text:
In *Zahariev v. North Macedonia*, the European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Borislav Zahariev Zahariev, a Bulgarian national, concerning domestic criminal proceedings and his claim of diplomatic immunity. The applicant worked as financial director of a telecommunications company in North Macedonia between 2004 and 2009. In January 2007 his wife began working as an official at the Bulgarian Cultural and Information Centre attached to the Bulgarian embassy. On 24 January 2012 an investigating judge opened an investigation against the applicant and another person for abuse of office and tax evasion allegedly committed in 2008 relating to his telecom employment. An indictment followed on 11 February 2013.

In June 2013 the applicant informed the Skopje Court of First Instance that he held a special identity card issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs granting him absolute immunity from prosecution. The card stated that he enjoyed immunity from criminal jurisdiction, arrest or police custody in North Macedonia. The applicant relied on his status as a family member of embassy administrative/technical staff under Article 37(2) of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. He argued that the exception in Article 37(2) applied only to civil and administrative jurisdiction, not criminal jurisdiction. He later relied on the ICJ *Arrest Warrant* case, arguing that immunity from criminal jurisdiction did not distinguish official and private acts and could only cease in limited circumstances, including express waiver by Bulgaria, which had not occurred.

The domestic courts did not accept his immunity claim. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed prosecutors and courts that the applicant had held special identity cards from 2007, extended through 30 May 2014, but that his immunity derived from his wife’s status. The Ministry noted that in February 2010 the embassy had asked to cancel his registration because Article 42 of the Vienna Convention prohibited diplomatic agents from engaging in professional or commercial activity for personal profit; that the applicant had been employed; and that after 2014, given pending criminal proceedings, only his wife’s card was extended. A Ministry representative stated that the applicant could not both be employed and enjoy immunities, and that he could not invoke immunity given Article 31(1)(c) and Article 42.

The applicant was convicted in absentia in 2015, but the appellate court remitted the case for reconsideration of immunity. On 24 December 2019 the trial court again convicted him in absentia of abuse of office and sentenced him to five years. It held that his immunity had ceased when he took private employment contrary to Article 42; that he had not invoked immunity during the investigation; and that the embassy had never waived or requested extension of his card after 2014. The appellate court confirmed the conviction on 9 March 2021, also relying on Article 31(1)(c). The Supreme Court confirmed on 3 November 2021, reasoning that the applicant had lost immunity due to breach of Article 42 and had not invoked it.

The ECtHR complaint, lodged on 27 May 2022, was communicated to the Government only under Article 6 of the Convention concerning the lack of a fair hearing. The central alleged violation was therefore that the domestic courts’ judgments dismissing the immunity argument lacked adequate reasoning and fair consideration, particularly regarding whether the applicant enjoyed criminal immunity at the time of indictment and the correct interpretation of the Vienna Convention. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

In *Kornilova v. Ukraine* (Application no. 47283/14), the applicant, Ms Tetyana Kornilova, a Jehovah’s Witness, complained under Articles 3, 9 and 14 of the Convention that the Ukrainian authorities had failed to adequately take into account the alleged religious-prejudice motive behind an assault against her.

On 7 March 2013, the applicant and another Jehovah’s Witness, Ms N.S., were conducting door-to-door visits in Nosivka, distributing invitations to a religious service. The invitations showed an image of Jesus Christ and the words “One Died for All,” with smaller text identifying the event as a Jehovah’s Witnesses’ meeting. At about 1 p.m., they called at the house of V.S., a fifty-year-old man they did not know. According to the applicant, when V.S. saw the invitations and Bible in their hands, he immediately punched her in the head, began cursing at them, called them “shtundas”—a colloquial term for evangelical Protestants—and threatened to set his dog on them.

On 9 March 2013, the applicant sought medical care and was diagnosed with concussion and a facial bruise. She was hospitalised until 19 March. The same day, she complained to the police. The case was preliminarily classified under Article 125 § 2 of the Criminal Code, covering intentional infliction of minor injury.

In her police statement, the applicant said she was a Jehovah’s Witness and that V.S. had cursed, called them “shtundas,” and hit her without reason. N.S. largely corroborated this, stating that V.S. hit the applicant immediately after seeing her and repeatedly cursed and called them “shtundas.” V.S. claimed the women had come onto his property, refused to leave, and tried to recruit him; he became angry and slapped one of them. He later said he acted due to the “sudden emergence of hostility,” alleging the applicant had insulted him about his “man’s health.” He denied religious intolerance, said he did not know she was a Jehovah’s Witness, and claimed “shtundas” had no religious meaning for him. A forensic expert found minor injuries with short-term health effects, possibly caused by a slap or a punch.

On 15 May 2013, the applicant asked the investigator to reclassify the offence as discriminatory acts under Article 161 § 2, arguing V.S. knew she was a Jehovah’s Witness and hit her for that reason. On 17 May, the investigator refused, finding that “sudden hostility” had been established and that no religious hatred motive was shown. At trial, the applicant again sought reclassification as discriminatory acts or hooliganism under Article 296, invoking Articles 3, 9 and 14 and arguing that the State had a duty to uncover any religious motive behind violence.

On 16 July 2013, the Nosivka District Court convicted V.S. under Article 125 § 2, fined him about EUR 78, awarded the applicant about EUR 278 in non-pecuniary damages, and found the injury was inflicted due to “sudden emergence of hostility.” No aggravating circumstances were found. The applicant appealed, arguing that the authorities had failed to examine religious hatred and that religious enmity should have been treated as an aggravating factor under Article 67. The prosecutor maintained that no religious motive had been identified. On 26 September 2013, the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, finding no religious motive established. On 8 January 2014, the High Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters upheld the lower decisions.

The key alleged violation was therefore that the authorities treated the attack as an ordinary minor assault motivated by personal hostility, despite evidence of the applicant’s religious activity, the use of a religious slur, and the immediate violent reaction to her religious materials. They refused to reclassify the offence as religiously motivated discrimination and did not consider religious enmity as an aggravating circumstance, thereby allegedly failing to protect her rights under Articles 3, 9 and 14.

In *Independent Newspapers (Ireland) Limited v. Ireland* (Application no. 28199/15, judgment 15 June 2017), the applicant company, publisher of the Irish daily newspaper the *Evening Herald* (now the *Herald*), alleged a violation of its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 ECHR. It complained that a disproportionately high defamation award against it reflected inadequate and ineffective domestic safeguards against excessive jury damages, creating a chilling effect on the press.

Between 30 November and 17 December 2004, the *Evening Herald* published eleven articles in nine editions about Ms L., a public relations consultant hired by government departments when Mr C. was a minister. The articles questioned government contracts awarded to her, tender procedures, her qualifications, remuneration and work; they discussed eight foreign trips with the ministerial entourage and a New York United Nations conference, initially claiming no record of the Minister’s attendance, later noting a record existed. They also referred to rumours of an intimate relationship between Ms L. and Mr C., her appearance and lifestyle, and used altered or cropped photographs. A front-page photomontage and headline—“The Minister, [Ms L.] and the Mystery Meeting”—suggested a romantic link. The Supreme Court later described the articles as a serious and sustained attack on Ms L.’s business and personal integrity.

Ms L. sued for defamation. In June 2009, a High Court jury found that the articles meant she had an extra-marital affair with Mr C.; it found the second alleged meaning not defamatory. The jury awarded EUR 1,872,000. The trial judge explained the compensatory and vindication functions of defamation damages but, under Irish law and the *Barrett* rules/*De Rossa* case-law, was not permitted to suggest a figure or range to the jury. He warned against “ridiculously large” awards and mentioned a lottery anecdote, but could give little concrete guidance. Judgment was entered for the award, with a stay pending appeal conditioned on interim payments of EUR 750,000 plus EUR 100,000 costs.

The applicant accepted liability but appealed quantum, arguing the award was grossly disproportionate and an unlawful interference with its constitutional and Convention rights. It later submitted that EUR 175,000 would have sufficed. On 19 December 2014, the Supreme Court found the award excessive and set it aside. The majority substituted EUR 1.25 million; one judge would have ordered a retrial or awarded EUR 1 million. The court applied the principle that an appellate court should disturb a jury award only if it was so disproportionate that no reasonable jury would have made it. The applicant paid an additional EUR 500,000 and later EUR 240,448.16 in costs.

Relevant to the alleged violation, the old regime left defamation damages to the jury, gave trial judges little power to provide meaningful guidance, and limited appellate intervention. Retrials before a new jury would not be told the prior award, the Supreme Court’s reasoning, or the original amount. The later Defamation Act 2009 introduced judicial directions, party submissions on damages, and express power for the Supreme Court to substitute damages, but it did not apply retroactively. The applicant’s Convention complaint therefore focused on the alleged inadequacy and ineffectiveness of domestic safeguards against disproportionately high defamation awards.

The case of *Rizzo Striano v. Italy* (Application no. 54800/16) concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a domestic court decision awarding the applicant damages and compensation in connection with land occupied for an aqueduct. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 September 2016 under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant, Maurizio Rizzo Striano, born in 1957, was represented by Mr I. Toscano, a lawyer practising in Rome. The Italian Government were given notice of the application.

The key domestic decision was issued by the Regional Public Water Court (Naples District Court), R.G. 2475/96, on 21 January 2002. It ordered the Reclamation Consortium of the Plain of Sybaris and the Middle Crati Valley (*Consorzio di Bonifica della Piana di Sibari e della Media Valle del Crati*, “the Consortium”) to pay the applicant damages for the occupation of his plot of land for the construction of an aqueduct and compensation for the establishment of an aqueduct easement over that land. The domestic judgment therefore established a clear monetary entitlement in the applicant’s favour against the Consortium.

According to the appended table, the non-enforcement period began on 27 September 2005. The end date of non-enforcement was recorded as pending, and the length of non-enforcement was stated as more than 18 years and 9 days. This means that for over eighteen years, the applicant had a domestic court order in his favour but did not receive the payments due from the Consortium. The applicant’s complaint before the European Court was therefore that the domestic decision awarding him damages and compensation had not been enforced.

The essence of the alleged violation is that the Italian State failed to ensure compliance with a final domestic judgment against a public or semi-public entity. The applicant had successfully obtained a ruling ordering payment for the occupation of his land and for the aqueduct easement, but the sums remained unpaid for an exceptionally long period. This prolonged failure to enforce the domestic decision deprived the applicant of the practical benefit of his successful litigation and formed the factual basis of his complaint to the Court.

Procedurally, the case was examined by the First Section sitting as a Committee, composed of Judges Wojtyczek, Hüseynov and Jelić, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court rejected the Government’s objection to the examination of the application by a Committee. The Committee deliberated in private on 14 December 2023 and adopted the judgment on that date; the judgment was delivered on 18 January 2024. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore relatively narrow: a final domestic decision of 21 January 2002 awarding damages and compensation; a debtor identified as the Consortium; a non-enforcement period beginning on 27 September 2005 and still pending; and a delay exceeding eighteen years and nine days. The applicant’s central complaint was that this continued non-enforcement breached his Convention rights, principally by denying him the effective enjoyment of a final judicial award and by leaving him without timely redress against a public debtor. The Court was thus called upon to assess whether Italy had failed to secure enforcement of the domestic decision within a reasonable time.

**Rizzo and Others v. Malta** (Application no. 36318/21, judgment 16 January 2024) concerns three Maltese nationals and the compatibility of Malta’s old rent laws with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

The applicants held the perpetual utile dominium of a property at No. 17, Triq Gort, Paceville, St Julian’s, inherited following their aunt’s death on 26 February 1994. In January 1972, their predecessor in title had leased the property under a temporary sub-emphyteusis for twenty-one years. When that expired on 18 January 1993, the tenant—a Maltese citizen using the property as his ordinary residence—relied on Act XXIII of 1979, amending Chapter 158, the Housing (Decontrol) Ordinance, to retain possession under a lease at the statutory annual rent of approximately €303. The rent later increased to about €454 in 2008, €502 in 2013, and €519 in 2016.

In April 2019, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings before the First Hall, Civil Court, in its constitutional competence. They alleged that the Ordinance, as amended, granted the tenant the right to retain possession under a unilateral lease for an indeterminate time without a fair and adequate rent, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They limited their claims to 31 December 2018, sought compensation, and did not demand the tenant’s eviction. A court-appointed expert valued the property in 2019 at €850,000 with development potential, or €320,000 in its existing state. Annual market rental values were estimated at €1,980 in 1993, €3,120 in 1998, €4,080 in 2003, €6,360 in 2008, €6,240 in 2013, and €10,560 in 2018.

By judgment of 25 January 2021, the First Hall found a violation of the applicants’ property rights, holding that they had suffered a disproportionate burden. It awarded €30,000 in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage for the violation until 10 April 2018, when new Article 12B of the Ordinance provided a further remedy. The applicants were not ordered to bear costs, despite not succeeding on all claims. No party appealed.

In parallel, Act XXVII of 2018, published on 10 July 2018 and in force from 1 August 2018, amended the Ordinance and introduced Article 12B. In April 2019, the applicants also instituted ordinary proceedings before the Rent Regulation Board. They sought recognition of the occupants as tenants, a means test, an increase in rent to no more than 2% of the open market value on 1 January 2019, or eviction within five years if the tenant failed the means test. On 2 December 2020, the RRB found that the tenants satisfied the means test and increased annual rent to €5,000 for the first two years and €7,500 for the following four. The tenants appealed and the applicants cross-appealed; the Court of Appeal confirmed the decision on 17 December 2021.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 July 2021. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13, declaring the remainder inadmissible. The case therefore concerns, in particular, the effectiveness of an appeal to the Constitutional Court for Article 13 purposes following developments in domestic case-law on old rent laws raising Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 issues.

The case *Tsaava and Others v. Georgia* concerns five applications brought by twenty-six Georgian nationals against Georgia under the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants include journalists, photographers, camera operators and demonstrators. They complain about the excessive use of force by police during the dispersal of a large demonstration in Tbilisi on 20–21 June 2019 and about the alleged failure to conduct an effective criminal investigation. Most invoke Articles 3 and 13; some also invoke Articles 10 and 11.

The protest began after a Russian State Duma member and IAO president, S.G., sat in the Georgian Parliament Speaker’s chair and addressed the assembly in Russian. Public anger led to a demonstration outside Parliament. Initially peaceful, it gathered around 12,000 people. Police formed a cordon blocking access to Parliament. As opposition politicians demanded resignations, snap elections and proportional representation, tensions grew. Some protesters tried to break through the cordon and enter the Parliament yard. Scuffles continued for hours, with demonstrators throwing bottles and other objects, seizing police shields and batons, and some officers being assaulted. Police responded with batons, shields, tear gas, rubber bullets and later a water cannon. Shooting began around 11:55 p.m. without warning. Tear gas and rubber bullets were fired repeatedly, sometimes simultaneously, as demonstrators returned to the area. Dispersal continued until about 6:45 a.m. In total, 342 people were arrested and over 200 injured, including about eighty police officers and forty journalists.

The applicants’ individual circumstances are central to the alleged violations. Many were injured by rubber bullets, tear gas or physical beatings. Several journalists were filming, photographing or livestreaming, wearing press badges, and allegedly posed no threat when hit. For example, Merab Tsaava was photographing when his hand was hit; Beslan Kmuzov was moving calmly and gesturing when hit in the head; Zaza Svanadze had his hands raised when hit in the thigh; other journalists were hit in the back, shoulder, hand or eye. Some demonstrators suffered grave injuries: one lost an eye, another lost most sight in an eye, others sustained a broken jaw, fractures, chest wounds or wounds from which rubber bullets were retrieved. Some applicants alleged they were beaten during arrest or detention. Medical reports classified several injuries as minor, serious or grave; some applicants were denied victim status in the domestic investigation.

On 22 June 2019 the General Prosecutor’s Office opened an ex officio investigation under Article 333 of the Criminal Code into alleged abuse of authority by MIA officers through violence or weapons during the dispersal. It was later extended to alleged unlawful interference with journalists’ work. All applicants were questioned, but some were refused victim status because the investigation had not established an offence against them. The Public Defender monitored the investigation and recommended examining the role of mid- and high-level MIA officials and the supervision of rubber-bullet use. The GPO later stated that decisions to use non-lethal projectiles had been taken by individual officers independently and that not all use was necessarily excessive. The case therefore concerns whether the police force was excessive and whether Georgia carried out an effective investigation.

Case Glavinić and Marković v. Croatia (ECtHR, 30 July 2020) concerned two Croatian nationals’ complaints that the length of judicial proceedings in their cases was excessive and that domestic authorities had failed to remedy the situation.

The first applicant, Jela Glavinić, was defendant in a civil action filed on 8 January 2003 in the Zadar Municipal Court seeking annulment of a gift contract. She responded in February 2003. The first-instance judgment was not delivered until 10 July 2014, dismissing the claim; it was served on 9 September 2014 and became final on 20 April 2015. The proceedings thus lasted about 11.5 years. She used domestic length remedies. In October 2013 she lodged a request for protection of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time with the President of the Zadar Municipal Court. In December 2013 the president found the request well-founded and ordered the judge to decide within six months. The time-limit was not met. In July 2014 she sought compensation from the Zadar County Court. In October 2014 the County Court awarded her HRK 1,000, finding the length excessive but also holding that she had contributed to the delay “to a certain extent” by failing to attend hearings on 9 April and 13 June 2014. She appealed, arguing that the April hearing was adjourned because another defendant had not been properly summoned and that the June hearing was held despite her absence. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in December 2014, served in January 2015. Her complaint was that the length was excessive and the compensation inadequate.

The second applicant, Aleksander Marković, applied on 20 July 2012 to the Karlovac Municipal Court for enforcement of a 27 January 2010 judgment ordering company T. to perform construction repairs. A writ of execution was issued on 14 February 2013, but company T. appealed on 27 February 2013. The appeal remained pending until 10 February 2017, when the Karlovac County Court quashed the writ and remitted the case. In fresh proceedings, on 5 July 2017 the Municipal Court issued a new writ ordering compliance within thirty days or payment of HRK 1,000 per day. However, on 10 April 2017 the Zagreb Commercial Court had opened “emergency administration proceedings” against company T.’s parent company A. and its subsidiaries under emergency legislation. As a result, all civil and enforcement proceedings were stayed, non-financial claims were transformed into financial claims, and creditors had to register claims. The applicant registered a claim of HRK 1,400,000; the administrator did not contest it. In July 2017 the company informed the Municipal Court, and on 17 October 2017 enforcement was stayed. In July 2018 a settlement was concluded and approved, entitling the applicant to 14.4% of his claim in financial instruments if implemented, or 2.6% in liquidation. Implementation was ongoing.

As to domestic remedies, in September 2014 the second applicant lodged an acceleratory request with the Karlovac County Court president, which was dismissed in November 2014 on the basis that three years had not elapsed and no breach was found. The Supreme Court dismissed his appeal in December 2014. In February 2015 he lodged a constitutional complaint under section 63 of the Constitutional Court Act, arguing that enforcement proceedings were urgent and statutory time-limits had been breached. The Constitutional Court treated it as a complaint under section 62 against the Supreme Court’s decision and declared it inadmissible, because such decisions were not subject to constitutional review. He alleged excessive length of the enforcement proceedings and failure of the domestic authorities to remedy the violation.

The legal context involved the 2013 Courts Act, which made a purely acceleratory remedy primary and a combined compensatory and acceleratory remedy available only if the set time-limit was ignored. Constitutional Court practice required exhaustion of those remedies before a length complaint. The ECtHR examined whether these remedies were effective and whether the applicants’ rights under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention were violated.

**Case: S.F. v. Finland (Application no. 35276/20), judgment of 8 October 2024**

The applicant, S.F., is an Eritrean national born in 1982 and living in Vantaa, Finland. She and her three minor children were granted asylum in Finland by the Finnish Immigration Service on 27 October 2016, and she was notified of that decision on 8 November 2016. She received refugee status because she was found to face persecution in Eritrea on account of her political opinions. The asylum decision included information, in Finnish, about family reunification procedures, including where and how to apply and the relevant time-limit. In particular, it explained that where the sponsor in Finland had refugee status and the family had been established before the sponsor arrived in Finland, a family member could apply for a residence permit without satisfying the maintenance requirement if the application was submitted within three months of notification of the positive asylum decision.

The Government submitted that immigration records showed the applicant had discussed family reunification with a social worker in November 2016 and January 2017, assisted by a Tigrinya interpreter. On the latter occasion she was allegedly specifically informed about the three-month deadline and the consequences of exceeding it, and was given application forms, the contact details of the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi, and information about applying online.

The applicant’s husband, also Eritrean, had refugee status in Uganda and lived in Kampala. On 30 January 2018—about fifteen months after the applicant was notified of her asylum decision—he applied for a residence permit on family reunification grounds at the Finnish Embassy in Nairobi. He presented an Eritrean passport issued on 18 May 2017. In his February 2019 interview, he said he had fled Eritrea in 2014 after being penalised for leaving military service without permission to visit his family.

By decision of 20 February 2019, the Immigration Service refused the husband’s application. It accepted that he was a member of the applicant’s family but found that the applicant did not meet the maintenance requirement under section 39 of the Aliens Act. The three-month exception in section 114(4) did not apply because the applicant had been notified on 8 November 2016, while the husband applied only on 30 January 2018. The required monthly income was EUR 2,900, or EUR 34,800 annually; the applicant’s income consisted only of social security benefits, and she had not shown continuous income sufficient to support her husband. It was assumed he would need social assistance.

The Immigration Service found no exceptionally serious grounds for derogating from the maintenance requirement. The couple had been partly imprecise about the delay. The husband claimed he had tried to contact Finnish consular authorities in Kampala in spring 2017, but the honorary consulate did not handle residence permits; he was advised to apply in Nairobi but did not do so before January 2018. The Immigration Service found this insufficient, noting that passport stamps indicated he had visited Kenya and Eritrea before then, that he was in good health, had refugee status and a support network in Uganda, and was settled there. It also considered the children’s best interests but found they did not warrant a permit for a father who had spent little time with them; the oldest child said he had never had a relationship with him, and the youngest was born after the father left Eritrea.

The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 6 September 2019, holding that the late application meant the maintenance requirement applied. It found the applicant depended on social welfare, the delay reasons were financial or passport-related, and the alleged health problems were unsubstantiated. It concluded that the children’s best interests did not require derogation merely because family ties might be interrupted. A minority of judges would have derogated because the required income was unrealistic in the applicant’s circumstances. The Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal on 26 February 2020. The case therefore concerns the refusal of family reunification and its compatibility with the applicant’s right to respect for family life.

**CASE OF AGGERHOLM v. DENMARK** (App. no. 45439/18), judgment 15 September 2020, final 15 December 2020, concerned a Danish national with paranoid schizophrenia. In 2005 he was convicted of five violent incidents and threats against a public servant and committed to a psychiatric hospital. He had a history of violence, was placed in a high-security unit under a dangerousness decree from 2007 to 2011, later treated in an open ward, and in September 2012 moved to a closed ward, P4, because of irritability and threatening behaviour.

The alleged violation arose from an incident on 8 February 2013. At 1:15 p.m. the applicant was strapped to a restraint bed with a belt, wrist straps, and ankle straps—a five-point restraint. He remained restrained until 9 February 2013 at 12:05 p.m., about 22 hours and 50 minutes. He complained that this breached Article 3 of the Convention.

The immediate background was that on the evening of 7 February he was angry and frustrated. He made remarks about the chief physician, H.H., which staff understood as threats, including “We have to do something about her” and that she should have “a bullet through her head.” Staff felt insecure. The next day, because of his anger, it was decided that he could not go on unsupervised day release. When H.H. informed him, he refused to sit or talk, appeared white-faced with his mouth set, and displayed pent-up anger. Dialogue failed for about an hour and a half. H.H. considered him dangerous to others and decided to restrain him. He walked voluntarily to the belt room.

While restrained, he was under constant watch. Doctors checked him at least four times. At 6:55 p.m. one foot strap was released and toilet visits were allowed; at 10:46 p.m. he was still considered potentially dangerous. On 9 February, after he became cooperative, he was released at 12:05 p.m.

Domestically, the Psychiatric Patients’ Complaints Board heard the applicant and, relying on his statement and a brief written statement from H.H. (who was ill and absent), found on 21 March 2013 that both the January and February restraints had been unlawful, because it was not documented that he posed an immediate risk of harm. The State Administration later dismissed his compensation claim. The Health Authority found no lack of care by H.H. In his civil action, the City Court heard witnesses and obtained a 2016 Medico-Legal Council report. The Council found that the conditions for restraint were present and that medical assessments were sufficiently frequent. The City Court in 2017 and the High Court in 2017 agreed, finding the restraint necessary to prevent an immediate risk to others and that less intrusive measures were insufficient. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in 2018.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key issue was whether the almost 23-hour five-point restraint amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3, considering the applicant’s mental illness, prior violence, perceived threats, necessity and proportionality, conditions during restraint—constant supervision, medical checks, partial release—and the available procedural safeguards. The Court found no violation of Article 3.

The case of *Guðmundur Gunnarsson and Magnús Davíð Norðdahl v. Iceland* concerns the 2021 Icelandic parliamentary elections and complaints under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 (right to free elections) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). The applicants were candidates in the Northwest constituency: Gunnarsson headed the Liberal Reform Party list, and Norðdahl headed the Pirate Party list. Althingi has 63 members: 54 elected in six constituencies by open-list proportional representation and nine national levelling seats allocated to parties receiving at least 5% nationally. The levelling seats aim to correct population imbalances among constituencies.

After the 25 September 2021 election, the initial Northwest count gave Liberal Reform 1,072 votes and the Pirate Party 1,082 out of 17,666. Gunnarsson therefore qualified for a levelling seat, while Norðdahl narrowly missed a constituency seat. The next day, the National Electoral Commission, noting a very narrow margin, suggested a recount. A recount lowered Liberal Reform to 1,063 and the Pirate Party to 1,081; a full recount confirmed those results. A South constituency recount produced no changes. The new Northwest result triggered a national reallocation of levelling seats: Gunnarsson lost his levelling seat, which went to the Centre Party in the Northwest, while Norðdahl remained unelected.

The applicants complained to the Preparatory Credentials Committee. They alleged that the recount lacked a legal basis; that ballots were improperly stored and handled between the initial count and recount; that party agents were not informed and could not observe the recount; and that vote totals, including blank and invalid ballots, changed without explanation. Gunnarsson also argued that Althingi’s power to decide electoral disputes conflicted with the Convention standard discussed in *Mugemangango v. Belgium*. They contended that the defects could or were liable to have affected the outcome.

The Preparatory Credentials Committee held an extensive inquiry. It found several defects: after the first count, ballots were not sealed and were left unattended in open boxes in a closed but unsupervised hotel room with multiple entrances and staff access; the commission chairman spent about half an hour alone in the room

In *Bielau v. Austria*, the applicant, Dr Klaus Bielau, was an Austrian general practitioner with a “holistic medicine” website on which he described himself as an expert on vaccinations and vaccine damage. The case concerned disciplinary proceedings brought against him over an article on vaccination posted on that website, dated 27 June 2016.

In the article, Bielau suggested that a tick bite could not cause death, that viruses were not proven pathogenic agents, and that conditions such as meningitis were healing reactions rather than the result of viral infection. He also claimed that chemical vaccinations could never protect against disease because people do not become ill through bacteria and viruses; that nature knew no diseases; and that vaccination had not eradicated or made a single disease disappear. The article used provocative language and referred ironically to “only vaccination protects.”

On 27 June 2017, after a hearing, the Disciplinary Commission for Styria and Carinthia of the Austrian Medical Association found Bielau guilty of disciplinary offences under section 136(1)(1) and (2) of the Medical Practitioners Act. Relying on an expert report by a prominent immunologist, the Commission found that he had denied the existence of pathogenic viruses, claimed vaccinations never protected against disease, claimed nature knew no diseases, and claimed that no disease had disappeared through vaccination. It considered these statements one-sided, negative, contrary to the state of science and medical experience, and therefore unobjective. They violated section 53 of the Medical Practitioners Act and the Regulation on Medical Practitioners and the Public, damaged the reputation of the medical profession, and breached professional duties. He was fined EUR 2,000, suspended for a one-year probationary period, and ordered to pay EUR 1,500 in costs.

Bielau challenged the decision before the Styria Regional Administrative Court, relying on his right to freedom of expression. He argued that the statements had to be read in context, were provocative rather than literal, were not directly related to his professional practice, and were not untrue or unobjective. The Regional Administrative Court held an oral hearing with a second expert, who also concluded that the statements contradicted current medical science. The court dismissed his complaint, finding that the statements were one-sided and scientifically unsupported. It stressed that doctors must provide objective information, especially about vaccination, and that the restriction served the protection of health and public trust in the medical profession. The Constitutional Court declined to consider the case, and the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his extraordinary appeal. The Supreme Administrative Court found that the website had an advertising purpose connected to his medical practice, that the statements were unobjective and potentially damaging to the profession’s reputation, and that the relatively low, suspended fine was proportionate under Article 10 § 2 of the Convention.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Bielau complained under Article 10 that the disciplinary sanction violated his right to freedom of expression. The key issue was whether the domestic authorities’ interference—punishing him for public statements about vaccination—was justified as necessary in a democratic society for the protection of health and the rights of others, or whether it disproportionately restricted his freedom to impart information and ideas.

**Case: Starishko v. Ukraine (Application no. 61839/12), ECtHR, 15 October 2020**

The case concerned Mr Anatoliy Petrovych Starishko, a Ukrainian national born in 1980 who is serving a life sentence in Vinnytsya Prison No. 1. He lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 July 2012. The Court gave notice to the Ukrainian Government of two main complaints: first, that his life sentence lacked any genuine prospect of release, i.e. was irreducible; and second, that restrictions on his right to receive visits during his post-conviction detention from 2000 to 2014 violated the Convention. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The applicant was represented by Ms Ganna Ovdiyenko, a lawyer practising in Kharkiv. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Ivan Lishchyna.

The key facts were as follows. On 14 December 1999 the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court found the applicant guilty of several counts of aggravated murder and theft and sentenced him to the death penalty. On 30 May 2000 the Supreme Court replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment and upheld the verdict in the remaining part. Thus, from 2000 onwards, the applicant was detained under a life sentence.

During the period from 2000 to 2014, the applicant received only ten short-term visits, each lasting between one and four hours, from his mother, his sister and, on three occasions, a friend. During these meetings, the applicant communicated with the visitors through a glass partition, and their conversations were listened to by a prison officer.

The relevant legal framework concerned both life imprisonment and visiting rights. Legal provisions on life imprisonment and presidential clemency were summarised in *Petukhov v. Ukraine (no. 2)* (no. 41216/13, §§ 75-90, 12 March 2019). Under the Correctional Labour Code of 1970, repealed with effect from 1 January 2004, life prisoners had the right to one short-term visit every six months, conducted in the presence of a staff member of the prison (Article 39). The Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences of 11 July 2003, in force from 1 January 2004, kept that rule unchanged until 16 February 2010, when life prisoners became entitled to one short-term visit every three months (Article 151). Further details on visiting entitlement and its evolution are found in *Trosin v. Ukraine* (no. 39758/05, §§ 26 and 29, 23 February 2012) and *Bigun v. Ukraine* (no. 30315/10, §§ 15-19, 21 March 2019).

Relevant Council of Europe documents and CPT reports on life imprisonment are cited in *Petukhov*. Material on family visits to prisoners is quoted in *Khoroshenko v. Russia* (no. 41418/04, §§ 58-67, ECHR 2015), while excerpts from relevant CPT reports are quoted in *Bigun* (no. 30315/10, § 22).

The alleged violations therefore centred on whether the life sentence regime—where release depended on presidential clemency rather than an ordinary parole mechanism—made the sentence de facto irreducible, and whether the severe restrictions on visits, including the limited number of visits, the glass partition and the monitoring of conversations, breached the applicant’s rights under the Convention, particularly regarding private and family life. The Court adopted its judgment on 22 September 2020 and delivered it on 15 October 2020.

**Case:** *Kotsev and Ermenkova v. Bulgaria* (Application no. 33864/03), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 10 May 2012.

The applicants were two Bulgarian nationals, Mr Valentin Konstantinov Kotsev and Ms Yarmila Anguelova Ermenkova. They lodged their application on 13 October 2003. Mr Kotsev died on 20 November 2005; his widow and minor son later expressed a wish to continue the proceedings on his behalf.

The applicants and the parents of a Mr B.I. were co-owners of a building and plot of land in Sofia. In 1992 B.I.’s parents sold him one quarter of the property. In 1993 B.I. began constructing an adjoining building. Between 1996 and 2005 the authorities five times ordered that the construction be halted or the building demolished. B.I. challenged all these orders by way of judicial review. Two sets of judicial-review proceedings, in which the applicants joined as interested parties, formed the background to the alleged violations.

**The 1996 proceedings:** On 21 March 1996 the mayor ordered demolition of the building erected by B.I., finding it could not be legalised. In April 1996 B.I. sought judicial review before the Sofia City Court. In March 1999 the court allowed the applicants, as well as B.I.’s wife and brother, to join the proceedings. At least fifteen hearings were held between 8 June 1999 and 26 October 2007, at intervals of four to eight months. Five hearings failed because various parties had not been duly summoned. At least six hearings between January 2005 and October 2007 were adjourned because a newly added party living in Toronto, Canada, had to be summoned by letter rogatory. The Sofia City Court rendered judgment in 2010; according to the applicants’ latest correspondence in October 2010, the case was then pending before the second-instance court.

**The 1999 proceedings:** On 16 June 1999, after being alerted by the applicants, the building control authorities ordered B.I. to pull down the building. On 13 July 1999 B.I. and his wife sought judicial review. At the first hearing on 26 November 1999 the applicants intervened as interested parties. Some twenty hearings were held until February 2006, scheduled at intervals of two to nine months. At least four hearings were adjourned because parties had not been properly summoned, including B.I.’s brother in Canada. After the brother’s death in 2002, at least six hearings were adjourned because his widow, also in Canada, could not be summoned by letter rogatory. As of October 2010 the proceedings were still pending before the Sofia City Court.

**Domestic complaints about delay:** On 23 November 2000, 18 December 2002, and again in 2007, the applicants complained to the Sofia City Court and the Supreme Judicial Council about the slow progress of the proceedings. In 2007 the Ministry of Justice replied that there were no delays attributable to the authorities. However, in 2002 the Ministry of Justice informed the local authorities that an inspection by a representative of the Supreme Judicial Council’s Inspectorate had established that a delay had occurred, caused by B.I.’s abuse of process and the high case-load of the Sofia City Court. The Inspectorate had written to the Chairman of the Sofia City Court about the delays.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore concern the prolonged duration of two sets of judicial-review proceedings, repeated adjournments due to summoning problems—especially of parties or relatives abroad—and the applicants’ unsuccessful domestic complaints about delay. The relevant domestic law on “complaints about delays” was summarised in *Finger v. Bulgaria* (no. 37346/05, § 43, 10 May 2011).

text:
In *Berkman v. Russia* (Application no. 46712/15), the applicant, Yelena Vladimirovna Berkman, complained about the Russian authorities’ response to an LGBTI public event and about her arrest and detention. On 27 September 2013, LGBTI rights activists notified the St Petersburg authorities of their intention to hold a meeting marking Coming Out Day on 12 October 2013 at the Field of Mars. The event was planned from 2 p.m. to 3.30 p.m., with about 150 people expected and some participants arriving at 1.30 p.m. to prepare. The authorities forwarded the notice to the police and reminded the organisers that they could be liable under domestic law for inciting hatred or for promoting “non-traditional” sexual relationships to minors. The police deployed around 540 officers, including special-purpose units, apparently because clashes with counter-demonstrators were anticipated. No crowd barriers or perimeter fence were installed at the site.

At about 1 p.m. the applicant arrived to help prepare the meeting. According to her, the participants—about twenty or thirty people—were unable to gather because the area was blocked by more than 100 aggressive counter-demonstrators. Many counter-demonstrators wore national costumes and some were armed with whips. They insulted, pushed and punched the LGBTI participants, surrounded them and followed them. The participants asked police officers for help, but the police did not react until counter-demonstrators insulted the police themselves. The police then arrested several counter-demonstrators, took them to a police bus and released them. The released counter-demonstrators continued their verbal and physical attacks.

At 1.55 p.m. police officers surrounded a group of twelve demonstrators, including the applicant, and said they had breached public order by using foul language. The officers ordered them to a police bus and took them to central police station no. 28 under Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The Government later stated that ninety-three people in total had been arrested for disorderly conduct and taken to three police stations before release. The applicant argued that only Coming Out Day participants were taken to police stations.

The applicant was detained under Article 27.3 of the Code from 2.30 p.m. to about 6.30 p.m. Administrative records stated that she had been detained at 1.55 p.m. for disorderly conduct under Article 20.1, namely using foul language and ignoring police warnings, and that she was taken to the station to ensure prompt examination of her case. She signed the records but noted her disagreement. On 8 November 2013, the Dzerzhinskiy District Court terminated the administrative proceedings against her for lack of evidence. Similar charges against other participants were mostly terminated; one conviction was later quashed on appeal.

The applicant brought civil proceedings challenging the lawfulness of her arrest and detention and later alleging that the authorities had failed to ensure the safety of the meeting participants. In October 2014 the district court dismissed her claim, relying on a video recording and finding that she had been an active participant in the conflict, that her arrest was lawful and that her detention had not exceeded forty-eight hours. The appellate court upheld that decision in March 2015, finding the arrest a lawful interim measure taken to facilitate administrative proceedings because the tension at the scene prevented police from identifying offenders. Cassation appeals were unsuccessful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 11 and 14 of the Convention because the authorities failed to ensure the peaceful conduct of the public meeting and allegedly discriminated against her because of her support for LGBTI people. She also alleged under Article 5 that her arrest, removal from the event and subsequent detention were arbitrary and unlawful.

**Case Summary: Albul and Others v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 18899/19 and 49871/19)**

This case is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 18 June 2020. The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention about the excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of any effective remedy in domestic law for that complaint. The Court deliberated in private on 28 May 2020 and adopted its judgment on 18 June 2020.

The factual details are set out in the appended table. Application no. 18899/19 was introduced on 29 March 2019 by Tamara Afanasiyivna Albul, born 26 May 1957, who was represented by Anatoliy Borysovych Bogachev of Odesa. The table records civil proceedings with start dates of 25 June 2012 and 2 March 2015, and end dates of 13 November 2014 and 3 October 2018. The total length was 5 years, 11 months and 22 days, across three levels of jurisdiction. Thus, by the time the application was lodged, the proceedings involving the applicant had lasted nearly six years cumulatively, passing through first-instance, appellate and cassation review.

Application no. 49871/19 was introduced on 13 September 2019 by Dmitriy Georgiyevich Lapin, born 19 December 1964, and Valentina Pavlovna Lapina, born 30 April 1939. Their civil proceedings began on 29 July 2009 and were still pending at the time the case was before the Court. The total length was more than 10 years, 9 months and 8 days, across three levels of jurisdiction. This application therefore alleged an ongoing and exceptionally long delay, far exceeding the duration in the first application.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the duration and procedural history of the domestic civil proceedings. In both applications, the proceedings passed through three levels of jurisdiction. In the first, the total length was just under six years. In the second, the proceedings had already exceeded ten years and nine months and had not concluded. These periods formed the basis for the applicants’ complaint under Article 6 § 1 that their civil cases were not heard within a reasonable time.

The applicants also complained under Article 13 that Ukrainian law did not provide any effective remedy through which they could challenge the excessive length of the civil proceedings. The Court’s review, as framed by the applications, concerned whether the length of the proceedings was compatible with the “reasonable time” requirement and whether the applicants had an effective domestic remedy for that length complaint.

The provided text does not set out the Court’s substantive findings or any award, but it identifies the factual matrix: two sets of civil proceedings against Ukraine, one lasting almost six years and another pending for over a decade, both involving three levels of jurisdiction. Those facts were the basis for the alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention.

The case originated in an application (no. 52682/07) against Azerbaijan lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by the Religious Community of Jehovah’s Witnesses in Baku and Mr Oddvar Hansen, a Norwegian national. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 6 (fair trial), 9 (freedom of religion), and 14 (non-discrimination) of the Convention. The Court communicated those complaints to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The applicant community is a local Jehovah’s Witnesses community registered in Baku. Hansen owned a private building and leased it, without payment, to the community for religious meetings. On 24 December 2006, about 200 Jehovah’s Witnesses met for worship at their meeting hall on the second floor of that building. According to the applicants, a raid involved more than forty officials, including officers from the Khatai District Police Department, a representative of the State Committee for Work with Religious Associations, officials from the Khatai district prosecutor’s office, and the Ministry of National Security. The authorities conducted search and seizure procedures to prevent an unauthorised religious meeting. An investigator’s record stated that eighteen items were seized in the presence of attesting witnesses, including computers, computing equipment, and religious literature.

On 7 February 2007, the applicants lodged a complaint in court supervisory proceedings before the Khatai District Court, relying on the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They asked the court to find the search unlawful and order the return of the seized property. Affidavits dated 2 and 30 March 2007 showed the property was returned to the community chairman. On 7 May 2007, the Khatai District Court partly allowed the complaint. It held that the search and seizure were unlawful because they had been carried out without a court order, contrary to the CCrP. It noted that the property had already been returned.

On 10 May 2007, the Khatai district prosecutor appealed, seeking to quash the favourable part of the decision. He argued that the authorities had not broken into the building because the doors were open and the owner had permitted entry. On 21 May 2007, the Baku Court of Appeal examined the case in the applicants’ absence but in the presence of the prosecutor and a police representative. It stated that the applicants had been notified but failed to appear or explain their absence. The appellate court allowed the prosecutor’s appeal and found the search and seizure lawful, relying on Article 177.6 of the CCrP, which provided that no court order was required when the owner permitted entry. That decision was not amenable to further appeal.

The applicants alleged that they had not received notice of the hearing or a copy of the prosecutor’s appeal. They said their lawyer learned only on 22 May 2007 that the first-instance decision had been appealed and quashed. Under domestic law, such court supervisory appeals are examined by a three-judge appellate chamber within three days in camera. A complainant has the right to participate, but non-attendance by notified parties does not prevent examination. The appellate decision is sent to the parties within three days and cannot be appealed.

The alleged violations therefore concerned whether the raid and seizure unlawfully interfered with freedom of religion under Article 9; whether the appellate proceedings were unfair under Article 6 because the applicants lacked notice and an effective opportunity to respond; and whether the measures or proceedings involved discrimination under Article 14. The applicants also relied on property rights under Protocol No. 1 in seeking return of the seized items.

In Aleksandrov v. Ukraine (Application no. 56483/09, judgment of 9 January 2020), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, examined a Ukrainian applicant’s complaint that domestic authorities hindered his right of individual petition under Article 34 of the Convention by refusing to provide him with copies of documents from his criminal case file for use in his application to the Court.

The applicant, Ruslan Alekseyevich Aleksandrov, born in 1978 and detained in Berdychiv, had been convicted by the Crimea Court of Appeal on 25 December 2008 of two counts of rape and one count of murder. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. On 21 May 2009 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that conviction. He was serving his sentence at Berdychiv correctional colony no. 70 in Zhytomyr Region.

On 5 October 2009 the applicant informed the European Court of Human Rights of his intention to file an application. By letter of 10 May 2010, the Court acknowledged receipt of his application form and attachments and asked him to submit copies of domestic courts’ decisions and other documents relevant to his case by 10 August 2010. This request made the criminal case-file documents important for his Strasbourg application.

Between 2009 and 2013, the applicant repeatedly asked the Crimea Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court of Ukraine for access to his case file or for copies of procedural documents. He stated that those documents had been requested by the European Court. The domestic authorities, however, largely refused or obstructed these requests. On numerous dates—including 2 February, 11 June, and 7 and 9 July 2009; 10 March, 28 April, 1 and 21 July, 4 August, and 5 November 2010; 16 March and 5 October 2011; and 10 May 2012—the Crimea Court of Appeal rejected his applications for access to the file. It explained that there was no legal basis for providing copies of documents from a criminal case file after the conviction had become final.

On 17 February 2012 the applicant again asked the Crimea Court of Appeal to provide documents from his file so that he could send them to the European Court. On 29 February 2012 Judge G. replied that he had already received all copies permitted by law. For additional procedural documents intended for the European Court, he would need to present confirmation that the Court had requested them and a list of those documents, both drafted by an authorised person. On 22 March 2012 the Crimea Court of Appeal rejected a further application because the proceedings concerning the applicant had ended. On 19 November 2012 the applicant asked the court to authorise his mother to study his criminal case file. On 4 December 2012 the Deputy President of the Crimea Court of Appeal refused, stating that only participants in criminal proceedings had a right of access to the file.

On 24 June 2013 the applicant again requested copies, indicating that the European Court had asked for them. On 11 July 2013 Judge T. told him that he had to pay a fee of UAH 46 and send confirmation of payment, after which the requested copies would be sent. The applicant did not pay. According to him, he had insufficient funds because he had no income and no legal counsel.

On 30 May 2018 the Government were given notice of the complaint under Article 34 concerning the authorities’ failure to provide copies of documents from the applicant’s case file; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The key alleged violation was therefore that the Ukrainian authorities, despite knowing the documents were needed for the applicant’s ECtHR application, failed to facilitate his access to them, thereby hindering his effective exercise of the right of individual petition.

In *Executief van de Moslims van België and Others v. Belgium* (ECtHR, 13 February 2024), the applicants were thirteen Belgian nationals and seven NGOs, including Muslim representative bodies, Turkish and Moroccan religious authorities, and Belgian nationals of Muslim and Jewish faith. They challenged regional bans on ritual slaughter without prior stunning in Flanders and Wallonia, alleging violations of Articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Previously, Belgian federal law required stunning before slaughter but exempted slaughter prescribed by religious rites. After animal welfare became a regional competence in 2014, Flanders and Wallonia ended that exemption. The Flemish Decree of 7 July 2017 amended the 1986 animal welfare law so that vertebrates may not be killed without prior stunning, except in cases of force majeure, hunting or fishing, and pest control. For religious slaughter, stunning had to be reversible and could not cause the animal’s death; for cattle, a transitional rule allowed stunning immediately after the throat was cut until reversible stunning became practicable. The Walloon Decree of 4 October 2018, in force from 1 September 2019, contained an equivalent rule: animals must be stunned or anaesthetised before killing, with limited exceptions, and religious slaughter required reversible, non-lethal stunning. Breaches were punishable by imprisonment and substantial fines. The Brussels-Capital Region retained the earlier exemption.

The applicants argued that Jewish and Islamic religious precepts, at least as understood by parts of those communities, require the animal to be fully conscious at the time of slaughter and to die solely from bleeding. They claimed that mandatory stunning—even reversible, non-lethal stunning—was incompatible with those precepts, making it difficult or impossible to obtain ritually slaughtered meat in the two regions. They alleged that this breached their freedom to manifest religion under Article 9 and discriminated against them under Article 14, particularly because hunting and fishing were exempted and because non-religious slaughter was treated differently.

Some applicants brought annulment proceedings before the Belgian Constitutional Court. That court referred preliminary questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union. In *Centraal Israëlitisch Consistorie van België* (2020), the CJEU held that EU law did not preclude a member State from requiring reversible, non-lethal stunning in ritual slaughter. It found an interference with religious manifestation but considered it limited, justified by animal welfare, and proportionate, with a wide margin of appreciation. The CJEU also rejected the discrimination complaint concerning hunting and fishing.

In 2021, the Belgian Constitutional Court dismissed the annulment actions. It held that the restriction was prescribed by law, pursued the legitimate aim of animal welfare and public morals, and was necessary and proportionate. It noted that reversible stunning was permitted, that import of non-stunned meat remained possible, and that there was no unjustified inequality. The applicants then brought the case to the ECtHR, which gave notice to Belgium of the complaints under Articles 9 and 14 and declared the remaining parts inadmissible. The key issue was whether the regional bans on unstunned ritual slaughter unjustifiably interfered with religious freedom and discriminated against Jewish and Muslim believers.

**Yukhymovych v. Ukraine** (Application no. 11464/12) concerned the fatal shooting by police of the applicant’s son, Ruslan Yukhymovych, during an attempted arrest in March 1999 and the subsequent investigation. The applicant, a Ukrainian national, alleged violations of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights—both the substantive right to life and the procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation—after his son was shot twice by police.

The events began when B. complained to the Lviv Regional Department for Combatting Organised Crime that unknown persons had threatened her and extorted USD 25,000. Police identified the applicant’s son and his friend Z. as suspects, allegedly members of an organised criminal group. On 1 March 1999, the DCOC approved an operation to arrest them using the “Sokil” special police unit. On 4 March 1999, the applicant’s son and Z. arrived by taxi at B.’s house. Z. entered first, followed by the applicant’s son. Police officer M. shouted “Freeze, police!” and Z. was arrested. The applicant’s son fled. Officers M. and O. chased him. During the operation, O. shot the applicant’s son twice. He died from his injuries.

The key disputed fact was whether the applicant’s son had a gun and posed a threat when shot. Police claimed he disobeyed orders, fled, and pointed a “Valtro” gas gun at officers. A “Valtro” gun was allegedly found near his body and later placed in a plastic bag inside the house. His fingerprints were found on the gun. However, witnesses to the on-site inspection did not clearly see a gun. The taxi driver initially said he saw a gun, then withdrew that statement. The alleged accomplice Z. initially said the applicant’s son had left his gun in the car and that the gun in the house was not his; he later changed his testimony. Forensic reports were also contradictory regarding the location, order, and distance of the shots. Initial examinations suggested death was caused by a chest wound, while later reports described two back wounds, with the fatal wound inflicted near the gate. Experts could not conclusively determine the order of shots. Additional injuries—a bruise on the forehead and wounds to the head and lip—were noted but never adequately explained.

The investigation was marked by repeated terminations and reopenings. An internal police inquiry quickly found the shooting lawful. The prosecutor initially refused to open a criminal case, then reopened it. Between 1999 and 2018, proceedings were terminated and set aside many times. Domestic courts repeatedly criticised the investigation for failing to resolve contradictions about whether the applicant’s son had a gun, failing to secure the scene, allowing the car to be towed without permission, losing evidence, and taking a formalistic approach. The applicant’s son’s clothes were returned to the applicant and later destroyed, preventing further forensic examination. As of 2018, the proceedings were still pending.

The applicant complained that the police used lethal force without justification and that the State failed to conduct an effective, independent, and prompt investigation into his son’s death. The case therefore centred on whether the shooting complied with Article 2’s strict requirements on the use of force and whether the prolonged, contradictory, and repeatedly defective investigation violated the procedural limb of Article 2.

This case, *Rrapo v. Albania*, concerned the extradition of Almir Rrapo, an Albanian and United States national, from Albania to the United States despite an interim measure issued by the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39. Before the Court, the applicant alleged breaches of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention because his extradition exposed him to the risk of the death penalty and related treatment, and a breach of Article 34 because the Albanian authorities failed to comply with the Court’s interim measure.

The applicant was arrested in Tirana on 2 July 2010 at the request of the United States Embassy, after applying to renew his American passport. The Embassy requested his provisional arrest for extradition under the 1933 Extradition Treaty. Albanian courts authorised and repeatedly extended his detention. On 30 August 2010, the United States formally requested his extradition. The diplomatic note listed nine counts, including membership in an organised racketeering enterprise, conspiracy to distribute large quantities of marijuana and controlled substances, robbery, firearms offences, kidnapping in aid of racketeering, and the murder of E.S. in aid of racketeering. Five charges carried a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, two carried forty years, one carried twenty years, and the murder charge carried either death or life imprisonment.

Albanian courts granted extradition. The applicant objected that the United States had not provided assurances against the death penalty. The District Court and Court of Appeal rejected that objection, holding that no legal obligation required such assurances. On 1 November 2010, the Court of Appeal ruled in favour of extradition. The Minister of Justice then ordered extradition by 16 November 2010 and asked the United States whether the applicant would face capital punishment. On 8 November 2010, the United States Embassy sent diplomatic note no. 91, assuring Albania that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed on Rrapo for the charges for which extradition was granted.

Meanwhile, the European Court had intervened. On 12 October 2010, the President of the Fourth Section indicated under Rule 39 that the applicant should not be extradited until ten days after notification of the Court of Appeal’s decision. On 2 November 2010, after the Court of Appeal’s decision, the measure was prolonged until fifteen days after notification of the Supreme Court’s decision. On 15 November 2010, the President decided that the Rule 39 measure remained in force despite the United States’ assurances. The Albanian authorities were explicitly reminded that failure to comply with a Rule 39 measure could breach Article 34.

On 24 November 2010, Albania extradited the applicant to the United States without prior notice to him or his lawyer. The Government later claimed the extradition was prompted by the United States’ assurances and by the imminent expiry of his detention on 1 December 2010, which would have required his release and created a risk of absconding. On 26 November 2010, the Supreme Court quashed the lower extradition decisions, finding that the courts had failed to obtain death penalty assurances and had not properly assessed evidence of guilt. By then, however, the applicant had already been extradited. In the United States, he later pleaded guilty and, in July 2012, was sentenced to 80 months’ imprisonment.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the capital nature of one charge, the timing and content of the United States’ death penalty assurances, the Albanian courts’ initial failure to obtain such assurances, and Albania’s decision to extradite while a binding Rule 39 interim measure remained in force.

The case *Livančić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Applications nos. 15313/15 and 7 others) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, in a judgment dated 20 February 2020. The eight applications were lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention between 20 March 2015 and 6 January 2017. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was given notice of the applications.

The applicants all complained of the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions. The key factual issue was that binding domestic decisions in their favour were not enforced for substantial periods, despite the authorities’ obligation to do so. These delays allegedly raised issues under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The individual facts are set out in the appended table. Jerko Livančić relied on a decision of the Novi Travnik Cantonal Court of 7 June 2012. The non-enforcement period began on 28 September 2012 and ended on 13 June 2016, a delay of 3 years, 8 months and 17 days. Tončo Livančić relied on the same decision and court; his non-enforcement period ran from 14 September 2012 to 3 June 2016, lasting 3 years, 8 months and 21 days.

Kebir Šehić’s case involved seventeen domestic decisions issued by the Bugojno First Instance Court between 2003 and 2008. The non-enforcement periods began between 2 July 2012 and 31 October 2012 and ended on various dates between 2015 and 2017. The delays ranged from 2 years, 11 months and 2 days to 4 years, 7 months and 29 days.

Vahid Dervišić relied on a Sarajevo First Instance Court decision of 10 July 2008. Non-enforcement ran from 15 June 2012 to 21 January 2016, a delay of 3 years, 7 months and 7 days. Jasminka Basara relied on a Bugojno First Instance Court decision of 30 September 2011; non-enforcement lasted from 2 April 2012 to 25 April 2016, a period of 4 years and 24 days. Fatima Čajdo relied on a Bugojno First Instance Court decision of 20 November 2006; non-enforcement ran from 23 February

The case of **Łabudek v. Poland** (Application no. 37245/13), a First Section Committee judgment of 4 June 2020, concerned an alleged violation of **Article 5 § 3** of the European Convention on Human Rights—the right to trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial—based on the excessive length of the applicant’s detention on remand after **23 July 2011**. The applicant, Zdzisław Łabudek, a Polish national born in 1961, was held in Wojkowice Detention Centre.

On 18 January 1999 the applicant was arrested and remanded in custody on charges of participating in an organised armed criminal group and committing numerous violent offences, including two murders. His trial before the Katowice Regional Court began on 20 February 2001. On 13 February 2008 the Katowice Regional Court convicted him, together with thirty-five other accused, of membership in an organised armed criminal group, arms trafficking, two murders, three robberies, three attempted robberies, illegal possession of firearms and other offences. He was sentenced to life imprisonment with eligibility for conditional release after thirty years. On 18 February 2010 the Katowice Court of Appeal partly quashed the judgment and remitted the case, particularly regarding the applicant. On 11 February 2011 the Supreme Court dismissed cassation appeals.

Meanwhile, on 25 May 2010, the applicant’s detention on remand in the present case was lifted, but he was then serving a prison sentence in another set of criminal proceedings until 22 July 2011. On 27 June 2011 the Katowice Regional Court again ordered his detention on remand in the same proceedings. It relied on the high probability that he had committed the offences and the severity of the possible penalty. It also cited a risk of obstruction because he had already been sentenced to life imprisonment and had close ties with co-accused and witnesses from the same organised criminal group. The court noted that the applicant had previously maintained discipline and punished disobedience within the group, had attempted to contact and influence one witness, had threatened another, and had planned to murder a witness in another case. It concluded that no other preventive measure could sufficiently secure the proceedings.

The detention was extended repeatedly: on 17 January, 21 June and 18 December 2012; 13 June and 10 December 2013; 9 June and 17 December 2014; 11 June and 3 December 2015; and 10 May and 12 October 2016. The courts relied on the same grounds: reasonable suspicion, the maximum possible penalty, risk of collusion, absconding or further serious offences, and witness interference. Some decisions noted that the crown witness evidence had not yet been obtained and that proceedings were interrupted because a co-accused was detained in another case. The applicant’s appeals against several extensions were dismissed, with the Katowice Court of Appeal agreeing that continued detention was necessary. Between 11 June 2015 and 6 April 2016 he served a prison sentence imposed in another case. On 12 October 2016 the Katowice Regional Court convicted him as charged and imposed life imprisonment with conditional release after thirty years. His appeal was pending.

The proceedings after remittal were extensive. From 26 May 2011 to 12 October 2016, 174 hearings were held: 28 in 2011, 44 in 2012, 34 in 2013, 26 in 2014, 24 in 2015 and 18 in 2016. Of 276 scheduled hearings, 102 were adjourned, mainly due to illness of witnesses, accused or judges, or justified absence of experts. The court heard numerous witnesses, including a crown witness, obtained forensic reports, and the case file reached 75,000 pages.

The applicant lodged his application on 15 April 2013. The Court gave notice only of the complaint under Article 5 § 3 concerning the length of detention on remand after 23 July 2011, declaring the remainder inadmissible. It rejected the Government’s objection to Committee examination. The key issue was therefore whether the detention on remand after 23 July 2011 was excessively long.

**Maçi v. Albania** (Application no. 21051/10) is a European Court of Human Rights case, Third Section, judgment of 4 July 2024. The applicants, Altin Maçi and Skënder Maçi, are heirs of Mr Sh. M. They complain about Albania’s failure to enforce domestic decisions given in favour of their predecessor.

The relevant facts begin with a 1996 decision by the Tirana Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties. On 5 November 1996, the Commission found that Mr Sh. M. had been the former owner of a plot of land confiscated during the communist era. Relying on a field report, the Commission noted that a two-storey building and a road had been built on the plot. Under the operative part of the decision, the Commission returned to Mr Sh. M. title to one-third of the land on which the building stood and granted him the right to erect an additional third floor. It also ordered that his ownership be registered with the Immovable Property Registration Office (“IPRO”). As regards the remainder of the plot, the Commission ruled that he should receive compensation in one of the ways provided by law. No appeal was filed, and the 1996 decision became final on 5 December 1996. Its enforcement has remained pending for more than 27 years.

In 2004, Mr Sh. M. brought a claim before the Tirana District Court against the Ministry of Economy, the Municipality of Tirana and the IPRO, seeking delimitation of the exact boundaries of the plot. The court ordered an expert report which identified and described the plot and its boundaries. The property bordered public property, initially described by the Government as a “public square” and later as a “public road.” Mr Sh. M.’s title was confirmed by a 1994 ownership certificate. According to the expert report, the total surface area was 720 sq. m. The Municipality and the IPRO accepted the claim, while the Ministry of Economy did not express a position.

On 27 April 2004, the District Court upheld Mr Sh. M.’s claim and ordered the IPRO to register his title as defined in the expert report. Mr Sh. M. died on 17 May 2004, and the applicants were recognised as his heirs. The 2004 judgment became final on 3 June 2004. About two weeks later, the same court issued an enforcement writ. The non-enforcement period for this judgment began on 3 July 2004 and has continued for approximately 20 years.

The enforcement difficulties centred on the remaining 129 sq. m of the 720 sq. m plot. The IPRO informed the applicants that it had registered only 591 sq. m in their name.
