It claimed that the remaining 129 sq. m formed part of a public square owned by the Municipality of Tirana and therefore did not belong to the applicants. According to the IPRO, the court-appointed expert had made a mistake in measuring the plot. The IPRO asked the State Attorney’s Office to begin proceedings to invalidate the applicants’ title over those 129 sq. m. The State Attorney forwarded the request to the Municipality, asking it to start proceedings; the Municipality responded that it was for the State Attorney to initiate them. In 2023, the State Attorney stated that it was still examining the possibility of challenging the 2004 judgment.

These facts are relevant to the alleged violations because final and binding domestic decisions in favour of the applicants’ predecessor were not fully enforced. The authorities’ contradictory positions and prolonged inaction left the applicants unable to secure full registration and enjoyment of the property. The case therefore concerns alleged breaches of the right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, particularly the execution of final judgments, and the right to protection of property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Mirgadirov v. Azerbaijan and Turkey* (App. no. 62775/14, judgment 17 September 2020), the applicant, Rauf Mirgadirov, is an Azerbaijani national and well-known journalist/political analyst. In July 2010 he moved to Turkey, where he lived in Ankara and worked as a correspondent for the newspaper *Zerkalo*. Turkish authorities had granted him a press card and residence permit valid until 31 December 2014. On 8 April 2014, however, the Turkish Directorate General of Press and Information annulled his press card; he was informed orally the next day, without written reasons. On 11 April he requested written confirmation, but received none. On 18 April the Migration Management authorities decided to deport him under Law no. 6458. That night, while travelling by bus to Georgia with his family, police stopped the bus, found his residence permit had been revoked, and took him to the Ankara Security Directorate. He was allegedly told he was arrested because he was no longer legally resident. Police documents stated he was notified of the deportation procedure, his illegal presence, administrative detention and his rights, including access to a lawyer, but he refused to sign them; he claimed he was never properly notified. His requests for a lawyer and to contact his wife were allegedly ignored. On 19 April he was taken to Esenboğa Airport, signed a twelve-month entry ban, and was placed on a flight to Baku under police control. The official deportation and administrative detention decision was issued on 21 April.

Upon arrival in Baku on 19 April 2014, Azerbaijani Ministry of National Security agents arrested him. At 5:15 p.m. he was recorded as a suspect for high treason under Article 274 of the Criminal Code. At 5:20 p.m. he was questioned in the presence of a State-appointed lawyer. He admitted meeting L.B., head of an Armenian NGO, and D.S., former head of Armenian intelligence, in Turkey, Armenia and Georgia to discuss the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and regional affairs, but denied providing any State secrets, military, socio-political or economic information, or the location of military units. On 21 April he was charged with high treason: the authorities alleged he had been recruited by Armenian intelligence and had collected and supplied State secrets, photographs and technical drawings for use against Azerbaijan. The same day, the Nasimi District Court ordered his pre-trial detention for three months, citing the serious nature of the charge and risks of absconding or obstructing the investigation.

The applicant complained that his Convention rights were violated by his arrest, detention and de facto deportation from Turkey and his subsequent detention in Azerbaijan. Against Turkey, he invoked Article 5 §§ 1 and 2 (unlawful detention on 19 April and lack of reasons), Article 5 § 3 (failure to bring him before a judge), Article 5 § 4 (inability to challenge detention), and Article 10 (freedom of expression as a journalist). Against Azerbaijan, he invoked Article 5 § 1(c) (no reasonable suspicion), Article 5 § 1 (unlawful detention from 19 to 20 November 2014), Article 5 § 3 (lack of justification for pre-trial detention), Article 5 § 4 (courts’ failure to assess release arguments and his lawyers’ absence from the 20 November 2014 Nasimi District Court hearing), Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), Article 8 (unlawful restrictions during the investigation), and Article 18 in conjunction with Article 5.

In *Dimović and Others v. Serbia* (Application no. 40238/16), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined a complaint by four Serbian nationals: Erika Dimović (b. 1975), Roža Dimović (b. 1971), Magdalena Kolompar (b. 1987), and Đenđi Kovač (b. 1983). They were represented by V. Juhas Đurić. The application was lodged on 21 June 2016 and concerned criminal proceedings in Serbia. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically that they could not comment on written observations submitted by the Higher Public Prosecutor in reply to their appeal.

The applicants had been convicted of attempted aggravated theft and sentenced to imprisonment by a first-instance court. Both the applicants and the Subotica Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office appealed against that judgment. The appeals were sent to the Novi Sad Court of Appeal. In the appellate proceedings, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office submitted written observations seeking dismissal of the applicants’ appeal, granting of the Subotica Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office’s appeal, and higher prison sentences for the applicants.

The Court of Appeal did not provide the applicants with a copy of those written observations. As a result, the applicants had no opportunity to review or respond to the prosecution’s arguments before the Court of Appeal decided the case. The Court of Appeal then issued a final judgment upholding the applicants’ conviction but reducing the prison sentences for all applicants. The applicants only learned about the Higher Public Prosecutor’s observations after receiving the Court of Appeal’s judgment. Therefore, the prosecution’s appellate submissions were disclosed, in effect, only after the appellate court had already ruled.

The applicants challenged this before the Serbian Constitutional Court. On 26 November 2015, the Constitutional Court dismissed their complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It noted that the Code of Criminal Procedure did not require second-instance courts to provide an accused person with a copy of the prosecutor’s observations filed in reply to the accused’s appeal. In other words, domestic law did not oblige the Court of Appeal to disclose the prosecution’s written response to the defence.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 about their inability to comment on the Higher Public Prosecutor’s written observations submitted in reply to their defence statements of appeal in the proceedings before the Court of Appeal. The central factual basis of the alleged violation was that the prosecution’s appellate submissions were not communicated to the defence, depriving the applicants of an opportunity to respond before the Court of Appeal reached its final decision.

The case was communicated to the Serbian Government, represented by Agent Zorana Jadrijević Mladar. The parties submitted observations. The Fourth Section Committee, composed of Judges Tim Eicke, Ana Maria Guerra Martins, and Mateja Đurović, deliberated in private on 22 October 2024 and delivered judgment on 19 November 2024. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are thus the non-communication of the Higher Public Prosecutor’s written observations, the applicants’ lack of any chance to comment on them, and the domestic Constitutional Court’s rejection of the complaint on the basis that such communication was not required by the Code of Criminal Procedure.

In **Pasquini v. San Marino (No. 2)** (Application no. 23349/17), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention concerning the presumption of innocence. The applicant, Enrico Maria Pasquini, an Italian national living in San Marino, was at the relevant time chairman and sole shareholder of S.M.I., a fiduciary company operating in San Marino.

Following a Central Bank inspection of S.M.I.’s headquarters, a report was submitted to the investigating judge alleging suspicious financial operations by the applicant and another person, B., the company’s director. Criminal proceedings were instituted. The applicant was charged with exercising fiduciary activity without a licence, three counts of obstruction of surveillance, misreporting to shareholders and supervisory boards, and continuing aggravated embezzlement. The prosecution alleged that between April 2009 and March 2010 the applicant had personally withdrawn EUR 2,633,055.77 from a fiduciary account opened by company S. and administered by S.M.I. It claimed he was the beneficial owner of company S. and had used fictitious invoices for non-existent services provided by foreign companies, thereby embezzling funds to the detriment of S.M.I. Company S.M.I., then in compulsory liquidation, joined the criminal proceedings as a civil party.

On 8 April 2014 the first-instance judge convicted the applicant and B. of all charges. The applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and a fine, and was ordered to compensate S.M.I. in an amount to be quantified in separate civil proceedings. An interim compensation order of EUR 2,633,055.77 was made in favour of the civil party. The judge found a complex system of foreign broker companies, simulated brokerage operations, tax-haven entities, and bank accounts formally registered to brokers but actually traceable to the applicant and B.

The applicant appealed, arguing that the limitation period for embezzlement had expired. On 1 December 2015 the Judge of Criminal Appeals acknowledged the limitation issue but referred a constitutional question concerning Article 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, because it allegedly prevented the appeal judge from deciding civil claims once an offence was time-barred. Law No. 189 of 2015 subsequently introduced Article 196 bis, allowing the appeal judge, when declaring an offence time-barred, to decide civil obligations arising from it. The Constitutional Court returned the file for reconsideration.

By judgment of 19 September 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted the applicant and B. of exercising fiduciary activity without a licence; acquitted the applicant of one obstruction count; and declared the remaining obstruction counts, misreporting, and aggravated embezzlement time-barred, discontinuing those charges. It upheld the compensation order. The appeal judge stated that the first-instance reasoning had not indicated that the alleged facts never occurred or that the accused had not committed them, so there was no room for any finding other than discontinuance. Nevertheless, he examined the evidence underlying the aggravated embezzlement conviction exclusively to decide civil compensation.

The applicant complained to the Court that his presumption of innocence had been violated: although there had been no finding of guilt, the appeal judgment reflected the judge’s conviction that he was guilty, and he was ordered to pay damages precisely on the basis of a declaration of criminal responsibility not ascertained in the criminal proceedings. On 4 September 2017, notice of the Article 6 § 2 complaint was given to the Government; the remainder was declared inadmissible. The Italian Government did not intervene.

**Summary of Ivashchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 41303/11)**

The case of *Ivashchenko v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Valeriy Volodymyrovych Ivashchenko, a Ukrainian national, on 27 June 2011. The applicant, a former Deputy and acting Minister of Defence of Ukraine, complained under Article 3 of the Convention that he had not received adequate medical treatment while in detention and was confined in a metal cage during court hearings. He further complained under Article 5 that his pre-trial detention was unlawful, lengthy, and lacked justification, and that no effective procedure existed to challenge its lawfulness.

The relevant facts began in August 2010. Following an operational inquiry by the Security Service of Ukraine into alleged unlawful activity at a State-owned enterprise managed by the Ministry of Defence, the General Prosecutor’s Office instituted criminal proceedings against the applicant on 20 August 2010. He was suspected of abuse of power for signing a financial rehabilitation plan that allegedly caused State property losses. On 21 August 2010, after appearing before an investigator, he was arrested on grounds that eyewitnesses had identified him and to prevent him from evading investigation or obstructing the truth.

On 24 August 2010, the Pechersk District Court of Kyiv ordered his pre-trial detention, citing risks of absconding and hindering the investigation, without further detail. This order was upheld on appeal, and subsequently extended multiple times on the same grounds. On 4 March 2011, the District Court decided he would remain in detention for an unspecified period without providing particular reasons. During trial, on 1 and 19 August 2011, the applicant requested removal from the metal cage used during hearings; the court refused, stating it was in accordance with domestic legislation and not for the court to decide.

Regarding medical treatment, the applicant had suffered since 1995 from chronic conditions including spinal osteochondritis, arthritis, and cerebral atherosclerosis, requiring inpatient treatment at least twice yearly. After his placement in the Kyiv Pre-trial Detention Centre (SIZO) on 25 August 2010, his health deteriorated. He was diagnosed with additional conditions in May 2011. Various medical examinations from June 2011 to January 2012 consistently noted his chronic diseases had worsened. Medical professionals, including the head of the Main Military Clinical Hospital (MMCH) and chief doctors, repeatedly stated that adequate treatment could not be provided at the SIZO, that he required inpatient neurological care and physiotherapy unavailable there, and that without timely treatment, his condition, including spinal dysfunction and muscle atrophy, could further deteriorate, potentially risking paralysis. Despite these recommendations and a court statement of no objection to his inpatient treatment at the MMCH, transportation was refused by the prison escort service in January 2012. Treatment recommendations were only partially implemented. The applicant was found guilty by the District Court on 12 April 2012 and sentenced to five years, but was released on 14 August 2012 after the Court of Appeal imposed a suspended sentence.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 due to inadequate medical care and the cage confinement, and of Article 5 due to unjustified, lengthy detention and lack of effective review.

The case *Baz v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40962/13) is a European Court of Human Rights Fifth Section Committee judgment delivered on 5 November 2020. The applicant, Mekhmet Takhır Dıno Baz, a Turkish national born in 1976 and living in Mykolayiv, complained under Article 5 § 1 (f) of the Convention that his detention in Ukraine in the context of extradition proceedings was unlawful. The Court communicated only that complaint; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The key facts concern the applicant’s immigration status, criminal proceedings in Ukraine, and Turkey’s extradition request. In 2004 the applicant arrived in Ukraine and on 23 March 2011 was granted refugee status. On 18 October 2012, however, the State Migration Service revoked that status, finding that he had provided false information: he had claimed political persecution in Turkey while concealing that he was wanted by Turkish law-enforcement authorities on suspicion of a criminal offence. Ukrainian courts upheld the revocation at three levels, with the final decision on 3 April 2013. Meanwhile, on 14 March 2013, the applicant applied for subsidiary protection. On 13 August 2013 that application was rejected as inadmissible because his refugee status had been revoked, but on 27 February 2014 the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court quashed that refusal and ordered the authorities to examine the application on the merits. Subsequent developments were not in the case file.

Separately, on 25 September 2012 the applicant was detained in Ukraine on suspicion of using forged documents. He was later released subject to an undertaking not to abscond, and on 14 March 2013 the Kharkiv Leninsky District Court convicted him and sentenced him to two months’ imprisonment. His appeal outcome is unknown.

The extradition context is central. On 20 June 2011 the Istanbul 13th Higher Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for the applicant on suspicion of participation in terrorist and separatist activities on 5 August 1998. On 3 October 2012 that court sent an extradition request to the Ukrainian judicial authorities, specifying that the charge would become time-barred on 15 August 2013 and assuring respect for Convention rights. On 14 November 2012 the State Security Service detained the applicant with a view to extradition. The next day the migration service confirmed he was not a Ukrainian national. On 16 November 2012 the Mykolaiv Tsentralny District Court ordered his detention pending extradition. On 17 June 2013 the Istanbul court issued a second arrest warrant on the same charge.

After being transferred to Kharkiv in connection with the domestic criminal case, the Kharkiv Zhovtnevy District Court on 17 July 2013 held that continued detention was justified, relying on the two Turkish warrants, the extradition request, and a prosecutor’s extradition inquiry finding no impediments. The court noted the applicant’s conviction but observed it was not final. On 30 August 2013 the Zhovtnevy Court released him because the limitation period for the offence had expired on 15 August 2013 and Article 10 of the European Convention on Extradition barred extradition in such circumstances. On 23 September 2013 the Ministry of Justice rejected Turkey’s extradition request.

Relevant Ukrainian law prohibited extradition of refugees or persons under subsidiary protection (Article 589 § 2 of the 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure) and barred extradition decisions while protection applications remained pending (Article 590 § 4). Detention pending extradition was permitted under Article 584, but for no more than twelve months and subject to judicial review. The applicant’s complaint therefore focused on whether his detention with a view to extradition remained lawful given the lapse of time, the extradition bar, and his protection-related proceedings.

M.A. and Others v. Bulgaria (Application no. 5115/18, ECtHR, 20 February 2020) concerned five Chinese Uighur Muslims from the Xinjiang Uighur Autonomous Region (“XUAR”). They alleged that their intended expulsion from Bulgaria to China would expose them to death or ill-treatment, in violation of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. The Court had issued an interim measure under Rule 39 indicating that they should not be removed to China.

The applicants fled China at different times, claiming persecution by Chinese authorities. The second applicant alleged that security agents demanded he collect data on clients; when he refused, charges were brought against him, his mother and sister were arrested, and he fled via Malaysia and Turkey. The third applicant alleged police monitoring of his family, childhood arrests for praying, detention and torture after discussing the 2009 Urumqi riots, later arrest for wearing a beard, and targeting after secretly teaching Uighur. He fled through Southeast Asia and Turkey. The fourth applicant alleged repeated detention and fines for breaching China’s family-planning rules after his children were born, then fled with his wife through Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand and Turkey. The first and fifth applicants similarly claimed persecution in the XUAR and arrived in Turkey.

In 2017, believing Turkey had agreed to deport Uighurs to China amid improving Turkey-China relations, the applicants left Turkey and entered Bulgaria unlawfully on 26 July 2017. Bulgarian border police apprehended them and issued repatriation orders. They were placed in an alien detention centre. On 1 December 2017 they applied for asylum. The State Refugees Agency rejected their applications on 18 December 2017, and the Haskovo Administrative Court upheld those decisions on 29 January 2018. It found that they had not shown individual persecution, accepted that Chinese counterterrorism measures in Xinjiang were justified, and said their past problems were not proven to be based on ethnicity or religion. It also found no indication that Turkey intended to repatriate Uighurs.

In parallel, in January 2018 the State Agency for National Security ordered their expulsion on national security grounds. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed judicial reviews for the second, third and fourth applicants in May 2019. It relied on confidential information alleging that after leaving China they had stayed in Syria, received training from the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (“ETIM”), a terrorist organisation, and had contacts with ETIM, Islamic State-linked persons, and human traffickers. It concluded that they could threaten Bulgaria’s national security. It further stated that any risk they would face on return to China concerned the implementation, not the lawfulness, of the expulsion.

International bodies and NGOs, including Amnesty International, the World Uighur Congress and members of the European Parliament, urged Bulgaria not to return the applicants to China. They cited documented cases of Uighurs forcibly returned to China who were detained, tortured, or sentenced to death. Country information described mass detentions, re-education camps, torture, severe restrictions on Uighurs in Xinjiang, and particular suspicion of Uighurs with foreign ties. The applicants’ central complaint was therefore that expulsion to China would expose them to a real risk of arbitrary detention, ill-treatment or death.

**Summary of *Stafeyev v. Russia* (Application no. 32984/06)**

**Background and Investigation**
The case concerns the applicant, Mr. Vyacheslav Vladimirovich Stafeyev, a Russian national born in 1978. On 19 February 2001, the bodies of the Sh. family (a man, his wife, and their thirteen-year-old son) were discovered in their flat, having apparently been killed the previous day. In November 2004, while detained for another crime, the applicant's fingerprints were entered into a police database. On 8 December 2004, investigating officers were informed that fingerprints found in the victims' flat matched the applicant's. A subsequent search of the applicant's home uncovered items stolen from the victims' flat.

Police officers visited the applicant in detention on 8, 9, and 10 December 2004, questioning him informally. The applicant alleged that he confessed on 10 December 2004 under duress; the Government maintained he spontaneously confessed on 8 December 2004. On 10 December 2004, the applicant was informed of his rights, waived his right to a lawyer, and reiterated his confession during an interview. He confessed again on 16 December 2004, again without a lawyer. On 20 January 2005, assisted by counsel, he retracted his confession.

**Trial Proceedings**
The Sverdlovsk Regional Court conducted the trial. On 15 September 2005, it excluded the applicant's statements of 10 and 16 December 2004 as inadmissible because they were made without a lawyer and later retracted. However, the court admitted the 8 December 2004 confession. The applicant denied guilt, claiming he had visited the family on 16 February 2001 (not 18 February) and that his confession was coerced.

On 14 December 2005, the Regional Court convicted the applicant of three counts of murder, robbery, and destruction of property, sentencing him to life imprisonment. The judgment relied on fingerprint evidence, the search results, police testimony that the applicant voluntarily confessed after being informed of the fingerprint match, and the 8 December 2004 confession.

**Appeal Proceedings and Alleged Violations**
The applicant's trial lawyer appealed on 14 November 2005, raising numerous factual and legal issues. The appeal hearing was scheduled for 15 May 2006. However, the lawyer failed to appear. The applicant, participating via video link, requested new counsel. The Supreme Court assigned lawyer R. and adjourned to 29 May 2006.

On 23 May 2006, R. visited the applicant, but detention facility authorities allegedly limited their meeting to fifteen minutes, with guards repeatedly interrupting. On 25 May 2006, the applicant requested additional time with R. via a letter to the Supreme Court, but the request apparently arrived after the hearing.

On 29 May 2006, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction. R. was present, and the applicant participated via video link. The applicant alleged poor video quality and that the court refused to admit his 25 May request. The Government claimed the applicant complained about video quality on 30–31 May 2006, but a 2013 certificate stated no transmission failures were recorded.

**The Complaint**
The European Court of Human Rights granted notice solely on complaints regarding the lack of effective legal assistance on appeal and the poor quality of the video link before the Supreme Court. The core alleged violation centers on whether the applicant had adequate time and facilities to consult his assigned appellate lawyer, R., given the fifteen-minute meeting constraint, and whether procedural fairness was compromised during the appeal hearing.

**Summary of W.R. v. The Netherlands**

The case of *W.R. v. The Netherlands* concerns the alleged unfairness of criminal proceedings due to the lack of legal assistance during initial police interviews, violating Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, a Dutch national, was arrested on 12 January 2014 on suspicion of manslaughter following the disappearance of his ex-wife. Police had discovered blood spatters and a pungent odour of a combustible substance at his home. Upon arrest, the applicant was informed of his right to consult a lawyer prior to questioning. He did not respond when asked if he wished to consult an assigned lawyer, so the Legal Aid Duty Roster Service was notified. He consulted with his lawyer later that morning.

That evening, police questioned the applicant without his lawyer present. After being informed of his right to remain silent, he gave a detailed confession, admitting to killing the victim and offering to show police relevant locations. This led to an on-site visit where the victim's body was discovered. In a subsequent interview on 13 January, again without counsel, he provided further details, including his admission that he had conceived a plan to kill the victim, laid out a knife and tarpaulins in his garage beforehand, and later executed this plan.

The core of the applicant's complaint stems from the use of these statements, made without a lawyer present, in his subsequent trial. In the first-instance proceedings, the Regional Court admitted the evidence, finding the police had acted in accordance with the case-law of the Supreme Court, which at the time only guaranteed the right to *consult* a lawyer, not to have one present during questioning.

However, the legal landscape evolved. The Supreme Court later accepted, in December 2015, that suspects had a right to have a lawyer present during police interviews, effective from March 2016. This change followed the European Court of Human Rights' *Salduz* judgment and EU Directive 2013/48/EU.

Despite this shift, the applicant's conviction for murder was upheld on appeal in December 2015. The Court of Appeal relied heavily on the detailed confession from 12 and 13 January 2014 to establish premeditation. The applicant's defence argued for the exclusion of these statements, but this was rejected. The Supreme Court later acknowledged the Court of Appeal had erred in its legal reasoning on the exclusion issue but ultimately dismissed the appeal, noting that the applicant had consulted a lawyer between his arrest and the first substantive interview.

The applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights centered on the unfairness of using evidence obtained during police interviews where he was not assisted by a lawyer, as this violated his right to a fair trial. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are the police interviews conducted on 12 and 13 January 2014, during which the applicant made incriminating statements without his lawyer being present, and the subsequent reliance on this evidence to convict him of murder.

**Case:** *Klopcovs v. Latvia* (Application no. 26902/13)  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section  
**Judgment date:** 13 February 2020

The applicant, Mr Boriss Klopcovs, a Latvian national born in 1951 and living in Riga, lodged his application on 11 April 2013. On 18 December 2013 the Latvian Government were given notice only of the complaint concerning the **length of proceedings**; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. Therefore, the key facts relevant to the admissible alleged violation concern the duration of the administrative proceedings he brought after prison authorities interfered with his correspondence.

In 2005 the applicant was detained in Riga Central Prison pending trial. During June, July and August 2005, the prison administration controlled and stopped his correspondence addressed to private persons and institutions. On 14 and 25 September 2005 he complained to the Prisons Administration about those actions and the reasons given. The Prisons Administration rejected his complaints on 11 and 24 October 2005. On 4 October and 16 December 2005, the Ministry of Justice found the prison administration’s actions and the Prisons Administration’s replies lawful.

On 22 September 2006 the applicant brought administrative proceedings against the Ministry of Justice. The Prisons Administration later joined the proceedings. On 21 October 2008 the Administrative District Court found the prison administration’s actions unlawful, but rejected the applicant’s claim for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages of 5,406 Latvian lats (approximately EUR 7,692). On 3 December 2009 the Administrative Regional Court quashed that decision and remitted the case to the first-instance court. On 27 April 2010 the first-instance court again found the actions unlawful and rejected the damages claim. The applicant appealed only as regards damages, but his appeal was not accepted because it was late. The opposing parties’ appeals were accepted, and appellate proceedings began.

On 15 February 2012 the Administrative Regional Court found that the prison administration had acted unlawfully only insofar as the applicant had not been informed of the reasons for stopping his letters and insofar as one letter had been stopped unlawfully. The remainder of his claims were dismissed. On 26 October 2012 the Senate of the Supreme Court gave a final decision upholding the appellate judgment and dismissing the cassation complaints of both the Prisons Administration and the applicant.

The administrative proceedings thus ran from 22 September 2006 to 26 October 2012, lasting over six years and passing through first instance, appeal, remittal, a second first-instance judgment, a second appeal, and cassation. There were ten hearings. None were postponed because of the applicant’s unjustified absence. However, after the hearing of 22 February 2008, the applicant failed to return 77 pages of case documents. On 23 May 2008 he explained that he believed the documents were for his personal use and did not know they had to be returned. The first-instance court reobtained them from another case file in September 2008, and at least one hearing was apparently adjourned because of this. The applicant also initiated several ancillary proceedings challenging various procedural decisions of the first-instance and appellate courts.

These facts were relevant to assessing whether the length of the administrative proceedings exceeded a reasonable time and whether any delays were attributable to the authorities or to the applicant. The only admissible Convention complaint was the length-of-proceedings complaint; the other complaints, including those concerning the stopping of his correspondence, were declared inadmissible.

In *Daugaard Sorensen v. Denmark* (App no. 25650/22), the applicant, a Danish national born in 2000, alleged that she was raped by A during the night of 6–7 June 2021. She reported the incident to the police on 7 June and was interviewed in the presence of a lawyer.

On 8 June 2021, the District Court remanded A in custody on suspicion of rape under Article 216 § 1 of the Penal Code and non-consensual sexual activity under Article 225. The court cited reasonable suspicion, outstanding witness interviews, and a risk that A might interfere with the investigation. Police investigated the case, interviewed the applicant and others, examined the crime scene and the applicant’s clothing, and searched A’s home. A was released on 18 June 2021.

On 30 July 2021, the first-instance prosecutor dropped the charges under section 721(1)(ii) of the Administration of Justice Act, finding insufficient evidence because there were two opposing statements and no conclusive corroboration. The applicant appealed on 18 August 2021. On 16 September 2021, the Regional State Prosecutor reversed the decision and decided to proceed with the prosecution.

Under section 724(2), notice of that decision had to be served on A by 30 September 2021—within two months of the initial drop decision—via Digital Post or registered letter. Due to a database typing error, the prosecutor wrongly assumed A could not receive Digital Post and sent a registered letter. Another database error omitted A’s c/o address, so the letter was returned on 23 September 2021 marked “addressee unknown at this address.” Internal guidelines required checking the address, whether A had moved, whether the deadline had expired, and whether to reattempt service. Because of a further error, the office did not recheck, and A was not notified before the deadline.

On 13 October 2021, the first-instance prosecutor filed an indictment. In November, A’s defence lawyer sought dismissal because the two-month time-limit had not been met. The prosecutor agreed, and on 16 November 2021 the District Court dismissed the case against A. It was therefore no longer possible to prosecute him for the alleged rape. On 30 November 2021, the prosecutor apologised to the applicant’s lawyer for the procedural error.

The applicant sought compensation. On 21 December 2021, she applied to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board for injury to feelings under the State Compensation to Victims of Crime Act. On 15 November 2022, the Board rejected her claim, finding she had not sufficiently established that she had been the victim of a crime. She did not bring civil proceedings against the Board.

In December 2022, the Director of Public Prosecutions informed her lawyer that she could claim compensation against the police and prosecutor for administrative errors and discussed the Chapter 93a summary procedure. On 31 January 2023, the applicant claimed pecuniary and non-pecuniary compensation from the prosecutor under Chapter 93a, including pain and suffering, medical and rehabilitation expenses, ruined clothes, and injury to feelings. Items relating to pain, medical costs, and clothes concerned the reported rape; injury to feelings concerned both the rape and the administrative errors. On 24 April 2023, the prosecutor rejected the claims as outside the scope of Chapter 93a. The Director of Public Prosecutions upheld that decision on 30 June 2023, noting she could ask a court to decide or bring civil proceedings. The applicant did not bring civil proceedings.

The applicant complained under Articles 3, 6, 8, and 13 of the Convention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the collapse of the rape prosecution due to the Regional State Prosecutor’s failure to comply with the statutory notification deadline, caused by multiple administrative errors, and the alleged lack of an effective remedy or compensation for that failure.

Talalikhina v. Ukraine (Application no. 13919/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case, Fifth Section, judgment of 22 October 2020, concerning the lawfulness and length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention, the length of the criminal proceedings against her, and the lack of effective remedies in that regard.

The applicant, Olga Vasilyevna Talalikhina, a Ukrainian national born in 1954 living in Sevastopol, was initially involved in criminal proceedings instituted on 5 September 2007 on charges of theft. She was questioned as a suspect and signed an undertaking not to abscond. On 30 October 2007 the theft case was referred to court for trial. While those proceedings were pending, on 13 April 2009, the applicant was involved in a drunken brawl with her cohabitant at home. She allegedly hit the man with a hammer. He was taken to hospital and died a few days later. On 17 April 2009 the applicant was arrested and questioned in relation to that incident.

On 20 April 2009 the Leninskyy District Court of Sevastopol ordered her pre-trial detention. On 15 June 2009 the Sevastopol City Prosecutor approved a bill of indictment charging her with aggravated infliction of serious bodily harm resulting in the victim’s death and referred the case to the District Court. The applicant remained in custody. On 6 July 2009 the Nakhimovskiy District Court of Sevastopol committed her for trial and ruled that the preventive measure should remain in place.

Her detention continued for over three years. On 5 August 2011 and 10 May 2012 the District Court dismissed her applications for release as unfounded, considering that there were no grounds to change the preventive measure. Only on 20 June 2012 did the District Court change the custodial preventive measure, accepting her relatives as guarantors, and the applicant was released. In the meantime, on 19 September 2012, the prosecutor dropped the theft charge against her for lack of constituent elements of the crime. On 6 February 2013 the District Court convicted her of unintentional homicide of her cohabitant and sentenced her to two years’ imprisonment.

The relevant legal framework included Article 156 of the 1960 Code of Criminal Procedure, then in force, which provided that detention during the pre-trial investigation should not exceed two months. A judge was, however, empowered to extend pre-trial detention following a request to that effect. The applicant’s complaints therefore focused on whether her detention from April 2009 to June 2012 was lawful and justified, whether the criminal proceedings—especially the homicide case, but also the earlier theft case—were excessively long, and whether Ukrainian law provided effective domestic remedies for those alleged violations. The Court gave notice of the application to the Ukrainian Government on 2 May 2019 and adopted its judgment on 22 October 2020.

In *Aggerholm v. Denmark* (Application no. 45439/18, judgment 15 September 2020), the applicant, a Danish national diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1999, complained under Article 3 of the Convention about a prolonged mechanical restraint.

In 2005 the applicant was convicted of five incidents of violence against a civil servant and threats of violence, and was sentenced to committal to a psychiatric hospital. From 2007 to 2011 he was held in a high-security psychiatric unit under a “dangerousness decree.” He was later treated in an open ward but was moved to a closed ward, P4, in September 2012 because of irritability and threatening behaviour.

The alleged violation concerned an incident on 8 February 2013. The previous evening, the applicant had been angry and had made remarks about the chief physician, H.H., including “We have to do something about her,” which staff interpreted as a threat. After speaking with the on-call doctor, he appeared calm. The next day, staff decided that he should not go on unescorted day release because he remained angry. When H.H. informed him that his day release was revoked, he refused to sit or talk, appeared white-faced and tight-lipped, and was described as having significant pent-up anger. Attempts at dialogue failed over about one and a half hours. H.H. considered him dangerous to those around him and decided to restrain him.

At 1.15 p.m. on 8 February 2013, the applicant was strapped to a restraint bed with a belt and wrist and ankle straps—a five-point restraint. He remained restrained until 12.05 p.m. on 9 February 2013, a total of twenty-two hours and fifty minutes. He went voluntarily to the restraint room and lay down. During the restraint, a staff member kept constant watch, and doctors assessed him four times. At 6.55 p.m. one foot strap was released and toilet visits and personal hygiene were permitted. At 10.46 p.m. he was still considered potentially dangerous. The following morning he was cooperative, and he was released at 12.05 p.m.

The applicant complained to the Psychiatric Patients’ Complaints Board. On 21 March 2013, the Board found both the January and February restraints unlawful, holding that the conditions for physical restraint had not been fulfilled and that it had not been documented that he posed an immediate risk of harm to himself or others. H.H. had submitted only a brief written statement and could not attend due to illness. The State Administration later dismissed the applicant’s claim for compensation and his Article 3 complaint. The Health Authority found no lack of care by H.H.

In subsequent civil proceedings, the Medico-Legal Council stated in 2016 that the conditions for the February restraint had been present, that medical assessments had been sufficiently frequent, and that H.H.’s assessment was justified. The City Court found against the applicant in 2017, relying on the medical records, testimony from H.H. and staff, and the Medico-Legal Council. The High Court upheld the restraint in November 2017, finding it necessary to prevent an imminent risk to others and that sufficient assessments had been made. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in March 2018.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged that the approximately twenty-three-hour five-point restraint amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment contrary to Article 3. The key issues were the duration and method of restraint, his mental illness and violent history, the threats and anger preceding the measure, the conflicting domestic findings, and the safeguards applied—constant supervision, regular medical checks, and gradual relaxation. The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 3.

**Case: Saakashvili v. Georgia (Apps nos. 6232/20 and 22394/20), ECtHR, 23 May 2024**

The case concerns two criminal prosecutions of Mikheil Saakashvili, former President of Georgia (2004–2013) and later a Ukrainian national. The applications alleged violations of Articles 6, 7 and 18 of the Convention—fair trial, legality of conviction, and improper political motive. The prosecutions formed part of the post-2012 Georgian Dream government’s “restoration of justice,” following thousands of complaints against former officials of the United National Movement. Saakashvili left Georgia in 2013, became a Ukrainian citizen, and was tried and convicted in absentia while represented by his chosen lawyers.

**First application (no. 6232/20): battery and misuse of authority.** On 14 July 2005, V.G., a member of parliament, was attacked in Tbilisi by armed men in riot-police uniforms. He was severely beaten, permanently disfigured, and his belongings were seized. V.G. linked the attack to an interview he had published shortly before, in which he insulted the President and his wife. An initial investigation was discontinued in 2005 but reopened in November 2012. Evidence included testimony from V.G., his bodyguard and driver; former Defence Minister I.O., who said Saakashvili personally ordered him to arrange the attack before it was reassigned to Interior Minister Merabishvili; former Parliament President N.B., who said Saakashvili implied V.G. deserved the beating; secret-surveillance officers who testified they monitored V.G. and tampered with his car brakes; riot-police participants who described the assault; and phone data showing contacts between Saakashvili and officials before and after the incident. In November 2014 he was charged with complicity in battery and misuse of authority. In June 2018 the Tbilisi City Court convicted him in absentia; the Supreme Court upheld the conviction in July 2019, imposing six years’ imprisonment plus a two-year ban on public service. He complained that the conviction relied on hearsay and politically hostile witnesses, but domestic courts found their testimony corroborated by other evidence.

**Second application (no. 22394/20): abuse of official authority.** In January 2006, Sandro Girgvliani and L.B. were abducted and beaten by Interior Ministry officers; Girgvliani was killed. Four officers were convicted in 2006. In November 2008, Saakashvili granted them presidential clemency, halving their sentences; they were released on licence in September 2009 after serving about three years. The ECtHR in *Enukidze and Girgvliani v. Georgia* (2011) found a procedural Article 2 violation and criticised the investigation and lenient treatment. After a 2012 repeat investigation, the four officers said they had acted on orders of CSD Director D.A., who allegedly promised them pardons, better prison conditions and compensation if they confessed and stayed silent about others, including the Interior Minister’s wife. Former officials I.O. and N.B. testified that Saakashvili knew the details and promised pardons to protect his political team. Clemency Commission members said the pardon bypassed normal procedure and no applications were considered. In November 2014 he was charged with abuse of power for granting the pardon to pervert justice. In January 2018 he was convicted in absentia. On appeal he argued judicial bias, reliance on hearsay, and that exercising presidential clemency could not constitute a crime. The alleged violations therefore concern whether the proceedings were fair, whether convicting him for the pardon breached the principle of legality, and whether the prosecutions pursued an improper political purpose.

In *Sigríður Elín Sigfúsdóttir v. Iceland*, the applicant, a former director of corporate banking at Landsbanki, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that her criminal proceedings were heard by a tribunal that was not independent and impartial and that her right to be presumed innocent was violated. The case arose from Iceland’s 2008 financial crisis. On 30 September 2008, the company Imon ehf., owned by investor M.A., purchased 250,000,000 Landsbanki shares using a loan from Landsbanki, secured by the shares and Imon’s capital certificates in Byr Savings Bank. The applicant, as a member of Landsbanki’s credit committee, approved the loan on 3 October 2008, four days before Landsbanki collapsed on 7 October 2008.

A Special Prosecutor later investigated. In March 2013, the applicant was indicted for fraud by abuse of position and market manipulation, along with two co-defendants. In June 2014, the District Court of Reykjavik acquitted her. In October 2015, the Supreme Court overturned the acquittal, convicted her of abuse of position and aiding and abetting market manipulation, and sentenced her to 18 months’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court panel consisted of Justices M.S., V.M.M., E.T., H.I.J. and Þ.Ö.

In December 2016, media reports revealed that several Supreme Court justices had owned shares in Icelandic banks before the 2008 crash, raising concerns about undisclosed conflicts of interest. The applicant stated that this was the first time she learned of these holdings. She requested information from the Committee on Judicial Functions. The Committee explained that Justice M.S. had inherited Glitnir shares but sold them in 2003 and 2007; Justices V.M.M. and E.T. were appointed only in 2010 and 2011 and had previously held shares lost in the bank collapse; the other judges had reported no shareholdings. The Supreme Court later published information and provided details to affected parties. Justice E.T. reported Landsbanki shares with a nominal value of ISK 87,383, purchased for ISK 374,112 and valued at ISK 1,738,922 on 3 October 2008, as well as Glitnir shares with a nominal value of ISK 287,124. Justice V.M.M. reported Landsbanki shares acquired between March and September 2007 with a nominal value of ISK 428,075, purchased for ISK 14,753,256 and valued at ISK 8,518,692 on 3 October 2008; they became worthless after the State takeover.

In December 2016, the applicant applied to reopen her case. She argued that the financial interests of Justices E.T., M.S. and V.M.M. meant the Supreme Court panel lacked impartiality under Article 70 of the Icelandic Constitution and Article 6 of the Convention. On 12 May 2019, the Committee on Reopening of Judicial Proceedings accepted the request under section 228(1)(d) of the Criminal Procedures Act. It found that Justice V.M.M.’s substantial Landsbanki shareholding and resulting financial loss could reasonably justify fears that the panel lacked impartiality. The Committee noted that the Supreme Court had stated that the applicant’s “imprudent decisions” on loans could have caused financial loss to Landsbanki shareholders, and that the information about V.M.M.’s holdings had not been known to the applicant at trial. The Committee did not decide the impartiality of the other justices. The reopening proceedings remained pending before the Supreme Court. The applicant’s ECtHR application, lodged on 2 June 2017, centred on these undisclosed shareholdings and the alleged resulting lack of objective impartiality.

In *Parinov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 48398/17), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 10 December 2020. The applicant, Mr Borys Parinov, a Ukrainian national born in 1953 and living in Lugansk, died in September 2018; his wife and son continued the application. He alleged violations of Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining that proceedings concerning his share in a limited liability company were excessively long and that, as a result, he could not recover that share. The Court communicated the duration-related complaints and declared inadmissible his complaint about the alleged lack of impartiality of the liquidation manager.

In April 2000 the applicant became a shareholder in a limited liability company. On 30 May 2005 he withdrew from the company, but the other shareholder failed to return his share. In December 2007 domestic proceedings began; by April 2008 a final ruling acknowledged his withdrawal. Meanwhile, the company sold two commercial buildings in December 2007 and January 2008 to company B., which resold them to company K. in January and February 2008.

In June 2008 the applicant sued for reimbursement of the value of his share. The Commercial Court opened proceedings and ordered seizure of the company’s assets. After learning of the property sales, in December 2009 he amended his claim to seek reimbursement and invalidation of the sale contracts. In February 2010 the court allowed part of his claim, but the appellate court amended that decision in April 2010. In November 2010 the Higher Commercial Court quashed the lower decisions and remitted the case. On 29 December 2011, on fresh consideration, the Higher Commercial Court terminated the reimbursement claim because the issue had been examined in insolvency proceedings; the invalidity claim was rejected for lack of standing.

Separately, in October 2010 insolvency proceedings began against the company at the request of company P., imposing a moratorium on debt payments. The applicant filed a creditor’s claim in December 2010. In April 2011 the Commercial Court recognized him as a creditor for UAH 4,100,439 (about EUR 356,560), corresponding to his share. The insolvency proceedings were repeatedly suspended and resumed from 2011 to 2013. In February 2014 the company was declared insolvent, liquidation began, and D. was appointed liquidator. The court found the company had only two vehicles, whose location was unknown.

From July 2014 to April 2015 the Commercial Court did not operate because of armed conflict in eastern Ukraine; it resumed in Kharkiv. In July 2015 the insolvency case was reopened. In August 2015 the liquidator asked to be dismissed. Between October 2015 and September 2019, the creditors’ committee repeatedly failed to decide on his withdrawal, despite court orders to convene meetings and appoint a new liquidator. Attempts to find a new liquidator via the automatic system failed because candidates did not consent or did not reply. The liquidator reported that liquidation was suspended because of the conflict and his relocation. Hearings in October 2019 and April 2020 were adjourned due to non-attendance, with no resolution on the liquidator. In July 2019 the applicant’s wife was admitted as a creditor/heir.

The applicant also filed a criminal complaint in September 2011 against company officials. A fraud case was opened, closed in February 2014 for lack of corpus delicti, quashed in September 2016, and the investigation remained ongoing. These facts underpinned the complaints that the proceedings were excessively long, lacked an effective remedy, and prevented him from recovering his company share, thereby interfering with his possessions.

**Summary of Chernov v. Ukraine (App. No. 16432/10)**

*Chernov v. Ukraine* concerned the right not to be tried or punished twice, protected by Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Mr Oleksandr Gennadiyovych Chernov, a Ukrainian national living in Sumy, was arrested on 20 June 2007 for an administrative offence.

On 21 June 2007, the Zarichnyy District Court of Sumy found that at about 10 p.m. on 20 June 2007, while drunk on Prokofyeva Street in Sumy, Chernov had uttered obscenities, reacted aggressively to police officers’ remarks, cursed them in obscene language, attempted to start a fight, and thereby breached public order and offended human dignity and morals. He was convicted of “minor disorderly acts” under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced to three days’ administrative detention. That decision became final and was not subject to appeal. Chernov served the detention from 21 to 23 June 2007.

Despite this administrative punishment, the same facts later formed the basis of criminal proceedings. On 16 July 2007, a prosecutor opened a criminal case under Article 296 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine concerning disorderly acts committed on 20 June 2007. Chernov was eventually charged under Article 296 § 3 for hooliganism causing physical injuries to two victims, Mu. and P. On 28 January 2008, the prosecutor lodged an objection against the earlier administrative decision, arguing that under Article 9 of the Code of Administrative Offences, administrative liability applies only where the underlying facts do not give rise to criminal liability. The prosecutor stated that Chernov’s actions gave rise to criminal liability. On 6 February 2008, the same district court annulled its earlier administrative decision; that annulment was upheld on appeal on 25 February 2008.

Meanwhile, Chernov was arrested in December 2007 and indicted on 29 January 2008. On 14 July 2008, the Zarichnyy District Court convicted him under Article 296 § 3 and sentenced him to two years’ imprisonment. The court made no mention of the earlier administrative proceedings or his three-day detention. On 7 October 2008, the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction because of inconsistencies, including the time of the offence, and remitted the case. On 29 December 2008, the district court again convicted Chernov, finding that he had pulled Mu.’s gold neck chain, beaten him, and later damaged P.’s t-shirt, punched her in the face, and damaged her glasses. He was sentenced to two years and one month’s imprisonment. On 10 March 2009, the appellate court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years. On 24 September 2009, the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that decision. It rejected Chernov’s double-jeopardy complaint, reasoning that the administrative decision had been annulled and the administrative case “closed,” so he had not been tried twice for the same offence.

The applicant complained under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 that, after serving a three-day administrative sentence for minor disorderly acts, he was subsequently tried and convicted in criminal proceedings for disorderly acts based on the same facts. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that the administrative and criminal proceedings concerned the same applicant, same time and place, and the same underlying conduct. The prosecutor’s objection expressly linked the two by stating that the criminal case was opened “on the basis of these facts” and that the conduct gave rise to criminal rather than merely administrative liability. The applicant had already served the administrative detention before the administrative decision was annulled and before the criminal conviction. The domestic courts rejected his double-jeopardy claim because the administrative decision had been annulled. The Court gave notice only of the complaint under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

**Summary of Mugemangango v. Belgium (Application no. 310/15)**

The case concerned a post-election dispute in Belgium. The applicant, Germain Mugemangango, was the top candidate on the PTB-GO! list for the Charleroi constituency in the 25 May 2014 elections to the Walloon Parliament. His list received 16,554 votes—fourteen votes short of the 16,567.83 threshold required to qualify for the "related lists" (apparentement) system, which could have won him a seat. Separately, 21,385 ballot papers in Charleroi were declared blank, spoiled, or disputed.

The day after the elections, the applicant requested a recount from the main electoral board and the Hainaut central electoral board. Both refused, stating they lacked jurisdiction and referring him to the Walloon Parliament.

On 6 June 2014, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Walloon Parliament under section 31 of the Special Law of 8 August 1980, seeking re-examination of the 21,385 ballot papers and a recount of any valid votes wrongly declared void. He alleged numerous irregularities: counting station fatigue (some counts lasted over twelve hours without breaks); poor physical conditions; hurriedly set-up stations and insufficiently trained officers; ballot papers discovered days after the election with no record of whether they were counted; ballot design problems (boxes too small, red pencils not marking pink ballots clearly); and witnesses reporting that ballot papers with non-identifying marks were wrongly declared spoiled despite validly cast votes. He submitted witness accounts and press articles.

The Credentials Committee, chosen by drawing lots, heard the applicant and his lawyer publicly on 10 June 2014, then deliberated privately. Notably, two committee members who had stood in the same constituency as the applicant chose not to vote on his complaint, though they remained present during deliberations and the vote. One member was absent for part of the proceedings. The committee initially rejected a proposal to declare the complaint admissible but ill-founded (2-2), then after further deliberations found it admissible and well-founded (3-1), proposing that blank and spoiled ballots be checked and all Charleroi ballots recounted. The committee's accompanying note concluded that the distribution of seats could change if the 21,385 ballots were recounted and deemed valid, potentially affecting other Hainaut constituencies through the related lists system.

On 13 June 2014, the committee presented its findings at the plenary session. The Walloon Parliament rejected them by 43 votes to 32. All members voted, including those elected in the applicant's constituency. A motion to approve all credentials then passed 43-28 with four abstentions. The Parliament's reasoned decision stated that most grievances concerned inherent features of the electoral system; press articles were inadmissible evidence; witness statements should have been recorded officially at the time; the number of spoiled ballots was lower than in 2009; and handwritten annotations spoiled ballots under Article 157 of the Electoral Code. Some members were alarmed that ballots marked with non-red pencils were inconsistently declared spoiled, but no official record existed.

Belgian courts consistently declined jurisdiction over election disputes, vesting final authority in Parliament. The applicant complained of a lack of safeguards against arbitrariness and the absence of a remedy before an independent and impartial authority, relying on Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13 of the Convention.

Smbat Ayvazyan v. Armenia (no. 49021/08), an ECtHR judgment dated 8 October 2020, arose from Armenia’s disputed 19 February 2008 presidential election and the ensuing opposition protests. The applicant, a former MP, government minister and opposition party council member, supported Levon Ter-Petrosyan and actively participated in daily rallies and sit-ins at Freedom Square in Yerevan. He stayed overnight at Freedom Square on 23–24 February 2008.

On 24 February 2008, while driving home, the applicant was stopped, taken to the police anti-organised-crime unit, and allegedly searched. Police claimed an anonymous tip had reported armed passengers. A spring baton was allegedly found in his coat, and a Makarov-type pistol was later found in his car. The pistol was subsequently found by an expert to be ineffective and not a firearm. The applicant claimed the baton was planted and that he was coerced into admitting ownership by threats to prosecute his friends instead. He denied any illegal possession.

That evening he was taken for a drug test, which was negative. On returning to Kentron Police Station, three officers alleged that he disobeyed orders, pushed officer K.H., and punched him in the chest. The applicant denied any such incident, saying he merely stated that his arrest was unlawful. Relatives, friends, a lawyer and a journalist had gathered outside expecting his release. A forensic medical examination found no injuries on K.H.

On 25 February 2008, a criminal case was opened under Article 316 §1 of the Criminal Code for non-life-threatening assault on a public official. An arrest record was drawn up at 1:35 a.m. On 27 February the applicant was charged, and the District Court ordered his detention for two months, finding risks that he might reoffend, abscond or obstruct the investigation. The applicant argued that the detention was unsubstantiated and politically motivated.

After the violent clearance of Freedom Square on 1–2 March 2008 and the declaration of a state of emergency, criminal proceedings no. 62202608 were opened concerning mass disorder. On 11 March the applicant’s case was joined to that investigation. On 12 March he was prohibited from contact with the outside world. His detention was extended on 21 April and 20 June 2008, with the courts citing generic risks and the investigation into case no. 62202608. The investigator later admitted that no sufficient evidence implicated the applicant in that case. On 18 June his case was disjoined, and on 26 June he was additionally charged under Article 235 §4 for illegally carrying a cold weapon—the baton. The investigation ended on 7 July and the case went to trial.

At trial, police officers testified against him. The applicant denied guilt and sought to call defence witnesses, including relatives, supporters, a journalist and two detained friends, who could confirm that no incident occurred outside the police station. The court refused, finding their evidence unnecessary or the persons unidentified. He also sought to question police officers S.H. and A.H., but that request was postponed and never revisited. On 19 November 2008 he was convicted of assaulting officer K.H. and illegally carrying the baton, sentenced to two years’ imprisonment and a fine. Appeals were dismissed and the Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible. He was later amnestied.

The case concerned alleged violations of Article 5 §§1, 3 and 4 (unlawful initial detention, insufficient reasons for detention, and refusal to examine his detention appeal), Article 6 §§1 and 3(d) (unfair trial and inability to call and question witnesses), and Articles 10, 11 and 14 (prosecution and conviction allegedly targeting his political activism and participation in peaceful opposition demonstrations, and discrimination on political grounds).

In *Stavropoulos and Others v. Greece* (Application no. 52484/18), three Greek nationals—Nikolaos Stavropoulos, Ioanna Kravari, and Stavroula-Dorothea Stavropoulou—complained about an entry in a birth register. The first and second applicants were the parents of the third applicant, born in 2007. The family lived in Oxford, United Kingdom.

On 17 August 2007, the first applicant, authorised by the second, went to the Amarousio registry office to register their daughter’s birth. When the registrar entered the child’s forename, he added in parentheses an abbreviation of the Greek word for “naming” (*ονοματοδοσία*). The applicants objected to this notation. They argued that Greek law did not require registry offices to specify whether a child had been named by a civil or Christian act. In their view, the note implied that the child had not been christened, thereby revealing their religious beliefs and the child’s religious status. They alleged violations of their right to freedom of religion and of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, because the register allegedly disclosed sensitive personal data.

On 19 October 2007, the applicants applied to the Supreme Administrative Court for annulment of the birth registration insofar as it contained the note “naming.” They claimed the entry referred to the fact that their child had not been christened and exposed their religious beliefs. On 6 March 2018, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the application as inadmissible, finding that the applicants lacked legal interest. It relied on Articles 25 and 26 of Law no. 344/1976. The court held that a child’s first name could be registered only through “naming”—a declaration by the parents or guardians before the competent registry office—regardless of whether the child was later christened. The note “naming” merely repeated the title of Article 25 and was the only legal way of acquiring a name. It therefore could not be said to discriminate against the applicants or cause the alleged harm.

The relevant legal framework reinforced the distinction between civil naming and religious christening. Article 25 of Law no. 344/1976 provided that a newborn’s name is recorded in the birth registration act following a declaration by the parents exercising parental responsibility, or by a guardian. Article 26 provided that a christening is recorded separately in the side section of the birth act within ninety days, upon declaration by the officiating priest, and includes the date of christening and any name given to the child. State Legal Council opinion no. 431/2006 stated that if parents did not declare a name simultaneously with or before a christening declaration, they had to make a special naming declaration; merely noting the name during christening registration did not suffice for the child to acquire a first name. A Ministry of Interior circular similarly stated that a christening declaration could not be treated as a naming declaration unless it met Law no. 344/1976’s conditions.

The Greek Ombudsman, intervening, observed that the view that only non-christened children are “named,” or that christened children need not be named, was inconsistent with the law and effectively forced citizens to register a religion inadvertently. The Ombudsman’s 2006 report noted wider problems concerning religious freedom and the administration’s reluctance to embrace the State’s religious neutrality.

The applicants’ core complaint was that the registry notation “naming” amounted to an official record distinguishing civil naming from religious christening, disclosing that the child had not been christened and thereby revealing their religious beliefs in breach of Articles 9 and 8 ECHR. The domestic court’s rejection on standing grounds was the final domestic act before the Strasbourg application.

**Case: Al-Habeeb v. Denmark (Application no. 14171/23)**

The case concerns an Iraqi national, Mr Hamza Azeem Thamer Al-Habeeb, who complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that his expulsion from Denmark with a twelve-year re-entry ban disproportionately interfered with his private and family life.

The applicant entered Denmark in 1998 at the age of seven. In 1999 he was granted residence under section 7(2) of the Danish Aliens Act (subsidiary protection), and in 2002 he received permanent residence. He grew up in Denmark, attended Danish primary, secondary and commercial/technical schools, speaks fluent Danish, and worked for four years as an assistant social educator. His parents and siblings live in Denmark. In 2020 he married a Danish national in a Muslim ceremony, and in March 2021 their daughter, also a Danish national, was born. He has no relatives in Iraq, speaks broken Arabic, and does not read or write Arabic.

The applicant had previous convictions: in 2010, attempted robbery at age 17, sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment; in 2011, attempted aggravated violence, sentenced to three months’ imprisonment; and in 2019, repeated violence, sentenced to three months’ imprisonment, when he was warned of the risk of expulsion.

The index offence occurred on 26 July 2020. By judgment of the District Court of Roskilde on 28 September 2021, the applicant was convicted under Article 245 § 1, read with Article 247 § 1, of the Danish Penal Code of assault of a particularly offensive, brutal or dangerous nature. The court found that he, together with three masked co-offenders, had stabbed the victim five times in the back, groin and lung; one stab hit the victim’s right lung and could have been fatal without medical treatment. He was sentenced to two years and three months’ imprisonment. The court also ordered his expulsion from Denmark with a twelve-year re-entry ban.

In deciding on expulsion, the District Court considered his long lawful residence, permanent residence status, Danish family and social ties, and his possible EU-law derived right of residence through his Danish daughter. It found no relationship of dependency that would compel his daughter to leave the European Union if he were expelled. It accepted that his ties with Denmark were stronger than those with Iraq but found that the gravity of the stabbing, his prior violent offences, and the risk of future serious offences outweighed the considerations against expulsion. It also noted that his family could maintain contact through visits, telephone or online communication. The High Court of Eastern Denmark upheld the judgment on 19 May 2022, and the Appeals Permission Board refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court on 20 December 2022. The applicant was expelled to Iraq on 5 July 2022 and later moved to Sweden to live with his family; his wife became pregnant with their second child in August 2023.

Relevant to the alleged Article 8 violation was the twelve-year re-entry ban. Under Danish law, courts may reduce a normally permanent ban if a longer ban would certainly breach Denmark’s international obligations. Re-entry after a time-limited ban depends on obtaining a residence permit or visa. Iraq is in visa group 5, meaning high immigration risk, and visas are generally granted only in extraordinary circumstances. Statistics showed very few expelled persons obtained residence permits or visas. Danish courts generally do not consider future readmission prospects when imposing time-limited bans. The applicant’s complaint therefore concerns whether expulsion and the lengthy ban disproportionately interfered with his private and family life given his settled status, Danish family ties, and practical barriers to returning.

**Case: M.S. v. Slovakia and Ukraine (Application no. 17189/11), ECtHR, 11 June 2020**

The applicant was an Afghan national who alleged he was born in 1993 or 1994, making him a minor at the relevant time, while Slovak and Ukrainian authorities recorded his date of birth as 14 January 1992. He fled Afghanistan after his father, who had worked for the National Security Department, was killed in about 2005 by unknown persons possibly linked to the Taliban. In 2010 his uncle arranged for him to leave after receiving a threatening letter. Smugglers took him through Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Russia, and he entered Ukraine in July 2010. In September 2010 he crossed illegally into Slovakia with three other Afghan nationals and no identity papers.

On 23 September 2010 Slovak border police arrested him. He was interviewed that evening with Slovak-English interpretation and another Afghan translating into Pashto. The record noted his date of birth as 14 January 1992 and stated that he did not request asylum in Slovakia and wished to go to western Europe. The applicant alleged that he received no proper information about asylum or access to a lawyer, that his attempts to ask for asylum and say he was a minor were ignored, and that he never signed the interview record. On 24 September 2010 Slovakia issued an expulsion decision and a five-year entry ban, and handed him over to Ukraine.

In Ukraine he was detained at the Chop Border Guard temporary holding facility. He alleged overcrowded conditions and restricted exercise, and claimed he told a guard and a Caritas NGO representative that he was fourteen and wanted asylum, but no action was taken. Ukrainian authorities ordered him to leave voluntarily and then sought forcible expulsion and detention. On 13 October 2010 a court ordered his expulsion and detention pending expulsion. **Project-Trade d.o.o. v. Croatia** (Application no. 1920/14) concerned a Croatian limited liability company that held 1,251 shares in Croatia Bank d.d., a privately owned joint-stock bank. In 1999 the Croatian National Bank (CNB) appointed a temporary administrator at the bank after finding large risky investments, potential losses, disputed claims and operating losses. On 18 June 1999 the CNB proposed recovery and restructuring. On 23 September 1999 the Croatian Government adopted the Decision on the recovery and restructuring of Croatia Bank, published on 27 September 1999.

The Government Decision had severe effects on shareholders. Point VII revoked and cancelled all existing shares of the bank; new shares were to be issued and owned entirely by the State Agency for Deposit Insurance and Bank Resolution (DAB). Point VIII extinguished the powers of the bank’s governing bodies and the rights of shareholders based on the existing shares. The applicant company therefore lost its shareholding without compensation. The restructuring process was completed in September 2000.

Several shareholders challenged the Government Decision before the Constitutional Court in 1999–2000, but the applicant company was not among them. In 2003 the Constitutional Court discontinued those proceedings because the 1994 Recovery and Restructuring of Banks Act, on which the Decision was based, had been repealed. It nevertheless noted that the Decision, although subordinate legislation, directly interfered with individual rights. It stated that former shareholders could seek protection in civil proceedings under the Obligations Act and the Courts Act and could ultimately lodge a constitutional complaint. Two dissenting judges disagreed, saying there was no effective remedy and that the Decision was unconstitutional.
