**Summary of the Case of Albertina Carvalho e Filhos Lda v. Portugal**

The case of *Albertina Carvalho e Filhos Lda v. Portugal* (Application no. 23603/14) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 March 2014. The applicant, a Portuguese company headquartered in Valongo, alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically concerning the excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy to address this delay.

The underlying facts pertain to enforcement proceedings initiated by the applicant company on 18 July 2005 against a debtor identified as M.C. The company sought to recover a debt of EUR 32,992.99 plus EUR 18,413.35 in accrued interest, totaling EUR 51,406, along with continuing interest until full repayment.

A judicial enforcement officer was appointed by the Valongo Court on 12 October 2005, accepting the role the following day. The debtor was summoned on 20 November 2005 and subsequently lodged an opposition to enforcement on 14 December 2005, which was joined to the main enforcement proceedings. The applicant replied to this opposition on 30 May 2006.

A significant period of procedural activity, marked by delays, followed. Between February 2007 and August 2008, steps were taken regarding the potential freezing of the debtor's bank accounts. Meanwhile, in the opposition proceedings, a preparatory decision was issued on 22 February 2008. A notable disruption occurred when the applicant's lawyer withdrew on 29 November 2010, and by January 2011, the court could not contact the applicant at its provided address.

In December 2011, a hearing in the opposition proceedings was scheduled for May 2012, but was postponed multiple times—first to November 2012 due to the illness of the debtor's lawyer, and finally held on 6 March 2013. Concurrently, the enforcement proceedings faced administrative hurdles. For reasons not specified, a new judicial enforcement officer was appointed on 3 January 2012. The transition between officers proved inefficient, with discussions regarding the transmission of case documents lasting from September to December 2012. Further correspondence between the new officer and the court about the applicant's legal representation occurred between April and October 2013.

A first-instance decision against the applicant in the opposition proceedings was rendered on 29 April 2013. The applicant appealed to the Oporto Court of Appeal, which upheld the decision on 20 May 2014. A subsequent appeal to the Supreme Court of Justice was rejected on 11 September 2014 by the Oporto Court of Appeal due to a failure to submit grounds of appeal. This final decision terminated the enforcement proceedings, concluding a process that had lasted over nine years.

The applicant company complained that the duration of these civil proceedings was excessive, violating the "reasonable time" requirement. It further argued that Portuguese law did not provide an effective remedy to challenge this delay. The case was communicated to the Portuguese Government on 18 November 2015, focusing on these two complaints, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

CASE OF GIANNAKOPOULOS v. GREECE (Application no. 20503/20) concerns an Article 8 complaint by Mr Georgios Giannakopoulos, a Greek national, that the Greek courts refused to examine his custody application after his children were taken to Germany by their mother. The applicant married E.B., a German national, in 2009; they lived in Rhodes and had two children, born in 2010 and 2012. After separating, E.B. applied for interim custody in Greece. In decision no. 590/2013 of 18 October 2013, the Rhodes One-Member Court of First Instance granted her custody, set the applicant’s contact schedule, and noted there was no evidence she would leave for Germany. E.B. had assured the court that she would remain in Rhodes with the children.

In December 2013, E.B. travelled with the children to Germany for a Christmas visit, saying she would return by 13 January 2014. She did not return and settled permanently in Germany. The applicant served the Greek decision on the German authorities in July 2014. In January 2015, the Greek court granted him interim custody in decision no. 26/2015, finding a substantive change of circumstances: E.B. had misled the court, moved to Germany, and obstructed his contact rights. The applicant also obtained enforceability certificates for that decision.

On 29 January 2015, the applicant sought sole custody of the children in Greece. The Greek courts declined jurisdiction. They found that, by the time he applied, the children were habitually resident in Germany. They had lived there for over a year, attended nursery or school, adapted well, spoke German, and had family and social ties there. The mother, who had sole custody, could determine their place of residence. The Dodecanese Court of Appeal (decision no. 302/2017) and the Court of Cassation (decision no. 927/2019) upheld that conclusion. They held that Article 10 of the Brussels II bis Regulation on child abduction did not apply because the mother had sole custody and there had been no wrongful removal. Article 12 on prorogation did not apply because E.B. had not accepted Greek jurisdiction.

The applicant argued that the Greek courts had wrongly ignored several key matters: that the children’s removal breached his contact rights under decision no. 590/2013; that E.B. had misled the Greek court to obtain custody; that decision no. 26/2015 had later granted him interim custody; that German courts had rejected the mother’s request to disregard that decision and had initially suspended proceedings pending the Greek courts’ clarification of jurisdiction; and that the children’s stay in Germany had not been long enough to establish habitual residence.

In parallel German proceedings, the Düsseldorf District Court ordered the children’s return to Greece in June 2015, but the Düsseldorf Court of Appeal reversed that decision in November 2015. It found that the Hague Convention return application had been lodged after the one-year period and that the children were settled in Germany. A constitutional complaint was dismissed. German custody proceedings were initially suspended pending the Greek courts’ jurisdiction decision; after the Court of Cassation ruling, a German court granted parental responsibility to E.B. in October 2021. Separately, a Greek misdemeanour court convicted E.B. in 2018 for breaching decisions nos. 590/2013 and 26/2015 between December 2013 and March 2015.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8 that the Greek courts’ rejection of his custody application for lack of jurisdiction violated his right to respect for family life. He alleged misinterpretation of the Brussels II bis Regulation, an erroneous finding that the children were habitually resident in Germany, and disregard of the wrongful removal, his contact and custody rights, and the related German proceedings.

In *Avto Atom Doo Kochani v. North Macedonia* (Application no. 21954/16), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 28 May 2020. The applicant, Avto Atom Doo Kochani, was a limited-liability passenger transport company registered in Kochani, North Macedonia. It was registered for VAT and regularly declared VAT on outgoing invoices. It also declared VAT on incoming invoices, allowing it to deduct input VAT from its periodic VAT obligations.

The dispute arose from the applicant’s VAT deductions for 2004 and 2005. One of its suppliers, a petrol station, issued invoices that showed a tax number and expressly charged VAT. The applicant paid those invoices in full and claimed the corresponding input VAT deductions. In March–April 2007, the Internal Revenue Office audited the applicant’s VAT obligations for 2004–2005. The audit found that the petrol station supplier had not been registered for VAT. On 2 May 2007, relying on that finding, the IRO issued a payment order imposing additional VAT of MKD 3,266,792. The IRO considered that the VAT deducted on the basis of the supplier’s invoices had been unlawful.

The applicant contested the payment order but paid the amount in several instalments during 2007 and 2008. Its administrative claim was ultimately dismissed by the Administrative Court on 28 January 2015, after two remittals. The Administrative Court held that the applicant was not entitled to the deduction because the supplier had not been VAT-registered, and it treated as irrelevant the fact that VAT had been declared on the supplier’s invoices. The Higher Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 20 October 2015, endorsing the same reasoning.

Additional facts were relevant. The supplier had been founded on 19 August 2003 and was struck off the companies list on 30 June 2006. Its founder and sole owner was convicted on 25 December 2009 of failing to register for VAT (tax evasion) and received a suspended prison sentence. He paid a tax debt of MKD 595,470 (about EUR 9,650). The supplier itself was not prosecuted because it had been liquidated.

Under the applicable domestic VAT Act, sections 33 and 34 governed deductions, and section 55 provided that an entity which declared VAT on an invoice despite not being registered for VAT owed the declared amount. The Court had previously summarised the relevant law in *Euromak Metal Doo v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (no. 68039/14, 14 June 2018).

The applicant company complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property). It alleged that the State’s additional VAT demand and the domestic courts’ refusal to allow the input VAT deduction amounted to an unjustified interference with its possessions. The key factual issue was that the applicant had relied on invoices that appeared VAT-compliant, had paid the supplier in full, and had otherwise complied with its VAT obligations, yet was required to bear the VAT burden after the supplier was found to be unregistered. On 21 February 2018, the Court gave notice of the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected. The case thus focused on whether the refusal of the VAT deduction imposed a disproportionate burden on the applicant.

Levchuk v. Ukraine (Application no. 17496/19), judgment of 3 September 2020, concerns Ms Iryna Levchuk, a disabled Ukrainian woman living in Rivne. She alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention arising from the dismissal of her civil eviction claim against her ex-husband, O.L., who had repeatedly subjected her and their minor children to psychological and physical violence.

In 2006 the applicant married O.L.; they lived in a flat co-owned by O.L. and his mother. They had triplets in 2007, and in 2008 Rivne City Council provided the family with social housing as protected tenants. According to the applicant, O.L. abused alcohol, harassed, threatened and physically assaulted her, often in the children’s presence. In 2009 a forensic report certified a broken nose and eye haemorrhages; in 2011 police refused criminal proceedings for an assault. In 2015 she reported O.L. kicking her; criminal proceedings under Article 125 were opened but later closed after she withdrew her complaint. She also reported child-support arrears and repeated harassment. In 2016 police issued warnings, and O.L. was charged with administrative domestic violence under Article 173-2 for insulting and threatening her and piercing a blanket with a knife. A family welfare assessment found the children were distressed by their father’s drunken arguments and neglect; school staff described psychological ill-treatment. In April 2016 she reported another violent outburst, and medical evidence showed haemorrhages and a foot sprain. In July 2016 a court found O.L. administratively guilty of domestic violence but relieved him of liability with an oral reprimand because the applicant requested this and the parties allegedly resolved their differences.

In June 2016 the applicant sued to evict O.L. under Article 116 of the Housing Code, arguing that living with him was impossible because he systematically abused alcohol, mistreated, threatened and harassed her and the children, creating constant risk of psychological and physical violence. She submitted medical certificates, police complaints, administrative and criminal proceedings, and evidence of child-support arrears. In April 2017 the Rivne Town Court allowed eviction, finding O.L. abused alcohol, caused scenes, intimidated the applicant in front of the children, threatened violence, and that earlier corrective measures had failed. The Rivne Regional Court of Appeal reversed in June 2017 and dismissed the claim. It found hostile relations between the former spouses but no proof that O.L. systematically breached living rules or that authorities had applied corrective measures; complaints alone, it said, did not justify the “extreme” measure of eviction. It merely warned O.L. to change his attitude. The Supreme Court upheld that decision in August 2018. The applicant and O.L. later became co-owners of the flat and still share it. In December 2019 she filed a fresh criminal complaint, and in November 2019 she began proceedings to deprive O.L. of parental rights.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged that the dismissal of her eviction claim breached Article 8 by failing to protect her private and family life from domestic violence, Article 6 by denying a fair hearing, and Article 13 by leaving her without an effective remedy. The key facts centre on the documented pattern of domestic violence, the authorities’ repeated inadequate responses, and the domestic courts’ refusal to remove the abusive ex-husband from the shared home despite prior findings against him.

**Dmytrenko and Bezdorozhniy v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 59552/11 and 7096/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning Ukraine’s alleged failure to pay a pension supplement to two Ukrainian nationals. The applicants, Mykola Dmytrenko and Mykhaylo Bezdorozhniy, both held the special status of “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act in force as of 1 January 2006. Under Article 6 of that Act, they were entitled to a special pension supplement amounting to 30% of the minimum pension.

The first applicant, born in 1943, lives in Donetsk. The second applicant, born in 1936, died in 2015. His son and heir later informed the Court of his death and expressed a wish to pursue the application. The applications were lodged with the Court on 12 September 2011 and 29 January 2012.

The applicants brought domestic court proceedings against the Pension Fund of Ukraine, claiming the pension supplement for the period between 2 April and 31 December 2006. Their claims were rejected by final decisions in 2011. The Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine, on 13 May 2011, and the Donetsk Administrative Court of Appeal, on 18 August 2011, found that amendments to the State Budget Act 2006 had, with effect from 2 April 2006, required the supplement to be introduced gradually during 2006 according to a procedure to be established by the Cabinet of Ministers. Because no such procedure had been adopted in 2006, the domestic courts concluded that there was no legal basis for allowing the claims.

Separately, the second applicant had obtained a judgment from the Kuybyshevskyy District Court of Donetsk on 31 December 2010. That court ordered the Pension Fund to calculate and pay him the pension supplement for the periods between 9 July and 31 December 2007 and between 22 May 2008 and 31 December 2010. The judgment became final on 18 August 2011 but remained unenforced.

Before the European Court, the Government were represented by their Agent, Mr I. Lishchyna. The Court decided to give notice to the Ukrainian Government only of the applicants’ complaints under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning the State’s failure to pay the pension supplement for the period between 2 April and 31 December 2006. The remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

The core alleged violation is therefore that, despite the applicants’ statutory entitlement as “children of war” to a 30% pension supplement, they did not receive that supplement for the relevant 2006 period because the domestic authorities had not adopted the required implementing procedure, and the domestic courts refused their claims. This, the applicants argued, amounted to an unjustified interference with their possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case was heard by the Fifth Section Committee, composed of Judges Mits, Yudkivska and Hüseynov, with Anne-Marie Dougin as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. Judgment was delivered on 2 July 2020. The relevant domestic law and practice were summarized by reference to *Sukhanov and Ilchenko v. Ukraine*.

**Summary of Arkania v. Georgia (Application no. 2625/12)**

The case of *Arkania v. Georgia* concerns an application lodged by Mr. Lasha Arkania, a Georgian national, against Georgia under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment) and Article 5 (right to liberty and security) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he was ill-treated by police during an unrecorded detention lasting four to five hours and that the subsequent investigation into his ill-treatment was ineffective.

The key facts are as follows: According to official records, the applicant was arrested at 3 a.m. on 15 June 2011 in the village of Muzhava on suspicion of unlawful possession of firearms and drugs. A search revealed a Kalashnikov rifle, cartridges, and a greyish substance. The detention report noted multiple scratches on his face and head, which the applicant claimed to have sustained prior to his arrest. Between 4:55 and 5:25 a.m., while questioned without a lawyer at the Jvari police department, the applicant confessed to the charges.

However, the applicant presented a different account. He claimed he was actually arrested on 14 June 2011 around 10 p.m. by plain-clothes officers while going to meet an acquaintance. He alleged he was forced into a car, taken to an abandoned factory in Tchale, and severely beaten with a rifle butt. He stated the ill-treatment continued at the Jvari police department, where he was threatened with rape, lost consciousness, and was subjected to beatings in the presence of investigator I.A. He further alleged that psychological pressure, including threats against his family, forced him to sign a self-incriminating statement.

Medical evidence supported the applicant's claims of injury. Upon admission to a temporary detention centre in Zugdidi on 15 June 2011, bruises, reddish spots on his back and behind his ears, and a haematoma on his left eye were documented. On 16 June, an emergency doctor diagnosed a post-concussion condition. Later forensic examinations in August 2011 found multiple haematomas and minor scars, as well as four red scars under his left armpit and two under his right, which the applicant claimed were cigarette burns inflicted by police. Comprehensive medical examinations also diagnosed post-concussion syndrome and post-traumatic stress disorder.

The applicant consistently raised his ill-treatment allegations with prosecutors, courts, and the Public Defender’s Office. He identified specific officers involved and requested identification parades. Despite this, the domestic courts failed to examine his allegations when ordering his pre-trial detention or during his trial, where he was convicted and sentenced to thirteen years’ imprisonment.

An investigation into the alleged torture was opened on 17 August 2011. During this investigation, several police officers corroborated the applicant's version of events, testifying that he was brought to the Jvari police department with visible injuries and was beaten by officers. The applicant also identified multiple officers in photo identification procedures. However, the investigation was marred by delays and failures. Key requests from the applicant’s lawyer, such as organizing identification procedures and questioning witnesses, were dismissed. The applicant was only granted victim status in May 2013, nearly two years after the investigation began. The proceedings remained ongoing at the time of the European Court’s judgment.

The applicant was released from prison on 16 January 2013 under an amnesty. He complained to the European Court that his ill-treatment during the unrecorded detention and the authorities’ failure to conduct an effective investigation violated Article 3 of the Convention.

In *Shebaldina v. Ukraine* (Application no. 75792/11), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Ms Alla Petrivna Shebaldina, a Ukrainian national born in 1959 and living in Bilgorod-Dnistrovskyy, Odessa Region. The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the domestic courts refused to award her a social allowance to which she was entitled under domestic law. She also raised a related complaint under Article 13 of the Convention. The Court gave notice of those complaints to the Ukrainian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

From 1988 until 2006 the applicant worked as a teacher in a State specialised child-care centre. Under Article 57 of the 1991 Education Act, as in force at the material time, she was entitled to seniority and recreation allowances. However, between 1997 and 2002 she did not receive those allowances. On 3 December 2007 she lodged a claim with the domestic courts against the centre and the regional department of the State Treasury. She sought arrears of UAH 2,244.30, an index-linked adjustment of UAH 4,336.17, compensation for non-pecuniary damage of UAH 10,000, and costs and expenses of UAH 1,484.

On 28 October 2010 the Bilgorod-Dnistrovskyy Town Court partly allowed the claim. It found that the applicant was entitled to the seniority and recreation allowances and that the centre was in arrears. It ordered the centre to pay her UAH 2,244.30 in arrears, UAH 4,336.17 as an index-linked adjustment, and UAH 1,400 in legal costs. The court dismissed her claim for non-pecuniary damage. It reasoned that the centre’s failure to pay had resulted from a lack of State budget funding, and that the centre could therefore claim reimbursement from the State budget.

On 29 April 2011 the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal quashed that judgment and dismissed the applicant’s claim. It found that the applicant had worked in the centre, which had dual status as a healthcare and educational institution, and that in 1997–2002 she had not received allowances due under Article 57, with arrears of UAH 2,244.30. However, under the 2004 Act on the Restructuring of Indebtedness under Article 57 of the Education Act, payments for that period were recognised as a debt to be paid by the State from the State budget. The arrears therefore constituted a State budget debt, not a debt of the centre, which had not received the relevant funds. The regional department of the State Treasury was not a proper defendant. The court also dismissed the index-linking and non-pecuniary damage claims because the 2004 Act did not provide for them. On 21 July 2011 the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court declined to examine the merits of the applicant’s cassation appeal.

The applicant submitted domestic case-law showing that the Court of Appeal had previously upheld claims by two other employees of the same centre for recovery of Article 57 allowances for 1997–2003, holding that payment was not conditional on the availability of State budget funds. The key alleged violation was therefore that, despite recognising her statutory entitlement, the domestic courts ultimately denied her the allowance and left her without payment. The Article 13 complaint concerned the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy for that breach.

In *Walczak v. Poland* (Application no. 45564/15, judgment 9 July 2020), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 8 ECHR by Damian Walczak, a Polish national. He alleged that during his pre-trial detention he was deprived of personal contact with his wife for a significant period.

Walczak was arrested on 16 December 2014 and charged with serious offences, including membership and leadership of an organised criminal group, armed robbery, extortion, severe beating, deprivation of liberty, and recidivism. He was remanded in custody by the Poznań-Nowe Miasto District Court until 16 March 2015. The Poznań Regional Court later prolonged detention until 16 June and then until 16 September 2015.

His wife, M.W., repeatedly asked to visit him. On 30 December 2014 she applied for permission. On 5 January 2015 the prosecutor refused because she was a witness in the proceedings. Requests on 26 February and 17 March 2015 were refused on 27 February and 24 March, again because evidence was needed from her. Neither the applicant nor M.W. appealed. On 3 April 2015 M.W. refused to testify and immediately reapplied to visit. On 7 April the prosecutor refused, saying she could still be asked to testify during the ongoing investigation. No appeal was lodged. A request on 27 May was refused on 5 June, again without appeal. On 10 June M.W. applied again; on 15 June the prosecutor refused, stating that a visit could impede proceedings because she knew other witnesses and had access to the applicant’s computer. The applicant appealed, but on 28 August 2015 the Poznań Regional Prosecutor dismissed the appeal. Further applications in June and July, and the applicant’s own request of 29 June 2015, were also refused.

On 27 August 2015 the prosecutor allowed M.W. to visit; the visit took place on 30 August 2015. On 3 September 2015 an indictment was lodged. On 10 September the Poznań Regional Court refused M.W.’s visit application because she remained a witness. On 24 September the court dismissed her appeal, reasoning that she could change her mind about testifying, the trial had not begun, and the prosecutor’s earlier decisions allowing visits could not be assessed by the court. On 2 October 2015, after M.W. stated she would rely on her right to refuse to testify, the court allowed her to visit; she visited on 11 October 2015. Later requests were granted. M.W. was not ultimately asked to testify at later hearings. Walczak was released from detention on 4 February 2016.

In *Filozofenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 72954/11), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint brought by Ms Lina Alekseyevna Filozofenko, a Ukrainian national born in 1938 and living in the Odessa Region. The applicant lodged her application on 18 November 2011. Her sole complaint before the Court was under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, alleging that the State had failed to pay a supplement to her pension. On 11 July 2018, the Court gave notice of that complaint to the Ukrainian Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The factual background concerns the applicant’s special status as a “child of war” under the Children of War Social Protection Act in force from 1 January 2006 (“the 2006 Act”). Section 6 of that Act entitled her to a special supplement to her pension equal to 30% of the minimum pension. The alleged violation therefore centred on the non-payment of that statutory pension supplement.

On 11 December 2008, the applicant brought a claim against the State Pension Fund in the domestic courts, asking them to recalculate her pension under section 6 of the 2006 Act for 2006–2008 and to pay the outstanding debt. On 10 June 2009, the Odessa Circuit Administrative Court partly allowed the claim. It held that in 2006 section 6 of the 2006 Act had been suspended by the State Budget Act 2006. Although amendments to the Budget Act, in force from 1 April 2006, empowered the Cabinet of Ministers to establish a mechanism for a pension increase, no such mechanism had been introduced in 2006. Consequently, the applicant’s claims relating to 2006 were rejected. As for 2007 and 2008, the court noted that section 6 had been suspended and modified respectively by the 2007 and 2008 State Budget Acts. However, the Constitutional Court had declared that suspension and modification unconstitutional on 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008. The first-instance court therefore held that the State Pension Fund should recalculate the applicant’s pension, but only for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008.

On 1 November 2010, the Odessa Regional Administrative Court of Appeal partly amended that judgment. It upheld the rejection of the applicant’s claims for 2006. It also upheld her right to a pension increase for the periods from 9 July to 31 December 2007 and from 22 May to 31 December 2008. However, because the applicant had missed a one-year statutory limitation period, the appellate court held that the 2007 claim could be allowed only for the period from 11 to 31 December 2007. On 18 May 2011, the Higher Administrative Court upheld that judgment, making the domestic proceedings final.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that the applicant had a legal entitlement to a pension supplement under the 2006 Act, that the domestic courts recognised that entitlement only for limited periods, and that the applicant nevertheless complained to the Strasbourg Court that the State failed to pay the supplement. The case thus concerned the State’s compliance with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 in the context of pension payments and the enforcement of domestic court

**Case of Lopata and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 84210/17 and 23 others) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, with judgment delivered on 10 December 2020. The Committee was composed of Judges Ivana Jelić (President), Ganna Yudkivska and Arnfinn Bårdsen, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The case originated in 24 applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates between 2017 and 2019. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications.

The applicants are Ukrainian nationals, born between 1956 and 1984, all serving life sentences imposed by Ukrainian courts between 1996 and 2017. The appended table shows that each applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment by different trial courts, mostly regional courts or courts of appeal. For example, Stepan Lopata was sentenced by the Cherkasy Regional Court of Appeal on 12 December 2006; Volodymyr Bala by the Chernihiv Regional Court of Appeal on 8 August 2003, upheld by the Supreme Court of Ukraine on 18 November 2003; Oleksiy Romanenko by the Kherson Regional Court on 19 September 1997; Nikolay Sili by the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal on 28 March 2007; and Sergey Khukalenko by the Sumy Court of Appeal on 23 June 2005. Other applicants received life sentences from courts in Lviv, Crimea, Kyiv, Ternopil, Odesa, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhya, Kharkiv, Luhansk and Khmelnytsk. In several cases, the convictions were upheld by the Supreme Court of Ukraine or higher courts, making the sentences final. The applicants therefore remained in detention serving life imprisonment.

The central alleged violation concerns Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The applicants complained that their life sentence had no prospect of release. In other words, they alleged that Ukrainian law and practice did not provide a real possibility of review, parole, commutation or release, leaving them subject to an irreducible life sentence. Under the Court’s case law, a life sentence is not automatically incompatible with Article 3, but it must be reducible both in law and in practice. There must be a mechanism allowing the continued detention of a life prisoner to be reviewed after a certain period to assess whether penological grounds still justify it. The applicants claimed that the absence of such a mechanism in Ukraine, or its purely discretionary nature, caused them ongoing mental suffering and a sense of hopelessness, amounting to inhuman or degrading treatment. Some applicants also raised other complaints under other provisions of the Convention.

The case therefore focuses on a systemic issue affecting life prisoners in Ukraine: whether a life sentence with no meaningful prospect of release violates Article 3. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are not the underlying criminal convictions themselves, but the nature of the life

The case of Makuchyan and Minasyan v. Azerbaijan and Hungary (Application no. 17247/13) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by two Armenian nationals: Mr Hayk Makuchyan, a member of the Armenian military, and Mr Samvel Minasyan, uncle of the deceased G.M., a lieutenant in the Armenian army. The case concerned the brutal murder of G.M. and the attempted murder of the first applicant by an Azerbaijani military officer, R.S., and the subsequent pardon and glorification of the perpetrator.

In January 2004, the first applicant and G.M. arrived in Budapest, Hungary, to participate in a three-month English language course under NATO's "Partnership for Peace" programme. Participants included two officers from the Azerbaijani army, one of whom was R.S. On 19 February 2004, at around 5 a.m., R.S. murdered G.M. while he slept by decapitating him with at least twelve blows of an axe. R.S. then attempted to break down the first applicant's door, allegedly yelling "Open the door, you Armenian! We will cut the throats of all of you!" He was stopped by police.

During questioning, R.S. admitted he strongly disliked Armenians due to losing relatives in the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and that he had decided to kill the Armenian participants on the anniversary of the conflict's beginning. He bought an axe and sharpening stone two days prior. He admitted murdering G.M. on account of his Armenian origin and showed no remorse.

On 13 April 2006, the Budapest High Court found R.S. guilty of exceptionally cruel and premeditated murder of G.M. and preparation of the murder of the first applicant. The court concluded the crimes were committed with vile motives and exclusively because of the Armenian nationality of the victims. R.S. was sentenced to life imprisonment with possibility of conditional release after thirty years. This was upheld on appeal in February 2007.

In 2012, Azerbaijan requested R.S.'s transfer under the Council of Europe Convention on the Transfer of Sentenced Persons. Azerbaijan's Ministry of Justice assured Hungary that enforcement would continue without conversion of the sentence and that a life sentence could only be released on parole after at least twenty-five years. On 17 August 2012, Hungary agreed to the transfer. On 31 August 2012, R.S. was transferred to Azerbaijan and immediately released on a presidential pardon issued the same day.

Following his release, R.S. was promoted to major, provided with a state-owned flat, and awarded salary arrears. Numerous Azerbaijani officials and public figures made statements glorifying R.S. and his actions, with some describing him as a patriotic role model for Azerbaijani youth.

The applicants alleged that Azerbaijan violated Article 2 of the Convention by granting the presidential pardon, and Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 2 because the Armenian ethnic origin of the victims was the main reason for the murder and subsequent actions, including the pardon and glorification of the perpetrator. They also complained that Hungary violated Article 2 by granting the transfer request without obtaining adequate binding assurances that R.S. would be required to complete his prison sentence in Azerbaijan.

In *Minyaylo and Others v. Ukraine*, three Ukrainian nationals complained to the European Court of Human Rights that police had ill-treated them and that domestic authorities had failed to investigate their complaints effectively. They also raised other complaints under Articles 5 §§ 1 and 5 and 6 § 1 of the Convention.

**Mr Minyaylo** alleged ill-treatment between 13 and 15 February 2005 at Mukacheve and Lviv railway police stations. He claimed officers hit him on the head and torso with water-filled plastic bottles, punched and kicked him, made him lie undressed on the floor, handcuffed his left foot to his right hand, and twisted his arms behind his back to force him to confess to stealing from train passengers. At Lviv, he was allegedly handcuffed to a radiator for hours without food or drink. Medical evidence included ambulance reports for hypertensive crises, a detention-facility certificate recording no injuries on arrival, and a later SIZO certificate noting abrasions on his left calf, right knee, and chin. A forensic report described the injuries as minor but could not establish their timing. He had been arrested on 12 February 2005 on suspicion of robbery, questioned without a lawyer, transferred to Lviv SIZO on 15 February, and gave self-incriminating statements before being remanded. He complained on 18 February 2005. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings; several decisions were quashed, and the courts ultimately found his ill-treatment complaint without merit. The authorities concluded he had not been ill-treated and that any minor injuries could have occurred during arrest.

**Mr Kindra** alleged that on 23 August 2008 plain-clothes police officers asked him into their car, handcuffed him, and took him to Krasnoarmiysk city police station. There, officers allegedly demanded that he confess to arson together with his son, repeatedly punched and kicked him for over an hour—including in his son’s presence—and denied him access to a lawyer. He was released after his son confessed. Hospital records the next day showed a displaced left cheekbone fracture, hematomas around the left eye, and haemorrhage; he underwent surgery and inpatient treatment until 15 September 2008. A forensic report classified the injuries as intermediately serious, with timing possibly consistent with his account. He complained on 24 August 2008. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open proceedings, but those decisions were quashed. Criminal proceedings began in January 2011 and were suspended in December 2011 because no perpetrator was identified. The investigation was marked by limited notification to the applicant.

**Mr Kharchenko** alleged that on 5 January 2010 Kremenchuk district police officers forced him to confess to theft, punched and kicked him, handcuffed him to a chair, and electrocuted his thighs with a black device containing two electrodes. A forensic report found multiple small burn marks on both thighs, classified as minor and possibly dating to 5 January. Later reports considered electric current a probable cause and cigarette or match contact improbable, though a stun-gun model stocked by Kremenchuk police was not considered probable. He was questioned without a lawyer and gave self-incriminating statements later retracted. He complained on 6 January 2010. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to institute proceedings; those decisions were quashed. An internal review found irregularities, including that his presence at the police station was undocumented. Criminal proceedings for police misconduct were opened in March 2013, closed and reopened several times, and finally closed in December 2013 for lack of evidence. The authorities concluded the origin of his injuries could not be established and that they could possibly have been self-inflicted.

The case thus centres on alleged police ill-treatment and allegedly ineffective domestic investigations under Article 3, along with additional Article 5 and Article 6 complaints.

**Case Summary: Aggerholm v. Denmark (Application no. 45439/18)**

The case concerns an Article 3 complaint by Mr Niels Lund Aggerholm, a Danish national suffering from paranoid schizophrenia. In 2005 he was convicted of five incidents of violence and threats against a civil servant and was sentenced to committal to a psychiatric hospital. From 2007 to 2011 he was held in a high-security psychiatric unit under a “dangerousness decree.” He was later treated in an open ward but was moved to a closed ward, P4, in September 2012 due to irritability and threatening behaviour. On 3 January 2013 he was restrained, but that measure is not the subject of the Court’s case.

The alleged violation concerns an incident on 8 February 2013. At 1:15 p.m. the applicant was strapped to a restraint bed with a belt and wrist and ankle straps—a five-point restraint—and remained restrained until 9 February 2013 at 12:05 p.m., approximately 22 hours and 50 minutes. He complained that this breached Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant appealed both restraint incidents to the Psychiatric Patients’ Complaints Board. The chief physician who ordered the measures, H.H., submitted a brief written statement but could not attend due to illness. On 21 March 2013 the Board found both measures unlawful. As to 8 February, it noted that the applicant did not want to participate in a medical consultation and was described as very angry, but concluded that it had not been documented that he exposed himself or others to an immediate risk of harm to body or health.

H.H. later told the Health Authority that she decided to restrain the applicant because he had a lot of pent-up anger after she revoked his day release, and she wanted to act before anyone was hurt. She acknowledged that the Board had declared the decision unlawful. The Health Authority found no lack of care or conscientiousness.

Daily records showed that on 7 February the applicant was frustrated and angry, and made remarks about H.H. that staff interpreted as threats, including “We have to do something about her.” After speaking with a doctor, he appeared calm. On 8 February, H.H. recorded that his day release was revoked, that he refused to sit or talk, was white-faced and showed pent-up anger, and after about 1.5 hours remained extremely angry and was considered dangerous. He came to the belt room voluntarily and was restrained. During the restraint, a social and healthcare assistant was constantly present, and doctors checked on him four times. One foot strap was released at 6:55 p.m., toilet visits were allowed, and at 10:46 p.m. he was still considered potentially dangerous. The next morning he was cooperative and was released at 12:05 p.m.

The applicant sought compensation and acknowledgment of an Article 3 violation. The City Court consulted the Medico-Legal Council, which found that the conditions for restraint were present, that it was necessary to avoid an immediate risk to others, that medical assessments were sufficiently frequent, and that the chief physician’s assessment was justified. The City Court dismissed the claim, finding the restraint and its duration necessary and less intrusive measures impossible. The High Court affirmed as regards the 8 February measure, finding no reason to overrule the chief physician and that sufficient evaluations had been made. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal.

Under the Mental Health Act, compulsory restraint may be used only when necessary to prevent an imminent risk of harm to body or health; it must be proportionate and least intrusive; a doctor must decide, the chief physician must approve straps, constant watch is required, and medical review must occur at least four times every 24 hours. The key factual tension is that the Complaints Board found no documented immediate danger, while later medical and court reviews found the restraint justified. The Court must assess whether the 22-hour-50-minute restraint and its review complied with Article 3.

In **Nicolaou v. Cyprus** (Application no. 29068/10, ECtHR, 28 January 2020), five Cypriot applicants—the parents and siblings of Athanasios Nicolaou—alleged that Cyprus had failed to conduct an adequate investigation into his death, contrary to the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Athanasios Nicolaou, born in 1979, was performing mandatory military service in Cyprus. On 28 September 2005 he was granted overnight leave and was due back at camp by 6:50 a.m. the next day. He left home around 6:30 a.m. on 29 September but never returned. Police later found his car near a bridge in Alassa and then his body under the bridge. A forensic pathologist, Dr P.S., attended the scene. According to police records, P.S. stated on-site that the death appeared to be suicide by falling from the bridge and that no criminal act was suspected. His later autopsy concluded that death resulted from injuries consistent with a fall from a height, including haemorrhages and internal ruptures, and found “no signs of criminal activity.”

The initial police investigation was led by the local police station and focused on an unnatural death/suicide. Although over fifty witnesses were interviewed, serious omissions occurred: the scene was not immediately properly cordoned off; no DNA samples were taken from the car; the gastric-fluid vial was unsealed and not tested; no tests were done on vomit, sand or water in the deceased’s mouth, or on his glasses, watch, wallet and clothes; mobile-phone data was not fully recovered; and not all soldiers from his squadron were interviewed. The first inquest in 2007 found death under conditions resembling suicide, but the Supreme Court quashed that verdict and ordered a second inquest. In 2009 the second coroner found death resulted from injuries caused by a fall from a height, while concluding there was insufficient evidence of either suicide or a criminal act. The Attorney General then decided no criminal proceedings were warranted.

The family obtained private forensic opinions which criticised the autopsy and investigation. Experts O.P., P.K., D.G. and M.G. argued that the internal injuries were incompatible with a fall from a 30-metre bridge, that external and skeletal injuries were absent, and that third-party violence or another mechanism could not be excluded. They also highlighted untested or contaminated evidence.

In 2011 the Council of Ministers appointed criminal investigators and an independent pathologist, M.M. M.M. found the scene inspection, autopsy and police investigation substandard. He noted that the body was found directly under the bridge, the glasses were intact, blood was found three metres away, and sand and water were in the mouth despite the river not flowing. He concluded that a fall from the bridge was unreliable, the cause of death was indeterminable, and a criminal act had not been ruled out. The investigators likewise found serious police deficiencies, possible criminal conduct, and recommended reinvestigation. The Attorney General initially refused but later ordered further police investigation in 2014. New DNA testing found DNA from three unknown men on the deceased’s clothes, though no match was made with tested soldiers; a new pathologist gave mixed findings.

The central alleged violation was Cyprus’s failure to conduct an effective, prompt and impartial investigation into a death occurring during compulsory military service. The key facts supporting that complaint were the premature suicide classification, reliance on disputed forensic conclusions, failure to secure and test crucial evidence, failure to pursue obvious lines of inquiry, prolonged delays, and unresolved expert conflicts. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 2 under its procedural aspect.

**Dykusarenko v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 7218/19 and 17854/19) is a European Court of Human Rights case against Ukraine. The applicant, Oleksiy Mykolayovych Dykusarenko, born 9 February 1985, was represented by Mr S.M. Rybiy, a lawyer practising in Dnipro. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 21 January 2019 and 11 March 2019 respectively. The Ukrainian Government were given notice. A Fifth Section Committee, composed of Judges Kucsko-Stadlmayer, Mits and Hüseynov, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 19 March 2020 and adopted its judgment on 9 April 2020.

The key facts concern the applicant’s detention in Dnipro detention facility no. 4. According to the appended table, he was held there from 27 October 2014 to 6 July 2019, a total period of 4 years, 8 months and 10 days. The available living space was reported as 3.65 to 3.95 square metres per inmate. The applicant alleged that the conditions of this detention were inadequate.

The specific grievances recorded for the detention period include: lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; lack of toiletries; lack or insufficient quantity of food; lack of or insufficient electric light; no or restricted access to a shower; lack of privacy for using the toilet; poor quality of potable water; and a mouldy or dirty cell. These conditions form the factual basis of his complaints.

As to the alleged violations, in application no. 17854/19 the applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that the conditions of his detention were inadequate, amounting to inhuman or degrading treatment. He also complained under Article 13 that there was no effective remedy in domestic law in respect of those conditions. In application no. 7218/19 he also raised complaints under Article 5 §§ 3 and 5 and Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. Article 5 §§ 3 and 5 concern the right to liberty and security, particularly the right to be brought promptly before a judge and the right to compensation for unlawful detention, while Article 6 § 1 concerns the right to a fair trial. The appended table records the same detention facility, period, space per inmate and specific grievances for both applications, indicating that the conditions of detention were central to both applications.

The case therefore centres on the applicant’s lengthy detention in Dnipro detention facility no. 4, the very limited personal space, and the multiple alleged deficiencies in material conditions—bedding, hygiene, food, lighting, shower access, toilet privacy, water quality and cell cleanliness. These facts underpinned his claims that Ukraine violated Article 3 and Article 13, and, in application no. 7218/19, also Article 5 §§ 3 and 5 and Article 6 § 1. The provided excerpt sets out the procedure and factual allegations but does not include the Court’s full merits analysis or final conclusions on the violations.

text:
In Chernyavskiy v. Ukraine (Application no. 54141/12), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined an application brought by Nikolay Kirillovich Chernyavskiy, born in 1963, against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention. The application was introduced on 6 July 2012, and the Ukrainian Government was given notice. A Committee composed of Judges Chanturia, Yudkivska, and Seibert-Fohr deliberated in private on 29 September 2020 and adopted the judgment on 22 October 2020.

The applicant’s principal complaints were that the conditions of his detention were inadequate and that no effective remedy existed in domestic law to address them. He also raised other complaints under the Convention, though the provided extract does not detail them. The factual core of the case concerns his detention at Odesa Detention Facility from 3 October 2011 to 21 November 2019, a total of 8 years, 1 month, and 19 days.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are set out in the appended table. Throughout the entire period, the living space available to the applicant was only 3.3 to 3.6 square metres per inmate. This level of personal space is significantly below the minimum standards generally required for humane detention and is central to assessing whether the conditions amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3 of the Convention. The applicant also alleged a broad range of specific deficiencies: lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities; lack of privacy for using the toilet; mouldy or dirty cells; lack or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; lack or inadequate furniture; lack of fresh air; lack or insufficient quantity of food; no or restricted access to a shower; poor quality of food; lack of toiletries; and lack or insufficient physical exercise in fresh air.

These allegations are not isolated incidents but describe continuous and cumulative conditions over more than eight years. In the Court’s assessment, the cumulative effect of overcrowding, poor sanitation, restricted shower access, inadequate food, lack of privacy, and limited outdoor exercise is particularly relevant. The duration of detention is also a significant factor: a lengthy period under such conditions can aggravate the severity of the treatment and strengthen the claim that it crossed the threshold of Article 3. The applicant further complained that Ukraine failed to provide any effective domestic remedy by which he could challenge these conditions or obtain redress, contrary to Article 13 of the Convention. Under the Convention, Article 3 is absolute, while Article 13 requires an effective remedy for arguable claims of such treatment.

The case therefore focuses on two main alleged violations: first, that the applicant was subjected to inhuman or degrading treatment because of the overall conditions at Odesa Detention Facility, especially the prolonged lack of adequate space and basic amenities; and second, that there was no effective domestic remedy for those complaints. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

**Summary of *Dobrovitskaya and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia***

The case of *Dobrovitskaya and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* comprises six applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by eleven Moldovan and Russian nationals against both Moldova and Russia. The applications concern actions taken by the authorities of the self-proclaimed "Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic" ("MRT"), an unrecognised entity in the Transdniestria region of Moldova.

The applicants alleged multiple violations of the European Convention on Human Rights, primarily under Articles 3, 5, 6, and 13, as well as Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. The respondent States are the Republic of Moldova and Russia.

In application no. 41660/10, Elena Dobrovitskaya was summoned as a witness in criminal proceedings against her mother, who had been declared wanted by "MRT" authorities. When she refused to disclose her mother's whereabouts, she was detained in the basement of Bender's remand centre from 16 to 19 June 2010. She complained of inhuman detention conditions, unlawful arrest by "MRT" militia lacking legal authority, being held as a hostage, and being prohibited from leaving Bender, which prevented her from continuing her university studies or seeking employment.

In application no. 25197/11, Alexandru Ursu was arrested on 21 July 2009 by "MRT" militia on charges of forgery and fraud. He was allegedly subjected to ill-treatment and psychological pressure during interrogation to extract self-incriminatory statements, including threats that his father would be arrested. He was convicted by the Bender district court to fifteen years' imprisonment, a decision upheld by the "MRT" Supreme Court. He complained of inhuman detention conditions, unlawful detention ordered by illegal courts, unfair trial proceedings, and lack of effective remedies.

In application no. 8064/11, Galina and Ivan Samatov complained regarding the second applicant's detention. Ivan Samatov was recruited into the "MRT" army in 2005, was arrested in March 2007 for leaving his military unit without permission, and was held in a cell measuring twelve square metres with eight to eleven other detainees. He complained of inhuman conditions and detention by virtue of decisions taken by unlawfully created "MRT" courts.

In application no. 6151/12, Mihail Petiş, Maxim Ciumacenco, Mihail Doagă, and Igor Gherghelejiu were arrested between 27 and 31 August 2009 on charges of rape of a minor. They were convicted to prison sentences ranging from seven to twenty years. They complained that their detention was unlawful, ordered by an authority not qualifying as a court, and that they were convicted by a tribunal not established by law in unfair proceedings.

In application no. 28972/13, Serghei Boltenco was arrested on 24 December 2005 on charges of organising theft of ferrous metal. He was detained in various facilities under conditions he described as inhuman, including overcrowding, lack of natural light, inadequate medical care, and insufficient treatment for serious heart conditions. He was convicted and sentenced to fifteen years' imprisonment. He died in November 2014 from a heart attack while the case was pending.

In application no. 29182/14, Vitalii Beşleaga and Serghei Bevziuc were arrested on 15 November 2013 on corruption charges. They complained of very poor detention conditions, including lack of heating, ventilation, and medical care, despite one suffering from diabetes and another requiring colon surgery.

All applicants complained of violations under Article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment), Article 5 (right to liberty and security), Article 6 (right to fair trial), and Article 13 (right to effective remedies), with some also invoking Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 (freedom of movement).

**Case Summary: Tasev v. North Macedonia (Application no. 9825/13)**

The case concerns Slavčo Tasev, a judge in the Štip Court of Appeal in North Macedonia, who complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the authorities’ refusal to register his self-declared ethnicity in the electoral roll for judges violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention. He also alleged unfairness in the administrative proceedings.

On 21 September 2012, a vacancy notice was published for five posts on the State Judicial Council (SJC), to be filled by sitting judges elected from among their peers. Under the State Judicial Council Act, the SJC had fifteen members, eight of whom were judges elected by their peers; three of those eight had to belong to ethnic-minority communities. Candidates could stand on general lists or on a single list of judges belonging to ethnic-minority communities. All judges registered in the electoral roll voted for candidates on the minority list.

On 28 September 2012, Tasev asked the Ministry of Justice to change his ethnicity entry in the electoral roll from Bulgarian to Macedonian. On 15 October 2012, the electoral roll was made available to the Štip Court of Appeal for inspection. Because his ethnicity had not been changed, he lodged a fresh request under section 17 of the State Judicial Act. On 18 October 2012, the Ministry refused. It reasoned that the request had been submitted after the SJC election announcement and was intended to secure an electoral right in that election. Allowing the change, it said, would put other judges at a disadvantage.

Tasev appealed to the Administrative Court, arguing that the refusal had no statutory basis and that determining his ethnicity was his personal right. The Ministry replied, attaching extracts from the 2006, 2008 and 2010 electoral rolls showing him registered as Bulgarian. On 26 October 2012, the Administrative Court upheld the refusal. It added that the request was not a rectification of an obvious error but concerned an ethnicity detail. It found that he had previously enjoyed rights as a Bulgarian concerning SJC elections, based on the earlier electoral rolls, although Tasev had not been given an opportunity to comment on those extracts. On 5 November 2012, the Higher Administrative Court dismissed his appeal, repeating that changing his ethnicity after the election announcement would disadvantage other judges and that the refusal did not restrict his right to assert his ethnic identity because it was sought after the announcement.

Separately, on 5 October 2012, Tasev stood for election to the SJC. He submitted a written statement affirming that he was of Macedonian ethnicity and applied under the general list of judges from courts within the Štip Court of Appeal’s jurisdiction. On 3 December 2012, the SJC struck his name from the general list because his declared Macedonian ethnicity did not match official records, which had registered him as Bulgarian since 1995. The SJC noted that it was not required to decide electoral-roll entries; rectification was governed by section 17.

Under domestic law, the Constitution defines free expression of national identity as a fundamental value. Section 17 of the Act provides that the Ministry of Justice administers the electoral roll, including ethnicity. Within five days of an SJC election being announced, the roll is available for inspection, and judges may seek rectification of their details for three days. The Minister decides within three days, subject to administrative appeal. The Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities also guarantees the right freely to choose to be treated or not as belonging to a national minority, without disadvantage.

The applicant alleged that the refusal to register his declared ethnicity interfered with his private life and that the administrative proceedings were unfair.

**Case: Bradarić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 84721/17), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, Judgment of 3 December 2019**

The case concerns an application lodged by Mr Nedžad Bradarić, a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1954 and living in Tuzla, against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant was represented by a Tuzla law firm, while the Government was represented by its Agent. The application was lodged on 14 December 2017.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violation concern the non-enforcement of a domestic settlement. On 26 April 2012, the applicant and his former employer, a private company based in Tuzla, concluded a settlement before the Tuzla Municipal Court concerning the applicant’s severance pay. On 29 August 2012, the applicant filed a request with the Tuzla Municipal Court for enforcement of that settlement.

Despite the settlement being enforceable, the enforcement proceedings did not result in payment. On 20 March 2017, the applicant lodged a constitutional appeal complaining about the non-enforcement. On 15 June 2017, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and ordered the Tuzla Municipal Court to expedite the enforcement proceedings. The Constitutional Court also awarded the applicant 1,000 convertible marks (approximately 500 euros) in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

Despite that finding, enforcement continued to be delayed. On 27 September 2017, following a request by a third party—a company which had brought a civil action against the applicant’s former employer in separate proceedings—the Tuzla Municipal Court postponed the enforcement proceedings until the end of the third-party proceedings. The applicant appealed against that decision. On 15 November 2017, the Tuzla Cantonal Court overturned the postponement decision, rejected the third party’s request, and ordered the third party to pay the applicant 1,053 convertible marks in legal costs.

Nevertheless, as of the latest information available to the European Court of Human Rights, dated 28 June 2019, the enforcement proceedings in the applicant’s case were still pending. The applicant therefore complained to the Strasbourg Court about the non-enforcement of the settlement. On 13 November 2018, the Court gave notice of the complaint concerning non-enforcement to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

The key issue before the Court was whether the respondent State had failed to enforce a final domestic settlement within a reasonable time, thereby violating the applicant’s rights under the Convention, in particular Article 6 § 1 and potentially Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The relevant facts include the long delay from the enforcement request in August 2012, the Constitutional Court’s earlier finding of a violation in June 2017, the subsequent third-party postponement, and the fact that enforcement remained pending more than six years after the initial enforcement request and nearly two years after the Constitutional Court’s decision. The case therefore focused on the effectiveness of domestic enforcement mechanisms and the State’s compliance with its obligation to ensure timely execution of final domestic decisions.

**Case: Šaranović v. Montenegro (Application no. 31775/16), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 5 March 2019.**

The applicant, Slobodan Šaranović, a Montenegrin national born in 1938, complained under Article 5 of the Convention about his pre-trial detention in Montenegro, particularly between 15 November and 15 December 2014, which he alleged was unlawful. He also alleged that his detention could last at most six months without an indictment and that the decisions extending detention and the Constitutional Court’s decision lacked adequate reasoning.

The background involved the 2009 murder of the applicant’s brother in Belgrade and the 2013 murder of X, whose brother had been identified as an organised-crime leader. Serbian authorities investigated the applicant on suspicion that he arranged X’s murder as revenge. He was arrested in Montenegro in July 2013, but Montenegro refused Serbia’s extradition request and released him in February 2014. Montenegro then authorised his prosecution locally.

On 8 April 2014 the applicant was arrested in Montenegro. An investigation was ordered on 9 April for aggravated murder through incitement. On 10 April an investigating judge ordered detention for up to one month under Article 175 § 1(2) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC), relying on reasonable suspicion, risk of influencing witnesses, and risk that release would seriously threaten public peace and order. Detention was extended monthly through 5 September 2014 on essentially the same grounds.

On 7 October 2014 an indictment was issued, and detention was extended “until a further decision of the court.” That decision was quashed on 16 October. On 17 October the High Court again extended detention under Article 175 § 1(4), adding a risk that the applicant might abscond; the Court of Appeals later described that finding as an obvious error but considered it irrelevant. On 22 October the indictment was returned for further investigation, and further investigation was ordered on 13 November.

The alleged violation focused on the period after 15 November 2014. Under CPC Article 179 § 2, before an indictment enters into force, a court must review whether detention grounds persist and issue a decision extending or revoking detention every 30 days. No such review occurred after 15 November 2014. On 15 December 2014 the applicant sought release, arguing that his detention had become unlawful from 15 November. The same day, the High Court extended his detention “until a further decision,” relying on Article 175 § 1(4) and Article 179 § 2 and repeating earlier reasons about the ongoing investigation, public peace and order, and the absence of less restrictive measures.

His appeals were dismissed on 25 December 2014. The Court of Appeals held that failure to review detention within 30 days did not mean detention had ceased, and that the indictment had been issued within six months, even though it had later been returned. It also found irrelevant that the indictment covered two offences while detention was extended on only one basis.

The applicant further complained that his detention exceeded the statutory six-month limit without an indictment entering into force, and that the detention decisions and the Constitutional Court’s decision were not properly reasoned. He argued that the courts merely copied earlier reasoning and failed to consider his age, health, family situation, prior clean record, or the overall length of detention, and did not specify how long detention would last. On 29 May 2015 the Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal, finding the decisions reasoned and not arbitrary.

Detention continued to be extended until he was released on 9 December 2016. The applicant was murdered on 11 March 2017; his wife pursued the application. Relevant domestic law included CPC Article 177, limiting investigation detention and requiring release if no indictment was issued by the statutory deadline, and Article 179 § 2, imposing a 30-day review duty.

The case *Nicolaou v. Cyprus* (Application no. 29068/10) concerned five Cypriot applicants, relatives of Athanasios Nicolaou, who died on 29 September 2005, aged 26, during mandatory military service. After overnight leave, he failed to return to camp. His car was found near a bridge in Alassa, and his body was discovered under the bridge. The initial forensic pathologist, Dr P.S., attended the scene and reportedly considered the death a suicide/fall from height with no suspicion of criminal activity. His autopsy concluded that death resulted from multiple severe injuries “which can also occur from fall from a height” and found “no signs of criminal activity.” Alcohol was detected in the blood.

The first police investigation was conducted by local police rather than specialist crime investigators and was oriented toward an unnatural death/suicide. Family members alleged that Mr Nicolaou had been bullied and humiliated at camp and suggested possible third-party involvement. The first inquest (2007) found death under conditions resembling suicide. The Supreme Court quashed that verdict, and a second inquest (2009) found death from injuries caused by a fall from a height, but with insufficient evidence of suicide or criminal act. The Attorney General declined to bring criminal proceedings.

The applicants’ core complaint before the European Court of Human Rights was that the investigation into the death was inadequate, contrary to the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the Convention.

Key facts relevant to that alleged violation included serious and repeated criticisms of the original forensic and police work. Private experts O.P., P.K., D.G. and M.G. challenged P.S.’s conclusions. They noted, among other things, that the stomach contents and vomit had not been properly tested; the gastric vial had not been sealed; DNA was not taken from the car, glasses, watch, wallet or clothing; blood was found about three metres from the body; the deceased’s glasses remained intact; and there were no external or skeletal injuries typical of a fall from a 20–30 metre bridge. They suggested the injuries could have been intentionally inflicted and that the body might have been moved.

In 2011 the Council of Ministers appointed criminal investigators. An independent forensic pathologist, Dr M.M., concluded that the scene inspection, autopsy and police investigation had been substandard. He found the fall-from-bridge conclusion unreliable and considered the cause of death indeterminable, with criminal action not ruled out. The investigators identified major police omissions: contamination of the scene, failure to conduct DNA and toxicological tests, failure to examine the scene thoroughly, failure to trace all soldiers and mobile phone data, and an early unquestioning reliance on P.S.’s suicide theory. They recommended re-examination as a possible criminal act. The Attorney General initially refused a fresh police investigation, but later ordered further inquiries. A second police investigation took place in 2015–2017; some DNA from soldiers did not match unknown male DNA found on the deceased’s clothing, while another forensic expert, S.S., partly supported P.S.

The Court found that the authorities had failed to conduct an effective investigation capable of establishing the cause of death and identifying those responsible. The procedural deficiencies, delays, loss of evidence and contradictory expert findings meant Cyprus had violated the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the Convention.
