text:
In *Souroullas Kay and Zannettos v. Cyprus* (Application no. 1618/18, judgment of 26 November 2024), the European Court of Human Rights examined two main complaints under Article 6: whether the applicants’ criminal trial was fair because their conviction rested to a decisive extent on the testimony of an accomplice granted immunity from prosecution, and whether the refusal to give them access to the prosecution’s forensic disk image breached Article 6 § 3(b) taken together with Article 6 § 1.

The case arose from a 2013 commission of inquiry into a suspicious land deal in Dromolaxia, near Larnaca airport. The land, originally owned by a Turkish Cypriot, had been sold to a private company and then resold to CYTA’s pension fund for an office complex. The authorities suspected bribery, money laundering, and an inflated price. During police searches, computer hard drives were seized and copied for forensic examination. Searches were conducted using terms including a misspelling of “Poleson.”

N.L., a property entrepreneur and chairman of the financially troubled ALKI Larnaca football club, was arrested in August 2013 with two police officers on suspicion of bribing officers to produce a false report about the landowner’s residency. He initially refused to answer questions. After being released, he promised to cooperate. An investigator told him to reveal everything, without making promises, but said that if his statements proved true, he might suggest using him as a prosecution witness. Between September and November 2013, N.L. made four written statements admitting complicity in a conspiracy and implicating several people, including the applicants Gregoris Souroullas and Venizelos Zannettos, and Polleson Holdings Ltd. He alleged that Souroullas was involved in laundering bribe money paid to a CYTA trade-union representative, and that Zannettos, AKEL’s financial director, threatened to block the deal unless N.L. repaid personal loans of former ALKI executives. The Attorney-General decided not to prosecute N.L. on 5 November 2013. The applicants were charged and tried with six co-accused before the Larnaca Assize Court.

At trial, the prosecution relied mainly on N.L. Five defence lawyers cross-examined him over five days, attacking his credibility and alleging collusion with politically motivated investigators. After N.L. testified, proceedings against him were discontinued. During the trial, the prosecution asked its forensic examiner to search the disk image again. She extracted two unsigned draft contracts between N.L.’s company and Polleson, which the prosecution used to support the claim that Souroullas knew of the illicit origin of funds. The defence argued that those documents must have been seen earlier and concealed. Investigators said they had overlooked them due to the volume of material and a misspelling.

The defence then sought access to the prosecution’s disk image. Although the defence had a copy, it claimed the hash value differed and the copy was inexact. It wanted its expert to inspect the prosecution’s image to determine when the documents had been opened, potentially proving collusion or that N.L.’s testimony had been dictated. The Assize Court refused the request.

In December 2014, the Assize Court convicted Souroullas of money laundering and Zannettos of extortion, sentencing them to six and a half and three and a half years respectively. It cautioned itself about accomplice evidence but found N.L. credible, describing his testimony as “indestructible and sincere,” and relied on it to a “most decisive” extent, with no corroboration. The Supreme Court upheld the convictions, calling N.L.’s testimony the “foundation” and finding no improper dealings. It also held that denial of access to the disk image did not disadvantage the defence because it had a copy containing all trial documents. The ECtHR thus considered whether these facts violated the applicants’ fair-trial rights.

**Case name:** *Kowalik v. Poland* (Application no. 37910/21), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Committee judgment of 8 February 2024.

The applicant, Paweł Kowalik, born in 1980, lodged an application against Poland on 15 July 2021 under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Polish Government were given notice of the application. The applicant complained of two principal matters: the excessive length of criminal proceedings concerning him, and the lack of any effective remedy in Polish domestic law for that excessive length. These complaints correspond to the reasonable-time guarantee under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

The key facts are set out in the appended table. The criminal proceedings began on 7 May 2017. At the time relevant to the application, they were still pending. The total length of the proceedings was recorded as more than 6 years, 6 months and 4 days. The proceedings had reached only one level of jurisdiction. This chronology is central to the alleged violation: the applicant did not complain principally about the substantive outcome of the criminal case, but about the State’s failure to conclude it within a reasonable time and its failure to provide effective domestic redress for the delay.

The table also records that the applicant made use of the domestic remedy under the Polish 2004 Act concerning complaints about breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The Warsaw-Praga Regional Court issued decisions on those complaints: on 6 December 2019 in case no. VI S 133/19, with a domestic award of PLN 2,000; and on 10 February 2021 in case no. VI S 12/21. The provided text does not set out the reasoning of those decisions or the later procedural history of the criminal case. Nevertheless, the fact that the applicant had already pursued the 2004 Act remedy and then applied to Strasbourg is significant, because it underpinned his allegation that the domestic remedy had not been effective in his case and that the criminal proceedings remained excessively long.

The Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Péter Paczolay, Gilberto Felici and Raffaele Sabato, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 18 January 2024 and adopted the judgment on 8 February 2024. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the criminal proceedings started on 7 May 2017; they remained pending; their total duration exceeded six and a half years; they had reached only one level of jurisdiction; and the applicant had obtained a domestic award of PLN 2,000 under the 2004 Act, plus a further decision in February 2021, yet still complained that the length was excessive and that no effective domestic remedy existed. No details concerning the nature of the criminal charge, the evidence, or the merits of the criminal case are included in the provided text. The case accordingly forms part of the Court’s recurring examination of Polish length-of-proceedings complaints under Article 6 § 1 and the effectiveness of domestic remedies under Article 13.

The case of *Bilal Akyıldız v. Turkey* concerns the arrest and pre-trial detention of the applicant, Mr. Bilal Akyıldız, in connection with a series of sexual assaults and attempted child abductions in Istanbul in 2002. The applicant primarily complained that there was no reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence, in violation of Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In 2002, several children were sexually assaulted in the Ümraniye district of Istanbul, and two attempts were made to abduct children in the nearby district of Samandıra. On 16 November 2002, following an anonymous tip, gendarmes arrested the applicant in Samandıra because he resembled a photofit of the perpetrator. The arrest report, signed by the applicant, stated he was suspected of attempted child abduction. However, a separate, handwritten report by three gendarmes claimed he was arrested during a routine patrol for failing to produce his identity card.

On the day of his arrest, an identification parade was held. A child witness identified the applicant with certainty, while two child victims stated he strongly resembled the perpetrator. Crucially, however, DNA testing conducted while he was in police custody proved he was not responsible for the sexual assaults.

On 18 November 2002, the gendarmerie station commander sent the investigation file to the public prosecutor. His letter noted the DNA results and the applicant's clean record, and he expressed his belief that the victims and witnesses had likely been influenced by intense media coverage of the "Ümraniye pervert" and had identified the applicant solely due to his resemblance to the photofit. Despite this, the applicant was brought before a judge that same day and ordered into pre-trial detention based on the evidence and the nature of the alleged offences.

The applicant’s lawyer objected, highlighting the exculpatory DNA test, contradictions in the victims' descriptions, and the irregularity of the identification parade, where the applicant—whose face was partially burned—was placed alongside two men with no distinguishing features. The lawyer also submitted an alibi, stating the applicant was at work far from the scene. The objection was rejected.

On 11 December 2002, the father of one victim submitted a petition to the court, stating his daughter had been influenced by media reports and was now convinced the applicant was not the perpetrator. On 13 December 2002, when confronted with the victims in court, they unequivocally stated the applicant was not the person who had attempted to abduct them. The Assize Court of Kartal immediately acquitted him, after 27 days in detention.

The applicant was subsequently awarded compensation for unlawful detention under the repealed Act No. 466. In a separate administrative action, the Council of State ultimately found that the authorities had violated the confidentiality of the investigation by leaking information to the press, which led to him being publicly identified as the "Ümraniye pervert," and awarded him non-pecuniary damages. The case before the European Court of Human Rights centred on the lack of reasonable suspicion for his initial arrest and detention.

In *Bezzina Wettinger and Others v. Malta* (App. no. 52673/15, 21 January 2020), six Maltese applicants complained about an expropriation and the compensation awarded for their land. In 1960, the applicants and/or their ancestors, together with C.Z. and Company W.J., acquired a perpetual emphyteusis over about 23,606 sq m of land at Tal-Ħriereb, within Birkirkara and Msida. The applicants held one third jointly, in different shares. In 1961, the Governor of Malta declared about 7,531 sq m of that land necessary for a public purpose, to be acquired by outright purchase.

In 1964, the Commissioner of Lands offered the emphyteutae and the dominus £631 for the expropriated land. They refused. The matter went before the Land Arbitration Board (“LAB”), which in 1978 fixed compensation at MTL 1,161 (about EUR 2,704) and set a date for the deed of transfer. The LAB did not indicate how the sum should be shared. In 1981, following rectification, the LAB corrected a measurement error but kept the compensation unchanged. It declined to determine the shares of the dominus and the emphyteutae, leaving that issue to the ordinary courts. Because the parties disagreed over apportionment, the compensation was not divided or paid.

The applicants then brought constitutional redress proceedings, alleging that the taking and non-payment violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and that the LAB proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1. In 2005, the Constitutional Court rejected their claims. In 2008, the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 concerning the length of the LAB proceedings ending in 1981, but only for certain direct victims. The Court rejected the complaint about inadequate compensation for non-exhaustion and found the no-payment complaint manifestly ill-founded because payment had not occurred because the applicants had failed to take steps to divide the compensation.

After the 2008 judgment, in 2011 the applicants and others brought fresh constitutional redress proceedings challenging the quantum of compensation. They argued that the LAB award was inadequate and breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They sought annulment of the LAB decision, adequate compensation, refund of ground rent, and damages. Their architect estimated the 2006 open-market value of the land at about MTL 3,780,000 (EUR 8,805,000), the 1964 value at about MTL 7,530 (EUR 17,319, or EUR 2.30 per sq m), and the 1978 value at about MTL 52,700 (EUR 121,210).

In 2014, the First Hall rejected the claim. It noted that the emphyteutae had originally paid about 0.08 euro cents per sq m; the expropriation concerned 6,774.54 sq m; and the LAB award gave them about 0.41 euro cents per sq m, more than their acquisition price. The Commissioner’s expert valued 1964 compensation at about EUR 3,610 because the land was then outside a development zone. The court found the award adequate.

On appeal, the applicants argued that proportionality required considering the passage of time, non-payment, ground rents paid (EUR 605.92 yearly), inflation, and the land’s building-land status. They relied on ECtHR case-law holding that compensation laws failing to account for time between taking and payment may breach the Convention. They also complained that the area used was wrong and that their challenge to the LAB award covered the law’s limitations. In 2015, the Constitutional Court confirmed the dismissal. It held that the applicants had challenged only the amount, that non-payment resulted from their failure to determine shares and use ordinary proceedings, that ground rents had been repaid, and that the land had been agricultural at the time of taking. It found a fair balance had been struck. The key alleged violation therefore concerned Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, namely whether the compensation was adequate and whether the delay and non-payment breached the applicants’ property rights.

text:
**Kálovics v. Hungary** (Application no. 46030/18) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings in Hungary. The application was lodged against Hungary under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Tamás Kálovics, born on 19 November 1977, was represented by Ms L. Horgos, a lawyer practising in Budapest.

The case was assigned to the Fourth Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Stéphanie Mourou-Vikström (President), Georges Ravarani, and Jolien Schukking, judges, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 29 August 2019 and delivered its judgment on 19 September 2019. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. Notice of the application was given to the Hungarian Government.

The factual background is set out largely in the appended table to the judgment. According to the procedure section, the application was lodged on 3 September 2018, although the appended table records the date of introduction as 23 September 2018. The applicant complained principally of the excessive length of civil proceedings. He also raised other complaints under the provisions of the Convention, though the provided text does not identify them in detail.

The key facts relevant to the length complaint are as follows. The civil proceedings at issue began on 27 July 2010 and ended on 8 May 2018. Their total duration was seven years, nine months, and twelve days. The proceedings passed through three levels of jurisdiction. This lengthy period formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the Hungarian authorities had violated his right to a hearing within a reasonable time, as guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant argued that the proceedings were excessively long, and the Court was called upon to assess whether the duration was compatible with the Convention’s “reasonable time” requirement.

Because the judgment provided is a short Committee judgment, it does not contain a detailed narrative of the underlying civil dispute. Instead, it relies on the appended table for the applicant’s personal details, the dates of the domestic proceedings, the total length, and the levels of jurisdiction involved. The central alleged violation therefore arises from the nearly eight-year span of civil litigation across three judicial instances. The case was communicated to the Hungarian Government, which had the opportunity to respond. The Court’s role was to determine whether the length of the domestic proceedings exceeded the reasonable-time standard, taking into account the complexity of the case, the applicant’s conduct, and the conduct of the authorities.

In summary, **Kálovics v. Hungary** concerns an applicant who pursued civil proceedings in Hungary from 27 July 2010 to 8 May 2018, a total of 7 years, 9 months, and 12 days over three jurisdictional levels. He alleged that this duration violated his Convention rights, principally the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1. He also raised unspecified additional complaints. The European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, examined the application and delivered its judgment on 19 September 2019. The key factual basis for the excessive-length claim is the long duration of the domestic civil proceedings, as recorded in the appended table.

In *Tamrazyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 42588/10), the applicant, Babken Tamrazyan, an Armenian national born in 1931, complained under Article 6 §1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the alienation to a third party of land he had possessed for about 23 years and about the Court of Cassation’s failure to give adequate reasons. The application was lodged on 21 July 2010; on 19 May 2014 the Government were given notice of the fair-trial and property complaints, while the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The key facts concerned a plot of about 1,300 sq.m. adjacent to Teghut village in the Tavoush region. From 1986 until 2009 the applicant possessed it: he erected a fence and garden shed, planted fruit trees, and arranged water supply. From 1986 to 1990 the land was registered in his name in the Kuybishev collective farm register. In 1994 Teghut village became a separate administrative unit from Haghartsin, but the plot was not included within either village’s administrative boundaries. From 1995 to 2007, except 1998 and 1999, the applicant paid rent to Teghut community administration, which transferred the money to the State budget.

In April 2008, while still possessing and cultivating the land, the applicant learned that in April 2007 the Tavoush Regional Administration had sold it to a third person, A.H., at public auction. A letter from the State Real Estate Registry dated 3 February 2009 informed him that A.H. had registered title on 23 April 2007, referring to a newspaper announcement and the Governor’s decision of 27 March 2007. The announcement, published on 21 February 2007, had advertised an auction on 20 March 2007 for a plot said to measure 1,394 sq.m. The applicant claimed he only obtained a copy of the Governor’s decision in 2009; it stated that A.H. had won the auction and that a sale contract was concluded on 3 April 2007.

On 21 April 2009 the applicant brought Administrative Court proceedings seeking annulment of the sale and registration and an order that the Governor conclude a direct sale agreement with him. He argued that, although his use was not legally registered, he had used the State land continuously, openly and in good faith for more than ten years, giving him a pre-emptive right to acquire it under Articles 65, 66, 67 and 72 of the Land Code and Court of Cassation case-law.

On 8 July 2009 the Administrative Court granted his claims. Relying on a certificate from the Teghut village head, rent payment evidence and witness testimony, it found that from at least 1995 until the auction the applicant had possessed the land continuously, openly and in good faith for over ten years. Under Article 72 §2 of the Land Code, he therefore had a pre-emptive right to acquire it. The Governor had unlawfully authorised a public auction instead of direct sale to a person with a pre-emptive right, contrary to Article 66.

A.H. appealed. On 2 April 2010 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment and rejected the applicant’s claims. It reasoned that payment of rent to Teghut was not decisive because the plot was outside Teghut’s administrative boundaries and therefore could not prove continuous, open and good-faith possession for ten years. It also held that Article 72 §3 referred adverse possession of land owned by persons other than the State to the Civil Code, and that Article 187 of the Civil Code was not applicable to State and community land, citing domestic case-law.

The alleged violations thus concerned whether the applicant’s long possession and payments created a protected pre-emptive/property interest under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and whether the Court of Cassation’s reasoning satisfied Article 6 §1 fair-trial guarantees.

**Ryabinin and Shatalina v. Ukraine** (Application no. 33006/07, ECtHR, 7 November 2019) concerned complaints by Valeriy Ryabinin (“the first applicant”), a Ukrainian national serving life imprisonment, and his mother, Yuliya Shatalina (“the second applicant”).

The first applicant had been released from prison in November 2004 after serving a twelve-year murder sentence. In May 2005 he began a relationship with S. After S. disappeared, body parts were found in the river Ingulets near the applicants’ home in June 2005. On 23 June 2005 police searched the home and seized a hacksaw, blades, a handcart, a TV and a kitchen cabinet. The second applicant was asked to telephone her son and tell him to come to the police station. He did so and was arrested at 7.20 p.m. on suspicion of S.’s murder.

The first applicant alleged that, after arrest, police beat him with plastic bottles filled with sand and liquid to force him to confess to murdering and dissecting S. He said he was later subjected to electric shocks from cables attached to his testicles and lower lip, lost consciousness several times, and was threatened with rape. Eventually he wrote a dictated confession. The next morning, he alleged, he was made to change into clean clothes brought by his mother because his own clothes were bloodied; the investigator allegedly told his mother to destroy the dirty clothes. He also alleged that when remanded by a judge on 25 June 2005, he was not allowed to complain about ill-treatment and the judge ignored visible facial injuries. The Government denied coercion, but noted that detention records from the Inguletskyy police station had been destroyed in 2012.

After initially confessing repeatedly, including with a lawyer present and during a reconstruction, the first applicant later complained of coercion. In August 2005 he told prosecutors he had confessed under moral coercion and threats concerning relatives. Prosecutors refused to institute criminal proceedings in February and April 2006, finding no criminal offence; domestic courts upheld those refusals. At trial in February 2006, he pleaded innocent, retracted his confession as the product of torture, but was convicted of aggravated murder, robbery and unlawful possession of weapons, and sentenced to life imprisonment. The trial relied on his earlier confessions, the reconstruction video showing no visible injuries, physical evidence, and witness testimony. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction in August 2006. His request to attend the cassation hearing was rejected as untimely. He also alleged that his correspondence in detention was routinely monitored and that he could not obtain case-file copies to substantiate his ECtHR application, although he received them in 2013.

The second applicant complained that her mobile telephone, seized from her son on 23 June 2005 although it belonged to her, was retained by the investigator without any procedural decision until August 2007. Her attempts to obtain a remedy through civil and administrative courts failed, and prosecutors repeatedly said no law had been violated.

The first applicant alleged violations mainly under Article 3 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation), Article 6 (unfair trial and absence from cassation hearing), and Article 8/Article 34 (monitoring of correspondence and obstruction of his application to the Court). The second applicant alleged arbitrary seizure and retention of her property and the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

In *Deli v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 42010/06), the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered judgment on 22 October 2019, final on 22 January 2020. The applicant, Teodor Deli, a Moldovan national born in 1960 and living in Chișinău, represented party X in civil proceedings before the Ciocana District Court against party Y.

The key events arose at a hearing on 15 June 2006 before a single judge, Judge B. According to the applicant, he objected when Judge B acted in an intimidating manner toward X. The judge allegedly threatened to have the applicant removed from court or jailed. When the applicant requested Judge B’s recusal, the judge dictated a sanction into the hearing minutes. The minutes recorded that the applicant had been cautioned for inappropriate behaviour, disrespectful remarks toward the defendant’s representative, disturbing order, using unacceptable words, shouting, and failing to heed warnings. He was fined 10 conventional units—200 Moldovan lei, about €12—under Article 200/7 of the Code of Administrative Proceedings for contempt of court. The minutes stated that a cassation appeal could be lodged with the Chișinău Court of Appeal within 10 days.

The applicant claimed that, after he persisted in challenging the judge, the proceedings were suspended and the recusal request was referred to another judge. In his recusal request, supported by his client, he alleged that Y had asked X the same question five times; when X said he had already answered, the judge raised her voice and insisted. The applicant objected that his client was being harassed. The judge warned him against misbehaving. When Y repeated the question and the judge shouted at X, the applicant requested recusal and asked that his complaint be recorded in the minutes. The judge then sanctioned him for contempt. The recusal request alleged that Judge B was biased and hostile toward X and the applicant while favouring Y. On 15 June 2006, the judge examining the recusal request rejected it, finding that the grounds did not correspond to Article 50 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The civil case continued. The Government asserted instead that the applicant repeatedly behaved improperly, used offensive language toward the opposing representative, was warned, and was then found in contempt, as recorded in the minutes.

On 19 June 2006, the applicant asked for a copy of the minutes. On 23 June 2006, he submitted objections. He complained that the minutes omitted his request that the judge not shout at or intimidate his client, falsely recorded that he had initially been cautioned, and omitted his repeated recusal request and the judge’s threats. He further objected that the fine decision had never been delivered publicly but had simply been dictated in response to his legitimate complaints. His client supported these objections. The applicant said he received no reply and saw no decision on the objections.

Also on 23 June 2006, he lodged a cassation appeal, which the Ciocana District Court forwarded to the Chișinău Court of Appeal. He alleged that the court did not annex his objections or any response to the case file, as required by law, and that he had never received a copy of the sanctioning decision. He argued that the decision breached Article 2651 of the Code of Administrative Offences and Article 6 of the Convention. On 6 July 2006, the Chișinău Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It reiterated the lower court’s decision and stated that the applicant had been summoned, but gave no further details. That decision was final. The underlying civil case was later settled, confirmed in December 2006.

Relevant domestic law included CCP provisions on recusal, measures against persons disturbing court order, minutes contents, and examination of comments; and administrative-offence provisions defining contempt and permitting appellate decisions without reasoning. The applicant’s principal complaints were that the judge who convicted him lacked impartiality and that the Chișinău Court of Appeal had not properly summoned him.

**Case Summary: Nicolaou v. Cyprus (Application no. 29068/10)**

**Key Facts Relevant to the Alleged Article 2 Violation**

The case concerns the death of Athanasios Nicolaou, a 26-year-old Cypriot national performing mandatory military service, and the subsequent investigation into his death. On 29 September 2005, after overnight leave, Nicolaou failed to return to his camp. His car was later found parked near a bridge in Alassa, and his body was discovered beneath it. A forensic pathologist, Dr. P.S., arrived at the scene and, according to police records, expressed the view that the cause of death was suicide due to a fall from the bridge, with no suspicion of criminal act. This initial assessment shaped the entire subsequent investigation.

Dr. P.S.'s post-mortem report concluded that death resulted from multiple fatal injuries consistent with a fall from a height, and stated that no signs of criminal activity were found. However, the report noted several unusual findings: the deceased's glasses were intact, his wristwatch was found beneath his body with a cut strap, and there was blood found three metres from the body, later confirmed to be the deceased's. Toxicological analysis revealed alcohol in his blood, and his DNA matched beer cans found nearby.

The police investigation, conducted by local officers rather than specialist investigators, obtained statements from over fifty witnesses. Fellow soldiers described Nicolaou as quiet and reserved. His mother and priest reported that he had complained of being bullied and humiliated at the camp. Two or three days before his death, another soldier had called him "the English," an incident reported to superiors. The police report concluded that death resulted from a fall from a height, excluding criminal act, without addressing the alleged bullying.

A parallel military investigation reached the same conclusion. The first inquest, held in 2007, found no evidence of criminal liability and concluded death occurred under conditions resembling suicide. However, the deceased's family sought private forensic opinions. Dr. O.P. and Dr. P.K. criticized the original post-mortem as flawed, noting the absence of testing on stomach contents, the failure to seal evidence, and the incompatibility of the deceased's injuries with a fall from such a height. They observed minimal external injuries despite severe internal trauma, questioned the position of the body, and noted evidence suggesting possible third-party involvement.

The Supreme Court quashed the first inquest verdict in 2008, finding the coroner had exceeded her powers by suggesting suicide without adequate evidence. A second inquest (2009) concluded that death resulted from injuries caused by falling from a height, but found insufficient evidence to establish suicide or criminal act.

Following persistent efforts by the family, the Council of Ministers appointed criminal investigators in 2011. An independent forensic pathologist, Dr. M.M., produced a report strongly criticizing the original investigation. He identified numerous shortcomings: the scene was not properly cordoned, DNA samples were not collected from the car or personal items, the gastric fluid was not sealed, and no proper examination of the blood found near the body was conducted. M.M. concluded that the absence of skeletal injuries made the fall-from-height finding unreliable and that criminal act could not be ruled out.

The investigators' 2012 report identified significant police oversights that rendered proper investigation extremely difficult. They concluded there was sufficient evidence to overturn the second inquest verdict and suggested the death possibly resulted from criminal act, recommending police re-examination.

The Attorney General initially declined further investigation in 2014, but later instructed a fresh police investigation. Additional forensic opinions were obtained, but by this time, the prolonged delay had irretrievably compromised the possibility of establishing the true cause of death.

The applicants—Nicolaou's parents and siblings—complained that the investigation into his death was inadequate, violating the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the Convention.

**Case: Sargsyan and Others v. Ukraine**  
**ECtHR, Fifth Section, Judgment of 9 January 2020**  
**Applications nos. 54012/07, 25697/08 and 17361/10**

The case concerned three Ukrainian nationals who complained that they had been subjected to police ill-treatment and that Ukraine had failed to carry out effective investigations into their allegations. Notice was given to the Government mainly concerning those complaints; other complaints were examined under well-established case-law, and parts of two applications were declared inadmissible.

**Applicant 1 – Vartan Sargsyan (no. 54012/07):** He alleged ill-treatment on 24–25 April 2007 at a Kharkiv district police station. Police allegedly sought to force him to confess to murder. Officers repeatedly pushed his face into foam rubber, twisted his handcuffed hands, made him sit naked, squeezed his genitals with a plastic bag, hit his head with a folder, spat at him, threatened his relatives, and applied electric current to wet rags pressed against his ears, chin and head. He was under administrative arrest from 24 April, confessed on 25 April, met a lawyer on 27 April, retracted the confession, and was released on 28 April. Medical evidence was mixed: a 24 April report found no injuries; a 29 April hospital certificate noted cranial contusions, ankle abrasions and painful genitals; a 21 May forensic report found no injuries. On 7 May 2007, prosecutors decided not to prosecute him for murder due to insufficient evidence. He complained on 28 April 2007. The same investigator handling the murder case issued decisions not to institute criminal proceedings on 4 May, 8 May and 18 June 2007, finding no ill-treatment and no identified officers. He was informed of only one decision much later and learned of others only from the Government’s observations. In 2009, an administrative court found prosecutorial inactivity.

**Applicant 2 – Igor Gordus (no. 25697/08):** He alleged two episodes. On 8 April 2006, at Debaltseve police station, after arrest on drug suspicion and questioning without a lawyer, officers allegedly handcuffed him to a radiator for twelve hours, punched and truncheon-beat him, including blows to his mouth, kidneys, arms and shoulders, causing him to fall and scratch his knees. On 18 June 2006, in the temporary detention unit, three plainclothes officers allegedly hit his arms and shoulders and threatened to place him with ordinary detainees as retaliation for complaints. Medical reports noted minor bruises, abrasions and lip erosion, possibly self-inflicted. Between 2006 and 2009, prosecutors repeatedly refused to institute proceedings, concluding the injuries were self-inflicted. Proceedings were marked by delays: a 2009 decision was notified only in 2011, and an appeal against a 2006 decision was heard only in 2008 because the prosecutor failed to submit the file.

**Applicant 3 – Konstantin Kravets (no. 17361/10):** He alleged ill-treatment from 28 January to 1 February 2008 in Dniprodzerzhinsk police custody. He was allegedly detained without procedural status, denied access to a lawyer and relatives, and pressured to confess to inflicting fatal injuries. Officers allegedly tied him to a chair, punched him, suffocated him with gas-mask smoke, threatened him, deprived him of food and sleep, forced him to memorise a confession and sign blank papers, removed his clothes, and made him participate in investigative actions in his underpants. After signing a confession, he was placed in an ITT, where a cellmate allegedly kicked and punched him. Medical evidence noted rib, shoulder and arm bruises. He retracted his confession; the criminal case against him was terminated in 2011 for lack of evidence. Prosecutors issued repeated refusals to institute proceedings between 2008 and 2010, then opened proceedings that were closed and reopened several times, finally closing them in 2016 and attributing the injuries to the deceased cellmate. The cellmate was never questioned; notifications were delayed; and Kravets was mostly treated as a witness, with victim status only for a limited period.

In essence, the applicants alleged Article 3 violations: ill-treatment in police custody and ineffective domestic investigations characterised by repeated refusals, delayed decisions, reliance on self-infliction or third-party responsibility, and failure to identify or question relevant officers.

In *D. v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 25397/09, judgment 8 December 2020), the applicant, a Moldovan woman born in 1990, complained of unlawful arrest and ill-treatment by police during mass arrests following Moldova’s 5 April 2009 parliamentary elections. The election results triggered protests in Chișinău over alleged electoral fraud. On 7 April 2009, protests turned violent, and after 1 a.m. on 8 April police and special forces launched a massive operation to restore order. A later parliamentary inquiry found that excessive force was used and that all people still present in the main square were arrested regardless of whether they had been violent.

On the evening of 7 April 2009, the applicant went with her roommate R. to the Great National Assembly Square, where they met her relative V. Boboc. She claimed they were part of a group of about fifty young people standing peacefully and discussing the day’s events. Around 1 a.m. on 8 April, their group was surrounded by police, masked special forces, and plain-clothed officers armed with automatic rifles and rubber sticks. The young people were ordered to lie down and were kicked and severely beaten with rubber sticks and rifles. The applicant’s head was hit against the pavement, and she received several blows. While being taken to a police car, she and R. saw police kicking Boboc, who was unconscious and no longer reacting. He died several days later.

At Buiucani police station, approximately twenty young men and three young women, including the applicant and R., were allegedly ordered to stand with their hands against the wall and were beaten whenever they tried to speak or move. The young men were taken one by one into an office and ordered to lower their trousers; sounds of beating and screams followed. The men returned with clear signs of ill-treatment, and one was released completely naked. The three women were insulted and shouted at but not physically assaulted. No explanation was given for the arrest. Around 5 a.m. on 8 April 2009, the women were released and advised to leave the city. The applicant alleged unlawful detention for over five hours without being informed of the reasons, without access to relatives, and without prompt judicial review.

On 13 April 2009, she gave a concealed-identity television interview. Authorities later sought to uncover her identity. On 14 April, a doctor found a 16 by 15 centimetre injury to her right foot; fearing for her life, she falsely attributed it to an unknown street attacker. On 4 May 2009, she complained to the Prosecutor General about ill-treatment and unlawful detention. Medical examinations at the Memoria Rehabilitation Centre between 4 and 15 May 2009 documented headaches, vertigo, insomnia, nightmares, heartache, anxiety, flashbacks, post-traumatic stress disorder, and consequences of cranial trauma.

On 1 June 2009, she was interviewed by an investigating judge and a prosecutor. Witness protection was refused, with authorities saying concealed identity was sufficient. On 22 July 2009, the military prosecutor’s office opened a criminal investigation into her allegations. It was joined to a broader investigation into police beatings, but was suspended on 15 January 2013 because, despite questioning about 200 special forces members and reviewing videos, investigators could not identify which officer used force against which victim or whether force was necessary. Separately, officer G. was convicted of negligence for failing to act while at Buiucani station when young people, including the applicant and R., were ill-treated; the Supreme Court upheld that conviction in 2016. In November 2012, the Government paid the applicant MDL 7,000 (about €447) under a compensation scheme. The parliamentary commission found that arrests continued until 12 April 2009. These facts underpinned her complaints under Articles 3 and 5 of the Convention and the alleged lack of an effective investigation.

In *Čivinskaitė v. Lithuania* (Application no. 21218/12, judgment of 15 September 2020), the applicant, Rita Čivinskaitė, was Deputy Chief Prosecutor of the Kaunas City District Prosecutor’s Office (“KCDPO”). She complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention that disciplinary proceedings against her were unfair because of a parallel parliamentary inquiry, prejudicial statements made by high-ranking politicians in the media, and intense media coverage of a high-profile criminal case.

The case arose from a pre-trial investigation opened in November 2008 into allegations that D.K.’s minor daughter had been sexually abused. The investigation was initially conducted by police and supervised by prosecutor G.R. After shortcomings were identified, the investigation was transferred to the KCDPO. In January 2009 the Chief Prosecutor of the KCDPO instructed the applicant to entrust the investigation to G.R.; the applicant did so. From 30 January to 11 June 2009, G.R. conducted the investigation under the applicant’s supervision. In February 2009 the applicant partly allowed suspect A.Ū.’s complaint and granted him access to part of the investigation file, excluding the minor’s interviews. The investigation later attracted national attention after two suspects were murdered, D.K. fled and died, and A.Ū. died.

In October 2009 the Prosecutor General’s Office conducted an inquiry into the investigation. It found multiple shortcomings, including that G.R. had failed to properly supervise police work, and that the applicant had entrusted the investigation to G.R. despite doubts about her competence, failed to supervise G.R., and unlawfully examined A.Ū.’s complaint instead of having it heard by a pre-trial judge. Disciplinary proceedings were opened against the applicant on 13 October 2009. On 22 October 2009 the Prosecutor General’s Office concluded that she had committed disciplinary offences, harmed the prosecutor’s office’s reputation and public trust, and recommended demotion. On 30 October 2009 the Prosecutor General demoted her; she was transferred to a prosecutor post in the KCDPO.

In parallel, in October 2009 the Seimas ordered its Legal Affairs Committee to conduct a parliamentary inquiry into the investigation. The Committee’s January 2010 report found the investigation incompetent and protracted, and stated that the responsible persons included the KCDPO prosecutor and the Deputy Chief Prosecutor—the applicant. The Seimas endorsed these conclusions and found that the prosecutors involved had failed to perform their duties. Meanwhile, high-ranking politicians, especially President Dalia Grybauskaitė, publicly demanded personal accountability and harsher decisions against prosecutors. Media reports repeatedly described the investigation as negligent and linked the applicant to the misconduct.

The applicant challenged her demotion before administrative courts. She argued, among other things, that the penalty had been influenced by political statements and media coverage. The Vilnius Regional Administrative Court dismissed her complaint in June 2010, annulling some findings but upholding that she had failed to properly supervise the investigation and had overstepped her remit regarding file access. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed her appeal in October 2011. Notably, neither court addressed her complaints about political and media interference. Later requests to reopen the proceedings were refused.

The ECtHR therefore had to examine whether the disciplinary proceedings, in the context of the parliamentary inquiry, political statements and media pressure, complied with Article 6 §§ 1 and 2, particularly the requirements of a fair hearing, an impartial tribunal, and respect for the presumption of innocence.

Svitlana Ilchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 47166/09) concerned the demolition of the applicant’s garage and her complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that this amounted to deprivation of property.

The applicant, born in 1951, lived in Kyiv and had used a one-car brick garage in the courtyard of her building since 1980. In April 1983 the Kyiv Leninsky District Council executive committee authorised her to use the garage. From 1993 to 1998 she leased the courtyard area occupied by the garage. In January 1995 the district executive committee stated it had no objection to her registering the garage in her name. In February 1995 the Kyiv Technical Inventory Bureau registered the garage as hers, relying on the 1983 decision and the 1995 letter. She later bought her flat privately, and in October 2002 a municipal housing agency certificate stated that she owned the 34 sq. m brick garage.

In 2002 the city and a private developer planned a new housing project on the site where the garage stood. Kyiv City Council allocated land to the city’s Housing Directorate in April 2003, and a lease was signed in July 2003. In November 2002 a municipal company told the applicant’s husband that the garage would need to be moved. On 29 May 2003 the Directorate wrote to the applicant, saying the land was designated for housing, that she used the garage without legal grounds, that her registration was invalid, and that the garage would be demolished. It offered monetary compensation because no alternative placement was available and invited her to sign an agreement; if she refused, the Directorate would sue. The file indicated she did not pursue negotiations.

In July 2003 the Directorate sued for demolition. The applicant counterclaimed for title to the land and annulment of the development documents. In February 2004 the Brovary Court dismissed the Directorate’s claim, finding the applicant owned the garage, had used the land openly since 1980, had acquired title by adverse possession, and could apply for free private title. It also found irregularities in the development approval, including excess land allocation, unresolved conflicting rights, and that the project was commercial rather than for public need.

In July 2005 the Kyiv Regional Court of Appeal reversed. It held that the applicant had not proved a right to the land; the adverse-possession rule under the 2001 Land Code required fifteen years counted from 2002; and her land use had never been properly granted. It ordered her to vacate the land by demolishing the garage. On 8 August 2005 she sought suspension of enforcement pending cassation appeal, warning of irreversible consequences. On 12 August 2005 State bailiffs demolished the garage. On 19 August 2005 the court granted suspension. In February 2006 the Supreme Court quashed the lower judgments and remitted the case, noting she was the garage owner, had paid land tax, and had used the land openly; the lower courts had to clarify whether she had applied to formalise her adverse-possession rights.

On remand, the first-instance court found for the Directorate in May 2007: the 1983 decision was merely temporary permission, no proper land grant existed, and her registration was unlawful; she was ordered to vacate. Appeals were upheld in October 2008 and March 2009. Her separate claim against the bailiffs was dismissed; the court found that although notification was delayed until 8 August, demolition occurred on 12 August. The ECtHR later communicated her Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint about the demolition.

**Keaney v. Ireland** (Application no. 72060/17) concerned an Irish national, Mr Vincent Keaney, who complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the delay of eleven years between the institution of his civil proceedings and the final judgment breached the “reasonable time” requirement. The case was also communicated with others raising similar delay complaints and a question under Article 13 as to whether an effective domestic remedy existed for such delay.

The facts arose from a failed business venture. In 1996, after winning money in the national lottery, the applicant bought the Scotts Building in Cobh, intending to operate it as a Titanic-themed bar and restaurant. He spent considerable sums renovating the premises but ran out of money due to structural defects. He borrowed further and sought professional advice from J.S., a financial and management consultant, who introduced him to M.N., a public house owner.

In 2000, the applicant and M.N. entered a series of transactions. The premises were assigned to them as tenants in common in equal shares. A company, Titanic Queenstown Trading Company Limited (“TQTC”), was incorporated, with the applicant holding 49% and M.N. 51%. The premises were leased to TQTC and the intoxicating liquor licence was transferred to it. The business traded until December 2002 but was not viable. Relations deteriorated. In July 2003, the applicant and M.N. entered legally binding heads of agreement and further deeds to separate their interests, but the re-leasing arrangement failed and M.N. took possession of the premises.

In February 2006, the applicant commenced High Court proceedings against eighteen defendants. He alleged deceit, fraud, misrepresentation or undue influence arising from the 2000–2003 transactions, and sought to set aside those transactions. The case was admitted to the Commercial List. Early proceedings were dominated by pleadings disputes. The High Court ordered a properly drafted, particularised statement of claim. Multiple motions sought to strike out the claim. On 16 January 2007, the High Court struck out all claims against several defendants and limited claims against others; further claims were struck out in March 2007. The applicant delivered several amended statements of claim, which were found non-compliant. After further orders and excisions, a final statement of claim was delivered on 1 July 2008.

On 19 December 2008, the High Court dismissed all remaining claims, noting that aspects of the case bordered on an abuse of process. Appeals were initiated between 2007 and 2009. There were lengthy procedural delays: books of appeal were filed only in 2014–2015. The first appeal was heard on 24 June 2015, with judgment on 23 July 2015. The second appeal was heard on 28 February 2017, with judgment on 5 April 2017. A third appeal was not pursued. Thus, final judgment came roughly eleven years after the proceedings began in February 2006.

The applicant complained that this delay violated Article 6 § 1. The Court also examined whether Irish law provided an effective remedy under Article 13. Although Irish law recognises a constitutional right to timely civil proceedings and possible damages, no clear statutory remedy had been established, and the McFarlane v. Ireland judgment had already found a breach of Article 13. The proposed compensation scheme remained stalled. These facts framed the alleged violations: excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for delay.

In *Abdi Ibrahim v. Norway*, the applicant, a Somali national, alleged under Articles 8 and 9 of the Convention that Norway violated her right to respect for family life and religious freedom by consenting to the adoption of her son, X, by his Christian foster parents.

The applicant left Somalia in 2009 while pregnant, gave birth to X in Kenya in November 2009 in traumatic circumstances, and fled with him to Norway via Sweden in February 2010. She received refugee status and temporary residence. In 2010, while caring for X, she stayed at a parent-child institution. On 28 September 2010, the institution notified child welfare services that X was at risk of harm, that his life would have been in danger without staff protection, and that he was suffering. X was placed in emergency foster care. The municipality applied for a care order. The applicant opposed it and asked for placement with her cousin or in a Somali/Muslim foster home. On 10 December 2010, the County Social Welfare Board issued a care order, granted her contact of two hours four times yearly, and X was placed with a Christian family on 13 December 2010.

She appealed. On 6 September 2011, the District Court upheld the care order but reduced contact to one hour six times yearly. It referred to X’s cultural background but found his vulnerability and need for stability did not favour frequent contact. She did not appeal further.

On 11 September 2013, child welfare services applied to withdraw her parental responsibility and consent to adoption by the foster parents, alternatively to deny contact. The Board heard the case in February 2014 and on 21 March 2014 granted adoption consent. It found X so attached to the foster parents that removal could cause serious problems and that the applicant would be permanently unable to provide proper care. It considered adoption in his best interests for stability, security, healing and identity. The District Court upheld this on 21 November 2014.

Before the High Court in May 2015, the applicant accepted that X had become attached and that return was difficult. She accepted contact had caused reactions but argued future contact should remain possible because of his cultural and religious roots. On 27 May 2015, the High Court found it agreed that removing X would seriously harm him. X had lived with the foster parents since age one, about four and a half years, and had only lived with his mother for his first ten months. He regarded the foster parents as his parents and was strongly attached. He was vulnerable, with special needs and possible early attachment disorder, and had suffered serious practical and emotional neglect. Contact caused trauma reactions—screaming, agitation, anxiety—and he calmed after contact stopped in 2013. He needed stability and continuity.

The High Court noted adoption breached the biological principle; the foster parents refused open adoption; and there were religious/cultural issues: the mother was Muslim, the foster parents Christian, intending baptism and name change. It assumed no culturally similar foster home was available. Because X identified with the foster parents’ values, cultural and religious considerations carried less weight. The majority found particularly compelling reasons for adoption; the minority disagreed but would deny contact. The Supreme Court refused leave on 23 September 2015.

The alleged violations concerned the adoption order’s effect on family life and the child’s religious and cultural identity, including the proposed Christian baptism and name change.

**Summary of *Panteleiciuc v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 57468/08)**

The case originated from an application lodged on 27 November 2008 by Mr. Viorel Panteleiciuc, a Moldovan national and farmer, against both the Republic of Moldova and Russia. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights, concerning his arrest, detention, and subsequent administrative proceedings conducted by the authorities of the self-proclaimed "Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria" ("MRT"), a region outside the effective control of the Moldovan Government but alleged to be under Russian influence.

The key facts center on an incident on 5 February 2008. While selling potatoes in Varnița, a village under Moldovan control, the applicant was approached by plain-clothed officers of the "MRT" customs authority who demanded import tax documents. The applicant, who had paid taxes to Moldovan local authorities, was subsequently attacked, forced into a car, and abducted by "MRT" officers. His brother alerted the Moldovan police, who arrived after the abduction. The applicant's car and merchandise were later seized by the "MRT" customs authority, allegedly in the presence of a passive Moldovan police officer.

The following day, 6 February 2008, the Bender city court, an "MRT" judicial body, tried the applicant for resisting customs officers. The proceedings were fundamentally flawed. Despite being a Romanian speaker, the hearing was conducted in Russian, a language he understood poorly, and without an interpreter. He was denied the right to counsel of his choice for preparation and received no effective assistance from the court-appointed lawyer present only at the hearing. Furthermore, he was not provided with a copy of the arrest record before trial or a copy of the court's decision. He was convicted and sentenced to three days' detention, which he served immediately.

Crucially, the location of the alleged offense—the jurisdictional basis for the "MRT" proceedings—was disputed. The applicant maintained he was on Moldovan-controlled territory. The initial "MRT" first-instance decision was later quashed by the "MRT" Supreme Court on 18 March 2008 for failing to specify the location of the offense. However, the applicant was not informed of this development. On 25 April 2008, the "MRT" Supreme Court accepted an extraordinary appeal and decided to re-examine the case itself. The applicant was again not notified. He received a late fax on 27 May 2008 summoning him to a hearing that same day, which prevented his attendance. At that hearing, his appeal was rejected, with the court asserting he had been arrested in Bender city after disobeying "MRT" customs orders.

While the "MRT" proceedings were ongoing, the applicant pursued remedies with Moldovan authorities. His brother filed a criminal complaint on 6 February 2008 regarding the unlawful arrest. A Moldovan criminal investigation into the abduction began on 28 February 2008, during which witnesses identified "MRT" officers. However, the investigation was suspended on 28 August 2008 due to Moldovan authorities' inability to prosecute individuals on "MRT"-controlled territory. It was later resumed in 2013 but remained pending.

The applicant also sent complaints to various embassies, including Russia's, thanking them for intervening via the Joint Control Commission, which he believed led to the return of his car and merchandise. The core of the alleged violation is the unfairness of the administrative proceedings before the "MRT" court, over which the respondent states were alleged to bear responsibility.

In *Denis and Irvine v. Belgium*, the applicants were both subject to compulsory confinement imposed under Belgium’s old Social Protection Act of 9 April 1930. They complained that their continued detention after a change in legislation violated Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that they lacked effective remedies under Articles 5 § 4 and 13. The key legal issue arose because Belgium’s new Compulsory Confinement Act of 5 May 2014 entered into force on 1 October 2016, narrowing the criteria for compulsory confinement and introducing discharge rules, including final discharge after a three-year probationary period.

The first applicant, Jimmy Denis, a Belgian national, was placed in compulsory confinement by the Turnhout Criminal Court in 2007 for theft. A psychiatrist had described him as having a psychotic personality, alcohol and drug dependence, and a severe mental disturbance making him incapable of controlling his actions and dangerous to society and himself. He received conditional discharges but these were repeatedly revoked for non-compliance. After the new Act entered into force, he sought final discharge, arguing that theft could no longer justify compulsory confinement and that his detention was therefore no longer lawful under Article 5 § 1. On 25 January 2017, the Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court refused final discharge and maintained his placement in the social protection unit of Merksplas Prison. It found that the new Act did not apply retrospectively to old confinement orders and that final discharge required a sufficiently stable mental condition and completion of a minimum three-year conditional discharge period. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, holding that Article 7 did not apply to preventive measures, that Article 5 § 1 did not invalidate a final confinement order merely because the law changed during execution, and that current dangerousness had to be assessed in light of the applicant’s present mental condition and risk factors, not only the original offence. On 18 July 2017, he was again conditionally discharged to a psychiatric hospital in Zoersel.

The second applicant, Derek Irvine, a British national, was placed in compulsory confinement in 2002 for attempted aggravated burglary under the 1930 Act. A psychiatrist found him to suffer from a serious personality disorder and psychotic disorder, making him incapable of controlling his actions. He was conditionally discharged in 2003 to a Scottish psychiatric hospital, but escaped and was found in Belgium in 2010. He was returned to the psychiatric wing of Turnhout Prison. Efforts to place him in Scotland failed, and although the Antwerp Social Protection Committee ordered his placement in a forensic psychiatry centre in Ghent or Antwerp, no bed was available, so he remained in prison. In December 2016, he sought final discharge, raising the same arguments as Denis. A psychosocial report and psychiatrist noted ongoing schizophrenic symptoms treated with injections, and recommended continued confinement in a forensic centre. On 25 January 2017, the Antwerp Post-Sentencing Court maintained his confinement in Turnhout Prison pending a bed and dismissed his final discharge request on the same grounds as in Denis’s case. The Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal on 21 February 2017. He was later placed in the Antwerp forensic psychiatry centre in 2018.

Both applicants alleged that their detention was no longer lawful under Article 5 § 1 because their original offences could no longer lead to confinement under the new Act, and that the three-year probation requirement denied them access to a court capable of ordering immediate release, contrary to Articles 5 § 4 and 13. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 June 2021.

**Garumov v. Ukraine (Application no. 70043/17)**

The case of *Garumov v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged by Mr Magomedganipa Gadzhiyevych Garumov, a Russian national born in 1967, against Ukraine. The applicant was arrested on 1 June 2017 on suspicion of kidnapping and subsequently placed in pre-trial detention at the Kyiv SIZO (pre-trial detention centre). His application to the European Court of Human Rights raised two principal complaints: (1) the lack of adequate medical treatment while in detention, and (2) the authorities' failure to provide relevant and sufficient reasons justifying his continued pre-trial detention.

Regarding the first complaint, the applicant suffered from serious medical conditions, including ischemic heart disease and second-stage hypertension, for which he received treatment in the SIZO medical unit from July 2017. On 3 September 2017, he suffered a haemorrhagic stroke and was diagnosed with third-stage hypertension; he was hospitalised until 8 September 2017. Subsequent medical consultations with a neurologist and cardiologist recommended further in-patient treatment at a neurology-specialised facility, along with an MRT scan, massages, and rehabilitation exercises. A neurologist warned that without adequate treatment, another intracerebral haemorrhage and disability could result. On 21 September 2017, during a court hearing, the applicant fell unwell and was taken to hospital by ambulance. The District Court ordered the SIZO administration to ensure an urgent forensic examination. A forensic examination completed on 2 February 2018 concluded that the applicant suffered from cerebrovascular disease, acute stroke, discirculatory encephalopathy, and third-degree hypertension, and that further examination and in-patient treatment at a neurology-specialised facility were imperative. Despite a court order on 8 May 2018 allowing his transfer to a medical facility at his or his relatives' expense, the SIZO authorities required documentation confirming the facility's readiness to admit him. He was eventually transferred to Kyiv City Hospital No. 4 on 4 June 2018, discharged on 22 June 2018 with only insignificant improvement, and recognised as a category 2 disabled person on 5 July 2018.

Regarding the second complaint, the applicant's pre-trial detention was repeatedly extended by courts at both pre-trial and trial stages, including on 27 July, 22 and 28 September, and 15 and 29 November 2017, and later on 9 February, 28 March, 24 April, 13 June, 11 September, 7 November 2018, and 11 February 2019. The courts consistently cited the severity of the possible sanction, the need for additional investigative steps, and the persistence of risks of absconding or obstructing proceedings, but provided no further details or individualised reasoning. Some decisions also referenced the applicant's Russian nationality, lack of a permanent residence, social ties, and employment in Ukraine, and the fact that he had not surrendered his passport. Notably, on 29 November 2017, the court maintained non-custodial preventive measures for two co-accused. The applicant objected to the extensions, citing his poor health following a stroke, stable family relationships in Ukraine (a civil partner and two children born there), a permanent residence permit, and the fact that he had not attempted to abscond. He also applied for house arrest on several occasions. The courts did not address these arguments in their decisions.

**Medyanikov v. Ukraine** (Application no. 31694/06) is a European Court of Human Rights case lodged by Ukrainian national Eduard Valeryevich Medyanikov on 19 September 2006. The applicant was convicted by the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal on 25 November 2004 of several crimes and sentenced to life imprisonment with confiscation of property; the Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 23 February 2006 with certain changes. He had been detained since 26 August 2003 in various facilities, initially pending investigation and trial, and later after sentencing. At the relevant time he was serving his life sentence in Ladyzhynska colony no. 39. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government in 2011 and, in 2017, specifically notified the complaints under Articles 3 and 34 concerning alleged lack of adequate medical treatment in detention and alleged hindrance of the right of individual petition. The remainder of the application, including complaints about the fairness of the criminal proceedings, was declared inadmissible.

The admissible Article 3 complaint concerned the applicant’s medical treatment, particularly for tuberculosis and hepatitis C. On 25 January 2007, while detained in SIZO No. 5 in Donetsk, he was diagnosed with tuberculosis; other evidence indicated the diagnosis may have been made on 1 February 2007. After the criminal proceedings ended, he was transferred to Ladyzhynska colony on 16 March 2007. A preliminary examination on 20 March 2007, including laboratory tests and an X-ray, placed him under medical supervision for residual tuberculosis. According to the Government, he was regularly examined and treated by colony doctors between 20 March 2007 and 26 February 2018, and his health improved after each treatment course. However, the Government did not specify the frequency of examinations or the nature of treatment.

In December 2011 a blood test revealed hepatitis C. The applicant claimed he was denied copies of the test results. The Government stated that on 28 February 2012 a colony doctor diagnosed chronic persistent hepatitis in remission and prescribed treatment. On 16 May 2012, doctors from the Vinnytsya Regional Centre for HIV/AIDS Control and Prevention diagnosed hepatitis C in remission without hepatic impairment; symptomatic treatment was allegedly prescribed, but its nature was not specified. The Government also claimed the applicant received necessary medicine and a special diet, again without specifying frequency or content. From 23 February to 20 March 2015 he received treatment in a multi-disciplinary hospital in Stryzhavska colony no. 81, after which his health reportedly improved, though the treatment type was not described. As of 26 February 2018, he remained under colony doctors’ supervision and his health was described as satisfactory. The applicant therefore alleged that his detention lacked adequate medical care for tuberculosis and hepatitis C.

The Article 34 complaint concerned alleged interference with his right to submit an application to the Court. The applicant stated that he made numerous requests to domestic authorities, especially the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, for copies of documents needed to substantiate his Strasbourg application. Between August and November 2006 he requested a copy of his indictment; this was refused on 8 August and 6 September 2006, partly because he had already received it and because no legal requirement obliged the court to provide it. A copy was eventually sent on 21 July 2008. Between April and August 2009 he requested court records from his criminal case and his accomplice’s case; these were initially refused as lacking legal basis. On 10 September 2009 he made another request. On 2 October 2009 the Court of Appeal sent some copies but excluded court hearing records, saying their transmission was not covered by then-applicable legislation. On 21 April 2011 the Government Agent’s Office sent the hearing records. In January 2017 the Court of Appeal refused his requests for a copy of his request to extend the cassation appeal time-limit and a copy of the 26 October 2016 ruling dismissing that request, stating the case file had been sent to the Higher Specialised Court for Civil and Criminal Matters. The applicant never received those documents. These facts formed the basis of his alleged hindrance of the right of individual petition.

In *Ifandiev v. Bulgaria*, the applicant, a Bulgarian journalist and writer, complained under Article 10 of the Convention about domestic defamation proceedings brought by K.T., a prominent politician and trade-union leader. In 2003 the applicant published a book, *The Shadow of Zion*, discussing Judaism, Zionism, Freemasonry and their alleged impact on world history. On pages 69–70, after comparing communists and Nazis to Freemasons, the text stated that after the “democratic changes” many communists and people connected with their secret services had become Freemasons. A list of names followed, including K.T., described as a “pseudo trade unionist.” A footnote cited a 2002 article by another author.

In September 2005 K.T. brought a tort action, alleging that the book falsely defamed him by presenting him as a Freemason, a communist connected with the former secret services, and a pseudo trade unionist. K.T. said he was a fervent Orthodox Christian, had never been a member of the Communist Party or its youth organisation, had no secret-service links, and had fought for human rights and democracy. He claimed the allegations humiliated him, harmed his national and international prestige, and caused non-pecuniary damage.

The applicant defended his statements, arguing that he had relied on earlier publications, including the one cited in the footnote. He also claimed K.T. had said he was a member of the Maltese Order, intended to prove secret-service connections through witnesses, and asserted that K.T. had bragged about links to leading communist figures. The applicant argued the expressions were not offensive or defamatory and that no damage had been shown. He was legally represented throughout.

In July 2008 the Sofia City Court allowed K.T.’s action and ordered the applicant to pay BGN 15,000 (about EUR 7,670) in moral damages plus default interest. Although it referred to Article 10, it found the applicant had exceeded acceptable criticism. It held the allegations untrue: Freemasonry contradicted K.T.’s Orthodox faith; secret-service links were disproved by official archive attestations and unconvincing witnesses; and “pseudo trade unionist” was a gratuitous offence aimed at discrediting him. The court treated insult as subjective, so K.T.’s feeling offended sufficed. It found serious harm to his honour and dignity within the trade-union community and internationally, aggravated by health problems and hospitalisation.

The Sofia Court of Appeal upheld the judgment in October 2009. It added that even if K.T. had mentioned the Maltese Order, the applicant had not shown this was equivalent to Freemasonry; earlier publications did not make the allegations less defamatory or truer; and K.T.’s status as a public figure justified higher damages. In August 2010 the Supreme Court of Cassation refused to accept the applicant’s appeal on points of law, confirming that whether an allegation is offensive depends on how the addressee and his social circle perceive it, even if that perception does not conform to common understanding of the facts.

K.T. later instituted enforcement proceedings. In October 2011 a bailiff calculated the total due at BGN 31,549 (about EUR 16,100), including principal, interest and costs. Enforcement was discontinued in 2016 after K.T. abandoned payment attempts; only BGN 4.55 (EUR 2.32) had been seized.

After the application was communicated, the applicant published blog comments in June 2018 accusing the Government Agent of lies and offensive language and making insulting remarks about Bulgarian judges and the Court. Notice of the freedom-of-expression complaint was given to the Government on 22 January 2018; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

**Summary of Balsamo v. San Marino (Applications nos. 20319/17 and 21414/17)**

The case of *Balsamo v. San Marino* concerns two Italian nationals, Ms. Valentina Balsamo and Ms. Angela Balsamo, who lodged applications against the Republic of San Marino with the European Court of Human Rights. Their central complaint was that a confiscation order was imposed upon them following their acquittal, which they argued was unlawful and disproportionate, violating Articles 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence), 7 § 1 (no punishment without law), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property).

The case originated from a criminal investigation in San Marino into money laundering activities allegedly involving the applicants and their father, identified as "B." The prosecution claimed the assets laundered, totaling approximately EUR 2,150,000, were proceeds from multiple offences committed by B. in Italy.

In July 2011, the investigating judge seized a current account, a bonds account, and a safe deposit box registered in the first applicant's name, with a total value of EUR 1,920,785.50. The prosecution alleged these funds were of criminal origin. The applicants and their father had deposited large sums of cash into these accounts between 2004 and 2008, with B. depositing EUR 950,000 in 2006. Information from Italian authorities in January 2012 indicated B. had a prior conviction for theft and receiving stolen goods, with the proceeds assessed at EUR 750,000.

In November 2014, the first-instance criminal judge found both applicants guilty of money laundering. The judge relied on "reasonable evidence" of the money's criminal origin, citing B.'s extensive criminal record, the disproportion between the applicants' legitimate income and the seized assets, their contradictory explanations regarding the funds' origin, and the use of foreign bank accounts to hide the money. The court sentenced the applicants and ordered the confiscation of the seized EUR 1,920,785.50, plus an additional EUR 499,000 from the first applicant for funds withdrawn before seizure.

However, on appeal in October 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals acquitted both applicants for lack of evidence demonstrating *mens rea*, as it was not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that they were aware of the assets' criminal origin, especially given their youth. Despite the acquittal, the appeal judge noted the money's criminal origin was established due to the absence of any licit explanation and upheld the confiscation order, characterising it as a preventive measure rather than punitive.

The applicants then sought revision before the judge for extraordinary remedies in January 2017, arguing the judgment breached their Convention rights. The judge rejected their request in May 2017, concluding the confiscation was lawful, proportionate, and preventive, as the funds had an illicit origin established in fair proceedings, and "crime cannot pay."

The applicants alleged before the Strasbourg Court that the confiscation, applied despite their acquittal, violated the presumption of innocence. They also argued it was not "in accordance with the law" and was disproportionate. They further complained about the lack of an effective remedy under Article 13. The case raises significant questions about the interplay between acquittal, the presumption of innocence, and the imposition of preventive confiscation measures.

The case *Kožul and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 38695/13) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 20 April 2013 by five Bosnian nationals: Ivan, Dinko, Dražen, Petar and Ruža Kožul. They live in the vicinity of Široki Brijeg. The applicants complained about the authorities’ prolonged failure to enforce a final demolition order concerning industrial buildings erected illegally next to their homes. On 10 July 2017, the Government were given notice of the complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The relevant domestic facts began on 4 February 2002, when the local authorities ordered a private company, Paškić d.o.o. Široki Brijeg, to demolish its industrial buildings. The buildings had been erected illegally next to the applicants’ homes. The decision became enforceable on 18 April 2002. However, it was not enforced.
