text:
In *Berardi and Mularoni v. San Marino* (Applications nos. 24705/16 and 24818/16), the applicants, Paolo Berardi and Davide Mularoni, were San Marino nationals and public officials responsible for construction-site safety supervision. A parliamentary commission investigating organised crime found evidence of entrenched corruption involving companies linked to “B,” a notary and lawyer. The commission reported that construction companies bribed safety officials to avoid compulsory inspections. The applicants were charged with the continuing offence of bribery under Articles 50, 73 and 373 of the Criminal Code, in particular for periodically receiving cash payments to omit safety checks, refrain from sanctioning violations, and give favourable treatment to companies controlled by B. They were charged in respect of events up to 1 January 2010. Evidence included witness statements, bank deposits by the applicants during 2005–2012, and testimony about brief meetings with a company administrator.

In 2014, the first-instance judge convicted both applicants of direct bribery under Article 373 § 1. They received five years and six months’ imprisonment, a four-year prohibition on public office and political rights, and a €25,000 fine. The judge found that B was the de facto dominus of the companies and had directed bribes to avoid safety checks. Because the applicants exercised discretionary powers and deliberately violated their duties, the conduct was classified as direct bribery.

On appeal, the applicants argued that the law had been applied retroactively, contrary to Article 7 of the Convention. Before Law No. 92 of 17 June 2008, they claimed, there was no offence of “bribery inducing omission”—that is, paying an official to omit or delay a legitimate act. At most, their conduct constituted indirect bribery, which carried a lighter penalty. The 2008 amendment expressly added omission or delay of duty, and payment after a past omission, to Article 373 § 1. Since it entered into force three months after publication, they argued it could not cover pre-2008 facts.

The Judge of Criminal Appeals upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to five years’ imprisonment, a four-and-a-half-year public-office ban, and a €20,000 fine. It reasoned that the bribery was a single continuing offence based on one corrupt pact between B and the applicants, renewed by each payment. Because it was a continuing offence, an amendment to the law during the period of the offence could apply to the whole offence. Alternatively, the applicants had not merely omitted duties; they had also carried out acts contrary to their office and shown general favouritism, conduct already covered by the old Article 373 § 1. The court concluded that the 2008 amendment did not create a new crime but only gave a more serious legal classification to existing criminal conduct.

The applicants alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that the criminal law had been applied retroactively to their disadvantage. The Chamber joined the applications, communicated the Article 7 complaint to the Government, and declared the remainder inadmissible. The key issue was whether convicting the applicants for pre-2008 conduct—especially omission-based bribery—violated the prohibition on retroactive criminal liability and harsher penalties. The domestic legal framework included Article 3 on non-retroactivity, Article 55 on the time of commission for continuing offences, and the pre- and post-2008 versions of Article 373. The Court therefore had to examine whether the domestic courts’ continuing-offence reasoning and their reliance on the old Article 373 were compatible with Article 7.

In *Yakuba v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national with prior drug-related convictions, complained under Article 3 that police ill-treated him during arrest; under Article 6 that he could not examine the video recording of an undercover drug purchase or examine the undercover agent; and under Article 34 that the authorities refused to provide copies of documents needed for his application to the European Court.

The case arose from an undercover test-purchase operation. P., apparently a private individual recruited by police as an undercover agent, was given cash before attesting witnesses and, out of their sight, allegedly made three drug purchases from the applicant on 26 February and 6 and 9 March 2007. The first purchase was video-recorded by hidden camera. On 9 March 2007 the applicant was arrested. Police pushed him to the ground and handcuffed him. The applicant alleged that after he was immobilised they continued to drag him around, causing pain and humiliation. He initially admitted having a drug-filled syringe in his sleeve and trying to destroy the drug during arrest, later denying possession of the syringe but still admitting buying drugs for personal use that day. The arresting officers reported that force was used because he tried to destroy evidence.

On 15 March 2007 his lawyer requested a medical examination, alleging beatings during arrest and later at a police station. A medical expert found abrasions on his right hand, shin and both knees, possibly sustained on 9 March; leg abrasions could have resulted from a fall. On 8 May 2007 prosecutors refused to open criminal proceedings against the police. The applicant did not appeal that refusal but continued to raise ill-treatment before the criminal courts, which rejected his complaints as unsubstantiated and held that force during arrest was lawful and the prosecutors had properly examined the matter.

As to the fair-trial complaint, on 20 April 2007 an investigator viewed the video with witnesses and recorded that it showed the applicant selling drugs to P. The applicant’s lawyer asked to watch it, but on 27 April 2007 the investigator refused, citing protection of P.’s identity. P. was questioned pre-trial. The indictment listed P. as a trial witness and the video report as evidence. During trial the applicant asked for the video to be disclosed and for P., a possible defence witness B., and a forensic expert to be examined. Those requests were refused for unknown reasons. On 26 June 2007 he was convicted of drug trafficking and sentenced to eight years, based largely on police and attesting-witness testimony, P.’s pre-trial statements, a banknote found on him, and forensic traces. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 25 March 2008, also relying on the investigator’s video report, and the Supreme Court refused cassation review on 4 September 2008.

Finally, while preparing his European Court application, the applicant asked the trial court for copies of procedural documents. On 10 October 2008 the trial court refused, saying domestic law provided no procedure for a convict to examine a case file after criminal proceedings ended. Similar refusals followed in 2009 and 2013, and the Court of Appeal gave a similar response in October 2008. These facts formed the basis of his Article 34 complaint that Ukraine obstructed his right to individual application.

**Case: Antonov and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia**  
(Applications nos. 315/10, 1153/10, 1158/10)  
European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, Judgment of 2 July 2019.

The case concerned six Moldovan, Russian and Ukrainian nationals detained in the Transdniestrian region of Moldova under the de facto authority of the “MRT”. The applicants alleged serious violations arising from their arrest, detention conditions, ill-treatment and denial of contact with relatives in facilities controlled by the “MRT” authorities, including IVS Tiraspol and Hlinaia prison in Grigoriopol. The Russian Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

In Application no. 315/10, Evghenii Antonov, a Russian national, was arrested in Tiraspol in August 2009 and accused of possessing a hunter’s knife and marijuana. He was held initially at IVS Tiraspol and later moved to Hlinaia prison. Shortly after arrest, he told Iryna Antonova that he was in a dark, damp cell lacking basic hygiene. She was refused permission to see him. On 19 October 2009, the OSCE was refused access to IVS Tiraspol, where about 90 detainees, including Antonov, were on hunger strike protesting ill-treatment and inhuman detention conditions. Complaints to Moldovan, Russian and “MRT” authorities were unsuccessful. Antonova saw him briefly at a court hearing in December 2009 and said he appeared tired and weak. He was convicted in November 2010, with proceedings pending before the “MRT” Supreme Court.

In Application no. 1153/10, Alexandru Băluţă, a Moldovan national, was arrested in Tiraspol in December 2004 and accused of murder and arson. He alleged he was severely beaten. Released in 2007, he left to work abroad and was rearrested in September 2009. He was held at IVS Tiraspol and then Hlinaia prison. He allegedly endured a dark, damp cell without basic hygiene or daily walks. His mother, Tamara Băluţă, claimed food and items she sent, except bread, did not reach him, and all requests to visit were refused. She learned in October 2009 that many detainees were on hunger strike against abuse and inhuman conditions. She alleged that on 16 October 2009 riot police entered the prison and beat prisoners. The OSCE was again refused access on 19 October 2009. Complaints to Moldovan, Russian and “MRT” authorities were unsuccessful. The “MRT” prosecutor’s office replied that investigators were not obliged to authorise detainee meetings with relatives and that visits had been refused, without further reasons.

In Application no. 1158/10, Oleksandr Bezrodnii, a Ukrainian national and NGO leader, was arrested in Tiraspol on 23 July 2009, accused of stealing roses and endangering militia officers and security agents. He was held at IVS Tiraspol and later Hlinaia. On 29 July 2009, Liudmila Bezrodnyaya saw him at court with blood on his face, a green substance on his head and bruises; he said he was being ill-treated to obtain self-incriminating statements. A court ordered his detention for an undetermined period. In September 2009 he described a basement cell with no daylight, shared with persons having HIV and tuberculosis, insufficient beds, one shower a month, a rarely cleaned toilet in the cell, dampness, no ventilation, parasitic insects, almost no hygiene products, inedible mouldy food and no medical assistance despite injuries. Food and items sent by Bezrodnyaya were rejected or destroyed. In October 2009, prison staff warned that riot police would be called if the hunger strike continued. A Moldovan anti-torture committee member reported ill-treatment and hunger strike, and the “MRT” Justice Minister admitted overcrowding in pre-trial detention centres. The OSCE was refused access. Bezrodnii later complained he had been severely beaten at arrest, with bruises, hematomas, head blows and a swollen leg requiring medical attention. He was convicted in July 2010, but the sentence was quashed and sent for re-examination.

The common factual core concerns alleged inhuman and degrading detention conditions, ill-treatment, denial of family visits and food parcels, obstruction of monitoring, and ineffective complaints to Moldovan, Russian and “MRT” authorities.

J.D. and A v. the United Kingdom concerned two British women whose Housing Benefit was reduced under the 2012 Housing Benefit (Amendment) Regulations, often called the “bedroom tax.” They alleged that the reduction discriminated against them contrary to Article 14 ECHR, taken with Article 8 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, on grounds of disability (J.D.) and gender/sex (A).

The scheme, Regulation B13, reduced Housing Benefit for social-sector tenants deemed to have more bedrooms than they needed: by 14% for one extra bedroom and 25% for two or more. Claimants could seek temporary Discretionary Housing Payments (DHPs) to cover shortfalls, but these were discretionary, cash-limited, and uncertain.

First applicant J.D. had lived since 1993 in a three-bedroom social rented house with her adult daughter, who has severe brain damage from oxygen deprivation, profound physical and learning disabilities, is a wheelchair user and registered blind. J.D. cares for her full-time. The house had been specially adapted to meet her daughter’s needs, including wide doors, an internal lift, ramps, ceiling hoists, an accessible bathroom and a changing bed. Because the household comprised two people in a three-bedroom home, J.D.’s Housing Benefit was cut by 14%, leaving a rent shortfall. DHPs were awarded only temporarily; her last award expired in March 2017, and no suitable smaller adapted accommodation was available. Her complaint was that the reduction discriminated on grounds of disability by failing to recognise her daughter’s need for the adapted home and by relying on discretionary payments.

Second applicant A had lived for over 25 years in a three-bedroom social rented house with her son. She had been allocated the larger house because of a shortage of smaller accommodation. A had been raped by a violent former partner, X, who had served a long prison sentence for attempted murder and continued to threaten her; her son was conceived as a result of the rape. Under a Sanctuary Scheme, her home was fortified and adapted with a “panic room,” security monitoring, police flagging and multi-agency support. Her Housing Benefit was also reduced by 14% for under-occupation. A received temporary DHPs, but in 2015 a refusal led to an eviction threat; the Secretary of State intervened and the local authority reversed the decision, accepting it had failed to consider the adaptations. A alleged sex/gender discrimination: the reduction jeopardised her ability to remain in the only safe, specially adapted home, and DHPs were not adequate protection.

In domestic proceedings, courts accepted prima facie discrimination on disability and sex, but the Supreme Court ultimately dismissed both claims. It applied the “manifestly without reasonable foundation” test to welfare policy and held that the Secretary of State could reasonably rely on DHPs for exceptional needs rather than creating exemptions in Regulation B13. The Strasbourg applications therefore asked the European Court to determine whether the benefit reduction violated Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8 and/or Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key factual issue was whether the applicants’ disability-related and gender-based safety needs made the under-occupancy deduction unjustifiably discriminatory.

**Summary of *Sanchyshyn v. Ukraine* (Application no. 81639/17)**

The case of *Sanchyshyn v. Ukraine* originated from an application lodged against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Bogdan Ivanovych Sanchyshyn, born on 31 October 1970, was represented by Mr O.V. Mytsyk, a lawyer based in Lviv. The application was introduced on 24 November 2017, and notice was subsequently given to the Ukrainian Government.

The central facts of the case concern the duration of criminal proceedings initiated against the applicant. According to the appended table, the proceedings began on 31 August 2009 and concluded on 25 May 2017. This amounted to a total length of 7 years, 8 months, and 26 days, spanning two levels of jurisdiction.

The applicant’s primary complaints before the ECtHR were twofold: first, that the length of the criminal proceedings against him was excessive, and second, that there was no effective remedy available in domestic law to address this delay. These complaints engage Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial within a reasonable time) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention. The applicant also raised other complaints under various provisions of the Convention; however, the judgment focuses on the excessive length and lack of effective remedy claims, as these were the grounds upon which the case was communicated to the Government.

The Court, sitting as a Committee of the Fifth Section, deliberated on 14 February 2019 and delivered its judgment on 7 March 2019. The judgment was adopted on the date of delivery and is final, though subject to editorial revision.

In its assessment, the Court would have considered the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant and the authorities, and what was at stake for the applicant. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the protracted duration of the criminal proceedings—over seven and a half years—and the absence of a domestic mechanism to challenge or remedy this delay. The proceedings spanned two jurisdictional levels, indicating that the case underwent review or appeal, further extending the timeline.

The Government did not present sufficient justification for the delay, and the Court likely found a violation of Article 6 § 1 due to the excessive length. Regarding Article 13, the Court would have examined whether Ukrainian law provided an effective remedy for the length complaint. If no such remedy existed or was accessible, a violation of Article 13 would also be found.

This case is emblematic of a broader pattern of similar applications against Ukraine concerning judicial delays and the lack of effective domestic remedies, which the ECtHR has addressed in numerous judgments. The facts here are straightforward: a criminal case that lasted nearly eight years across two instances, with the applicant arguing that this duration was unreasonable and that he had no means to expedite or obtain compensation for the delay at the national level.

The judgment in *Sanchyshyn v. Ukraine* thus rests on these core factual elements—the lengthy criminal proceedings and the absence of a domestic remedy—which form the basis for the alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention. The Court’s findings would typically include a declaration of violation and, where appropriate, an award of just satisfaction under Article 41, though the full text of the judgment would specify such details. For the purpose of this summary, the essential facts relevant to the violations are the extended duration of the proceedings and the ineffective domestic remedy, which are sufficient to establish the context of the case.

text:
In *Clasens v. Belgium*, the applicant, John Clasens, a Belgian national born in 1983, was serving a final criminal sentence in Ittre Prison when a prison staff strike affected Brussels and Wallonia from 25 April to 22 June 2016. Because Belgian law at the time did not guarantee minimum prison services during strikes, ordinary detention regimes were suspended to varying degrees. Ittre Prison had 386 prisoners and 420 places; most cells were single-occupancy, about 9 m², with a wash basin and partitioned toilet.

From 26 April 2016, the regime at Ittre deteriorated sharply. According to a 3 May 2016 urgent order by the President of the Walloon Brabant Court of First Instance, prisoners had telephone calls only on 26, 29 and 30 April and 1 May; showers on 27 and 29 April and 1 May; exercise on 28 and 30 April; healthcare and medicines continued normally; but there were no family visits. Pickets blocked food-delivery lorries, raising the prospect that food supplies would stop by 5 May. The applicant and other prisoners brought an urgent application under Article 584 of the Judicial Code, alleging that these conditions violated Article 3 of the Convention. The judge partly granted relief, ordering the State to provide three meals per day, one hot; showers every other day; phone access every other day; two family visits per week; and access for lawyers and the Supervisory Board, subject to a €10,000 fine per infringement.

The State sought further court orders prohibiting blockades at prison entrances and mobilised police, prison directorates, civil protection, the Red Cross and the army. The CPT visited Ittre from 7 to 9 May 2016. It reported limited access to showers, medicines for anxiety and stress, collective exercise once a week, 24-hour cell confinement, interrupted canteen supplies, no cleaning or hygiene products, no visits, and insufficient staff to top up telephone accounts. After the strike ended, the Ittre Prison Supervisory Board found on 23 June 2016 that prisoners had had no lawyer visits before 16 June, almost no family visits, only one meal per day, telephone contact about every three days, and until 16 June left their cells only once every three days for exercise or a shower. No other activities were provided. A 25 May 2016 unannounced visit noted staff presence varying from 4 to 20, with police reinforcements and a night regime.

On appeal, the Brussels Court of Appeal largely upheld the 3 May 2016 order by judgment of 26 April 2017, though it reduced the fines to a maximum of €250 per day. Applying *Vasilescu v. Belgium* and *Muršić v. Croatia*, it found a prima facie breach of Article 3: prisoners were treated as objects at the mercy of striking staff, uncertain when the strike would end, confined to cells without activities, deprived of family and lawyer contact, and exposed to distress exceeding the suffering inherent in imprisonment.

Enforcement difficulties continued, and the applicant forwarded an order to pay outstanding fines; the State appealed. No minimum-service legislation existed during the strike, although a new Act of 23 March 2019 was adopted to guarantee minimum services from 1 July 2019. The CPT later issued a public statement describing the 2016 strikes as crossing a “red line” and creating conditions that could amount to inhuman or degrading treatment. The applicant alleged that his detention conditions violated Article 3 and that he lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

In *Oddone and Pecci v. San Marino* (Applications nos. 26581/17 and 31024/17), two Italian nationals—Mr David Oddone, a journalist, and Mr Alessandro Pecci, a lawyer—complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention that they were denied the opportunity to cross-examine two co-accused, G. and L., who had given incriminating statements against them.

The case arose from a San Marino police investigation into suspicious car accidents believed to be staged for insurance fraud. Oddone had been involved in three accidents over three and a half years; one charge was later dropped. On 6 and 12 July 2012, police questioned G. and L. as witnesses, without counsel. Initially, both described ordinary accidents, but then retracted and admitted the accidents had been simulated. G. said Oddone planned the fraud and later paid him EUR 2,000. L. said Pecci recruited her and that Oddone paid her about EUR 5,000.

On 31 August 2012, the investigating judge questioned G. and L. with counsel present, but without the applicants. They confirmed their earlier statements. The investigation file had been classified on 6 August 2012 and was not declassified until 29 November 2013. The applicants were only informed of the charges in December 2013 and summoned for questioning in February 2014. Through counsel, they requested that the investigation be reopened so they could cross-examine G. and L. On 26 February 2014, the investigating judge refused. She reasoned, among other things, that co-accused persons could not participate in the questioning of other co-accused; that only statements made before her had been used; and that the investigation was sufficient. The same day, the applicants were indicted.

At trial, G. and L. were themselves co-accused, not prosecution witnesses; the prosecution witness list named only police officer P. The applicants again objected that their defence rights had been violated because they had never been able to question G. and L. The trial judge rejected their requests to reopen the investigation or cross-examine G. and L. In August 2015, all accused were convicted. Oddone received two years and five months’ imprisonment; Pecci and the others received two years. The judgment relied on G. and L.’s statements but also cited other elements, including anomalies in the accidents and phone records.

On appeal, the applicants repeated that the classified investigation and inability to confront G. and L. breached their defence rights. In October 2016, the Judge of Criminal Appeals upheld the convictions, holding that domestic law did not require exclusion of evidence collected without adversarial examination; admissibility depended on the judge’s free assessment. L.’s offence was later declared time-barred after a reduced penalty for a “useful and spontaneous confession.” A subsequent extraordinary/revision request by Oddone was rejected in January 2019.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants’ core complaint was that G. and L.’s incriminating statements were used against them even though they had never had an opportunity, at the investigation or trial stage, to cross-examine them as witnesses. The key alleged violation therefore concerned the lack of adversarial confrontation with co-accused whose statements helped establish the fraud charges.

Keaney v. Ireland concerned an Irish national, Vincent Keaney, who complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the delay of eleven years between commencing his civil proceedings and the final judgment violated the “reasonable time” requirement. The case was also communicated together with others raising similar delay complaints, with a specific question whether Ireland provided an effective domestic remedy under Article 13 for such Article 6 delay.

Factually, in 1996 Keaney used lottery winnings to buy the Scotts Building in Cobh, intending to run it as the Titanic Bar and Restaurant. He bought an intoxicating liquor licence and began renovations. Structural defects exhausted his funds, and further borrowing proved insufficient. He sought advice from J.S., a financial consultant, who introduced M.N., a publican. Around 2000, Keaney and M.N. entered a series of agreements: the premises were assigned to them as tenants in common in equal shares; TQTC was incorporated with Keaney holding 49% and M.N. 51%; the premises were leased to TQTC and the liquor licence transferred. Relations deteriorated, TQTC traded until December 2002 and failed, and a July 2003 attempt to separate their interests through “heads of agreement” and further transactions also failed. M.N. ultimately took possession of the premises.

On 8 February 2006, Keaney issued High Court plenary proceedings against eighteen defendants, alleging deceit, fraud, misrepresentation and undue influence arising from the 2000–2003 transactions, and seeking to set those transactions aside. The case was admitted to the Commercial List on 3 April 2006. From the outset, the pleadings were poorly particularised. The High Court repeatedly ordered amended statements of claim. Defendants brought motions to strike out all or part of the claims. On 16 January 2007, the High Court struck out claims against numerous defendants and limited claims against others; further strike-outs followed in March 2007. By early 2007, claims against fourteen of the eighteen defendants had been struck out. Keaney delivered several further amended statements, some of which the High Court found non-compliant or nonsensical, while allowing final opportunities to amend. A final statement of claim was delivered on 1 July 2008. On 19 December 2008, the High Court dismissed all remaining claims, finding Keaney had failed and that aspects of his case bordered on abuse of process.

Keaney issued notices of appeal between February 2007 and February 2009. Appellate progress was then extremely slow. In February 2014, the Supreme Court directed books of appeal within four weeks; they were filed in March 2014. In March 2015, the respondents said the books were incomplete, and the Supreme Court made a peremptory order. Submissions were eventually filed in June 2015. The first appeal was heard on 24 June 2015 and judgment delivered on 23 July 2015, upholding the strike-out and criticising unsubstantiated allegations as an abuse of process. In the second appeal, the Supreme Court in September 2014 required books or dismissal; later, in March 2016, it directed submissions within six to eight weeks, but Keaney filed only in February 2017. That appeal was heard on 28 February 2017 and judgment delivered on 5 April 2017, finding no basis to overturn the High Court. A third appeal was not pursued.

The alleged Article 6 § 1 violation was therefore the cumulative delay from institution on 8 February 2006 to final judgment on 5 April 2017. As to Article 13, Irish law recognised a constitutional right to reasonable expedition and possible damages, and the ECHR Act allowed damages where no other remedy existed. However, following McFarlane v. Ireland, the Committee of Ministers found that Ireland still lacked an effective remedy for excessive length, despite proposed legislation. These facts framed Keaney’s complaint that the lengthy proceedings lacked an effective domestic remedy.

**Case A.S. v. Norway** (Application no. 60371/15) concerned a Polish national, A.S., living in Norway, and her son X, born in December 2009 after artificial insemination. X had no registered father, and A.S. had sole parental responsibility. From April 2010, when X was under four months old, child welfare services received numerous notifications from health visitors and family members alleging a lack of interaction between A.S. and X. After attempts at assistance and guidance failed, X was placed in an emergency foster home on 27 March 2012, aged two years and three months.

On 18 September 2012, the County Social Welfare Board ordered that X be placed in long-term foster care, finding pervasive and extensive deficiencies in A.S.’s caregiving and serious neglect of X’s physical and emotional needs. Contact rights were set at two hours twice a year under supervision, later reduced to one hour twice a year. The Board indicated that the placement was intended to be long-term, so contact was meant only to let X know his origins, not to maintain an attachment or prepare for reunification. The City Court confirmed the care order on 25 February 2013.

In spring 2014, A.S. sought termination of the foster placement or, alternatively, extended contact. On 5 November 2014, the County Social Welfare Board rejected her request after a two-day hearing with eleven witnesses. It denied her contact rights and also decided she should not be informed of X’s whereabouts. A.S. brought the case to the City Court, which heard fourteen witnesses, including her GP, psychiatrist, a counsellor, and two privately engaged psychologists. The court refused to appoint its own expert or to allow the private experts to observe A.S. and X together.

In its judgment of 27 March 2015, the City Court found that A.S. would not be able to provide X with proper care at that time or in the future. It relied heavily on X’s vulnerability and special needs. Before entering care, X had shown low cognitive, motor and linguistic functioning, emotional flatness, eating problems, compulsive behaviour, and excessive sleep needs, with possible autism-spectrum symptoms. After placement, he improved significantly and formed a secure attachment to his foster parents, whom he called mum and dad. An expert testified that X had suffered relational and developmental trauma while in his mother’s care, leaving him highly vulnerable to change and stress. Returning him to A.S. would seriously jeopardise his mental health. The court also found A.S.’s basic intuitive parenting skills remained inadequate and that courses and work experience had not changed this. Contact sessions showed she still could not see X’s perspective, and X had severe reactions after contact, especially in November 2014, including regression, bed-wetting, and retching, lasting two months. The court therefore denied contact, finding exceptional and strong reasons because the risk of harm to X outweighed A.S.’s interests. It also withheld the foster parents’ address, concluding that although kidnapping risk was not substantiated, A.S. would likely make unannounced contact, causing disproportionate harm to X.

The High Court refused leave to appeal on 22 May 2015, and the Supreme Court’s Committee on Leave to Appeal rejected her appeal on 3 July 2015. A.S. alleged that the refusal to terminate foster care, the denial of contact, and the withholding of information about X’s whereabouts violated her and X’s right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention.

**Case Summary: Živanović and Others v. Serbia (Application nos. 29171/16 and 8 others)**

The case of *Živanović and Others v. Serbia* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) by nine Serbian nationals. The applications, lodged between May 2016 and January 2017, all shared a common complaint: the excessive length of civil proceedings in violation of their right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were represented by a single lawyer, Ms. R. Dugošija.

The key facts of the case revolve around the prolonged duration of civil litigation for each applicant, which occurred across two or three levels of jurisdiction. The proceedings for the majority of the applicants began in 2005 or 2006 and concluded in 2013, with total lengths ranging from approximately six years and eight months to nearly eight years.

The specific details for each applicant are as follows:

- **Bogoljub Živanović:** Proceedings lasted from 20 September 2005 to 22 May 2013, a total of 7 years, 8 months, and 3 days. The case went through two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Zoran Stojković:** Proceedings lasted from 11 January 2006 to 5 June 2013, a total of 7 years, 4 months, and 26 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Mileta Joksimović and Dragan Tabaković:** Both applicants' proceedings lasted from 8 September 2005 to 21 August 2013, a total of 7 years, 11 months, and 14 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Goran Jolić:** Proceedings lasted from 28 August 2006 to 8 May 2013, a total of 6 years, 8 months, and 11 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Siniša Savković:** Proceedings lasted from 3 October 2005 to 20 February 2013, a total of 7 years, 4 months, and 18 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.
- **Dragan Savić and Ljubiša Đorđević:** These applicants had the longest proceedings, lasting from 8 September 2005 to 3 June 2016. This amounted to a total of 10 years, 8 months, and 27 days, spanning three levels of jurisdiction.
- **Vene Aleksov:** Proceedings lasted from 8 September 2005 to 23 October 2013, a total of 8 years, 1 month, and 16 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.

In all nine cases, the applicants sought redress at the national level by lodging a constitutional appeal with the Serbian Constitutional Court. However, in every instance, between November 2015 and September 2016, the Constitutional Court declared their appeals inadmissible.

The applicants subsequently turned to the ECtHR, alleging that the Serbian judicial system had failed to ensure their cases were heard within a "reasonable time," as required by Article 6 of the Convention. The ECtHR's judgment, delivered on 19 September 2019, addressed these common grievances regarding the systemic issue of judicial delays in Serbia.

Fil LLC v. Armenia (Application no. 18526/13, judgment of 31 January 2019) concerned an Armenian construction company’s complaint that civil proceedings against a debtor were excessively long and that Armenia provided no effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The applicant, Fil LLC, contracted with company S. on 7 May 2007 to carry out construction work on premises owned by company H. Claiming that it had completed the work but had not been fully paid, Fil LLC initiated compensation proceedings against company S. in the Yerevan Civil Court on 18 January 2008. The claim was admitted on 21 January 2008.

The main source of delay was a repeated forensic technical examination. On 20 February 2008, the Civil Court ordered an expert examination of the construction work and stayed the proceedings. The expert soon stated that he needed access to company H’s premises, but H was not a party to the case. On 4 April 2008 the court resumed the proceedings and summoned H as a third party. On 15 May 2008 it ordered the same examination again and stayed the case. On 28 October 2008, the expert reported that he still could not access H’s premises and therefore could not conduct the examination. The court resumed the case and, on 19 February 2009, granted Fil LLC’s claim.

Company S. appealed. On 23 April 2009 the Civil Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and remitted the case, essentially because there was no expert opinion on the disputed construction work. The case was later transferred to the Shengavit District Court of Yerevan. The same pattern continued: on 26 August 2009 the District Court ordered a forensic examination and stayed proceedings; on 31 May 2010 the expert again reported that lack of access to H’s premises made examination impossible. The court resumed on 7 June 2010, but on 16 July 2010 ordered another examination, this time with assistance from the Department for Enforcement of Judicial Acts, and stayed proceedings again. On 21 June 2012, another expert concluded that access to H’s premises was still lacking. The court resumed on 27 June 2012, and on 3 October 2012 ordered yet another examination and stayed the case.

The examination then remained pending for years. In late 2014, Fil LLC wrote to the Bureau of Forensic Examinations. The Bureau replied that the examination had not been carried out because no qualified expert was available, but said experts had been recruited and the examination was expected in January 2015. Fil LLC complained again in February 2015 and then wrote to the Ministry of Justice in May 2015 about the delay. The Minister replied that although the examination itself would take about one day and the report about five days, it had not been done because of the lack of an expert, difficulty accessing H’s premises, and the Bureau’s workload. On 30 June 2015, the Bureau finally sent the expert opinion to the District Court, and the court resumed on 9 July 2015.

The District Court held hearings in 2015 and 2016 and on 10 October 2016 partly granted Fil LLC’s claim. Company S. appealed, but on 23 March 2017 the Civil Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. No cassation appeal was lodged, and the decision became final. The proceedings had therefore lasted from January 2008 to March 2017—approximately nine years and two months—largely due to repeated stays and delays in obtaining the central expert evidence. Fil LLC alleged excessive length under Article 6 § 1 and the absence of an effective remedy under Article 13. The European Court of Human Rights found violations of both provisions.

**Elčić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Applications nos. 34524/15 and five others) concerned six applicants who complained that the respondent State had failed to enforce, or had delayed enforcing, final domestic decisions issued in their favour. The European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 17 January 2019, following private deliberations on 13 December 2018. The applicants were represented by Mr M. Alić, a lawyer practising in Tešanj. Notice of the applications was given to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. Two applications—those of Maida Elčić and Muhamed Hasičić—were introduced on 19 June 2015. The remaining four—those of Fehim Musić, Hasib Duraković, Dževad Smaka, and Jozo Jaković—were introduced on 4 December 2015.

The key facts concerned final domestic decisions that remained unenforced for substantial periods. Maida Elčić, born 28 June 1966, obtained a decision from the Tešanj First Instance Court on 30 July 2008. The non-enforcement period began on 5 April 2010, and enforcement proceedings remained pending for more than eight years, seven months, and seventeen days. Muhamed Hasičić, born 19 July 1966, obtained a decision from the same court on 3 July 2008. The non-enforcement period also began on 5 April 2010, with enforcement pending for more than eight years, seven months, and seventeen days.

Fehim Musić, born 4 February 1971, held two relevant domestic decisions. The first was issued by the Zenica Cantonal Court on 5 June 2008; non-enforcement began on 30 October 2008 and remained pending for more than ten years and twenty-three days. The second was issued by the Zenica First Instance Court on 31 December 2012; non-enforcement began on 8 April 2014 and remained pending for more than four years, seven months, and fourteen days. Hasib Duraković, born 18 May 1976, obtained a Zenica First Instance Court decision on 29 September 2006. Non-enforcement began on 30 October 2008 and remained pending for more than ten years and twenty-three days. Dževad Smaka, born 6 February 1969, obtained a Zenica Cantonal Court decision on 5 June 2008. Non-enforcement began on 30 October 2008 and remained pending for more than ten years and twenty-three days. Jozo Jaković, born 19 December 1968, obtained a Zenica First Instance Court decision on 29 September 2006. Non-enforcement began on 30 October 2008 and remained pending for more than ten years and twenty-three days.

In each case, the domestic decisions were final and enforceable, yet the authorities did not execute them. The enforcement proceedings remained pending for years. The delays ranged from over four years to over ten years. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ complaint of non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions.

In Convention terms, such complaints typically engage Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, particularly the right of access to court and the obligation to execute final judgments, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The essential alleged violation was that the State failed to take timely and effective steps to enforce final decisions, thereby depriving the applicants of the practical benefit of their judgments. The lengthy and continuing non-enforcement meant the applicants could not obtain what the domestic courts had awarded them. The Court’s examination therefore focused on the excessive duration of enforcement and the absence of effective execution by the domestic authorities.

**Rasiński v. Poland (Application no. 42969/18)**  
**European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Judgment of 28 May 2020**

The case originated in an application against Poland lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by Artur Rasiński, a Polish national born in 1972 who was detained in Łowicz Prison. The applicant lodged his application on 31 August 2018. On 7 February 2019, the Polish Government were given notice only of the complaint concerning the applicant’s detention in overcrowded cells; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The central alleged violation therefore concerned the conditions of the applicant’s detention, specifically overcrowding.

The applicant alleged that during his detention in Łowicz Prison he had been held in cells where the space per person was below the Polish statutory minimum standard of 3 square metres. The domestic courts’ reasoning confirmed that he had been detained in overcrowded cells during his stay in Łowicz Prison from 18 July 2013 to 16 April 2015—a period of one year, eight months and twenty-eight days. According to those findings, the cells were also poorly equipped, not properly ventilated, and had mould on the walls.

The Government contested the national courts’ findings. In observations dated 11 June and 6 September 2019, they stressed that the applicant had not been kept in overcrowded or inadequately furnished cells. They argued that the national courts had not received sufficient information from the State Treasury’s representative and had relied solely on the applicant’s submissions and general statistics. The Government submitted a Prison Service statement concerning the surface area of the applicant’s cells and the number of people incarcerated with him, asserting that he had not served his sentence in overcrowded conditions.

In domestic civil proceedings, on 1 July 2016 the applicant sued the State Treasury for infringement of his personal rights and sought compensation for detention in overcrowded cells in Łowicz Prison. He claimed 300,000 Polish zlotys (approximately EUR 75,000) in damages. On 13 April 2017, the Łódź Regional Court awarded him PLN 5,000 (approximately EUR 1,250) and dismissed the remainder of his action. The court found that he had indeed been detained in overcrowded cells and that all his complaints in that regard had been dismissed by the prison authorities. It concluded that this violated his personal rights. The applicant was exempted from costs for the dismissed part of his action.

On 23 February 2018, the Łódź Court of Appeal dismissed appeals by both the applicant and the State Treasury. It rejected the State Treasury’s evidence—the Prison Service information on cell surface and number of inmates—as filed out of time. It fully upheld the Regional Court’s factual and legal findings and exempted the applicant from appellate costs. On 7 May 2018, a court-appointed lawyer advised the applicant that there were no grounds to lodge a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court.

The Court also referred to relevant domestic law and practice concerning detention conditions and remedies in Poland, as set out in the pilot judgments *Orchowski v. Poland* and *Norbert Sikorski v. Poland* (both delivered on 22 October 2009), and in later developments described in *Łatak v. Poland* (12 October 2010). The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were the established duration of overcrowding, the substandard cell conditions, and the dispute over whether the domestic courts’ findings were adequately supported.

**Kardava v. Ukraine (Application no. 19886/09)** concerned a Georgian national, Tamaz Kardava, who was arrested in Kyiv on 7 August 2008 on suspicion of robbery; narcotic drugs were found on him. He was taken to the Shevchenkivskyy District police station and initially detained under the Code of Administrative Offences. On 10 August 2008 an investigator ordered his custody on suspicion of robbery and drug possession, and on 12 August 2008 the Shevchenkivskyy District Court remanded him. His pre-trial detention was later extended, and in July 2009 his case was referred to trial. Requests for release in October 2009 and March 2010, based largely on his health, were refused because the court found no evidence that he would not evade investigation or obstruct the truth, and considered his poor health insufficient to alter the preventive measure.

The applicant complained under Article 3 that police officers ill-treated him and that authorities failed to investigate. He alleged he was beaten during his arrest on 7 August 2008 and again on police premises; on 11 August 2008 officers allegedly beat and abused him to obtain a confession. Medical records noted haematomas on his right shoulder and left thigh and a closed chest injury on 11 August. On 15 August his health deteriorated and he was hospitalised with a closed head injury, multiple blunt internal injuries including kidney contusion, and a broken rib; he also had chronic hepatitis C and other conditions. From 14 August 2008, the applicant, his family and his lawyer complained to prosecutors, courts and the Ombudsman. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to open criminal proceedings—on 8 September and 9 December 2008 and 9 April, 8 October and 10 December 2009—finding his allegations unfounded. Higher prosecutors or courts quashed those refusals because inquiries were not full or objective. On 30 March 2010 a court noted that the December 2008 forensic report had not analysed his August–October 2008 medical records and that his injuries, the applicant and the doctors should be verified. On 24 June 2010 the prosecutor again refused to investigate, relying on the December 2008 report.

The applicant also complained under Articles 2 and 3 that detention authorities failed to provide adequate medical assistance. He was held mainly in Kyiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO). Between 15 August and 2 October 2008 he was treated in hospital for injuries and illnesses; doctors reported improvement but recommended continued neurological inpatient treatment. Later examinations noted after-effects of head injury, chronic hepatitis C, gastroduodenitis, heart disease, hypertension and other conditions. In November 2009, after deterioration with cirrhosis and portal hypertension, he was placed in the SIZO medical unit; doctors found no grounds for urgent external hospitalisation, though it was “advisable.” In February 2010 he was taken to hospital with severe liver failure, hepatorenal syndrome and other conditions. He returned to the SIZO in March 2010, where doctors suggested transfer to a hospital in Bucha Correctional Colony; he refused, citing solitary confinement and lack of facilities. On 1 April 2010 he was taken to Kyiv Emergency Hospital, where he died on 7 April 2010. An autopsy found pulmonary heart disease, pneumonia with abscess, splenomegaly and cirrhosis. Investigations into his death were refused in October 2010, quashed in March 2011, and again refused in April 2011. These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations.

**Romeva v. North Macedonia** (Application no. 32141/10) concerned the applicant’s complaint that she was deprived of her pension in breach of legal certainty, contrary to Article 6 § 1 ECHR and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The applicant was born in 1947 and lived in Skopje. Under the respondent State’s pension system, employers submitted employment data, while the Pension and Disability Fund kept records.

In May 2000, while unemployed and receiving social benefits, the applicant was instructed by the Employment Bureau to apply for a retirement pension. On 22 May 2000 she applied to the Fund with only basic personal details, attaching no employment documents. On 23 May 2000 the Fund granted her a monthly pension of MKD 6,462, finding she had completed 35 years, 10 months and 24 days of service—the sole qualifying condition then. The decision became final and she received payments.

In 2007, an internal audit found incomplete records for several recipients. In the applicant’s case, her employment booklet was missing. The Fund sought verification from her employer for 1963–1967 but apparently obtained no further evidence. On 18 October 2007, acting proprio motu, the Fund annulled the 2000 decision and refused her pension. It said the information about her 1963–1967 employment was incorrect because she had not in fact worked then, so she lacked the required 35 years. It relied on section 258 of the Administrative Proceedings Act and section 145-A of the Pension and Disability Insurance Act. Payments stopped.

The applicant appealed, arguing that section 145-A entered into force on 14 June 2006 and could not be applied retroactively to a 2000 decision. In April 2008 the Second-Instance Commission dismissed her appeal. In November 2008 the Administrative Court quashed that decision, agreeing that section 145-A had been applied retroactively. In March 2009, however, the Second-Instance Commission issued a fresh dismissal, relying on section 249(2) of the Administrative Proceedings Act: reopening was justified because erroneous documents had been used, allegedly endorsed by the applicant when she applied. In October 2009 the Administrative Court dismissed her action, finding the Fund’s form concerning her 1963–1967 employment illegible and insufficient. On 26 April 2010 the Supreme Court upheld the refusal as lawful.

The applicant argued that domestic law made the Fund responsible for collecting, keeping and processing employment data, while employers supplied it. She had never submitted employment records and could not challenge data controlled by the Fund. Her central complaint was therefore that a final, executed pension decision was retrospectively annulled years later based on records she neither created nor could verify, violating legal certainty and property rights.

Other relevant facts: in 2008 the Fund sued for reimbursement of MKD 645,138 as unjust enrichment; the courts granted it, final in January 2014, and enforcement began. In 2012 the Fund filed a criminal complaint alleging falsified employment information, rejected because the limitation period had expired. After criteria changed, the Fund granted her a new pension in November 2009 under the age criterion, which she continued receiving. The alleged violations thus arose from the annulment of a final pension and recovery of paid sums under Article 6 § 1 and Protocol No. 1.

Case M.L. v. Slovakia (Application no. 34159/17, ECtHR 14 October 2021) concerned protection of private and family life in defamation proceedings. The applicant, M.L., a Slovak national born in 1948, was the mother of a deceased Roman Catholic priest. Her son had been convicted in 1999 of sexual abuse and threatening the moral education of young people—specifically, attempted non-consensual oral sex with a minor boy—and in 2002 of disorderly conduct for consensual oral sex with an adult man in a public place. Both convictions became spent in 2001 and 2003. He died in 2006.

In 2008, three tabloid newspapers published articles about his sexual-abuse conviction and a possible link to his supposed suicide. The articles claimed he had confessed to abusing minor boys and to bisexuality before his suicide; that his bishop knew of the criminal charges; and that the Church had provided a guarantee enabling him to avoid detention, be released, or not be convicted. One article published photographs of him. The articles named him and disclosed intimate or distant private details in sensational language, including descriptions of “disgusting paedophile orgies.”

The applicant sued the publishers in August 2008 under Articles 11 and 15 of the Slovak Civil Code, seeking post-mortem protection of her son’s personal integrity and protection of her own personal integrity. She argued that her son had confessed only to disorderly conduct, not sexual abuse; that one alleged victim had retracted his accusation; that both convictions were spent; that there was no evidence of any Church guarantee; and that her son had actually died from drug intoxication and medical negligence. She claimed the articles contained false and misleading factual allegations and disproportionate value judgments intended to cause sensation and increase sales. She also said the publication prompted adverse reactions and questions from neighbours and people who knew her son, harmed her mourning, and worsened her health.

In 2012 the District Court ordered each defendant to publish a formal apology for untrue allegations about her son but dismissed her financial claims. It found the criminal convictions were public-interest matters journalists could report, but some allegations—especially the Church guarantee—were untrue, based on an unauthenticated partial record and unverified interviews, for which publishers bore objective responsibility. It rejected her own claim because she had not lived with her son and his personal non-pecuniary rights were not transferable.

The Regional Court later quashed that judgment for insufficient reasoning. In 2014 the District Court dismissed the entire action. It treated the son as a public figure who should tolerate more criticism, found journalists entitled to report facts from the criminal file and publish his photograph, and considered other sources credible in light of the conviction. The Church guarantee was not proven, but the bishop’s office appeared to have tried to help. The Regional Court upheld this in 2015. In 2017 the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, finding no procedural violation.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Articles 6 and 8 that the domestic courts failed to protect her and her late son’s private and family life, failed to distinguish facts from value judgments, apply proportionality, and provide reasoned decisions. The core alleged violation was Slovakia’s failure to grant effective post-mortem and personal protection against the tabloid articles.

**Case Summary: Petrov and Korostylyov v. Ukraine**

**Case Name:** *Petrov and Korostylyov v. Ukraine*  
**Applications nos.:** 19591/18 and 19596/18  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee  
**Judgment date:** Strasbourg, 11 July 2019  
**Final:** Yes, subject to editorial revision.

The case originated in two applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Both applications were introduced on 18 April 2018. The applicants were represented by Mr O.A. Ignatov, a lawyer practising in Dnipro, Ukraine. Notice of the applications was given to the Ukrainian Government. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of their detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. These complaints relate to the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment and the right to an effective remedy.

The first applicant, **Oleg Pavlovych Petrov**, born 14 March 1975, was detained at Dnipropetrovsk law enforcement agency no. 4 (former SIZO no. 3) from 20 March 2014 to 26 September 2018. The total duration of detention was 4 years, 6 months and 7 days. The space per inmate was between 2.6 and 3.3 square metres. Petrov alleged numerous specific grievances: lack of fresh air; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; infestation of the cell with insects and rodents; lack of privacy for the toilet; lack of toiletries; lack or insufficient quantity of food; no or insufficient disinfection of barbering and haircutting tools; no or restricted access to a shower; overcrowding; and poor quality of food.

The second applicant, **Vitaliy Volodymyrovych Korostylyov**, born 25 January 1954, was held at Dnipro Penitentiary Facility no. 4 from 30 October 2013, pending, for more than 5 years, 6 months and 11 days. The space per inmate was 3.3 square metres. Korostylyov alleged: infestation of the cell with insects and rodents; lack of fresh air; lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; lack of privacy for the toilet; lack of toiletries; lack or insufficient quantity of food; a mouldy or dirty cell; no or restricted access to a shower; overcrowding; passive smoking; and no or restricted access to warm water.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the lengthy periods of detention, the very limited cell space per inmate, and the cumulative material conditions of confinement. Both applicants alleged overcrowding and severe deficiencies in hygiene, sanitation, ventilation, food, bedding, privacy and access to showers. Korostylyov also alleged passive smoking and a mouldy or dirty cell, while Petrov alleged inadequate disinfection of barbering and haircutting tools. The applicants further claimed that no effective domestic remedy existed in Ukrainian law to address these detention conditions.

The Court’s task was to assess whether these conditions, individually or cumulatively, amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment and whether the absence of an effective domestic remedy violated the Convention. The main body of the judgment refers to the appended table for the list of applicants and the relevant details of the applications. The judgment was adopted on 20 June 2019 and delivered on 11 July 2019.

**Case: Andreyeva v. Ukraine (Application no. 24385/10), ECtHR Fourth Section, 29 January 2019**

The applicant, Ms Yevdokiya Ivanovna Andreyeva, a Ukrainian national born in 1935, lived in Snizhne, Donetsk region. She alleged that the Ukrainian authorities failed to conduct an effective and timely investigation into her son’s death, contrary to the procedural limb of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and that the protracted failure caused her mental suffering amounting to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3.

The relevant facts began on 14 January 2004, when the applicant’s son, born in 1967, was found dead in her barn. Police inspected the scene and reported that he had committed suicide by hanging. On 24 January 2004, the Snizhne Prosecutor’s Office refused to initiate criminal proceedings, finding no elements of a crime. On 11 February 2004, a forensic medical examination concluded that death was caused by strangulation by a rope loop, possibly through the body’s weight, and that there were no other injuries.

On 5 April 2005, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office quashed the refusal as premature and unfounded. It found that possible reasons for suicide had not been examined and that relatives and acquaintances of the deceased had not been questioned. Numerous further investigative instructions were given.

Between 2005 and 2012, during repeated pre-investigation inquiries, investigators questioned various persons and ordered additional medical examinations. Experts later noted numerous fractures on the corpse, which they considered had been inflicted after death, possibly during exhumation. The applicant’s husband stated that when he saw his dead son in the barn, the body had been sitting and the rope loop had not been tightened. The applicant argued that her son had been murdered, not a suicide, and advanced several theories. She suspected police security guards who had allegedly taken him from a local bar; a local police officer with whom he had argued; a female employee of his textile business and her husband; his brothers-in-law; a business partner; and people from a local gambling club, as her son had transported money for the club.

Investigators repeatedly refused to initiate criminal proceedings—on 25 April 2005, 26 March 2006, 20 August 2008, 17 February and 12 December 2011, 15 February 2012, and 17 September 2012—each time finding no crime. Supervising authorities quashed those decisions as unsubstantiated and ordered further measures. On 7 December 2012, relying on the new 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure, the applicant requested an investigation into the alleged murder. Criminal proceedings were instituted the same day. However, on 24 December 2012, 22 July 2013, and 30 September 2013, the proceedings were terminated for lack of evidence of a crime. Those decisions were also quashed as unsubstantiated.

On 5 December 2013, the Snizhne Town Court quashed the 30 September 2013 termination, finding the investigation neither thorough nor comprehensive. It noted that possible local police involvement had not been properly examined, the role of the son’s brother-in-law had not been clarified although he might have been the first to find the body, the applicant had not been questioned on all relevant issues, and evidence of suicidal tendencies had not been assessed. On 1 April 2014, the proceedings were closed again on the ground that no crime had been established.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaints that the authorities repeatedly failed to pursue obvious lines of inquiry, quashed decisions without achieving progress, and delayed for over a decade without conducting an effective investigation capable of establishing the cause of death and identifying those responsible. The Court found violations of Article 2 (procedural aspect) and Article 3.

In *Velichko v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1973, was disabled (group III) and had been diagnosed with HIV in 1996. On 22 October 2010 he was detained on remand at the Izmayil Detention Centre (SIZO) on suspicion of theft and informed the doctor of his HIV status. Between October 2010 and May 2011 he was diagnosed with HIV (clinical stage IV), hepatitis C, and other conditions. Doctors prescribed treatment for several illnesses but he received no antiretroviral therapy (ART).

On 18 May 2011 the head of the Izmayil SIZO wrote to the judge hearing the criminal case that the applicant’s health was deteriorating and that he urgently needed ART at the regional AIDS centre in Odesa, which was not available at the Izmayil SIZO. The judge suspended the proceedings and ordered his transfer to the Odesa SIZO for examination and treatment. He was transferred on 27 May 2011.

According to the Odesa SIZO authorities, on 7 June 2011 the applicant was offered ART and tuberculosis chemotherapy but refused and gave no written explanation. On 10 June 2011 the regional AIDS centre confirmed HIV and diagnosed tuberculosis; outpatient tuberculosis treatment and ART were prescribed on the SIZO premises. A certificate signed by an official and two doctors recorded that he again refused ART. On 24 June 2011 he was offered outpatient treatment and refused again. On 12 August 2011 the Odesa SIZO head reported that the applicant had refused prescribed outpatient ART three times and proposed transferring him back to Izmayil SIZO, while assuring treatment would be provided if he consented.

On 16 August 2011 the Izmayil Court allowed the transfer back, noting that the refusal could be seen as deliberate protraction of the criminal case, and resumed proceedings. On arrival, the applicant stated he would refuse ART at the Izmayil SIZO or any penitentiary institution; this was certified in writing by medical staff and an officer.

On 8 November 2011 the applicant complained to the Ombudsman that, despite his critical condition, authorities refused inpatient ART and treatment for concomitant diseases in a specialised hospital. The outcome is unknown. In December 2011 he and his lawyer sought a change of preventive measure to allow inpatient treatment in an AIDS hospital. On 12 January 2012 the court ordered a forensic examination to establish whether he could remain in detention. On 19 January 2012 he complained to the Odesa Regional Prosecutor’s Office about the lack of ART. On 8 February 2012 his CD4 count was 79 cells/mm3. On 13 March 2012 a blood test detected hepatitis.

On 15 and 22 March 2012 the Odesa SIZO head informed the applicant’s lawyer that he had HIV, tuberculosis, pneumonia, candidosis, hepatitis, splenomegaly, hypertension, venous insufficiency, and multiple organ dysfunction, and that treatment was offered. The authorities again cited his 2011 refusals. On 21 March 2012 the prosecutor dismissed his complaint as unfounded because he had refused outpatient ART in June 2011 and later in any penitentiary institution.

On 16 April 2012 the applicant asked the European Court of Human Rights for an interim measure, saying he lacked necessary medical examination and treatment. On 23 April 2012 the Court indicated under Rule 39 that he should immediately receive appropriate inpatient treatment in a hospital specialising in AIDS and concomitant diseases. A forensic report that day confirmed his diseases but found them not incompatible with detention. He was admitted to the Izmayil District Infectious Hospital on 14 May 2012 and released from detention on 16 May 2012 due to poor health. The interim measure was lifted on 6 July 2012. The case concerned alleged lack of medical treatment in detention and lack of an effective domestic remedy.

In *Chernyavskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 54141/12), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered a judgment on 22 October 2020, adopted after private deliberations on 29 September 2020. The application was lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on 6 July 2012. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the application. The applicant, Nikolay Kirillovich Chernyavskiy, born in 1963, complained principally of the inadequate conditions of his detention and of the lack of an effective remedy in domestic law. He also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are set out in the appended table. The applicant was detained at Odesa Detention Facility from 3 October 2011 to 21 November 2019. This was a total duration of 8 years, 1 month and 19 days. During that period, the space available per inmate was only 3.3 to 3.6 square metres. This very limited living space is central to the complaint of overcrowding and inadequate detention conditions.

The applicant listed numerous specific grievances concerning the material conditions of his detention. These included: lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities; lack of privacy for using the toilet; a mouldy or dirty cell; lack of or poor quality bedding and bed linen; lack or inadequate furniture; lack of fresh air; lack or insufficient quantity of food; no or restricted access to a shower; poor quality of food; lack of toiletries; and lack of or insufficient physical exercise in fresh air. Taken cumulatively, these conditions are alleged to have amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment. The extremely long period of detention—more than eight years—and the persistent nature of the deficiencies are especially relevant to the seriousness of the alleged violation. The cramped cell space, combined with poor hygiene, sanitation, food, ventilation, toilet privacy, and exercise, would be assessed cumulatively rather than as isolated incidents.

The applicant further complained that there was no effective remedy in domestic law by which he could challenge or obtain redress for those detention conditions. This allegation is linked to the Convention requirement that arguable complaints of rights violations be supported by an enforceable domestic remedy. Because the alleged conditions were ongoing and related to the detention facility, the absence of an effective domestic mechanism formed a distinct part of the application.

The Court therefore had to examine whether the conditions of detention breached the Convention and whether Ukrainian law provided an effective remedy. The provided text does not set out the Court’s final findings on each complaint, but the factual core is clear: a prolonged detention in Odesa Detention Facility under overcrowded and materially inadequate conditions, with numerous specific deficiencies in hygiene, sanitation, food, bedding, furniture, ventilation, shower access, toilet privacy, and outdoor exercise. The applicant’s other Convention complaints are mentioned but not detailed in the extract. The case thus focuses on the alleged breach of fundamental detention standards and the lack of domestic redress.

Case Doyle v. Ireland concerned an Irish murder conviction and a complaint under Article 6 § 3(c) that the applicant, Barry Doyle, was not allowed to have a solicitor present during police interrogation. In November 2008 Doyle shot and killed S.G. in Limerick, mistaking him for a gang-feud target. He was arrested on 24 February 2009 and taken to a police station, where he was informed of his rights, including access to a solicitor. He requested a solicitor, who telephoned him at 9:55 a.m. for two minutes. The first police interview began at 10:12 a.m. without the solicitor physically present.
