**E.G. v. the Republic of Moldova** (Application no. 37882/13), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 13 April 2021 (final 13 July 2021). The applicant, E.G., is a dual Moldovan and Romanian national born in 1977, living in Chișinău. The case concerns the non-enforcement of a prison sentence imposed on one of the perpetrators of a sexual assault against her, raising issues under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention.

On the night of 9–10 February 2008, the applicant was sexually assaulted by three individuals: P.G., R.G., and V.B. Criminal proceedings were opened. The three defendants were initially placed in pre-trial detention but later released pending trial; V.B. was released on 12 March 2008 against a security deposit.

On 17 June 2009, the Centru District Court in Chișinău convicted all three of gang sexual assault under Article 172 § 2(c) of the Criminal Code and imposed suspended sentences. The applicant appealed. On 2 December 2009, the Chișinău Court of Appeal affirmed the convictions and additionally convicted P.G. and R.G. of gang rape under Article 171 § 2(c), sentencing them to six and five and a half years’ imprisonment respectively. It also imposed a five-year prison sentence on V.B. That judgment was immediately enforceable. P.G. and R.G. were taken into custody from the courtroom, but V.B., who was not present, was not detained. On 7 December 2010, the Supreme Court of Justice affirmed the Court of Appeal’s judgment with final effect.

V.B. remained at large. A wanted notice was issued on 14 May 2010. In April 2011, V.B. applied through his lawyer for amnesty under the 2008 Amnesty Act. A similar application by R.G. was rejected in October 2011 because his conviction post-dated the Act and section 5 was inapplicable. On 20 December 2011, the District Court rejected V.B.’s amnesty claim for the same reason. On appeal, however, the prosecution supported V.B., and on 22 May 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal granted him amnesty, reasoning that the offence pre-dated the Act. Subsequent proceedings repeatedly reopened and reversed this decision. On 29 June 2012, the Court of Appeal set aside the amnesty and restored the refusal, but the Supreme Court later annulled that decision for lack of jurisdiction and remitted the case. On 7 March 2013, the Court of Appeal refused to entertain a further reconsideration request.

Meanwhile, on 22 October 2012, the authorities arrested V.B. but released him the same day based on the 22 May 2012 amnesty decision. In September 2013, the District Court reopened the amnesty proceedings and set aside the amnesty; the Court of Appeal affirmed on 18 November 2013, noting that the earlier court had been unaware that V.B. had breached the conditions of his release against security.

Afterwards, the applicant asked whether V.B. was serving his sentence. On 10 January 2014, the police informed her lawyer that no wanted notice had been issued and no search steps taken because neither the prosecution nor the Court of Appeal had directed a search. On 28 January 2014, the prosecution asked the police to enforce the decision setting aside the amnesty. On 31 January 2014, police found that V.B. had left Moldova for Ukraine on 16 November 2013. The prosecution later stated that the courts had failed to forward the final decision of 18 November 2013 to the police within the ten-day period required by Article 468 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. A CIS wanted notice was issued on 20 February 2014, and an international notice on 29 April 2015. According to the Government’s submissions in March 2020, V.B. had still not been found.

The applicant’s complaints under Articles 3 and 8 concerned the State’s failure to enforce the final prison sentence imposed on V.B., including delayed and contradictory amnesty proceedings, failure to search for him, and failures to transmit enforceable decisions to the police. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

**Asanović v. Montenegro** (App. No. 52415/18, judgment 20 May 2021) concerns the applicant’s alleged unlawful deprivation of liberty and the lack of an effective domestic remedy, contrary to Articles 5 § 1 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Nebojša Asanović, is a Montenegrin lawyer and longtime representative of an opposition media outlet. In December 2016 the Tax Administration reported to the police that there were indications he had committed tax evasion in relation to his professional activities. The police forwarded the matter to the State Prosecution Office (SPO) in January 2017. On 12 September 2017 a state prosecutor allegedly orally ordered police officer G.M. to gather information from the applicant “as a citizen” regarding the suspected offence. The next morning, G.M. informed the prosecutor that the applicant had not been found at his address and that his phone was switched off. The prosecutor, apparently believing the applicant was hiding, ordered police to find him and “deprive him of liberty.”

At about 9:30 a.m. on 13 September 2017, G.M. and three other officers approached the applicant outside the Court of First Instance in Podgorica and served him with a summons requiring him to come to the police “at once” to provide information as a citizen. The summons warned that non-compliance could lead to him being brought in by force. The applicant claimed he was put into a vehicle and taken to the police station; the Government claimed he was offered a ride without force. After giving a statement, an official report stated that he had been deprived of liberty at 10:40 a.m. on the prosecutor’s order under Article 264 § 1 of the Criminal Code, in conjunction with Article 49, and that he would be brought before the prosecutor. His fingerprints were taken, he was photographed, his belongings—including his glasses—were removed, and he was placed in a windowless cell. At 12:10 p.m. he was handcuffed and taken to the prosecutor, questioned from 12:30 to 13:54 p.m., and then released. He denied the offence and explained that he had been visiting a client in prison, where phone use was prohibited and there was no signal.

The applicant filed a constitutional appeal on 15 September 2017. The Bar Association protested. On 1 November 2017 the Council for Civic Control of Police found the police had acted unlawfully because, as a lawyer, the applicant could not be deprived of liberty without a court decision. On 11 July 2018 the Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal, finding the police and SPO acted lawfully; it said he had not complied with the summons and had been deprived of liberty at 10:40 a.m. following the prosecutor’s order. It did not address other effective remedies.

On 2 October 2018 the Ombudsperson found breaches of Article 29 of the Constitution and Article 5 § 1 (c) of the Convention. It concluded that the applicant had not first been allowed to comply voluntarily with the summons, but was told to go “at once” with police, contrary to Article 259 § 1 of the Criminal Procedure Code. It found he was de facto deprived of liberty from 9:30 a.m., under police control, without legal grounds, since no Article 175 detention reason was indicated.

On 12 October 2018 the applicant brought civil proceedings against the State, seeking compensation and publication for unlawful deprivation of liberty. Those proceedings were later stayed pending criminal proceedings. An indictment for tax and social contributions evasion was issued in April 2019, and the criminal case remained ongoing. The case therefore centers on whether the police and prosecutor’s actions from 9:30 a.m. until release amounted to unlawful deprivation of liberty and whether domestic remedies were effective.

**Jallow v. Norway** (Application no. 36516/19) concerns complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Ebrima Pa Jallow, a Gambian national, sought parental responsibilities for G., his biological son born in Norway in 2011 to K.J. The applicant had been married to K.J., but they divorced around 2003. K.J. later moved to Norway; G. was conceived during her 2010 visit to Gambia and was born in Norway. The applicant never went to Norway, never had custody or parental responsibilities for G., and did not formally recognise paternity, so G. was registered with an unknown father.

G. lived in Norway with his mother and half-brother. The applicant met G. in Gambia in 2015, but the parties disputed the extent of contact and telephone communication; the Government noted G. did not speak English at the relevant time. G.’s mother died on 25 June 2017. G. then stayed with a family friend, later with a maternal uncle, and eventually in a foster home.

Because no one had parental responsibilities after the mother’s death, the City Court had to decide applications under the Children Act. In 2017, a family friend applied then withdrew; G.’s maternal aunt, A.J., applied; and the applicant also applied from Gambia. In January 2018, the City Court dismissed both A.J.’s and the applicant’s applications. It found the applicant had never been to Norway, wanted G. to move to Gambia, knew little of G., had probably met him only once, and had shown limited interest after the mother’s death. It concluded there was a significant danger of inadequate care if he were granted parental responsibilities. A.J. appealed; the applicant was initially not treated as a party due to communication problems, but later joined the High Court proceedings.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the applicant’s inability to attend the High Court hearing. He applied for a Schengen visa in November 2017; it was refused, and his appeal rejected in April 2018. He applied again in June 2018; that application was refused in July 2018, and the Immigration Appeals Board dismissed his appeal on 7 January 2019. The Board found the risk that he would not return outweighed welfare reasons, but noted he could follow proceedings by Skype and that his lawyer could protect his interests.

The High Court had itself written in November 2018 that the applicant’s presence was important for the case and for equality of arms, including to question A.J. and witnesses, and that Skype was not optimal. Nevertheless, after the visa refusal, the High Court refused the applicant’s request to reschedule the January 2019 hearing. It considered the visa decision probably not flawed, found Skype acceptable, emphasised G.’s need for stability, noted the applicant had counsel, and distinguished *Cılız v. the Netherlands* because the applicant had never lived with G. and had met him only twice.

At the hearing on 10–11 January 2019, technical problems meant the applicant was not initially on Skype; his counsel consented to proceed, and he joined later. The High Court dismissed the appeals in February 2019, finding that granting the applicant parental responsibilities was not in G.’s best interests. It noted the applicant did not seek daily care, that parental responsibilities would have no immediate practical effect, and that he lacked sufficient knowledge to participate in decisions. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in April 2019.

In later judicial-review proceedings, the City Court in June 2020 found no “family life” under Article 8 between the applicant and G., but invalidated the visa decision for procedural error because the Board had assessed incorrect facts about the applicant’s ties to Gambia. The applicant lodged his ECtHR application in July 2019, alleging violations of Articles 6 and 8.

In *Milovanović v. Serbia*, the applicant, Ms Mirjana Milovanović, a Serbian national, complained that Serbian authorities failed to enforce domestic child-custody decisions and to facilitate her reunion with her children. The case concerns a prolonged custody dispute.

The applicant had twins, D. and K., in May 1996 with M.M. She left the matrimonial home in March 2001. In January 2002, while returning from a medical check-up, M.M. intercepted her, took the children, and until 2010 systematically prevented contact, threatening violence. He moved with the children into a house he had begun building.

In 2002 the applicant sought divorce, sole custody and maintenance. In June 2002 the Belgrade Second Municipal Court divorced the parties and awarded custody to her; in September 2002 the District Court upheld the divorce but quashed the custody decision. In November 2002 she sought interim custody. On 27 February 2003 the Municipal Court issued an interim custody order requiring M.M. to hand over the children within 24 hours. It became enforceable on 14 June 2003 but was never enforced.

On 6 October 2005 the Municipal Court granted the applicant sole custody, set M.M.’s contact rights and maintenance, and barred his contact for three months. It noted his destructive behaviour and the children’s appalling living conditions—lack of hygiene, windows and water—requiring immediate removal. The judgment became final on 16 November 2006 and enforceable on 9 January 2007, but remained unenforced.

Enforcement efforts included fines of RSD 5,000, 20,000 and 25,000, but bailiffs found no assets. Attempts in 2003–2004 to reunite the family failed because M.M.’s house was empty or he was absent. A June 2005 transfer at the children’s school failed: the children were terrified and rejected their mother, and the social care centre sent only a lawyer, not its expert team. A September 2005 social report found the applicant had good parental capacity but considered disrupting the children’s current living arrangement not to be in their best interests; enforcement was terminated, then that decision was quashed in April 2006. In 2007 social services advised that enforcement was in the children’s best interests, but in February 2008 the enforcement court terminated enforcement of the interim order because it was no longer valid and told the applicant to file a new request under the final judgment.

In March 2008 enforcement was ordered for the final judgment. M.M.’s appeal was rejected in April 2009. Hearings followed in 2009–2010. In October 2009 the children said they wished to meet their mother and suggested weekend visits; the court ordered counselling and weekend stays, but M.M. obstructed contact. Social services advised against forcible enforcement; in April 2010 contact was reduced to Tuesdays and Sundays. The file was later transferred to criminal and constitutional courts, causing further delay. The final custody judgment remained unenforced, and contact was sporadic.

M.M. was convicted in 2006 of child abduction for failing to hand over the children, receiving a suspended sentence; he was acquitted in December 2012, with appeal pending. Deprivation of parental rights proceedings were later withdrawn.

In February 2009 the applicant filed a constitutional appeal. In May 2012 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a fair trial due to protracted enforcement of the final custody judgment, ordered expedited enforcement, dismissed the interim-order complaint as out of time, and awarded no damages.

The applicant alleged that, despite enforceable interim and final custody orders, Serbian authorities failed to take effective measures—fines, bailiff action, social-service and police support, and forcible transfer where necessary—to enforce custody and facilitate her reunion with her children.

In *Cilei and Rosip v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 48145/10 and 8387/15), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints arising from arrests and detention in Transdniestria, the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The applicants, Moldovan nationals Alexandr Cilei and Ivan Rosip, alleged unlawful detention; Rosip also alleged inhuman detention conditions, unlawful seizure of property, and lack of effective remedies.

Cilei was arrested by MRT authorities on 30 January 2008 on attempted murder charges. On 5 June 2009, MRT courts convicted him and sentenced him to eleven years’ imprisonment. He sought annulment before Moldova’s Supreme Court of Justice, but on 10 May 2010 that court returned his extraordinary appeal without examination, stating it lacked competence to review MRT court judgments. He was released on 1 August 2012 after an MRT presidential pardon. His complaint concerned unlawful detention.

Rosip was founder and director of an MRT company. On 20 December 2012, MRT authorities arrested him for allegedly misappropriating funds; detention was repeatedly extended. On 24 December 2012, his personal property—two cars, gold rings, a gold watch, 159 MRT roubles, a company share, and two mobile phones—and company property were seized. On 16 June 2014, the Bender City Court convicted him of abuse of position of trust, sentenced him to one year and eight months and a fine, upheld a civil claim for 1,899,050 MRT roubles, ordered execution against his personal property, and lifted restrictions on company property. On 5 August 2014, the MRT Supreme Court increased the civil award to 2,553,000 MRT roubles (about EUR 212,750), dispensed him from serving the sentence due to limitation expiry, and released him. Enforcement against his property followed; an expert later valued it at 106,002 MRT roubles (about EUR 8,832).

As to detention conditions, Rosip was held in several facilities. In IVS Tiraspol (20 December 2012–14 January 2013), he alleged high humidity, overcrowding, no ventilation, no natural light, smoking, wooden bunks, no bed linen, unsanitary conditions, scarce/inedible food, and parasites. In Hlinaia prison no. 1 (14–22 January 2013), cells were overcrowded and unheated; relatives supplied food and medication. Mainly in Tiraspol prison no. 3 (22 January 2013–5 August 2014), he alleged overcrowding, no bed linen, bad tap water, small windows admitting damp/cold air, very short daily walks, a 20 kg monthly package limit, and hunger. Transfers were in an unheated metal truck with no toilet, sometimes for nine hours in freezing temperatures. He also complained of inadequate medical staff and reliance on relatives’ medication.

After an extraordinary appeal, on 7 April 2015 Moldova’s Supreme Court quashed the MRT judgments against Rosip, finding MRT courts unconstitutional. Rosip complained to Moldovan and Russian prosecutors about unlawful deprivation of liberty and property execution. Russia answered that the complaint did not concern Russian territory. Moldova opened but suspended a criminal investigation for lack of identified perpetrators; no property protection measures were granted because Moldovan law did not provide for them.

**Case: Hodžić and Sirćo v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**  
**Applications nos. 34526/15 and 34530/15**  
**European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section**  
**Judgment delivered 27 June 2019**

The case originated in two applications lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 18 June 2015. The applicants, Adis Hodžić and Adil Sirćo, were represented by Ms. H. Kapetan, a lawyer practising in Travnik. Notice of the applications was given to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Mourou-Vikström, Ravarani, and Schukking, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 6 June 2019 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment was delivered on 27 June 2019 and is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applicants’ central complaint was the non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions. The appended table sets out the relevant facts. Both applicants had obtained domestic decisions from the Sarajevo First Instance Court, both dated 30 August 2013. Despite these decisions, the authorities allegedly failed to enforce them within a reasonable time, and enforcement remained pending.

For Adis Hodžić, born 29 June 1967, the relevant domestic decision was issued by the Sarajevo First Instance Court on 30 August 2013. The start date of the non-enforcement period was 17 December 2013. At the time the case was before the Court, the end date of the non-enforcement period was still pending. The length of the enforcement proceedings therefore exceeded five years, four months and twenty days. This prolonged failure to enforce the domestic decision formed the factual basis of his complaint.

For Adil Sirćo, born 25 June 1962, the relevant domestic decision was also issued by the Sarajevo First Instance Court on 30 August 2013. The non-enforcement period began on 8 April 2014. As with Hodžić, enforcement was still pending, and the length of the enforcement proceedings exceeded five years and twenty-nine days. This delay similarly grounded his complaint.

Both applications were introduced on 18 June 2015. At that point, the domestic decisions had not been enforced for a substantial period: approximately one and a half years for Hodžić and just over one year for Sirćo. However, the enforcement remained unresolved for years afterward, eventually exceeding five years in each case. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the existence of final domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour, the dates on which non-enforcement began, the absence of any completed enforcement, and the extensive duration of the pending enforcement proceedings.

The applicants alleged that the failure to enforce the domestic decisions violated their Convention rights. The Court’s task was to determine whether the State had complied with its positive obligation to enforce final domestic decisions within a reasonable time and whether the applicants had an effective remedy for the delay. The case thus concerned the respondent State’s alleged failure to execute final court decisions, the protracted nature of the enforcement, and the resulting deprivation of the applicants’ rights under those decisions. The Court gave notice of the applications to the Government and considered the complaints on the basis of the facts set out in the appended table.

**Summary of Špadijer v. Montenegro (Application no. 31549/18)**

The case of *Špadijer v. Montenegro* concerns allegations of workplace bullying (mobbing) affecting the applicant’s psychological integrity and the failure of domestic authorities to protect her, in violation of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Ms. Daliborka Špadijer, a Montenegrin national born in 1978, worked as a prison guard at the Institute for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions (IECS) in Podgorica since 1998. At the relevant time, she held the position of head of shift in the women’s prison.

The events began in January 2013 when the applicant reported five colleagues for indecent behaviour on New Year’s Eve, during which male guards entered the women’s prison and one had physical contact with inmates. Following this report, the applicant faced retaliation. On 12 January 2013, a colleague, N.R., warned her by phone that she should not have reported the others, that many colleagues were against her, and that she should "be prepared for anything." The next night, the windscreen of her car was smashed outside her home. She filed a police complaint, but the State prosecutor found no criminal offence.

Further incidents followed. In March 2013, a prison driver refused to take her home, citing her "sharp tongue." The colleagues she had reported were later fined in disciplinary proceedings. In June 2013, one of them, A.V., insulted her publicly, calling her a "stinking bitch" and spitting near her. When she reported this, the governor confronted her with A.V., who denied it; her request to review video footage was dismissed with the false claim that cameras were not working. She also alleged that between January and August 2013, she was forbidden to organise duty shifts, ignored by colleagues, ordered to make coffee for a prisoner, and that her reports were disregarded.

On 16 August 2013, the applicant formally requested her employer to initiate protection proceedings against bullying. A mediator dismissed her request as unfounded, reasoning that the conduct was not continuous and that some incidents occurred outside the workplace. She then instituted civil proceedings. An expert found she suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder and an adjustment disorder, with a 20% permanent reduction in functioning capacity.

On 19 February 2015, the Court of First Instance ruled against her, finding that the incidents lacked the frequency required for bullying—at least once a week for six months. The High Court and Supreme Court upheld this, adding that the assault did not relate to the employer. On 10 February 2015, just before the civil ruling, the applicant was physically assaulted in a car park by an unknown attacker who warned her to "be careful." Police efforts to identify the perpetrator failed.

The applicant’s constitutional appeal was dismissed in November 2017. She retired in May 2016 due to complete loss of working capacity, with her psychological problems traced to workplace stress in 2013. The case highlights the domestic courts’ narrow definition of bullying, requiring high frequency, and their failure to address the cumulative effect of the incidents or the criminal complaints she filed.

In *Shabelnik v. Ukraine (No. 3)* (Application no. 54806/18), the European Court of Human Rights considered the applicant’s complaint under Article 7 that a judicial review of his previous conviction resulted in a new punishment imposed after the statutory limitation period had expired.

The underlying events occurred in 2001. In October 2001, an elderly woman, K., was murdered in her flat. In December 2001, a minor, S., was abducted and murdered. The applicant was arrested on 10 December 2001 and charged in connection with S.’s abduction and murder. In February 2002, while questioned as a witness and without a lawyer present, he confessed to K.’s murder and took part in an on-site reconstruction. Criminal proceedings concerning K. were later joined with those concerning S.

On 11 July 2002, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal convicted the applicant of crimes against both victims. For the murders, he was sentenced to life imprisonment under Article 115 § 2 (2), (3), (6), (9) and (13) of the Criminal Code, with lesser sentences for abduction, hostage-taking, robbery and extortion absorbed into the life sentence. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 10 October 2002.

In the applicant’s first case before the ECtHR, he alleged that his conviction for K.’s murder had been based on self-incriminating evidence obtained without a lawyer, in violation of Article 6. On 19 February 2009, the Court found a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3. After that judgment became final, the Supreme Court reviewed the case. On 9 September 2010, it excluded the applicant’s confessions but upheld his conviction for K.’s murder on the basis of other evidence.

In his second ECtHR case, the applicant complained about that review. On 1 June 2017, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that only a full retrial could adequately examine the impact of excluding the confessions on the remaining evidence concerning K. That judgment became final on 1 September 2017.

Following the second judgment, the applicant’s lawyer sought review of the 2002 and 2010 decisions. On 16 May 2018, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court partly allowed the request. It quashed the 2002 sentence and the 2010 decision insofar as they concerned the robbery and murder of K., remitting that part for fresh examination. However, it resentenced the applicant on the remaining charges concerning S. under Articles 146 § 3, 147 § 2, 189 § 4 and 115 § 2 (2), (3) and (6), imposing terms of imprisonment and, ultimately, a merged life sentence with confiscation of property under Article 70. Three judges dissented, arguing that the partial severance and resentencing was erroneous and effectively maintained a life sentence despite the reduction in charges.

The Article 7 complaint arises from this 2018 judicial review. The crimes concerning S. were committed in 2001, and the original conviction was in 2002. Under Article 49 of the Criminal Code, a fifteen-year limitation period applied to especially grave offences. Where such an offence was punishable by life imprisonment, the court had to decide whether limitation applied; if it ruled out limitation, life imprisonment could not be imposed and had to be commuted to a determinate term. The applicant alleged that the Supreme Court’s 2018 decision imposed a new life sentence for the S.-related offences outside the statutory time-limit. The key issue is therefore whether the judicial review and fresh sentencing violated Article 7’s prohibition on unlawful or retroactive punishment.

The case *Baralija v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 30100/18) was brought by Irma Baralija, a Bosnian national born in 1984 and resident of Mostar. She is president of the local branch of the political party *Naša stranka*. She complained of her inability to vote and stand in local elections. Mostar, with a population of 105,797, is the cultural and economic capital of Herzegovina and one of the largest cities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its last local elections were held in 2008.

The electoral deadlock stemmed from the legal regime for the Mostar City Council. Under the Election Act 2001 and the Statute of the City of Mostar, the 35-member Council was elected in a city-wide constituency and in six city-area constituencies, each electing three councillors. Residents of the Central Zone could vote only for the 17 city-wide councillors; they could not vote for area councillors and had no committee representation. In 2010, following a request from the Croat caucus, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared sections 19.2(1)-(3) and 19.4(2)-(8) of the Election Act 2001 and section 17(1) of the Mostar Statute unconstitutional. It found that the arrangement failed to secure equal suffrage, was incompatible with Article 25(b) of the ICCPR, and violated the constitutional prohibition of discrimination. The Court gave the Parliamentary Assembly six months to amend the provisions.

The Parliamentary Assembly did not do so. On 18 January 2012, the Constitutional Court adopted a ruling on non-enforcement, and the invalid provisions ceased to have effect on 28 February 2012. No new provisions regulating Mostar city council elections were adopted. As a result, local elections could not be held in Mostar in the 2012 or 2016 election cycles. By September 2019, the relevant legal framework still had not been adopted. The mayor, elected by the city council in 2009, continued in a “technical mandate.” Because the council could not be constituted, from 2013/2014 special entity legislation allowed the mayor to adopt the city budget in its place, renewed each fiscal year.

The applicant alleged that she was unable to exercise her right to vote and to stand for election in Mostar, contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 to the Convention. The Court gave notice of that complaint to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The key alleged violation was therefore the State’s prolonged failure to provide a legal framework for local elections in Mostar, leaving the applicant and other residents unable to participate in municipal elections. International bodies repeatedly highlighted the situation: the High Representative reported that political parties had failed to agree on amendments to the Election Law; the Council of Europe Congress and Parliamentary Assembly urged a solution; and the European Commission noted that Mostar citizens had not been able to elect a municipal council since 2008. These facts formed the background to the applicant’s discrimination complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

**Summary of *Gawlik v. Liechtenstein* (Application no. 23922/19)**

The case concerns the dismissal without notice of Lothar Gawlik, a German national and deputy chief physician at the Liechtenstein National Hospital, the only public hospital in Liechtenstein. He worked under an indefinite contract and was directly subordinate to Dr H., the chief physician. In September 2014, after a colleague indicated an unusual rise in patient deaths, Gawlik examined the hospital’s electronic medical files. He found notes suggesting that four patients had died after morphine administration and concluded that Dr H. had practised active euthanasia.

On 9 September 2014, Gawlik met with the President of the Parliamentary Control Committee and voiced his suspicions. On the President’s advice, he lodged a criminal complaint against Dr H. with the Public Prosecutor’s Office on 11 September 2014. The prosecution opened proceedings concerning suspected killing on request and participation in another person’s suicide. Police seized the patients’ paper files and questioned Dr H. On 19 September 2014, after further electronic research, Gawlik informed the prosecutor that he suspected active euthanasia in six additional patients and was questioned by police. He stated that his aim was to avert harm to hospital patients.

The hospital had an internal anonymous reporting system, the Critical Incident Reporting System, but it is unclear whether a change in its handling was communicated within the hospital. Gawlik did not use it. Hospital-commissioned reports, including one by an external Swiss palliative expert, concluded that no active euthanasia had occurred. The patients were in palliative situations; morphine had been used for pain and breathing difficulty, not to end life. Some prescriptions “without upper limit” might not have been necessary, but such doses had not actually been administered. The reports suggested that if Gawlik had consulted the paper files, he would have realised his suspicions were clearly unfounded.

Gawlik was suspended on 26 September 2014 and dismissed without notice on 17 October 2014. The hospital claimed the trust relationship was irretrievably destroyed because he had failed to verify his allegations and had not raised them internally before going to external bodies. Criminal proceedings against Dr H. were discontinued in December 2014; proceedings against Gawlik for deliberately casting false suspicions were also later discontinued.

Gawlik sued for unlawful dismissal, arguing that his whistleblowing was justified. The Regional Court dismissed his claim, finding an important reason for dismissal under the Civil Code. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding that the dismissal was unjustified and that the disclosure was covered by freedom of expression. The Supreme Court then reinstated the dismissal, finding that Gawlik, a senior employee, had relied only on incomplete electronic files despite having access to full paper files, and had thus seriously breached trust.

The Constitutional Court dismissed Gawlik’s complaint. It accepted that Article 10 of the Convention applied indirectly to the employment relationship and that there was a public interest in proper medical treatment. It also accepted that Gawlik was a whistleblower and did not act from personal motives. However, it found that he had failed to verify his serious allegations in the patients’ paper files and had acted irresponsibly given the gravity of accusing a colleague of euthanasia. Therefore, his dismissal did not violate his right to freedom of expression. The court left open whether he should first have attempted internal reporting. The alleged violation therefore centred on whether the dismissal for external whistleblowing about suspected euthanasia breached Article 10.

E.H. v. Norway (Application no. 39717/19) concerns an Article 8 complaint by a Norwegian father, E.H., about the replacement of foster care with adoption of his son, X. X was born in June 2015 to B, the applicant’s former partner. The parents were not in a relationship at the time of birth. During pregnancy and after birth, a midwife and social workers raised serious concerns about both parents’ caregiving abilities. On 15 June 2015, when X was only weeks old, he was emergency placed in a foster home; the County Social Welfare Board authorised the placement the next day. The mother contested the emergency order, but the father was not initially a party.

In July 2015, the child welfare services requested a care order. The father had five supervised visits with X before the Board issued a care order on 21 October 2015. The Board found that B had mild mental retardation and an expressive language disorder, lacked fundamental caregiving abilities, and that X would risk serious neglect if left with her. Assistance measures were considered inadequate. The father was granted supervised contact of two hours, four times a year. He supported the care order but sought more contact.

A psychologist’s expert report in March 2016 found X had extraordinary care needs, including epilepsy, severe eczema, and significant far-sightedness. B could not meet his ordinary or special needs. The father had clear cognitive and reflective limitations, weak interaction skills, low stress tolerance, and could become loud and hot-tempered with X, but he was positive and more able to use guidance. The expert recommended that X remain in foster care with limited contact—three two-hour sessions yearly per biological parent. B later withdrew her City Court challenge, making the care order final.

In November 2017, the child welfare services applied to withdraw the parents’ parental responsibilities and authorise X’s adoption by his foster parents. X was then two and a half and had lived with the foster parents since he was three weeks old. The Board granted adoption in January 2018. It found reunification unrealistic, a point both parents accepted, and concluded adoption was in X’s best interests because of his attachment to the foster parents, lack of attachment to his biological parents, vulnerabilities, need for stability, difficult contact sessions, and the risk of future uncertainty or litigation.

The father and mother challenged the decision. They argued the City Court should appoint an expert on adoption but made no formal request. The City Court declined to appoint an expert and relied on general research and knowledge. After a hearing in June 2018, it upheld adoption, finding X exceptionally vulnerable, closely attached to his foster parents, and without attachment to his biological parents. Adoption would provide safety and predictability; otherwise, X would remain in long-term foster care with possible future proceedings. The biological principle had to yield. The foster parents had not consented to post-adoption contact. A dissenting lay judge considered general research insufficient and adoption too drastic.

The High Court refused leave to appeal in November 2018, and the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in January 2019. Under the Child Welfare Act, parental responsibilities may be withdrawn and adoption authorised if parents are permanently unable to provide proper care or if the child has become so attached to the current environment that removal would cause serious problems. The applicant alleged that the adoption decision violated his right to family life under Article 8, raising issues of proportionality, the child’s best interests, less restrictive alternatives, expert evidence, contact rights, and biological ties.

**Case Name:** *Haddad v. Spain* (Application no. 16572/17), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 18 June 2019.

The applicant, Mr Wael Haddad, a Syrian national living in Madrid, fled Syria in January 2012 with his Spanish wife and their three minor children because of the armed conflict. One month after arriving in Spain, his wife lodged a criminal complaint of domestic violence. On 2 February 2012, the Coslada judge no. 1 issued a protection order barring the applicant from approaching or communicating with his wife and children, requiring him to wear a tracking bracelet, and temporarily withdrawing his parental responsibility and contact rights. His wife nevertheless twice left an emergency shelter and returned to live with him despite the barring order; the applicant was arrested for violating it but released.

In June 2012, after the mother said she could no longer care for the children, the Madrid regional government declared the three children abandoned and assumed guardianship under the urgent procedure. The applicant was not informed. The children were placed in residential care in Murcia, and in July 2012 Murcia took over guardianship; the mother was allowed visits. In February 2013, the applicant, through the Spanish Muslim Association, sought information and contact, but the child protection department said there were no plans to return the children and that visits by outsiders were undesirable. A guardianship hearing notice was published in the official gazette, and child protection staff telephoned him twice. He did not attend, saying he would appeal if necessary. In April 2013 the children were placed in the care of the child protection department; a notification was sent but left at the post office and not collected.

Reports in June and July 2013 referred to alleged physical and emotional abuse by the applicant and criticised the mother’s vulnerable personality, instability, lack of resources and parenting capacity. They recommended placing the daughter in foster care with a view to adoption and suspending birth-family contact. In September 2013, the regional child protection board decided on temporary foster care with a view to adoption. The daughter was placed with a foster family, and the pre-adoption proposal made no provision for visits by her birth parents.

A key development was the applicant’s acquittal. On 27 September 2013, the criminal court acquitted him of all domestic-violence charges and set aside the earlier criminal and civil measures. The acquittal became final in November 2013. The applicant then contacted child protection, reported stable work and income, and requested contact with his children. In February/March 2014, the department refused contact with his daughter and provisionally refused contact with his sons, noting the daughter’s good adjustment to pre-adoption fostering and the sons’ fear of their father.

In May 2014 the applicant appealed the daughter’s foster placement. In February 2015 the Murcia first-instance judge authorised her placement in foster care with a view to adoption, finding it served her development and best interests. The applicant appealed, arguing that he had been acquitted, had never been assessed as a possible carer, and that abandonment had resulted from the mother’s conduct and their flight from war. The regional government replied that he had shown no interest after June 2012 and had not appealed the administrative care decision. In April 2016 the Audiencia Provincial dismissed his appeal, relying on the child’s best interests, her strong bonds with the foster family, and the serious harm removal would cause. His two sons were returned to him in February 2016. His constitutional amparo appeal was declared inadmissible in October 2016 for lack of constitutional significance.

The case concerns an alleged violation of Article 8 of the Convention arising from the declaration of abandonment, the daughter’s foster-care/adoption-oriented placement, the denial of contact, and the alleged failure to consider the father’s rights and his subsequent acquittal.

In *Omdahl v. Norway*, the applicant, Olav Omdahl, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the administration and division of his grandfather’s estate had exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement. The deceased, O.A. Knutsen, died in April 1993, leaving an estate worth approximately NOK 100 million, with NOK 10 million in debt, consisting mainly of property, shares, securities and moveable assets. Public administration began on 5 May 1993 before the Probate Court, with an advocate appointed as administrator. The process lasted 22 years and 4 months, ending with final distribution in April 2015.

The length was largely caused by numerous legal disputes. Early proceedings concerned heirs’ rights to receive assets in kind under the deceased’s will and codicil. These tied up proceeds until 2005/06, while Probate Court decisions to convert assets into cash were quashed or amended on appeal. A Bahamas trust managed by a London bank came to light after 2002; in December 2005 each child and grandchild received NOK 5.5 million. The trust generated disputes over whether funds belonged to the estate and complex inheritance-tax questions, clarified only by winter 2010. An interim distribution of NOK 10 million per family branch occurred in July 2010, upheld after appeals ending in November 2011. Further disputes concerned share sales, a judge-disqualification motion, and the sale of shares in a property company and a fish-oil factory. These concluded by 2012, share sales were largely completed in 2013, and remaining companies were wound up in December 2013. The Probate Court decided final distribution on 1 August 2014; the High Court dismissed an appeal in November 2014, and the Supreme Court refused leave in April 2015. Final distribution was paid on 16 April 2015.

The applicant brought domestic proceedings against Norway in March 2016, seeking a declaratory judgment and compensation for violation of Article 6 § 1. The Oslo City Court found no violation: although 22 years was long, the estate was highly complex, other heirs brought many proceedings, no periods of inactivity were proven, and the State could not be blamed. The High Court agreed in March 2018. It noted that normal estate administration takes one to three years and that the total duration was longer than desirable. However, it characterised the case as extraordinary: extensive assets, multiple complex disputes, tax and trust issues, difficult property sales, and the 2008 financial crisis. It found no pure inactivity and no practical legal steps the State could have taken to speed up the process. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in June 2018.

The ECtHR examined whether this length was compatible with the “reasonable time” requirement. The central facts were the extraordinary complexity of the estate, the numerous legal actions by heirs, the trust and tax complications, and the absence of proven inactivity attributable to the authorities. The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 6 § 1, concluding that the duration was justified by the exceptional circumstances and that the Norwegian authorities had not failed to ensure progress.

text:
**Moroşanu and Others v. Romania** (ECtHR, Fourth Section, Committee, 16 March 2021; Applications nos. 84271/17 and 4 others) concerned the prolonged criminal investigations into injuries and deaths arising from the Romanian Revolution of December 1989. The five applicants were Romanian nationals who either were shot and injured during demonstrations or were close relatives of persons killed by gunshot. They complained mainly under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the domestic authorities had failed to carry out an effective investigation within a reasonable time.

The underlying events occurred in Bucharest and Reșița during December 1989, when demonstrations led to the fall of the communist regime. Applicant Cristian Florinel Moroşanu was shot on 23 December 1989 in Bucharest; his injuries required medical care for one year and three months and left him with a permanent infirmity. Aurel Iordan was also shot in Bucharest on 23 December 1989 and needed between twenty-three and twenty-five days of medical care. Floarea Portasă and Nicoleta Cîrjă were, respectively, the wife and daughter of a victim killed by gunshot in Bucharest on 23/24 December 1989. Maria Ruvineanțu was the mother of a victim killed by gunshot in Reșița on 25 December 1989.

In 1990, the military prosecutor’s office attached to the High Court of Cassation and Justice opened investigations of its own motion into illegal detention, ill-treatment, and injury suffered by the applicants and other participants in the December 1989 events. The main investigation was registered under file no. 97/P/1990, later no. 11/P/2014. Between 1991 and 2006, in separate proceedings concerning the applicants or their deceased relatives, prosecutors either declined to open investigations or discontinued proceedings. Those cases were nevertheless examined within the main criminal investigation, and the applicants pursued civil claims.

The procedural history of the main investigation resembled that in other Romanian revolution cases, including *Association “21 December 1989” and Others v. Romania* and *Sidea and Others v. Romania*. On 14 October 2015, the military prosecutor’s office closed the main investigation. It found that some complaints were statute-barred, some were covered by amnesty, some were ill-founded, some facts could not be classified as offences, and some were res judicata. That closure was subsequently annulled by the Prosecutor General on 5 April 2016, a decision confirmed by the High Court of Cassation and Justice on 13 June 2016. On 1 November 2016, the military prosecutor ordered a criminal investigation in rem for crimes against humanity concerning the same factual circumstances.

On 5 April 2019, the military prosecutor’s office sent to trial several individuals—including a former Romanian president, a former prime minister, and a former commander of the Romanian air force—for crimes against humanity. At the same time, it discontinued the investigation as to other individuals because some charges were res judicata, some suspects had died, or some facts could not be classified as criminal offences. Those proceedings remained pending before the Preliminary Chamber of the High Court of Cassation and Justice.

The key alleged violation was therefore procedural: that the Romanian authorities had not conducted an effective, prompt, and thorough investigation into the December 1989 events in which the applicants were injured or their relatives killed. The investigation spanned decades, involved repeated decisions to close or discontinue proceedings, and had not reached a final resolution. The Court gave notice only of the complaints concerning the lack of an effective investigation within a reasonable time; the remainder of the applications were declared inadmissible. The case thus centered on whether Romania complied with its Article 2 obligation to investigate deaths and serious injuries caused by state action during the Revolution.

The case of *Gilligan v. Ireland* concerned four Irish nationals—John, Geraldine, Treacy and Darren Gilligan, members of the same family—who complained that proceedings brought against them under the Proceeds of Crime Act 1996 (“the Act”) exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In November 1996, the Criminal Assets Bureau (“CAB”) applied to the High Court to freeze properties belonging to the applicants, including houses, land and cars, alleging that they represented proceeds of crime. An interim order was made on 21 November 1996. A temporary order under section 3 of the Act followed on 5 December 1996. The first applicant was then in custody in Belmarsh prison, London; he was later extradited to Ireland, convicted of drug offences in 2001 and sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment, ultimately released in 2013. Further section 3 orders were made in December 1996 and on 16 July 1997. The July 1997 order was later held by the Supreme Court, in April 2005, to be the final and operative freezing order.

A key feature of the Act was that a section 3 “interlocutory order,” despite its name, was in substance a final measure: it froze property until, after seven years, the State could seek a disposal order under section 4. A person affected could, however, apply at any time under section 3(3) to vary or discharge the order if the property was not proceeds of crime or if the order caused injustice.

The applicants made numerous attempts to challenge the freezing order. The first applicant brought a constitutional challenge, dismissed in 1997 and upheld on appeal in 2001. In 1998 and 2000, efforts were made to have the order discharged or proceedings struck out on procedural grounds. In December 2004, CAB applied under section 4 for a disposal order, but that application did not progress until the applicants’ other challenges were resolved. In 2008, the Supreme Court rejected the argument that the freezing order could be challenged for alleged procedural unfairness; it held that the proper remedy was an appeal or a section 3(3) application, and that the applicants’ advisers should have understood this since 1997.

The applicants eventually brought section 3(3) applications in 2009. After hearings in 2010, the High Court ruled in January 2011 against them. It found that the first applicant’s evidence about the source of funds was untruthful and implausible, and that most properties were probably acquired through drug trafficking proceeds. It also held that delay was attributable to the applicants, who could have invoked section 3(3) much earlier. The applicants appealed in June 2012. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals on 1 February 2017, stating that the applicants had “slept on their rights” and failed to challenge the orders promptly. The properties were confiscated in June 2017.

The applicants lodged their Convention application on 31 July 2017. The only admissible complaint concerned the length of the proceedings. The key facts for that alleged violation were therefore the nearly 21-year period from the 1996 freezing orders to the 2017 final appeal and confiscation, the unusual final nature of the section 3 order, the availability of the section 3(3) remedy, the applicants’ delayed use of that remedy, their multiple and repetitive challenges, and the domestic courts’ findings that much of the delay was caused by the applicants themselves rather than the State.

**Summary of *Bliznyuk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 20789/14)**

The case of *Bliznyuk v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms. Galina Fedorovna Bliznyuk against Ukraine on 5 March 2014. The applicant complained under Article 2 of the Convention (right to life) about the death of her son in suspicious circumstances allegedly involving State agents and the subsequent ineffective investigation.

The key facts begin on 11 August 2001. The applicant's thirty-four-year-old son was stopped twice by separate traffic police patrols for traffic violations. On both occasions, he exhibited signs of severe alcohol intoxication and was taken to a medical centre for testing. The narcologist recorded high alcohol levels in his urine (2.66‰ and 3.7‰) and found him heavily intoxicated. According to police and the narcologist, he behaved adequately, refused medical assistance, and was released after each test. Some witnesses, however, testified that during the second stop, police officers forcibly pulled him from his car, handcuffed him, and beat him with rubber truncheons. These accounts were denied by police, and a later forensic opinion suggested the minor injuries found on his body were unlikely to have been caused by such truncheons.

The next day, 12 August 2001, the applicant's son was found dead in his abandoned car. The initial autopsy concluded he died from acute ischaemic heart disease, complicated by circulatory disturbance, with internal bleeding and minor scratches on his leg unrelated to death. Two experts partly dissented, attributing death to acute heart failure of toxic origin.

An investigation was initiated, but between 2001 and 2012, over twenty decisions refusing to institute criminal proceedings were made and subsequently set aside by higher prosecutors and courts. These authorities repeatedly identified critical shortcomings: contradictory expert evidence on the cause of death; failure to check the applicant's claims that her son had no heart condition; disregard of witness testimonies alleging police beating; failure to investigate the danger posed by the rising alcohol level and its cause; unclear origin of the internal bleeding; and procedural irregularities, such as different police patrols using the same attesting witnesses for offence reports. The applicant consistently alleged that police had beaten her son and forced him to consume alcohol.

In 2013, criminal proceedings were finally instituted against police officers for abuse of power and separately against the narcologist for failure to provide medical assistance. Forensic examinations conducted in 2013 reaffirmed the heart disease as the cause of death, found no causal link between the lack of medical aid and death, and suggested the son likely continued drinking after leaving the medical centre. Consequently, the proceedings against the police officers were terminated in April 2013 for lack of evidence, and this decision was upheld by domestic courts. The proceedings against the narcologist were also terminated multiple times, but those decisions were repeatedly set aside, and the investigation remained ongoing.

The applicant's key allegations before the Court were that her son died at the hands of State agents (police officers) who ill-treated him and forced alcohol consumption, and that the State failed to conduct an effective investigation into these events, thereby violating its positive obligation to protect the right to life.

**Sławiński v. Poland** (ECtHR, First Section, App. No. 61039/16, 15 April 2021)

The applicant, Mariusz Grzegorz Sławiński, a Polish national born in 1958 and living in Gniewkowo, complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the criminal proceedings against him were unreasonably long and that there was no effective domestic remedy for that delay. The application was lodged on 11 October 2016, and the Court gave notice to the Polish Government of the complaints concerning the length of the criminal proceedings and the right to an effective remedy.

The underlying criminal case began in 2001, when the Toruń District Prosecutor opened an investigation into alleged fraudulent activity by the applicant’s company, which dealt with debt vindication. The applicant and his business partner were suspected of failing to transmit to a bank several hundred monthly instalment payments collected from individuals who had taken out consumer loans. On 26 February 2002 the applicant was charged with fraud, and the prosecutor placed him under police supervision. On 24 June 2002 he and a co-accused were indicted before the Toruń District Court.

The first hearing was not held until 4 December 2003, almost eighteen months after the indictment. The trial court then held hearings at regular intervals, approximately 100 in total. By 7 March 2006, it had heard over 300 witnesses listed in the bill of indictment. After that point, however, the proceedings progressed very slowly. The first-instance court eventually convicted the applicant of defrauding payments received from over 300 persons, sentencing him to one year and eight months’ imprisonment, suspended on probation, plus a fine. The applicant appealed.

On 23 October 2014 the Toruń Regional Court quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. Between 9 April and 16 June 2015 the trial court held four hearings. On 22 June 2015 the Toruń District Court acquitted the applicant of some charges and convicted him of fraud in a more limited scope, imposing one year’s imprisonment, suspended, and a fine. The applicant again appealed.

On 17 March 2016 the Toruń Regional Court quashed the conviction and discontinued the proceedings because the offences had become time-barred. The judgment was given at a hearing attended by the applicant and his lawyer. The court gave oral reasons, informed the parties that written reasons would be prepared within fourteen days, and explained that the judgment was final and that a cassation appeal was possible. The applicant was served with the written grounds on 12 April 2016.

Separately, on 6 July 2015 the applicant lodged a complaint under the Polish 2004 Act concerning undue delay. On 20 August 2015 the Toruń Regional Court partly allowed the complaint and found that the proceedings had been excessively long. It awarded the applicant 2,000 Polish zlotys (approximately 475 euros). The court noted that the first hearing had been scheduled almost eighteen months after the indictment; that after all meaningful evidence had been gathered by 7 March 2006, the next seven and a half years produced only four more witnesses and a bank evidence request, amounting to a flagrant lack of procedural efficiency; and that the trial court had also taken too long to prepare written reasons for the first-instance judgment. It further observed that the trial court should have been more active in securing the attendance of the applicant and his lawyer, who had contributed to some delays. After the case was remitted, the Regional Court found no further delays attributable to the courts.

The relevant domestic law included the 2004 Act remedy for excessive length and Article 457 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, under which written reasons are prepared automatically when a second-instance court quashes a judgment and discontinues the case, but a party must apply to be served with them. The key alleged violations therefore concerned the unreasonable length of the criminal proceedings and the lack of an effective remedy for that delay.

**Feilazoo v. Malta** concerns a Nigerian national who, after serving a drug-related prison sentence in Malta, was placed in immigration detention and later alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 6 and 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In 2010, the applicant was convicted of drug offences and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment and a €50,000 fine, later converted into a further term of imprisonment in default. Shortly before his release in April 2018, he was questioned about his plans. He wished to return to Spain, where he had previously held a residence permit, but the Spanish authorities allegedly refused to accept him. On 10 April 2018, instead of being taken to an emergency shelter as he expected, he was escorted to the Immigration Office. Inspector D.B. informed him that he could not return to Spain and would be removed to Nigeria, while being detained in the meantime. A Return Decision and Removal Order was issued that day under Article 5(2)(d) of the Immigration Act because he had been convicted of an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment. The Government claimed he requested voluntary departure, which was refused because he was considered a risk of absconding and a threat to public policy or security; the applicant claimed he was not informed of any right to appeal.

When the applicant objected to detention, a violent scuffle occurred. The officers alleged that he became aggressive, resisted handcuffing and bit one officer, leading them to use pepper spray and restraints. The applicant alleged that officers grabbed him by the neck, twisted him to the floor, kicked him in the private parts, knelt on his face and neck, and pepper-sprayed him; he said he could not breathe and passed out. Medical reports documented a fractured left radial head, bruising and abrasions on his face, ears, neck, shoulder and wrists, a swollen thumb, a haematoma on the mastoid process, and severe lower back pain. An expert found blunt-trauma injuries and handcuff abrasions, describing the elbow fracture as grievous.

Criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant for assaulting and resisting correctional officers, causing slight injuries, disobeying lawful orders and disturbing public order. He was placed in pre-trial detention on 12 April 2018. He complained that he was questioned without a lawyer and without being informed of the charges, and that he refused to sign an incomplete statement. In February 2019 he was convicted and sentenced to two years’ imprisonment and a €5,000 fine; on appeal in May 2019 his guilt was confirmed but the sentence was reduced to two years suspended for three years and a €4,000 fine, with immediate deportation ordered after payment. Because he could not pay the fine, it was converted into six months’ imprisonment. He was then moved between prison and immigration detention, including the Safi Detention Centre.

The alleged violations concerned: Article 3, in relation to the alleged ill-treatment on 10 April 2018 and the conditions of his immigration detention; Article 5, concerning the lawfulness of his immigration detention and removal order, including the alleged lack of information about appeal or voluntary departure and his continued detention without a realistic prospect of removal; Article 6, regarding the fairness of the criminal proceedings, particularly the absence of a lawyer and inadequate information about charges; and Article 34, concerning interference with his correspondence and ineffective domestic legal aid representation, including alleged obstruction of access to medical documents and the legal aid lawyer’s failure to contact or represent him. The Court ultimately removed the domestic legal aid representative and granted legal aid for the Strasbourg proceedings.

Lacatus v. Switzerland (Application no. 14065/15) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by Violeta-Sibianca Lacatus, a Romanian national of Roma origin, against Switzerland. She alleged violations of Articles 8, 10 and 14 of the Convention arising from her prosecution and punishment for begging in Geneva under section 11A of the Geneva Criminal Law Act, which makes begging on public highways an offence punishable by a fine.

From 2011, the applicant lived intermittently in Geneva. Unable to find work, she resorted to begging. On 22 July 2011 she was fined CHF 100 under section 11A. On the same occasion, police confiscated CHF 16.75 from her after a body search; no seizure order was issued. Between February 2012 and January 2013, she received eight further summary penalty notices, each imposing a CHF 100 fine for begging on public highways using a cup. On 21 February and 4 March 2012 she was also taken into police custody for three hours each time. Each fine could be replaced by one day of imprisonment if unpaid.

On 14 January 2014 the Police Court of Geneva found her guilty of begging. It imposed a CHF 500 fine, convertible into five days’ imprisonment if unpaid, and upheld the confiscation of CHF 16.75.

She appealed, alleging infringement of her freedom of communication under Article 16 of the Swiss Constitution and Article 10 ECHR; indirect discrimination under Article 14 ECHR and Article 8 § 2 of the Swiss Constitution, read with section 11A; infringement of personal liberty under Articles 7, 10 and 36 of the Swiss Constitution and Article 8 ECHR; and arbitrary interpretation of section 11A because begging was not legally defined. She also requested return of the confiscated CHF 16.75 with interest.

On 4 April 2014 the Criminal Appeals Division dismissed her complaints. It held that the ban did not infringe freedom of expression because it did not prevent her from making her social situation known by other means. It found no indirect discrimination because the law did not target only Roma people and poverty was not a protected ground.

On 10 September 2014 the Federal Supreme Court also dismissed her appeal. It held that the ban breached neither Article 8 nor Article 14 ECHR. On Article 10, it found that her begging was non-verbal conduct. She had not reported any spoken message or political dimension. The message was confined to her private impoverishment or need for help, not addressed to the public as a whole but to individual passers-by to elicit pity and generosity. The communicative aspect was therefore substantially reduced, and Article 10 did not protect her conduct. The Federal Supreme Court further found that confiscation of the CHF 16.75 was not arbitrary, since she had not explained its provenance and it could be viewed as proceeds of begging.

From 24 to 28 March 2015, the applicant was detained in Champ-Dollon short-term prison for failure to pay the fine.

Relevant domestic law provided that section 11A punishes begging with a fine; if begging is arranged or the person is accompanied by minors or dependants, the minimum fine is CHF 2,000. Federal criminal law allows an alternative custodial sentence of one day to three months for negligent non-payment. The Federal Supreme Court had previously upheld Geneva’s blanket ban as a proportionate restriction of personal liberty, justified by public order, safety, tranquillity, and prevention of exploitation and harassment, noting that social assistance was available. It had also rejected indirect discrimination claims absent concrete evidence.

The key alleged violations thus concerned whether criminalising and punishing begging interfered with private life/personal liberty (Article 8), freedom of expression (Article 10), and amounted to indirect discrimination against Roma (Article 14).
