**Case: K.I. v. France (Application no. 5560/19), European Court of Human Rights, 15 April 2021**

The applicant, K.I., is a Russian national of Chechen origin born in 1994. He alleged that his deportation from France to Russia would violate Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, exposing him to a real risk of death or inhuman and degrading treatment.

K.I. claimed that in Russia his father had been a Chechen guerrilla fighter. In November 2010, he was allegedly arrested, held in custody, and beaten with an iron bar by Russian law-enforcement officers, who pressured him to infiltrate rebel groups. After he refused, he was arrested again in May 2011, interrogated, insulted, and beaten. Shortly before fleeing Russia, he was arrested a third time, assaulted, and threatened with death. He fled in 2011, transited through Poland, and left his Russian external passport there before reaching France.

In France, K.I. applied for asylum in March 2012 and was granted refugee status in January 2013. The French authorities accepted that he had family ties to Chechen separatists and had refused to cooperate with the Russian authorities. However, in November 2013, about nine months after obtaining refugee status, he was arrested in France on suspicion of involvement in a terrorist conspiracy. In April 2015, the Paris Criminal Court convicted him of participating in a criminal conspiracy to commit acts of terrorism. The court found that he had travelled to Syria in August 2013, via Germany, Poland, Ukraine, and Turkey, to undergo military training and fight with a jihadist group composed of Chechen, Dagestani, and Ingush fighters. He was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment.

Following his conviction, the French Office for the Protection of Refugees and Stateless Persons revoked his refugee status in June 2016 under Article L. 711-6 of the Immigration and Asylum Code, on the grounds that he had been finally convicted of a terrorism offence and that his presence in France constituted a serious threat to society. The National Asylum Court confirmed that decision in January 2019, and the Conseil d’État dismissed his further appeal in July 2020.

A deportation order had been issued in November 2015, and in February 2019 the prefect set Russia as the destination country. K.I. argued that he would still be at risk in Russia because of his family ties to Chechen fighters, his refusal to collaborate, and his membership in a Chechen “teip” allegedly opposed to the regime. He relied on statements that Russian or Chechen authorities had repeatedly questioned his relatives, that FSB agents had told family members he would be imprisoned upon return, and that a friend with refugee status in Germany had been arrested after returning to Russia. He also claimed that Russian officials had contacted him by telephone and Skype after he arrived in France.

The French Government disputed the reliability of this evidence, noting that some witness statements were undated or unauthenticated. Domestic courts found that K.I. had not demonstrated a real and personal risk of ill-treatment if returned. They observed that he had used his Russian external passport to travel to Syria and that there was no evidence he was wanted or charged in Russia. They also referred to reports indicating that returnees from Syria were monitored but that Chechen authorities had reception programmes for some returnees.

Before the European Court, K.I. requested an interim measure under Rule 39 to prevent his deportation. The Court initially granted temporary protection, discontinued it when no enforceable removal decision existed, and then extended it while the application was examined. The central issue was whether enforcing the deportation order would expose K.I. to treatment contrary to Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

**Summary of *Abdi v. Denmark* (Application no. 41643/19)**

The case concerns the expulsion of a settled migrant from Denmark and a permanent re-entry ban imposed in criminal proceedings, raising issues under the applicant’s right to respect for private and family life.

The applicant, Mohamed Hassan Abdi, is a Somali national born in 1993. He entered Denmark in 1997 at age four with his mother and was granted asylum in December 1997. His father and sister came in 2000, and a younger brother was born in Denmark. By the time of the proceedings, he had lawfully resided in Denmark for about twenty years and two months. His parents and siblings lived in Denmark; he lived with his sister and brother. He had no family in Somalia, had not returned there since leaving as a child, spoke Danish, and had only basic Somali. He had attended primary school and completed a basic commercial programme, and while in custody was enrolled in vocational upper secondary education. He was unmarried, had no children, and no girlfriend in Denmark.

The applicant had a criminal history. As a minor, he was convicted of robbery at age 15 and burglary at age 17, receiving suspended or partly suspended sentences. As an adult, he was convicted and fined seven times, mainly for controlled-substance offences and driving under the influence of psychedelic substances, most recently in December 2016.

In May 2018, the District Court convicted him of illegal possession of a fully loaded 9 mm firearm with ammunition in a public place, committed around midnight on 5 November 2017 jointly with three others, and of two controlled-substance violations: possession of 1.2 grams of cannabis for personal use and 7.4 grams intended for handover to a prison inmate. The firearm had been brought in a car parked 200 metres from the clubhouse of a motorcycle gang, S. The applicant and co-accused were affiliated with or meeting members of another gang, R. Although no ongoing conflict between S and R was proved, police testified that S had been on high alert. The District Court found joint possession in particularly aggravating circumstances under Article 192a of the Penal Code and sentenced him to two years and nine months’ imprisonment.

The immigration authorities gathered personal-circumstances information. The District Court, by a majority, decided on conditional expulsion with a two-year probation period. It found expulsion disproportionate given his long residence, lack of ties to Somalia, and the absence of any prior expulsion order, despite the seriousness of the offence. The dissenting judge favoured unconditional expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban.

On appeal, the Western Denmark High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years and six months. By a majority of five to one, it ordered expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban. The majority found very compelling reasons due to the serious firearm offence and prior convictions. It accepted that expulsion would burden him because of his ties to Denmark, but noted he lacked spouse, children, completed education, or regular labour-market ties. It also considered that he spoke basic Somali and likely knew Somali customs and culture through his family, so he was not entirely without ties or qualifications for return. It concluded that expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban was proportionate to prevent disorder and crime. The dissenting judge would have made expulsion conditional. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in January 2019.

Under the Aliens Act at the time, a permanent re-entry ban automatically followed a prison sentence exceeding two years. A 2018 amendment, not applicable to this crime, lowered that threshold to one year and six months but allowed courts to reduce bans if necessary to comply with international obligations. The key proportionality facts were therefore the applicant’s long lawful residence from childhood, family ties in Denmark, absence of ties to Somalia, limited Somali language, education and employment limitations, serious gang-related firearm offence, prior criminal record, and the permanent re-entry ban.

Apap Bologna v. Malta (App. no. 47505/19), judgment of 9 December 2021, concerned a Maltese national, Mr Louis Apap Bologna, and a unilaterally imposed commercial lease under Chapter 69 of the Laws of Malta. The applicant alleged that the statutory rent regime forced him to receive an insufficient, controlled rent for his Valletta shop, imposing a disproportionate burden on his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. He also questioned the effectiveness of domestic remedies.

The applicant originally owned one-half undivided share of premises at 295 and 296 Republic Street, Valletta, inherited in 1980. The property had been leased in 1922 for four years at GBP 100 per year. Although originally contractual, 1933 Act XXI—now Chapter 69—introduced perpetual protection for tenants, renewing the lease indefinitely and preventing eviction. In 1964 the owners negotiated rent of GBP 150. In 1980, after partition with the co-owner, the applicant became full owner of the interconnected shop at no. 296. Around the same time, the tenancy passed through successions and transfers to three tenants, K., I., and V., who were not recognised by the landlords; attempts to evict them also failed.

Rent remained very low. From 18 April 2001, the landlords refused rent and deposits were made in court: the first was MTL 2,828.84, covering rent from 1982 to 2001; later deposits were MTL 150 (about EUR 395) per annum until 2009. Act X of 2009 raised rent by 15% annually for 2010–2013: EUR 401.82, EUR 462.09, EUR 531.41, and EUR 611.11. From 2014, because the Index of Commercial Value of Property was never published, rent rose by 5% yearly: EUR 641.67, EUR 673.75, EUR 707.44, EUR 742.81, EUR 779.95, and EUR 818.95 for 2014–2019.

In 2017 the applicant filed constitutional redress proceedings, claiming a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. A court-appointed architect valued the entire property at EUR 1.5 million and its annual market rent at EUR 86,540. The legal rent due in 2017 was about EUR 743 annually. The total market rent since 1986 was estimated at EUR 1,603,499. On 4 June 2018 the Civil Court, in its constitutional competence, found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but not of the Constitution, and awarded EUR 100,000 compensation with costs split equally.

Both parties appealed. On 29 March 2019 the Constitutional Court confirmed the violation but reduced compensation to EUR 55,000—EUR 50,000 for pecuniary damage and EUR 5,000 for non-pecuniary damage. It refused to order eviction, considering it lacked jurisdiction, but declared Chapter 69 provisions without effect between the applicant and the tenants, so the tenants could no longer rely on them to justify occupation. Costs were apportioned: first-instance costs remained as before; appeal costs were divided equally between the Attorney General and the applicant; the tenants bore their own cross-appeal costs. The Constitutional Court noted that the architect’s valuation covered the entire shop, whereas the applicant’s interest was limited to his divided part.

After the judgment, the applicant negotiated a new lease at EUR 140 daily—EUR 51,100 yearly—effective 1 October 2019, exceeding the expert’s estimate, plus a lump sum to make up fair rent from the Constitutional Court judgment. Later, due to COVID-19, he agreed to EUR 50 daily. The core alleged violation was the disproportionate burden arising from the perpetual statutory lease and inadequate rent, and whether domestic remedies sufficiently redressed that breach under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Chernika v. Ukraine* (Application no. 53791/11), the applicant, Mykhaylo Chernika, was a former Ukrainian police investigator. He was charged with stealing opium that had been seized as evidence in a case he was investigating. According to the prosecution, he siphoned opium from the evidence jar, diluted the remaining liquid, and gave the stolen opium to his friend, Ms N.Sh., to help sell it. N.Sh. allegedly involved Mr V.G. and Mr I.S., who came from Crimea to Lutsk, to transport the opium back to Crimea for sale.

During the pre-trial investigation, N.Sh., V.G., and I.S. made statements implicating the applicant. Confrontations were held between them and the applicant. However, the applicant and his lawyers did not have access to the investigation file at that stage. The case later became centrally concerned with the use of these witnesses’ statements at trial.

At the first trial before Judge V.D., N.Sh. appeared and confirmed her pre-trial statement. V.G. and I.S. were repeatedly summoned but failed to appear. The Security Service could not locate them. The trial court read out their pre-trial statements and, on 26 August 2008, convicted the applicant of theft and illegal possession of a large quantity of drugs with intent to sell, sentencing him to eight years’ imprisonment. The Court of Appeal quashed the conviction on 10 March 2009 because the trial court had read V.G.’s statement without knowing why he had failed to appear. The case was remitted for retrial before a different judge.

At the retrial before Judge V.B., N.Sh., V.G., and I.S. were again repeatedly summoned but did not appear. V.G. and I.S. were reported to be seriously ill—V.G. hospitalised and I.S. suffering from infectious tuberculosis—and unable to travel from Crimea to Lutsk. N.Sh. could not be found. Other witnesses testified, including N.Sh.’s friends and colleagues, who said the applicant and N.Sh. were close, that drugs were discussed, and that V.G. and I.S. had visited N.Sh.’s flat. A police officer also testified that the applicant and N.Sh. were friends.

On 11 December 2009, the retrial court again convicted the applicant and imposed the same eight-year sentence. It relied essentially on the same evidence, including the pre-trial statements of N.Sh., V.G., and I.S. The court found those statements reliable because they were mutually consistent and had been confirmed during pre-trial confrontations, where the applicant had been able to examine and question the witnesses. It therefore rejected the claim that defence rights or the principle of immediacy had been breached. It also relied on corroborating testimony from N.Sh.’s friends, documentary evidence concerning the opium jar, and expert and police evidence about the reduced drug quantity. The applicant appealed, arguing that the three key witnesses had not been examined at the retrial, were not credible, and had given contradictory accounts. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 2 March 2010, and the Supreme Court rejected a cassation appeal on 15 March 2011.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) that the criminal proceedings were unfair. The key complaint was that the domestic courts admitted in evidence statements of three witnesses despite the fact that N.Sh. had been examined only in the original trial, not the retrial before a different judge, and V.G. and I.S. had never appeared before the trial court. Thus, the central facts were the reliance on absent or previously examined witnesses’ statements and the applicant’s inability to cross-examine them effectively at the retrial.

The case of *Strøbye and Rosenlind v. Denmark* concerned two Danish nationals who had been deprived of their legal capacity and were consequently denied the right to vote in Denmark’s 2015 parliamentary elections. The first applicant, born in 1966, was declared legally incompetent in 1984 by the Copenhagen City Court under the then applicable legal competence rules. The second applicant, born in 1987, was placed under financial guardianship and deprived of legal capacity in 2009 by the Roskilde District Court. That court found he could not manage his financial affairs because of mental disability and needed protection against further debt. Under Article 29 of the Danish Constitution and section 1 of the Parliamentary Elections Act, persons declared legally incompetent were not entitled to vote in general elections. The applicants were therefore excluded from the parliamentary election held on 18 June 2015.

A 2016 statutory amendment gave persons deprived of legal capacity the right to vote in European Parliament elections and in local and regional elections, but not in national parliamentary elections. The applicants, together with two others, brought proceedings against the Danish Ministry of Social Affairs and the Interior, claiming that their disenfranchisement violated Article 29 of the Constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights, and the UN Disability Convention. Before the European Court of Human Rights, they complained specifically of a breach of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, taken alone or in conjunction with Article 14, arguing that their exclusion from the right to vote was arbitrary and disproportionate.

The domestic courts rejected their claims. The High Court of Eastern Denmark held in 2017 that the longstanding constitutional interpretation excluded persons deprived of legal capacity and that Denmark’s international obligations did not require an absolute right to vote for this group. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 18 January 2018. It accepted that the restriction pursued a legitimate aim—ensuring that only citizens capable of assessing the consequences of their decisions participated in public affairs. It also found the Danish scheme narrower than the Hungarian measure condemned in *Alajos Kiss v. Hungary*: only persons fully deprived of legal capacity under section 6 of the Guardianship Act were disenfranchised, not all persons under guardianship. The Supreme Court considered that strict conditions governed full deprivation and that about 1,850 persons were affected. It held that an individual assessment of voting capacity was not always required and found no violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 or Article 14.

Key facts relevant to the alleged violation included the automatic nature of the disenfranchisement: it followed from the civil-law status of full deprivation of legal capacity, without an individualised judicial assessment of the applicants’ actual ability to vote or their political awareness. The applicants’ personal circumstances suggested they could participate meaningfully. The first applicant had brain damage but could express views and described sharing a single vote with his guardian mother as humiliating. The second lived in a group home, worked at a reception desk, read newspapers, watched news, and was interested in politics; he felt excluded from society. Denmark later amended the law in 2018–2019 to allow partial deprivation of legal capacity, under which partially deprived persons retained voting rights. The first applicant’s incapacity order was quashed in 2019, and the second was only partially deprived, so both regained national voting rights. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, holding that the blanket, automatic disenfranchisement of persons fully deprived of legal capacity, without individual assessment, exceeded Denmark’s margin of appreciation.

**Case: Chernov v. Ukraine (Application no. 16432/10), ECtHR, 10 December 2020**

The applicant, Oleksandr Gennadiyovych Chernov, a Ukrainian national, complained that he had been tried and punished twice for the same conduct, in violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights (the right not to be tried or punished twice).

The case arose from events on 20 June 2007 at about 10 p.m. on Prokofyeva Street in Sumy. According to the administrative findings, the applicant, while drunk outdoors, uttered obscenities, reacted aggressively to police remarks, cursed the officers, attempted to start a fight, and thereby breached public order and offended human dignity and morals. On 21 June 2007 the Zarichnyy District Court of Sumy found him guilty of “minor disorderly acts” under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences and imposed three days’ administrative detention. That decision became final and was not subject to ordinary appeal. The applicant served the detention from 21 to 23 June 2007.

Later, the same facts became the basis of criminal proceedings. On 16 July 2007 a prosecutor opened a criminal case against the applicant for disorderly acts under Article 296 of the Criminal Code, later under Article 296 § 3, alleging that on 20 June 2007 he had committed hooliganism and caused minor physical injuries to two victims, Mu. and P. The applicant was arrested in December 2007, indicted in January 2008, and convicted in July 2008. That conviction was quashed on appeal in October 2008 for factual inconsistencies and remitted for fresh examination.

Meanwhile, on 28 January 2008, the prosecutor lodged an objection against the earlier administrative decision. The prosecutor argued that administrative liability under Article 173 applied only where the facts did not give rise to criminal liability, and that the applicant’s actions actually amounted to a criminal offence. On 6 February 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court annulled its own decision of 21 June 2007; this annulment was upheld on appeal on 25 February 2008.

In the renewed criminal proceedings, the judge who had handled the administrative case withdrew, noting that she had found the applicant administratively liable and later annulled that decision because the prosecutor’s investigation revealed a criminal offence. On 29 December 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court convicted the applicant under Article 296 § 3 and sentenced him to two years and one month’s imprisonment. On 10 March 2009 the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years. The applicant appealed, arguing, inter alia, that he had been tried twice for the same offence. On 24 September 2009 the Supreme Court of Ukraine rejected that complaint, reasoning that the administrative decision had been annulled and the administrative case “closed,” so the applicant had not been tried twice.

The key issue before the ECtHR was whether the administrative proceedings and the subsequent criminal proceedings concerned the same facts and constituted a second trial or punishment. The applicant had already been finally convicted and had served a three-day administrative detention for the disorderly conduct before the criminal prosecution for the same events proceeded. The domestic authorities sought to avoid double jeopardy by annulling the administrative decision after it had become final and after the sanction had been served. The ECtHR found that this amounted to a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, as the applicant had been tried and punished twice for substantially the same conduct.

In *Alimpiev v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*, the applicant, Alexandru Alimpiev, a Russian national born in 1950 and living in Tiraspol, was president of the Tiraspol People’s Court in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). On 31 August 2006 the “MRT” prosecutor’s office began a corruption investigation into him. He was arrested on 17 May 2007 and formally charged with corruption. He remained in detention pending trial until 25 December 2008, when the “MRT” Supreme Court convicted him and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. That judgment was upheld on 18 March 2009. On 24 July 2009, in extraordinary proceedings, the sentence was reduced to five years and he was released under an amnesty.

The case concerned the applicant’s alleged detention in inhuman conditions, failure to observe his rights during detention pending trial, and censorship of his correspondence in prison. On 2 November 2017 the respondent Governments were given notice of complaints under Article 3, Article 5 §§ 3 and 4, Article 6 § 1, Article 8, and Article 13 of the Convention; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Russian Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

As to detention pending trial, the prosecutor periodically sought extensions of the applicant’s detention, and each time a judge granted the request. The applicant was unable to obtain copies of the decisions extending his detention. On 21 July 2008 his lawyer sent a telegram to the president of the “MRT” Supreme Court asking for a copy of a decision of 18 July 2008 extending detention, and asked that the applicant’s Article 34 rights not be hindered by refusal. By reply of 23 July 2008, the president stated that “MRT” law did not provide for defence representatives to obtain copies of decisions issued in response to applications before the courts. On 15 August 2008 the lawyer asked to make copies of selected parts of the criminal file; the request was refused the same day by handwritten note, again on the basis that “MRT” law did not provide such a right. On 18 August 2008 the lawyer asked for copies of all detention-extension decisions, stressing that he had not been involved at the pre-trial stage and needed them for an effective defence, and relying on Article 34.

In applications to replace detention with an alternative measure, the lawyer relied on Articles 3, 5, 6, 8 and 13, arguing that the “MRT” courts had extended detention by merely citing abstract risks—absconding, reoffending or interfering with the investigation—without evidence specific to the applicant. He also described the applicant’s detention conditions and worsening health. On 11 November 2008 the lawyer issued a press release about the case.

Regarding conditions of detention, the applicant described the temporary detention facility in Tiraspol and prison UIN-3 as follows: the cell had no separate toilet or shower; he received no hygiene products or bed linen; the cell was infested with parasites; tap water was bad; the window was very small and allowed damp and cold air; daily walks were very short. Relatives could send only 30 kg of items per month, including bottled water, and the facility food was inedible; combined, he alleged torture through hunger. During trial he was held in a metal cage. On 6 August 2008 his lawyer asked that he sit next to counsel rather than in a cage and that cages in courtrooms be declared unlawful; it is unclear whether a reply was received. A medical certificate showed that on 23 June 2008 an emergency team attended him, diagnosed respiratory problems and moderate persistent asthma, and prescribed medication. He alleged heavy smoking by cellmates exposed him to passive smoke.

Finally, the applicant alleged that all his correspondence was censored during detention. He submitted a copy of a letter sent to him personally by his lawyer; the envelope bore a stamp reading “Verified. Censor (signature), 8/09/2008.”

**Mucha v. Slovakia** (Application no. 63703/19, ECtHR First Section, judgment 25 November 2021) concerned alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 (impartial tribunal) and Article 6 § 2 (presumption of innocence) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Pavel Mucha, a Slovak national born in 1979 and serving imprisonment, complained that the same tribunal that had previously approved his co-perpetrators’ plea bargains later convicted him, and that those earlier decisions had effectively treated him as guilty before his own trial.

The facts concerned an organised criminal gang operating in Bratislava and other Slovak regions. In 2012, the applicant and nine others were charged with setting up, conceiving and maintaining a criminal enterprise, along with multiple violent offences. Prosecution was initially joint, but eight co-perpetrators were later prosecuted separately after entering plea-bargaining agreements with the Public Prosecution Service. Those agreements required confessions and contained precise factual descriptions of the offences, legal classifications, and penalties. The Specialised Criminal Court (SCC), sitting in the same three-judge chamber of career judges, approved the agreements in judgments dated 19 December 2012 and 7 March 2013. The judgments found the eight co-perpetrators guilty and sentenced them.

Crucially for the applicant’s complaints, the operative parts of those judgments included factual definitions of the criminal acts that referred to the applicant by initials, and sometimes by alias. They described him as a mid-ranking member of the gang who gave instructions, received percentages from extortion, imposed and enforced financial penalties on members, ordered forcible debt collection, arranged the setting of operations, and received and distributed proceeds. The judgments contained little reasoning beyond reciting procedural history and finding the plea bargains lawful and the penalties adequate. They became final on delivery.

The applicant was then tried separately by an SCC chamber with identical composition. On 7 August 2013, he was found guilty as charged and sentenced to twenty-three years’ imprisonment. The factual definitions of four sets of criminal actions attributed to him were identical to those previously summarised in the co-perpetrators’ plea-bargain judgments. The trial court relied on complex evidence, including testimony from co-perpetrators, some of whom were cooperating “penitents.” In its reasoning, it noted that the co-perpetrators’ convictions were a “factual and homogenous part” of the case and were contained in the file.

The applicant appealed, lodged an appeal on points of law, and filed a constitutional complaint. He argued that the prior plea-bargain judgments, delivered by the same judges who later decided his case, had prejudiced the assessment of his guilt and violated his right to an impartial tribunal and to be presumed innocent. His appeals were dismissed, ultimately by the Constitutional Court on 25 June 2019. The Constitutional Court relied on a 2017 unifying decision of the Supreme Court, which held that approving a plea bargain involves no evidence-taking, binds only the convicted person, and does not disqualify the judge from later proceedings against another accused. It also stated that mentioning another person in an earlier conviction does not violate the presumption of innocence, and that such persons should preferably be identified by initials. The Constitutional Court distinguished cases such as *Ferrantelli and Santangelo v. Italy* because the applicant had not argued that the trial court cited extensive extracts from the earlier judgments.

Domestic law and EU law were also relevant: Article 4(1) of Directive 2016/343 and CJEU case-law (*AH and Others*, *UL and VM*) permit references to other accused persons in plea agreements only where necessary for legal categorisation and where it is made clear that their guilt has not been legally established and will be determined separately. The case therefore centred on whether the same tribunal’s earlier plea-bargain findings improperly prejudged the applicant’s guilt or created an appearance of bias.

In *Rovshan Hajiyev v. Azerbaijan* (Applications nos. 19925/12 and 47532/13, judgment of 9 December 2021), the applicant was an Azerbaijani journalist and editor of the newspaper *Azadlıq*. The case concerned requests for information about the Gabala Radar Station, a Soviet-era military early warning radar located in Azerbaijan and operated by Russia under a lease until 2012. The applicant alleged that the station caused serious environmental and public-health problems in Gabala and nearby districts. Presidential orders in 2001 and 2003 created Azerbaijani-Russian commissions, chaired by the Minister of Healthcare, to assess the station’s environmental and public-health impact. The applicant sought related reports and information from State authorities under Azerbaijan’s Law on Access to Information, but claimed he was denied access. He also alleged that the domestic proceedings concerning his requests lacked fairness. The applications were lodged under Articles 6 and 10 of the Convention.

In application no. 19925/12, on 27 July 2010 the applicant wrote to the Ministry of Healthcare as editor of *Azadlıq*, invoking the Law on Access to Information. He asked whether the State commission assessing the Gabala Radar Station’s environmental and public-health impact was still active and requested copies of reports prepared by relevant State commissions. On 6 August 2010, the Ministry replied that a report prepared under the presidential order of 26 February 2001 had been transmitted to the Cabinet of Ministers. The applicant considered this response inadequate and sued, seeking an order requiring the Ministry to provide a copy of the report. The Ministry argued that it no longer possessed the report and had given a comprehensive reply. On 3 February 2011, the Nasimi District Court dismissed the claim, finding that the Ministry had complied because it no longer held the report and had informed the applicant. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 2 May 2011, adding that the Ministry had assisted by identifying the Cabinet of Ministers as the holder. The Supreme Court upheld the lower judgments on 5 September 2011.

In application no. 47532/13, on 6 December 2010 the applicant wrote to the Cabinet of Ministers requesting a copy of the same report. The Cabinet received the request but did not respond. In February 2011, the applicant sued in Baku Administrative Economic Court No. 1, arguing that the failure to respond breached the Law on Access to Information and Article 10 of the Convention. The Cabinet of Ministers did not send representatives or submit written pleadings during the proceedings. The applicant reapplied in April 2011 but again received no response. On 23 December 2011, the first-instance court dismissed the claim, reasoning that Article 29.1 of the Law on Access to Information did not obligate information owners to disclose reports of commissions created for a specific purpose. The applicant appealed, arguing that Article 29.1 merely listed types of information to be proactively disclosed and did not limit obligations to provide non-restricted information upon request. He contended that the report was not restricted and was of public interest, needed for his professional work as a journalist. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment on 15 March 2012, and the Supreme Court upheld it on 11 July 2012.

Under the relevant law, State bodies were “information owners” required to ensure access to information, respond to requests, assist in locating information if not possessed, and forward requests to the proper owner within five working days. Refusals had to be written and substantiated. Article 29.1 listed information subject to proactive disclosure, while Article 29.2 generally prohibited requesting those listed types individually, subject to exceptions. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 6 and 10 arising from the denial of access to requested information and the alleged unfairness of the domestic proceedings.

Monir Lotfy v. Cyprus (Application no. 37139/13, ECtHR Third Section, 29 June 2021) concerned an Egyptian national with a long immigration history in Cyprus. He first arrived in 1991, was deported twice, and although granted Cypriot citizenship, it was later revoked. After a second deportation in June 2012, he unlawfully re-entered Cyprus. On 10 February 2013 police arrested him during a random identity check. On 11 February 2013, deportation and detention orders were issued under the Aliens and Immigration Law because he was a prohibited immigrant. He remained in immigration detention until 8 July 2014, when he was deported to Egypt, moving between Nicosia Central Prisons Block 10, Menoyia detention centre, and various police stations.

The main Article 5 §1 complaint was that this detention pending deportation was unlawful. After more than five months, he lodged a first habeas corpus application. On 30 July 2013 the Supreme Court granted it, ordered his immediate release, and found the Government had not shown his continued detention was justified: it had failed to explain steps taken to deport him or whether the Minister had reviewed detention as required. The same day, while still at court, he was rearrested. New deportation and detention orders were issued on the same grounds. A second habeas corpus application was rejected on 28 January 2014; the Supreme Court viewed the detention as continuous since February 2013 and lawful because extensions were based on the lack of Egyptian travel documents, partly due to the applicant’s refusal to cooperate. His judicial-review challenge to the new orders also failed; a provisional suspension was initially ordered subject to a €10,000 guarantee, but he could not provide a guarantor. The main recourse was later dismissed as moot after deportation. His asylum claim, lodged in January 2014, was rejected and his appeal dismissed in 2015 after deportation.

Under Article 5 §4, he alleged there was no effective remedy for challenging his detention, given the rearrest after the habeas corpus release, the rejection of the second habeas corpus, and the ineffective recourse proceedings.

Under Article 3, he alleged poor detention conditions, denial of medical treatment, and ill-treatment. He complained of overcrowding and inadequate facilities, including at Menoyia, where an 18.36 sq m cell held up to eight detainees (he shared with four to seven), and smaller police cells. He alleged refusal of medication and delays in hospital access. He claimed that on 17 July 2013 he was handcuffed to a chair for six hours and assaulted; the Government denied this. On 9 October 2013 he alleged officers beat him at Menoyia; the Government said he assaulted two officers, who were injured. Criminal proceedings against him were discontinued after deportation. On 19 October 2013 he alleged beating when requesting hospital; the Government recorded that he had drunk shampoo and had abrasions but no fracture. On 29 October 2013 he alleged forced showering and humiliation. He was also held in solitary confinement in April and May 2014 for misconduct; the Ombudsman did not investigate after his deportation. Medical records showed he was examined or hospitalised many times.

**Summary of *Mikeladze and Others v. Georgia* (Application no. 54217/16)**

The case concerns four Georgian nationals of the Muslim minority who complained that police physically and verbally assaulted them during arrest and detention, using discriminatory insults, and that the ensuing criminal investigation was ineffective, in breach of Articles 3 and 14 of the Convention.

The events arose from a dispute over an old building in the village of Mokhe, claimed by the local Muslim community as an ancient mosque, which municipal authorities decided to reconstruct as a public library. On 22 October 2014, between sixty and one hundred police officers and municipal representatives gathered as reconstruction began. Fifty to one hundred local Muslim residents, including the applicants, protested. The police formed a cordon separating protesters from officials. The first applicant was a village trustee; his father, the second applicant, accompanied him; the third applicant joined from a neighbouring village; and the fourth applicant, a school librarian, became involved after leaving work.

Accounts of the events differ. The applicants alleged that police used excessive force during arrests and shouted insults, calling them "Tatars"—a term they considered an insult implying their Muslim faith was incompatible with being Georgian. They claimed violence continued at the police station. The Government maintained that the applicants resorted to physical and verbal violence and attempted to break the police cordon; arrests were for resisting lawful orders and breaching public order, with no excessive force or derogatory remarks used.

Fourteen individuals were arrested. The first three applicants faced criminal charges of resisting police; the remaining eleven, including the fourth applicant, faced administrative charges of minor hooliganism and disobeying police. All were released on 23 October 2014.

The first applicant's arrest report recorded redness around his left eye, an excoriation on a wrist, and a bump on his head; he stated injuries occurred during arrest and refused medical assistance. He later complained of headache and disorientation, and medical examination noted a haematoma around the left eye. The second applicant complained of breathing difficulties the following morning. The third and fourth applicants' reports recorded no injuries or complaints.

On 5 November 2014, the first three applicants and seven others complained to the Chief Prosecutor's Office about derogatory language (including "Tatar") and excessive force during arrest and at the police station. They requested that the prosecutor's office, rather than the implicated police, conduct the investigation. The first applicant alleged he was beaten and assaulted at the station; the third applicant claimed seven officers beat him for approximately ten minutes.

A criminal investigation was split in December 2014: one strand concerning the applicants' alleged offences against police, another concerning alleged police exceeding of official powers. Investigative steps in 2014–2015 produced conflicting witness accounts—some confirmed hearing "Tatar" insults and witnessing beatings; others denied any ill-treatment. In April 2021, prosecutors granted the first applicant victim status, finding that officers G.P. and B.A. had punched and kicked him at the police station, and charged both (by then no longer serving) under Article 333 § 3(b) of the Criminal Code. Proceedings against them remain ongoing, and no progress was made regarding the other three applicants' complaints.

Levon Barseghyan, an Armenian journalist and political activist who chaired a journalists’ club in Gyumri, complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 11 of the Convention about being prevented from holding and participating in a rally and being fined for disobeying police orders.

The case arose after Armenia’s 19 February 2008 presidential election. Opposition supporters, led by candidate Levon Ter-Petrosyan, began daily protests in Yerevan, centring on Freedom Square. On 1 March 2008, police cleared the square; later that day, protests escalated into clashes, resulting in ten deaths, injuries and property damage. The President declared a state of emergency in Yerevan for twenty days, banning meetings, rallies, demonstrations, marches and other mass events. Although the decree was formally limited to Yerevan, reports by Armenia’s Ombudsman, PACE and the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights indicated that restrictions on rallies were also applied in other major cities, including Gyumri.

On 2 March 2008 at about 12:30 p.m., Barseghyan went to Theatre Square in Gyumri and tried to enter the square to hold a protest. Police officers stationed there to prevent demonstrations refused him entry. According to the authorities, he called on people present to gather and hold a demonstration. Police ordered him to leave and stop inciting others to assemble. He did not comply and was taken to a police station.

An administrative case was opened under Article 182 of the Code of Administrative Offences for disobeying lawful police orders. The police then sought an administrative penalty, claiming that no notification or authorisation had been given to hold a demonstration at Theatre Square. Barseghyan counterclaimed that the factual basis was unsubstantiated: he had not intended to organise a rally, no rally was taking place, “calling on people” was not a punishable act, and there was no evidence that 100 or more people had gathered. Under the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, only “mass public events” of 100 or more participants required prior written notification; non-mass events of fewer than 100 participants did not. He therefore argued that the police orders were not lawful.

The police responded that well-known facts did not need proof, including the tense post-1 March situation, a previous unauthorised rally at Theatre Square, and an announcement that Barseghyan would speak at the next rally. They contended that his appearance was not accidental and that the administrative case was justified.

On 10 June 2008, the Administrative Court granted the police claim and fined Barseghyan 50,000 Armenian drams (about €110). It found that police were at the square to prohibit an unnotified demonstration and that there had been no legal basis for holding one. Although the state of emergency was formally in force only in Yerevan, the court reasoned that a mass public event in Gyumri, Armenia’s second-largest city, could have endangered public order and public health, especially without notification. It concluded that the police orders he disobeyed were lawful.

Barseghyan appealed, arguing that the fine violated his Article 11 rights and that the judgment failed to explain the restriction on his right to hold and participate in a rally. On 2 October 2008, the Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible for lack of merit.

He lodged his application with the European Court on 1 April 2009. The complaint concerned the prohibition on holding and participating in a rally and the administrative penalty for disobeying police orders, raising issues under Article 11 regarding freedom of peaceful assembly. The key dispute was whether the interference was lawful and justified, particularly given that the state of emergency was formally limited to Yerevan, that restrictions were nonetheless applied in Gyumri, and that domestic law allegedly did not require notification for gatherings of fewer than 100 people.

**J.B. and Others v. Malta** (Application no. 1766/23) concerns six Bangladeshi nationals who claimed to be unaccompanied minors aged 16–17 when they arrived in Malta on 18 November 2022 after being rescued at sea. They were initially held at the Ħal Far Initial Reception Centre (“China House”). The applicants alleged that they were detained without any document or explanation in a language they understood and in inadequate conditions. They claimed they were held with adults in small rooms, with insufficient and poorly maintained washrooms, no meaningful access to outdoor or common areas, no prayer room, limited access to telephones—including for contacting lawyers—no leisure or educational activities, no heating, inadequate winter clothing, limited drinkable water, and insufficient medical and psychosocial support. The Government disputed these accounts.

On 30 November 2022, the Principal Immigration Officer issued detention orders to determine or verify the applicants’ identity or nationality and to obtain elements supporting their possible international protection claims, citing a risk of absconding. On 6 December 2022, the Immigration Appeals Tribunal (“IAB”) confirmed the legality of the detention in a single mass hearing concerning the whole group that had arrived by boat. The IAB noted that all applicants except the first were minors and that a legal guardian should be appointed, but still found the detention of the entire group lawful.

The applicants’ lawyers accessed them in January 2023. The applicants confirmed they were minors and said they had informed the authorities, including at the IAB hearing. Their representatives referred them to the Agency for the Welfare of Asylum Seekers and filed an urgent review request for some applicants, which remained unanswered. On 11 January 2023, the European Court of Human Rights indicated interim measures under Rule 39, asking Malta to ensure conditions compatible with Article 3 and with the applicants’ status as unaccompanied minors. The applicants were later transferred to Safi Detention Centre, where they were held with other minors; they alleged conditions were similar apart from room size and one hour of daily outdoor access.

Age-assessment proceedings concluded in January 2023 that the applicants were adults. The applicants alleged the process was hasty, not holistic or multidisciplinary, and that in one case a bone test was conducted without knowing consent. They appealed. Procedural problems followed: only the first applicant’s appeal was initially scheduled; detention officers told the IAB that the others wished to withdraw, and the IAB accepted this without consulting their lawyers; declarations of adulthood were later signed without representatives or an interpreter. Vulnerability reports later showed elevated anxiety, depression, PTSD, and in some cases suicidal thoughts. Release requests based on vulnerability were not answered in writing. In May 2023, the IAB rejected the first applicant’s appeal, finding him adult due to a genuine passport showing birth in 2002, but upheld the others’ minority claims. Most were released to an open centre for minors; the first was moved with adults and later left Malta.

The Court gave notice to the Government of complaints under **Article 3** (conditions of detention), **Article 5 §§ 1 and 4** (lawfulness and judicial review of detention), and **Article 13 in conjunction with Article 3** (effective remedy regarding conditions). The key alleged violations concern the detention of presumed minors, inadequate reception and detention conditions, failure to treat them as minors or conduct proper individual assessments, and ineffective remedies.

**Case Summary: Aslanian v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 74433/11)**

The case of *Aslanian v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* is a judgment delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, sitting as a Committee) on 13 July 2021. The applicant, Rostom Aslanian, is a Russian national born in 1989 who lives in Vărăncău, Moldova. He lodged his application against the Republic of Moldova and Russia on 28 November 2011, complaining under Articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The case concerns the applicant’s conviction for refusing military service on religious grounds in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The applicant is a member of the religious community of Jehovah’s Witnesses in the “MRT.” When he became eligible for the draft, he requested the “MRT” authorities to assign him to civilian service instead of compulsory military service, relying on his religious conscience and beliefs.

In December 2010, the “MRT” authorities denied his request and initiated a criminal investigation against him on charges of draft evasion. On 29 March 2011, the “Rîbnița City and Region Court” convicted the applicant of draft evasion and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment. He was taken into custody in the courtroom. On 7 June 2012, the “MRT” Supreme Court upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant had already been released from detention on 29 March 2012, after having fully served his sentence.

These facts are central to the alleged violations. The applicant’s complaint under Article 9 concerns freedom of thought, conscience, and religion. The essence of the allegation is that he was criminally punished for refusing compulsory military service because of his religious beliefs, and that the authorities failed to provide an alternative civilian service as required by his conscientious objection. The complaint under Article 14 concerns discrimination, apparently alleging that he was treated differently because of his religion or religious community.

The broader context of the “MRT” is also relevant. The Court has previously addressed the situation in Transdniestria in cases such as *Ilaşcu and Others v. Moldova and Russia*, *Catan and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*, and *Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*. The judgment notes that relevant materials concerning the “MRT” are summarised in *Mozer*. This context matters for questions of jurisdiction and the responsibility of the respondent States, although the extract provided focuses primarily on the applicant’s individual facts.

Procedurally, the Court gave notice of the application to both Governments, and the parties submitted observations. The Russian Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The Committee was composed of Judges Carlo Ranzoni, Egidijus Kūris, and Pauliine Koskelo, with Hasan Bakırcı as Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was adopted on 22 June 2021 and delivered on 13 July 2021. It is final, though subject to possible editorial revision.

In sum, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant was a Jehovah’s Witness in the “MRT”; he sought civilian service instead of military service on religious grounds; his request was denied; he was criminally prosecuted and convicted of draft evasion; he was sentenced to one year’s imprisonment; the conviction was upheld on appeal; and he fully served his sentence. Those facts form the basis of his claims under Articles 9 and 14. The provided text does not include the Court’s final merits reasoning or conclusion.

**Case:** *Khan v. Denmark* (Application no. 26957/19), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 12 January 2021.

**Core alleged violation:** The applicant, Shuaib Khan, a Pakistani national born in Denmark in 1986, complained that an order expelling him from Denmark with a six-year re-entry ban breached Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

**Key personal and family facts:** Khan was born and raised in Denmark. His parents and four siblings lived in Denmark; two sisters lived abroad. He had no spouse, live-in partner, or children. He attended Danish kindergarten and school and completed the ninth grade, but he had no completed education or stable employment. He had limited ties to Pakistan: he had visited only a few times, most recently in 2007, spoke broken or some Punjabi, and claimed he could not read the language. Pakistan later became relevant because the authorities noted a family property and an address on his Pakistani ID card, though Khan disputed that these indicated genuine ties.

**Criminal history and gang involvement:** Khan had a criminal record since 2003, with thirteen convictions. These included serious violent offences: in 2008 he received eight years’ imprisonment for aggravated violence, including fatal violence; in 2013 he received three years and six months for aggravated violence and theft; and in 2015 he received six months for aggravated violence in prison. The 2015 judgment also imposed a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period. Khan was the leader of the gang Loyal to Familia (“LTF”), later dissolved by a Danish court because it had an unlawful purpose and operated through violence.

**Immediate offence:** On 31 July 2017, in a stop-and-frisk zone at Blaagaard Square, Copenhagen, established due to armed gang conflict, Khan was frisked by police. As LTF leader and surrounded by LTF affiliates, he threatened police inspector S.E. He allegedly said “Remember his face,” “Watch out,” “Watch out carefully,” and “Watch your back,” while an affiliate photographed the inspector. The atmosphere was tense and his conduct was found threatening. He was charged under Article 119(1) of the Danish Penal Code for threatening an on-duty public official.

**Domestic proceedings:** In October 2017, the Copenhagen City Court convicted Khan, sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment, and issued a suspended expulsion order. The High Court upheld the conviction, reduced the sentence to 60 days, but found unconditional expulsion disproportionate. On 20 November 2018, the Supreme Court increased the sentence to three months and ordered unconditional expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. Because the offence occurred during the probation period of the earlier suspended expulsion order, section 24b(3) of the Aliens Act required expulsion unless it was certainly contrary to Denmark’s international obligations.

**Proportionality factors:** Khan’s strong ties to Denmark—birth, upbringing, family, schooling—were weighed against his extensive criminal history, approximately ten years’ imprisonment, gang leadership, continued offending during probation, and risk of future violent crime. The Supreme Court majority found expulsion necessary for public safety and crime prevention and not disproportionate. One judge dissented, viewing the latest offence as spontaneous and too minor—only three months’ imprisonment—to justify expelling a settled alien. The ECtHR ultimately found no violation of Article 8.

text:
**Avci v. Denmark** (Application no. 40240/19), European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, judgment of 30 November 2021, concerned the expulsion of a settled migrant imposed in criminal proceedings. The applicant, Cihan Avci, was a Turkish national born in Denmark in 1993. He later lived in Turkey. The case raised issues under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Article 14(1) of the Association Agreement between the EU and Turkey, particularly whether his expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban was a disproportionate interference with his private and family life.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were as follows. In 2013, the applicant was convicted of attempting to free a detainee in August 2012 and, in February 2013, participating in a crowd that caused public insecurity. He received a 20-day suspended prison sentence. In September 2018, the District Court convicted him of serious drug offences under section 191(2), read with section 191(1), of the Danish Penal Code, committed between January and April 2017. As part of an organised network, he had received, possessed, and transferred one kilogram of cocaine through extensive sales and deliveries to identified and unidentified buyers. He was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment and given a warning about expulsion.

The Immigration Service gathered information on his personal circumstances. He was born in Denmark, lived with his parents and three siblings, was unmarried, and had no children. He had not completed the ninth grade or any further education. After lower secondary school, he had worked in various jobs, including in a supermarket and as a waiter, and was receiving unemployment benefits when arrested. His maternal aunt and grandfather lived in Turkey. He reportedly spoke Turkish/Kurdish, though not as well as Danish, and had visited Turkey several times on holiday.

On appeal, the applicant disputed parts of this information. He stated that his father’s sister in Turkey had died, that he had no maternal aunt there, and that his maternal grandfather suffered from dementia and he had no relationship with him. He spoke only a little Kurdish, mainly with his father, and mostly Danish with his parents. He did not speak Turkish beyond a few words. He had only visited Turkey as a tourist. He said he had committed the offences because of a gambling debt.

In January 2019, the High Court unanimously confirmed the conviction and sentence but overturned the District Court’s refusal to expel him. It ordered his expulsion with a permanent re-entry ban. The High Court found that the drug offences were very serious, organised, committed with others over several months, and that his personal behaviour represented a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to society. It also found a risk of future offending if he were not expelled, and rejected his gambling debt explanation as mitigating. Although it acknowledged that he was born and raised in Denmark, had family there, and would suffer a particular burden from expulsion, it found he had certain ties to Turkey through his grandfather, Kurdish language, and previous holidays. It concluded that he could establish a life in Turkey and maintain contact with family by phone or internet. The circumstances favouring expulsion were sufficiently compelling to outweigh those against it, and expulsion was not disproportionate under Article 14(1) of the Association Agreement or Article 8 ECHR.

The Appeals Permission Board refused leave to appeal to the Supreme Court on 8 March 2019, and the deportation order was enforced on 24 January 2020. Under the Aliens Act at the time of the offence, a permanent re-entry ban was imposed if the sentence exceeded two years. A later 2018 amendment, not applicable to this case, allowed courts to reduce such bans if they would breach Denmark’s international obligations.

In *Memishaj v. Albania*, the applicant, Enver Memishaj, an Albanian national born in 1944, worked as an accountant for Tirana City Hall. On 10 December 2001 he was dismissed, effective 11 January 2002. He challenged the dismissal. On 6 February 2002 the Civil Service Commission (“CSC”) quashed the dismissal and ordered his reinstatement. By final decision of 8 May 2003, the Supreme Court upheld the CSC decision. On 15 May 2003 the Tirana District Court supplemented the CSC decision by ordering Tirana City Hall to pay the applicant’s salary for the period between 10 December 2001 and the date of reinstatement. The employer’s request for revision was dismissed on 10 October 2003. An enforcement writ was issued on 4 June 2003.

Despite those final decisions, reinstatement was delayed. On 31 March 2006 the Constitutional Court, acting on the applicant’s constitutional complaint, acknowledged a breach of his right of access to court because the Supreme Court’s decision had not been enforced, but it made no award. Meanwhile, on 1 March 2006 the applicant took up employment with the Ministry of Tourism, Culture, Youth and Sports. On 10 March 2006 Tirana City Hall appointed him to a position in a maintenance company responsible to the City Hall. The applicant challenged that appointment, and on 15 May 2006 the CSC quashed the appointment decision. That decision became final because no party appealed.

Separate proceedings concerned payment of accrued interest. In 2004 and 2006 the applicant successfully sought interest arising from delay in payment of his salary. On 9 April 2008, following a third action, the Tirana District Court found in his favour and ordered Tirana City Hall to pay ALL 774,076 in salary arrears and ALL 105,258 in accrued interest. The court reasoned that, because the applicant had begun employment with the Ministry on 1 March 2006, Tirana City Hall was obliged to pay salary arrears only for the period from 11 January 2002 to 28 February 2006; that obligation ceased *ipso lege* as of 1 March 2006. Relying on an expert report, the court found that salary arrears for that period amounted to ALL 1,720,261, of which ALL 946,185 had already been paid. Accrued interest for the corresponding period was ALL 105,258. An enforcement writ was issued on 11 November 2009. The decision became final around 12 February 2010 after the Supreme Court dismissed the defendant’s appeal. On 31 March 2010 Tirana City Hall paid the salary arrears. The case file did not indicate whether the accrued interest was paid.

In 2010 the applicant lodged a fourth civil action seeking accrued interest for the period between 9 April 2008 and 31 March 2010, and payment of social security contributions by Tirana City Hall. On 30 June 2010 the Tirana District Court found in his favour, ordering Tirana City Hall to pay accrued interest resulting from delayed payment of salary arrears from 9 April 2008 to 31 March 2010 and social security contributions based on his indexed salary. No quantification of the amount was made. On 8 July 2011 and 23 December 2011, respectively, the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld that decision.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 July 2008; it was communicated to the Government on 11 July 2011. The facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore concern the prolonged non-enforcement and delayed enforcement of final domestic decisions awarding reinstatement, salary arrears, accrued interest, and social security contributions. The Constitutional Court had already found a breach of access to court due to non-enforcement of the Supreme Court’s decision, but awarded no compensation, and later enforcement remained protracted. The case thus raises issues under the Convention, particularly access to court, fair trial, and protection of property, based on Albania’s alleged failure to secure timely execution of final judgments in the applicant’s favour.
