text:
In *Ibrišimović and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (ECtHR, Fourth Section, 11 February 2021; applications nos. 15634/20 and 3 others), four applicants complained of the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 11 March 2020. The applicants were represented by Mr O. Eterović, a lawyer practising in Sarajevo. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was given notice. A Fourth Section Committee composed of Judges Armen Harutyunyan (President), Jolien Schukking and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 21 January 2021 and adopted the judgment on 11 February 2021.

The factual core appears in the appended table. Each applicant obtained a decision from the Sarajevo Municipal Court, but the domestic authorities did not enforce it. The applicants alleged that this non-enforcement violated their Convention rights. The key facts are as follows.

Fikret Ibrišimović, born 1969, application no. 15634/20, had two relevant Sarajevo Municipal Court decisions, dated 12 January 2015 and 6 May 2016. The non-enforcement periods began on 15 April 2016 and 3 November 2016, respectively. At the time of the application, enforcement proceedings were still pending: more than 4 years, 7 months and 25 days for the first decision, and more than 4 years, 1 month and 7 days for the second.

Tarik Ćosić, born 1972, application no. 15641/20, relied on a Sarajevo Municipal Court decision of 21 August 2014. The non-enforcement period began on 10 February 2016. Enforcement remained pending for more than 4 years and 10 months.

Ivica Franjić, born 1975, application no. 15644/20, relied on a Sarajevo Municipal Court decision of 21 October 2014. The non-enforcement period began on 25 March 2016. Enforcement remained pending for more than 4 years, 8 months and 15 days.

Senad Ćubara, born 1967, application no. 15651/20, relied on a Sarajevo Municipal Court decision of 5 February 2016. The non-enforcement period began on 28 April 2016. Enforcement remained pending for more than 4 years, 7 months and 12 days.

All four applications were introduced on the same date, 11 March 2020. The common factual pattern is that each applicant had a final domestic court decision in his favour, but Bosnia and Herzegovina failed to enforce it. The enforcement proceedings were still pending in each case, with delays exceeding four years from the start of the non-enforcement period to the introduction of the applications. The alleged violation therefore concerns the State’s prolonged failure to execute final and enforceable domestic decisions. The most relevant facts for that complaint are the dates and identity of the domestic decisions, the start dates of the non-enforcement periods, the absence of completed enforcement, and the length of the delays. The excerpt does not set out the Court’s legal assessment or final conclusions, but the factual basis is clearly the continued non-enforcement of domestic judgments.

**Summary of W.A. v. Switzerland**

The case of *W.A. v. Switzerland* concerns the applicant's challenge to his subsequent preventive detention (*nachträgliche Verwahrung*) following the completion of a twenty-year prison sentence. The applicant, a Swiss national born in 1960, was convicted by the Zurich Jury Court in 1993 of murder and intentional manslaughter and sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. The court found that he had murdered a man in a particularly violent manner in 1983 and, in 1990, had induced his partner to strangle an acquaintance, whose corpse he subsequently dismembered. Psychiatric expert G. diagnosed the applicant with a personality disorder and alcohol intoxication, concluding that his capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of his acts was substantially diminished at the time of both offences.

Importantly, the sentencing court decided *not* to order preventive detention under Article 43 § 1 of the then-applicable Criminal Code. It reasoned that preventive detention in practice rarely lasted more than five years, whereas a long prison term would better serve the aim of protecting society from the applicant, who was considered very dangerous due to his abnormal mental state.

The applicant served his full sentence until 8 October 2010. In 2009, while he was still incarcerated, the Public Prosecution Office applied for his subsequent preventive detention under Article 65 § 2 of the Criminal Code, a provision that had entered into force in 2007. This provision permits courts to order preventive detention after sentencing if new facts or evidence reveal that the requirements for such detention were already met at the time of conviction but were unknown to the court.

In 2012, the Federal Court found that new facts justified reopening the proceedings. A 2009 psychiatric report by expert P., using new analytical methods unavailable in the 1990s, concluded that the applicant had not been alcohol-dependent but suffered from dissocial personality disorder and psychopathy—conditions deemed untreatable and associated with a very high risk of further violent offences. These facts had not been known to the Jury Court in 1993.

Following the reopening, the Zurich District Court ordered the applicant's subsequent preventive detention in 2013, relying on reports from experts P. and R. It found that the requirements for preventive detention had been met both at the time of conviction and currently, citing the applicant's serious mental disorder and the very high risk he posed if released. Appeals to the Zurich Court of Appeal and the Federal Court were dismissed in 2014 and 2015 respectively.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 5 § 1 (right to liberty), Article 7 § 1 (prohibition on retrospective punishment), and Article 4 § 1 of Protocol No. 7 (right not to be punished twice). The Federal Court rejected these claims, finding that preventive detention measures were comparable to penalties and thus subject to the *nulla poena sine lege* principle, but concluded that the retrospective application did not impose a heavier sanction than the law applicable at the time of the offence. It further held that reopening to the convicted person's detriment had been permissible under the old law and that the detention had a sufficient causal connection with the original conviction.

The case of *Sociedade de Construções Martins & Vieira, Lda and Others v. Portugal* involves five applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights against the Portuguese Republic by a construction company and its two managing partners. The core of the case concerns the excessive length of domestic criminal proceedings for tax fraud, which were suspended for years pending the outcome of related administrative tax litigation.

The events began in September 1999 when Portuguese authorities launched an investigation into the applicant company’s fiscal activities between 1994 and 1997. This led to two separate sets of criminal proceedings.

The first set was instituted in the Porto Criminal Court in November 2003, with charges brought against the applicant company and the third applicant. After several delays, the trial began in September 2005. However, a key development occurred in November 2006 when the applicants informed the court that they had sought a judicial review of a tax adjustment in the Porto Administrative and Fiscal Court. In accordance with Article 50 § 1 of the Legal Framework for Non-Customs Tax Offences (RJIFNA), the criminal proceedings were suspended on 29 November 2006 until the administrative court issued a final, unappealable decision.

Similarly, a second set of proceedings was brought before the Barcelos Criminal Court in April 2003 against all three applicants for tax offences related to an earlier period. This case was also suspended in November 2003 under the same legal provision, pending the outcome of the same administrative judicial review. The Barcelos court repeatedly sought updates, but the fiscal proceedings remained pending. In April 2007, it formally extended its suspension.

In December 2008, the applicants attempted to expedite both sets of criminal proceedings by applying to the High Council of Magistrates. These applications were dismissed in May 2009 and January 2009, respectively. The Council reasoned that the delays were attributable to the Administrative and Fiscal Court, not the criminal courts, and advised the applicants to direct their requests to the High Council of the Administrative and Fiscal Courts.

Consequently, the criminal proceedings in both Porto and Barcelos remained suspended for years, awaiting the conclusion of the administrative tax case. The applicants also instituted separate tort proceedings against the State in 2006, claiming damages for the excessive length of the criminal proceedings, but these too were still pending as of early 2014.

The central factual issue relevant to the alleged violation is that the suspension of the criminal proceedings, mandated by domestic law, had no statutory time limit when the relevant provision was Article 50 § 1 of the RJIFNA. This contrasted with the general Code of Criminal Procedure, which imposes a one-year maximum for such suspensions. This legal feature effectively resulted in criminal proceedings being stalled for an indefinite period, dependent entirely on a separate administrative process. The applicants argued that this lengthy suspension violated their right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *Chernov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 16432/10), the applicant, Mr Oleksandr Gennadiyovych Chernov, a Ukrainian national born in 1965 and living in Sumy, complained under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention that he had been tried and punished twice for the same offence. The case concerned events on 20 June 2007, when, at about 10 p.m., the applicant was drunk outdoors on Prokofyeva Street in Sumy. He uttered obscenities, reacted aggressively to remarks by police officers, cursed them, attempted to start a fight, and thereby breached public order and offended human dignity and morals.

On 21 June 2007 the Zarichnyy District Court of Sumy found the applicant guilty of “minor disorderly acts” under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced him to three days’ administrative detention. That decision became final and could not be appealed. The applicant served the sentence from 21 to 23 June 2007.

On 28 January 2008, however, the prosecutor lodged an objection against the administrative decision. The prosecutor argued that the same facts gave rise to criminal liability under Article 296 of the Criminal Code, because Article 9 of the Code of Administrative Offences provided that administrative liability applied only where the underlying facts did not lead to criminal liability. On 6 February 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court annulled its earlier decision, and on 25 February 2008 the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal upheld that annulment.

In parallel, criminal proceedings had been initiated. On 16 July 2007 a prosecutor opened a criminal case against the applicant under Article 296 of the Criminal Code concerning the same events of 20 June 2007, alleging disorderly acts and physical injuries to two victims, Mu. and P. Forensic examinations in June and September 2007 found minor physical injuries that may have been inflicted on 20 June 2007. The applicant was placed on a wanted list on 4 August 2007, arrested on 23 December 2007, and indicted on 29 January 2008 under Article 296 § 3.

On 14 July 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court convicted the applicant under Article 296 § 3 and sentenced him to two years’ imprisonment. The court did not mention the earlier administrative proceedings or the three-day detention. On 7 October 2008 the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal quashed the conviction because of inconsistencies—particularly as to the time of the offence—and because the sentence was too lenient, and remitted the case for fresh examination. Judge Ma., who had decided the administrative case, withdrew from the criminal case on 29 October 2008, noting that she had annulled the administrative decision after criminal elements became apparent.

On 29 December 2008 the Zarichnyy District Court again convicted the applicant. It found that on 20 June 2007 he had pulled Mu.’s gold neck chain, damaged it, beaten Mu., and later damaged P.’s t-shirt, punched her in the face, caused minor injuries, and damaged her glasses. He was sentenced to two years and one month’s imprisonment. On 10 March 2009 the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to two years. On 24 September 2009 the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that decision. It rejected the applicant’s double-jeopardy complaint, reasoning that the administrative decision had been annulled and the administrative case closed, so he had not been tried twice.

The applicant’s central complaint was therefore that, despite serving an administrative detention for the same conduct, he was later criminally convicted and punished for the same facts. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the complaint under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

In *Sandu and Others v. Romania* (Application no. 27855/17 and 19 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) examined 20 applications against Romania. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of detention in various Romanian police facilities and prisons. One applicant, Ion-Daniel Tudor, died in 2021; his children informed the Court that they wished to continue the application. The Romanian Government was given notice of the applications.

The applicants were detained between 2012 and 2017 at numerous facilities, including Bucharest Police no. 6, Rahova, Jilava, Galați County Police and Prison, Bihor County Police, Oradea, Satu Mare, Arad, Baia Mare, Deva, Gherla, Colibași, Târgu-Jiu, Ploiești, Timișoara, Bistrița, and Târșorul Nou. Detention periods ranged from about five months to nearly five years.

The central alleged violation was overcrowding. The appended table provides square metres per inmate for most applicants, often showing very low personal space. For example, Jan Marian Sandu had 1.52–2.44 m² over three years, two months and thirty days. Costică Caranfil had 1.5–1.8 m² for six months and twenty-one days. Serafim-Dorinel Șipoș had 1.31–2.77 m² for three years, seven months and seven days. Levente-Lorand Pal had 1.45–2.77 m² for almost two years. Emil-Gheorghe Florian had 1.33–2.77 m² for three years, seven months and twenty-three days. Daniel-Tomas Cozma had 1.30–2.94 m² for four years and six months. Mihai-Levente Băla had 1.30–2.29 m² for four years and eleven days. Adrian-Felician Sava had 1.43–2.79 m² for four years, two months and twenty days. Sorin-Andi Pandele had 1.12–2.44 m² for three years and twenty-one days. Zoltan Lingurar had 1.16–2.89 m² for one year, nine months and three days. Other applicants, such as Radu-Lucian Silaghi, Ioan Petran, and Mariana Iordăchescu, had slightly more space but still alleged overcrowding or related defects. In several cases, overcrowding was not continuous; the table notes specific periods when it was absent.

Beyond overcrowding, applicants alleged many specific conditions: bunk beds, lack of fresh air, insufficient natural or electric light, constant electric light, insect or rodent infestation, mouldy or dirty cells, inadequate furniture, poor bedding and bed linen, insufficient outdoor physical exercise, no or restricted access to warm water, no or restricted access to running water, restricted or no shower, poor food quality or quantity, poor potable water, inadequate temperature, lack of toiletries, no or restricted toilet access, lack of privacy for toilet, and lack of leisure or educational activities. These grievances were often cumulative and accompanied the overcrowding allegations.

The case therefore concerned whether these material conditions of detention—especially severe overcrowding, poor hygiene, sanitation, ventilation, lighting, food, and exercise—amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under the Convention. The Court had to assess the facts in the appended table to determine whether Romania violated the applicants’ rights.

In *Beganović v. Slovenia* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, Application no. 6625/10, judgment of 3 April 2014), the applicant was Nenad Beganović, a Slovenian national born in 1986. He alleged that the conditions of his detention in Ljubljana prison violated Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights and that he lacked an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

The applicant served his prison sentence in Ljubljana prison from 1 July 2009 to 4 November 2009. He was then transferred to Celje prison until 9 December 2009, when he was transferred back to Ljubljana prison, Section Novo mesto. His complaints did not concern his detention in Celje prison.

From 1 July to 23 September 2009, he was held in the closed section of Ljubljana prison. He occupied three different cells: cell 7 measured 16.8 square metres, while cells 4 and 3 each measured 18 square metres, including a separate sanitary facility of 1.72 square metres. Each cell had furniture and five sleeping places—two bunk beds and one single bed. The applicant claimed that five prisoners occupied each cell; the Government said the number varied between four and five. Each cell had a 107 x 110 cm double casement window that prisoners could open and close. General material, sanitary and health-care conditions were referenced to the Court’s earlier judgment in *Štrucl and Others v. Slovenia*. As to out-of-cell time in the closed section, sentenced prisoners were locked in their cells and could leave only if they applied for activities, most of which took place in a recreation room. There was only one 50-square-metre recreation room per floor, intended for no more than ten inmates.

From 23 September to 4 November 2009, the applicant was held in the semi-open section, in cell 3, measuring 18 square metres including a sanitary facility. According to the Government, cell doors in that section were unlocked except from 9:45 p.m. until 6:00 a.m., and on weekends or holidays until 8:30 a.m. Prisoners could then move freely in a 35.7-square-metre corridor, in co-prisoners’ living quarters, and in indoor or outdoor exercise areas under prison rules. However, the applicant had been transferred to the semi-open section only because of overcrowding, and while there he was not granted outside visits or unsupervised leave.

From 9 December 2009 to 1 April 2010, he was held in the closed section of Section Novo mesto. Unit 5 measured 58.83 square metres and contained four separate rooms: an ante-chamber of 9.98 square metres, a sanitary facility of 1.4 square metres, a smaller room of 18.61 square metres with three beds, and a larger room of 28.84 square metres with five, occasionally six beds. The applicant was mostly held in the larger room with three other prisoners. The unit held seven prisoners in total. Inner doors were unlocked, allowing free movement within the unit 24 hours per day. From 3:30 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., prisoners could also move in the shared corridor and recreation areas. The applicant spent six hours daily outside the unit: two hours outdoors in a 300-square-metre area and four hours in a shared corridor of 108.64 square metres or shared living quarters of 59.04 square metres. He also had access to an outdoor recreation yard for two hours daily.

During imprisonment, he had three consultations with a general practitioner and one psychiatric treatment. He never requested a psychologist or dentist. Temperature data showed that in the second half of July and August 2009, the average late-afternoon cell temperature was about 28°C, exceeding 30°C on seven days. Relevant domestic law, practice and international documents were set out in *Štrucl and Others*. The Court gave notice to the Government and decided to rule on admissibility and merits together, granting the case priority.

The case of *Vajnai v. Hungary (No. 4)* (Application no. 6061/10) concerned an application against Hungary lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention by Mr Attila Vajnai, a Hungarian national born in 1963 and living in Budapest. The applicant was represented by Mr G. Magyar, while the Hungarian Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi. The applicant complained under Article 10 of the Convention that a police measure taken against him for wearing a red star violated his right to freedom of expression. The application was lodged on 23 January 2010 and communicated to the Government on 17 October 2013. The Government objected to the application being examined by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The key facts concerned events on 18 May 2009. On that date, the applicant, a left-wing politician, participated in a peaceful demonstration. He wore a five-pointed red star on his jacket. A police patrol present at the demonstration called on the applicant to remove the star. He did not, or at least the star was then confiscated by the police. This police measure formed the basis of his later complaint that his expression had been unlawfully restricted.

The applicant first complained to the Head of the National Police, but without success. He then challenged the police measure in court. On 29 June 2010, the Budapest Regional Court dismissed his action. The Regional Court held that the display of the red star contravened section 269/B of the Hungarian Criminal Code. Consequently, it found that the confiscation of the star was justified under sections 115(1) and 151(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The applicant sought review. On 8 June 2011, the Supreme Court upheld the Regional Court’s decision. It held that the police measure had been lawful. Importantly, the Supreme Court acknowledged the earlier judgment of the European Court of Human Rights in *Vajnai v. Hungary* (no. 33629/06, ECHR 2008), but reasoned that applying that judgment was not a task of the police officers present at the demonstration. The applicant incurred legal costs of approximately EUR 1,115.

The facts relevant to the alleged Article 10 violation were therefore that the applicant wore a five-pointed red star as part of political expression during a peaceful demonstration; that police officers intervened, demanded its removal and confiscated it; and that the domestic courts upheld that interference by relying on the Criminal Code prohibition on displaying the red star. The domestic courts also declined to give effect to the earlier Strasbourg judgment in the applicant’s favour when reviewing the police action. The applicant’s central complaint was that this measure constituted an unjustified interference with his freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

In *Omdahl v. Norway*, the applicant, Olav Omdahl, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the public administration and division of his grandfather’s estate lasted an unreasonable time. The estate belonged to O.A. Knutsen, who died on 24 April 1993. It was substantial, worth approximately NOK 100 million with NOK 10 million in debt, and consisted mainly of properties, shares, securities, and moveable assets. The heirs were three children and two grandchildren; two of the children, including the applicant’s mother, died before final distribution. Public administration began on 5 May 1993 before the Probate Court, with an advocate appointed as administrator. It ended 22 years and 4 months later, after final distribution on 16 April 2015.

The long duration was largely due to numerous legal disputes. Early proceedings concerned heirs’ rights to receive assets in kind under the deceased’s will and a codicil; these tied up proceeds until 2005/06, and Probate Court decisions to convert assets were quashed or amended on appeal. A trust in the Bahamas, discovered after the applicant’s mother died in 2002, led to further disputes over ownership and taxation. In December 2005, each child and grandchild received NOK 5.5 million from the trust, but tax issues were not clarified until winter 2010. An interim distribution in July 2010 gave each branch NOK 10 million; appeals were dismissed in 2011. Disput

In *Valdís Fjölnisdóttir and Others v. Iceland* (Application no. 71552/17), Third Section, judgment of 18 May 2021, the applicants were two Icelandic women, Valdís and Eydís, and a child, Mr X. The first two applicants were a married couple who used a US surrogacy agency and travelled to California, where the third applicant was born in February 2013 through gestational surrogacy. The child was conceived with donor gametes and had no biological link to either intended parent. A California birth certificate named the first two applicants as parents, and the surrogate waived legal parenthood.

Three weeks after birth, the applicants travelled to Iceland. The intended parents applied to Registers Iceland to register the child as an Icelandic national born abroad, relying on the US birth certificate. After being asked further questions, they disclosed that the child had been born via surrogacy. On 18 June 2013, Registers Iceland refused registration. Under Icelandic law, the woman who gives birth is regarded as the mother. The child therefore did not automatically acquire Icelandic citizenship through the applicants and was treated as a foreign national. The Ministry of the Interior confirmed that decision on 27 March 2014.

Because the child was considered a foreign unaccompanied minor, the local child protection committee took legal custody and appointed a guardian, Ms M. The child was initially placed with the first two applicants under a foster-care arrangement. The applicants sought judicial review, asking that the Ministry’s decision be annulled and that Registers Iceland be required to register the first two applicants as the child’s parents based on the US birth certificate.

While the domestic proceedings were pending, the child was granted Icelandic citizenship by Act No. 128/2015 and entered in the national register as a citizen. However, the first two applicants were still not registered as his parents. The first two applicants divorced in May 2015, which invalidated the permanent foster-care agreement and affected their earlier adoption application. The adoption process had already been stalled because the District Commissioner considered the surrogate mother and her husband to be the legal parents/guardians whose consent was needed, and because adoption rules prohibit payment linked to consent. The applicants withdrew the adoption application after divorcing.

In March 2016, the District Court rejected the claims. It held that Icelandic family law treats the birth mother as the legal mother and that recognising foreign surrogacy parentage would conflict with fundamental Icelandic principles and the domestic ban on surrogacy. It accepted that family life existed and that the refusal interfered with it, but found the interference justified to uphold the surrogacy ban and protect others, noting counterbalancing measures such as foster care, residence, and later citizenship. The Supreme Court upheld the rejection in March 2017, but found that no protected family life existed at the time of the registration decision, since the ties had not been lawfully established under Icelandic law until the foster-care approval.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 8, concerning the right to respect for private and family life, and Article 14, concerning the prohibition of discrimination. The key alleged violation was the State’s non-recognition of the parent-child relationship between the first two applicants and the child, and the resulting refusal to register them as his parents, despite the US birth certificate, the child’s residence with them, and the foster-care arrangements.

The case *Kiisa v. Estonia* (Applications nos. 16587/10 and 34304/11, judgment of 13 March 2014) concerned two Estonian nationals, formerly married from 1989 to 2006, and protracted civil proceedings over child maintenance. The first applicant, Karin Kiisa, gave birth to child K. in September 2002; the second applicant, Aare Kiisa, was recorded as the father. In October 2003 the first applicant filed for divorce and division of marital property.

In October 2004 the first applicant sued the second applicant in Harju County Court for child alimony. After preliminary hearings and evidence requests, the second applicant in April 2005 filed a separate action to establish that he was not the child’s father and to contest the civil status record. In June 2005 he requested suspension of the alimony case pending the filiation proceedings. In October 2005 the County Court suspended the alimony proceedings until judgment in the filiation case.

In the meantime, in May 2005 the County Court in the filiation case ordered DNA analyses of the child and the second applicant and obliged the first applicant to take the child for sampling. She appealed unsuccessfully; the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in January 2007. However, the first applicant did not take the child for DNA testing. The filiation action was eventually dismissed by the Harju County Court on 10 May 2012.

In June 2007 the first applicant asked for the alimony proceedings to be resumed, relying on Supreme Court practice that contesting the civil status record did not remove the obligation to provide child support. The County Court resumed proceedings on 20 June 2007 and scheduled a hearing, which was postponed at the second applicant’s request. In July 2007 the second applicant made a compromise proposal; time-limits were extended. Between September and November 2007 the parties exchanged evidence and submissions, and the second applicant requested further adjournments. In October 2007 the court requested evidence from banks and the Tax and Customs Board and ordered the second applicant to submit documents. A hearing was held on 30 November 2007.

On 11 January 2008 the County Court partly granted the first applicant’s action, ordering monthly alimony of EEK 3,000 (about €192). Both parties appealed. On 9 May 2008 the Tallinn Court of Appeal upheld the judgment. Both applicants appealed to the Supreme Court. On 19 November 2008 the Supreme Court quashed the Court of Appeal judgment and remitted the case for renewed examination. On 21 May 2009 the Court of Appeal quashed the County Court judgment and remitted the case to the first-instance court. The first applicant’s further appeal was refused by the Supreme Court on 7 September 2009.

In January 2010 the first applicant amended her claim, submitted voluminous new evidence and sought interim measures. On 17 February 2010 the County Court ordered interim monthly alimony of EEK 2,175 (about €139). In April 2010 the second applicant sought postponement because his representative was ill. The first applicant submitted further evidence in April and May 2010. A hearing took place on 3 June 2010. On 5 July 2010 the County Court ordered monthly alimony of EEK 5,000 (about €320). Both parties appealed. On 6 October 2010 the Tallinn Court of Appeal reduced the monthly amount to EEK 3,550 (about €227). Both applicants sought leave to appeal, but the Supreme Court refused on 26 January 2011.

The proceedings therefore lasted from October 2004 to January 2011, over six years, including a suspension of about one year and eight months, repeated adjournments, appeals and remittals. Domestic law included constitutional provisions on effective remedies and compensation, the State Liability Act, and Supreme Court decisions indicating that compensation for excessive length of proceedings should be sought before an administrative court. The alleged violations concerned primarily the excessive length of the civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the lack of an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

**Case: Tsukur and Others v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 53132/18 and 2 others), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, Committee judgment, Strasbourg, 17 October 2019.

The case originated in three applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of their detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. The relevant facts are set out in the appended table.

**Application no. 53132/18**, introduced on 2 November 2018, was brought by Mykola Volodymyrovych Tsukur (born 3 December 1978), represented by Sergiy Mykolayovych Rybiy (Dnipro). He was detained in Kyiv SIZO from 11 March 2016 to 9 August 2018—a duration of 2 years, 4 months and 30 days. The space per inmate was 2.5 m². His specific grievances were overcrowding; lack of fresh air; a mouldy or dirty cell; lack of toiletries; lack of privacy for the toilet; no or restricted access to warm water; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; poor quality of food; no or restricted access to potable water; and no or restricted access to a shower.

**Application no. 53181/18**, introduced on 5 November 2018, was brought by Borys Pavlovych Gulchuk (born 16 February 1993), also represented by Sergiy Mykolayovych Rybiy. He was held in Kyiv SIZO from 21 June 2015 to 18 September 2018—3 years, 2 months and 29 days. The space per inmate was 2.6–3.5 m². He alleged overcrowding; lack of fresh air; infestation of the cell with insects or rodents; a mouldy or dirty cell; lack of privacy for the toilet; no or restricted access to warm water; lack of toiletries; poor quality of potable water; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; poor quality of food; and no or restricted access to a shower.

**Application no. 59802/18**, introduced on 27 November 2018, was brought by Vadym Sergiyovych Koval (born 24 December 1991), represented by Oleksandr Anatoliyovych Ignatov (Dnipro). He was detained in Dnipropetrovsk detention facility No. 4 from 7 November 2014 to 26 November 2018—4 years and 20 days. The space per inmate was 3.1 m². His complaints were lack of fresh air; overcrowding; poor quality of food; no or restricted access to a shower; lack or insufficient quantity of food; lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen; lack of or insufficient natural light; lack of or insufficient electric light; lack of or inadequate hygienic facilities; and lack of toiletries.

These facts were central to the alleged violations. The complaints about detention conditions engage Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. Relevant factors include the length of detention, cell space, overcrowding, ventilation, hygiene, sanitation, access to showers and potable water, food quality and quantity, bedding, lighting, privacy and infestation. The applicants also alleged that no effective domestic remedy existed, engaging Article 13 of the Convention, because they could not obtain redress in Ukraine for the allegedly inadequate conditions.

The Court, sitting as a Committee composed of André Potocki, President; Ganna Yudkivska; Yonko Grozev; and Liv Tigerstedt, Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 26 September 2019 and delivered judgment on 17 October 2019. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The provided text does not include the Court’s substantive findings or any award, but the key alleged violations concern prolonged detention in overcrowded and inadequate conditions in Kyiv SIZO and Dnipropetrovsk detention facility No. 4, together with the absence of an effective remedy in domestic law.

The case of *Osakovskiy v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged by Mr Sergey Valeryevich Osakovskiy, a Ukrainian national, against Ukraine. He alleged ill-treatment in custody, unreasonable detention, a lack of access to a procedure to challenge his detention's lawfulness, and excessively lengthy criminal proceedings.

The case involves two sets of criminal proceedings.

**First Set of Proceedings:** In August 2003, a cashier, F., was found fatally injured at his workplace. On 8 June 2004, the applicant was arrested and confessed to the crime. He later claimed this confession was false and extracted through ill-treatment, specifically alleging police applied electric current, suffocated him with a gas mask, and used other torture techniques.

After his arrest, the applicant was assigned a legal-aid lawyer. He participated in a crime scene reconstruction and was indicted on 10 June 2004, when a court remanded him in custody. On 11 June 2004, a pre-trial detention facility (SIZO) medical examination found no bodily injuries on him.

In July 2004, a private lawyer replaced his legal-aid counsel. On 31 July 2004, the applicant, represented by his new lawyer, retracted his confessions, stating they were given under duress, and pleaded innocent. On 4 August 2004, the prosecutor’s office refused to open a criminal inquiry into his ill-treatment allegations for lack of objective evidence; the applicant did not appeal this decision.

On 14 December 2004, the applicant complained in court about ill-treatment and was released on an undertaking not to abscond. However, on 16 March 2005, the court remitted his case for further investigation and again remanded him in custody, fearing he might abscond. This decision was upheld on appeal in July 2005.

Throughout 2005 and 2006, courts repeatedly ordered further inquiries into the applicant’s ill-treatment complaints, but the prosecutor’s office consistently refused to institute criminal proceedings. A forensic medical examination in September 2005 could not establish whether he had sustained injuries in June 2004. The prosecutor’s office rejected his accounts as improbable, noting it was physically impossible to smoke in a gas mask and that the police station had no basement.

The applicant’s requests for release were repeatedly denied. On 18 August 2006, the District Court acquitted him, citing procedural breaches and doubts about the genuineness of his initial confessions. However, on 30 October 2007, a higher court quashed the acquittal and ordered a further investigation. The investigation was suspended in January 2008 but resumed in July 2012. As of June 2013, the proceedings were still pending.

**Second Set of Proceedings:** In May 2004, D.’s body was found in a river. In August 2004, the applicant, then in the Kharkiv SIZO, was identified as a potential suspect. On 25 August 2004, his cellmates reported he had engaged in self-injury. The applicant explained he had cut his arm with a razor blade due to anguish over his divorce and potential long-term sentence. SIZO authorities concluded the injuries were self-inflicted.

On 21 September 2004, the applicant confessed to killing D. He was indicted but the charges were dropped on 9 October 2004 due to inconsistencies with objective evidence, and the proceedings were discontinued in November 2004. Two other individuals were later convicted.

On 14 December 2004, the applicant complained that SIZO authorities had pressured and ill-treated him in August and September 2004 to coerce a confession to D.’s murder, including having his cellmates threaten him. He alleged warden K. and detainee L. had beaten him. Complaints to the prosecutor’s office resulted in repeated refusals to institute proceedings. In September 2006, the prosecutor’s office again found no ill-treatment case to answer, concluding he had volunteered his confession without pressure. The applicant did not inform the Court whether this decision was appealed.

**Case summary: Ancient Baltic Religious Association “Romuva” v. Lithuania (App. no. 48329/19)**

The applicant is the Ancient Baltic religious association “Romuva,” a registered Lithuanian religious association whose communities follow the old Baltic pagan faith. One affiliated community was registered in 1992, and Romuva itself was registered in 2002. Under Lithuanian law, religious associations may be merely registered, traditionally recognised, or granted State recognition. State-recognised status carries additional privileges: religious education in public schools, religious marriages with civil effect, national broadcaster airtime, State pensions for clergy, and land-tax exemptions. Non-traditional associations may obtain State recognition if they have support in society and their teaching and practices do not contravene law or public morals; they may apply 25 years after initial registration, with the Seimas deciding after the Ministry of Justice’s conclusion.

In 2017 Romuva sought State recognition. The Ministry of Justice concluded that it met the legal criteria: it had operated long enough, its teachings did not violate law or public morals, and it had sufficient public support. The Ministry noted that more than 5,000 people identified with the “Baltic faith” in the 2011 census, that the movement had grown, that it was the sixth largest religious movement in Lithuania, and that surveys viewed it positively. Seimas committees, the Government, and the Seimas Law Department supported the draft resolution.

Debates took place on 25 and 27 June 2019. Supporters stressed Romuva’s links to Lithuanian history, freedom of religion, and pluralism. Opponents questioned whether Romuva was truly a religion rather than an ethno-cultural heritage group; argued that the ancient Baltic faith had never been uniform; disputed the comprehensiveness of its beliefs; claimed public support was too small (about 0.17% in 2011); and warned that recognising it would “hollow out” the concept of religion. Some framed paganism as opposed to Christianity. One MP alleged Soviet/KGB/Kremlin links. On 26 June, the Lithuanian Bishops’ Conference sent a letter to members of the parliamentary group “For the Family,” arguing that the notion of an ancient Baltic religion lacked scientific basis, that its beliefs were incomplete, and that public support required wider study. The letter was forwarded among group members.

On 27 June 2019, the Seimas voted: 40 in favour, 31 against, 15 abstentions. The draft resolution failed. Romuva complained to the Seimas Ethics Commission about the KGB allegation. The Commission found that the MP had knowingly spread false and defamatory claims, noting that old Baltic believers had been persecuted by Soviet authorities. A court upheld those findings but held there was no legal basis to order an MP to retract statements made in parliamentary debate; that case remained pending on appeal.

Romuva alleged violations of Articles 9 (freedom of religion), 14 (prohibition of discrimination), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention. Key facts relevant to those complaints include that other non-traditional Christian associations—Evangelical Baptist, Seventh-day Adventist, Pentecostal, and New Apostolic Churches—had been granted State recognition between 2001 and 2017, often with little debate, while Romuva was refused despite the Ministry’s positive conclusion. Domestically, administrative courts generally cannot review Seimas acts of State governance, and an individual constitutional complaint requires a prior decision based on the challenged legal instrument violating rights and exhaustion of remedies. The case thus concerns whether the refusal, amid hostile parliamentary statements and the Bishops’ Conference letter, amounted to unjustified interference with religious freedom, discriminatory treatment, and a lack of effective domestic remedy.

**Cēsnieks v. Latvia** (Application no. 9278/06) concerned a Latvian national who alleged that police ill-treated him to extract a confession and that this confession was later used to convict him. He lodged the application on 26 January 2006. He alleged violations of Article 3 (ill-treatment), Article 13 (lack of effective investigation), and Article 6 § 1 (use at trial of evidence obtained in violation of Article 3). In 2012, after the Government made a unilateral declaration acknowledging ill-treatment in custody and a lack of effective investigation, the Court struck out the Article 3 and Article 13 complaints. Only the Article 6 fair-trial complaint remained for judgment.

The key facts began on 21 March 2002, when police telephoned the applicant and asked him to attend the State Police station. According to the applicant, before any formal charges were laid, officers accused him of murdering Ģ.Č. and used physical force to obtain a confession. As a result, he made a written confession. He remained at the police station after questioning, was taken into custody at 8 p.m. that day, but was not transferred to a short-term detention facility until 1 a.m. on 23 March 2002. On 23 May 2002, police opened an investigation into the alleged misconduct of officers during his questioning. In June 2005, a prosecutor concluded that the complaint was no longer subject to review, referring to a Supreme Court judgment that had dismissed the ill-treatment allegation.

The applicant’s pre-trial statements included questioning as a witness on 21 March 2002, a handwritten confession on 22 March 2002, and questioning as a suspect later that day and again that night. In the confession, he described debts, a trip to Moscow, money transfers involving Ģ.Č., and an acquaintance, O.O. He later stated that he had sought Ģ.Č.’s killing and asked O.O. to kill him. The transcripts recorded that he wished to give statements without a lawyer.

At trial, the Riga Regional Court acquitted the applicant on 11 October 2004. It found his ill-treatment claim credible, noting that he had bodily injuries while in custody confirmed by expert reports, and that police witnesses could not explain why he had not been released after questioning as a witness. The court found that Article 3 had been violated. It rejected an expert report stating that the confession had not been written under anxiety, fear, or ill-treatment, finding the report lacked a study section. It held that the applicant’s 22 March 2002 statements could not be used for conviction. It found no other evidence that he had organised, assisted, or incited the murder.

On appeal, the Supreme Court overturned the acquittal on 26 April 2005 and convicted the applicant of aggravated murder, sentencing him to eleven years’ imprisonment. It reasoned that the Regional Court had groundlessly rejected the confession, that the file lacked impartial evidence that the statements were given because of ill-treatment or police dictation, and that the criminal case against the police officers had been terminated. It admitted the 22 March 2002 statement and relied on it.

The defence appealed on points of law, arguing that the conviction violated Articles 3 and 6 because it rested on statements obtained through ill-treatment, that his injuries were unexplained, and that no other evidence supported guilt. On 26 August 2005, the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without a hearing, saying it sought re-evaluation of evidence and that the Convention complaint was formal. The decision was not appealable. The central alleged violation was therefore that the domestic appellate courts used the confession despite the first-instance finding of ill-treatment, undermining the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1.

**CASE OF L.M. v. SLOVENIA** (Application no. 32863/05), European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, judgment of 12 June 2014.

The applicant, L.M., a Slovenian woman born in 1971 with a long history of psychotic disorder, complained under Article 5 and Article 8 of the Convention about two consecutive psychiatric confinements between July 2005 and January 2006.

**First confinement – Idrija Psychiatric Hospital.** On 10 July 2005 the police informed L.M.’s family physician that she had broken into an unoccupied house, was difficult to communicate with, and was behaving psychotically. She was referred to the Idrija Psychiatric Hospital and admitted the same day to its closed ward. She signed a consent form for confinement and treatment, but told staff she was “possessed by energetic and physical people” sent through cameras operated by President Bush. She was diagnosed with schizophrenia and given antipsychotic and sedative medication. On 11 July she asked how long she would have to stay and said she would resist. The hospital notified the local court. The court appointed a lawyer and held a hearing on 15 July, at which L.M. said she would rather be at home and did not understand why she had been hospitalised. Medical records suggested she continued to agree to therapy, but on 30 July she gave power of attorney to a lawyer, D.P., saying she was receiving treatment against her will but feared refusing it because medication might be forced on her. On 2 August D.P. informed the hospital that L.M. did not consent to treatment and asked for information about side effects; on 6 August D.P. asked the hospital to stop forcibly administering medication. On 8 August L.M. was transferred to the open ward, and the court terminated the confinement proceedings. She was discharged on 12 August at her own request.

**Second confinement – Ljubljana Psychiatric Hospital.** On 15 August 2005 police took L.M. to emergency services, where she said she was being “raped by the police, the emergency medical technicians, everybody.” She was referred to the Ljubljana Psychiatric Hospital. Her admission record noted dissociated speech, paranoia and megalomaniac delusions; the psychiatrist indicated that she accepted hospitalisation owing to the staff’s presence and that no compulsory measures were necessary. On 17 August she was placed in the closed ward. She received Haldol, Akineton, Lorsilan, later Moditen and Leponex. On 21 August she notified the local court of her confinement and sought an interlocutory order to stop treatment and release her, and lodged a constitutional complaint. On 23 August the court appointed a lawyer, held a brief hearing, and, based on an expert opinion, ordered her confinement in the closed ward until 23 September. Her interlocutory request was dismissed on 24 August. On 3 or 4 September she was transferred to the open ward. The Higher Court allowed her appeals on 9 September and 10 November, finding the lower court’s reasoning inadequate and holding that interlocutory relief was legally possible and that her request to stop medication required separate consideration. Nevertheless, on 12 December the local court terminated the confinement proceedings because she was in the open ward. On 5 January 2006 the Higher Court dismissed her appeal, holding that non-contentious confinement rules no longer applied and referring her to civil injunctive relief. She was released on 19 January 2006 with a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia.

**Relevant legal context.** Domestic law permitted involuntary admission where mental illness posed danger or grave harm, with notification to a court within 48 hours. Only closed-ward confinement was subject to judicial review; transfer to an open ward could end proceedings. The Constitutional Court had already found the confinement procedure unconstitutional, requiring counsel, reasoned notification, shorter time-limits, effective judicial review, and regulation of treatment. Ombudsman reports noted that involuntary patients in open wards were not supervised and forced treatment was unregulated.

L.M. alleged under Article 5 that her closed-ward confinements were unnecessary and unlawful, that her open-ward stays were not voluntary, that she was not informed of the reasons, and that she had no effective legal protection or compensation. Under Article 8 she alleged that forced medication and therapeutic procedures interfered with her physical and mental integrity, and that no remedy existed to challenge that forced treatment.

In *N.H. and Others v. France* (ECtHR, Fifth Section, judgment of 2 July 2020), five single adult asylum-seekers in France alleged that the authorities failed to provide the in-kind and financial support required by national law, forcing them to sleep rough in inhuman and degrading conditions for months. They relied on Article 3 of the Convention. Two applicants also complained under Article 13 read with Article 3, and N.H. additionally invoked Article 8, alone and with Article 13.

N.H., an Afghan national, arrived in France in March 2013. He obtained a mailing address and tried to lodge an asylum claim on 4 April 2013, but was given an appointment for 9 July 2013 because of administrative delays. His urgent application for interim relief was rejected; the Conseil d’État found that a three-month wait did not amount to a serious and manifestly unlawful interference with the right of asylum. At the July appointment, a Dublin II procedure began because his fingerprints had been registered in Denmark under another identity. His claim was eventually registered, but in October 2013 the prefect refused him permission to stay, treating the asylum claim as abusive. Until then he had no material support, lived rough near the Canal Saint-Martin, had only occasional emergency accommodation, limited meals and showers, and no State medical aid until late October. OFPRA later granted him subsidiary protection.

S.G., K.T. and G.I. arrived in France in 2013 and claimed asylum in the Languedoc-Roussillon region. They were offered Asylum Reception Centre accommodation subject to availability and accepted it because doing so was necessary to qualify for the Temporary Waiting Allowance. OFII then told them no places were available and placed them on the National Reception Scheme waiting list, advising them to call the 115 emergency accommodation helpline. Because emergency facilities were at capacity, they lived in tents on the banks of the Aude river. S.G. also suffered from leg injuries and chronic hepatitis C. Their urgent applications for accommodation were rejected in October 2013 on the grounds that facilities were full, priority had to be given to families and vulnerable persons, and the State’s conduct did not amount to a serious and manifestly unlawful interference with the right of asylum. Legal aid for appeals to the Conseil d’État was refused or considered futile. G.I. later withdrew his asylum claim and sought voluntary return.

A.J., an Iranian journalist, arrived in France in September 2014. On 23 October 2014 he tried to lodge an asylum claim, but it was not registered; he received an appointment for 7 January 2015. Without asylum-seeker status, he could not obtain material support. The prefect said the national reception scheme was full and told him to call 115. He spent only a few nights in an overcrowded emergency centre. His urgent applications were dismissed by the Paris Administrative Court and the Conseil d’État. On 22 January 2015 he finally received a provisional stay, an asylum form and an accommodation offer. Pôle emploi refused the Temporary Waiting Allowance until OFPRA registered his claim in February 2015; he was later housed and recognised as a refugee.

The legal context was that French law at the time required asylum-seekers to obtain permission to stay before lodging an asylum claim, and access to reception support depended on status. Reception Directive 2003/9/EC required minimum material reception conditions throughout the asylum process. The applicants alleged that delays in obtaining appointments, registration and status created gaps in which they were left without lawful status, accommodation or financial aid, and were forced to live rough. The Government disputed some facts, arguing that notices allowed them to remain, that emergency accommodation was available through 115, and that some applicants did not make sufficient use of it or voluntarily left facilities.

In *Ruiz Rivera v. Switzerland*, the applicant, Carlos Humberto Ruiz Rivera, a Peruvian national living in Zurich at the material time, complained that the Swiss procedure refusing to discharge him from confinement violated Article 5 § 4 and Article 13 of the Convention. The confinement had been imposed because he was declared not criminally responsible for killing his wife.

In April 1995 the applicant’s wife was found dead. He had stabbed her 49 times, cut off her head and thrown it out of a window. Toxicological examinations indicated that he was under the influence of alcohol and cocaine. After a psychiatric assessment in October 1995, Dr R. diagnosed chronic paranoid schizophrenia and drug addiction, found that the offence was directly related to his illness and drug abuse, concluded that he had lacked criminal responsibility at the material time, and recommended confinement because he posed a serious danger to public safety. On 31 May 1996 the Zurich District Court found that he had killed his wife and had been totally lacking in criminal responsibility, and ordered his confinement under Article 43 of the Criminal Code.

From 29 August 1996 the applicant was held at Pöschwies Prison. His discharge was refused in 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2000. In June 2001 a second psychiatric report was prepared. It noted that he had worked in the prison as a bookbinder, in the dispensary, as a gardener and as a cook, but showed no awareness of his illness and no capacity for introspection. The experts found that he still suffered from chronic paranoid schizophrenia; although positive symptoms were less noticeable in prison, he still gave a delusional interpretation of his offence. His condition had changed little since 1995. Because he was not receiving treatment, the experts saw no basis for alternative arrangements or discharge on probation. Further discharge requests were refused in 2002 and 2003, and an appeal against the September 2002 refusal was dismissed in December 2002.

A March 2004 therapy report confirmed the 2001 findings and gave an unfavourable prognosis. It noted that the applicant denied being ill and refused prescribed treatment. On 24 June 2004, after interviewing him, the Judicial Enforcements Office refused discharge on probation, relying on a prison report, the 2004 therapy report and the 2001 psychiatric assessment. The applicant appealed with a lawyer, seeking a fresh expert assessment, legal aid and a hearing. The Directorate of Justice and Internal Affairs denied legal aid in September 2004 because his appeal appeared to have no prospect of success, as discharge had repeatedly been refused and nothing had changed.

The Administrative Court dismissed his appeal in January 2005, finding the 2001 report still valid and no need for the expert to testify. The Federal Court dismissed his further appeal in October 2005. It held that a fresh assessment was unnecessary, that the diagnosis was confirmed and unchanged, and that confinement remained proportionate. It also found that Article 5 § 4 required review only at reasonable intervals, which could be longer for persons of unsound mind. Since the last court decision was December 2002 and no clear change had occurred, his appeal lacked prospects, so denying legal aid was legitimate. The alleged violation therefore concerned the refusal to discharge him without a fresh neutral expert, an oral adversarial hearing or legal assistance, in breach of Article 5 § 4 and Article 13.

The case *Duranspahić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 47761/16 and nine other applications) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) on 9 May 2019. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention at various dates in 2016. The 26 applicants were represented by S. Zaklan, a lawyer practising in Mostar. Notice of the applications was given to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The case concerned the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions. Each applicant had obtained a final decision from either the Mostar Cantonal Court or the Mostar First Instance Court. The relevant domestic decisions were issued between 10 June 2010 and 26 January 2011. Enforcement proceedings were either initiated or should have begun shortly afterwards, but they remained pending. The appended table identifies a “start date of non-enforcement period” for each application, ranging from 21 January 2011 to 11 October 2011.

The ten applications were grouped by domestic decision. In application no. 47761/16, three applicants relied on a Cantonal Court decision of 26 November 2010; non-enforcement began on 21 January 2011 and had lasted more than 8 years, 1 month and 27 days. In application no. 48433/16, four applicants relied on a decision of 23 September 2010; non-enforcement began on 24 February 2011 and lasted more than 8 years and 24 days. In the European Court of Human Rights case *Golub v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 48020/12, judgment of 30 November 2021), the applicant was Nikolay Golub, a Russian national born in 1993. He complained about compulsory military service in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). He alleged that his service amounted to forced labour, that he was unlawfully detained, and that no effective remedies existed. The Court gave notice to Moldova and Russia of complaints under Articles 4, 5 and 13 of the Convention and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The key facts are as follows. In September 2011 the applicant was called up for compulsory military service in the “MRT”. Although he was the sole caretaker of his disabled mother and entitled under “MRT” law to deferral, he and his mother opted for his enrolment in a military education institution under the “MRT” Ministry of Defence. This counted as military service and allowed him to obtain an education diploma. As a cadet, his passport was taken away, he was issued a recruit card, and he was not allowed to leave the premises without the commander’s authorisation.

In November 2011 he left the premises several times to seek medical treatment after alleged ill-treatment or to care for his mother. Upon his return, from 17 to 24 November 2011, he was disciplined for absence without leave and placed in isolation in the Tiraspol Military Command. There he was held in a cell with eight other persons and could leave only once per day to use the toilet.

On 2 December 2011 the “MRT” authorities opened a criminal investigation against him for absence without leave. It was discontinued on 27 January 2012 on non-rehabilitation grounds. On 20 December 2011 he was excluded from the military institute for lack of discipline and unwillingness to continue his military education. He was sent to “MRT military unit no. 40896” in Dubăsari to complete compulsory military service.

On 25 December 2011 the applicant left the military unit on authorised leave but returned several hours late. According to him, as an informal sanction he was ordered to dig a trench. When he refused, he was disciplined and placed in isolation from 26 December 2011 to 9 January 2012 in the military unit’s prison (“гауптвахта”). On 25 February 2012 the “MRT” Minister of Defence granted his request for early dismissal as sole caretaker of his disabled mother and placed him in the reserve. On 27 February 2012 he was informed of this order and left the military unit.

As regards remedies, on 17 May 2012 the applicant complained to the Moldovan and Russian Prosecutor General’s Offices about his unlawful deprivation of liberty. On 9 and 22 June 2012 the Russian Military prosecutor informed him that his complaint had been redirected to the Moldovan and “MRT” authorities. On 19 June 2012 the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office told him that a criminal investigation into his unlawful detention had been initiated that day. On 17 August 2012 the investigation was suspended until the perpetrators could be identified. The relevant materials were summarised in *Mozer v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia*.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the conscription and enrolment in an “MRT” military institution, the confiscation of the applicant’s passport, restrictions on leaving the premises, disciplinary isolations in the Tiraspol Military Command and military-unit prison, the criminal charge for absence without leave, the alleged forced trench-digging, and the failure, redirection, and suspension of investigations by the Moldovan and Russian authorities. These facts underpin the complaints of forced labour, unlawful detention, restrictions on movement, and lack of effective remedies.

In *Zalevskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 3466/09, ECtHR, 16 October 2014), the applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 1964, alleged that he had been ill-treated by police during his arrest and that Ukraine had failed to carry out an effective investigation. The case arose from a long-running domestic dispute. The applicant had been given a flat in Vinnytsya in 1995. He married S. in 1995, they had a son in 1997, and they divorced in 2001, but both continued living in the same flat. Conflicts were frequent. In December 2005 a district court found the applicant guilty of domestic violence against his son and former wife and imposed a fine.

The alleged ill-treatment occurred on 14–15 February 2006. At about 11 p.m. on 14 February, three police officers arrived at the flat after S. complained about the applicant. The applicant refused to let them in, saying they had not identified themselves, it was late, and the corridor light was off. The police could not enter. According to the Government, a neighbour had called, the applicant was shouting and threatening S., and S. said the applicant had a knife. At about 2 a.m. on 15 February, S.’s two brothers arrived and persuaded the applicant to open the door, saying the police had left. The applicant claimed that, after he opened the door, the two brothers and three police officers burst in and beat him. He did not resist, but while handcuffing him the police twisted his arms and broke his right arm. He was allegedly ill-treated on the way to and at the police station. The Government disputed this, claiming the applicant tried to close the door, was pushed backwards, fell onto a chair and floor, and then resisted arrest; his arm was broken unintentionally during handcuffing.

At the police station the applicant complained of arm pain and was taken by ambulance to hospital. He was diagnosed with a displaced fracture of the right humerus, radial nerve neuritis, crushed soft tissue, and bruises on both wrists and jaw. He underwent surgery on 16 February and remained in hospital until 1 March 2006.

On 21 February 2006 the applicant complained to the district prosecutor about ill-treatment by police officers and S.’s brothers. The prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings several times—on 14 March, 6 May, and 26 September 2006, and again on 12 February 2007. Some earlier refusals were quashed as unfounded or incomplete by higher prosecutors and a court. A key expert report of 18 August 2006 concluded that the arm fracture had been caused by a rotary application of force, consistent with the applicant’s arms being twisted behind his back, and not by a direct fall. Another expert said the wrist bruises could have been caused by handcuffs, while other bruises might have resulted from the fall. The final refusal of 12 February 2007 found that the police and S.’s brothers had acted lawfully and necessarily; the fracture possibly occurred when the applicant resisted having his arms twisted, and other injuries came from the fall or handcuffs. That decision was upheld by the Staromiskyy District Court on 23 March 2007, the Vinnytsya Region Court of Appeal on 17 May 2007, and the Supreme Court on 12 July 2008.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 of the Convention, both substantive—ill-treatment during arrest—and procedural—failure to investigate effectively. The key factual disputes concerned whether the force used was necessary and lawful, the true cause of the fractured arm, and whether the authorities conducted a thorough and independent investigation. The European Court of Human Rights ultimately found violations of Article 3 in both respects.

Case Husayn (Abu Zubaydah) v. Poland (Application no. 7511/13) concerned allegations that Poland facilitated the CIA’s secret detention and torture of Zayn Al-Abidin Muhammad Husayn, a stateless Palestinian known as Abu Zubaydah. He is currently detained at Guantánamo Bay. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 3, 5, 8, 6 § 1, and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

After the 11 September 2001 attacks, the CIA established the High-Value Detainees Programme, a covert system for detaining and interrogating suspected terrorists in secret “black sites” abroad, in cooperation with host states. Abu Zubaydah was the first High-Value Detainee, captured in Pakistan in March 2002. CIA documents, including the 2004 CIA Inspector General’s Report and the 2009 DOJ Report, describe “Enhanced Interrogation Techniques” applied to him: attention grasp, walling, facial hold, insult slap, cramped confinement, insects, wall standing, stress positions, sleep deprivation (up to 11 days), and waterboarding. These were designed to create “learned helplessness” and were used cumulatively.

text:
In *Lindström and Mässeli v. Finland*, two Finnish prisoners at Riihimäki Prison alleged that prison authorities subjected them to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3 of the Convention, with the case later re-communicated under Article 8. The first applicant, Mark Kristian Lindström, convicted of aggravated drug offence, aggravated theft and a firearms misdemeanour, began serving his sentence in early 2004. The second applicant, Jouni Kristian Mässeli, convicted of attempted manslaughter, began serving his sentence around November 2003.

The alleged violations arose from isolation imposed because authorities suspected each applicant of concealing drugs or other unlawful substances inside his body. Lindström was isolated from 13 to 16 November 2004 after an unsupervised family meeting. Mässeli was isolated from 9 to 16 May 2004 after returning from leave. During isolation, they had to wear closed overalls covering them from feet to neck. Prison staff sealed the overalls with plastic strips, so the applicants could not remove them without help. To use the toilet, they had to call guards, who escorted them and removed the overalls. Lindström claimed that once the guards did not come quickly enough and he had to relieve himself in the overalls. Mässeli was given laxatives on his second day, with his consent but without prior medical consultation. When the laxatives took effect, he called for a guard, but the guard took a long time to arrive and he defecated in the overalls. He alleged that he then had to put the same dirty overalls back on and was not allowed to wash. Both applicants said they were not permitted to wash during isolation, and that the dirty overalls caused skin irritation; Mässeli’s skin broke.

In February 2005, the applicants reported the matter to the police. In January 2007, the public prosecutor charged the Riihimäki Prison director and two chief guards with breach of official duty for failing to respect the applicants’ human dignity during isolation. The applicants also brought charges for coercion and defamation. On 15 June 2007, the Riihimäki District Court dismissed all charges. It found that the use of closed overalls was acceptable to control and prevent drug smuggling. Defecation was not intended; prisoners were supposed to use separate, supervised toilets. The court found no evidence that the overalls affected how quickly prisoners were taken to a toilet, and no evidence that guards delayed their responses. It held that the overalls were not meant to humiliate and did not restrict privacy more than isolation itself. Lindström had defecated as a protest, while Mässeli, as a legally isolated prisoner, needed escorting to a separate toilet and did not reach it in time. The court also found no proof that they lacked washing opportunities.

On 30 September 2008, the Kouvola Appeal Court upheld the judgment, concluding that the suffering and humiliation caused by the overalls did not exceed the inevitable suffering and humiliation of legal isolation and did not violate human dignity. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 4 November 2009.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 2 May 2010. Domestic law permitted isolation on suspicion of concealment for up to seven days, under medical supervision. Prison rules required closed overalls sealed with plastic strips, supervised eating, smoking, washing and toilet use, and laxatives only before noon. In 2012, the Parliamentary Ombudsman found that the use of closed overalls lacked a sufficient legal basis, and their use was prohibited from 15 March 2013.

**Tershiyev v. Azerbaijan** (Application no. 10226/13, judgment 31 July 2014) concerned a Russian national of Chechen ethnic origin, Mr Ramazan Tershiyev, who alleged that his extradition from Azerbaijan to Russia would expose him to a real risk of torture or ill-treatment, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention, and that Azerbaijan lacked an effective remedy by which he could challenge the extradition on that ground, contrary to Article 13.

The applicant arrived in Azerbaijan in 2009. In July 2009 he was arrested while attempting to cross illegally from Azerbaijan to Russia. In April 2011 the Azerbaijani Assize Court convicted him and others of serious offences committed in Azerbaijan in 2009, including creating an illegal armed unit, illegal border crossing, illegal possession of firearms and explosives, and setting up clandestine flats in Baku for members of illegal armed units operating in Chechnya. He was sentenced to fourteen years’ imprisonment and was serving that sentence in Baku when the extradition dispute arose.

In Russia, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant in September 2011 under Article 208 § 2 of the Russian Criminal Code for participation in an illegal armed unit. The Russian authorities suspected that between 2000 and 2007 he had been an active member of an illegal armed unit in the Vedeno district of Chechnya and that he remained a member. He was placed under search, formally charged in April 2012, placed on an international wanted list in July 2012, and remanded in custody in absentia by the Vedeno District Court in Chechnya.

Meanwhile, in January 2012 the applicant applied to the UNHCR office in Baku for asylum. By agreement between the UNHCR and the Azerbaijani Government, asylum applications from people originating from Chechnya were handled directly by the UNHCR. His application was rejected at first instance, and an appeal was pending.

In August 2012 the Russian Deputy Prosecutor General requested the applicant’s extradition under the Minsk Convention. Alternatively, because the applicant was serving a sentence in Azerbaijan, Russia sought his temporary extradition for three months for procedural steps in the Russian criminal case. The request contained assurances that he would be prosecuted only for the offence charged, would not be subjected to torture or ill-treatment, and would be returned to Azerbaijan within three months if temporarily extradited.

On 26 November 2012 the Azerbaijani First Deputy Prosecutor General granted the request and ordered the applicant’s temporary extradition to Russia for three months. The applicant appealed, arguing that he faced a serious risk of torture or ill-treatment by Russian law-enforcement authorities. The Sabayil District Court asked the UNHCR about his asylum claim. The UNHCR replied that his application had been rejected at first instance but that an appeal was pending, and it “strongly requested” that his forced return be prevented until a final decision was taken.

On 24 January 2013 the Sabayil District Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It found no legal grounds precluding temporary extradition, noted that he did not have refugee status, and relied on the Russian assurances. It refused to examine his torture-risk complaint because he had submitted no evidence. On 1 February 2013 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld that decision. Its judgment was silent about the pending UNHCR asylum appeal and the applicant’s allegations of a risk of torture or ill-treatment. No further appeal lay against that decision.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 February 2013. The Court indicated an interim measure under Rule 39 that he should not be extradited to Russia during the proceedings and granted the case priority treatment. The Russian Government later intervened as a third party. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the claimed risk of ill-treatment in Russia, especially Chechnya; the Russian assurances; the pending UNHCR asylum appeal; and the Azerbaijani courts’ refusal or failure to assess the alleged risk, with no further avenue of appeal.

**Summary of *Milinković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* (Application no. 21175/13)**

The case of *Milinković v. Bosnia and Herzegovina* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 February 2013 by Mr. Dragan Milinković, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1977 and residing in Banja Luka. The application was directed against Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the applicant represented by Ms. R. Plavšić and the Government represented by its Agent, Ms. M. Mijić. The crux of the case concerns the prolonged non-enforcement of a final and enforceable domestic judgment against the Republika Srpska, one of the two Entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a matter similar to the earlier case of *Momić and Others v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows. On 23 February 2009, the Banja Luka Court of First Instance issued a judgment ordering the Republika Srpska to pay the applicant, within 15 days, 34,000 convertible marks (BAM) in respect of non-pecuniary damage, along with default interest at the statutory rate. The judgment also awarded the applicant BAM 4,667 for legal costs, again with default interest. This judgment became final and enforceable on 11 May 2009. To initiate the enforcement process, the Banja Luka Court of First Instance issued a writ of execution (rješenje o izvršenju) on 29 June 2009. Despite these legal steps, the Republika Srpska failed to comply with the judgment.

Consequently, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the non-enforcement. On 16 January 2013, the Constitutional Court delivered a decision in the applicant's favour, finding a breach of Article 6 of the Convention (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property). This finding by the highest domestic court acknowledged that the applicant's rights had been violated due to the authorities' failure to enforce a final judgment. However, the critical fact is that despite this domestic finding of a violation, the final judgment of 23 February 2009, awarding the applicant compensation and costs, remains unenforced to this day.
