The relevant domestic law and practice in this case were previously outlined by the European Court in the *Momić and Others* judgment. The Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina objected to the examination of the application by a Committee of the Court, but after consideration, the Court rejected this objection. The application was communicated to the Government on 7 May 2013.

In summary, the central factual circumstances relevant to the alleged violations are the issuance of a final and enforceable domestic judgment in favour of the applicant against the Republika Srpska in 2009, the subsequent issuance of a writ of execution, the domestic Constitutional Court's confirmation in 2013 of a breach of the applicant's rights under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to non-enforcement, and the continued, indefinite failure of the respondent State to enforce that judgment, leaving the applicant without the awarded compensation and costs. This situation forms the basis for the applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights.

In *Kowalski v. Poland* (Application no. 4771/20), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 8 February 2024. The applicant, Piotr Kowalski, born in 1979, was represented by Dawid Cupiał, a lawyer practising in Warsaw. He lodged his application with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention on 2 January 2020. The Polish Government was given notice of the application.

The applicant’s central complaints were that the criminal proceedings in his case had been excessively long and that Polish domestic law did not provide him with an effective remedy for that delay. These allegations correspond to the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

According to the appended table, the criminal proceedings began on 30 June 2014 and ended on 10 June 2020. They therefore lasted 5 years, 11 months and 12 days, and were examined at two levels of jurisdiction. The table does not set out the nature of the charges, the complexity of the case, the number or length of hearings, or the specific reasons for the delay. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are thus the start and end dates, the total duration, and the fact that the case went through two judicial instances.

A significant domestic-remedy fact is that the applicant made a complaint under the Polish 2004 Act concerning the breach of the right to have a case heard within a reasonable time. The Warsaw Regional Court decided that complaint on 14 November 2019 in case no. X S 146/19. The appended table labels this as a “Domestic award (in Polish zlotys),” but the excerpt provided does not specify the amount awarded. The timing is important: the domestic complaint was decided more than five years after the criminal proceedings started, and the criminal case continued for approximately another seven months after that decision. The applicant nevertheless maintained that this mechanism did not amount to an effective remedy for the length of the proceedings.

The Court, composed of President Péter Paczolay and Judges Gilberto Felici and Raffaele Sabato, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 18 January 2024 and adopted the judgment on 8 February 2024. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In summary, the facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant was involved in criminal proceedings lasting almost six years across two levels of jurisdiction; that he attempted to use the domestic length complaint under the 2004 Act, obtaining a decision from the Warsaw Regional Court in November 2019; and that he then applied to Strasbourg, complaining that the overall length was excessive and that domestic law lacked an effective remedy. The excerpt does not include the Court’s detailed reasoning or final holding, but it identifies the case as one concerning prolonged criminal proceedings and the adequacy of Poland’s domestic remedial response.

Case Stauder and Gabl v. Austria (Application no. 10711/09) concerned criminal proceedings in Austria arising from suspected aggravated fraud. The applicants were Wolfgang Stauder, a German national born in 1948, and Bernhard Gabl, an Austrian national born in 1964. They were represented by R. Gabl, while Austria was represented by H. Tichy. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 10 February 2009 and communicated to the Austrian Government on 21 October 2011.

In 1997 the Wels Regional Court began preliminary investigations against the two applicants and several others. The suspicion was that they had set up and managed an internationally operated gambling system based on a pyramid scheme, amounting to aggravated fraud. On 19 January 1999, the Regional Court decided to separate the proceedings against the applicants from those against the co-suspects in order to avoid delays.

As regards Mr Stauder, the Regional Court issued an international arrest warrant in December 1997. He was held in detention on remand from 26 to 27 May 1998. On 18 February 2008, he filed a request for acceleration of the proceedings under Section 91 of the Courts Act. The Linz Court of Appeal dismissed that request on 11 September 2008, stating that such a request could only be directed against delays caused by the courts, not by the Public Prosecutor. On 2 May 2013, the Regional Court acquitted Mr Stauder of all charges. The decision was served on his counsel on 15 October 2013. His proceedings therefore lasted approximately sixteen years from the start of investigations to acquittal.

As regards Mr Gabl, the Regional Court issued an international arrest warrant in April 1997. He was in detention on remand from 22 May 1997 until 6 August 1999. On 12 April 2002, the preliminary investigations against him were closed and the file was transferred to the Wels Public Prosecutor for further processing, but no indictment was brought at that time. On 4 December 2007, Mr Gabl filed a request for acceleration of the proceedings under Section 91 of the Courts Act. The Linz Court of Appeal dismissed it on 11 September 2008, again holding that the request could only target delays attributable to the courts, not to the Public Prosecutor. On 2 April 2010, the Public Prosecutor eventually brought an indictment against Mr Gabl. He appealed against the indictment and requested discontinuation of the proceedings. On 28 February 2011, the Court of Appeal rejected the indictment but did not discontinue the proceedings. On 13 October 2011, the Public Prosecutor discontinued the proceedings against him. His proceedings thus lasted more than fourteen years without a trial on the merits.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Convention violations are the substantial length of both sets of criminal proceedings and the applicants’ inability to obtain an effective domestic remedy to accelerate delays caused by the prosecution. Both applicants attempted to use the Section 91 Courts Act acceleration request, but the Court of Appeal refused to examine delays attributable to the Public Prosecutor. The case therefore raised issues concerning the right to a hearing within a reasonable time and the availability of an effective remedy for protracted criminal proceedings.

In *Karagjozi and Others v. Albania* (applications nos. 25408/06, 37419/06, 49121/06, 1504/07, 19772/07, 46685/07, 49411/07, 27242/08, 61912/08 and 15075/09), the European Court of Human Rights’ Fourth Section delivered judgment on 8 April 2014. Ten applications were lodged by 52 Albanian nationals between 13 June 2006 and 7 March 2009. They alleged violations of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention because Albanian authorities failed to enforce final administrative decisions awarding them compensation in lieu of restitution of nationalized properties.

The underlying issue was already the subject of the Court’s pilot judgment in *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*. In each application, property commissions recognized the applicants’ inherited title to land, restored some parcels where possible, and ordered compensation—state bonds, in-kind compensation, or other statutory forms—for occupied or unrestorable portions. These final decisions remained unenforced.

In *Karagjozi*, the 1996 Tirana Commission recognized title to 1,214 sq. m occupied by buildings housing foreign embassies; compensation was due but not paid. *Budini* concerned a 1995 Mat Commission decision recognizing 7,984 sq. m, restoring 4,797 sq. m and awarding state bonds for 3,187 occupied sq. m; it remained unenforced. A separate 11,112 sq. m claim had been rejected in 1996. *Koco* involved 1,154.62 sq. m occupied by a stadium, with compensation due but unenforced.

*Hajnaj* concerned 8,900 sq. m recognized in 1994; 7,727 sq. m were initially restored but occupied by Urban Transportation Company buildings. Later court decisions annulled that restoration and substituted compensation; Constitutional Court appeals failed in 2005 and 2006. The decision remained unenforced for 6,342 sq. m. *Shehu* concerned 3,600 sq. m recognized in 1994; some warehouses and plots were restored, but 2,240 occupied sq. m required unpaid compensation. *Dvorani and Dume* concerned 2,250 sq. m recognized in 1993; 278 sq. m were restored and 1,972 occupied sq. m were to be compensated by state bonds, but the decision remained unenforced.

*Sallabanda and Hoxha* involved 10,056.7 sq. m occupied by a national park; compensation was due but unenforced. *Goga and Others* concerned 12,000 sq. m recognized in 1996; 600 sq. m were restored, 4,950 sq. m were to be compensated in state bonds and 5,000 sq. m in kind, with no decision for 2,050 sq. m; compensation for 9,350 sq. m remained unenforced. *Tartari* involved 1,100 sq. m recognized in 1995, with 142 sq. m restored and 958 occupied sq. m requiring compensation. A third party nonetheless received a building permit in 1997. The applicant’s compensation claim was dismissed in 2009 for lack of funds, though he later received ALL 6,000,000 for a different plot.

*Okaj* concerned Shkodër Commission decisions in 1995 restoring 8,430 sq. m, awarding compensation for 2,833 sq. m, and granting first refusal over 14,537 sq. m. The applicants bought 2,194 sq. m, but third parties occupied their properties and challenged their title; litigation ended in 2001. No compensation was paid for 2,833 sq. m, and occupation continued.

The Court noted domestic and Council of Europe materials, including the Committee of Ministers’ repeated concern about Albania’s structural failure to enforce such property compensation decisions and the pilot judgment deadline of 17 June 2014. The key alleged violation was therefore the prolonged non-enforcement of final administrative decisions awarding compensation, impairing court access, effective remedy, and property rights.

Zalevskiy v. Ukraine (no. 3466/09) concerns a Ukrainian national’s complaint that police ill-treated him during his arrest and that Ukraine failed to conduct an effective investigation, contrary to Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant lived in Vinnytsya in a flat provided in 1995. He married S. in 1995, and they had a son in 1997. They divorced in 2001 but continued living in the same flat, where conflicts repeatedly occurred. In December 2005 a court fined the applicant for domestic violence against S. and his son.

On the night of 14 February 2006, after S. or a neighbour called the police, three officers arrived at about 11 p.m. The call reported that the applicant was shouting and threatening S., allegedly with a knife. The applicant refused to open the door, saying the police had not identified themselves, it was late, and the corridor light was off. At about 2 a.m. on 15 February, S.’s two brothers arrived and asked him to open. Seeing only the brothers through the peephole, he opened the door. According to the applicant, the brothers and three police officers then burst in and beat him; he did not resist. Police twisted his arms while handcuffing him and broke his right arm. He was allegedly further ill-treated on the way to and at the police station. The Government’s account differed: when the applicant opened the door and saw police, he tried to close it; the officers and brothers pushed in; he fell onto a chair and floor. Because he resisted arrest, officers used force to handcuff him, unintentionally breaking his arm.

At the police station, the applicant complained of pain. An ambulance took him to hospital. He was diagnosed with a displaced fracture of the right humerus, radial nerve neuritis, crushed soft tissue, and bruises on both wrists and jaw. He had surgery on 16 February and remained in hospital until 1 March 2006.

On 21 February 2006 the applicant complained to the prosecutor about ill-treatment by police and S.’s brothers. Domestic authorities repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings, on 14 March, 6 May, 26 September 2006 and 12 February 2007. Higher prosecutors and courts quashed several refusals as incomplete, ordering further inquiry into the medical evidence, the roles of police and S.’s brothers, the applicant’s personality, and the family situation. A key expert report of 18 August 2006 concluded that the arm fracture resulted from a rotary force—the arm being turned about its axis—consistent with the applicant’s account that his arms were twisted behind his back; it could not have been caused by a direct fall. Another expert accepted that wrist bruises could have come from handcuffs, while some other bruises might have resulted from a fall.

The final refusal of 12 February 2007 accepted the authorities’ version: police and the brothers acted lawfully to arrest the applicant and stop dangerous conduct; force was necessary; the fracture occurred while he resisted arm-twisting, wrist bruises came from handcuffs, and other bruises from the fall. This decision was upheld by courts in March 2007 and on appeal to the Vinnytsya Region Court of Appeal and Supreme Court in 2007–2008. The applicant alleged that these facts disclosed ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation.

The case Șcerbinina v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia (Application no. 76892/14) concerns a Moldovan national, Ms Irina Șcerbinina, born in 1981 and living in Tiraspol, the administrative centre of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transdniestria” (“MRT”). The factual background is set against the Transdniestrian armed conflict of 1991–1992 and the subsequent establishment of the MRT, an internationally unrecognised separatist entity. The European Court of Human Rights has previously examined this context in cases such as Ilaşcu and Others v. Moldova and Russia, Catan and Others v. Moldova and Russia, and Mozer v. Moldova and Russia. Those cases establish that Russia exercised effective control over the MRT, while Moldova retained positive obligations towards persons within its internationally recognised borders but outside its effective control.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations began in 2013, when the applicant was dismissed from her employment. Seeking to challenge the dismissal, she brought reinstatement proceedings against her employer before the courts of the “MRT”. The case proceeded through the MRT judicial system and ended with a final judgment of the Supreme Court of the “MRT” on 5 June 2014. That judgment dismissed the applicant’s action, thereby confirming her dismissal and denying her reinstatement.

The applicant also complained to the authorities of the Republic of Moldova. In response, the Bender District Prosecutor’s Office initiated a criminal investigation into her complaints. However, the criminal proceedings were later discontinued. The stated reason was that the facts she complained about did not disclose the elements of a criminal offence. The excerpt does not specify the exact nature of the criminal complaint, but it appears to have been linked to the circumstances of her dismissal and/or the proceedings before the MRT courts.

These facts are relevant to the alleged violations because they raise questions about the fairness and lawfulness of judicial proceedings conducted by the MRT, whose courts are not part of the Moldovan legal order and are not established under Moldovan law. The applicant’s reliance on MRT courts to challenge her dismissal engages the right to a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal established by law, typically under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The subsequent complaint to Moldovan authorities and the discontinued criminal investigation may also be relevant to assessing Moldova’s positive obligations and the effectiveness of domestic remedies.

The legal framework includes reports by inter-governmental and non-governmental organisations, relevant Moldovan domestic law and practice, and material summarised in Mozer. The Court therefore had to consider the distribution of responsibility between Moldova and Russia in the Transdniestrian context. The key factual issues were: the applicant’s dismissal in 2013; the MRT court proceedings and the final judgment of 5 June 2014; her complaint to Moldovan authorities; the criminal investigation by the Bender District Prosecutor’s Office; and its discontinuation for lack of elements of a criminal offence. Those facts formed the basis for examining whether the applicant’s Convention rights were violated and which respondent State bore responsibility.

In *Toțchi and Others v. the Republic of Moldova, Russia and Ukraine* (Application no. 8833/10), the applicants were two Russian nationals, Mr Iurie Toțchi and Mrs Tatiana Toțcaia, and one Ukrainian national, Mr Marc Fașcevschii. They lived in Bender. Their complaint concerned the death of Ms Iana Faşcevscaia, the first two applicants’ daughter and the third applicant’s wife, after she consumed poisonous mushrooms bought from a public market in Tiraspol, a city controlled by the self-proclaimed Moldovan Republic of Transnistria (“MRT”). The applicants alleged that the authorities failed to protect the victim’s right to life and to conduct an effective investigation into the circumstances of her death.

On 6 July 2001, two persons, K.S. and K.V., collected mushrooms in the woods and sold them at a market in Tiraspol. On 8 July 2001, two people who had eaten mushrooms from these sellers were admitted to the intensive care unit of the Republican Clinical Hospital in Tiraspol. More poisoned consumers followed. On 9 July 2001 at 10:35 a.m., hospital staff urgently called the Republican Centre for Hygiene and Epidemiology, reporting the incident and identifying the marketplace where the mushrooms had been bought.

Later that same day, at around 5 p.m., Ms Iana Faşcevscaia bought mushrooms from K.S. and K.V. They showed her a certificate from the market’s veterinary and sanitary laboratory confirming the mushrooms were suitable for consumption. She prepared dinner for her family. At about 4:10 a.m. on 10 July 2001, she felt stomach discomfort and was admitted to the hospital at 6 a.m. Her condition worsened, and on 13 July she was transferred to a hospital in Chișinău, where she died on 15 July 2001.

On 19 July 2001, the Tiraspol Prosecutor’s Office opened criminal investigations against the sellers and the market laboratory expert. On 31 May 2002, both investigations were discontinued. It was found that the sellers could not have known that some mushrooms were poisonous, especially since they had a certificate. The laboratory expert had used a rudimentary method—visual inspection and boiling mushrooms with an onion to observe colour changes—and no market laboratory in the MRT had equipment for biochemical mushroom testing. She was also covered by an amnesty law. The investigation against the sellers was later reopened and discontinued several times; ultimately, they were relieved of criminal responsibility because the limitation period had expired.

The investigation was extended to three officials from the Centre, accused of negligence for failing to react promptly to the hospital’s urgent call on the morning of 9 July 2001 and for not preventing further sale of the dangerous mushrooms despite having time to do so. On 14 May 2009, the Tiraspol city court convicted two officials of negligence. It found that had they properly discharged their duties, further sale would have been prohibited and the victim’s death avoided. They were sentenced to three years’ imprisonment but released due to the limitation period. The court also noted serious systemic shortcomings: old regulations for veterinary and sanitary laboratories no longer applied, no new regulations had been adopted, the laboratories lacked testing equipment, and prosecutorial delays allowed responsible persons to avoid liability. The MRT Supreme Court upheld the judgment on 30 July 2009. The Supreme Court of Moldova refused to examine the applicants’ appeal, stating that the judgments had been issued by unconstitutional courts and inviting them to pursue constitutional procedures; it appears they did not do so.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged violations: the authorities’ failure to protect life after knowing of the poisoning risk, and the failure to conduct a prompt and effective investigation, with delays and limitation periods preventing accountability.

In *Volyanyk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 7554/10), the applicant, Mr Oleg Markiyanovych Volyanyk, a Ukrainian national, worked as a deputy chief guard at “Lviv Railways”, a State-owned company. On 26 October 2009 the police instituted criminal proceedings against him on suspicion that, in conspiracy with S. and D., he had accepted bribes to cover up thefts from the company’s premises. This led to his pre-trial detention and a series of extensions, which formed the factual basis of his application to the European Court of Human Rights.

On 3 November 2009 the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv ordered the applicant’s pre-trial detention. It stated that he had committed serious crimes, did not admit guilt, and, if at liberty, would influence witnesses and other persons involved. The court also said that because the applicant worked as a policeman, he was well aware of how to obstruct the investigation and justice. However, there was no evidence in the case file that the applicant had worked as a policeman before or during the relevant events. It also remained unknown whether S. and D. had been arrested or remained at liberty. The Lviv Regional Court of Appeal upheld this detention decision on 9 November 2009.

On 25 December 2009 the Galytskyy Court extended the applicant’s detention until 26 February 2010. It relied on the grounds that not all his alleged accomplices had been detained, that the investigative authorities kept receiving complaints from persons who had given bribes to the applicant, and that if released he could obstruct the investigation or abscond. The Court of Appeal upheld this extension on 30 December 2009. On 22 February 2010 the Galytskyy Court extended detention again, until 26 April 2010, stating that the accused had committed serious crimes, did not admit guilt, and refused to testify, while if at liberty he—having higher education and extensive work experience as a guard—might influence witnesses, obstruct the investigation, or abscond. On 22 April 2010, the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal prolonged detention until 26 July 2010, citing the need to carry out further investigative measures, the seriousness of the charges, and the risk that he might abscond, obstruct the investigation, or continue criminal activities.

Subsequently, the pre-trial investigation was completed and the case was submitted to the Sykhiv District Court of Lviv for trial. On 17 August 2010, at a preliminary hearing, the Sykhiv District Court upheld the applicant’s preventive measure without providing any reasons and without fixing a time-limit for his detention. On 16 February 2012, the Sykhiv Court allowed the applicant’s request to change the preventive measure on health grounds. He was released the same day against an undertaking not to abscond.

The applicant lodged his application on 22 January 2010. The Ukrainian Government were represented by Ms Olga Davydchuk, and the application was communicated to them on 6 May 2013. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the repeated judicial authorisation and extension of his pre-trial detention, the alleged lack of relevant and sufficient reasons, the reliance on an apparently incorrect assumption that he was a policeman, the uncertainty about his co-suspects’ status, the lengthy period of detention, and the 17 August 2010 decision upholding detention without reasons or a time-limit. These matters were central to the applicant’s complaints under Article 5 of the Convention about the lawfulness, length, and judicial review of his detention.

Peter v. Germany (Application no. 68919/10) concerned a German applicant’s complaint about the length of proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. The applicant, born in 1948, entered into a civil partnership in October 2001 after Germany introduced civil unions for same-sex couples. His partner died in June 2002. In September 2002 the applicant applied for a survivor’s pension from the German Pension Fund. The Fund rejected the claim in November 2002, and his administrative appeal was dismissed in February 2003.

The applicant sought judicial review before the Fulda Social Court, arguing that “widow or widower” in the Social Security Code should include a surviving civil partner. In November 2004 the Social Court dismissed his claim, finding that a civil partner could not be considered a “widower” and that, in any event, the partnership had not lasted longer than one year—a requirement that would also exclude married couples. During the appeal, the respondent acknowledged a pension from 1 January 2005, following legislative amendments. The Federal Social Court dismissed the remaining leapfrog appeal in December 2005, leaving only the period July 2002 to December 2004 in dispute.

On 20 January 2006 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. In 2007 another case was brought before the Federal Constitutional Court concerning pension rights of a surviving civil partner in the civil servants’ pension scheme. In July 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court ruled in that 2007 case that denying such a pension violated the constitutional equality principle. The applicant then asked for a comparable decision. On 11 June 2010 a three-judge panel declined to review his complaint, reasoning that no pressing constitutional question remained because the relevant social-security provision had been amended, and that even if it had been unconstitutional, the Court could not require the legislature to amend a void provision. The decision was served in July 2010.

The applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights in November 2010. On 3 June 2013 the Court communicated his complaint concerning the length of the Federal Constitutional Court proceedings and the lack of an effective remedy; the remainder was declared inadmissible. Meanwhile, after the pilot judgment in Rumpf v. Germany, Germany enacted the Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations, effective 3 December 2011, which created a compensation remedy for excessively long proceedings, including before the Federal Constitutional Court. The Strasbourg Court invited the applicant to use this new remedy.

On 6 February 2012 the applicant filed a complaint under the new Act, claiming compensation for constitutional proceedings lasting four years, six months and one day. The judge rapporteur explained that the applicant’s complaint had been postponed pending the 2007 case by agreement with the previous rapporteur. Later it became clear the 2007 case did not involve retroactivity and did not affect the outcome, and he conceded the applicant’s complaint could have been dealt with earlier. He nevertheless said waiting had been in the applicant’s interest. The applicant replied that his complaint had received no attention in the first year and that the cases were not interdependent.

On 1 October 2012 the Federal Constitutional Court’s complaints panel dismissed the applicant’s compensation complaint. It accepted that chronic backlog cannot justify excessive length, but stressed the Constitutional Court’s special constitutional function, limited capacity for acceleration, and the binding effect of its decisions. It found the four-and-a-half-year duration unusually long but not excessive, distinguishing three phases: over one year before postponement, two years until the 2007 decision, and eleven months until determination. It found the delay not arbitrary and decided in due time after the 2007 case. The applicant therefore alleged before the ECtHR that the length of the constitutional proceedings violated the reasonable-time requirement and that Germany lacked an effective remedy.

**Summary of Omelchenko v. Ukraine (Application no. 34592/06)**

The case concerns an application lodged by Mr Sergey Vladimirovich Omelchenko, a Ukrainian national, against Ukraine on 13 July 2006. The applicant alleged breaches of his right against self-incrimination and his right to legal assistance during criminal proceedings.

The facts arose from the murder of Ms V., whose body was discovered on 27 October 2004 in Simferopol. She had suffered numerous knife wounds, and her mobile telephone and an earring were missing. On 28 October 2004, police obtained an expert opinion that a fingerprint on V.'s notebook possibly belonged to the applicant.

On 29 October 2004, police officers arrived at the applicant's home, approximately 120 kilometres from Simferopol, inspected it, seized clothing, and took him to the police station. Critically, no formal record of his arrest was drawn up. He was questioned as a witness on 29 and 30 October 2004, and on 30 October he confessed to murdering V. for her belongings, stating he had stolen her mobile telephone and killed her with a kitchen knife.

On 31 October 2004, the applicant was questioned as a suspect. He was informed of his suspicion of simple murder under Article 115 § 1 of the Criminal Code and waived his right to legal assistance in writing. An undertaking not to abscond was selected as a preventive measure. According to the applicant, he was not released until 1 November 2004. On that afternoon, he was arrested for breaching public order through swearing, spitting, and vagrancy and detained for ten days as an administrative punishment. While in administrative detention, he was questioned again on 4, 9, and 10 November 2004 concerning the murder, each time signing waivers of his right to legal representation.

On 11 November 2004, the court remanded him in custody. Lawyer E. was admitted on 16 November 2004, but according to the applicant, did not visit until 26 December 2004. On 12 January 2005, the charges were reclassified from simple murder to murder for profit under Article 115 § 2, which carries a potential life sentence. A new lawyer, R., was admitted on 10 February 2005.

On 28 February 2005, the applicant was questioned for the first time as an accused in the presence of lawyer R. He retracted his confessions, pleaded innocent, and alleged he had confessed under police pressure during unlawful detention. The prosecutor's office refused to investigate these allegations.

On 5 April 2005, the Court of Appeal convicted the applicant of armed robbery and murder for profit, sentencing him to fifteen years' imprisonment. The court issued a separate ruling noting the absence of any arrest record for 29 October 2004. The Supreme Court quashed the conviction on 21 July 2005, ordering additional investigation, noting that the confessional statements had been obtained during detention partly covered by administrative decision and partly by no records, and that the applicant's allegations concerning ulterior motives in detaining him should have been investigated.

On 18 November 2005, the Court of Appeal again convicted the applicant, relying on his initial confessions. It found no reason to exclude them, noting medical evidence showed no injuries and that the applicant had voluntarily waived legal representation. As he was initially suspected of simple murder, not carrying a life sentence, the waiver was deemed compatible with law. The Supreme Court upheld this judgment on 16 March 2006.

The applicant complained that his confessions were taken during unlawful detention without proper records, and that his right to legal representation was breached because the investigation deliberately delayed reclassifying charges to obtain confessions from an unrepresented suspect.

The case concerns José Antonio Fernández Martínez, a Spanish national born in 1937. Ordained as a Catholic priest in 1961, he applied to the Vatican for dispensation from celibacy in 1984 but received no immediate response. He married civilly in 1985 and had five children. From October 1991 he taught Catholic religion and ethics at a State secondary school in Murcia under a renewable one-year contract. Under the 1979 Spain–Holy See Agreement and a 1982 Ministerial Order, such teachers were appointed by the education authority from candidates proposed annually by the diocesan Ordinary; renewal was automatic unless the Ordinary objected.

In November 1996 a regional newspaper reported on a gathering of the Movement for Optional Celibacy (MOCEOP). The article named the applicant as a married priest and former seminary director who advocated optional celibacy and a more democratic Church, and discussed birth control and abortion. In August 1997 the Pope granted his long-pending dispensation from celibacy. The rescript removed his clerical state and barred him from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the local bishop decided otherwise, provided there was no scandal. On 29 September 1997 the Diocese informed the Ministry that he had ceased service, and the Ministry terminated his employment. The Diocese later explained that once his situation became public knowledge, the bishop could no longer authorise him to teach Catholic religion, citing risk of scandal and the sensitivity of parents; it described the reasons as religious.

The applicant challenged the non-renewal. An employment tribunal found he had been discriminated against because of his marital status and MOCEOP membership, declared the dismissal null, and ordered reinstatement. The Murcia High Court reversed, holding that the teacher–bishop relationship was based on trust, that the bishop had a prerogative to refuse to propose him, and that publicity had caused scandal. The Constitutional Court dismissed his amparo appeal. It found no discrimination, noting that he had voluntarily made his situation public. It balanced the Catholic Church’s collective religious freedom and parents’ rights to religious education against the applicant’s freedom of thought, religion, and expression, and held that the non-renewal was justified by exclusively religious reasons and proportionate, given State religious neutrality.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8, alone and with Article 14, that the non-renewal unjustifiably interfered with his private life because publicity about his family and personal situation as a married priest caused his termination. He also invoked Articles 9 and 10, arguing that the measure punished his thoughts, expression, and religious stance. The Government defended the non-renewal as necessary to protect Church autonomy, the trust required for religious teaching, and the avoidance of scandal.

The Grand Chamber, in its judgment of 12 June 2014, held that there had been no violation of Article 8 and found no separate examination under Article 14 necessary. It accepted that the non-renewal interfered with the applicant’s private life but pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights of the Catholic Church and parents regarding religious education. Given the special nature of Catholic religion teaching, the annual renewal system dependent on diocesan proposal, and the applicant’s public status and advocacy, the domestic authorities had not exceeded their margin of appreciation. The State’s duty of neutrality required respect for the Church’s assessment of suitability, subject to limited judicial review. The key facts were therefore the applicant’s public married-priest status and MOCEOP activity, the Church’s withdrawal of suitability on scandal grounds, and the State’s implementation of that decision in a publicly funded teaching post.

**Case: Vieira Gomes Bezerra v. Portugal (Application no. 60786/10)**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Second Section (Committee)  
**Judgment date:** 28 January 2014  

The applicant, Ms Tomásia Vieira Gomes Bezerra, is a Portuguese national born in Silves and living in Bonn, Germany. She lodged an application against the Portuguese Republic under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 4 October 2010. The Portuguese Government were represented by Ms M. F. Graça de Carvalho, Deputy-Attorney General. On 17 October 2012, the application was communicated to the Government.

The domestic facts concerned a civil dispute over land. On 28 February 2007, the applicant started civil proceedings against two companies before the Court of Vila Nova de Gaia in Portugal (domestic proceedings no. 1908/07.8TBVNG). She claimed that the defendants were occupying land that belonged to her. The defendants contested the claim. The court ordered an expert analysis to determine the size of the land, and that procedural stage ended on 18 December 2007. During the first trimester of 2008, an attempt at conciliation between the parties took place.

On 18 July 2008, the domestic court suspended the proceedings because the property was not registered in the applicant’s name at the Land Registry Office (Conservatória do Registo Predial). Later, on 20 January 2010, the court ordered the interruption of the proceedings. On 18 July 2010, the applicant submitted an additional supporting document to the court, informing it that the land had been registered. The judge then ordered the proceedings to be resumed. According to the last information received by the European Court on 3 May 2013, the domestic proceedings were still pending.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation centre on the duration of these civil proceedings. The case began on 28 February 2007 and was still unresolved more than six years later, as of 3 May 2013. The principal Convention complaint was therefore the excessive length of the civil proceedings, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time.

The chronology shows several important periods. The initial proceedings and the expert analysis lasted about ten months. A conciliation attempt occurred in early 2008. However, from July 2008 to July 2010, the case was suspended and then interrupted because the land was not registered in the applicant’s name. That issue appears to have been a central procedural obstacle. The applicant sought to revive the case on 18 July 2010 by filing proof of registration, after which the domestic court resumed the proceedings. Nevertheless, the case remained pending for nearly three more years as of May 2013.

These facts would be relevant to assessing whether the total length of the proceedings was excessive and whether any delay was attributable to the applicant, the domestic authorities, or the complexity of the land-ownership dispute. In particular, the Court would examine the period of suspension/interruption due to the registration problem, the applicant’s conduct in eventually providing the registration document, and the continued pendency of the case after resumption. The alleged violation was thus the failure to determine the applicant’s civil claim within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The case *Pikhun v. Ukraine* concerned a Ukrainian national and former police officer. A criminal investigation for illegal arms possession began in September 2006. He was arrested and detained several times, then released. Later, charges of murder, threats, and abuse of power were brought against him. On 30 November 2009 he was arrested on new charges of firearms theft.

The applicant’s main Article 3 complaint concerned alleged police ill-treatment on 30 November 2009. He claimed that, after refusing to answer questions about the new charges, three police officers physically assaulted him at the prosecutor’s office: they throttled him, handcuffed him, and hit his head against a parked car. The alleged ill-treatment continued at the police station, where officers allegedly stubbed a cigarette out on his left hand and demanded that he not assert his rights during the investigation. A temporary detention centre report of 22 December 2009 recorded a head wound, scratches on his head and neck, and bruises on his wrists; he complained of headache and stomach sickness and received ambulance care. He repeatedly requested medical-examination documents, but these requests were refused. From 1 December 2009 he submitted numerous complaints to the prosecution authorities and gave a detailed account on 3 December 2009. The Government stated that on 29 January 2010 an investigator refused to open criminal proceedings, finding no offence: the police had forcibly stopped and handcuffed him after he attempted to flee, no cigarette burns were found, and wrist bruises resulted from handcuffs. The applicant reportedly did not challenge that decision. Prosecutors later said his ill-treatment complaints had not been forwarded because the criminal case was before the trial court. In February 2010 his challenge to that reply was discontinued because no procedural decision had been taken. In November 2013 the trial court noted that the events could indicate ill-treatment and notified the regional prosecutor; in February 2014 the Regional Court quashed that ruling and instructed the trial court to examine the complaints. It was not clear whether that instruction was implemented.

Regarding Article 5, on 3 December 2009 the District Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. On 28 January 2010 the same court, in the absence of the applicant and his defence lawyer, extended his detention until 30 March 2010. His appeal was returned unexamined on 4 February 2010 because the case was already before the trial court. On 26 February 2010 the District Court remitted the case for additional investigation and ordered continued detention without giving reasons or time-limits.

As to Article 6, the criminal proceedings were lengthy. On 4 October 2011 the District Court convicted the applicant of threats, theft, and unlawful use of firearms, sentencing him to four years’ imprisonment. On 13 December 2011 the Regional Court quashed the sentence, remitted the case, and released him with an undertaking not to abscond. The prosecution later limited the charges to firearms theft. On 22 November 2013 he was convicted but exempted from liability due to expiry of time-limits. On 20 February 2014 that decision was quashed and remitted. According to the applicant, on 11 December 2018 the trial court terminated the proceedings after charges were dropped. The trial held 86 merits hearings; 66 were adjourned because the prosecution, victim, expert, or witnesses failed to appear; 21 due to the applicant’s or defender’s absence; and 18 due to the judge’s inability to sit. The latter adjournments extended the proceedings by about one year and six months.

In *Beketov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 44436/09, judgment of 19 February 2019), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by a Ukrainian national under Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention. The applicant, born in 1970, had undergone surgery for an umbilical hernia in April 2007.

On 9 or 10 February 2008 he was arrested in connection with suspicion of abduction and murder and placed in a cell at the Shevchenkivskyy district police station in Kyiv. He alleged that between 10 and 16 February 2008 police officers beat him to force a confession. In particular, Officer G., the first deputy head of the police station, allegedly kicked him in the face and abdomen, injuring the area of his prior hernia operation. On 16 February 2008 he confessed and signed undated documents. That same day he was transferred to the Kyiv Temporary Detention Facility (ITT), where a medical examination noted a bruise under his right eye, classified as a minor physical injury.

According to the applicant, the Kyiv Pre-trial Detention Centre (SIZO) refused to admit him because of his poor health. He was returned to the ITT, and an ambulance took him to the Kyiv Medical Emergency Hospital, where he stayed from 20 to 25 February 2008 and was treated for “contusion to the abdomen and facial tissue.” On 26 February 2008 he was placed in the SIZO, where a doctor diagnosed a post-operative condition following his 2007 hernia operation.

His defence lawyer complained to the prosecutor’s office about ill-treatment in May and August 2008, naming Officer G. Between September 2008 and 2013, the prosecutor’s office repeatedly refused to institute criminal proceedings, finding no constituent elements of an offence. Domestic courts quashed those decisions multiple times because investigators failed to question the applicant, Officer G., cellmates, ITT and SIZO staff, emergency medical personnel, and arresting officers; failed to establish the origin of the applicant’s injuries; and failed to follow court instructions. In 2013 the matter was entered into the Unified Register of Pre-Trial Investigations, but proceedings were again terminated and decisions quashed. No final information about further developments was provided.

The applicant also alleged inadequate medical treatment in detention. He suffered constant abdominal pain, navel fistula, suture sinus, omphalitis, a urachal cyst, and cardiac and other conditions. SIZO doctors provided outpatient treatment and antiseptics, and surgeons recommended elective surgery. In September 2009, during a court hearing, an ambulance team suspected peritonitis and recommended urgent hospitalisation, but the prison escort allegedly refused. In October 2009 the Court applied an interim measure under Rule 39 requiring appropriate medical treatment; it was lifted in December 2009. In January 2010 the applicant was hospitalised at Buchanska Prison Hospital and underwent surgery to remove the navel fistula. The Government later said medical documentation after February 2010 had been lost.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant alleged that SIZO cells lacked natural light, had dim electric light constantly on, beds without mattresses or linen, and poor-quality and insufficient food. He also alleged that on court hearing days he received no food or water because Ukrainian law made no provision and court buildings had no facilities. Under Article 13, he complained that no effective domestic remedies existed for these violations. These facts formed the basis of his Article 3 complaints concerning ill-treatment, ineffective investigation, inadequate medical care, poor detention conditions, and lack of food and water on hearing days, as well as his Article 13 complaint.

In *Placì v. Italy*, the applicant, Luigi Placì, born in 1975, was called up for compulsory military service in 1993 at age eighteen. On 3 December 1993, a combined psychological and physical examination found him fit for service. The detailed report, not disclosed to him until 2010, described him as slow in understanding and executing tasks but logical, prone to giving up, and scoring 4/10 in language/cultural skills, motivation, mental performance and behaviour. A further medical examination on 14 June 1994 again found him fit and suffering from no illness. He was assigned to Battalion no. 123 in Chieti, where he underwent intensive physical and mental training, including firearms training.

On 9 July 1994 he was transferred to the provincial command in Aquila until 30 December 1994, temporarily serving in a logistical battalion from 1 September to 2 November. There he received eight punishments between July and December, amounting to twenty-four days’ confinement, including solitary confinement, for minor matters such as negligent care of his camp-bed area, failure to report, or informal behaviour toward a superior. He was also hospitalised at least four times for unrelated medical care.

On 30 December 1994 he was transferred to Lecce, where a commander noted nervous tics, difficulty socialising and learning, and absent-minded behaviour, and ordered a specialised fitness assessment. On 24 January 1995 he was hospitalised and diagnosed with anxiety disorder and a fragile mental state. A 6 February 1995 NHS report described pre-existing affection-relational problems and learning difficulties, physical weakness, insecurity, low learning aptitude, isolation, impaired cognitive functions, and an IQ of 67. It said military life caused him anxiety and fear of fellow soldiers and that longer service would worsen his anxiety. He remained on medical leave until April 1995, when he was found to suffer from dysphoria and borderline personality disorder and discharged as unfit.

Later reports linked his mental health problems to military service or at least saw a causal contribution. In 1996 he sought damages from the Defence Ministry. In 1999 a Medical Commission diagnosed obsessive-compulsive disorder, found it pre-existing and not caused or aggravated by military service, and considered his request out of time; this was confirmed in 2000 and the Ministry rejected damages.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3, claiming that Italy failed properly to assess his fitness before conscription and then subjected him to compulsory military service, training and punishments causing treatment contrary to Article 3. He also complained under Article 6 about unfairness in the domestic proceedings. Relevant facts included repeated difficulties accessing medical and disciplinary records, inconsistent disclosure of punishment days, and the late disclosure of the 1993 pre-conscription report.

In domestic proceedings, the TAR appointed an expert in 2002 who failed to report; when the applicant sought replacement in 2007, the TAR treated this as a renewal request, rejected it due to inactivity, and decided the case. It found a pre-existing condition but noted the June 1994 fitness examination had been inaccurate. On appeal, the Supreme Administrative Court ordered a Medical Board examination. The Board, largely composed of military/police doctors with an external neurologist, reported in 2010 that the applicant’s chronic OCD and intellectual disability were pre-existing and not directly caused or aggravated by ordinary military service. The applicant challenged the Board’s impartiality and non-disclosure. In February 2011 the Supreme Administrative Court rejected his appeal, relying on the Board and finding the condition antecedent and not detectable in 1994. The ECtHR application was lodged on 3 August 2011.

In *van de Kolk v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 23192/15, ECtHR, 28 May 2019), the applicant, Hugo van de Kolk, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention that he lacked legal assistance during police interviews after his arrest.

On 19 August 2009, aged 19, he was arrested on suspicion of distributing child pornography—three photographs of a 16-year-old girl—in April 2009. He was informed of his right to consult a lawyer. At the police station, before his lawyer was available but with his consent, officers conducted a “social interview” about his personal circumstances and personality, not the suspected offence. He disclosed a brain disorder: cavernous hemangiomas in his brain and spinal cord, which affected his trust in others and meant he could not head a football. When his lawyer became available, the interview was suspended so he could consult by telephone. Following his lawyer’s advice, he refused to answer further questions, and the interview ended. He met his lawyer later that day.

On 20 August 2009, police interviewed him twice about the suspected offence. At the start, he asked for his lawyer to be present. He was told this was not possible, and questioning proceeded; he answered questions. During the interview, officers noticed a spasm-like arm movement and asked if he was having an epileptic fit. He confirmed he was. They interrupted the interview, called a doctor, and resumed after he said the seizure might have been caused by stress and other factors. A final interview took place on 21 August; all interviews were audio-recorded. He was released from custody that day.

Domestically, the Regional Court of The Hague convicted him on 25 March 2011 of distributing child pornography and imposed a suspended two-week prison sentence and 80 hours’ community service. It found he should have been allowed to consult a lawyer before the first interview, but treated this as a procedural defect because later interviews did not substantially differ. On appeal, the Court of Appeal of The Hague quashed and reconvicted him on 3 July 2013, imposing 40 hours’ community service. It rejected his complaint about lawyer presence, finding no indication that the officers knew he had a mental age of 15 or 16 or that his brain disorder could cause epileptic seizures. Since he was an adult, under the *Salduz* case-law as then applied, he was not entitled to have a lawyer present during police questioning. The conviction relied on the victim’s complaint and statement, his 20 August police statement that he had sent and uploaded photographs, a third party’s statement, and a police record showing images accessible online via a profile using his name. The Supreme Court dismissed his further appeal on 18 November 2014 with summary reasoning under section 81 of the Judiciary (Organisation) Act.

At the relevant time, Dutch law did not generally provide a right to consult a lawyer before police questioning or to have one present during interviews. After *Salduz*, the Supreme Court held on 30 June 2009 that adult suspects could consult a lawyer before the first interview but had no right to a lawyer present during interviews. Only on 22 December 2015 did the Supreme Court accept that right, applying from 1 March 2016, with legislation following in March 2017.

The applicant applied to the ECtHR on 8 May 2015. Notice was given only on the complaint concerning lack of legal assistance during police interviews. In 2016 the Government filed unilateral declarations admitting a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) and offering compensation and costs, seeking a strike-out. The applicant objected because Dutch law allows revision of a final conviction only on the basis of an ECtHR judgment finding a violation, not a strike-out. On 23 January 2018 the Court refused to strike the case out and adjourned it pending *Beuze v. Belgium*.

In *Milošević v. Croatia* (Application no. 12022/16), the European Court of Human Rights examined whether Croatian authorities punished the applicant twice for the same conduct, contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 (the *ne bis in idem* principle). The applicant, a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina living in Bosanski Brod, owned a truck inspected on 29 June 2012 by the Vukovar Customs Office with police assistance. The inspection found that the truck was using red-tinted, state-supported heating oil, which could not lawfully be used as motor-vehicle fuel.

On the same day, the Customs Office found the applicant guilty of a minor offence under the Excise Duties Act for using the heating oil contrary to section 74(2). He was fined HRK 4,800 (about EUR 640) under section 80(3). The penalty notice stated that, as owner, he was responsible; it also warned that an unpaid fine could be enforced and, if enforcement failed, converted into imprisonment. The applicant did not appeal, the decision became final, and he paid the fine.

Also on 29 June 2012, the Customs Office sent inspection and sampling records to its administrative department to calculate tax surcharges. On 2 July 2012, the Osijek Customs Office ordered the applicant to pay HRK 123,000 (about EUR 16,700) in excise duties. This sum consisted of excise duties for the quantity of heating oil involved, increased one hundred times because of its illegal use, under section 76(2) of the Excise Duties Act.

The applicant challenged that decision. On 31 October 2013, the Ministry of Finance quashed it because the quantity of oil subject to excise duty had not been properly determined. On 15 January 2014, the Osijek Customs Office issued a fresh decision ordering payment of HRK 83,025 (about EUR 11,300), again applying the one-hundred-times increase for the illegal use on 29 June 2012. This decision was upheld on appeal. The applicant then brought an administrative action, but the Osijek Administrative Court dismissed it on 20 January 2015, and the High Administrative Court upheld that judgment.

The applicant subsequently lodged a constitutional complaint, arguing, among other things, that he had been punished twice for the same act, contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. On 20 January 2016, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, without addressing his *ne bis in idem* complaint. He applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 22 February 2016.

The relevant law included the Excise Duties Act: section 73 required heating gas oils to be labelled; section 74(2) prohibited using such oils to power motor vehicles or for purposes other than heating; section 76(2) required the owner of a vehicle found using such oil illegally to pay excise duties equal to the fuel-tank volume multiplied by one hundred; and section 80 made such use a minor offence punishable by a fine of HRK 2,000 to HRK 10,000 for natural persons. In 2015, the Act was amended to remove the one-hundred-times increase, with the final proposal stating that the increase had been contrary to the *ne bis in idem* principle and EU jurisprudence and practice. The minor offence for illegal use remained.

The alleged violation therefore arose from two consequences based on the same facts: a final minor-offence fine for using prohibited heating oil, and a later administrative excise-duty charge for the same illegal use, increased one hundred times. The key question was whether these amounted to two criminal punishments for the same offence contrary to Article 4 of Protocol No. 7.

In *Khan v. Denmark* (Application no. 26957/19), the applicant, Shuaib Khan, a Pakistani national born in Denmark in 1986, complained that a Danish expulsion order and six-year re-entry ban imposed on him violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects private and family life.

Khan was born and raised in Denmark. His parents and four siblings lived in Denmark; two other siblings lived in the United Kingdom. He had no spouse or children. He stated that he had only broken Punjabi and could not read it, had visited Pakistan two or three times, most recently in 2007, and had no family or friends there. The Danish Immigration Service calculated that, after deducting about ten years of imprisonment, he had been lawfully resident in Denmark for approximately 20 years and 10 months. It also noted that his family owned property in Pakistan and that a Pakistani ID card later listed a permanent address there. His residence permit had been renewed in 2017 until 2021, though he had earlier been charged with staying in Denmark without the required permit after failing to renew it from 2010 to 2015.

Khan had a long criminal record since 2003, including thirteen convictions. These included weapons offences, violence, drugs, driving offences, and unlawful mobile phone possession in prison. Most significantly, in 2008 he received eight years’ imprisonment for aggravated violence, including fatal violence; in 2013 he received three years and six months for aggravated violence and theft; and in 2015 he received six months for aggravated violence. In 2015 he was also given a suspended expulsion order with a two-year probation period. He was released in March 2017. He was the leader of the gang Loyal to Familia (LTF), which was later dissolved by a City Court in 2020 for having an unlawful purpose and operating through violence.

The offence underlying the expulsion arose on 31 July 2017. Amid an armed conflict between gangs, police established stop-and-frisk zones, including at Blaagaard Square in Copenhagen. During a frisk there, Khan, as LTF leader, allegedly threatened a police inspector on duty. According to the courts, he said something about the inspector having an attitude problem, then told other LTF affiliates “Remember his face” and told the inspector “Watch out,” “Watch out carefully,” and “Watch your back,” while at least one affiliate photographed the inspector. The courts found his tone and attitude threatening and the atmosphere tense. He was charged under Article 119(1) of the Penal Code for threatening a public official, and also for staying without the requisite permit.

In October 2017 the Copenhagen City Court convicted him, sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment and a fine, but issued only a suspended expulsion order, finding that immediate expulsion of someone born and raised in Denmark with limited ties to Pakistan would be disproportionate. In March 2018 the High Court upheld the conviction but reduced the prison sentence to 60 days, again finding expulsion disproportionate. In November 2018 the Supreme Court increased the sentence to three months and imposed unconditional expulsion with a six-year re-entry ban. The majority emphasized his serious prior violence, roughly ten years’ imprisonment, LTF leadership, commission of the offence during the suspended-expulsion probation period, and risk of reoffending. One judge dissented, finding the latest offence too minor—spontaneous and short-sentenced—to justify expelling a person with strong Danish ties and weak Pakistani ties. Khan then brought his Article 8 complaint to the European Court of Human Rights.

This case, *Vasilyev and Others v. Ukraine*, was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) by 249 Ukrainian nationals against Ukraine. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The central facts of the case are consistent across all applicants and concern the non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions. On various dates, Ukrainian domestic courts and labour disputes commissions issued decisions in favour of the applicants. These decisions entitled them to receive various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour, such as the payment of owed wages, pensions, or other social benefits. The judgment explicitly states that these decisions became final and enforceable.

Despite the final and binding nature of these rulings, the Ukrainian authorities failed to enforce them in a timely manner. The applicants were therefore unable to obtain the payments or actions they were legally entitled to for prolonged periods. This failure by the state authorities to execute the final judgments formed the basis of their applications to the ECtHR. The applicants complained that this non-enforcement violated their rights under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) of the Convention.

The case was a composite of many individual applications, the details of which were appended in a table. For instance, the lead applicant, Aleksandr Nikolayevich Vasilyev, had a final decision from the Suvorivskyy District Court of Kherson dated 27 September 2005, which remained unenforced. The table shows that the final domestic decisions originated from a wide range of courts across Ukraine, including district courts, regional courts of appeal, and circuit administrative courts. The dates of these decisions span from as early as 1997 to as late as 2011. The entities responsible for the payments were often state-owned or former state enterprises, such as the "Sodovyy Zavod" in Slovyansk, or various state bodies responsible for social payments.

The judgment also noted several procedural developments. A number of the applicants died during the proceedings before the ECtHR, and their next of kin expressed a wish to continue the applications. In other applications, the applicants claimed to be the lawful successors in title of deceased relatives who had been awarded judgments.

The ECtHR's judgment, delivered on 13 February 2014, focused on the systemic problem of non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in Ukraine. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were the existence of final and binding court decisions in the applicants' favour and the state's subsequent failure to enforce them, thereby depriving the applicants of their lawfully awarded entitlements. The case is a clear example of a repetitive application concerning Ukraine's long-standing failure to ensure the timely execution of court judgments.

In *Y v. Latvia* (Application no. 61183/08, judgment of 21 October 2014), the applicant, Ms Y, a Latvian national born in 1959, lived in Liepāja. On 1 November 2007, while she was in the courtyard of her apartment building, two municipal police officers, J.M. and J.L., arrived in a car in connection with an alleged administrative violation—washing a car in a public courtyard. After a conversation, the officers twisted the applicant’s arms behind her back and forced her towards their car. She was eventually released, apparently after neighbours intervened. Soon afterwards she felt ill and called an ambulance; she received an injection. The next day a general practitioner issued sick leave until 12 November 2007 and prescribed painkillers and sedatives. She claimed ongoing health effects more than a year later.

On 2 November 2007 the applicant asked the prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings. She alleged that one officer grabbed and twisted her right arm, shouted that he would teach her a lesson about resisting police, and that the second officer twisted her left arm. She said the officers tried to push her into their car and that she later had haematomas on her upper arms. On 4 November she also complained to the municipal police, seeking an investigation and compensation for mental anguish and material and psychological harm.

A forensic medical expert found two haematomas on each upper arm. The expert concluded they could have arisen in the circumstances described by the applicant but classified them as minor injuries not causing adverse health effects for more than six days. The applicant’s longer medical treatment was considered irrelevant. Three eyewitnesses said the applicant ignored police requests and resisted; the officers twisted her arms behind her back and released her once she stopped resisting. An internal police inquiry disciplined J.M. and J.L. only for failing to properly document the administrative infraction, not for using force.

On 21 January 2008 an inspector terminated the criminal proceedings. He found that the applicant had intentionally disobeyed a lawful police order and that the officers had grounds to detain her. However, they violated section 13 *in fine* of the Law on Police, which prohibited the use of special restraint techniques against women except in exceptional circumstances, such as danger to life or health or armed resistance. The applicant had sustained minor injuries under section 130 of the Criminal Law. Nevertheless, the inspector found no exceeding of official authority under section 317 because there was no substantial harm to state authority, administrative order, or individual rights, given the applicant’s disobedience and resistance. The proceedings were terminated for absence of *corpus delicti*. The applicant was informed she could pursue a private prosecution under section 130.

She did not appeal the termination but lodged a private prosecution complaint with the Liepāja Court, dated 29 April 2008 and received on 30 April, claiming damages under sections 130 and 156. On 7 May 2008 a judge refused to initiate proceedings, holding that the six-month limitation period had expired and that the complaint had been received on 6 May; she also failed to specify the relevant paragraph of section 130. On appeal, the Kurzeme Regional Court dismissed her appeal on 2 June 2008. It held that the last day to bring charges was 1 May 2008 and that, although the complaint was lodged on 30 April, it was physically impossible to complete the necessary procedural steps by 1 May. It also noted she could bring a civil claim. That decision was final.

The applicant alleged that she had been subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment and that she had no possibility of obtaining compensation for the damage sustained. The key facts relevant to those alleged violations are the use of special restraint techniques against a woman contrary to domestic law, the documented minor injuries, the termination of criminal proceedings, the classification of the offence as privately prosecuted, the restrictive six-month limitation period, and the resulting inability to obtain compensation through criminal or private prosecution.

The applicants, the Norwegian Confederation of Trade Unions (LO) and the Norwegian Transport Workers’ Union (NTF), complained under Article 11 ECHR that the Norwegian Supreme Court’s decision declaring their planned boycott unlawful violated their right to freedom of association and collective action.

The dispute concerned dockworkers in Norway. LO/NTF had a Framework Agreement with NHO and the Norwegian Logistics and Freight Association, covering fixed pay and employment for dockworkers at major ports, including Drammen. Clause 2(1) gave registered dockworkers priority to load and unload vessels of 50 dwt or more sailing between Norwegian and foreign ports, except at a company’s own facilities. In Drammen, the Administration Office for Dock Work managed and permanently employed dockworkers. Holship Norge AS, a Norwegian subsidiary of a Danish freight group, was not an NHO member or party to the Framework Agreement. Until 2013 it used the Administration Office; then it employed four workers who also performed loading and unloading.

In 2013 NTF demanded that Holship sign a collective agreement accepting the Framework Agreement. Holship did not respond. After mediation, NTF notified a boycott on 11 June 2013: a blockade of ships calling at Drammen involving Holship’s loading/unloading work. NTF stated the purpose was to secure a collective agreement and enforce the priority clause. NTF sought an advance declaration under the Boycott Act that the boycott was lawful.

The Drammen City Court and Borgarting High Court found the boycott lawful. They rejected unlawful purpose, relied on the 1997 Port of Sola Supreme Court precedent, ILO Convention No. 137, public interests in trained dockworkers, and NTF’s willingness to negotiate. They found no breach of negative freedom of association or competition law.

On Holship’s appeal, the Supreme Court, sitting plenary, ruled 10–7 on 16 December 2016 that the boycott was unlawful. It had sought an EFTA Court advisory opinion. The EFTA Court said the priority clause and Administration Office system restricted EEA freedom of establishment, protected a limited group of workers to the detriment of others, and could affect negative freedom of association; justification was for the national court.

The Supreme Court majority balanced the possible Article 11 right to boycott against Holship’s EEA freedom of establishment under Article 31. It accepted that protecting workers can justify restrictions, but found the boycott’s principal effect was to limit market access and shield the Administration Office from competition, rather than protect Holship’s employees, whose jobs were not seriously threatened. It therefore held the restriction unjustified and disproportionate; the boycott had an unlawful purpose under section 2(a) of the Boycott Act. The minority found a legitimate aim and proportionality, relying on ILO Convention No. 137 and the Viking/Laval line.

The ECtHR examined whether that Supreme Court decision breached Article 11. It ultimately found no violation, holding that the domestic courts had adequately balanced the competing rights and that the interference with the applicants’ collective-action rights was justified. The key facts were therefore the priority clause, Holship’s non-membership and use of its own employees, NTF’s boycott notice aimed at securing the Framework Agreement, and the Supreme Court’s EEA-based finding that the boycott unlawfully restricted freedom of establishment.
