text:
In *Luca v. the Republic of Moldova* (ECtHR, 17 October 2023), the applicant, Lilia Luca, alleged that Moldova failed to protect her from domestic violence and to support her contact with her children, relying on Articles 3, 8 and 14 of the Convention. She lived with A.I. as an unmarried couple in Italy, where their two children were born in 2006. A.I. returned with the children to Moldova in 2012; the applicant stayed in Italy to work and support the family, joining them in 2015.

According to the applicant, A.I. began psychologically and physically abusing her in October 2015. She reported physical violence on 13 July and 4 November 2016, plus verbal abuse, harassment, emotional abuse, attempts to turn the children against her, and utility disconnections. On 1 August 2016 she sought a protection order for herself and the children. On 2 August 2016 the Ialoveni District Court granted a 90-day order requiring A.I. to leave the common residence, avoid contact, and stay at least 50 metres away; this was upheld on appeal.

The applicant repeatedly complained to police and child protection services that A.I. violated the order. She said he moved into his sister’s part of the same house, that the children moved in with him on 22 August 2016, that he continued making negative statements about her, removed her belongings, and cut off water. She alleged authorities failed to monitor compliance. On 24 October 2016 police said her facts were unconfirmed; a prosecutor had refused criminal proceedings on 7 October 2016, treating the conflict as essentially civil/family.

She sought extension of the protection order. On 2 November 2016 the District Court refused, finding no evidence of non-compliance and describing the conflict as a family dispute without violence; the children lived with their father. Her appeal was dismissed on 24 January 2017. On 4 November 2016 A.I. physically assaulted her, causing bruises to her forehead, arms and buttocks and a concussion; she was hospitalised for eight days. Further protection requests in November 2016 and February 2017 were rejected. Courts found insufficient evidence, no imminent danger, doubted her credibility, and said she was using domestic-violence proceedings for divorce/custody or revenge; they also relied on the children’s wish to live with their father.

Criminal proceedings were opened in November 2016 for breach of the protection order and domestic violence. An earlier administrative fine against A.I. for the 13 July incident was quashed. In November 2019 A.I. was convicted on both counts, given a suspended sentence of two years and three months, and ordered to pay damages; this became final in 2021.

As to contact rights, while the protection order was in force, the children moved in with A.I. and stopped answering the applicant’s calls. On 15 September 2016 the child protection authority declined to set a contact schedule, based on the children’s statements that they preferred their father and refused their mother. A court ordered a schedule on 11 November 2016, and on 26 January 2017 a schedule was set for every second week. The applicant complained A.I. refused compliance; police replied that the children voluntarily refused. In May 2017, at a school visit, the children refused to speak to her or accept gifts. A working group was reportedly created in September 2017, but no records were provided. Divorce proceedings initiated by A.I. in July 2016 ended in 2018 with the children living with their father; the decision became final in 2022. A criminal complaint concerning psychological abuse of the children was discontinued in 2018 after expert reports found no trauma.

The alleged violations therefore concern Moldova’s failure to protect the applicant from domestic violence, enforce protection orders, investigate abuse effectively, and support her parental contact despite A.I.’s alleged interference and the children’s alienation.

In *Irodotou v. Cyprus* (Application no. 16783/20), the applicant, Mr Marios Irodotou, a Cypriot national born in 1964 and living in Paphos, complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of private criminal proceedings brought against him, and under Article 13 about the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy. The Court gave notice only of those complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations began with a civil judgment of 18 June 2013, in which the District Court of Paphos ordered the applicant to pay EUR 300 monthly to the Cooperative Credit Company of Geroskipou and East Paphos until a debt plus interest was paid off. On 2 March 2015, Paphos Cooperative Savings Bank Ltd brought a private prosecution against him (case no. 1312/15) for failing to pay instalments due between 1 September 2013 and 1 January 2015.

On 3 April 2015 the applicant was notified of the case for the first time. He pleaded not guilty, and the hearing was set for 5 November 2015. From 5 November 2015 to 22 March 2017, the hearing was adjourned four times, mainly because the District Court lacked time to hear the case. On 28 September 2017, the prosecution notified a change of name after the bank transferred its assets and liabilities to Cooperative Central Bank Ltd, later renamed Cyprus Cooperative Bank Ltd. On 6 November 2017, the court again adjourned for lack of time. On 29 March 2018, the case was postponed at the applicant’s request for health reasons.

On 14 September 2018, the prosecution filed a second change of name, from Cyprus Cooperative Bank Ltd to Cooperative Asset Management Company Ltd. On 24 September 2018, a hearing was postponed because a prosecution witness was absent. On 15 November 2018, the applicant challenged whether the company could prosecute as a legal entity capable of operating as a credit institution, arguing that no counsel could appear for it and the criminal proceedings could not continue. The prosecution sought an adjournment, which was granted, and the case was rescheduled for 15 January 2019. Further adjournments followed on 15 January 2019, 26 March 2019, and 24 May 2019, largely by agreement or for procedural exchanges.

By letter of 5 September 2019, the prosecution applied to the Attorney General to discontinue the case. It explained that mergers had created an issue whether a non-existent prosecutor could initiate a prosecution, that a related Supreme Court decision was pending, that a similar case had ended in a prima facie acquittal at the pre-trial stage, and that continuation no longer served a purpose. It also feared that a dismissal could harm the merged credit institution’s rights in a future prosecution for unpaid instalments. On 23 September 2019, the Attorney General ordered discontinuance by granting a nolle prosequi. On 2 October 2019, the District Court informed the parties that the case was discontinued and the applicant discharged.

The applicant attempted to challenge the discontinuance, arguing that he had not been consulted by the Attorney General, that he had raised the capacity issue on 15 November 2018 but it remained unresolved because of repeated adjournments, that he could not claim losses or expenses, and that he had been treated unfairly after appearing in court for four and a half years. The court replied that discontinuance was an exclusive constitutional power of the Attorney General, not subject to judicial review, and that no discretion could be exercised as to substance, procedure, or costs. The case was closed without an order for costs against the applicant.

In *A.M.A. v. the Netherlands*, the applicant, a Bahraini national and Shiite Muslim, applied for asylum in the Netherlands in August 2017. He claimed membership in the opposition group “Barbar Revolutionary Youth,” wrote critical articles about the Bahraini regime, and feared persecution because his brother was a political activist who had fled to Germany. He alleged that after a group member was arrested and allegedly tortured, he fled Bahrain for Iran and later the Netherlands. His first asylum application was rejected as implausible and incoherent: the authorities found no evidence of his online activity, noted inconsistencies, considered it unlikely he was wanted given he left Bahrain legally with a valid passport, and found his fear based on his brother unsubstantiated. Judicial review was initially dismissed for late electronic filing; the Council of State quashed that decision, but the Regional Court again declared the review inadmissible in September 2018. The applicant did not further appeal.

In October 2018, removal preparations began. The applicant refused return to Bahrain, claiming he would be arrested immediately and was on a terrorism wanted list; he was willing to go to Iran or Georgia, but those options proved impossible. A detention order was issued. On 18 October, during a final return interview, he was told he could submit a new asylum application but that this would not automatically cancel his flight. He tried but failed to reach his lawyer.

On 19 October, his lawyer emailed him documents from his brother: copies in Arabic bearing the Bahraini Public Prosecutor’s letterhead. He submitted a subsequent asylum application that afternoon. On 20 October, he was transferred to Schiphol Airport and interviewed without a lawyer. He said he had just received the documents, that his name appeared and he was charged with participating in a terrorist organisation, and that the documents were a record of the questioning of someone who had named him. He could not explain how his brother had obtained the originals. At the end of the interview, an officer orally rejected the application, stating the documents were not original and were in Arabic, that there was no time, and refusing a one-week extension. A written decision the same day declared the subsequent application inadmissible because no new elements had been presented. It found the documents had no probative value as they were untranslated, not original, and of unexplained provenance, and concluded the application was merely intended to delay removal. The applicant was ordered to leave immediately. The decision and interview report were faxed to his previous lawyer, and objection and interim-relief remedies were available, but the applicant did not use them. He was expelled to Bahrain later that day.

After removal, he was immediately arrested and detained. His lawyer asked the Dutch authorities to set aside the removal and return him, citing a likely risk of torture; this was refused. His subsequent asylum application was formally rejected in February 2019. On 28 February 2019, he was convicted in Bahrain of possessing weapons and ammunition and participating in terrorist activities, sentenced to life imprisonment and a fine, and initially lost his nationality. He alleged he had been tortured to extract a confession, had an unfair trial, and faced poor detention conditions, restricted family and lawyer contact, and later participated in a hunger strike.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Articles 3 and 13 that the Dutch authorities had failed to sufficiently assess the risk of ill-treatment before expulsion, despite the late evidence, and that this risk materialised. He also alleged that he had no effective remedy to challenge the final risk assessment or the last-minute rejection before removal.

In *Sukhanov and Ilchenko v. Ukraine* (Apps. nos. 68385/10 and 71378/10), judgment 26 June 2014, two Ukrainian nationals with “child of war” status complained to the European Court of Human Rights that they had not been paid social benefits—pension supplements—in the amount claimed. Their applications were lodged in November 2010 and communicated to the Government in August 2011.

Under section 6 of the Children of War Social Protection Act, from 1 January 2006 “children of war” were entitled to a pension supplement of 30% of the minimum pension. Section 3(2) stated that these guarantees could not be limited or annulled by other legal acts.

The first applicant, Mr Sukhanov, sued in May 2008 for recalculation of his pension for 2006–2008 and related payments. On 22 July 2008 the Lugansk Regional Administrative Court rejected his claims for 2006 because the State Budget Act 2006 had suspended section 6 and empowered the Cabinet to create a mechanism for the increase, but no mechanism was adopted. For 2007–2008, the State Budget Acts had again suspended or modified section 6, but the Constitutional Court declared those provisions unconstitutional on 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008. The court ordered recalculation for 9 July–31 December 2007 and from 22 May 2008. This was upheld on appeal on 19 December 2008; the Higher Administrative Court dismissed cassation on 28 July 2010.

The second applicant, Mr Ilchenko, sued in December 2009 seeking recalculation from January 2006. On 2 March 2010 the Zhovtovodsky Town Court partly granted his claim, holding that he was entitled only from 9 July 2007, not from 1 January 2006. It ordered recalculation for 9 July–31 December 2007 and 22 May 2008–2 March 2010. The Dnipropetrovsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld this on 10 August 2010, making it final. In February 2011 he brought further proceedings for the supplement from 3 March 2010; on 17 May 2011 the town court granted recalculation from that date, upheld on appeal on 14 October 2011.

The domestic legal background was central. The State Budget Act 2006 suspended section 6; amendments made the supplement gradual and subject to a Cabinet decision, but none was taken. The 2007 and 2008 State Budget Acts suspended or modified section 6, and the Constitutional Court found the relevant changes unconstitutional on 9 July 2007 and 22 May 2008. Because Constitutional Court decisions were not applied retrospectively, the Higher Administrative Court in 2009 advised that supplements for 2007–2008 could be awarded only from those judgment dates, and that 2006 benefits had not been implemented.

The key issue was therefore the conflict between the Children of War Act’s guarantee and successive State Budget Acts that suspended or reduced it, together with non-retrospective Constitutional Court rulings. The applicants alleged that, despite domestic court recognition of entitlement, they did not receive the pension supplements in the full amount claimed, especially for periods before the Constitutional Court decisions.

The case of *Janáček v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 9634/17), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 2 February 2023, concerns an alleged breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention arising from the Czech Constitutional Court’s failure to communicate to the applicant written observations submitted by the general courts involved in his case.

The applicant, Ladislav Janáček, a Czech national born in 1957, was involved in proceedings concerning the division of matrimonial property with his former wife. On 17 December 2013, the Zlín District Court ruled on the division and ordered the applicant to pay substantial sums to his former wife. The case turned heavily on expert valuation evidence. The District Court relied on an expert, S., after other experts were unavailable or delayed. The applicant later submitted an expert opinion by expert M. The presiding judge then emailed expert S. directly for comments on that opinion, and S. responded the next day. The court preferred S.’s report.

On appeal, the Brno Regional Court partially altered the judgment on 24 March 2015, increasing the total amount the applicant was ordered to pay. It relied on expert S.’s opinion, heard S. and other experts, and rejected the applicant’s objections. The applicant’s subsequent appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 12 January 2016 as manifestly ill-founded. Execution proceedings followed, and the bailiff eventually ordered the sale of the applicant’s immovable property.

On 14 April 2016, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint. He argued, inter alia, that the lower courts had relied solely on expert S. without sufficient justification, that the Regional Court had refused an alternative expert report, and that the courts’ formalistic approach had led to an incorrect division of property to his detriment. He invoked Article 11 and Article 36 § 1 of the Czech Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms, Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Constitutional Court invited the District Court, Regional Court, and Supreme Court to submit comments. In May 2016, those courts provided written observations. The Supreme Court explained why the appeal on points of law had been rejected as inadmissible. The District Court judge addressed, among other things, his direct email contact with expert S., explaining that he had approached S. only to speed up the proceedings and that he had not previously known him. A Regional Court judge also commented on expert S.’s appointment and valuation.

These written observations were not sent to the applicant. On 19 July 2016, after a written procedure and without an oral hearing, the Constitutional Court dismissed the constitutional complaint as manifestly ill-founded. The applicant’s representative only learned of the observations after inspecting the file following the decision. When the applicant asked why he had not been given an opportunity to respond, the Constitutional Court replied that, since the observations had not been sent to him, the judge rapporteur had probably considered that they contained no new information or legal arguments.

The alleged violation under Article 6 § 1 therefore concerns the lack of adversarial proceedings: the applicant was unable to familiarise himself with the general courts’ written observations or to comment on them before the Constitutional Court decided his complaint. Relevant domestic law, including the Constitutional Court Act, grants parties and joined parties the right to submit views and inspect the file, while evolving Constitutional Court practice following *Milatová* recommended communicating observations containing potentially new facts, allegations, or arguments.

**Case: Li v. Russia (Application no. 38388/07), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Judgment of 24 April 2014**

The applicant, Roman Mikhaylovich Li, is a Russian national born in 1966 who lives in Magadan. He lodged his application against the Russian Federation on 20 July 2007 under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The application was communicated to the Russian Government on 14 January 2013. The Government were represented by Mr G. Matyushkin.

The facts concern the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment awarding the applicant compensation. On 28 January 2003, the Magadan City Court awarded him 30,000 Russian roubles as compensation for unlawful conviction. That judgment became final on 16 February 2003. On 5 March 2003, the applicant obtained the corresponding writ of execution.

According to the applicant, in 2004 the writ of execution was stolen from his office. In September 2007, he therefore asked the domestic courts to issue a duplicate of the writ. On 13 September 2007, a national court refused to issue the duplicate. The decisive reason was that the time-limit for submitting the writ for execution had expired under Article 14 of the Russian Federal Law on Enforcement Proceedings. That provision, in force at the material time, allowed writs of execution to be submitted for execution within three years from the date on which the underlying court decision entered into force. Since the judgment became final on 16 February 2003, the three-year period had expired in February 2006, before the applicant sought the duplicate in 2007.

On 27 September 2007, the applicant also asked the Ministry of Finance of the Russian Federation to execute the 2003 judgment. The Ministry replied that execution was not possible without submission of the writ of execution.

The relevant domestic law reinforced this position. Article 242.1 § 1 of the Budget Code of the Russian Federation provided that enforcement of judicial decisions recovering funds from the budgetary system had to be carried out on the basis of enforcement documents, such as a writ of execution or court order, and in accordance with domestic requirements and time-limits for submission. Article 14 of the Federal Law on Enforcement Proceedings required that such writs be submitted within three years from the entry into force of the court decision on which they were based.

The applicant’s alleged Convention violations therefore centred on the failure of the Russian authorities to enforce a final and binding domestic judgment in his favour. The key facts relevant to those allegations are: the existence of a final judgment awarding him compensation for unlawful conviction; the issuance of a writ of execution in March 2003; the alleged loss or theft of that writ in 2004; the applicant’s attempts in 2007 to obtain a duplicate and to have the judgment enforced; the domestic court’s refusal to issue a duplicate because the three-year enforcement period had expired; and the Ministry of Finance’s refusal to execute the judgment without the writ.

Those facts raised issues under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the right to a fair hearing and the effective enforcement of final judicial decisions, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning the applicant’s right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions, since the compensation award could be regarded as an asset or legitimate expectation. The central question was whether the Russian authorities’ reliance on formal enforcement requirements and the expired time-limit effectively deprived the applicant of the benefit of a final judgment that had never been executed.

In *Potoroc v. Romania* (Application no. 37772/17, judgment 2 June 2020), the European Court of Human Rights examined the applicant’s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention concerning his continued detention and prison conditions despite serious illness. The applicant, born in 1953, suffered from brain damage following strokes, hemiparesis, prostate adenoma, impaired hearing, and severe psycho-organic syndrome comparable to pre-senile dementia. He used a wheelchair, required permanent assistance, and needed continuous medical care.

In 2009, he received a final 15-year prison sentence for international drug trafficking. He was imprisoned at Rahova Prison from February 2011. Although he spent 350 of 529 days in prison hospitals until August 2012, he refused placement in Rahova’s medical wing because it was on the first floor, had no ramps, and made outdoor access difficult; he was therefore placed in a regular cell. Disability commissions concluded he did not need a personal assistant and had no functional deficiency.

In May 2012, the applicant applied for interruption of his sentence on health grounds, relying on Article 3. A July 2012 forensic report recommended Colibaşi Prison Hospital and found prison healthcare adequate, but could not guarantee treatment would actually be provided. In August 2012, the Argeş County Court allowed his release due to his “deplorable” health and humanitarian considerations. On appeal, a February 2013 report found his health serious, with possible unpredictable complications including prostate neoplasm, and noted he needed permanent care and supervision. It stated Colibaşi Prison could not provide adequate care, but the National Prison Service hospital network could. In September 2013, the Piteşti Court of Appeal confirmed his release with restrictions.

After release, he suffered an ischemic stroke in October 2012. In December 2014, on the authorities’ application, the Bucharest County Court reassessed his health. An October 2014 report by ten NIFM experts concluded the prison hospital network could provide adequate care, that he needed a personal assistant, and that the criteria for interrupting the sentence were not met. He was reimprisoned in early 2015 after the judgment became final.

From March 2015 to September 2017, he was held in various prisons and prison hospitals, including Mioveni (Colibaşi) Prison Hospital for almost two years. The Government claimed he generally had at least 4.22 square metres of personal space, except for 13 days in Giurgiu Prison when he had 3.06 square metres. The Giurgiu room was not fit for a disabled person, though ramps existed. In Colibaşi Prison Hospital, medical assistance was provided by a team of inmates collectively. At Jilava, another inmate, V.I., was appointed as his personal assistant but also assisted two other inmates.

The applicant made further applications to interrupt his sentence in 2016, alleging deterioration, lack of treatment, hearing loss, bed confinement, and confusion. An April 2016 medical report said prison healthcare could provide necessary treatment, frequent hospitalisation was needed, and he required constant assistance. Domestic courts dismissed his applications. In September 2016, he sought transfer from Colibaşi Prison to Colibaşi Prison Hospital; in October 2016, the Argeş County Court allowed it, finding his health very precarious, Article 3 applicable, and the prison unable to provide necessary care.

Eventually, after the Court found an Article 6 violation in a related case, the High Court on 20 September 2017 quashed his sentence and released him, relying on his serious health and good behaviour. In April 2018, he was acquitted in dubio pro reo without re-examination because he could no longer communicate.

The key Article 3 facts include his severe multiple illnesses and disability, wheelchair dependence, need for permanent care, prolonged detention despite medical evidence, conflicting domestic findings on prison healthcare adequacy, alleged lack of a personal assistant and disabled access, a 13-day period of cramped personal space, and reliance on inmate assistance in prison hospitals.

**Case summary: Lambertné Bársony v. Hungary (Application no. 48689/10)**

The case of *Lambertné Bársony v. Hungary* was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, Committee) on 25 March 2014. The applicant, Ms Klára Lambertné Bársony, was a Hungarian national born in 1955 and living in Miskolc. The case concerned the excessive length of civil proceedings and the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations began on 20 April 1998, when the applicant brought a civil action against Mr F. seeking division of the property of their common-law partnership. The dispute proceeded through three levels of Hungarian jurisdiction. The first-instance court was the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Court. On appeal, the case was heard by the Debrecen Court of Appeal. The final judgment was delivered by the Supreme Court on 2 March 2010.

Accordingly, the domestic civil proceedings lasted approximately 11 years, 10 months and 11 days. This lengthy period formed the central factual basis of the applicant’s complaint before the European Court of Human Rights.

The applicant lodged her application under Article 34 of the Convention on 18 August 2010. The Hungarian Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi, Agent, Ministry of Public Administration and Justice. On 6 March 2013, the application was communicated to the Government.

The applicant’s principal alleged violation was that the length of the civil proceedings was incompatible with the “reasonable time” requirement of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. She complained that a straightforward private property dispute between former common-law partners took nearly twelve years to resolve, despite passing through only the ordinary three judicial instances. The proceedings involved no exceptional complexity apparent from the facts, and no significant delay was attributed to the applicant. The Government contested the complaint.

The applicant also relied on Article 13 of the Convention. She alleged that Hungarian law did not provide an effective remedy by which she could complain about the excessive length of the civil proceedings. The key fact for this complaint was the absence of any domestic mechanism capable of providing adequate redress for the delay. At the relevant time, the Court’s case law held that Hungarian law did not offer such an effective remedy for length complaints in civil cases.

The Court assessed the period from 20 April 1998 to 2 March 2010 and found that the length of the proceedings was excessive and failed to satisfy the reasonable-time requirement. It therefore found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. It further found a violation of Article 13, as the applicant had no effective domestic remedy for her length complaint. The Court awarded the applicant compensation for non-pecuniary damage and reimbursement of costs.

In summary, *Lambertné Bársony v. Hungary* is a repetitive Hungarian length-of-proceedings case. Its key facts are that a civil property division claim, begun in April 1998, was not finally resolved until March 2010, after nearly twelve years and three judicial levels. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 about the unreasonable duration and under Article 13 about the lack of an effective domestic remedy. The Court found violations of both provisions.

Bokal v. Slovenia (no. 34386/10) concerned the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings in Slovenia. The applicant, Lidija Bokal, a Slovenian national born in 1955 and living in Ljubljana, lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 26 May 2010.

On 21 July 1997 the applicant instituted civil proceedings before the Ljubljana Local Court against M.P. and N.M. She sought a determination that a sale contract between the defendants concerning an apartment in a building partly owned by her was invalid, and she requested that a note on dispute be entered in the Land Register. She stated the disputed value as SIT 500,000 (approximately EUR 2,100).

The early proceedings were marked by delays and service problems. On 20 August 1997 the Local Court rejected her proposal to enter the note on dispute in the Land Register. After unsuccessful attempts to serve her appeal on the first defendant, the appeal was posted on the court’s notice board on 18 February 1998. On 4 March 1998 the Ljubljana Higher Court dismissed her appeal. Following a supervisory appeal to the Ministry of Justice, the court reported on 18 February 1998 that the case could not be given priority. The applicant requested a hearing on 21 April 1998 and requested priority on 27 March 2000; that request was dismissed on 5 April 2000. On 16 June 2000 a third party, D.S., who had bought the apartment, joined the proceedings.

The delay continued. The first hearing was scheduled only for 13 February 2004, but it was postponed to 26 March 2004. On 18 March 2004 the applicant raised the claim value to SIT 1,100,000 (approximately EUR 4,600). At the first main hearing on 26 March 2004, the court modified the disputed value as requested. Further hearings were held between 9 April and 4 June 2004. On 4 June 2004 the Local Court issued a judgment partially upholding the applicant’s claim. Service on the first defendant and the third party was again effected by posting the documents on the court’s notice board.

The applicant appealed on 27 September 2004. On 7 December 2005 the Higher Court returned the file to the first-instance court, instructing it to serve the appeal documents on the first defendant in accordance with the Civil Procedure Act and to decide the applicant’s request for an interim order. On 6 January 2006 the Local Court requested the applicant to pay court fees and supplement her interim-order proposal. On 3 March 2006 the judgment and appeal were served on the first defendant by posting them on the notice board. The Local Court dismissed the interim-order request on 20 March 2006. On 21 June 2006 the Higher Court dismissed the applicant’s appeals against both the judgment and the interim-order decision. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law.

On 23 October 2008 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal on procedural grounds. It held that the Local Court had wrongly allowed the disputed value to be modified at a late stage of the proceedings. It therefore used the value originally stated in the claim and concluded that the threshold for an appeal on points of law had not been met. On 26 November 2009 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional appeal. That decision was served on the applicant on 1 December 2009.

Overall, the proceedings lasted from 21 July 1997 until at least 1 December 2009—approximately twelve years and four months—across the Local, Higher, Supreme, and Constitutional Courts. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the repeated delays, the long period before the first hearing, service difficulties, the return of the file for procedural corrections, and the eventual rejection of the appeal on points of law on a procedural technicality. The applicant complained that the length of the civil proceedings violated her right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 §1 of the Convention, and that she lacked an effective domestic remedy

Császy v. Hungary (Application no. 14447/11) is a European Court of Human Rights case from the Second Section, with judgment delivered on 21 October 2014 and final on 21 January 2015. The applicant, Zsolt Béla Császy, a Hungarian national born in 1965 and living in Budapest, was represented by G. Győző. The Hungarian Government was represented by Z. Tallódi. The applicant alleged that the refusal by the authorities in charge of his detention to allow him to attend the funeral of a close relative amounted to an unjustified interference with his family life, in breach of Article 8 of the Convention. The application was lodged on 28 February 2011 and communicated to the Government on 6 September 2013.

The key facts concerned events on 31 August 2010. At 8:04 a.m., the applicant was apprehended at his home, and a house search was conducted until 11:12 a.m. During the search, he told officers that he intended to attend a funeral later that day. He claimed that his request was “unofficially” dismissed immediately, although the Government denied this. After the search, he was taken to the Central Investigating Prosecutor’s Office, about seven kilometres from the cemetery.

From 1:35 p.m., the applicant was interrogated as a suspect in an investigation into attempted misappropriation of funds. At the beginning of the interrogation, he formally requested permission to attend his stepmother’s funeral, which was scheduled for 2:15 p.m. the same day. The request was rejected on the ground that granting it would have contravened the purpose of his arrest. The interrogation ended at 2:29 p.m., after the funeral had already begun.

The applicant complained to the Attorney General. On 10 September 2010, that office rejected the complaint. It stated that the relevant domestic decree did not allow arrestees—as opposed to persons in pre-trial detention—to attend funerals. Consequently, the refusal of his request was considered lawful.

The alleged Article 8 violation centred on whether this refusal constituted an unjustified interference with the applicant’s family life. The applicant’s complaint was not that he was detained as such, but that the authorities categorically prevented him from attending a significant family event—his stepmother’s funeral—without any individualised assessment of his circumstances. The timing and logistics were central: he had informed officers during the house search, made a formal request at the start of interrogation at 1:35 p.m., and the funeral was only forty minutes later. The prosecutor’s office was approximately seven kilometres from the cemetery. The refusal was initially justified by reference to the purpose of the arrest and later defended by a blanket rule excluding arrestees from funeral attendance. The Government disputed that he had made an informal request during the house search.

The Attorney General’s response relied on the asserted lawfulness of the refusal under domestic rules rather than a case-specific balancing of security, flight risk, or investigative needs against the applicant’s family-life interests. The Court examined whether there was a legal basis, a legitimate aim, and whether the interference was necessary in a democratic society and proportionate. The key facts relevant to that assessment included the closeness of the relative, the fixed time of the funeral, the short distance, the applicant’s timely notification and formal request, the immediate rejection, and the blanket nature of the domestic rule. The Court found a violation of Article 8, concluding that the authorities had not demonstrated sufficient justification for the refusal or adequately balanced the applicant’s right to respect for family life against the needs of the criminal proceedings. The case illustrates that detention may restrict family life, but restrictions on attending a close relative’s funeral require individualised justification and cannot rest solely on a categorical rule.

In *S.A.S. v. France* (Application no. 43835/11), Grand Chamber, 1 July 2014, the applicant is an anonymous French national born in 1990. She is a devout Muslim who wears the burqa and niqab in accordance with her religious faith, culture, and personal convictions. The burqa is a full-body covering including mesh over the face; the niqab leaves only the eyes visible. She states that neither her husband nor any family member pressured her. She does not wear the full-face veil systematically: she may not wear it when visiting a doctor, meeting friends in public, or socialising. She wishes to wear it when she chooses, depending on spiritual feelings, particularly during Ramadan, to express faith and feel inner peace. She accepts removing it for security checks, at banks or airports, and agrees to show her face for necessary identity checks.

On 11 April 2011, Law no. 2010-1192 of 11 October 2010 entered into force throughout France. Section 1 prohibits anyone from wearing, in public places, clothing designed to conceal the face. Section 2 defines public places as the public highway and any places open to the public or assigned to public service; exceptions apply for clothing prescribed or authorised by law, health or occupational reasons, and sports, festivities, artistic or traditional events. Section 3 punishes breach with a fine of up to €150 or a citizenship course. Section 4 inserted Article 225-4-10 into the Criminal Code, punishing anyone who forces another to conceal their face by threat, duress, coercion, or abuse of authority on account of gender, with one year’s imprisonment and a €30,000 fine, increased for minors. The Constitutional Council upheld the law but reserved religious freedom in places of worship open to the public.

The applicant complained that the ban deprived her of the possibility of wearing the full-face veil in public. She alleged violations of Articles 3, 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the Convention, separately and in conjunction with Article 14. Central to her claim were that her dress was voluntary and based on religion, culture and personal identity; the ban directly restricted her manifestation of religion and private life; and it stigmatised Muslim women. She did not object to showing her face where identification was necessary.

The French legislature relied on the 2010 parliamentary report, which found the full-face veil a recent phenomenon affecting about 1,900 women. It described the practice as contrary to Republican values of liberty, equality, fraternity, dignity, gender equality, and “living together” (*vivre ensemble*), and as raising public-order and safety concerns. The CNCDH opposed a general absolute ban, and the Conseil d’État considered a ban on the full veil alone legally weak, preferring limited restrictions and penalties for duress. The National Assembly adopted a resolution, and the bill passed in 2010. The Government argued the ban protected public safety, the rights and freedoms of others, and minimum social interaction. The Court of Cassation later upheld the law under Article 9 as protecting public order and safety by requiring faces to be shown in public.

The Grand Chamber ultimately found no violation of Articles 8 and 9, no separate issues under Articles 10 and 11, and no violation of Article 14, accepting that France’s aim of preserving living together was legitimate, while stressing the wide margin of appreciation.

**Summary of the Case of Emin Huseynov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2)**

The case of *Emin Huseynov v. Azerbaijan (No. 2)* concerns the termination of the applicant’s Azerbaijani citizenship, which rendered him stateless. The applicant, Mr. Emin Huseynov, is a stateless person of Azerbaijani origin, an independent journalist, and the chairman of the Institute for Reporters’ Freedom and Safety (IRFS), a non-governmental organization focused on protecting journalists’ rights.

The events leading to the case began in April 2014, when the Prosecutor General’s Office of Azerbaijan opened a criminal case concerning alleged financial irregularities within several NGOs. As part of this investigation, the bank accounts of numerous NGOs and civil society activists, including the applicant and the IRFS, were frozen. Various human rights defenders were also arrested. In July 2014, the applicant learned that tax authorities had launched an investigation into the IRFS. On 5 August 2014, he was prevented from leaving Azerbaijan at Baku Airport. Fearing imminent arrest after being summoned for questioning, he went into hiding. On 18 August 2014, he clandestinely entered the Swiss embassy in Baku, where he found refuge. The following day, Azerbaijani authorities charged him with illegal entrepreneurship, large-scale tax evasion, and abuse of power, and a court ordered his arrest.

While at the Swiss embassy, on 10 February 2015 and again on 4 June 2015, the applicant submitted requests to the President of Azerbaijan to renounce his Azerbaijani citizenship. On 9 June 2015, the Swiss authorities paid USD 236,281 to Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Finance to cover the applicant’s tax debt. Consequently, the Nasimi District Court revoked the order for his arrest and quashed the decision declaring him a wanted person. On 12 June 2015, the applicant left Azerbaijan for Switzerland.

On 27 June 2015, the State Migration Service informed the applicant that his Azerbaijani citizenship had been terminated by a presidential order dated 10 June 2015. The applicant was never provided with a copy of this order, nor was its text made public. On 19 October 2015, he was granted asylum in Switzerland.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that he had been forced to renounce his citizenship, in violation of Articles 8 (right to respect for private and family life), 10 (freedom of expression), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights. He also alleged under Article 18 that his Convention rights had been restricted for purposes other than those prescribed in the Convention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant, a journalist and human rights defender, was facing criminal prosecution and was effectively trapped in the Swiss embassy when he applied to renounce his citizenship. His tax debt was paid by the Swiss authorities, after which his arrest order was lifted and he was allowed to leave. Shortly thereafter, his citizenship was terminated by a presidential order, leaving him stateless, as he possessed no other nationality. The applicant argued that this sequence of events demonstrated that his renunciation was not voluntary but was forced upon him under pressure from the Azerbaijani authorities. The respondent Government did not provide the Court with a copy of the presidential order terminating his citizenship or the earlier court decisions regarding his arrest. The case raises significant issues under international law, particularly the United Nations Conventions on Statelessness, which prohibit states from depriving individuals of nationality if it would render them stateless.

text:
Cēsnieks v. Latvia (no. 9278/06) concerned a Latvian national, Valters Cēsnieks, who alleged that police ill-treatment produced incriminating statements later used to convict him, violating Article 3, Article 13, and Article 6 § 1. The Court later struck out Articles 3 and 13 after a Government unilateral declaration acknowledging ill-treatment and an ineffective investigation, leaving the Article 6 § 1 complaint for judgment.

The key facts are as follows. On 21 March 2002 State Police telephoned the applicant and asked him to attend their station. Before any formal charges were laid, he was accused of murdering Ģ.Č. He alleged that police officers used physical force to obtain a confession and that he made a written confession as a result. He remained at the Riga police station until 23 March 2002, when he was transferred to a short-term detention facility. On 23 May 2002 an investigation was opened into the alleged police misconduct. On 25 June 2005 a prosecutor closed the complaint, relying on the Supreme Court’s judgment of 26 April 2005 dismissing the ill-treatment allegation. In the partial striking-out decision, the Government acknowledged that the applicant had been ill-treated in police custody and that there had been no effective investigation.

During the pre-trial investigation, the applicant was questioned as a witness on 21 March 2002 and gave an account concerning money transfers. He wrote a confession on 22 March 2002. He was questioned as a suspect later that day and confirmed the confession. In a further interview, he stated that he had wanted Ģ.Č. killed in order to obtain LVL 17,000, had asked O.O. to arrange the killing, and had discussed telephone calls. The transcripts recorded that he wished to give statements without a lawyer.

At trial, the Riga Regional Court on 11 October 2004 acquitted the applicant and O.O., while convicting V.Z. and J.G. of aggravated murder. Regarding the applicant, the Regional Court found his ill-treatment claim credible: he had been held at the police station from 21 to 23 March without explanation; expert reports confirmed bodily injuries in custody; and Article 3 had been violated. It found his 22 March statements contradictory and excluded them, also rejecting an expert report as lacking a study section. It found no other evidence that he had organised, assisted, or incited the murder.

The prosecution, victim, and convicted co-accused appealed. On 26 April 2005 the Supreme Court overturned the acquittal and convicted the applicant of aggravated murder, sentencing him to eleven years’ imprisonment. It held that the Regional Court had groundlessly rejected the confession; that there was no impartial evidence the statements resulted from ill-treatment; that the police case had been terminated; and that the expert report validly showed the confession was written in the applicant’s free style without signs of anxiety, fear, or physical ill-treatment. It admitted the 22 March statement and relied on it.

The defence appealed on points of law, arguing that the conviction violated Articles 3 and 6 because the statements relied on were obtained through ill-treatment, the injuries were unexplained, and no other evidence existed. On 26 August 2005 the Senate of the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal without a hearing, holding that cassation could not re-evaluate evidence and that the Convention complaint was formal and not based on the case materials. The application was lodged on 26 January 2006; the remaining Article 6 § 1 issue concerns the use at trial of evidence allegedly obtained in violation of Article 3.

In *Jaeger v. Estonia* (Application no. 1574/13, judgment 31 July 2014), the applicant, Egon Jaeger, an Estonian national serving a prison sentence in Tartu Prison, complained that a body search carried out on him was degrading and violated his privacy. The European Court of Human Rights communicated only the complaint concerning the body search; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The key facts concerned events of 10 October 2010. After taking a walk with other detainees, the applicant entered the accommodation block and was searched by two prison guards in the stairwell. According to the applicant, he was required to lower his trousers and underpants twice and lift his sexual organ. One guard also felt his underpants to check whether tobacco products had been hidden there. The applicant alleged that he was visible to other detainees because the stairwell doors had transparent windows; another door leading to the corridor also had a transparent window, and detainees or female prison officers could have seen him or entered the stairwell at any time. He named three detainees who had been behind him and sought 25,000 kroons (approximately EUR 1,600) in non-pecuniary damages.

The prison administration rejected his claim, relying on statements from one of the guards. According to the guard, the search was conducted privately: detainees entered the stairwell one by one, one guard searched jackets while the other searched detainees, and if a detainee was suspected, the door was closed to create a private space. Only the detainee and two guards were present. The applicant then complained to the Tartu Administrative Court, repeating his allegations and submitting written statements from two of the named detainees. By judgment of 21 September 2011, the Administrative Court rejected the claim, finding the guard’s account reliable and the applicant’s privacy respected.

On appeal, the applicant submitted that the stairwell door windows measured 1 metre by 30 centimetres and that some days after his complaint they had been covered with metal sheets. By judgment of 16 March 2012, the Tartu Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal. It found the search lasted at most a few minutes, that the applicant had not been certain whether other detainees were present, and that he could not explain exactly where the named detainees had seen the search. It concluded that his privacy had not been violated. It further held that, to manage a large number of detainees, the prison had to be able to carry out a body search when necessary in a location other than a designated private room. A suspicion that a detainee re-entering after a walk had hidden prohibited cigarettes in his underwear was sufficient.

By judgment of 17 October 2012, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, upholding the findings that his privacy and dignity had not been infringed. One judge dissented, reasoning that it was not decisive whether third persons had actually seen the search. A person being searched cannot simultaneously establish what others saw. If a body search occurs where it is not guaranteed that third persons will not see the person’s nudity, the person is bound to feel that his privacy has not been respected and that others might have seen the procedure. Such a situation damages dignity and can cause insecurity, anguish, and degradation.

Relevant domestic law included the Constitution’s protection of private life; the Imprisonment Act, allowing searches for prohibited items by same-sex officers; and ministerial regulations requiring full searches to be conducted where privacy is secured. Prison rules banned keeping tobacco except in designated smoking areas, with cigarettes distributed at the beginning of walks and unused cigarettes deposited afterwards. The Government also noted that the applicant had prior reprimands, including for unauthorised possession of a cigarette, and later received numerous disciplinary punishments mainly involving cigarettes.

In *Liebscher v. Austria* (Application no. 5434/17), the applicant, Christoph-Herwig Liebscher, an Austrian national born in 1957, complained about Austrian land-register requirements and their impact on his privacy and property rights.

In May 2013, he and his wife divorced by mutual consent. Their divorce settlement, concluded before the Döbling District Court under section 55a(2) of the Marriage Act, regulated the division of matrimonial assets, custody and residence of their two minor children, alimony, and included an overview of the applicant’s assets and income.

In December 2015, seeking to transfer his share of joint real estate to his former wife, the applicant applied to the same District Court, sitting as land-register court, for registration. Instead of filing the entire divorce settlement, he submitted a partial engrossment/excerpt issued by the family court on 1 December 2015. It was labelled an excerpt and reproduced only the chapter concerning real estate; it also stated that it contained all agreements pertaining to the property.

The land-register court rejected the application on 25 February 2016. It found that a partial engrossment was not the “original” required by section 87(1) of the Land Register Act (LRA). Under section 94(1) LRA, the court had to examine the application and enclosures comprehensively and could not assess from an excerpt whether the settlement contained conditions or legally relevant facts that might impede registration. An original could only be the complete version; an excerpt was not sufficient. The applicant appealed, arguing that the refusal infringed his right to dispose of his property. He also argued that requiring the full divorce settlement violated data-protection laws and Article 8 ECHR because highly personal and sensitive data—names and places of abode of his minor children and former spouse, alimony payments, and custody arrangements—would become publicly accessible in the land-register document archive. He claimed there was no legitimate aim or public interest outweighing his privacy.

The Vienna Regional Civil Court dismissed the appeal on 25 April 2016, agreeing that the excerpt did not meet section 87 LRA and that the land-register court itself had to examine the complete settlement. It found a legal basis for any Article 8 interference. The Supreme Court rejected his extraordinary appeal on 11 July 2016. It relied on its earlier decision no. 5 Ob 250/15y, holding that a partial engrossment is insufficient under section 87(1) LRA. The family court’s note could not bind the land-register court, which had to examine all documents under section 94(1). On data protection, the Supreme Court stated that examining the entire document was mandatory and served protection of registered property; the inclusion of documents in the document archive was not the subject of the decision, so no preliminary ruling or constitutional review was required.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged: (1) violation of Article 8, because the obligation to present the entire divorce settlement, rather than an excerpt

Case *Yavorovenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 25663/02 and 30 others) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 17 July 2014. It concerns 31 applications against Ukraine brought by Ukrainian and Russian nationals and by companies registered in Ukraine, Cyprus, and Romania. The central alleged violation is Ukraine’s prolonged failure to enforce final domestic court decisions that had awarded the applicants money or required certain actions to be taken in their favour.

The applications were lodged between 2002 and 2010. In each case, domestic courts issued decisions that became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. The appended table lists numerous final decisions from various Ukrainian courts—district, commercial, appellate, and arbitration—between 1997 and 2008. For example, applicant Yavorovenko relied on five decisions of Vinnytsya district courts from 2004 to 2007; Lindsell Enterprises Limited relied on Odesa commercial court decisions from 2000–2004; other applicants relied on decisions of courts in Crimea, Kyiv, Lviv, Donetsk, Sumy, Dnipropetrovsk, and elsewhere. These decisions concerned pecuniary amounts or specific actions. The common factual thread is that, despite being final and binding, they remained unenforced for extended periods. Some applicants also raised unrelated factual and legal matters, but the principal issue was non-enforcement.

Procedurally, two applications (nos. 23056/07 and 24245/10) had initially been struck out after the Government made unilateral declarations. Later, the applicants informed the Court that Ukraine had paid the compensation but had still failed to enforce the domestic judgments. The Government confirmed that the relevant judgments remained unenforced; in application no. 23056/07, enforcement proceedings were later terminated on 17 April 2013 because the decision had been fully enforced. The Court restored both applications to its list on 28 May 2013 and 17 December 2013 under Rule 43 § 5. In one application, an applicant died and the next of kin wished to maintain the case; in another, the applicant died and no one sought to continue it. There were also successor issues concerning a deceased father-in-law and a liquidated legal entity. The Cypriot and Romanian Governments declined to intervene.

The alleged violations therefore arose from the state’s failure to secure enforcement of final, binding domestic decisions. Such failure engaged the applicants’ right of access to a court and to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, because the awards or required actions became illusory. The applicants also complained, in substance, of the lack of an effective domestic remedy for the non-enforcement, contrary to Article 13. The case thus illustrates systemic problems with enforcement of domestic judgments in Ukraine, particularly where final decisions favourable to individuals or companies were not executed in due time.

**Case: Efgan Çetin and Others v. Türkiye (Application no. 14684/18)**

The case concerned five Turkish nationals—Efgan Çetin, Şermin Çetin, Ayşe Çetin, Hasanali Çetin, and Şerife Yıldız—who lived near planned geothermal energy plants in Aydın. The first applicant owned an olive grove; the remaining applicants lived in the vicinity. Their complaints under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention arose from their inability to obtain judicial review of an administrative decision that no environmental impact assessment (“EIA”) was required for a geothermal plant near their property and homes.

In 2012, the Aydın Governorship issued an EIA non-requirement decision dated 10 January 2012 for a private geothermal plant. A group of claimants, including the applicants, challenged that decision before the Aydın Administrative Court. During an on-site inspection on 27 March 2015 relating to that first plant, the parties noticed a second geothermal plant under construction nearby. The applicants and Government later accepted that this date could be treated as the point when the applicants learned of the second plant.

On 6 May 2015, some other claimants—not the applicants—submitted a freedom-of-information request asking whether the second plant had undergone an EIA procedure. On 18 May 2015, the Governor’s Office replied that on 24 July 2014 it had issued an EIA non-requirement decision for that second plant as well. On 19 June 2015, the applicants brought an administrative action challenging the 24 July 2014 decision. They argued that geothermal energy, although renewable, was not exempt from EIA requirements because such projects could cause chemical pollution, water-quality deterioration, and harm to health and the environment.

The Administrative Court ordered an on-site inspection and expert examination. The expert report of 18 December 2015 found that the project file complied procedurally but lacked scientific, technical, and legislative detail. Experts stated that energy generation could adversely affect flora, fauna, and air quality; gas emissions could pollute the environment and affect human and animal health; olive groves had already suffered irreversible damage; no alternative-site survey had been conducted; and construction had begun without required permits and before the EIA non-requirement decision. By the inspection date, construction was virtually complete.

Nevertheless, on 26 February 2016 the Aydın Administrative Court dismissed the claim as out of time. It held that the thirty-day fast-track period began on 27 March 2015, when the applicants became aware of the second plant during the earlier inspection. It noted there was no proof the EIA decision had been notified, but found that construction was nearly complete by March 2015 and that the applicants’ claim of learning only later was improbable. The Supreme Administrative Court upheld the dismissal on 17 November 2016, observing that the administration had not shown the EIA decision was publicly announced as required, but agreeing that the applicants knew by 27 March 2015 and that their June 2015 claim was late.

The applicants complained to the Turkish Constitutional Court that the domestic courts’ formalistic time-limit interpretation breached their right of access to a court. They also relied on the expert report to complain about risks to life, health, home, and their right to a healthy environment, and about not being informed of the plant decisions. On 1 November 2017, the Constitutional Court declared the applications inadmissible: the access-to-court complaint was manifestly ill-founded; the healthy-environment complaint was incompatible ratione materiae; and the private/family-life and home complaints were inadmissible for failure to exhaust remedies.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the key alleged violations were therefore the inability to access a court to challenge the EIA non-requirement decision and the failure to protect the applicants’ private lives, homes, and environmental surroundings. The central disputed fact was when the applicants should be deemed to have learned of the second EIA non-requirement decision, and whether the strict thirty-day deadline improperly barred their challenge.
