text:
**Case: Strassenmeyer v. Germany (Application no. 57818/18)**

The case concerned the applicant, Marco Straßenmeyer, a German national convicted of murder in 2016. The European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention, namely whether his trial was fair and whether he had been able to examine witnesses against him. The central alleged violation was that his conviction was based largely on pre-trial statements made by co-accused who later refused to testify at trial. In addition, before police questioning, the accused persons were not informed of their right to court-appointed counsel.

The underlying offence dated back to 1994, when G. was killed in the Czech Republic. His body was found but not initially identified. In 2012, N. contacted the German police and said that F., who had died in 1994, had confessed involvement in killing a co-worker in the Czech Republic. In 2014, K., a former co-worker, was arrested. Before questioning, he was informed of his rights to remain silent and to consult a lawyer, but, because police used an outdated form, he was not told of his right to court-appointed counsel under Article 136 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. K. implicated the applicant as the killer.

The applicant was arrested the following day and received the same defective rights warning. He denied knowing the victim or going to the Czech Republic. Other accused persons, S. and V., were later questioned. V. gave a detailed statement describing the plan to drug G., drive him to the Czech Republic, and beat him. According to V., the applicant struck G. with a truncheon, later threw a rock at his head, and the body was burned. V. admitted assisting in moving the body. All accused were informed of their rights in the same manner, without the court-appointed counsel warning. After being brought before the investigating judge, they were assigned lawyers and made no further statements.

At trial before the Erfurt Regional Court, the applicant made only a statement about drug abuse; the co-accused exercised their right to remain silent. The Regional Court therefore heard police officers about the pre-trial interviews, over defence objections. It also heard witnesses N., L. and B., Czech police officers, and forensic experts. Experts contradicted parts of V.’s account, including his claim that G. had moved after being set on fire, and noted discrepancies about the distance from the cars. The defence requested a psychological expert opinion on V.’s veracity, but this was refused.

In June 2016, the Regional Court convicted the applicant and K. of murder and deprivation of liberty resulting in death; V. was convicted of murder, and S. was acquitted. The applicant received life imprisonment. The court relied heavily on V.’s pre-trial statement, finding it corroborated by K.’s statements and witness testimony. It admitted the statements despite the failure to inform the accused of their right to court-appointed counsel, citing the seriousness of the offence, the State’s strong prosecution interest, and the unintentional nature of the error. The court also noted that the accused had remained silent at trial and that no recordings of the police interviews existed.

The applicant appealed, arguing that his conviction rested primarily on untested pre-trial statements by co-accused whom he could not examine, and that the rights warning defect rendered the statements inadmissible. The Federal Court of Justice dismissed the appeal in 2018, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint. The alleged violations therefore arose from the use of untested co-accused statements as decisive evidence and the failure to inform the accused of the right to court-appointed counsel before police questioning.

In *Lobchuk and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 36871/20 and six others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 9 February 2023. Seven applicants complained under Article 34 ECHR about inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. Applicant Lobchuk also raised other Convention complaints. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications.

The appended table sets out the key facts relevant to the alleged violations. Gennadiy Lobchuk (b. 1975) was held at Dnipro Penitentiary Facility No. 89 from 23 June 2014 to 28 December 2021—7 years, 6 months and 6 days—with only 1–2 m² per inmate. He alleged poor food quality due to his gallstone disease, lack of fresh air, insufficient natural light, inadequate hygienic facilities, restricted showers, insufficient outdoor exercise, no toilet privacy, inadequate temperature, insufficient electric light, and overcrowding.

Oleksandr Kanivets (b. 1988) was held at Dnipro Penitentiary Facility No. 4 from 24 June 2019 and remained there at filing—over 3 years, 5 months and 20 days—with 2.5–4 m² per inmate. He complained of lack of fresh air, insufficient electric light, poor bedding and linen, lack of toiletries, insufficient food, restricted potable water and showers, poor food quality, and overcrowding.

Oleksandr Millyer (b. 1978) was in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 17 October 2019 to 28 October 2021 (2 years and 12 days), with 1.91 m² per inmate. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient natural light, and poor or insufficient food.

Yevgeniy Svyntsov (b. 1983) was in the same Cherkasy facility from 25 January 2019 to 30 August 2021 (2 years, 7 months and 6 days), with under 3.3 m² per inmate. He complained of overcrowding, lack of fresh air, and insufficient or poor food.

Mark Chaus (b. 1974) was held at Poltava Penitentiary Facility from 8 August 2019 to 12 February 2021 (1 year, 6 months and 5 days), with 2.42 m² per inmate. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, no toilet privacy, lack of toiletries, and restricted showers.

Maksym Glyebov (b. 1981) was in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 15 October 2018 to 17 March 2021 (2 years, 5 months and 3 days), with 2.9–7.9 m² per inmate. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient electric and natural light, insufficient outdoor exercise, poor bedding, no toilet privacy, lack of toiletries, insufficient or poor food, a mouldy or dirty cell, restricted potable water, and restricted showers.

Vyacheslav Podvarchan (b. 1972) was held at Romny Detention Facility No. 56 from 17 November 2004 to 3 February 2021—16 years, 2 months and 18 days—with 3.9 m² per inmate. He raised similar complaints: overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient electric and natural light, insufficient outdoor exercise, poor bedding, no toilet privacy, lack of toiletries, insufficient or poor food, a mouldy or dirty cell, restricted potable water, and restricted showers.

The applications were introduced between 20 July 2020 and 2 August 2021. The common allegations concern prolonged detention in overcrowded or materially inadequate facilities, with insufficient space, ventilation, lighting, hygiene, food, water, and exercise, and no effective remedy in domestic law. The excerpt records the procedure and facts but not the Court’s final findings.

In *N.A. v. Norway*, the applicant, a Norwegian national, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that, despite being acquitted of criminal charges, a Norwegian court ordered her to pay compensation to the victims, thereby undermining her presumption of innocence. She also alleged that the compensation decision was not sufficiently reasoned, in breach of her fair-hearing rights.

In September 2009 N.A. and her former husband, U.A., were indicted in Norway. They were charged with causing, or aiding and abetting, aggravated bodily harm to their daughter A, including skull fractures, brain bleeding, retinal bleeding, an elbow dislocation, and permanent brain injury, and with seriously and repeatedly ill-treating their son B, including an arm fracture and other injuries. The alleged acts occurred between August 2005 and January 2008, while the children were in the parents’ care.

In January 2010 the Oslo City Court convicted N.A. and U.A. It found that the children had suffered gross ill-treatment by adults while in the family’s small flat. Although evidence from the defendants and witnesses was contradictory and it could not identify exactly who inflicted each act, the City Court found that each parent had aided and abetted the violence by failing to intervene or prevent it. N.A. received a prison sentence and was ordered to pay compensation.

On appeal, the Borgarting High Court held a jury trial in August–September 2010. The jury answered all questions negatively, and the professional judges accepted the acquittal. In the same judgment, however, the professional judges—sitting without the jury—examined the children’s civil claims for non-pecuniary damages under the Damage Compensation Act. They noted that acquittal did not prevent compensation because the civil evidentiary standard was less stringent than the criminal standard, though Article 6 § 2 set limits. Applying a “clearly probable” standard, the High Court found it clearly probable that N.A. and U.A. had ill-treated the children or aided and abetted such ill-treatment over a long period, and had inflicted or aided in inflicting serious injuries. It relied on medical evidence that the injuries were not accidental, signs of strong violence, B’s post-traumatic stress syndrome, and neighbours’ accounts of children’s screams. It awarded NOK 300,000 to A and NOK 100,000 to B. The High Court stated that this civil decision, based on a lower evidentiary threshold, did not contradict the acquittal.

N.A. appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court’s evidence assessment and reasoning violated Article 6 § 2 and that the compensation award was insufficiently reasoned under Article 6 § 1. In November 2010 the Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave to appeal. N.A. then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 3 May 2011.

The key alleged violation was that, despite her formal acquittal, the national court’s compensation judgment effectively found her responsible for the same criminal acts, undermining the presumption of innocence. She also alleged a fair-hearing violation because the judgment allegedly failed to explain why the civil findings did not conflict with the acquittal. The case therefore raised the tension between a criminal acquittal and civil liability based on a lower standard of proof.

In *Aleksandr Vladimirovich Smirnov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 69250/11, judgment 13 March 2014), the applicant, a Russian national, alleged that his detention conditions in the Slavyanoserbsk Colony were incompatible with human dignity and that his right to mount a defence in criminal proceedings had been breached.

The criminal proceedings began on 5 December 2002, when Ukrainian police stopped Smirnov at an Odessa bus station for lacking identity documents and detained him. He alleged that he was held until 23 December 2002 in a facility for vagrants and in Kakhovka, Kherson and Mykolayiv police detention facilities, where he was questioned off the record about alleged involvement with a terrorist group plotting to restore a communist state. He claimed he was beaten and tortured during these sessions. Official medical records showed that examinations on 9 and 14 December 2002 found no bodily injuries and that he made no complaints of ill-treatment.

On 14–18 December 2002, Kakhovka police questioned Smirnov as a witness. He described being a member of a Russian-based NGO, “Z.”, and distributing the newspaper *Soviet rabochikh deputatov* and other communist materials in Ukraine. On 23 December 2002 he gave a handwritten statement to the Security Service of Ukraine in Mykolayiv confessing that he had distributed materials and that he and two others had blown up a rubbish bin near the SSU headquarters in Kyiv in October 2002. He was arrested that day on suspicion of a terrorist offence and remanded in custody. Although notified of his right to legal assistance and initially requesting a lawyer, on 24 December 2002 he signed a consent to be questioned without a lawyer and repeated his earlier statements. A lawyer engaged by his mother joined the proceedings on 26 December 2002. On 29 December, with counsel present, he admitted communist affiliation and political activity but denied the bombing and terrorist activity.

In July 2003, defence counsel requested further investigation, alleging that Smirnov had been unlawfully detained and tortured between 5 and 23 December 2002 to extract self-incriminating statements, in breach of his defence rights. The investigator refused, stating that Smirnov had been arrested only on 23 December, that no investigative actions had involved him before then, and that no ill-treatment complaints had been recorded.

At trial, Smirnov pleaded not guilty, admitted acquaintance with co-defendants and newspaper distribution, but denied involvement in the rubbish-bin explosion and any criminal activity. He alleged ill-treatment and said medical staff refused to record his injuries; he had not complained earlier because he feared reprisals. Prosecutors later refused to institute criminal proceedings over the ill-treatment allegations. In July 2004 he was convicted of affiliation with a criminal association, distribution of material promoting violent revolt, and participation in a terrorist act. The court relied partly on his 23 and 24 December 2002 statements, finding no indication they had been extracted by ill-treatment or procedural breach. He was sentenced to eight years’ imprisonment. In July 2005 the Supreme Court upheld the conviction for distribution and terrorism but dropped the criminal-association charge.

Regarding detention, from November 2005 to September 2007 Smirnov was held in the Slavyanoserbsk Colony. He alleged that a cell of about thirty square metres held ten to sixteen inmates, with confinement all day except one hour’s exercise; heavy smoking without ventilation; refusal of transfer or a fan; poor heating, opaque windows, poor light, and inadequate food. He also alleged lack of medical care, including an unanswered January 2006 request for examination and delayed dental treatment until May 2007. The Government disputed these claims, stating the cell measured thirty-two square metres for eight inmates and that heating, lighting, ventilation, food and medical checks were adequate.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman detention conditions, ill-treatment and inadequate medical care) and Article 6 (right to a fair trial and defence, including use of self-incriminating statements and lack of effective legal assistance).

**Summary of *Mamasakhlisi and Others v. Georgia and Russia* (Applications nos. 29999/04 and 41424/04)**

This case before the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) concerns applications lodged by Georgian nationals against Georgia and Russia, stemming from events in the disputed territory of Abkhazia. The applications allege multiple violations of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The first and third applicants, Mr. Levan Mamasakhlisi and Mr. Grigol Nanava, were arrested and tried by the de facto Abkhaz authorities. The second applicant, Ms. Dinara Mamasakhlisi, was the first applicant’s grandmother, complaining of a breach of family life.

**Key Facts:**

On 7 August 2001, an explosive device accidentally detonated in the first applicant's hands in Pitsunda, Abkhazia, causing severe injuries, including the loss of his right hand. He was subsequently detained by the de facto Abkhaz security forces. He alleges that during his detention and questioning, he was subjected to ill-treatment, including beatings, mock executions, and psychological torture, to coerce a confession. He was held incommunicado in a small, dark, unheated cell, denied adequate food and water, and provided with no medical care for his festering wounds for months. Despite his condition, he was convicted of high treason and sabotage by the Abkhaz Military Court on 15 February 2002, after a two-hour trial. The court-appointed lawyer remained silent, and he was ultimately sentenced to twelve years' imprisonment. He was released on humanitarian grounds on 14 February 2007. Subsequent medical examinations diagnosed him with post-traumatic stress disorder and major depression, consistent with his account of torture.

Similarly, the third applicant, Mr. Nanava, was arrested in June 2003 for illegally crossing the border into Abkhazia. He was accused of terrorism, allegedly beaten, and threatened with death to extract a confession. He was convicted and sentenced to six years’ imprisonment in September 2003, again without access to a lawyer of his choosing. He was denied medical care despite his advanced age and ill health. He was released in May 2005.

The applications, lodged in 2004, raised complaints under Articles 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman/degrading treatment), 5 (right to liberty and security), 6 (right to a fair trial), 8 (right to respect for family life), and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention, as well as Article 2 of Protocol No. 7 (right of appeal in criminal matters).

The applicants primarily blamed Russia for its role as the de facto controlling power in Abkhazia and Georgia for its failure to protect its citizens and investigate the crimes. A significant development was the Russian Federation's cessation of Council of Europe membership in March 2022, which led the Court to appoint an *ad hoc* judge to continue proceedings against it.

In *Halet v. Luxembourg* (Application no. 21884/18), the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights delivered judgment on 14 February 2023. The applicant, Raphaël Halet, a French national, was a former employee of PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) in Luxembourg. PwC provided auditing, tax advice and consultancy services, including obtaining Advance Tax Agreements (ATAs or “tax rulings”) from the Luxembourg tax authorities for multinational clients.

Between 2012 and 2014, hundreds of ATAs and tax returns prepared by PwC were leaked to the media, revealing highly advantageous tax agreements between PwC and the Luxembourg tax authorities. A former PwC auditor, A.D., had copied about 45,000 pages of confidential documents in 2010 and provided them to journalist E.P.; these were used in a first *Cash Investigation* broadcast in May 2012.

After that broadcast, Halet contacted E.P. in May 2012 and offered further documents. Between October and December 2012, he transferred sixteen confidential documents—fourteen tax returns and two covering/notification letters—by creating a Gmail account and placing the documents in its “Drafts” folder so that E.P. could retrieve them. Some documents were used in a second *Cash Investigation* programme in June 2013, and in November 2014 the documents were published online by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists as part of “LuxLeaks.” PwC’s internal investigation identified Halet, and he was dismissed in December 2014. PwC then filed a criminal complaint.

In 2016, the Luxembourg District Court convicted Halet of theft from his employer, fraudulent access to a data-processing system, breach of commercial secrecy, breach of professional secrecy, and laundering/possession. He received a nine-month suspended prison sentence and a €1,000 fine. On appeal in 2017, the Court of Appeal acquitted him of some charges, including breach of commercial secrecy, but upheld convictions for theft, fraudulent retention/access to a data system, breach of professional secrecy, and laundering of the proceeds of theft. It rejected his defence that he was a protected whistle-blower under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The Court of Appeal accepted that the disclosed information concerned a matter of public interest—tax optimisation and ATAs—and that the documents were authentic. It also accepted that media disclosure may have been the only realistic alternative. However, it found that the sixteen documents were of limited relevance: they were not essential or fundamentally new, the ATA practice had already been exposed through A.D.’s earlier leak, and Halet knew of the prior broadcast. It also found that his selection of documents was influenced by the fame of the companies involved, and that the disclosure caused reputational harm to PwC and breached professional secrecy. Balancing the interests, it concluded that the harm to PwC outweighed the public interest, so Halet could not benefit from full whistle-blower protection. He was fined €1,000, with no prison sentence due to mitigating circumstances. In January 2018, the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal.

Halet then applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that his criminal conviction following disclosure of the sixteen documents subject to professional secrecy amounted to a disproportionate interference with his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The Grand Chamber examined the whistle-blower criteria, including public interest, good faith, authenticity, subsidiarity, harm and proportionality. It ultimately found that Luxembourg had violated Article 10, holding that the criminal conviction and fine were not necessary in a democratic society and had a chilling effect on whistle-blowing.

text:
The case of **Filatova and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 12424/06 and 15 others) was a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 31 July 2014 by a Fifth Section Committee. It originated in 16 applications lodged against Ukraine by Ukrainian nationals and Ukraine-based companies under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants alleged principally that final domestic court decisions in their favour had not been enforced in due time, in breach of Article 6 §1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The facts are set out in an appended table. In each application, domestic courts had delivered decisions entitling the applicants either to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable. However, the applicants were unable to obtain enforcement in due time. That failure of enforcement formed the central factual basis of the alleged violations. The domestic decisions covered a wide period: some were issued as early as 11 August 1997 (Lyudmila Filatova, Berdyansk Court) and 22 June 1998 (Nataliya Pogurnets, Suvorivskyy District Court of Odessa), while others were issued between 2004 and 2009. The applications themselves were introduced between 10 March 2006 and 9 October 2010. Thus, by the time the case reached Strasbourg, some applicants had waited many years for enforcement of final judgments.

The applicants included individuals such as Filatova, Pryadko, Plokhotnyuk, Nikonenko, Pogurnets, Molchanov, Alfyorov, Sokur, Dymytriyenko, Lutsenko (two applicants), Yakunenkov and Khlebnikov, as well as corporate entities SSV PP, SOLO TOV, VFK INTELSOYUZ TOV and DONBASNAFTOPRODUKT DP. The domestic decisions had been given by various courts, including district courts in Berdyansk, Dobropillya, Bila Tserkva, Kyiv, Odessa, Konotop, Vinnytsya and Mariupol, and commercial courts in Sevastopol, Donetsk, Lugansk, Dnipropetrovsk and Kirovograd. Some applicants had more than one relevant domestic decision; for example, Filatova relied on decisions of 1997 and 2001, Khlebnikov on decisions of 2004 and 2005, and the company SOLO TOV on five commercial court decisions from 2006 to 2008.

Two applicants died during the proceedings before the Court: Lyudmila Filatova (application no. 12424/06) and Valentin Molchanov (application no. 23509/08). Their next-of-kin expressed the wish to pursue the applications. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government on various dates. In applications no. 7436/08 and no. 40893/09, the Government submitted unilateral declarations, on 15 December 2011 and 15 September 2011 respectively, aimed at resolving the non-enforcement issues raised in seventeen applications. The Government asked the Court to strike those applications out of the list under Article 37 §1(c) of the Convention. The Court examined the declarations but found that they did not provide a sufficient basis for concluding that respect for human rights did not require continued examination of the applications.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore that the applicants held final and enforceable domestic decisions granting them pecuniary or other entitlements, but the Ukrainian authorities failed to enforce those decisions for lengthy periods. The applicants complained that this non-enforcement violated their right to a fair trial and their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions. Some applicants also raised submissions on factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issue, but the common and principal complaint concerned the prolonged failure to execute final domestic judgments.

**Summary of *Jestcov v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 33567/15)**

The case of *Jestcov v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* concerns a complaint under Article 2 (Right to Life) of the European Convention on Human Rights regarding the failure of Moldovan and Russian authorities to enforce a custodial sentence for murder, resulting in the alleged impunity of the perpetrator. The applicant, Mr. Petru Jestcov, a Moldovan national, lodged the application in 2015.

The facts are as follows: On 9 November 2010, the applicant’s wife was robbed and murdered in Chișinău, Moldova. An investigation led to the arrest

**Y v. France (Application no. 76888/17), European Court of Human Rights, 31 January 2023**

The applicant, a French national born in 1951, is an intersex individual whose birth certificate records him as “male.” Medically, his intersex status was established shortly after birth: he has ambiguous external genitalia, no gonads, neither testicles nor ovaries, and his body has never produced sex hormones. He did not develop male or female secondary sex characteristics or go through puberty. Although he has a male XY karyotype, medical certificates describe “intersex formation” and “clear intersexuality” of the external genitalia. At age 21 he was perceived socially as female; at around 40 he was prescribed testosterone as part of a male administrative assignment, which caused a beard and voice change. He describes this forced alteration as a violation of bodily integrity and a trauma.

The applicant also says he is psychologically and socially intersex. His psychotherapist stated that he had long been forced to “pretend to be a man” and lacked a legal identity reflecting who he is. He is married and has an adopted child.

In January 2015, the applicant asked the Tours tribunal de grande instance to replace the “male” marker on his birth certificate with “neutral” or, failing that, “intersex.” In August 2015, the tribunal granted his request. It found that his sex could not be defined from a genital, hormonal, or psychological standpoint; that the male marker was fictitious; and that replacing it with “neutral” would respect his private life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It considered this a rectification of incorrect civil status, not recognition of a third sex.

In March 2016, the Orléans Court of Appeal reversed. It accepted that the applicant was sexually ambiguous and that a fair balance under Article 8 might permit exceptions to civil-status rules. However, it found that his physical appearance and social behaviour were male, noting his marriage and adoption of a child. It also held that French law did not allow any permanent sex marker other than “male” or “female.” Granting the request would effectively recognise another sex category, a matter for the legislature, not the courts.

In May 2017, the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It held that French law does not permit a sex marker other than male or female on civil-status documents. While gender identity falls within Article 8, the binary nature of sex markers pursued a legitimate aim and was necessary for the social and legal system. Recognising a “neutral” sex would have far-reaching consequences and require multiple legislative changes. The Court of Cassation concluded that the interference with the applicant’s private life was not disproportionate.

The applicant complained before the European Court of Human Rights that the refusal to allow “neutral” or “intersex” on his birth certificate violated his right to respect for private life under Article 8. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: his medically documented intersex status and ambiguous sex characteristics; his lifelong assigned male status despite this; his intersex gender identity and social recognition; the domestic courts’ refusal based on the French binary civil-status system; and the claimed impact on his identity, bodily integrity, and private life.

**X and Others v. Ireland** (Applications nos. 23851/20 and 24360/20) concerns two challenges to Ireland’s child benefit rules. The applicants alleged that the domestic requirement that a parent be “habitually resident”—which, under section 246(5) of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, excludes anyone without a right to reside in Ireland—discriminates against claimants who are lawfully present in the State but have not yet been granted, or recognised as having, a right to reside. They relied on Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, read with Article 14.

In the first application, X, a Nigerian national, arrived in Ireland in November 2013 and applied for asylum. Her daughter E was born in December 2014 and is an Irish citizen through her father. X and E lived in Ireland’s “direct provision” system for asylum seekers. In September 2015, X applied for residence as the mother of an Irish citizen child. In October 2015, while that application was pending, she applied for child benefit for E. The application was refused in November 2015 because she did not satisfy the habitual residence condition, as she had no right to reside. X was granted a right to reside in January 2016 and thereafter received child benefit. Her domestic claim was limited to the period from E’s birth to the grant of residence, just over twelve months. She argued that E’s Irish citizenship, under the Zambrano case-law of the CJEU, entitled her to benefit from E’s birth.

In the second application, Y, an Afghan national, arrived in Ireland in May 2008 with her husband and first child and applied for asylum, living in direct provision. Her son M was born in April 2013. The family initially used false Pakistani identity documents; their asylum claim was rejected and removal orders were issued in 2012. After establishing their true nationality, they applied again. M was granted asylum in December 2014, communicated in January 2015. The other family members applied for family reunification. While that was pending, Y applied in February 2015 for child benefit for her four children. It was refused in April 2015 because she did not meet the habitual residence condition. Family reunification was granted in September 2015, and child benefit was then paid from that date. Her claim was limited to the eight-month period between M’s asylum grant and the family reunification decision. Y argued that recognition of refugee status declared an already existing status, so entitlement should begin when M was granted asylum, relying on Article 28 of the EU Qualification Directive.

The High Court rejected both claims, holding that child benefit vested in the “qualified person” parent rather than the child, and that the habitual residence rule was generally applied and justified. The Court of Appeal allowed X and E’s appeal, finding that excluding a resident Irish citizen child from a universal child benefit because of her mother’s immigration status breached constitutional equality, but rejected Y and M’s claim. The Supreme Court reversed, holding that child benefit is payable to the qualified person, not the child; the habitual residence requirement applied neutrally to claimants; any indirect effect on the children was justified by the State’s interest in regulating migration and residence; and no discrimination or breach of Article 28 of the Qualification Directive arose. The ECtHR case accordingly concerns whether that regime, as applied to these applicants, violated Article 14 read with Article 8 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Grima and Others v. Malta* (Application no. 18057/20), eight Maltese nationals from the Grima and Parnis England families complained about the effects of Maltese rent-control legislation on their co-owned property at No. 35 Dingli Street, Sliema.

The property was occupied by a tenant under a lease governed by Act XXIII of 1979, which amended Chapter 158 of the Laws of Malta (the Ordinance). Article 12(7) of the Ordinance allowed the tenant to maintain occupation. The rent paid was approximately EUR 466 per year in March 1979, increasing to EUR 685 in 1994, EUR 741 in 2009, EUR 803 in 2013, and EUR 819 in 2016. A court-appointed expert assessed the annual market rental value as EUR 1,398 in 1977, EUR 1,677 in 1982, EUR 2,516 in 1987, EUR 3,075 in 1992, EUR 4,193 in 1997, EUR 5,590 in 2002, EUR 6,150 in 2007, EUR 6,709 in 2012, and EUR 7,268 in 2017. The applicants therefore alleged that the controlled rent was far below market levels.

As to ownership, the Grima family’s predecessor in title acquired a half undivided share in 1982, aware that the property had been occupied under a temporary emphyteusis since 1960 for seventeen years, renewable once. That share belonged to him and applicant Georgina Grima. His share was inherited *ab intestato* in 2015 by applicants Doreen, Georgina, and Joseph Grima in different shares. Today Georgina Grima owns three-eighths of the undivided share of the entire property, while the siblings jointly own one-eighth. The bare ownership of the other half undivided share was vested in the Parnis England siblings (Nicholas, Robin, Stephen, and Johanna Petreski) as of 2004, as universal heirs of their father. Their mother, Margaret Parnis England, held the usufruct over the property after her husband’s death in 2004.

In 2019, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings, complaining of a breach of their property rights and seeking compensation for the period from 1977 to 2017. By judgment of 21 October 2019, the Civil Court (First Hall) in its constitutional competence found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention and awarded EUR 20,000 in compensation. However, contrary to domestic case law (*Ian Peter Ellis v. Maggur Cassar Reynaud*, Constitutional Court, 27 January 2017), the court held that the applicants’ ancestors had never complained about the situation and that the applicants should not financially benefit from their predecessors’ passivity. It therefore limited compensation to the period after the applicants inherited the property: 2015 for the Grima family and 2004 for the Parnis England family.

The applicants then applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 22 April 2020. They complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and in conjunction with Article 13 of the Convention that they remained victims of the violation found domestically because the compensation awarded was too low and because the tenants had not been evicted. The Court gave notice of the complaints concerning the effects of Act XXIII of 1979 to the Maltese Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

**Mesić v. Croatia (No. 2)** (Application no. 45066/17, judgment 30 May 2023) concerned former Croatian President Stjepan Mesić’s complaint that Croatia violated Article 8 of the Convention by dismissing his civil defamation action over an online article linking him to bribery in the Patria armoured-vehicle procurement.

In 2013 Finnish authorities indicted employees of the Finnish company Patria for aggravated bribery concerning the sale of AMV armoured vehicles to Croatia in 2007. A Finnish Prosecutor General press release stated that bribes were suspected of being promised or given in exchange for actions of the President of Croatia and a Croatian State-owned company director. On 16 February 2015, the Kanta-Häme District Court convicted two Patria employees of promising and giving a bribe to the Croatian company director. However, as regards Mesić, the court found that the mere fact he was considered an important lobbying target did not prove he was promised or given a bribe. It stated that the bribe allegedly promised to Mesić was not sufficiently evidenced. The charges against a third accused were dismissed. Mesić was never charged in Finland.

On 17 February 2015, the Croatian Internet news portal Dnevno.hr published an article about the Patria case. It alleged that Mesić had received a €630,000 bribe from persons who had just been convicted of giving bribes; that two Patria managers directly charged with giving bribes to Mesić and the Croatian company director had been sentenced to one year and eight months’ imprisonment; and that the joint investigation had “undoubtedly established” that Mesić and the director had participated in criminal activities. The article relied on the Finnish indictment and an alleged telephone interview with the Finnish Prosecutor General, and suggested that Croatian authorities, especially USKOK, should investigate Mesić.

Mesić requested a correction, arguing the statements were false because the Finnish court had not found that anyone gave or promised him a bribe. The portal refused. He then sued Dnevno.hr for defamation, seeking HRK 40,000 (about €5,290) in non-pecuniary damages. He argued he had no role in the procurement, that no one contacted him before publication, and that the article portrayed him as a corrupt criminal.

The Zagreb Municipal Civil Court dismissed his claim on 31 December 2015. It held that the journalist had acted in good faith on sufficiently verified information, relying on the Finnish press release and indictment. It considered the Finnish judgment non-decisive and did not examine the truth of the bribe allegations, partly because Mesić had not been charged in Finland. The Zagreb County Court upheld that judgment on 19 April 2016, finding the article objective and not violating the presumption of innocence. On 8 December 2016, the Constitutional Court dismissed Mesić’s constitutional complaint, finding the decisions sufficiently reasoned and no breach of the presumption of innocence.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Mesić complained only under Article 8 that the domestic courts had failed to protect his reputation and private life. The key issue was whether Croatia had adequately balanced his right to reputation against the media’s freedom of expression. The Court found that the domestic courts had failed to properly protect Mesić’s Article 8 rights. In particular, they treated the Finnish indictment and press release as sufficient verification despite the Finnish court’s finding that no bribe to Mesić had been proven, refused to assess the truth of the serious allegations, and dismissed relevant evidence that USKOK had not investigated him. The Court therefore found a violation of Article 8.

**Case: Camara v. Belgium (Application no. 49255/22), Judgment of 18 July 2023**

The case concerns Mr Abdoulaye Camara, a Guinean national who applied for international protection in Belgium. He arrived on 12 July 2022 and filed his asylum application on 15 July 2022. When he went to Fedasil, the agency responsible for reception, he was told that the reception network had reached saturation point and that no accommodation could be provided. He had no private network or means of support in Belgium.

From 15 July to 4 November 2022—112 days—the applicant lived on the street. He slept at Brussels Nord and Midi railway stations, in parks, and on makeshift mattresses or cardboard. His bag, containing Guinean documents relevant to his asylum claim, was stolen. He could shower about once a week through the Hub Humanitaire, had only sporadic access to toilets, and relied on associations for food, which was not provided daily; he sometimes ate from dustbins and remained hungry. In October, he suffered from rain and cold as temperatures often fell below 10°C at night.

On 19 July 2022, his lawyer wrote to Fedasil, arguing that the refusal to accommodate him breached the Reception Act of 12 January 2007 and Belgium’s international obligations. On 20 July, the applicant made an ex parte urgent application to the Brussels French-Language Employment Tribunal. On 22 July, the Tribunal ordered Fedasil to secure accommodation—in a reception centre, hotel, or other appropriate establishment—and to provide material support under the Reception Act. It imposed a €1,000 fine for each night he was left outside the reception network, declared the decision immediately enforceable, and granted legal aid for service and enforcement.

Fedasil was notified on 29 July 2022 but did not lodge a third-party appeal. The decision became final on 29 August 2022. It was not enforced. On 12 October, the applicant served an order to comply and a final notice to pay. On 20 October, he requested an interim measure from the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39. The Court granted the measure on 31 October 2022, requiring Belgium to provide accommodation and support. On 3 November, Fedasil invited him to the initial processing centre, and on 4 November he was assigned to the Evere Red Cross centre, later transferred to the Koekelberg Samusocial centre. His asylum application remained pending.

Before the Court, the applicant alleged violations of Article 3 (inhuman and degrading treatment due to months of homelessness and destitution despite a legal entitlement), Article 6 § 1 (non-enforcement of the Employment Tribunal’s final decision), and Article 8 read with Article 13 (interference with private life and lack of an effective remedy). The Court communicated those complaints.

The broader context was systemic: Belgium’s reception network had been saturated since September 2021. Fedasil prioritised vulnerable groups and later maintained waiting lists, often accommodating applicants only after they obtained a domestic court order or an ECtHR interim measure. Thousands of similar ex parte applications succeeded, and by 1 March 2023 Fedasil had been ordered more than 7,000 times to accommodate applicants. The Government cited migratory pressure, floods, staffing shortages, local authority restrictions, and processing delays, but domestic courts found Fedasil’s failure to comply with the Reception Act manifest and unjustified.

The key issue is that, despite a final enforceable domestic order recognising the applicant’s right to material support, he remained homeless and without basic assistance for months, requiring ECtHR interim relief before compliance.

**Summary of *Georgiou v. Greece* (Application no. 57378/18)**

The case of *Georgiou v. Greece* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) by Mr. Andreas Georgiou, a Greek national and former president of the Hellenic Statistical Authority (ELSTAT). The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair trial) of the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically arising from the Greek Court of Cassation's failure to provide reasoning for its tacit refusal to seek a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) during criminal proceedings against him.

The applicant served as ELSTAT president from August 2010 to August 2015. On 10 November 2010, he transmitted revised data on Greece's 2009 fiscal deficit to Eurostat without first presenting it for approval to ELSTAT's seven-member administrative board. He claimed this action complied with the principle of professional independence under the European Statistics Code of Practice, particularly Principle 1.4, which grants the head of a national statistical authority "sole responsibility" for decisions on statistical releases.

Criminal proceedings were subsequently initiated against the applicant for breach of duty. On 6 December 2016, the Athens Criminal Court acquitted him of all three charges: (i) breach of the duty of full and exclusive employment with ELSTAT due to his concurrent position at the International Monetary Fund; (ii) breach of the duty to convene ELSTAT's board from November 2010 to September 2011; and (iii) breach of duty for releasing the 2009 fiscal deficit data without communicating it to or obtaining consent from ELSTAT's administrative board.

The prosecutor appealed. On 1 August 2017, the Athens Court of Appeal overturned the acquittal in part, finding the applicant guilty of the third charge—breach of duty—and sentenced him to two years' imprisonment, suspended. The appellate court determined that he had transmitted the data to Eurostat without ELSTAT's consent, in violation of Article 10 § 2 A of Law no. 3832/2010. It found he acted intentionally to gain an illegal moral benefit by strengthening his power as president and effectively usurping the board's powers.

The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. In a memorandum dated 21 March 2018, he explicitly requested that the Court of Cassation seek a preliminary ruling from the CJEU under Article 267 TFEU regarding the correct interpretation of Principle 1.4 of the European Statistics Code of Practice. He argued that without such a reference, his right to a fair hearing under Article 6 would be violated. On 7 June 2018, the Court of Cassation rejected his appeal (judgment no. 977/2018) without any reference to or reasoning regarding his preliminary ruling request.

The ECtHR noted that the relevant domestic and EU legal framework is described in prior judgments, including *Gorou v. Greece (no. 2)*, *Baydar v. the Netherlands*, and *Ilias Papageorgiou v. Greece*. Principle 1.4 of the European Statistics Code of Practice states that heads of national statistical institutes have "sole responsibility" for deciding on statistical methods and the content and timing of statistical releases.

The key issue before the ECtHR was whether the Court of Cassation's tacit refusal of the applicant's request for a preliminary ruling, without any reasoning, violated his right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The Court declared the remainder of the application inadmissible and gave notice to the Greek Government solely on this complaint.

In *Tanda-Muzinga v. France*, the applicant, a Congolese national born in 1970, complained under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights that obstacles encountered in obtaining visas for his wife and children under France’s family reunification procedure for refugees violated his right to respect for family life.

The applicant was granted refugee status by UNHCR in Cameroon in 2000, together with his wife and two daughters, Vanessa and Michelle. A third child, Benjamin, was born in Cameroon in 2004 after the applicant had left for France to seek asylum. Although OFPRA initially rejected his asylum claim in 2004, the Refugee Appeals Board granted him refugee status in February 2007. He then received a ten-year residence permit, and OFPRA issued civil-status documents, including a marriage certificate and a family record book.

In June 2007, relying on the family reunification procedure for recognised refugees, he applied for long-stay visas for his wife and three children. The Ministry contacted OFPRA to verify family ties, and the consulate in Yaoundé summoned his wife for an interview in February 2008. She was asked to provide UNHCR/Cameroon travel documents. She submitted such a document in March 2008, but no acknowledgement of the visa application was issued. In June 2008, OFPRA confirmed that it had certified the applicant’s family situation in July 2007, listing his wife and all three children.

After the consular authorities implicitly refused the visas, the applicant appealed. The French Government contended that the birth certificates for Michelle and Benjamin were fraudulent. Checks allegedly showed that certificate no. 1271, presented for Michelle, actually concerned a boy, and certificate no. 78/2004, presented for Benjamin, actually concerned a girl. The Minister argued that the fraudulent documents justified refusing visas for the whole family. The applicant disputed this, arguing that any anomalies arose from dysfunction in Cameroonian civil-status administration. He relied on hospital birth declarations, UNHCR documents, travel documents, photographs, bank transfer records, and later a UNHCR certificate of parenthood.

In September 2008, the Conseil d’État refused an urgent stay of execution, and in July 2009 it dismissed his appeal. It held that the fraudulent nature of at least one submitted document justified refusing all the requested visas. A psychologist later reported that the applicant’s mental health had deteriorated because of the prolonged separation from his family.

Following that decision, UNHCR/Paris indicated that the consulate was willing to issue visas to his wife, Vanessa and Benjamin, but that Michelle required a supplementary civil-status judgment in Cameroon. The applicant’s wife began proceedings there. In April 2010, the consular authorities again refused long-stay visas, maintaining that Michelle’s birth certificate remained doubtful, although Benjamin’s was later authenticated. In June 2010, the Yaoundé tribunal de grande instance reconstituted Michelle’s birth certificate, finding that the original document was a forgery obtained by a third party and that her actual birth declaration was genuine.

In October 2010, the Nantes Administrative Court ordered a stay of execution and directed the Minister to re-examine the application, noting the length of separation and the uncertainty concerning only one child. In December 2010, the French consular authorities finally issued long-stay visas to the applicant’s wife and children. The Government stated that the June 2010 judgment had been provided during re-examination. The case therefore concerned alleged excessive obstacles, delays and refusals in the refugee family reunification process, and their impact on the applicant’s family life under Article 8.

The case *Vasilyev and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 29266/08 and 248 others) was a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 13 February 2014. It concerned 249 applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by Ukrainian nationals whose details were listed in appended tables. The Government was represented by Agent Nazar Kulchytskyy. The applications were communicated to the Government on 24 June 2013.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violations were largely repetitive. On the dates set out in the appended tables, Ukrainian domestic courts and labour disputes commissions issued decisions in the applicants’ favour. Those decisions entitled the applicants either to various pecuniary amounts or to have certain actions taken in their favour. The decisions became final and enforceable. Nevertheless, the applicants were unable to obtain their enforcement in due time. This prolonged failure to enforce final domestic decisions formed the basis of their complaints before the Court.

The appended table lists numerous applicants and final domestic decisions given between the late 1990s and 2012. For example, applicant Aleksandr Vasilyev had a final decision from the Suvorivskyy District Court of Kherson dated 27 September 2005. Other decisions came from courts and labour dispute commissions in Kherson, Ordzhonikidze, Antratsyt, Zhytomyr, Chernigiv, Kyiv, Donetsk, Lviv, Zaporizhzhya, Kharkiv, Sevastopol, and elsewhere. Many decisions were several years old by the time the applications were lodged, indicating a systemic problem of non-execution of binding judgments. Some decisions concerned labour disputes and were issued by enterprise labour disputes commissions, such as the Slovyansk “Sodovyy Zavod” commission. The table also shows multiple decisions in some applicants’ favour.

The case also contained procedural developments. Several applicants—Mr Bulavko and Mr Ponomaryov (application no. 49765/08), Mr Zavarzin (application no. 62187/12), and Mr Bondar (application no. 62247/12)—died during the proceedings. Their next of kin expressed a wish to maintain the applications. In other applications (nos. 60126/12, 60150/12, 60165/12, 60177/12, 60179/12, 60250/12, 60396/12, 62582/12, and 62588/12), domestic court decisions had been delivered in favour of the applicants’ deceased relatives, and the applicants claimed to be lawful successors in title. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues.

The alleged violations therefore concerned Ukraine’s failure to enforce final domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour within a reasonable time. In Convention terms, such complaints are typically examined under Article 6 §1 (right to a fair trial) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The key facts relevant to those alleged violations are that valid, final and enforceable decisions existed; the applicants were entitled to payments or actions; and the State authorities failed to enforce those decisions promptly. The case is essentially a repetitive non-enforcement case, reflecting a widespread Ukrainian practice of delaying or failing to execute final judgments, which deprived applicants of effective judicial protection and the practical benefit of their property rights.

text:
The case *Derkach v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 23537/20 and 23615/20) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee and delivered in Strasbourg on 9 February 2023. The Committee was composed of Mārtiņš Mits (President), Mattias Guyomar and Mykola Gnatovskyy (judges), with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention. Both were introduced on 12 May 2020. The applicant, Kostyantyn Yuriyovych Derkach, born in 1982, was represented by Mr A.V. Pustyntsev, a lawyer practising in Dnipro, Ukraine. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The Court deliberated in private on 19 January 2023.

The applicant complained principally of the inadequate conditions of his detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. He also raised other complaints under the Convention. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are set out in the appended table and are identical for both applications.

According to the table, the applicant was detained at the Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 13 April 2018 to 14 August 2020. The duration of that detention was 2 years, 4 months and 2 days. The amount of living space per inmate was between 1.7 and 2.6 square metres. This level of personal space indicates significant overcrowding.

The applicant also listed specific grievances about the material conditions of his detention. He alleged infestation of the cell with insects and rodents, lack of fresh air, lack of or poor quality of bedding and bed linen, lack of privacy for the toilet, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack or insufficient quantity of food, no or restricted access to a shower, overcrowding, and passive smoking. These conditions, cumulatively and over a prolonged period, formed the factual basis of his complaint under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The applicant argued that the combination of overcrowding, poor hygiene, inadequate ventilation, lack of toilet privacy, restricted shower access, insufficient food and exposure to passive smoking made his detention intolerable. The length of detention—more than two years—was also relevant to the severity of the alleged treatment.

In addition, the applicant complained that there was no effective remedy in domestic law by which he could challenge those conditions or obtain redress. That complaint corresponds to Article 13 of the Convention, which guarantees an effective remedy for arguable violations of Convention rights. The Court was therefore required to examine whether the conditions of detention met the standards of Article 3 and whether the Ukrainian authorities provided an effective domestic remedy as required by Article 13.

Both applications concern the same applicant, the same detention facility, the same period and the same factual allegations. They were introduced on the same date, 12 May 2020. The case therefore centres on the cumulative effect of the alleged detention conditions and the absence of an effective remedy in Ukraine.

In *Golovin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 47052/18, judgment 13 July 2023), the European Court of Human Rights examined the dismissal of a judge of Ukraine’s Constitutional Court, which the applicant alleged violated Articles 6, 8 and 18 of the Convention. The applicant, Anatoliy Sergiyovych Golovin, a Ukrainian national born in 1952 and living in Kyiv, lodged his application on 23 September 2018.

In August 2006, Parliament appointed Golovin as a judge of the Constitutional Court of Ukraine for a non-renewable nine-year term. On 24 February 2014, Parliament dismissed him “for breach of his judicial oath.” The dismissal was connected to his participation in the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 30 September 2010. The same parliamentary resolution also concerned the applicants in *Ovcharenko and Kolos v. Ukraine*. After his dismissal, on 27 February 2014, Golovin challenged the resolution before the Higher Administrative Court (HAC), relying on the Code of Administrative Justice. On 3 March 2014, he also submitted a statement of resignation to Parliament.

On 11 December 2017, the HAC declared the parliamentary resolution unlawful with respect to Golovin’s dismissal. It relied on international and domestic principles of judicial independence and found that Parliament had not respected them. In particular, it cited the Constitutional Court Act provision that judges could not be held liable for the results of their votes. It further found that Parliament had failed to follow the procedure for dismissing a Constitutional Court judge and that no individual liability of Golovin had been established.

Parliament appealed. On 14 March 2018, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court quashed the HAC’s judgment and dismissed Golovin’s claim as unfounded; the full text was issued on 23 March 2018. The Supreme Court held that in its 2010 judgment the Constitutional Court had acted beyond its powers by invalidating binding provisions of the Constitution. It found that the Constitutional Court had failed to ensure the supremacy of the Constitution, had changed the Constitution and constitutional system, had violated fundamental principles of democracy and separation of powers, and had undermined the legitimacy of State authorities. It concluded that Golovin’s participation in that judgment and its consequences were manifestly inconsistent with his judicial oath. It also found that his dismissal procedure had complied with the Constitution and Parliament’s rules.

Crucially for the alleged violations, the Supreme Court distinguished *Oleksandr Volkov v. Ukraine*. It observed that the Constitutional Court is formed through a political process, acts as a “negative legislator” when declaring legislation unconstitutional and as a “positive legislator” when interpreting the Constitution, and is therefore more political than judicial. Relying on *Fischer v. Austria* and *Zumtobel v. Austria*, it considered the Constitutional Court not to be a “court” within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. It concluded that the body that appointed a Constitutional Court judge may apply political accountability where the judge’s conduct does not meet the high standards expected by society.

These facts are central to Golovin’s complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 18. They concern whether he had access to a fair judicial process for contesting his dismissal, whether the dismissal based on his judicial activity unjustifiably interfered with his rights, and whether the measure pursued an improper purpose rather than a legitimate one.

text:
The case concerned four British nationals who alleged that the admission of witness statements at their criminal trials rendered the proceedings unfair under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights, because they had no opportunity to cross-examine the absent witnesses. The applications arose from two separate prosecutions.

In the first, P.R., a registered alcoholic, was attacked in his flat in May 2005 and suffered extensive injuries. In June 2005 he made a police statement saying three men had attacked him. He described a “bigger male,” a “male on crutches,” and a third man called “Horncastle.” He also said his memory was vague and that he had drunk heavily. P.R. died in July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness. Horncastle and Blackmore were charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent. The prosecution alleged they had gone with D. to recover stolen property and had attacked P.R.; the defence admitted presence but denied involvement in the assault. The prosecution applied to read P.R.’s statement under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 because the witness was dead. The defence objected under PACE, arguing the statement was the only evidence of participation, could not be tested, and was unreliable. The judge admitted it, finding no unfairness. Other evidence included blood on a television removed by Horncastle, Blackmore’s admission that he stepped over the victim, forensic evidence, and a witness suggesting M. had attacked P.R. The judge warned the jury that the statement was untested but central. Both were convicted.

In the second, H.M. was kidnapped in November 2007. Six men entered her home, threatened her with a knife, took her away, demanded ransom, and later released her. She made a police statement but later retracted it because she was scared. Before trial, she and her partner failed to attend; police had warned them the men were dangerous and advised relocation. In April 2008 she made a video statement saying she was terrified and would not attend court. The prosecution applied to read her statement under section 116(2)(e) of the 2003 Act as a witness in fear. The judge admitted it, finding genuine terror, even though police advice contributed to her fear; the Act did not require the fear to be caused by the defendants. G.P.’s statement was not admitted. At trial, the victim’s statement did not identify Marquis or Graham. Other evidence included CCTV of Graham entering the house, his arrest in the stolen car with a knife, Marquis’s phone being used for ransom calls, and a pink phone seen at his hotel. Both were convicted.

The applicants argued that admitting the statements without cross-examination violated Article 6, especially because the hearsay was sole or decisive. The UK Court of Appeal and Supreme Court dismissed their appeals, relying on statutory safeguards: judicial gatekeeping, cautionary jury directions, the ability to challenge reliability through other evidence, and the power to stop a case if hearsay evidence was unconvincing.

The European Court of Human Rights found no violation. It held that the statutory safeguards and counterbalancing measures were sufficient. In Horncastle and Blackmore’s case, the statement was decisive but adequately counterbalanced; in Marquis and Graham’s case, it was not decisive. The Court reiterated that sole or decisive hearsay is not automatically incompatible with Article 6. The trials were therefore fair.

**Case Summary: Nezdymovskyy v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 56163/21 and 879/22)**

The case of *Nezdymovskyy v. Ukraine* concerns two applications lodged against Ukraine with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant, Pavlo Leonidovych Nezdymovskyy, born in 1983, was represented by Mr V.V. Kushnir, a lawyer practising in Dnipro, Ukraine. The applications were introduced on 6 November 2021 and 18 December 2021. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the applicant’s detention at the Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility. According to the appended table, the applicant had been held in that facility since 20 February 2015, and his detention was still pending at the time of the proceedings. The duration of detention in that facility was therefore more than eight years, four months and twenty-three days. The two applications relate to the same detention facility and the same ongoing period of detention, although they were lodged on separate dates.

The applicant complained of inadequate conditions of detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. The specific grievances recorded in the appended table include overcrowding, with the space available per inmate ranging between only 2.5 and 2.9 square metres. The applicant further alleged a lack of fresh air, a lack of privacy for using the toilet, and the lack or poor quality of bedding and bed linen. He also complained of passive smoking, a lack of toiletries, and a lack or inadequacy of hygienic facilities. In addition, he described a mouldy or dirty cell, no or restricted access to warm water, and no or restricted access to shower facilities.

These factual allegations form the basis of the complaint that the conditions of detention were inadequate, and that no effective domestic remedy existed to address or prevent those conditions. The case therefore raises issues under the Convention concerning the prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment and the right to an effective remedy, although the provided excerpt refers generally to the applicant’s complaints under the Convention and notes that he also raised other complaints.

Procedurally, the case was heard by the Fifth Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee composed of Carlo Ranzoni (President), Lado Chanturia, and María Elósegui, judges, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 14 September 2023 and delivered its judgment on 5 October 2023 in Strasbourg. The judgment was adopted on that date, is final, but may be subject to editorial revision.

In summary, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations are the applicant’s prolonged detention at the Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 20 February 2015 onwards, lasting more than eight years and four months at the time of the applications, combined with severe overcrowding and multiple material deficiencies in detention conditions. The applicant alleged that these conditions breached the Convention and that Ukrainian domestic law provided no effective remedy for his complaints.

In *Ohanjanyan v Armenia*, the applicant, Suren Ohanjanyan, complained under Article 2 of the Convention about the death of his son, T. Ohanjanyan, during compulsory military service and the alleged failure of the authorities to conduct an effective investigation.

T. Ohanjanyan was drafted in November 2006 and transferred in May 2007 to military unit no. 28418 in Gegharkunik. According to the official account, on 30 August 2007, after the evening roll-call, he left the armoury towards a backup checkpoint and accidentally touched the guy-wires of the antenna mast of an R-419 radio relay station belonging to nearby military unit no. 28233. He was allegedly electrocuted and died instantly. Junior Sergeant A.G. found him lying under the wires; A.G. also received an electric shock when he touched a wire. The body was taken to hospital and then to Yerevan for autopsy.

Military police recorded a 180-volt current in the guy-wire when the radio relay station was switched on. Criminal proceedings were opened for negligence in military duties. The autopsy concluded that death resulted from electrocution, citing electrical wounds on the neck, left wrist, fingers and right toe, plus other abrasions. The applicant disputed this account. He submitted photographs taken before autopsy allegedly showing injuries not recorded by the expert, including missing teeth, head, ear and jaw injuries, and burn marks. A serviceman, D.H., stated that the former unit commander had slapped T. Ohanjanyan; the commander denied it and was not prosecuted.

The investigation had significant problems relevant to Article 2. The scene was not properly inspected at night; the radio relay station was dismantled despite a prosecutor’s order to preserve it; the key guy-wire was examined 38 days later and showed no skin or blood traces; clothing was examined 56 days later. The initial electrical expert concluded in November 2007 that damaged insulation and lack of earthing had connected the mast and guy-wires to mains current, causing electrocution, and that the station had been operated in breach of technical requirements. However, the Ministry of Defence earlier said no electric current was possible there.

Two servicemen, R.A. and K.T., were charged. At trial, a court-ordered combined expert report in 2009 found that the station subframe operated at 27 volts and could not produce 180 volts. It could neither confirm nor reject electrocution. In January 2010 the Regional Court acquitted R.A. and K.T., citing conflicting electrical and medical evidence, procedural defects, failure to establish the exact time and circumstances, and the inconsistency that the same current killed T. Ohanjanyan but only lightly injured A.G. The acquittal was upheld on appeal and by the Court of Cassation.

Further investigation followed. Additional reports upheld the autopsy and confirmed that the station malfunction could not have supplied mains current. In 2016 a domestic court upheld the applicant’s complaint that the post-acquittal investigation was not effective, prompt or diligent, and had failed to address his photographs and alleged injuries. In 2018 the Criminal Court of Appeal found the suspension of proceedings deficient because the specific radio relay station had not been found or examined and other possible causes of death had not been adequately investigated. It concluded that the investigation was not effective within the meaning of Article 2. Nevertheless, by 2022 the investigation remained incomplete, repeatedly suspended and resumed. The applicant died in 2017, and his widow continued the application.

In *Göthlin v. Sweden*, the applicant, Sven Olof Göthlin, born in 1943, owed approximately SEK 246,199 in tax debts. In September 2009, the Swedish Enforcement Authority issued a writ attaching his mobile sawmill, valued at about SEK 300,000. The sawmill remained in his possession, but he was prohibited from selling, disposing of, or otherwise reducing its value. He appealed, and an interim stay was granted, but the District Court upheld the attachment in February 2010. Further appeals were refused, and the writ became final on 6 May 2010.

In April 2010, while the Authority planned to sell the sawmill, the applicant stated that he had removed and hidden it. On 5 May 2010, the Authority visited his property, confirmed the sawmill was gone, and served him with a summons for questioning and an injunction to provide information needed to recover it. The injunction warned that he could be detained under Chapter 2, section 16, and Chapter 4, section 14, of the Enforcement Code. At questioning on 7 May, he admitted knowing the sawmill was attached and that he could not dispose of it. He said he hid it because he believed the tax debt and attachment were wrong, accepted responsibility, stated no one else was involved, and refused to reveal its location. He also said he had moved it by car and had considered burning it. His wife said she had no information.

On 17 May 2010, the Authority asked the District Court to detain him for refusing to cooperate. On 27 May, the District Court refused. It found no “extraordinary reasons” for detention, noting that only a short time had passed since the case became final and that the Authority had not tried less severe measures, such as a conditional fine, which might change his attitude.

The Authority appealed, arguing that a conditional fine would be futile and that the applicant had been reported to the police for breach of an official order. On 28 June 2010, the Court of Appeal quashed the refusal and ordered detention. It found extraordinary reasons and proportionality based on the size of the debt, the value of the hidden sawmill, and the applicant’s continued refusal. It held that no prior conditional fine was required. He was detained on 29 June 2010. A hearing on 30 June maintained the detention, with reviews every two weeks, release if he disclosed the location, and a maximum of three months. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 6 July.

The District Court reviewed detention on 13 and 27 July and continued it. The applicant maintained his refusal, argued that detention was disproportionate and akin to imprisonment to obtain a confession, and cited health problems including high blood pressure, panic anxiety, prostate cancer treatment, and asthma. The Authority said no investigative steps were possible because the sawmill’s location was unknown.

On 9 August 2010, the District Court found continued detention disproportionate and no longer justified; he was released the same day after 42 days. Appeals by the Authority were rejected, and the Supreme Court dismissed the further appeal. The police investigation for breach of official order was discontinued in April 2011 by waiver of prosecution. In October 2011, the Authority revoked the writ because the sawmill’s location could not be discovered and no further measures would help.

The applicant sought SEK 80,000 in damages from the Chancellor of Justice for the 42 days’ deprivation of liberty, but the claim was rejected. The Chancellor found the detention had been ordered by a court under relevant law and no erroneous grounds were shown.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 5 § 1 about the proportionality of the detention order. The key issue was whether detention to compel disclosure of an attached asset’s whereabouts was lawful and proportionate, or whether less coercive measures should first have been used.

In *Fernández Martínez v. Spain* (Application no. 56030/07), the applicant, a Spanish national born in 1937, had been ordained a Catholic priest in 1961. In 1984 he asked the Vatican for dispensation from celibacy; receiving no immediate reply, he married civilly in 1985 and later had five children. From October 1991 he worked as a teacher of Catholic religion and ethics in a State-run secondary school in Murcia under renewable one-year contracts. Under the 1979 Spain–Holy See Agreement and a 1982 ministerial order, such teachers were appointed by the education authority only from persons proposed annually by the diocesan Ordinary; renewal was automatic unless the Ordinary objected. His employment therefore depended on the bishop’s continuing approval.

In November 1996, a regional newspaper reported a gathering of the Movement for Optional Celibacy of priests (MOCEOP). The article identified the applicant as a former seminary director and included him among married priests advocating optional celibacy, a more democratic Church and reform of Church rules; it also reported critical views on sexuality, abortion and birth control. In August 1997 the Pope granted the applicant a rescript dispensing him from celibacy and removing his clerical state, but stating that he was barred from teaching Catholic religion in public institutions unless the local bishop decided otherwise and provided there was no scandal. On 29 September 1997 the Diocese of Cartagena informed the Ministry of Education that his service should end; the Ministry terminated his employment. In November 1997 the Diocese explained that once the applicant’s married-priest situation had become public and common knowledge, the bishop could no longer authorise him to teach because of the risk of scandal and the sensitivity of parents. It noted that he was entitled to unemployment benefit.

The applicant challenged the non-renewal. An employment tribunal declared the dismissal null and void, finding discrimination based on his marital status and MOCEOP membership, with press publicity being the cause. The Murcia High Court reversed, holding that teaching Catholic religion required a bond of trust with the bishop; the relationship was not neutral, and the bishop could decline to propose him. It also treated the contract as temporary and expired. The Constitutional Court dismissed his amparo appeal. It found no discrimination on account of marital status and no private-life violation because he had voluntarily made his situation public. Balancing the Catholic Church’s collective religious freedom and parents’ rights against the applicant’s freedom of thought, religion and expression, it held that the non-renewal was justified by exclusively religious reasons and by State neutrality.
