**Lagoshenko and Others v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 47045/21 and 5 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered in Strasbourg on 6 July 2023. The judgment was adopted after private deliberation on 15 June 2023 and is final. The case originated in six applications filed against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants’ central complaints were that criminal proceedings against them were excessively long and that Ukrainian law provided no effective remedy for that delay.

The relevant facts are set out in the appended table. Oleksandr Volodymyrovych Lagoshenko (born 1983), application no. 47045/21, introduced his application on 13 September 2021. His criminal proceedings began on 25 March 2015 and were still pending at the relevant time. They had lasted more than eight years, two months and two days, and had been considered at only one level of jurisdiction.

Yuriy Vasylyovych Andriychuk (born 1974), application no. 56240/21, applied on 10 November 2021. His proceedings started on 27 April 2011 and remained pending. Their total duration exceeded twelve years and one month, across three levels of jurisdiction. This was the longest period among the applications.

Rostyslav Romanovych Didukh (born 1965), application no. 58210/21, applied on 19 November 2021. He was represented by Oleg Volodymyrovych Mytsyk of Lviv. His proceedings began on 12 August 2014 and were still pending. They had lasted more than eight years, nine months and fifteen days, at two levels of jurisdiction.

Kostyantyn Sergiyovych Zheludchenko (born 1972), application no. 1398/22, applied on 20 December 2021. Unlike most of the other cases, his proceedings ended on 22 December 2021. They had begun on 26 January 2017 and lasted four years, ten months and twenty-seven days, involving two levels of jurisdiction.

Volodymyr Volodymyrovych Chyrkov (born 1975), application no. 8393/22, applied on 31 January 2022. His proceedings started on 29 August 2017 and were still pending. They had lasted more than five years, eight months and twenty-eight days, at one level of jurisdiction.

Dmytro Valeriyovych Nemazanyy (born 1986), application no. 48029/22, applied on 22 September 2022. He was represented by Anatoliy Volodymyrovych Mulko of Solone. His proceedings began on 10 May 2018 and were still pending. They had lasted more than five years and seventeen days, involving two levels of jurisdiction.

Thus, in five of the six applications, the criminal proceedings were still pending when the applications were introduced. The proceedings lasted from approximately four years and eleven months to more than twelve years. Some applicants’ cases had passed through one, two, or three levels of jurisdiction. These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ allegations that the length of the criminal proceedings was excessive and that no effective domestic remedy existed to address or prevent the delay. The Court, sitting as a Committee, considered these complaints in the light of the facts summarized in the appended table.

Axel Springer SE, a Berlin-based publishing house, publishes the daily newspaper *Die Welt*. On 4 October 2013, *Die Welt* published an article headlined “The Stasi woman by Gregor Gysi’s side.” It concerned Ms K., executive director of the political party Die Linke, then chaired by Gregor Gysi. The article alleged that K. had been an agent for the former GDR Ministry of State Security (the Stasi) and discussed the post-1989 disappearance of billions in assets belonging to the SED, East Germany’s former Communist Party. It stated that K.’s name stood for a “particularly unsavoury chapter” in the party’s handling of SED assets; that at the end of 1989 the SED still possessed extensive holdings and 6.2 billion East German marks in cash; that secret bank accounts might exist; that there was no evidence K. was involved in possible criminal activities; but that, according to documents, she remained directly or indirectly involved with companies whose assets derived from the SED’s heritage. It named companies FEVAC and Vulkan, said K. held shares in them as a private individual, and noted that in 1995 the Berlin Higher Administrative Court found that two companies in which she held stakes managed PDS assets on a fiduciary basis. The article also linked K. to the “Association of Friends of the ND,” which allegedly promised large sums to save the party newspaper *Neues Deutschland*, and named her honorary chairwoman.

Two days before publication, Axel Springer sent K. questions, including about her membership in the Association of Friends of the ND. K. refused to answer. After publication, on 11 October 2013, K.’s lawyer demanded a rectification. K. asserted she had nothing to do with the disappearance of SED assets; that FEVAC and Vulkan were founded in 1992 with PDS money on the recommendation and with approval of the Treuhandanstalt; that she became a FEVAC shareholder only in 1998; and that she had joined the Association around 2000 and chaired it since 2002. She also said she had not been a member of the party’s Federal Arbitration Commission since 1 January 2013.

Axel Springer refused to publish the rectification. K. sought an injunction. The Berlin Regional Court initially dismissed her application, finding that the article did not make the alleged connection. K. appealed. On 18 November 2013, the Court of Appeal ordered Axel Springer to publish a rectification under section 10 of the Berlin Press Act. In the main proceedings, the Regional Court again dismissed K.’s application, but on 16 January 2014 the Court of Appeal again ordered publication, on page 8, while rejecting a front-page placement. It reasoned that although the article did not explicitly allege K. concealed SED assets, the average reader would infer such involvement; the statement that there was no evidence of criminal activity did not offset that implication. It found the rectification’s length and content were limited to what was necessary and that K.’s refusal to answer pre-publication questions did not remove her legitimate interest. The date on the rectification was not manifestly incorrect because the first request dated from 11 October 2013, even if later revised.

On 3 February 2014, Axel Springer published the rectification, adding an editor’s note that the information was correct and that the newspaper had no knowledge connecting K. to the disappearance of SED assets. On 14 August 2017, the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider Axel Springer’s constitutional complaint without giving reasons. Axel Springer applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 14 February 2018, alleging that the German courts’ order requiring publication of K.’s rectification violated its right to freedom of expression and press under Article 10 of the Convention. The key alleged violation is therefore the compulsory right-of-reply publication imposed on the newspaper.

In *Pleshkov and Pleshkova v. Ukraine* (Application no. 5783/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered a judgment on 9 March 2023. The applicants are two Ukrainian nationals: Mr Dmytro Gennadiyovych Pleshkov, born 1974, and his daughter Ms Alisa Dmytrivna Pleshkova, born 2011. They live separately, in Kyiv and Irpin respectively, and were represented by Ms M. Korniyenko. They lodged their application on 13 January 2020.

The case concerns the alleged failure of Ukrainian authorities to enforce a domestic judgment establishing contact arrangements between father and daughter. On 24 October 2016, the Dniprovskyi District Court of Kyiv issued a judgment, later amended by the Kyiv Court of Appeal on 21 February 2017, setting out arrangements for contact between the first and second applicants, who were living separately. The second applicant lived with her mother, L. The mother failed to comply with those arrangements.

Enforcement proceedings began in September 2018 and were still ongoing at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings. According to the facts, the bailiffs imposed two fines on L for non-compliance, but she did not pay them. They also ordered a temporary suspension of her driving licence. Because L repeatedly failed to respond to their summons, the bailiffs unsuccessfully sought the initiation of criminal proceedings against her and a temporary ban on her leaving the country.

On 10 November 2018, the bailiffs organised the only meeting between the applicants. It took place in the presence of L. During that meeting, the second applicant refused to communicate with the first applicant because she was afraid of him. Subsequently, on 26 June 2019, a psychological examination of the second applicant was ordered by the bailiffs. The psychologist concluded that the child’s negative attitude towards her father was linked to the conflict between the first applicant and L. The psychologist indicated that improving the relationship between the first applicant and L. was a precondition for re-establishing “psychological contact” between the applicants.

The Government submitted that a representative of the local child welfare services had been involved in the enforcement proceedings, but they did not provide any further details about that involvement.

The applicants complained under Article 8 of the Convention about the non-enforcement of the contact arrangements. The Court decided to give notice to the Ukrainian Government of the complaint under Article 8 concerning the non-enforcement of the judgment on contact arrangements between the applicants, and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The application was given priority under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. The key issue before the Court was therefore whether the Ukrainian authorities had taken adequate and effective steps to enforce the father’s contact rights and to protect the family life of both applicants, or whether the prolonged failure to secure compliance with the domestic judgment violated Article 8. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In *O’Keeffe v. Ireland* (Application no. 35810/09, Grand Chamber, 28 January 2014), the applicant, Louise O’Keeffe, complained that Ireland’s primary education system failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973 and that she had no effective domestic remedy for that failure.

The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. Although State-funded, the school was owned through trustees by the Catholic Bishop of Cork and Ross, and the local parish priest acted as manager on behalf of the bishop. One of the two teachers, L.H., was the school principal. In 1971, a parent complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. The complaint was not reported to the police, the Department of Education, or any other State authority, and the manager did not act on it.

During the first six months of 1973, L.H. sexually assaulted the applicant approximately twenty times during music lessons in his classroom. The applicant and her parents were unaware of the 1971 complaint. In September 1973, other parents raised similar allegations. L.H. went on sick leave and then resigned. Again, these allegations were not reported to the police, the Department, or any other State body. The Department was later merely informed that L.H. had resigned and been replaced. L.H. subsequently taught at another national school until his retirement in 1995. State inspectors had visited Dunderrow, but no complaint about L.H. was made to them.

The applicant suppressed the abuse. In 1996, police investigating another complaint contacted her. She made a statement in 1997. L.H. was charged with 386 sexual offences involving about twenty-one former pupils. In 1998, he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was imprisoned. His teaching licence was withdrawn. The applicant then realised the connection between her psychological difficulties and the abuse.

The applicant applied to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal and accepted an ex gratia award. She also brought a civil action against L.H. and the State Defendants—the Minister, Ireland, and the Attorney General. Against the State, she alleged negligence in the recognition, examination, and supervision of the school; failure to put protective measures in place; vicarious liability for L.H.; and liability under the Constitution, relying on her right to bodily integrity and the State’s duty to provide primary education under Article 42. She obtained default judgment against L.H. However, the High Court non-suited the negligence claim for lack of a prima facie case. In 2006, the High Court found no vicarious liability because national schools were State-funded but clerically managed; L.H. was employed by the manager, not the State. It also rejected the constitutional claim. The Supreme Court dismissed her appeal in 2008, with the majority holding that the State was not vicariously liable given the unique managerial system; one judge dissented.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant mainly alleged a violation of Article 3 because the primary education system failed to protect her from sexual abuse in 1973. She also alleged a violation of Article 13 because she had no effective domestic remedy. She further relied on Article 8, Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, and Article 14. Complaints about the length of the civil proceedings were settled and struck out. The Grand Chamber found a violation of Article 3 and a violation of Article 13. It did not consider it necessary to examine the remaining complaints separately. The key facts were therefore the State-funded but Church-managed school structure, the ignored 1971 complaint, the abuse during lessons, the lack of State reporting or supervision, and the domestic courts’ refusal to hold the State liable.

text:
The case of *Kapitonov and Others v. Russia* concerns 26 applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights against Russia. The applications were introduced on various dates, primarily between 2017 and 2018. The core of the applicants' complaints revolves around what they allege were disproportionate measures taken against them by Russian authorities in response to their participation in or organization of public assemblies.

The facts, as detailed in the appended table, reveal a consistent pattern across the applications. The applicants were involved in a series of public events, predominantly in Moscow, St Petersburg, and Voronezh. These events were mostly political in nature, including manifestations against corruption (often linked to investigations concerning A. Navalnyy and D. Medvedev), in support of political prisoners and Ukraine, against the re-election of Mr Putin as President, and in support of free elections.

For their participation in these assemblies, the applicants faced administrative charges under the Russian Code of Administrative Offences (CAO). The most frequently cited charges were under Article 20.2, which penalizes violations of the established procedure for organizing or holding a public event. Specifically, they were charged under various parts of this article, including § 5 (failure to comply with the procedure), § 6.1, and § 8. Additionally, many applicants were charged under Article 19.3 § 1 of the CAO, which relates to disobedience of a lawful order by a police officer.

The penalties imposed on the applicants were varied and included both fines and administrative detention. The fines ranged significantly, from a low of RUB 500 to a high of RUB 250,000. Several applicants were also subjected to administrative detention, with sentences ranging from 2 to 17 days. For instance, in one of the larger applications (no. 71203/17), which grouped 11 applicants involved in an anti-corruption manifestation in Moscow on 26 March 2017, penalties included fines up to RUB 20,000 and up to 10 days of administrative detention for three of the applicants. Another applicant, Mr. Zheksimbayev (application no. 21998/18), received two separate sentences of 15 and 17 days of administrative detention for his role in a manifestation in St Petersburg.

These administrative sanctions were challenged in domestic courts, but the final decisions in each case were rendered by various regional city and regional courts, including the Moscow City Court, St Petersburg City Court, and Moscow and Voronezh Regional Courts, upholding the lower courts' rulings between 2016 and 2021. The applicants brought their case to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that these measures violated their rights under the Convention, specifically regarding the disproportionate interference with their freedom of assembly and expression.

The case of **Horncastle and Others v. the United Kingdom** (Application no. 4184/10) concerned four British applicants who alleged that the admission of witness statements at their criminal trials made the proceedings unfair, in violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The central complaint was that they had no opportunity to cross-examine the absent witnesses whose statements were read to the jury.

The first two applicants, Michael Horncastle and David Blackmore, were charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent to P.R., a registered alcoholic. In May 2005 P.R. was attacked in his flat and suffered severe injuries. He gave a police statement in June 2005 describing the attack. He admitted he had drunk heavily, said his memory was vague, and identified one attacker as “Horncastle” while describing two others as a “bigger male” and a “male on crutches.” P.R. died in July 2006 from an alcohol-related illness before trial. The prosecution applied to read his statement under section 116(2)(a) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 because the witness was dead. The defence opposed admission, arguing that the statement was inherently unreliable and was the only admissible evidence of their participation. The judge admitted it, finding the statutory condition satisfied and that fairness could be protected through directions and other evidence. At trial, the judge warned the jury that the statement was untested and carried less weight. Horncastle and Blackmore were convicted. The Court of Appeal accepted that the statement was decisive to a degree but found sufficient independent evidence and counterbalancing measures. The Supreme Court dismissed their appeal.

The second two applicants, Abijah Marquis and Joseph Graham, were charged with kidnapping H.M. in November 2007. H.M. made a police statement describing masked men entering her home, threatening her with a knife, demanding money, and taking her away in a car. She later retracted her statement out of fear, but in April 2008 made a video statement confirming that she was terrified. She and her partner, G.P., failed to attend trial. The prosecution applied to read H.M.’s statements under section 116(2)(e) of the 2003 Act on the ground that she would not give evidence through fear. The applicants argued that her fear was caused or increased by police warnings about dangerousness rather than by them. The judge found H.M. genuinely petrified, admitted her statement, and declined to admit G.P.’s statement. Marquis and Graham were convicted. On appeal, they argued that H.M.’s statement was the only evidence of kidnapping and should not have been admitted. The domestic courts found other evidence—CCTV, telephone records, a knife, and witness testimony—meant the conviction did not rest decisively on her statement.

The alleged violation was that admitting absent witnesses’ statements, especially where sole or decisive, denied the applicants the right to confront their accusers. The key factual issues were the reasons for the witnesses’ absence, the reliability of their statements, whether the evidence was decisive, and whether judicial warnings and other evidence sufficiently counterbalanced the lack of cross-examination. The Strasbourg Court ultimately found no violation of Article 6, holding that the UK statutory safeguards and trial directions were sufficient to secure fair proceedings.

In *Sharashkin and Others v. Russia*, the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered judgment on 11 May 2023, adopted on 13 April 2023. The case comprised Application no. 57223/19 and 21 other applications. The applicants lodged their applications under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, and the Russian Government was given notice of them. The case concerned administrative sanctions imposed on individuals who organised or participated in public assemblies in Russia, mainly in Moscow.

The appended table identifies the applicants and the events at issue. These included an anticorruption manifestation in Moscow on 26 March 2017; a manifestation in support of I. Golunov on 12 June 2019; manifestations for fair elections to Mosgorduma (the Moscow City Duma) on 27 July 2019 and 3 August 2019; a manifestation against political repressions on 31 August 2019; and a manifestation in support of A. Navalnyy on 2 February 2021. The majority of the applications concerned the 27 July 2019 Moscow City Duma protest, which was the central event in the case.

The applicants were charged under Article 20.2 of the Russian Code of Administrative Offences, in various paragraphs: § 5, § 6.1, § 2, and § 8. These provisions concern violations of the procedure for organising or holding public events, participation in unauthorised public events, organising unauthorised events, and repeated violations. The penalties imposed included administrative fines and administrative arrest or detention. Fines typically ranged from RUB 10,000 to RUB 20,000, although some were higher or lower. For example, Sharashkin received 7 days’ administrative arrest under § 6.1. Solovyev received an 8-day administrative detention under § 2 for the 27 July 2019 event and a 20-day administrative detention under § 8 for the 31 August 2019 event. Other applicants received fines such as RUB 20,000, 18,000, 15,000, 12,000, or 10,000. Some applicants were sanctioned for more than one event, including Burkhanov, Golovenko, Kravchenko, Pospelov, and Tamkovich. Final domestic decisions were issued by the Moscow City Court on various dates between 2017 and 2021.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained of disproportionate measures taken against them as organisers and participants of public assemblies. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The key alleged violation concerned interference with the right to freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 11 of the Convention, through administrative charges, fines, and short-term detention. The facts indicate that the penalties were imposed in connection with peaceful protests, many of which concerned electoral or political issues, and that the domestic courts upheld those sanctions. The applicants argued that the measures were not necessary in a democratic society and were disproportionate. The full text provided does not set out the Court’s legal reasoning or final conclusions on the merits, but it identifies the factual basis relevant to the alleged violations. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

In *Zajmi v. Albania* (Application no. 83907/17, judgment of 20 June 2023), the applicant, Ms Çetina Zajmi, an Albanian national born in 1957, had been convicted in criminal proceedings. On 13 March 2013 the Tirana District Court found her guilty of aggravated fraud and sentenced her to fourteen years’ imprisonment. Her appeal was dismissed by the Tirana Appeal Court on 8 November 2013, and the Supreme Court dismissed her further appeal on 25 May 2015. The criminal conviction therefore became final at the latest at that point.

The alleged violation arose from the subsequent constitutional-complaint procedure. On 8 November 2016, Law no. 99/2016 was published in the Official Journal. It shortened the time-limit for lodging a constitutional complaint from two years to four months “of obtaining knowledge of the interference [with a constitutional right or freedom]”. The new time-limit was to enter into force on 1 March 2017. This statutory change was central to the case.

On 27 February 2017—shortly before the new law entered into force—the applicant sent a constitutional complaint through a post office. On the envelope, she wrote the address as “Gj – K.SH, Tirané”. This was incomplete. The postal service did not deliver the mail because the recipient could not be identified. On an unspecified date, the applicant checked with the post office and learned that her complaint had not reached the Constitutional Court. She then re-sent the constitutional complaint on 22 May 2017 to the proper address of the Constitutional Court.

On 16 June 2017 the Constitutional Court declared the applicant’s complaint inadmissible as being lodged outside the new four-month time-limit. The same day, the Constitutional Court adopted two separate decisions in the cases of *Pajova* (decision no. 157) and *Ibrahimi* (decision no. 152). In those decisions, it applied the newly introduced four-month time-limit to Supreme Court decisions adopted respectively on 7 May 2015 and 25 June 2015, counting the time-limit from the date of the Supreme Court’s adoption of those decisions. Those parallel decisions are relevant because they demonstrate how the Constitutional Court applied the shortened deadline to earlier final decisions, including decisions issued well before the new law entered into force.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the applicant’s final criminal conviction; the legislative reduction of the constitutional-complaint deadline from two years to four months; her attempt to lodge a constitutional complaint before the new law entered into force; the postal non-delivery caused by an incomplete address; her later re-submission on 22 May 2017; and the Constitutional Court’s refusal to examine the complaint as out of time on 16 June 2017. The applicant’s complaint before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the resulting restriction on her access to the Constitutional Court and/or her right to a fair hearing in the criminal case, in so far as the domestic court refused to consider her constitutional complaint on the merits. The case thus focuses on whether the application of the shortened time-limit, combined with the postal delivery problem, disproportionately and unforeseeably barred her from obtaining constitutional review.

The case B.F. and Others v. Switzerland (ECtHR, Third Section, 4 July 2023) concerns four applications brought by Eritrean and Chinese nationals whose requests for family reunification in Switzerland were refused. The applicants had all been recognised as refugees under the 1951 Refugee Convention, but they were not granted asylum. Instead, they received provisional admission because the Swiss authorities found that the grounds for their refugee status arose only after their departure from their countries of origin and as a result of their own actions (“subjective post-flight grounds”). Under Swiss law, this distinction mattered greatly: refugees granted asylum could bring their nuclear family to Switzerland under section 51 of the Asylum Act without a waiting period or other conditions, whereas provisionally admitted refugees had only a discretionary entitlement under section 85(7) of the Aliens Act, subject to cumulative requirements, including a three-year waiting period and non-reliance on social assistance.

The applicants sought reunification with minor children or a spouse and children. In each case, the Swiss authorities rejected the requests primarily because the applicant remained reliant on social assistance. In some cases, the three-year waiting period or a time-limit for children over 12 was also not met. The Federal Administrative Court accepted that the applicants had de facto settled status and that Article 8 of the Convention was engaged, but it found that the refusals did not breach Article 8. It emphasised that their asylum claims of pre-departure persecution had been rejected as not credible, that their separation from family members had been voluntary or foreseeable, that they could maintain contact and visit relatives abroad, and that the public interest in avoiding social assistance outweighed their private interests.

The specific facts varied. B.F., an Eritrean national provisionally admitted in 2014, sought reunification with her daughter D.E., who was living in precarious conditions in Sudan. B.F. was fully reliant on social assistance, had health problems, and was later found 100% unfit for work; her request was rejected for failure to meet both the waiting period and the non-reliance condition. She alleged violations of Article 8 and Article 14 read with Article 8, arguing discrimination compared with refugees granted asylum. Another applicant, a Chinese national of Tibetan origin provisionally admitted in 2010, sought reunification with his wife and two children in India. He worked full-time as a nursing assistant but earned too little to support the family; his wife had epilepsy. His request was rejected for reliance on social assistance. A third applicant, an Eritrean woman provisionally admitted in 2010, sought reunification with her eldest daughter in Sudan. She worked part-time while caring for three minor children alone and remained largely dependent on social assistance; her request was rejected for the time-limit and lack of financial independence. The fourth applicant, an Eritrean woman provisionally admitted in 2014, sought reunification with her two daughters living in an Ethiopian refugee camp. She had health issues and had never found work, though she was not deemed completely unfit; her request was rejected for reliance on social assistance.

The alleged violations centred on Article 8, because the refusals allegedly amounted to a disproportionate interference with family life and, given the applicants’ inability to meet the social-assistance condition, a de facto permanent separation. Some applicants also alleged Article 14 discrimination, arguing that provisionally admitted refugees were treated less favourably than refugees granted asylum without objective justification.

In *El-Asmar v. Denmark*, the applicant, a Danish national, complained under Article 3 of the Convention that prison guards pepper-sprayed him in an observation cell on 4 April 2017 and that the subsequent investigation was ineffective. The Court declared inadmissible his complaint concerning his later confinement to a restraint bed.

The applicant had a violent criminal history. Arrested on 24 March 2017 and remanded in custody, he was assessed as possibly dangerous and transferred to Enner Mark Prison on 30 March after aggressive and threatening behaviour. Records show repeated threats to kill staff, property damage, and attacks, leading to observation and security cell placements. On 3 April he attempted to attack a guard with a pencil and later tried to kick officers; five officers restrained him.

On 4 April he was in an observation cell. Prison records state he shouted threats, threw food, urinated under the door, destroyed his mattress, and kicked the door while yelling that he would kill staff. At about 4:25 p.m. guards D1, M1, R1 and J opened the door. The guards’ account was that the applicant rushed at D1 and tried to punch his head; D1 pushed him back and both D1 and M1 used pepper spray. The applicant’s account was that he was passive and had surrendered; D1 and M1 entered and sprayed him in the face and back; he briefly fainted; guards then dragged him to the security cell. The guards denied he fainted and said he continued insulting them and refused water and care.

After the spray, guard D1 contacted prison doctor T, who said that if only pepper spray had been used, no attendance was needed, but asked for a report in an hour. Later T was told the applicant appeared unharmed but agitated. The applicant was moved to a security cell/restraint bed. He refused examination by prison doctors, considering them biased.

The applicant reported D1 and M1 to the police on 6 April 2017 for aggravated violence. Police interviewed him on 13 November 2017 and the guards in January 2018. There was no video in the observation or security cells or corridor. On 26 January 2018 the police discontinued proceedings because accounts conflicted, the applicant had refused a medical examination, and there were no witnesses or video. The Regional Prosecutor upheld that decision. Separately, the Department of Prisons and Probation on 29 August 2017 found the pepper spray justified under section 62 of the Sentence Enforcement Act to avert imminent violence; although no warning was given, it was not possible in the situation. A procedural complaint found a seven-month investigative delay excessive but the investigation not ineffective; this was upheld in January 2020.

Before the ECtHR, the applicant alleged substantive Article 3 ill-treatment (excessive pepper spray, no warning, inadequate medical care) and procedural Article 3 deficiencies (delayed investigation, late interviews, failure to secure video, lack of independent medical examination). The Court found a violation of the procedural limb of Article 3, while the substantive complaint was not upheld.

**Case of Vasilyev and Others v. Ukraine** (Application no. 29266/08 and 248 others) is a European Court of Human Rights case against Ukraine, decided by the Fifth Section Committee on 13 February 2014. The judgment is final, though subject to editorial revision. The case originated in 249 applications lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by Ukrainian nationals whose details appear in appended tables. The applicants complained chiefly about Ukraine’s failure to enforce final domestic decisions in their favour.

According to the facts, on dates listed in the appended tables, Ukrainian domestic courts and labour disputes commissions issued decisions entitling the applicants to various pecuniary amounts or requiring certain actions to be taken in their favour. These decisions became final and enforceable under domestic law. However, the applicants were unable to obtain their enforcement in due time. This non-enforcement formed the central factual basis for the alleged violations.

The appended table shows the scale and variety of the claims. For example, application no. 29266/08, brought by Aleksandr Nikolayevich Vasilyev, concerned a final decision of the Suvorivskyy District Court of Kherson of 27 September 2005. Other applicants relied on decisions from local, regional, administrative and appellate courts, as well as labour disputes commissions, issued between 1997 and 2011. Many of these decisions concerned unpaid wages, social benefits, pensions or similar employment-related entitlements. The applicants applied to the Strasbourg Court between 2008 and 2012, often several years after the domestic decisions had become final, reflecting prolonged enforcement problems.

Some procedural developments affected the applications. Several applicants—Mr Bulavko, Mr Ponomaryov, Mr Zavarzin and Mr Bondar—died during the proceedings. Their next of kin expressed a wish to maintain the applications. In other applications, domestic court decisions had been delivered in favour of the applicants’ deceased relatives, and the applicants claimed to be lawful successors in title. Some applicants also made submissions concerning factual and legal matters unrelated to the non-enforcement issues.

The Court communicated the applications to the Ukrainian Government on 24 June 2013. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Nazar Kulchytskyy.

The alleged violations arose from the State’s failure to secure timely execution of final and binding domestic judgments. In Convention terms, such non-enforcement typically engages Article 6 § 1, which guarantees the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The applicants essentially alleged that the prolonged inability to enforce decisions in their favour rendered their judicial victories ineffective and imposed a disproportionate burden on them. The case therefore formed part of a broader line of applications against Ukraine concerning systemic non-enforcement of domestic court decisions. The Court was asked to determine whether these delays and failures amounted to violations of the applicants’ Convention rights.

E.K. v. Latvia (Application no. 25942/20) concerns an Article 8 complaint by a Latvian father that the authorities failed to enforce a final court judgment granting him contact with his daughter, D.K. The applicant married I.B.; their daughter was born in 2013. In October 2016, I.B. left the family home and moved more than 200 km away, taking D.K. Divorce and contact proceedings followed. Interim orders granted the applicant contact, but I.B. obstructed it, including by removing D.K. from preschool and homeschooling her. In 2018, the courts dissolved the marriage and set detailed contact rights: initially every other Saturday, later overnight weekend contact, holiday contact, summer contact, and weekly telephone/video calls. The judgment, final in November 2018, warned that non-compliance could lead to fines, suspension of parental authority, or criminal liability.

After the judgment, contact was almost never exercised. I.B. frequently claimed D.K. was ill. On other occasions, D.K. was brought to the meeting place but immediately driven away or refused to go with the applicant. Sometimes no one appeared. Telephone contact was also restricted. A bailiff issued enforcement reports, but the regional court annulled them, reasoning that the bailiff could only verify presence, not assess why the child refused; a child could not be forced, and the issue had to be addressed through review of contact arrangements. The State Inspectorate for the Protection of Children’s Rights agreed that the bailiff or court could not resolve the child’s refusal; the guardianship institution could assess malicious exercise of parental authority or use a contact person.

The applicant repeatedly asked courts to review contact arrangements and asked the Guardianship Institution to suspend I.B.’s parental authority. Domestic courts acknowledged that the judgment was not being enforced. They modified the order: the mother was to hand over the child, third parties were excluded, video calls were required, and later sessions were to begin at the Guardianship Institution with a neutral contact person. Between June 2020 and January 2021, at least 23 such sessions produced no actual contact. Guardianship assessments found that the parental conflict harmed D.K.; I.B. did not prepare the child for meetings, spoke negatively about the father, took the child to numerous specialists, and did not cooperate. It found I.B. used parental authority maliciously by not complying with the judgment, but it refused to suspend her authority because separating D.K. from her mother would cause greater harm.

The Administrative District Court initially ordered suspension of I.B.’s parental authority, finding she had consciously created fear and obstructed contact. The appellate court reversed, holding that forced contact would traumatise the child and that both parents were partly at fault. The Supreme Court upheld that reversal. Psychological assessments noted D.K.’s hostility toward her father, possible maternal influence, acute stress, and dissociation. Criminal proceedings against I.B. for malicious non-compliance began in 2019, with charges brought in 2021. The mother’s civil claim to change contact was dismissed, and her restraining-order requests against the applicant failed.

The alleged violation is that, despite the final contact judgment and domestic recognition that the mother obstructed contact and influenced the child, Latvian institutions failed to secure practical enforcement of the applicant’s family life. The key issue is whether the State’s positive obligations required more effective measures—bailiff enforcement, guardianship action, parental-authority suspension, or contact-person arrangements—to ensure contact while protecting the child’s best interests.
