**Case Summary: Selimyan and Others v. Armenia (Applications nos. 2991/16 and 2 others)**

The case *Selimyan and Others v. Armenia* concerns three applications lodged against Armenia before the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The judgment was delivered by the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, on 16 April 2026. The applicants are Davit Selimyan, Arine Sukiasyans Salmasi, and Taron Simonyan. The core complaint is that they were unlawfully deprived of their liberty, contrary to Article 5 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to liberty and security and requires any deprivation of liberty to be lawful and justified under one of the permitted exceptions.

The key factual details are set out in the appended table to the judgment. All three applicants were arrested on the same date: 23 June 2015. Davit Selimyan was born in 1996 and was represented by Ani Chatinyan, located in Vanadzor. Arine Sukiasyans Salmasi was born in 1979 and was represented by Hasmik Harutyunyan and Araks Melkonyan, both located in Yerevan. Taron Simonyan was born in 1988 and was represented by the same two lawyers from Yerevan. Each applicant introduced their application to the European Court of Human Rights on 23 December 2015—exactly six months after the date of arrest. The applications were registered as nos. 2991/16, 5234/16, and 5294/16.

The Armenian Government was given notice of the complaints under Article 5 § 1 concerning the lawfulness of the applicants’ arrest. This indicates that the central issue communicated to the Government was whether the arrest and subsequent deprivation of liberty complied with the requirements of Article 5 § 1. That provision permits deprivation of liberty only in specific circumstances, such as lawful arrest or detention on reasonable suspicion of an offence, and only in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law. The applicants’ common allegation is therefore that their arrest on 23 June 2015 lacked a proper legal basis, was not carried out in accordance with domestic procedural rules, or otherwise fell outside the exhaustive list of permissible grounds for detention under Article 5 § 1.

The provided judgment extract does not contain a detailed narrative of the circumstances surrounding the arrests. It does not state where the arrests occurred, what suspicions or charges, if any, were involved, which authorities carried them out, how long the applicants were detained, or what domestic legal remedies were pursued. Nor does the extract include the Court’s legal reasoning or final conclusions on the merits. Instead, the factual foundation is limited to the information in the appended table: the applicants’ identities, dates of birth, representatives, date of arrest, and date of application.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are thus narrow but significant. First, all three applicants were deprived of their liberty by Armenian authorities on 23 June 2015. Second, each complained to the European Court that this deprivation of liberty was unlawful under Article 5 § 1. Third, the Government was notified of that specific complaint. Fourth, the applications were filed on 23 December 2015, six months after the arrest. Because the full judgment excerpt does not elaborate on the arrest’s legal basis or the Court’s assessment, the summary is necessarily confined to these essential procedural and factual elements. Any finding of a violation would depend on missing details about whether the arrest complied with Armenian law and whether it fell within an Article 5 § 1 exception.

**Summary of *Dimaksyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 29906/14)**

The case concerns the death of the applicant’s 18-year-old son, M. Dimaksyan, during compulsory military service in the Armenian army, and the subsequent investigation. The applicant, Mr Aleksandr Dimaksyan, lodged the application against Armenia under Articles 2 (right to life) and 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

**Key Facts:**

In November 2010, M. Dimaksyan was drafted and assigned to a military unit of the Nagorno-Karabakh armed forces. On 5 February 2012, while on watch duty at a base near Hadrut, he was shot and killed by a fellow serviceman, G.A. The incident allegedly occurred when G.A.’s assault rifle discharged unintentionally. A criminal investigation was immediately initiated.

The investigation established that on the evening of the incident, G.A. and M. Dimaksyan responded to a noise. G.A. loaded his rifle out of fear. Later, while repositioning, G.A. failed to close the rifle’s trigger guard despite M. Dimaksyan reminding him it was loaded. As G.A. moved, his finger touched the trigger, causing an accidental discharge that fatally wounded M. Dimaksyan. The forensic report confirmed death from a gunshot wound but also noted non-fatal blunt-force injuries on the body (e.g., bruising to the head), which the investigation did not explain.

Critically, an internal military investigation found significant shortcomings: forged safety-training signatures for G.A., poor supervision by commanding officers, and technical failure of the military medical vehicle during the emergency transport of the wounded soldier. The report concluded the death resulted from poor supervision by battalion administration. Disciplinary penalties were reportedly imposed on six officers, though no documents were submitted.

G.A. was charged with breaching weapon-handling rules causing death by negligence. He pleaded guilty. In April 2013, the Regional Court convicted him and sentenced him to four years and six months’ imprisonment. The court’s judgment focused only on G.A.’s actions and did not address the responsibility of the military command for the systemic failures identified, nor did it investigate the unexplained injuries, the delay in medical evacuation, or whether the broken-down vehicle contributed to the death.

The applicant, as the victim’s legal successor, appealed, arguing he could not fully participate (trial held in Stepanakert), and that the courts failed to examine the command’s responsibility and other critical circumstances. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction, stating the first-instance court had fully assessed the arguments. The Court of Cassation declared his appeal inadmissible in September 2013.

**Alleged Violations:**

The applicant complained that the State failed to protect his son’s life (Article 2), that the investigation into the death was inadequate (Article 2), and that he had no possibility to claim compensation for non-pecuniary damage from the State (Article 13). The case raises issues regarding the State’s positive obligation to safeguard the lives of conscripts, the effectiveness of investigations into deaths in military service, and the availability of effective remedies for such violations.

Mokgadi Caster Semenya is a South African international middle-distance athlete and Olympic/world champion. She was born female, raised as a woman, legally recognised as female, and has always identified as a woman. She has a 46 XY difference of sex development (DSD) and naturally elevated testosterone. In 2018, World Athletics (then IAAF) introduced the “Eligibility Regulations for the Female Classification (Athletes with Differences of Sex Development)” (DSD Regulations). These required “Relevant Athletes”—46 XY DSD athletes with testosterone above 5 nmol/L—to take hormone treatment to lower their natural testosterone if they wished to compete in restricted female events, including the 800m, 1500m and mile. Semenya refused, saying the treatment was medically unnecessary, had serious and poorly understood side effects, and forced her to alter her natural body to compete. As a result, she could no longer take part in international competitions.

The background facts relevant to her alleged Convention violations include earlier sex testing after her 2009 World Championships victory, when she was reportedly tested to determine whether she was “biologically male” and told to reduce her testosterone. She underwent hormone treatment despite side effects, then won the 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympic gold. After the 2015 Dutee Chand CAS interim award suspended the previous hyperandrogenism rules, she stopped treatment and won 2016 Olympic gold. The 2018 DSD Regulations applied only to 46 XY DSD athletes, not to XX women with elevated testosterone. Semenya did not dispute that she was a Relevant Athlete but challenged the regulations’ validity.

She lost before the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in an award of 30 April 2019. The CAS majority accepted that the DSD Regulations were discriminatory but found them necessary, reasonable and proportionate to ensure fair competition in female athletics. It accepted evidence that 46 XY DSD athletes had a significant testosterone-related performance advantage in restricted events and that oral contraceptives could lower testosterone without disproportionate side effects. It nevertheless expressed grave concerns about practical compliance, testosterone fluctuations above 5 nmol/L, confidentiality risks, and sparse evidence for the 1500m and mile events. It did not invalidate the regulations. On 25 August 2020, the Swiss Federal Supreme Court dismissed Semenya’s appeal, holding the rules appropriate, necessary and proportionate. It treated the CAS’s seat in Lausanne as the only link with Switzerland and reviewed the award under Swiss arbitration law.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Semenya relied on Articles 3, 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The key alleged violations were: (1) discrimination on grounds of sex and/or DSD status, because only 46 XY DSD women were required to lower natural testosterone; (2) breach of private life, bodily integrity and dignity through compulsory hormone treatment, sex testing/virilisation assessments, and risks of disclosure; (3) inhuman or degrading treatment due to medically unnecessary treatment and side effects; (4) lack of an effective remedy and fair trial, because the CAS arbitration and Swiss Federal Supreme Court review allegedly failed to provide adequate judicial protection. Switzerland’s responsibility arose from the CAS having its seat in Lausanne and the Swiss courts’ refusal to set aside the CAS award.

**Summary of A.T. and Others v. Italy (Application no. 47287/17)**

The case of *A.T. and Others v. Italy* concerns the detention and accommodation conditions of thirteen applicants in an Italian reception facility, or "hotspot," and raises issues under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and 5 (right to liberty and security) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The judgment was delivered by the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) on 23 November 2023.

The key facts are as follows: On 22 May 2017, the thirteen applicants, all young men claiming to be minors at the time, arrived on the Italian coast aboard a makeshift vessel. Their nationalities include Gambian, Guinean, Senegalese, Malian, Ivoirian, Bangladeshi, and Ghanian. Upon arrival, they alleged that they declared themselves to be minors. Despite these claims, they were transferred to the Taranto Early Reception and Aid Centre (CSPA), which had been designated as an Italian hotspot under Decree-Law no. 13 of 17 February 2017. While at the hotspot, their photographs and fingerprints were taken. The following day, on 23 May 2017, they formally requested international protection.

The core of the applicants' complaint centres on their confinement within this hotspot facility. They alleged that they were effectively detained there and that the conditions of their accommodation were poor and inadequate. They remained in this facility for a significant period. The situation changed only after they submitted a request to the European Court of Human Rights under Rule 39 (interim measures). In response to this request, on 13 July 2017, applicants Mr I.C., Mr M.J., and Mr K.I.S. were transferred to facilities specifically for unaccompanied minors. Another applicant, Mr A.T., was transferred to a facility for minors on 15 July 2017.

Subsequent legal developments were inconsistent. According to information provided by the Italian Government, the Taranto Juvenile Court decided on 28 July 2017 that three of the applicants (I.C., M.J., and K.I.S.) should be taken into the care of social services and have a legal guardian appointed. However, no such information was provided regarding Mr A.T. It appears that the public prosecutor did not submit a request on his behalf because he had been transferred to a region outside the Taranto Juvenile Court's jurisdiction.

The applicants were represented by Mr D. Belluccio, and the Italian Government by Mr L. D’Ascia. The Court also received third-party interventions from several organizations, including Defence for Children International, the International Commission of Jurists (ICJ), the AIRE Centre, the European Council on Refugees and Exiles (ECRE), and the Dutch Council for Refugees.

The central factual allegation is that these individuals, who claimed to be minors and were therefore entitled to special protection, were held in a hotspot facility under conditions that amounted to a deprivation of liberty and constituted ill-treatment, before eventually being moved to more appropriate facilities for minors following the Court's intervention.

**Summary of O.G. v. Latvia (Application no. 66095/09)**

The case of *O.G. v. Latvia* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by a Latvian national, Mr O.G., who alleged that his confinement to a psychiatric hospital was illegal. The key facts revolve around two sets of criminal proceedings and the subsequent imposition of compulsory psychiatric measures.

In March 2004, criminal proceedings for internet fraud were initiated against the applicant. During this first set of proceedings, he underwent two inpatient psychiatric examinations and was found to have full mental capacity. In October 2006, he was convicted and given a suspended sentence. However, during the appeal hearings in early 2007, the Riga Regional Court noted the applicant's aggressive and illogical behaviour and ordered an outpatient psychiatric assessment. In April 2007, a psychiatrist diagnosed him with chronic paranoid schizophrenia and recommended outpatient treatment. Consequently, in June 2007, a judge initiated proceedings to apply a compulsory medical measure. A crucial decision was made to examine the case in the applicant's absence, appointing his mother as his legal representative. When she could not attend a subsequent hearing, the court, with the consent of the applicant's counsel, appointed D.A., a psychiatrist involved in his treatment, as his legal representative.

A further inpatient assessment in November 2007 concluded that the applicant was unable to control his actions at the time of the offence and recommended relieving him of criminal liability. On 18 February 2008, the Riga Regional Court imposed a compulsory measure of outpatient psychiatric treatment. This decision was not appealed and became final.

A second set of criminal proceedings for fraud was initiated in March 2007. Based on a new forensic psychiatric assessment in October 2007, which again found him unable to participate in proceedings, the prosecutor decided to pursue a compulsory medical measure. In February 2008, D.A. was again appointed as his legal representative.

On 19 August 2008, the Riga Regional Court held a hearing in the applicant's absence to decide on the compulsory measure. He was represented by a lawyer, A.Ā., and D.A. was also present. The court heard testimony from D.A. and an expert psychiatrist, both of whom recommended involuntary inpatient treatment, a view concurred with by the defence counsel and prosecutor. The following day, the court ordered the applicant's inpatient treatment in a psychiatric hospital. This decision was not appealed in time by his representatives and became final on 2 September 2008.

The applicant only learned of this decision later and attempted to appeal, but was informed by the court that he lacked the standing to do so as his representatives had not appealed. He was taken to a psychiatric hospital by police on 22 October 2009. He was released on 7 June 2010.

**Key Facts Relevant to the Alleged Violation:**

The central issue is the lawfulness of the applicant's involuntary confinement. The key facts are:
- The final decision ordering his inpatient treatment (20 August 2008) was made in his absence.
- He was represented by a court-appointed psychiatrist (D.A.) who was also his treating doctor and recommended inpatient treatment.
- The applicant himself was not present at the hearing and was not represented by a lawyer of his own choosing.
- After the decision became final, he was not permitted to appeal against it because he had not been present at the hearing, a procedure explicitly permitted by domestic law.
- The decision was not enforced until over a year later, after he had been complying with a previous, separate outpatient treatment order.
- He was not informed of the final decision for a significant period.

The case of *Vanesyan and Others v. Armenia* concerns three applications lodged against Armenia with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants all complained of the excessive length of their pre-trial detention. In one application, no. 38190/23, the applicant also raised a complaint under Article 5 § 1 (c) of the Convention. The Armenian Government was given notice of the applications. The Fifth Section Committee, composed of Andreas Zünd, Diana Sârcu and Mykola Gnatovskyy, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 5 February 2026 and delivered judgment on 26 February 2026. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The first application, no. 35710/22, was introduced on 12 July 2022 by Samvel Vanesyan, born in 1954, represented by Hayk Alumyan in Yerevan. Vanesyan was detained from 3 June 2020 to 23 January 2023. His detention therefore lasted 2 years, 7 months and 21 days. The detention order and related appeals were examined by the First Instance Court of General Jurisdiction of Yerevan, the Lori Regional Court and the Criminal Court of Appeal. His complaint before the European Court focused on the excessive length of this pre-trial detention.

The second application, no. 8336/23, was introduced on 4 February 2023 by Hovsep Ashkarian, born in 1999, represented by Liparit Simonyan in Yerevan. Ashkarian was detained from 7 October 2020 to 13 October 2023. His total detention lasted 3 years and 7 days. The relevant detention order and appeal review were handled by the First Instance Court of General Jurisdiction of Yerevan and the Criminal Court of Appeal. He likewise complained that the length of his pre-trial detention was excessive.

The third application, no. 38190/23, was introduced on 7 October 2023 by Samvel Grigoryan, born in 2001, also represented by Liparit Simonyan in Yerevan. Grigoryan was detained from 21 August 2021 to 21 August 2025, a total length of 4 years and 1 day. The courts identified in connection with his detention were the Syunik Regional Court, the First Instance Criminal Court of General Jurisdiction of Yerevan and the Criminal Court of Appeal. In addition to the excessive-length complaint, Grigoryan also alleged a violation of Article 5 § 1 (c) of the Convention, concerning the lawfulness of his arrest or detention.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the prolonged periods of pre-trial detention imposed on each applicant. The shortest period complained of exceeded two years and seven months, while the longest exceeded four years. Each period was authorised or reviewed by domestic courts at first-instance, regional and appellate levels. The applicants’ central complaint was that these detentions were excessively long. For Grigoryan, the case also raises the additional issue of whether his detention satisfied the requirements of Article 5 § 1 (c). The appended table supplies the core factual details, while the available text does not set out further background such as the specific charges, evidence, or reasons given by the domestic courts for continuing detention.

In *V v. the Czech Republic*, the European Court of Human Rights examined the death of the applicant’s brother, P.Z., a 30-year-old man suffering from paranoid schizophrenia, after police used a taser at a psychiatric clinic and a nurse administered tranquillisers. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention concerning both the death and the ensuing criminal investigation.

On the evening of 5 November 2015, P.Z.’s family called an emergency line after he became aggressive and threatened relatives. He was taken by ambulance, accompanied by police, to the Psychiatric Clinic of Olomouc University Hospital and admitted to acute care. After examination, he calmed down, agreed to antipsychotic medication (Haloperidol and Apaurin), and was placed in an ordinary room.

Early on 6 November, at about 4 a.m., P.Z. became restless. Staff began preparing an intensive/seclusion room. Following a verbal altercation, he damaged fixtures and doors. When an orderly tried to stop him taking a fire hose, P.Z. knocked him down and severely beat him; staff said he tried to strangle the orderly with the hose. He later ripped ceiling tiles, pulled out electrical wires, and sprayed water on them. Two unarmed security guards failed to subdue him. A nurse called the police at 4:53 a.m.; four officers arrived around 5 a.m.

The applicant, relying on the Public Defender of Rights’ report, disputed the official account. She claimed P.Z.’s behaviour was largely defensive and triggered by realisation that a seclusion room was being prepared. She alleged police acted hastily, only briefly consulted a nurse who had not witnessed the attack, made no attempt to communicate with P.Z., and did not shut off water or electricity. The police claimed immediate intervention was necessary because P.Z. was spraying water onto live electrical wires, threatening everyone present. In a narrow 2.25-metre corridor, officers used a mattress as a shield and forced P.Z. to the ground, but could not restrain him. Officer T. warned P.Z., then fired a taser at his lower back from about 1.5 metres. Because P.Z. continued resisting, the taser was fired repeatedly at another officer’s request. The taser record showed three discharges lasting eight, eleven, and ten seconds. A nurse then administered Apaurin and Tisercin injections at 5:05 a.m. P.Z. became cyanotic, had no palpable pulse, and resuscitation failed. He was pronounced dead at 6:08 a.m., likely from cardiac arrest.

A medical expert report found the immediate cause of death was cardiac arrhythmia. It could not establish unequivocally whether or to what extent natural causes were responsible. Possible contributory factors included stress from the psychotic episode, medication, and the repeated taser use, though the darts were not aimed at the chest or heart. An autopsy revealed a coronary artery anomaly of unclear relevance. Experts were not asked about any interaction between the medication and the taser.

The General Inspectorate of the Security Forces investigated suspected negligent homicide. On 6 April 2016, it set aside the case, finding the police intervention lawful. It concluded that P.Z. posed a direct threat, no other means were available, and the repeated tasering was justified by continuing resistance and aimed away from vital organs. Prosecutors rejected the family’s complaints, and the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s constitutional appeal. The Public Defender of Rights later criticised the legal classification and training regarding tasers, inadequate police oversight, and the general disproportionality of tasering a person already on the ground restrained by officers, unless exceptional circumstances existed, such as a risk of electric shock. She also questioned whether the danger remained imminent and noted that positional asphyxia had not been examined. The applicant’s Article 2 and 3 complaints concerning the death and investigation were communicated to the Government.

Humpert and Others v. Germany (ECtHR Grand Chamber, 14 Dec 2023) concerns four German nationals—Karin Humpert, Kerstin Wienrank, Eberhard Grabs, and Monika Dahl—who were State school teachers with civil servant status (Beamte) in different German Länder. All belonged to the Trade Union for Education and Science. During working hours they participated in union-organised strikes, including demonstrations, protesting worsening working conditions and seeking collective bargaining advances for contractual State employees in education, with results transferred to civil servants.

They were disciplined. Humpert, a primary teacher, was reprimanded for a strike on 3 June 2010 and missed lessons. Wien

The case *Borzenkov and Others v Russia* concerns three applications against Russia lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained principally of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment, with some also raising other Convention complaints. The key facts concern alleged physical ill-treatment by Russian law-enforcement officers, contemporaneous medical evidence, and largely unsuccessful domestic complaints.

**Application no. 5841/23 – Daniil Konstantinovich Borzenkov (born 2001).** On 24 February 2022 at about 9:15 p.m., Russian Guards officers apprehended Borzenkov while he was on his way to a Moscow demonstration against the war in Ukraine. He alleged that officers hit him with rubber truncheons on the ribs, head and legs. He was taken to the Mezchanskiy police station in Moscow, where an administrative offence record was drawn up. A medical certificate dated 25 February 2022 from Moscow City Polyclinic No. 62 recorded a contusion of the soft tissues of the left thigh. On 4 March 2022 he complained to the Tverskoy District Investigative Department in Moscow; on 28 March 2022 the complaint was transferred to the Internal Security Department of the Moscow Police, and he received no further information. His appeal under Article 125 of the Russian Code of Criminal Procedure against the authorities’ inaction was dismissed on 28 July 2022 for lack of subject-matter, upheld by the Moscow City Court on 4 October 2022. He was fined under Article 20.2(5) of the Administrative Offences Code, final on 9 September 2022.

**Application no. 7877/23 – Natalya Borisovna Krisko (born 1967).** On 1 June 2020 at about 7 p.m. in the Krasnodar region, Krisko alleged that intoxicated police officers grabbed her by the wrists and pushed her down, causing her to hit the back of her head on the steps of a bank. She was allegedly held against the railing of the stairs for 20–30 minutes in front of passers-by. Medical evidence included an ambulance call card of 1 June 2020 and an extract from her medical record of 2 June 2020 from Kurganinskiy Central District Hospital, recording bruises to the chest and upper limbs and bruising; photographs of injuries were also taken. She complained on 3 June 2020 to the Labinskiy Inter-district Investigative Committee. Between 3 July 2020 and 23 October 2021, there were nine refusals to open a criminal case. Her Article 125 appeal against the last refusal was dismissed on 9 August 2022 and upheld by the Krasnodar Regional Court on 20 October 2022. She was not charged with any offence.

**Application no. 11065/23 – Kseniya Vladimirovna Viktorova (born 1977).** On 21 April 2021, while on her way to a rally protesting the arrest of opposition politician A. Navalnyy, Viktorova was forcibly apprehended by police. Officers allegedly used a rubber truncheon and a stun gun against her. She was taken to a police station for preparation of an offence report. The following day she saw a doctor, who documented contusions to the left forearm, right and left hips, and left knee joint. She first complained to the 16th police department in St Petersburg on 15 May 2021. Refusals to open a criminal case were issued on 27 July 2021 and 28 July 2022. Her Article 125 appeal against the refusal of 28 July 2022 was dismissed by the Oktyabrskiy District Court in St Petersburg on 2 November 2022, upheld on appeal on 18 January 2023.

In essence, each applicant alleged physical ill-treatment by police or Guards in the context of protests or public encounters, supported by medical documentation, and each faced refusals, inaction, or unsuccessful domestic court challenges. The case therefore centres on alleged Article 3 ill-treatment and the effectiveness of domestic investigation and remedies.

**Case: Ugulava v. Georgia (Application no. 5432/15)**

The case concerns Giorgi Ugulava, a Georgian national, former Tbilisi mayor and a leader of the opposition United National Movement. He complained under Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention that his pre-trial detention was unlawful and arbitrary, and under Article 18 read with Article 5 § 1 that it was politically motivated.

After the Georgian Dream coalition came to power in 2012, several criminal proceedings were opened against Ugulava. In earlier cases, he was charged with embezzlement, money laundering and related offences. Courts initially refused bail or imposed lesser measures, but the cases formed a backdrop to later detention decisions.

The key detention arose from a fourth set of proceedings. On 5 June 2014 an investigation began into an alleged violent incident at the Marneuli district electoral commission. Separately, a money-laundering investigation was opened after two individuals alleged that Ugulava had invited them into an offshore scheme. On the evening of 2 July 2014, an investigator summoned Ugulava for questioning at 10 a.m. on 4 July. Ugulava stated that he had a pre-planned business trip to Kyiv on 3 July but would shorten it and return early on 4 July. Later that night, a key witness, G.K., alleged that Ugulava had threatened him.

On 3 July 2014 at 5:57 a.m., Ugulava was arrested at Tbilisi International Airport. The arrest report cited aggravated money laundering and relied on the risk of absconding under Article 171 § 2(e) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, without a prior judicial warrant. His lawyers were allegedly denied immediate access to him for four to five hours and denied access to the case file. On 4 July 2014, the money-laundering case was merged with the Marneuli case, and he was charged with money laundering, forgery, coercion and organising activity disrupting public order.

The prosecution sought pre-trial detention, arguing flight risk based on his foreign contacts, frequent travel and attempt to leave despite the summons; risk of influencing witnesses, relying on G.K.’s statement; and risk of reoffending because he had allegedly committed offences while on bail. The defence argued that the arrest was unlawful, lacked factual basis, and that Ugulava had cooperated and informed authorities of his travel. On 4 July 2014, the Tbilisi City Court remanded him in custody, citing reasonable suspicion, gravity of charges, flight risk, obstruction and witness influence. The Court of Appeal upheld this on 8 July 2014.

In February 2015, Ugulava unsuccessfully sought release on bail. The court found the original grounds still valid and said the witness-tampering risk had increased after the prosecution witness list was confirmed. Meanwhile, a fifth set of proceedings was opened concerning the Imedi television company and Lynx Ltd. In March 2015, new charges were brought. The prosecution requested a fresh pre-trial detention order even though the original nine-month detention period was due to expire on 2 April 2015. The defence objected that this was unconstitutional, that the investigation was complete, and that the charges duplicated earlier proceedings. On 15 March 2015, the Tbilisi City Court granted a new detention order without addressing the time-limit objection. The appellate court held that the nine-month period could be calculated separately for different criminal cases.

Ugulava lodged a constitutional complaint. On 15 September 2015, the Constitutional Court ruled that Article 205 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was unconstitutional insofar as it allowed detention where the accused had already spent nine months in pre-trial detention in any other pending case at the time of the new indictment. On 17 September 2015, after fifteen months in detention, Ugulava was released. He alleged that his detention had been arbitrary, inadequately reviewed and politically motivated.

In *Lang v. Ukraine* (Application no. 49134/20), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) considered whether Ukraine’s decision to extradite the applicant, Craig Austin Lang, to the United States would violate Article 3 of the Convention. The applicant, a US national and former US Army serviceman, had travelled to Ukraine several times between 2015 and 2019 and served in Ukrainian armed formations fighting in eastern Ukraine. He was arrested on 21 August 2019 while re-entering Ukraine from Moldova and was later released on his own recognisance.

On 25 September 2019, the United States requested his extradition under the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime. In February 2020, the US expanded the request and added further charges. The amended request listed federal charges in Florida, Arizona, and North Carolina. In the US District Court for the Middle District of Florida, the applicant faced charges including conspiracy to interfere with commerce by violence; interference with commerce by violence; conspiracy to carry and use a firearm during a crime of violence; use and discharge of a firearm during a crime of violence resulting in murder; conspiracy to kill, kidnap, maim or injure persons in Venezuela; and violation of the Neutrality Act. The potential penalties included life imprisonment for the firearm-murder charge and for conspiracy to murder or kidnap, as well as the death penalty for the firearm-murder charge. The Florida charges alleged that the applicant and a co-conspirator had proposed to sell firearms to lure a victim to a meeting with cash, then shot and killed the victim and another person, took the money, and planned to use the funds to travel to Venezuela to fight the regime there.

The applicant also faced charges in Arizona for misuse of a passport, and in North Carolina for passport fraud, aggravated identity theft, visa fraud and misuse, and false representation of a Social Security number.

On 15 October 2019, the US Embassy in Kyiv assured the General Prosecutor’s Office of Ukraine (“GPO”) that the death penalty would not be sought or imposed on the applicant and that he would not be prosecuted for offences committed before extradition other than those for which extradition was granted. On 17 October and 4 November 2019, the applicant asked the GPO to request assurances that he would not be sentenced to death and that he would have an opportunity to seek reduction of any life sentence imposed. He relied on *Trabelsi v. Belgium*, where the Court held that the power of presidential pardon in the US did not satisfy Article 3 requirements. The GPO replied that death penalty assurances had been requested. On 4 August 2020, the US Department of Justice reiterated the death penalty assurances.

On 28 August 2020, the GPO granted the extradition request, finding legal grounds and noting the death penalty assurances. The applicant appealed, arguing that no adequate assurances had been provided concerning the reducibility of any life sentence. On 15 March 2021, the Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld the extradition decision, finding that the charges were extraditable, not time-barred, and that his asylum applications had been rejected.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that extradition would violate Article 3 because, if convicted, he risked receiving an irreducible life sentence. The Court gave notice of the Article 3 complaint, declared the remainder inadmissible, and indicated an interim measure under Rule 39. The central alleged violation was therefore that Ukraine sought to extradite him despite the risk of irreducible life imprisonment and without sufficient assurances that any life sentence would be reducible.

In *Zubco and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Applications nos. 49508/15 and 2 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 19 February 2026. The case mainly concerns alleged restrictions by the authorities of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”) on the applicants’ rights to freedom of expression and freedom of assembly, in the territory of the Republic of Moldova. Several applicants also alleged unlawful deprivation of liberty and inhuman detention conditions. The applicants relied principally on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention; some also invoked Articles 3, 5 § 1, 6, 8 and 13, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

The first applicant, Alexandru Zubco, was born in the “MRT” and was a member of an NGO defending human rights in the region. His family continued to live in the “MRT”. On 15 April 2014, he was denied access to the “MRT” after the “KGB” imposed a ban on him because of his human rights activities. He challenged the ban in the “MRT courts” but was unsuccessful. The “Supreme Court of Justice of the MRT” gave a final decision on 26 February 2015, served on him on 8 April 2015. His main complaint was under Article 10, alleging interference with his freedom of expression.

The second application was brought by Vladimir Yegorov, a Russian journalist and human rights activist, and NP “IPC Apriori”, an “MRT”-based human rights NGO. The NGO invited Yegorov to act as an international observer to monitor and publicly cover the “MRT presidential elections” of 11 December 2016. He was also invited to speak at several public events organised by the NGO. On 8 December 2016, when he attempted to enter the “MRT” from territory under the sovereign control of Moldova, the “KGB” refused him entry. The applicants challenged that refusal in the “MRT courts”. On 11 May 2017, the “Supreme Court of Justice of the MRT” rejected their claims without examining them, on the ground that they had failed to submit valid powers of attorney. The applicants complained under Article 10 (interference with freedom of expression) and Article 11, namely Yegorov’s restriction on participation in a public event and the NGO’s restriction on organising a public event.

The third application, *Jukoveţ and Others*, concerned a peaceful public meeting held in Tiraspol (“MRT”) on 2 June 2018, organised by the “Communist Party”. The “Tiraspol district court” imposed administrative sanctions on the applicants for participating in an unauthorised meeting. Maria Jukoveţ received six days’ administrative arrest and was detained from 7 to 13 June 2018 in cells nos. 3 and 6 of the “Tiraspol militia” pre-trial detention centre. Alexandr Samonii received fourteen days’ arrest and was detained from 11 to 25 June 2018 in cell no. 15. Alexander Nevskiy received ten days’ arrest and was detained from 2 to 12 June 2018 in cells nos. 20, 3 and 15. Antonina Samonii, Vera Kaput and Nadezhda Bondarenko were each fined 368 Transnistrian roubles (about €19.50 at the time).

These applicants alleged that they were held for between 6 and 14 days in the same detention centre in inhuman conditions. They claimed overcrowding, with under 4 sq. m of personal space per detainee, and a deplorable state, including insufficient electric lighting, clogged toilets not separated from the cell, inadequate bedding and linen, lack of fresh air, toiletries, adequate food, potable water, showers and medical assistance. Some challenged the district court decisions before the “Supreme Court of Justice of the MRT”, without success. Their complaints concerned Article 11 (punishment for participating in a peaceful public assembly); some also alleged Article 3 (inhuman conditions of detention) and Article 5 § 1 (unlawful deprivation of liberty).

The case *Shkuropatskyy and Others v. Ukraine* comprises four applications against Ukraine (nos. 9085/24, 6025/25, 11089/25 and 14768/25) lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Fifth Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 16 April 2026, adopted after private deliberations on 26 March 2026. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law.

The appended table provides the key facts relevant to those allegations.

**Anton Yevgenovych Shkuropatskyy** (born 1991), represented by O. O. Pogibko (Odesa), introduced application no. 9085/24 on 29 February 2024. His civil proceedings began on 25 November 2021 and were still pending. The total duration was recorded as more than 4 years, 1 month and 29 days, involving two levels of jurisdiction. Because the proceedings had not ended, the alleged excessive length was ongoing.

**Anatoliy Anatoliyovych Govorukha** (born 1972), represented by R. V. Serdyuk (Prosyana), introduced application no. 6025/25 on 14 February 2025. His civil proceedings began on 16 March 2016 and ended on 16 October 2024. They lasted 8 years, 7 months and 1 day, across three levels of jurisdiction.

**Yevgeniya Valeriyivna Pankina** (born 1986) introduced application no. 11089/25 on 7 April 2025. Her civil proceedings began on 2 April 2018 and ended on 9 December 2024. They lasted 6 years, 8 months and 8 days, across three levels of jurisdiction.

**Volodymyr Anatoliyovych Shylin** (born 1969) introduced application no. 14768/25 on 10 April 2025. His civil proceedings began on 13 January 2022 and ended on 16 April 2025. They lasted 3 years, 3 months and 4 days, at one level of jurisdiction.

The central alleged violation is therefore the unreasonable duration of civil litigation. The longest periods are those of Govorukha, whose case lasted over eight and a half years, and Pankina, whose case lasted almost seven years; both involved three judicial levels. Shkuropatskyy’s case is significant because the proceedings remained pending after more than four years. Shylin’s case is shorter but still exceeded three years at a single level. The applicants also allege that Ukrainian law did not provide an effective domestic remedy by which they could challenge or obtain redress for those delays. These complaints ordinarily engage the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and the right to an effective remedy.

The provided extract sets out the procedural background and factual details from the appended table, but it does not include the Court’s full legal reasoning, findings on admissibility or merits, or the final operative order. The key factual focus for assessing the alleged violations is the total duration of each civil proceeding, the number of jurisdictional levels involved, whether the proceedings were pending or concluded, and the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy.

Zaghini v. San Marino (no. 3405/21) concerns San Marino’s confiscation of EUR 1,892,700 connected to Gianluca Zaghini, an Italian national, after money-laundering proceedings against other persons, not him. He alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, complaining he could not recover the money despite an Italian judgment ordering restitution.

In 2003 Italy investigated Zaghini for tax evasion and unjust profits of about EUR 15 million. Through international letters rogatory, San Marino authorities searched assets linked to Zaghini’s father, G.A. and P.A. They found a bank account in Zaghini’s name and a safe deposit box in G.A.’s name containing EUR 1,892,700. Zaghini’s father had withdrawn EUR 939,500 and EUR 1,006,700 in cash from Zaghini’s account in December 2003. Evidence showed the father gave EUR 1,903,700 to P.A., who asked G.A. to open the safe deposit box; G.A. deposited EUR 1,892,700, while the father and P.A. kept EUR 12,000 and EUR 11,000. In January 2004 San Marino began money-laundering proceedings against the father, G.A. and P.A., not Zaghini. Zaghini’s Italian pre-trial statements admitted depositing about EUR 1.8 million in San Marino from illegal activity.

In 2005 the three co-accused were convicted of money laundering; confiscation of the seized sum was ordered. In 2008 the appeal confirmed the father’s and P.A.’s guilt and confiscation, while G.A.’s case became time-barred. The San Marino courts found the money came from crimes with which Zaghini was charged in Italy; a final Italian judgment was unnecessary, and Zaghini had asked the accused to hide the money while under house arrest. A 2008 execution order confiscated EUR 1,892,700 plus interest under Article 147(3) of the Criminal Code, which made confiscation mandatory for money laundering.

In Italy, Zaghini was convicted at first instance in 2012, but in 2016 the Court of Appeal of Bologna declared the proceedings time-barred and ordered restitution of money preventively seized. From 2017, Zaghini unsuccessfully asked San Marino’s judge for international cooperation to release the funds. The judge rejected the requests because the sums had already been confiscated in the San Marino criminal case and Zaghini was not an extraneous third party: he was the predicate offender and was only spared money-laundering charges because domestic law then barred prosecuting him for laundering. Appeals failed.

In 2018 Zaghini asked the Enforcement Judge to annul the confiscation based on the Italian judgment. This was rejected: the illicit origin of the funds had been established by San Marino courts independently of any Italian conviction, and the Italian time-bar did not mean innocence. The judge relied on Zaghini’s own statements and found he had instigated the movement of money and had not shown a licit origin. The second-instance judge in 2019 upheld the decision, finding the Enforcement Judge competent and that Zaghini had had an adversarial hearing but could not overturn final criminal findings. The third-instance judge rejected further appeals in 2020, confirming the confiscation could not be revoked.

The key alleged violation was therefore that confiscation of Zaghini’s funds in proceedings to which he was not a party left him without an effective remedy to recover his property, despite the Italian restitution order. The Court gave notice only of the Article 1 Protocol No. 1 complaint.

**Case Remez v. Ukraine (Application no. 25395/19)** concerns the alleged ineffectiveness of Ukraine’s investigation into ill-treatment suffered by a minor, Sofiya Andriyivna Remez, during her father’s failed attempt to kidnap her. The applicant, a Ukrainian national born in 2014, was represented by her mother, Anastasiya Viktorovna Gaybadulova. The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 June 2019. The applicant complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention.

The key facts begin on 8 June 2017, when the applicant—then two years and eight months old—was walking on a suburban street in Kherson with her grandmother. Her father, the former husband of her mother, grabbed her from her grandmother’s hands and pushed her into a nearby car. Bystanders intervened and stopped the attempted kidnapping. The same day, the applicant’s mother complained to the Korabelnyi District Police Department in Kherson, which immediately ordered a forensic medical examination.

On 8 June 2017, a paediatrician diagnosed the applicant with abrasions and haematomas of the upper limbs and torso. On 9 June 2017, a forensic medical doctor examined her and found abrasions and haematomas on both forearms and a bruise on the left abdomen beneath the costal arch. The doctor concluded that the injuries were minor and could not have resulted from a fall from the applicant’s height. That same day, the police opened criminal case no. 12017230020002105 concerning the infliction of minor bodily injuries under Article 125 § 1 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.

On 30 June 2017, the police closed the criminal case for lack of evidence. On 10 October 2017, the Kherson City Court quashed that closure, citing lack of reasoning and the police’s failure to take any procedural action other than ordering the forensic examination. On 25 December 2017, the police again closed the case for lack of evidence. On 5 April 2018, the Kherson City Court quashed that decision for procedural irregularities, including the failure to send the closure decision to the applicant, represented by her mother, or to submit it to the court.

The applicant’s mother repeatedly sought procedural action. On 19 December 2017, 17 May, 30 July, and 27 November 2018, she lodged applications with the police asking for specific investigative steps. On 16 January, 6 June, 16 August, and 17 December 2018, she complained to the Kherson City Court about police inactivity, and the court ordered the police to examine her applications.

On 16 November and 28 December 2018, the Kherson Regional Police Department wrote to the applicant’s mother acknowledging the ineffectiveness of the investigation. It informed her that investigator B. had been dismissed for failing to perform his duties and that investigator K. had been assigned to the case. The new investigator was given instructions from the prosecutor’s office dated 23 February 2018 and was ordered to accelerate the investigation.

On 8 January 2019, the mother again asked the police to perform procedural actions, including questioning her as a victim, questioning eyewitnesses, and informing her of the investigation’s results. On 12 February 2019, the Kherson City Court ordered the police to examine that application. On 13 February 2019, the police rejected it on the ground that the applicant was not a party to the criminal proceedings. On 27 March 2019, the Kherson City Court overturned that refusal and found the refusal to perform certain procedural actions unlawful. On 8 September 2021, the police closed the criminal case for lack of evidence.

These facts—prompt medical evidence of injury, repeated closures for lack of evidence, repeated judicial findings of procedural defects, prolonged failure to question the victim and witnesses, refusal to recognise the mother’s procedural role, acknowledged investigative ineffectiveness, and eventual closure years later—form the factual basis for the applicant’s complaints that the investigation was ineffective and that she lacked an effective remedy.

In **Lukashuk v. Ukraine** (Application no. 9079/24), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined an application lodged on 13 March 2024. The applicant, Artem Mykhaylovych Lukashuk, born in 2002, complained under Article 3 of the Convention that Ukraine had failed to conduct an effective investigation into ill-treatment he suffered at the hands of private individuals.

The key underlying facts occurred on 1 March 2019, when the applicant was 16 years old. He was punched in the face by a certain Ch., who was 15 years old. As a result, the applicant sustained a fracture of his nasal bones. On 3 March 2019, the applicant’s mother lodged a criminal complaint. An investigation was launched on 14 March 2019, and a preliminary medical examination was carried out on 19 March 2019. Thus, the initial reaction of the domestic authorities was relatively prompt.

However, the investigation did not proceed effectively thereafter. It was terminated several times by the investigator’s decisions—on 23 September 2019, 25 December 2019, 27 May 2020, and 27 February 2023. Each of those termination decisions was subsequently quashed as unsubstantiated by a prosecutor or an investigating judge—on 5 November 2019, 6 February 2020, 23 November 2020, and 27 April 2023. This repeated cycle of termination and reversal meant that the investigation failed to make meaningful progress for years.

It was only in July 2023—more than four years after the incident—that the investigator obtained a statement from Ch. Finally, on 26 June 2024, the investigation was closed due to the lack of constituent elements of a crime. By that time, more than five years had passed since the applicant’s injury.

The applicant’s Article 3 complaint did not concern the original alleged assault itself, but rather the State’s procedural obligation to investigate. Under Article 3, where there is a credible allegation of ill-treatment, the authorities must conduct an effective, prompt, thorough, and impartial investigation capable of identifying and, where appropriate, punishing those responsible. Even where the alleged ill-treatment is inflicted by private individuals, the State may be required to maintain effective criminal-law mechanisms and to investigate adequately.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation therefore include: the applicant’s young age and serious facial injury; the timely criminal complaint and initial investigative steps; the repeated termination of proceedings and subsequent quashing of those decisions; the lengthy delay in obtaining the alleged perpetrator’s statement; and the final closure of the investigation in June 2024 for lack of constituent elements of a crime. These circumstances formed the basis for the applicant’s claim that the domestic investigation was not effective for the purposes of Article 3.

The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the application. The Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Andreas Zünd, Diana Sârcu, and Mykola Gnatovskyy, deliberated in private on 18 December 2025 and adopted the judgment on 22 January 2026. The provided text sets out the procedural history and factual background relevant to the Article 3 complaint; it does not include the Court’s final merits conclusion.

**Dzyon v. Ukraine (Application no. 44249/17)** concerns an Article 2 complaint by Mr Valentyn Dzyon, a Ukrainian national, that State agents were responsible for his son’s death and that the ensuing investigation was ineffective.

The applicant’s son, a police investigator at the Staromiskyi district police station in Vinnytsya, died on 19 May 2010 from a gunshot wound to the chest in his office. He also had scratches and bruises on his head. The pistol found at the scene belonged to his superior, S. The same day, the police station was inspected.

Forensic examinations concluded that the bullet entered the front of the chest, exited the back, was fired from close range from in front of the deceased, and followed a downward trajectory. Experts ruled out a shot from behind. The son could have been sitting behind his desk. There was no objective evidence that his body had been moved after death. The head injuries could have occurred shortly before death, possibly through contact with blunt objects such as the pistol bolt or surrounding objects during a fall. No other injuries suggesting assault or struggle were found. Experts also noted no signs of increased suggestibility, fantasising, or suicidal ideation.

The applicant testified that his son had had work-related disputes with superiors K. and S. On the day of his death, the son allegedly told his mother that K. and S. were “bitches.” Later, K. telephoned the applicant, saying the son had barricaded himself in his office and that K. “did not want to go to prison.” The applicant later alleged that K. and S. had pressured his son to arrest a suspect, L., in order to take a bribe; when he refused, he was allegedly beaten and shot by superiors and colleagues. His wife and other son corroborated this. L.’s lawyer confirmed an argument about the arrest.

S. claimed he had left his service pistol in a safe, with the key in a drawer. He said that after access to the son’s office was obtained, he heard a gunshot and found the son had shot himself. K. partly confirmed this, describing the son as quiet and introverted but without open conflict. Another investigator, Ts., saw the son slumped over the desk with a pistol in his right hand after the shot. Other colleagues described a generally friendly atmosphere but noted the son was isolated and often stayed late.

The investigation was lengthy and contradictory. Initially opened for official negligence, it led to S. being charged and, in 2013, convicted with a suspended sentence. The court rejected the applicant’s murder allegations. However, the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal quashed that decision due to numerous contradictions and inconsistencies in witness statements and forensic evidence, ordering a fresh investigation. It noted that the authorities had not properly examined the lack of motive for suicide, the murder allegation, or the claim that the son had stolen S.’s pistol.

A new investigation was opened in 2013 into murder, theft of a weapon, abuse of power, and expert misconduct. Numerous further examinations and witness interviews followed. In 2020, proceedings against S. for negligent storage of a weapon and official negligence were terminated because the limitation period had expired, a decision upheld on appeal and by the Supreme Court. In 2022, an additional forensic medical report found that the head bruises could not have resulted from an agonal fall and questioned witness accounts of the son’s position when shot. In 2024, an investigation was opened into alleged torture and murder by colleagues and joined to the main proceedings. The investigation remains ongoing.

The applicant complains under Article 2 that State agents caused his son’s death and that the investigation was ineffective, delayed, and failed to resolve serious contradictions in the evidence.

In *Novák v. the Czech Republic*, the applicant is a Czech father of two daughters, born in 2014 and 2018. In April 2021, after he and the children’s mother separated in Brno, they agreed to share custody. In September 2021, the mother petitioned for divorce and sought sole custody, while the applicant sought shared custody. From January 2022, the mother refused shared custody, though the applicant maintained regular contact, including Tuesday overnight visits and alternate weekends. Attempts at counselling did not produce agreement.

In May 2022, the Brno Municipal Court granted the applicant interim shared custody, but on 14 June 2022 the Brno Regional Court reversed that decision, finding no urgent need for an interim measure because the mother was caring for the children and the applicant had regular contact. On 14 July 2022, the Municipal Court awarded shared custody on a weekly basis, relying on a counselling report and the children’s guardian ad litem, who considered both parents capable and the children’s relationships positive. The mother appealed, and her appeal had suspensive effect.

On 28 August 2022, the mother unilaterally relocated with the children from Brno to Prague and enrolled them in school there. She proposed that the applicant see them every other weekend and during holidays, plus telephone/online contact. The applicant informed the social welfare authority, which declared the children “endangered.” On 7 September 2022, he applied for interim measures seeking custody or, alternatively, the children’s return and re-enrolment in their original schools, arguing that the mother had breached Article 877 of the Civil Code by changing their residence without his consent.

On 12 September 2022, the Municipal Court dismissed the interim shared-custody application, citing the Regional Court’s June decision and finding no urgent need because the applicant retained contact and the mother cared for the children. It dismissed the return application because the required deposit had not been paid on the day of filing. The applicant filed a second return application on 20 September 2022, which was dismissed on 21 September 2022: the court found no sufficient endangerment under the Special Court Proceedings Act and held that residence and schooling should be determined in proceedings on the merits. The appeals were dismissed on 2 December 2022. The Regional Court acknowledged the mother had relocated without agreement but found the applicant had not shown that the children’s care was seriously impaired or endangered; it also considered further change contrary to their best interests. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 5 April 2023 as manifestly ill-founded.

On 20 April 2023, the Regional Court overturned the shared-custody judgment and granted the mother sole custody, with the applicant having contact every second weekend and during holidays. It found both parents capable but held that circumstances had significantly changed: the children had adapted well to Prague over eight months, lived near other family, and the distance of over 200 km made shared custody impractical. It also relied on the children’s wishes to remain with their mother in Prague and visit the applicant in Brno. The mother was ordered to collect the children from Brno and share travel costs. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal on 17 October 2023.

Later enforcement proceedings revealed repeated refusals by the mother to hand over the children, fines imposed on her, and an expert finding no danger from the applicant; in February 2025 she was convicted of obstructing contact. The ECtHR application concerns the appellate court’s refusal to uphold the first-instance shared-custody judgment after the mother’s unilateral relocation and the refusal of interim measures, raising issues under Article 8 of the Convention regarding the applicant’s right to family life.

In **Felemez and Others v. Türkiye** (Applications nos. 30027/20 and 3 others), the European Court of Human Rights’ Second Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 22 January 2026. The case concerns four Turkish applicants who were dismissed from their employment and whose requests for reinstatement were examined by domestic courts. Their common complaint before the European Court was that the domestic court decisions lacked reasoning or contained inadequate reasoning. The applications were lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, and the Turkish Government were given notice.

**Öner Felemez** (born 1986), represented by Mervan Eren Gül of Diyarbakır, introduced application no. 30027/20 on 29 June 2020. He sought reinstatement to his post after being dismissed from a private firm that was a subcontractor of Mardin Municipality under an emergency legislative decree, based on alleged links with the PKK. The Mardin Court of First Instance decided on 27 April 2018, and the Gaziantep Regional Court of Appeals decided on 19 February 2019. The Turkish Constitutional Court decided on 31 December 2019 (no. 2019/11080).

**Zeynep Yorgun** (born 1988), represented by Sabahattin Kaya of Van, introduced application no. 34403/20 on 13 July 2020. She requested reinstatement after dismissal on suspicion of affiliation with the PKK/KCK. The Van 2nd Labour Court decided on 2 May 2018, and the Erzurum Regional Court of Appeals decided on 8 November 2018. The Constitutional Court decided on 9 December 2019 (no. 2018/37791), with notification on 11 December 2019.

**Fırat Gümüş** (born 1971), represented by Hediye Saltan of Diyarbakır, introduced application no. 11548/21 on 21 January 2021. He requested reinstatement following dismissal on grounds of suspicion of affiliation with a terrorist organisation. The Diyarbakır 6th Labour Court decided on 19 June 2018 (2017/1174 E., 2018/842 K.). The Constitutional Court decided on 4 November 2020 (no. 2019/2868).

**İbrahim Ay** (born 1980), represented by Rehşan Bataray Saman of Diyarbakır, introduced application no. 36831/24 on 21 November 2024. He sought reinstatement after dismissal on suspicion of affiliation with a terrorist organisation under legislative decree no. 677. The Diyarbakır Labour Court decided on 7 June 2017; the Gaziantep Regional Civil Court decided on 15 November 2017; and the Court of Cassation decided on 2 July 2018. The Constitutional Court decided on 24 October 2024 (no. 2023/2579), notified on 1 November 2024.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are that, in each case, the applicants’ dismissal and reinstatement disputes were reviewed by first-instance courts, appellate bodies, and the Turkish Constitutional Court, but the applicants considered those decisions to be insufficiently reasoned. The applicants therefore complained of a lack of reasoning or inadequate reasoning in court decisions. The ECtHR Committee, composed of Judges Stéphane Pisani, Juha Lavapuro, and Hugh Mercer, deliberated in private on 18 December 2025 and adopted the judgment on that date. The appended table provided the applicant details, representatives, dates, and domestic court decisions. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In *Taranenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 1386/24 and 4 others), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 12 March 2026. The judgment was adopted after private deliberations on 19 February 2026 and is final, though subject to editorial revision. The applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, and the Ukrainian Government was given notice.

The case concerns complaints by detained applicants about inadequate conditions of detention and the absence of an effective domestic remedy. Some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention. The factual details are set out in the appended table.

**Roman Grygorovych Taranenko** (born 1983), represented by Yolkin, filed applications nos. 1386/24 and 13429/24. He was held in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 30 April 2015 to 13 February 2024—a total of 8 years, 9 months and 15 days. The space per inmate was 2.5–3.6 m². He alleged overcrowding, except for an unspecified short period when he had more than 3 m² of personal space, along with lack of fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, no privacy for toilet, restricted warm water, poor bedding and bed linen, mouldy or dirty cell, passive smoking, inadequate temperature, insufficient electric and natural light, restricted potable and running water, restricted shower access, lack of toiletries, insects/rodents, and poor or insufficient food.

**Yevgeniy Vasylyovych Shnyakin** (born 1985), represented by Pustyntsev, filed application no. 36481/24. He has been held in Poltava Detention Facility no. 23 since 25 September 2023—over 2 years, 4 months and 12 days. The space per inmate was 2.5–2.9 m². He complained of overcrowding, insects/rodents, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygiene, insufficient natural and electric light, insufficient food, lack of toilet privacy, lack of toiletries, mouldy or dirty cell, restricted shower access, passive smoking, and poor food.

**Mykola Viktorovych Tolmachev** (born 1977), also represented by Pustyntsev, filed application no. 36527/24. He has been held in Poltava Detention Facility no. 23 since 20 July 2022—over 3 years, 6 months and 17 days. The space per inmate was 2.5–3.1 m². His allegations included overcrowding, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, mouldy or dirty cell, insects/rodents, inadequate hygiene, no toilet privacy, poor bedding and bed linen, insufficient food, lack of toiletries, restricted warm water, poor food, restricted shower access, and insufficient electric and natural light.

**Oleg Viktorovych Kapelyushnyy** (born 1971), represented by Kulbach, filed application no. 4790/25. He has been held in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility since 29 March 2024—over 1 year, 10 months and 8 days. The space per inmate was 2.5 m². He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, poor bedding and bed linen, inadequate hygiene, lack of toiletries, insufficient physical exercise in fresh air, restricted warm water, passive smoking, and restricted shower access.

The common allegations concern prolonged detention in overcrowded and materially inadequate conditions, often with less than 3 m² of personal space. The applicants complained that this amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment and that no effective domestic remedy existed. The provided excerpt sets out the procedural and factual background but does not include the Court’s operative findings on the merits.

**Summary of the Case of Pavlov and Others v. Ukraine**

The case of *Pavlov and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 30722/21 and 2 others) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) by three Ukrainian nationals. The applicants lodged their complaints under Article 34 of the Convention, alleging inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of an effective domestic remedy, in violation of Articles 3 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The judgment was delivered on 11 May 2023.

The first applicant, Dmytro Yuriyovych Pavlov (born 1985), was held in Dnipro Detention Facility No. 4 from 24 February 2020 to 25 February 2021 (1 year and 2 days) and again from 11 March to 7 April 2021 (28 days). During his detention, he had only 2.6 square meters of personal space. He complained of severe overcrowding, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, insect and rodent infestation, a mouldy and dirty cell, lack of privacy for the toilet, restricted access to warm water, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack of toiletries, poor-quality bedding and bed linen, poor-quality food, restricted access to showers, and insufficient natural light.

The second applicant, Mykhaylo Oleksandrovych Malyshko (born 1988), was detained in Zaporizhzhya Pre-Trial Detention Facility over four separate periods: 12–22 January 2021 (11 days), 23 February to 2 June 2021 (3 months and 11 days), 9 September to 4 November 2021 (1 month and 27 days), and 26 November to 7 December 2021 (12 days). Throughout these periods, he had approximately 2.7 square meters of personal space. His grievances included overcrowding, lack of or insufficient physical exercise in fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, and lack of toiletries.

The third applicant, Yevgen Igorovych Kondratenko (born 1992), was held in Kharkiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 11 April 2013 to 10 May 2021—a period of 8 years and 1 month. His personal space ranged from 2.5 to 4.4 square meters. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient electric and natural light, poor-quality bedding and bed linen, poor-quality food, restricted access to showers and potable water, passive smoking, a mouldy and dirty cell, insect and rodent infestation, lack of privacy for the toilet, and lack of toiletries.

All three applicants complained that the conditions of their detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment and that they had no effective remedy in Ukrainian law to address these violations. The Court, sitting as a Committee, examined the applications and delivered its judgment based on the facts presented in the appended table, finding violations of the Convention.

In *Romani and Cancelli v. Italy* (Applications nos. 54213/19 and 61041/19), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) considered two applications against Italy concerning the effectiveness and duration of civil proceedings arising from alleged medical negligence that resulted in the deaths of the applicants’ next of kin.

The first application, *Romani v. Italy* (no. 54213/19), was introduced on 10 October 2019 by Nazzareno Romani and Stefano Romani, born in 1964 and 1967 respectively and residing in Pesaro, represented by Fabrizio Dini. Their mother was hospitalised from 2 to 17 January 2004 and died on 18 January 2004. On 29 April 2005, the applicants brought a civil action against the hospital seeking compensation for damage resulting from their mother’s death, which they alleged had been caused by negligence on the part of the medical staff. The civil proceedings lasted 14 years across three levels of jurisdiction and ended with a judgment of the Court of Cassation on 15 April 2019.

The second application, *Cancelli v. Italy* (no. 61041/19), was introduced on 14 November 2019 by Giovanni Cancelli, born in 1959 and residing in Maglie, represented by Lilia Lucia Petracchi and Federico Di Salvo. His daughter, who had suffered from congenital heart problems since birth, was hospitalised from 12 to 20 December 1999. On 29 December 1999, the hospital decided not to readmit her, and she died the same day. On 18 January 2001, the applicant brought a civil action against the hospital seeking compensation for damage allegedly caused by medical negligence in his daughter’s treatment. The proceedings ended with a judgment of the Court of Appeal on 14 May 2019, after the case had been remitted to that court by the Court of Cassation on 10 January 2017. In total, the civil proceedings lasted 16 years and 7 months over four levels of jurisdiction. In parallel, Cancelli sought and obtained €3,660 in compensation for the excessive length of the proceedings under Law no. 89 of 24 March 2001 (the “Pinto Act”); that compensation was awarded in 2020.

Before the European Court, the applicants relied on Articles 2 and 6 of the Convention. They complained of the ineffectiveness and length of the domestic civil proceedings concerning the alleged medical negligence that had resulted in the deaths of their next of kin. In particular, the core alleged violation concerned the procedural limb of Article 2, namely the State’s obligation to ensure an effective and timely judicial response to deaths allegedly caused by medical negligence. The Court gave notice of the complaint concerning Article 2 in its procedural limb to the Italian Government, represented by Agent Mr L. D’Ascia. The remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible. Thus, the case focused on whether the Italian civil proceedings provided an effective procedural mechanism under Article 2 and whether their duration undermined that effectiveness.

In *Locascia and Others v. Italy*, nineteen Italian nationals living in Caserta and San Nicola La Strada (Campania) complained under Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention that Italy’s poor management of municipal waste collection, treatment and disposal, and its failure to protect them from pollution from the “Lo Uttaro” landfill, violated their rights to life and to private/family life and health/environment.

Campania was under a waste emergency from 1994 to 2009, managed largely by deputy commissioners. By 2007–2008, mayors in Caserta and San Nicola La Strada issued orders describing huge accumulations of uncollected waste, fires releasing dioxin, unbearable smells, traffic obstruction and a public health emergency. Schools and markets were closed or suspended. WHO studies found elevated cancer mortality and congenital malformations in the Naples/Caserta area, especially where illegal hazardous waste disposal and uncontrolled burning occurred, though other factors were also noted.

The “Lo Uttaro” site had previously hosted a landfill operated by Ecologica Meridionale in the late 1980s–early 1990s. In 2001, a technical report declared the area absolutely unsuitable for a new waste plant, citing extremely serious pollution and a predictable environmental disaster. In 2005, a regional remediation plan included permanent safety measures for the site. Nevertheless, in 2006 authorities agreed to open a new waste disposal plant there, and in 2007 the deputy commissioner authorised the ACSA CE 3 consortium to operate it.

Residents brought an urgent civil action. In July 2007, the Naples District Court ordered the plant to cease operating, finding no proper environmental impact assessment, existing pollution, and failure to protect public health. On appeal, the plant was allowed to operate pending an expert report. In October 2007, the expert found groundwater already contaminated and concluded that adding more waste would worsen risks and complicate remediation. The mayor temporarily closed the plant in November 2007.

In November 2007, a criminal judge seized the landfill. The GIP found hazardous waste had been disposed of contrary to authorisation, certifications were forged, groundwater was contaminated, safety measures were absent, the site was unsuitable, and waste exceeded authorised volumes by 4.5 times. In 2016, the ACSA CE 3 managing director and a deputy commissioner were convicted of illegal waste trade; the manager was also convicted of environmental disaster. In 2017, the Court of Appeal acquitted them because the limitation period had expired but upheld civil damages and remediation orders; the Court of Cassation later quashed that judgment for inadequate reasoning.

Environmental characterisation in 2013–2016 confirmed groundwater contamination by arsenic, nickel, antimony, iron, manganese, mercury and fluorides. ARPAC recommended urgent safety measures, a ban on groundwater use, and removal of asbestos-containing hazardous waste. Mayors prohibited groundwater use and cultivation. Remediation was repeatedly delayed, and wells were seized in 2019. The applicants alleged no remediation had occurred by March 2020, while the Government claimed securing work and tenders were underway.

EU Court of Justice judgments also found Italy failed to clean illegal landfills and ensure an adequate waste disposal network in Campania; millions of tonnes of “ecobales” remained. A parliamentary commission found hazardous waste had been disposed of at Lo Uttaro and that authorities failed to monitor and even certified false information. The applicants therefore alleged that the prolonged waste crisis and the reopening/operation of Lo Uttaro, despite known contamination and unsuitability, exposed them to serious environmental and health risks, engaging Italy’s positive obligations under Articles 2 and 8.
