text:
In **Grespik v. Hungary** (Application no. 47018/10), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application lodged by Mr László Grespik, a Hungarian national born in 1964 and living in Budapest. The underlying facts concerned his removal from a senior public office and the ensuing protracted domestic litigation.

In February 2002, the applicant was head of the Budapest Public Administration Authority. On 22 February 2002 he was dismissed from the civil service as a disciplinary measure. In the resulting labour dispute, the parties reached a friendly settlement on 22 March 2002: the applicant was reinstated and received damages. However, on the same day, the Prime Minister revoked his mandate to preside over the Authority. Consequently, the applicant left the Authority. This dispute gave rise to four sets of proceedings.

On 2 May 2002 the applicant brought a labour action claiming that the revocation of his mandate had been unlawful. In parallel, the Authority brought a civil action against him seeking invalidity of the friendly settlement and reimbursement of the compensation he had received. The applicant also brought labour proceedings claiming that the disciplinary measure of 22 February 2002 was unlawful, together with a claim for salary arrears.

The domestic proceedings were lengthy and fragmented. The friendly settlement was annulled by a final judgment of the Baranya County Regional Court, acting as a second-instance court, on 3 November 2005. On 2 February 2010, the same court adopted a final judgment establishing that the revocation of the applicant’s mandate on 22 March 2002 had been unlawful. In the labour action concerning the disciplinary sanction, the Zalaegerszeg Labour Court found for the applicant in an interim judgment on 3 April 2007 and established the unlawfulness of the sanction. By contrast, the applicant’s claim for salary arrears and the Authority’s action for repayment of compensation remained pending before the Kúria and the Budapest Surroundings High Court, respectively.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 1 August 2010. The application was communicated to the Hungarian Government on 5 April 2013. The Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi, Agent, Ministry of Public Administration and Justice. The case was considered by the Second Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges Helen Keller, András Sajó and Egidijus Kūris, with Stanley Naismith as Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 25 March 2014 and delivered judgment on 22 April 2014.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation were the multiple, interconnected civil and labour proceedings arising from the applicant’s 2002 dismissal and the revocation of his mandate. The litigation began in 2002; some branches were resolved only in 2005, 2007 and 2010, while others were still pending before domestic courts by the time the Strasbourg proceedings were under way. This prolonged duration, the parallel nature of the proceedings, and the repeated delays formed the factual core of the applicant’s complaint that the domestic proceedings had exceeded a reasonable time and failed to satisfy fair-trial guarantees, principally under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

In *Vykhor v. Ukraine* (Application no. 36618/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The applicant, Pavlo Oleksandrovych Vykhor, a Ukrainian lawyer born in 1978 and living in Kostyantynivka, lodged the application on 30 April 2014.

The applicant was a defendant in criminal proceedings initiated in May 2013, which remained ongoing at trial stage as of January 2024. He was charged with defrauding V.O., his client, by inciting him to hand over money allegedly demanded by judicial and police authorities to ensure favourable treatment of V.O.’s criminal case.

The alleged violations arose mainly from covert investigative measures used against the applicant. On 23 May 2013, an investigating judge of the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, relying in particular on Articles 246–248 and 263 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, issued two similarly worded orders authorising the tapping of the applicant’s two mobile telephones and audio and video monitoring. The judge stated, without further detail, that there were sufficient grounds to believe that information of fundamental importance for preventing, detecting and ending criminal offences could be obtained. The judge also noted the police’s argument that the information could not be obtained by other means.

On 31 May 2013, a prosecutor from the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office authorised the police to organise a “controlled transaction”, under which V.O. would receive marked bills to hand over to the applicant.

By November 2013, the applicant learned that key evidence in his case had been obtained through those covert measures. The prosecution file included transcripts of his telephone conversations and of a meeting with V.O., recorded by law-enforcement authorities under the 23 May 2013 authorisations. Copies of those authorisations were also included in the file.

On 28 February 2014, the Higher Specialised Civil and Criminal Court declined to consider the applicant’s appeals against the investigating judge’s authorisations, finding that they were not subject to appeal. The applicant subsequently lodged numerous criminal, disciplinary and civil complaints challenging the covert measures. He alleged, in particular, that the 23 May 2013 authorisations had been given unlawfully and without an assessment of whether there was a reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence. He further alleged that the measures constituted an unlawful and disproportionate interference with the confidentiality of his private communications. In March 2017, he applied to the Kostyantynivka City District Court seeking exclusion from his criminal file of evidence obtained through the disputed measures.

According to the parties’ latest submissions, as of January 2024 the criminal proceedings were still at the trial stage, and no decision had yet been taken on his complaints concerning the covert measures.

The ECtHR gave notice of the applicant’s complaints under Articles 6, 8 and 13: that the covert investigative measures were incompatible with his right to respect for private life and correspondence; that he lacked effective remedies for that complaint; and that the criminal proceedings against him were excessively long. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. In its judgment of 22 January 2026, the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, examined those issues.

In *Gazin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 43898/19), the applicant, Mr Andriy Yuriyovych Gazin, a Ukrainian national born in 1967 and living in Dnipro, complained to the European Court of Human Rights that domestic proceedings concerning alleged medical malpractice were ineffective. The application was lodged on 10 August 2019.

The facts concern medical treatment in 2012. On 3 August 2012, the applicant was admitted to Dnipro Municipal Clinic No. 4 with acute flank pain. He was diagnosed with a ureteral stone and renal colic. In the early hours of 4 August 2012, duty doctor M.P. performed urinary catheterisation. The applicant alleged that his condition later deteriorated: he developed fever, lower abdominal pain, and increased urinary frequency. He was diagnosed with acute pyelonephritis and received treatment. He was discharged on 17 August 2012 in satisfactory condition.

In October 2012, the applicant was readmitted to the same clinic with complaints of increased urinary frequency—up to once every hour—and blood in his urine. Medical tests revealed a urethral stricture, described as a traumatic narrowing of the urethra, and chronic cystitis. On discharge, doctors noted that despite treatment his urinary frequency had not significantly improved.

On 6 June 2013, following a complaint by the applicant against M.P., the police instituted criminal proceedings into medical malpractice. During the investigation, police obtained the applicant’s medical records and questioned both the applicant and M.P. Three forensic examinations were performed. The final forensic report, completed in December 2015, concluded that the applicant’s injuries—including urethral stricture, cystitis, and chronic urinary retention, classified as medium-severity injuries—had resulted from an improperly performed catheterisation.

Within the criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged a civil claim, first against the clinic and then against M.P. He argued that M.P.’s medical intervention had caused him severe pain and suffering. He sought more than UAH 3 million, equivalent to more than EUR 100,000 at the relevant time, in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

On 28 September 2016, M.P. was formally notified of suspicion of medical negligence under Article 140 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 5 December 2016, the criminal case against him and the applicant’s civil claim were referred to the Leninskyi District Court of Dnipro for trial.

During the trial, the court heard the applicant and four witnesses. Both the applicant and M.P. submitted new forensic evidence. M.P. relied on a report stating that his actions had corresponded to medical practice standards and that the applicant’s complications might have been caused by reasons unrelated to the catheterisation. The applicant submitted a report indicating otherwise.

As of October 2025, the trial against M.P. remained pending at first instance, with no decision taken either on the criminal charges or on the applicant’s civil claim. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the serious medical harm allegedly caused by the catheterisation, the forensic finding that it resulted from improper performance, and the prolonged failure of the domestic criminal and civil proceedings to reach any final determination for over a decade. The applicant’s complaint before the Court is that these domestic proceedings were ineffective, depriving him of timely adjudication and an adequate remedy for the alleged medical malpractice.

The case *A.N. and Others v. Greece* concerns applications brought by Afghan unaccompanied minors who sought international protection in Greece and were accommodated at the Samos Reception and Identification Centre (“Samos RIC”) between February 2019 and May 2020. The applicants alleged that their living conditions and treatment violated the Convention, essentially complaining of inhuman and degrading reception conditions and failure to protect them as vulnerable minors.

The general factual background was severe overcrowding. The Samos RIC had an official capacity of 648 persons but in practice hosted several thousand, including families, single men, and unaccompanied minors. An informal settlement known as “the Jungle” developed on adjacent land, consisting of tents and makeshift shacks without electricity, running water, toilets, or waste disposal. Medical and psychosocial support was extremely limited. The “safe zone” for unaccompanied minors had insufficient capacity, accommodating fewer than one hundred minors while hundreds remained outside. Containers were overcrowded, lacked heating and adequate bedding, and provided little privacy. Temporary guardianship by prosecutors was formalistic and ineffective in practice. Transfers to mainland shelters were delayed for months, even after the European Court of Human Rights indicated interim measures under Rule 39 requiring suitable accommodation.

Individually, D.F. arrived on 4 February 2019 and was registered as an unaccompanied minor. He remained in the Jungle until mid-May 2019, then moved to the minors’ section. A place was found in November 2019 but delayed owing to bedbugs and medical checks. After a Rule 39 measure in December 2019, he was transferred to Thessaloniki in January 2020. A.N. arrived on 6 June 2019 and was placed in the safe zone; after Rule 39, he was transferred to Attica in January 2020 and then to Switzerland. S.N. arrived on 4 February 2019, initially registered as an adult, but was recognised as a minor in April 2019; he stayed in the Jungle until mid-May 2019 and was transferred to Athens in February 2020. A.A. arrived on 13 September 2019, stayed in the Jungle, was registered in November 2019, and was transferred in January 2020 after Rule 39. M.H. arrived on 3 March 2019, initially recorded as born in 2002, corrected to 2004 in November 2019; he stayed in the Jungle until mid-April 2019 and was transferred in January 2020. A.N. (application no. 13892/20) arrived on 24 July 2019, was initially registered as an adult born in 1993, arrested and detained as an adult in October 2019, then recognised as a minor in November 2019. He attempted suicide in February 2020 and was transferred only in May 2020 after further interim measures. A.M. arrived on 13 September 2019 and was registered as an unaccompanied minor; he was transferred to the safe area in June 2020, where a 22 sq. m dormitory housed eleven other minors, and then relocated to Finland.

The applicants alleged they were left for months in overcrowded and unsanitary conditions without adequate supervision, psychological support, or legal guardianship. They slept on the ground or wooden pallets covered with plastic, lacked regular sanitation, and were exposed to violence, theft, and illness. Some suffered skin infections, respiratory problems, and PTSD symptoms; one attempted suicide. They argued that the situation reflected structural deficiencies and that authorities failed to transfer them promptly despite knowing their minor status and vulnerability. The Government acknowledged overcrowding and the informal settlement but maintained that basic services were provided, that transfers were prioritised, and that deficiencies were temporary due to migratory pressure and COVID-19. Third-party interveners supported the applicants’ accounts of inadequate shelter, hygiene, healthcare, and guardianship. The core alleged violations concerned the failure to provide humane, age-appropriate reception conditions and effective protection for unaccompanied minors.

**Summary of *Pavlov and Others v. Ukraine* (Application nos. 30722/21 and 2 others)**

The case of *Pavlov and Others v. Ukraine* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) against Ukraine. The applicants lodged their applications under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The case concerns allegations of inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of effective domestic remedies, primarily raising issues under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applications were filed by three Ukrainian nationals: Dmytro Yuriyovych Pavlov (born 1985), Mykhaylo Oleksandrovych Malyshko (born 1988), and Yevgen Igorovych Kondratenko (born 1992).

**Applicant 1: Dmytro Yuriyovych Pavlov (Application no. 30722/21)**

Pavlov was detained at Dnipro Detention Facility No. 4 from 24 February 2020 to 25 February 2021 (1 year and 2 days), and again from 11 March 2021 to 7 April 2021 (28 days). During his detention, he had approximately 2.6 square metres of personal space. He alleged numerous specific grievances, including severe overcrowding, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, infestation of his cell with insects and rodents, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of privacy for the toilet, restricted access to warm water, inadequate hygienic facilities, lack of toiletries, poor-quality bedding and bed linen, poor-quality food, restricted access to showers, and insufficient natural light.

**Applicant 2: Mykhaylo Oleksandrovych Malyshko (Application no. 38250/21)**

Malyshko was held at Zaporizhzhya Pre-Trial Detention Facility across four separate periods: 12–22 January 2021 (11 days), 23 February–2 June 2021 (3 months and 11 days), 9 September–4 November 2021 (1 month and 27 days), and 26 November–7 December 2021 (12 days). Throughout these periods, he had approximately 2.7 square metres of personal space. His complaints included overcrowding, insufficient physical exercise in fresh air, inadequate hygienic facilities, and lack of toiletries—conditions that persisted across all four detention periods.

**Applicant 3: Yevgen Igorovych Kondratenko (Application no. 3587/22)**

Kondratenko was detained at Kharkiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 11 April 2013 to 10 May 2021—a period of 8 years and 1 month. His personal space ranged from 2.5 to 4.4 square metres. He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, insufficient electric and natural light, poor-quality bedding and bed linen, poor-quality food, restricted access to showers and potable water, passive smoking, a mouldy or dirty cell, insect and rodent infestation, lack of privacy for the toilet, and lack of toiletries.

**Key Legal Issues**

The applicants collectively complained that the conditions of their detention amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of Article 3 of the Convention, primarily due to severe overcrowding (with personal space consistently below international standards) and inadequate sanitary and living conditions. They further alleged that no effective domestic remedy existed in Ukrainian law to address these conditions, in violation of Article 13. The Court examined these complaints based on the factual details provided in the appended table.

In **Hakobyan v. Armenia** (Application no. 21350/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Hrayr Hakobyan, born in 1959, that his criminal trial had been unfair. The applicant was represented by Diana Shakhramanyan, a lawyer in Yerevan. The application was lodged on 15 April 2019. The final domestic decision was given by Armenia’s Court of Cassation on 16 October 2018. Hakobyan had been convicted of misappropriation of State funds, specifically swindling in particularly large amounts and forgery of official documents.

The alleged violation concerns the defence’s inability to question a witness, identified only as H.Z., whose testimony was central to the conviction. According to the appended factual details, H.Z.’s statement was the only direct evidence implicating Hakobyan in the swindling of State funds. It played a decisive role in his conviction on that count. There was no other direct evidence linking the applicant to the crimes with which he had been charged.

H.Z. was interviewed twice during the pre-trial investigation. She made incriminating statements against Hakobyan only during the second interview. Later, in court, she retracted those statements. She claimed that the investigator had inaccurately recorded them and had tried to confuse her. This made it particularly important for the defence to question her about the contradictions in her accounts and the circumstances surrounding her earlier incriminating statement, including an alleged passing of money to the applicant.

However, the presiding judge did not allow H.Z. to answer defence questions concerning the charges against Hakobyan or her relevant incriminating statement. The reasons given were formalistic. In particular, the applicant’s representative was not allowed to question H.Z. about discrepancies between her statements, including the alleged handing over of money to the applicant and the circumstances surrounding it. The judge reasoned that H.Z. had been summoned for an additional examination only in relation to the criminal case against her, and therefore she could not be questioned about other matters.

The applicant complained that this restriction deprived him of an opportunity to put questions in court to the witness whose testimony had played a significant role in securing his conviction. The complaint therefore engages the fair-trial guarantee, particularly the right of a criminal defendant to examine or have examined witnesses against him. The key issue is whether the domestic court’s refusal to permit defence questioning of H.Z. breached Hakobyan’s right to a fair trial.

The Court sat as a Committee of the Fifth Section, composed of Judges Andreas Zünd, Diana Sârcu, and Mykola Gnatovskyy, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. It deliberated in private on 12 March 2026 and delivered judgment on 2 April 2026. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. In essence, the case concerns an alleged violation of the defence’s right to challenge the decisive witness evidence through effective questioning in court.

**Kovárová v. Slovakia (Application no. 46564/10)**

The applicant, Eva Kovárová, a Slovak national born in 1947 and living in Bratislava, lodged an action on 9 May 2007 with the Bratislava V District Court. She sought a ruling that a meeting of flat owners in her block of flats held on 24 April 2007 was contrary to law and that the decisions adopted at that meeting were void. The defendant was a community of owners of residential and non-residential premises in the building, an entity with legal personality registered with the local District Authority.

On 2 January 2008, a lawyer acting for the defendant informed the District Court that the defendant had ceased legally to exist on 14 December 2007, having been struck out of the relevant register because administration of the building had been transferred to a specialised agency. On 24 January 2008, the applicant requested that the hearing scheduled for 28 January 2008 be postponed sine die, stating that she had just learned of the striking out and needed time to analyse the situation. The hearing was adjourned.

On 3 March 2008, the District Court discontinued the proceedings on the grounds that the defendant had ceased to exist and had no legal successor. It held that neither the individual flat owners nor the newly contracted administration agency could be considered as having succeeded to the defendant's position.

On 20 March 2008, the applicant appealed, arguing first that the administration agency was the successor and proceedings should have continued against it, and second that the court should have stayed the proceedings pending the outcome of separate proceedings challenging a decision taken at another meeting of flat owners on 11 September 2007 to wind up the defendant. If those proceedings ended with a ruling declaring the winding up void, the striking out would lose basis and proceedings could continue.

On 30 May 2008, the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the first-instance decision, noting that the defendant had lost capacity to be a party and that there was no alternative to discontinuance. No reasons were offered for the latter conclusion. On 7 July 2008, the applicant appealed on points of law under Article 237(f) of the Code of Civil Procedure, arguing that the Regional Court had provided neither factual nor legal grounds for its conclusion, rendering it unreviewable. On 7 May 2009, the Supreme Court declared the appeal inadmissible, holding that the alleged shortcomings did not fall within Article 237(f) and that staying proceedings was an option, not a duty. It did not examine the merits.

On 17 August 2009, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against all three levels of the ordinary courts, arguing that the discontinuance was unlawful, that the courts had wrongly failed to examine the merits of her claim, and that this breached her rights of access to court and to a fair hearing under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 16 December 2009, the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. Regarding the Regional Court, it found the complaint out of time. Regarding the Supreme Court, it found that relevant reasons had been given and the decision was not arbitrary. It noted that if the separate proceedings declared the winding up void, the applicant could seek reopening, though the defendant would not automatically come back into existence without an incorporation decision by the District Authority.

The applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 concerning access to court and a fair hearing.

**PSMA, spol. s r.o. v. Slovakia** (Application no. 42533/11, judgment 9 June 2015) concerned a Slovak company’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged that a final and binding judgment in its favour had been quashed after the Prosecutor General lodged an extraordinary appeal on points of law, following a petition by the opposing party. The central issue was whether this extraordinary review breached the applicant’s right to a fair trial, particularly the principles of legal certainty and finality of judicial decisions.

In 1995 the applicant company contracted with Slovak Radio, the national public-service broadcaster, to act as exclusive agent for selling advertising broadcasting time. The contract was amended several times and was valid until 31 December 2007. In 2004 the relationship deteriorated over the amount of business generated in 2003. Slovak Radio billed the applicant for the difference between estimated and actual profit. When the applicant did not pay, Slovak Radio terminated the contract for fundamental breach. The notice period expired on 30 September 2005.

In 2006 the applicant sued Slovak Radio for indemnity of approximately €693,000, calculated as average yearly commission over five years and including barter transactions. On 14 May 2007 the Bratislava I District Court granted the claim in full. It proceeded under Article 101 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure because Slovak Radio, despite being represented, filed no observations and failed to attend hearings without valid excuse. The court found the termination valid because it had not been contested and held that barter transactions were properly included in the indemnity calculation.

Slovak Radio appealed. It acknowledged the legal basis for some indemnity but disputed the barter component. On 28 November 2007 the Bratislava Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. It found Slovak Radio’s procedural passivity unjustified and held that the barter-related compensation claim was distinct from the indemnity claim. The judgment became final on 9 January 2008 and enforceable on 12 January 2008.

Slovak Radio then filed a constitutional complaint, which was declared inadmissible on 3 July 2008 for failure to exhaust an ordinary appeal on points of law. It also petitioned the Prosecutor General. On 23 October 2008 the Prosecutor General lodged an extraordinary appeal against both judgments. He argued that the lower courts had erred by treating the termination as valid merely because it was uncontested, and that they should have examined the validity of the contract and the notice independently. He also challenged the inclusion of barter transactions. The Supreme Court suspended enforceability on 8 December 2008.

The applicant argued that the extraordinary appeal was inadmissible because Slovak Radio could have used an ordinary appeal on points of law; that the Prosecutor General exceeded the petition’s scope; and that the principal had relied on, rather than challenged, the termination notice. It also complained that the Supreme Court ignored its observations and denied access to the case file. On 12 August 2009 the Supreme Court allowed the extraordinary appeal, quashed both lower judgments, and remitted the case for fresh examination, finding failures to examine the contract’s and notice’s validity.

The applicant’s constitutional complaint was dismissed as manifestly ill-founded on 25 November 2010. Before the European Court, the applicant maintained that the quashing of a final judgment in its favour through an extraordinary appeal initiated at the losing party’s request violated Article 6 § 1, undermining legal certainty and res judicata.

In *Mogyla and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 1129/18, 50410/18 and 34853/24), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 26 February 2026. Three applications were lodged against Ukraine. All applicants complained under Article 6 that their access to a court had been restricted. In application no. 1129/18, the applicant also raised other Convention complaints.

Application no. 1129/18, introduced on 21 December 2017 by Vadym Mykolayovych Mogyla (born 1986), concerned an administrative claim of 24 November 2008 challenging a local council’s refusal to allocate him a plot of land. The case was repeatedly reconsidered on jurisdiction. On 26 January 2011, the Higher Administrative Court confirmed that it should be examined in administrative proceedings. On 30 September 2014, in the second round, that court again remitted the case to the first-instance administrative court. On 21 June 2017, however, it ruled that the claim should be examined in civil proceedings and terminated the case. Consequently, his claim was never determined on the merits. He alleged this restricted his access to court.

**Case Summary: Pentikäinen v. Finland (Application no. 11882/10)**

**Key Facts**

The case concerns Markus Pentikäinen, a Finnish photojournalist for the weekly magazine *Suomen Kuvalehti*, who was arrested while covering a demonstration in Helsinki on 9 September 2006. The "Smash ASEM" protest against the Asia-Europe Meeting was anticipated to be confrontational. Prior risk assessments by security intelligence indicated the event would be hostile, and two earlier demonstrations that year had turned violent. The police deployed 480 officers—an exceptionally large number by Finnish standards.

The demonstration began at 6 p.m. near the Kiasma Museum of Contemporary Art. Shortly after it started, bottles, stones, and paint-filled jars were thrown at police and bystanders, and some demonstrators physically assaulted officers. By 6:30 p.m., police declared the event a riot and sealed off the area to contain the violence. Over loudspeakers, police repeatedly announced that the demonstration was stopped and ordered the crowd to disperse. Hundreds left voluntarily through designated checkpoints, while media representatives and families with children were allowed to pass through the cordon.

Pentikäinen remained inside the cordoned area to continue photographing. He later claimed the police order to disperse only became clear to him around 8:30 p.m., and after consulting his employer, he decided his presence was journalistically necessary. At approximately 9 p.m., a police officer personally warned him he had one last chance to leave. Pentikäinen identified himself as a journalist for *Suomen Kuvalehti* and stated he intended to follow the event to its end. The officer left him alone.

About twenty demonstrators remained seated inside the cordon. The situation had been peaceful for roughly an hour when police moved to break up the group and make arrests. According to Pentikäinen, an officer shouted "Get the photographer!" before he was apprehended while taking photographs. He again identified himself as a journalist and was allowed to stow his camera equipment. The stated basis for his apprehension was "contumacy towards the police" under Chapter 16, section 4(1), of the Penal Code.

Pentikäinen was detained from 9:26 p.m. on 9 September until 3:05 p.m. on 10 September—seventeen and a half hours. He was interrogated the following afternoon. He claimed he repeatedly identified himself as a journalist to officers at the bus and police station, but was ignored. He also alleged that his camera equipment and memory cards were confiscated, though the Government maintained his journalistic materials were never seized once his profession was known. His editor-in-chief attempted to contact the police station but received no information, and only after calling a senior Ministry of the Interior official were preparations made for Pentikäinen's release.

**Criminal Proceedings**

On 23 May 2007, the public prosecutor charged Pentikäinen with contumacy towards the police for failing to obey the order to disperse. On 17 December 2007, the Helsinki District Court found him guilty but imposed no penalty, invoking Chapter 6, section 12(3), of the Penal Code, which allows punishment to be waived when the act is deemed "comparable to an excusable act." The court reasoned that, as a journalist, Pentikäinen faced conflicting expectations from police and his employer. The court found the police actions and orders legal, and determined the orders manifestly applied to everyone in the crowd. Pentikäinen appealed, but the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal on 30 April 2009, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal on 1 September 2009.

**Alleged Violations**

Pentikäinen complained under Article 10 of the Convention that the police order to leave the demonstration, his inability to transmit information during his seventeen-and-a-half-hour detention, and his subsequent prosecution and conviction constituted an unjustified interference with his right to freedom of expression, producing a "chilling effect" on his journalistic work.

**Usatyuk v. Ukraine** (Application no. 1902/25) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), delivered on 13 May 2026. The applicant, Volodymyr Viktorovych Usatyuk, born in 1986, is a Ukrainian national. He was represented before the Court by Ms K.O. Chuyeva, a lawyer practising in Odesa. The application was lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 30 December 2024. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the application. The Court sat as a Committee composed of President Andreas Zünd, Judges Diana Sârcu and Mykola Gnatovskyy, and Acting Deputy Section Registrar Viktoriya Maradudina. It deliberated in private on 9 April 2026 and adopted the judgment that date.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are set out in the appended table. The applicant was held in pre-trial detention from 6 December 2023 to 22 May 2025. The total length of that detention was one year, five months, and seventeen days. The application was introduced on 30 December 2024, while the applicant was still in detention, and approximately five months before the detention ended on 22 May 2025. The applicant complained of the excessive length of his pre-trial detention. He also raised other complaints under the provisions of the Convention, though those additional complaints are not specified in the available text.

The central alleged violation concerns the right to liberty and security under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. That provision guarantees that everyone arrested or detained on suspicion of a criminal offence shall be entitled to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. The applicant’s complaint is that the Ukrainian authorities kept him in custody for an unjustifiably long period before trial. Under the Court’s case-law, the reasonableness of pre-trial detention depends on the particular circumstances of the case, including the complexity of the proceedings, the conduct of the applicant and the authorities, and the existence of risks such as absconding, interference with evidence, or reoffending. However, the extract provided does not contain the Court’s assessment of those factors or its conclusion on the merits. It also does not describe the charges, the domestic detention orders, or the reasons given by Ukrainian courts for extending detention.

The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. Because the case was decided by a Committee, it likely concerns issues already covered by the Court’s established case-law, although the provided text does not state the outcome. The available facts focus primarily on the duration of detention: from 6 December 2023 to 22 May 2025, a total of 1 year, 5 months, and 17 days. This period forms the main factual basis for the excessive-length complaint. The applicant lodged his application while still detained, and the detention ended roughly five months later. The Government were notified, and the Fifth Section Committee adopted the judgment on 9 April 2026, delivering it on 13 May 2026.

In sum, **Usatyuk v. Ukraine** concerns an allegation that Ukrainian authorities violated the Convention by maintaining the applicant in pre-trial detention for approximately one and a half years. The applicant complained of excessive length of detention and raised other unspecified Convention complaints. The full text excerpt does not reveal the Court’s reasoning or final disposition on the merits; it mainly identifies the parties, procedural history, and the length of the contested detention.

In *Gatsko and Panov v. Ukraine*, the applicants were two Ukrainian nationals and leaders of political party D. The case concerns their conviction for holding a peaceful demonstration and related proceedings.

In December 2012, the second applicant had been found guilty of violating the procedure for holding public events, but the criminal proceedings were closed as time-barred. That decision was not part of the application.

On 1 April 2013, the first applicant notified the Novi Petrivtsi Village Council that on 10 April 2013 he intended to organise a demonstration outside the President of Ukraine’s residence at 19 Ivana Franka Street, Novi Petrivtsi. The aim was to draw attention to poor road infrastructure. Up to 500 participants were expected. The Village Council asked the Kyiv District Administrative Court to prohibit the demonstration. On 5 April 2013, that court banned the D. party from holding it, citing a local executive committee decision of 31 July 2012 on public events and possible disruption of flood-damage roadworks at the location. Both applicants were present when the decision was announced and did not appeal.

According to the applicants, on 10 April 2013 they went to the President’s residence with journalists to check whether the roadworks mentioned by the court were actually taking place. While leaving, police stopped them, took them to a police station and later to the Vyshgorodskyy District Court. They were accused of breaching Articles 185 and 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences. The same day, the first applicant was fined UAH 170 (about EUR 16) for participating in a demonstration and refusing to follow a police officer. Although he said he did not appeal, the Government produced a Kyiv Region Court of Appeal decision of 3 June 2013 rejecting his appeal. The second applicant was also fined for disobeying a police officer under Article 185, and the court ordered further investigation into the remaining accusations. He did not appeal that fine.

On 11 April 2013, the second applicant appeared again before the Vyshgorodskyy District Court, which found him guilty of conducting a demonstration on 10 April despite the 5 April ban. The court found that he had organised the demonstration and sentenced him to seven days’ administrative detention under Article 185-1 § 2. It relied on police witness statements and statements by the Head of the Novi Petrivtsi Village Council, who said the second applicant had told him he planned to organise the demonstration. The court also noted the earlier December 2012 decision, whose proceedings had been closed as time-barred. After the hearing, the second applicant was taken to a temporary detention centre, where he met his lawyer. The lawyer appealed the same day, arguing that the second applicant had merely been checking for roadworks and had not been demonstrating. A Court of Appeal hearing was scheduled for 19 April 2013; the lawyer requested witness testimony and video footage, but the court allegedly refused without justification. On 19 April 2013, the Kyiv Region Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.

On 12 April 2013, the first applicant went to Novi Petrivtsi intending to demonstrate for the second applicant’s release. He was detained, brought before the Vyshgorodskyy District Court, met his lawyer and signed a legal representation contract, then was released. On 13 April 2013, the same court sentenced him to five days’ administrative detention under Article 185-1 § 2 for repeatedly violating the procedure for holding demonstrations under 1988 Soviet-era rules, referring also to Article 39 of the Constitution. It found that he had organised the meeting, relying on statements of people who had been with him and on the fact that he had notified the authorities only one hour before the planned demonstration. His appeal was dismissed by the Kyiv Region Court of Appeal on 28 May 2013.

The application was lodged on 9 August 2013. In 2018 the Court informed the applicants that the case file had been lost and invited them to resubmit. A new application form signed on 29 January 2019 was received on 3 April 2019, along with a copy of the original. These facts underpin the applicants’ complaints about interference with peaceful assembly, their prosecution and administrative detention, and procedural fairness in the administrative offence proceedings.

**Summary of K.F. v. Cyprus**

The applicant, K.F., was a Syrian national of Kurdish origin. He entered Cyprus illegally in February 2005 and applied for asylum. He claimed that after participating in the 2004 Qamishli Kurdish demonstrations, he was arrested, detained for fourteen days and ill-treated, then held for two and a half months in Damascus prison. After bribing officials, he was released but later learned that an arrest warrant had been issued against him. He also claimed that the family of a woman with whom he had eloped had killed her and was seeking him, prompting his flight from Syria.

In August 2008, the Asylum Service rejected his application. It found contradictions between his written application and his interview: he had initially said he came to Cyprus “for living,” but later claimed persecution. The Reviewing Authority dismissed his appeal in June 2009, again finding his account inconsistent and not credible. It also doubted an Arabic document he submitted, which allegedly ordered his arrest, because he had not produced the original and because the translation predated his claimed receipt. In January 2012, the Supreme Court dismissed his recourse, upholding the credibility findings and concluding that he had left Syria for personal reasons and had not shown a risk of persecution if returned.

In August 2009, deportation and detention orders were issued against him; he was detained but released in December 2009 after those orders were revoked. In May 2010, he joined a Kurdish protest encampment in Nicosia against the asylum authorities’ policies. On 11 June 2010, police carried out a mass early-morning operation involving about 250 officers. A total of 149 protesters were transferred to police headquarters; 22 were deported the same day. The applicant was among 44 people arrested. Authorities treated them as unlawful residents or “prohibited immigrants.” Some already had deportation orders, while the applicant was charged with unlawful stay. Deportation and detention orders were also issued against 53 detainees, including the applicant, under the Aliens and Immigration Law.

The applicant alleged that he was not informed of the reasons for his arrest and detention. The Government claimed he was informed orally and later served with written notice on 18 June 2010, but refused it; the applicant denied refusing service and said he only learned of the orders from his lawyer after Rule 39 proceedings before the European Court of Human Rights. On 12 June 2010, he and others sought an interim measure; on 14 June 2010, the Court indicated that Cyprus should not deport him to Syria. The measure was maintained in September 2010 for five cases, including his, and lifted in June 2012 after he left Cyprus for Northern Iraq.

He remained detained at Larnaca Police Station. In March 2011, he escaped, was injured, hospitalised, and returned to custody. He was released on 20 April 2011 after the deportation and detention orders were revoked. He filed habeas corpus proceedings in January 2011, arguing that his detention violated EU and Convention standards. The Supreme Court dismissed the application in March 2011, and his appeal was later dismissed as moot because he had been released.

Before the European Court, K.F. complained that deportation to Syria would breach Article 3; that there was no effective remedy under Article 13; that his detention violated Article 5 §§ 1(f), 2 and 4; and that deportation would breach Article 4 of Protocol No. 4, concerning collective expulsion. The key facts relevant to these alleged violations were the rejection of his asylum claim on credibility grounds, the mass arrest and removal operation against Kurdish protesters, the boilerplate deportation and detention orders, the alleged failure to inform him of the reasons for detention, the prolonged immigration detention, and the intended deportation to Syria.

In *K.A. v. Austria*, the applicant, a Kosovo national living in Austria, was convicted of prolonged domestic violence against his wife and four children and ordered confined in a forensic-therapeutic centre (then called an institution for mentally ill offenders). His complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 and Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d)–(e) arise from that confinement and from the examination of the child witnesses.

Family life was marked by frequent violence. In May 2021, after the applicant allegedly beat his children, his daughter B. called the police. His son C. told police that the applicant had struck their mother with a drill and threatened C. with a knife; C. fled. Police issued a restraining order, but the applicant refused to leave and was arrested. C. also alleged that the applicant later telephoned and threatened to kill the family. The applicant was taken into pre-trial detention on 31 May 2021 and denied the allegations.

During the pre-trial investigation, the three younger children were cross-examined as particularly vulnerable victims on 30 June 2021 via audio-video link. The applicant, his defence lawyer and the prosecutor were in a separate room and could see and question them. An Albanian interpreter provided only summary translations during breaks, not continuous interpretation. The children gave detailed accounts of longstanding violence. The applicant and his lawyer asked few or no questions. The wife and eldest daughter refused to testify. At trial in December 2021, the children did not attend; they said further testimony would be too distressing and asked that recordings or transcripts of their cross-examinations be used. Over defence objection, the court played the recordings and read the transcripts. The defence requested that the children be summoned for additional questioning, but the court refused because they had lawfully refused to testify.

Psychiatric expert Dr K. found the applicant had an accentuated personality structure or suspected personality disorder and alcohol abuse. Her examination was practically impossible because he denied everything and blamed his family. Assuming the children were credible, she described him as a classic “family tyrant” — narcissistic, dominance-oriented, lacking empathy, with sadistic tendencies. She considered him criminally responsible but found that, if the children’s statements were credible, the criteria for confinement under Article 21 § 2 were met: a severe mental or emotional abnormality and a high probability of serious violence against testifying family members. The Regional Court convicted him, sentenced him to eight years, and ordered confinement. It relied on the children’s credible statements and Dr K.’s report. Appeals were dismissed. The Supreme Court held that the applicant and counsel had been present at the cross-examinations, could ask questions, and that the summary translation did not violate his rights. The Court of Appeal upheld the confinement, later confirming in 2024 that a “severe and persistent mental disorder” need not match ICD or DSM categories and that the risk persisted.

The alleged violations were therefore twofold. First, under Article 5, the applicant argued that it had not been reliably shown that he was a person of “unsound mind” and that his confinement and subsequent review were unjustified. Second, under Article 6, he complained that he could not effectively challenge or question the prosecution witnesses because the child witnesses had been examined with only summary interpretation and later refused to testify at trial, while their recorded statements were admitted as evidence against him.

In *Milić and Nikezić v. Montenegro* (Apps. 54999/10 and 10609/11, judgment 28 April 2015), two Montenegrin nationals detained at the Institution for the Execution of Criminal Sanctions (IECS) alleged that prison guards tortured and ill-treated them on 27 October 2009, and that Montenegro failed to conduct an effective official investigation. They shared a cell with five other detainees. On that date, the first applicant was to be transferred to a disciplinary unit and the cell was to be searched.

The applicants alleged that guards entered the cell, grabbed the first applicant, threw him onto the concrete corridor floor, handcuffed him, and beat him with batons and fists while swearing at him. They further alleged that two rows of guards beat him as he was taken away. The second applicant alleged that when he protested, four guards kicked and beat him with fists and batons; after he was taken into the corridor, eight more guards continued beating him, and the beating resumed after he returned to the cell. The Government disputed this, claiming the applicants resisted and obstructed guards, and that the second applicant attacked a guard without reason.

Medical and witness evidence was mixed but significant. The first applicant initially refused examination by the prison doctor, saying he was healthy and not ill-treated. Later, his mother observed bruises on his face and body, and his lawyer saw a bruise under his eye and a large bruise on his calf, describing him as frightened and mentally broken. The second applicant was examined by a prison doctor after the Deputy Ombudsman intervened; the Ombudsman described the resulting reports as barely legible and inconsistent. An external forensic examination on 4 November 2009 found light injuries: a 10-day-old haematoma 8 x 15 cm on his left thigh and haematomas under both eyes, with an undated report also noting bruises around his eyes. Several detainees said they saw the first applicant beaten; three confirmed the second was beaten by guards in the cell and corridor. Some guards admitted using force, including one who said he hit the first applicant once with a baton.

The Ombudsman visited the applicants, noted visible injuries, and in March 2010 found their rights had been violated, concluding they had not resisted and that force was unjustified. Disciplinary proceedings against three guards followed; they were found responsible and fined 20% of their salaries for abuse of position or exceeding authority, having used disproportionate force. However, criminal complaints were rejected. In February 2010 the State prosecutor found that two guards had used force within official powers to overcome resistance, and in October 2010 rejected the complaint regarding other guards. Attempts at subsidiary prosecution failed: the indictment was treated as a criminal complaint, and the request for an investigation was dismissed in March 2011, upheld on appeal, for lack of reasonable suspicion that torture or ill-treatment occurred, the courts finding the force necessary. The Constitutional Court rejected the applicants’ constitutional appeal on procedural grounds.

The applicants also complained that the video recording omitted the corridor beating, that another camera recording was not obtained, and that there was a conflict of interest because a deputy State prosecutor was the prison governor’s daughter and the Deputy Supreme State Prosecutor was his wife. In civil proceedings, the Supreme Court ultimately awarded them EUR 1,500 each, holding the force unjustified and degrading but not amounting to torture or inhuman treatment. The ECtHR case therefore concerned the alleged substantive violation of Article 3 and the alleged failure to investigate effectively.

In *A.V. v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national, was arrested on the evening of 29 December 2006 on a street in Kyiv and taken to the Shevchenkivskyy District Police Department. According to him, police officers struck him down, handcuffed him, took him to their car, allegedly planted small bags of cocaine on him, and continued to beat him, with threats of sexual abuse, until they reached the police station. At the station, he was asked to empty his pockets in the presence of two attesting witnesses and produced bags containing cocaine.

At 10 p.m. the police ordered his administrative detention under Article 263 of the Administrative Offences Code for violating drug-circulation rules under Article 44. He was interviewed and wrote a confession admitting that he had unlawfully bought cocaine for personal use. He later claimed that the confession was forced and dictated by a police officer. He was placed in a police cell and alleged that he received insufficient food and water, was held in poor sanitary conditions, and was locked for one night in a dirty, stinking toilet. He felt unwell and suffered acute lower back pain.

On 2 January 2007, after a specialist report found 1.18 grams of cocaine, criminal proceedings were instituted against him under Article 309 § 2 of the Criminal Code for illegally purchasing and storing narcotic drugs in large quantities. That day the investigator ordered his arrest and detention as a criminal suspect for up to 72 hours. He was questioned again and gave details about purchasing the drugs. His lawyer, hired by his parents, joined only after the interview had gone on for a considerable time. In the lawyer’s presence, the applicant complained of poor health. The Government said a medical examination diagnosed intercostal neuralgia and considered his health satisfactory.

On 5 January 2007 the prosecutor refused to approve pre-trial detention, and the applicant was released on a written undertaking not to abscond. After release, ambulance teams diagnosed acute pyelonephritis and lumbosacral radiculitis. Further examinations followed, and from 9 to 19 January he received inpatient neurological treatment for spinal osteochondrosis, vertebrogenic lumbodynia, and pain/muscular tonic syndrome. A psychiatrist later noted signs of post-traumatic stress disorder.

On 22 January 2007 the District Court found that the investigator’s 2 January decision to arrest and detain the applicant as a criminal suspect had been unlawful because the grounds for such arrest had existed from 29 December 2006. On 9 February 2007 the prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers over the applicant’s allegations, finding no elements of an offence and relying on police explanations and custody records. A linguistic expert later reported that the 29 December confession had been written by the applicant with another person dictating the text. At trial, the applicant sought to exclude his 29 December and 2 January statements as obtained in breach of his rights, but the court refused.

Throughout trial, the applicant denied the charges, claiming the drugs had been planted and that he had been psychologically pressured and physically ill-treated. The officers and investigators denied the allegations. The attesting witnesses stated that when the applicant produced the bags, he told them they contained cocaine and showed no visible injuries. On 8 July 2008 the District Court convicted him and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment, suspended with two years’ probation, finding no indication of ill-treatment or procedural violations at the time of his initial self-incriminating statements. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 7 November 2008, and the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on 22 May 2009, relying in part on the original self-incriminating statements.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged ill-treatment by police contrary to Article 3, lack of access to a lawyer at the initial stage of investigation under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c), and use of evidence obtained through ill-treatment to secure his conviction under Article 6 § 1.

**Case: Begić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina (Application no. 5067/23), European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, Judgment of 3 February 2026.**

The applicant, Zlatan Begić, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina born in 1975 and living in Tuzla, is a high-ranking official of the Democratic Front and a member of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He does not declare affiliation with any of the “constituent peoples”—Bosniacs, Croats, or Serbs—and therefore belongs to the constitutional category of “Others.”

The applicant complained under Articles 14 and 17 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 about his ineligibility to stand for election to the position of Chair/Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives. The Court gave notice of those complaints to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The relevant constitutional framework derives from the 1995 Dayton Agreement. Bosnia and Herzegovina consists of two Entities, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska, plus the Brčko District. The Constitution distinguishes “constituent peoples” from “Others and citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.” At State level, power-sharing arrangements include a vital interest veto, an Entity veto, a House of Peoples composed of five Bosniacs, five Croats and five Serbs, and a tripartite Presidency with one Bosniac, one Croat and one Serb. Although no ethnic requirement applies to election to the House of Representatives, Article IV § 3(b) of the Constitution requires each chamber to select from its members one Serb, one Bosniac and one Croat to serve as Chair and Deputy Chairs, with the position of Chair rotating among those three persons. Consequently, persons who do not declare affiliation with a constituent people, such as the applicant, are not eligible to serve as Chair or Deputy Chair of that chamber.

On 1 December 2022, two members of the House of Representatives nominated the applicant for the position of Chair/Deputy Chair. According to the minutes of that meeting, his nomination was not put to a vote because it did not comply with the House’s Rules of Procedure. This refusal is central to the alleged violations, as it is said to result from the constitutional requirement that the position be held only by a Serb, a Bosniac or a Croat.

The Constitution provides that the Convention and its Protocols apply directly in Bosnia and Herzegovina and have priority over all other law, and that rights under listed international agreements are secured without discrimination. Article IX § 3 further states that officials appointed to institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be generally representative of its peoples. However, the Constitutional Court has held in decisions nos. U 5/04 and U 13/05 that the Convention does not have priority over the Constitution and that it lacks jurisdiction to review the Constitution’s conformity with the Convention. The relevant constitutional provisions have neither been amended nor declared unconstitutional.

The case therefore concerns whether the applicant’s exclusion, based on his status as an “Other,” from candidacy for Chair/Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives breaches his rights under the Convention and its Protocols, particularly the prohibition of discrimination and the right to free elections.

Gazsó v. Hungary (Application no. 48322/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Second Section on 16 July 2015; it became final on 16 October 2015. The applicant, György Gazsó, a Hungarian national born in 1963 and living in Telki, lodged his application on 24 July 2012 under Article 34 of the Convention. He was represented by D. Karsai, a Budapest lawyer. The Hungarian Government was represented by Z. Tallódi of the Ministry of Justice.

The applicant’s central complaint concerned delay in Hungarian labour litigation. He alleged that proceedings in his labour dispute had lasted an unreasonably long time and that Hungarian law provided no effective remedy for that delay. He relied on Article 6 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair trial within a reasonable time, and Article 13, which requires an effective remedy at national level for Convention violations.

The underlying facts began with earlier litigation between the applicant and his former employer from 25 February 2002 to 18 May 2005. That case ended with the employer being obliged to re-employ him. However, the applicant did not accept the position offered in pursuance of the re-employment order. As a result, a new labour dispute began on 5 January 2006.

In this second set of proceedings, the Budapest Labour Court dismissed the applicant’s action on 18 November 2008. The applicant appealed. On 9 July 2010, the Budapest Regional Court reversed the first-instance decision and found in his favour. The respondent then sought review before the Kúria, Hungary’s supreme court. On 29 February 2012, the Kúria reversed the Regional Court’s judgment and found for the respondent. Thus, the second labour dispute ran from 5 January 2006 until 29 February 2012—roughly six years and nearly two months—through three court levels. When viewed together with the earlier related employment litigation from 2002 to 2005, the applicant’s dispute with his former employer spanned a considerable period.

Procedurally, the application was communicated to the Government on 13 November 2014. At the same time, the Court proposed the pilot judgment procedure under Rule 61 of the Rules of Court. That procedure is used where a case may reveal a systemic or structural problem—here, potentially the repeated failure of Hungarian courts to dispose of labour and civil cases within a reasonable time, and the absence of an effective domestic remedy. The parties submitted comments on the pilot judgment proposal.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: the length of the labour proceedings from 2006 to 2012; the earlier related proceedings from 2002 to 2005; the successive decisions at three judicial levels; and the alleged lack of any effective domestic remedy capable of providing timely relief or compensation for the delay. The case thus focuses on whether Hungary violated the applicant’s right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 and his right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

In *Micu v. Romania* (Application no. 41040/11, ECtHR, 13 January 2015), the applicant was a Romanian border guard officer investigated by the National Anticorruption Department (NAD) for bribe-taking. The case concerned his complaints under Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention arising from events on 9–10 March 2010.

On 8 March 2010 a NAD prosecutor authorised a warrant to appear for the applicant. On 9 March 2010, two police officers enforced it at his workplace at 8:40 a.m. and took him to the NAD offices. The warrant stated only that his presence was required for him to be heard as an accused; it gave no further reasons. He was left waiting until noon, when he was informed of the criminal investigation and accepted a publicly appointed lawyer after initially refusing to appoint his own. He told the prosecutor he had diabetes and needed insulin treatment from his workplace, and asked that his wife be notified if he were placed in custody. The record of his statement indicated he was heard from noon until 9:34 p.m.; the Government later claimed this was a clerical error and that questioning actually ended at 12:34 p.m., after which the prosecutor dealt with co-accused and witnesses. At 7:08 p.m. he was charged with bribe-taking; he refused to make a further statement. At 9:15 p.m. the NAD placed him in police custody for 24 hours on suspicion of accepting money from Turkish nationals to allow them to leave Romania. He alleged that from 8:40 a.m. until formal custody he was effectively deprived of liberty at the NAD, beyond the lawful purpose of a warrant to appear, contrary to Article 5.

He also alleged Article 3 violations. He had suffered from type-two diabetes since 1997 and had been on insulin since 2009, requiring two injections daily. He claimed that while under the authorities’ control he was not allowed food, was denied medical examination or treatment, and at the detention centre his syringe, insulin and glucose meter were confiscated. He said he had not eaten all day and was not given food suitable for his condition or utensils, causing physical and psychological suffering. The Government disputed this: it stated that once he informed the prosecutor, his treatment kit was retrieved from his workplace within 30 minutes and he used it without restriction, and that a police officer bought him food. However, on 9 March at 10:30 p.m. the detention nurse recorded that his condition was relatively good but that he required insulin morning and evening and had high blood sugar. A doctor on 10 March confirmed the insulin regimen.

Domestically, the Court of Cassation refused pretrial detention on 10 March 2010, finding the evidence inconsistent and no grounds other than offence seriousness; this was upheld on 8 April 2010. The applicant was convicted in 2011 but acquitted on appeal in 2013. He filed criminal complaints against prosecutors G.B. and L.P. for abuse of office, unlawful arrest, improper investigation and torture. These were dismissed as non-existent offences, with courts saying his complaints concerned investigative acts and should be raised within the pending criminal proceedings, not through separate criminal complaints. He therefore alleged Article 13 because no effective domestic remedy existed for his Article 3 and 5 complaints.

In *Hakobyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 21350/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) delivered judgment on 2 April 2026. The applicant, Hrayr Hakobyan, born in 1959, was convicted in Armenia of misappropriation of State funds—specifically swindling in particularly large amounts and forgery of official documents. The final domestic decision was given by the Court of Cassation on 16 October 2018. Represented by lawyer Diana Shakhramanyan, Hakobyan lodged his application with the Court on 15 April 2019, and the application was communicated to the Armenian Government.

The applicant’s central complaint was that his criminal trial had been unfair. In particular, he alleged that he had not had an opportunity to put questions in court to the witness whose testimony played a significant role in securing his conviction. This complaint engages the fair-trial guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention, especially the defence’s right to examine or have examined witnesses against the accused.

The key witness was identified by initials as H.Z. According to the appended table, H.Z.’s statement was the only evidence directly implicating Hakobyan in the act of swindling State funds. It also played the decisive role in his conviction on that count. There was no other direct evidence linking the applicant to the crimes he had been charged with. This made H.Z.’s credibility and the reliability of her statements central to the case.

The circumstances surrounding H.Z.’s evidence were disputed. During the pre-trial investigation, H.Z. was interviewed twice. She made incriminating statements against Hakobyan only during the second interview. Later, in court, she retracted those statements. She claimed that the investigator had inaccurately recorded them and had tried to confuse her. Because the witness had retracted the incriminating account, questioning by the defence about the inconsistencies and circumstances of her statements was especially important.

However, the presiding judge did not allow H.Z. to respond to the defence’s questions concerning the charges against the applicant and her relevant incriminating statement. The refusal was based on formalistic reasons. In particular, the judge did not permit the applicant’s representative to question H.Z. about discrepancies between her statements, including the allegation that she had passed money to the applicant and the circumstances surrounding that alleged transfer. The judge reasoned that H.Z. had been summoned for an additional examination only in relation to the criminal case against her, and therefore she could not be questioned about other matters.

As a result, the defence was unable to test the reliability, consistency, or credibility of the main witness whose evidence was decisive for Hakobyan’s conviction. The applicant argued that this lack of any effective opportunity to question H.Z. violated his right to a fair trial. The case therefore focuses on whether the domestic courts’ refusal to allow defence questioning of H.Z., despite her decisive role and her retraction of the pre-trial incriminating statements

In *Lunev v. Ukraine*, the applicant, a Ukrainian national, was arrested in January 2012 on drug-trafficking suspicion and placed in Starobilsk SIZO. On admission he was diagnosed with HIV (clinical stage 3), chronic bronchitis, toxic encephalopathy/neuropathy from drug use, and residual tuberculosis changes. The Government claimed he refused a CD4 test in February 2012 and sought no medical help until January 2013, though records showed a TB examination and X-ray in September 2012 and bronchitis/kidney pain in November 2012. On 8 January 2013, after coughing and fever, he was treated for chronic bronchitis. On 9 January he was found unconscious. The SIZO head asked the court to expedite proceedings or release him for urgent specialised treatment; the court kept him detained but ordered placement in a specialised prison or civilian hospital. From 9 to 11 January he was hospitalised with acute serose meningoencephalitis and was in a soporose state. He returned to the SIZO medical unit until 15 February and was also held at Alchevsk ITT.

On 17 January 2013 he requested a Rule 39 interim measure for hospital placement, citing need for psychiatric examination, antiretroviral therapy (ART), correct TB staging, and epilepsy treatment. Medical information indicated he had been HIV-positive since 2010 but had refused treatment. The Government said he received treatment for acute serous cerebromeningitis between 11 January and 15 February, was seen by a TB specialist and X-rayed on 5 February, and had only residual TB needing no treatment. On 6 February a neuropathologist diagnosed HIV stage 3 and toxic encephalopathy. On 19 February he was sentenced to six and a half years’ imprisonment. On 26 February his CD4 count was 119. On 7 March the Government told the Court no hospitalisation was needed. On 12 March an infectious diseases specialist recommended ART; on 14 March his admission to Lugansk hospital was approved. He was hospitalised from 20 to 25 March, also diagnosed with over 10% weight loss and chronic hepatitis C. On 22 March the Court refused the Rule 39 request. Further hospital stays followed; on 3 April his CD4 count was 13.5% and on 16 April ART was prescribed. His conviction was quashed on 24 May. On 19 June he was released under house arrest, the court noting he required treatment unavailable in detention.

As to ill-treatment, the applicant was placed in Alchevsk ITT on 25 January 2013. On 30 January an ambulance was called for acute liver pain; he was examined, taken to hospital, and returned around 4 p.m. He alleged that at about 5.25 p.m. two policemen from the regional police office beat him and told him to write that the SIZO had provided adequate medical treatment. He claimed one officer hit his liver six or seven times and the other hit his kidneys four times; he then wrote the requested statement. On 31 January his lawyer complained in court; an ambulance diagnosed possible blunt abdominal trauma, but a surgeon found his abdomen soft and pain-free, no acute surgical pathology, and said he could remain in ITT. The applicant and his lawyer complained to the prosecutor that unknown policemen had pressured him physically and psychologically to withdraw his complaint about inadequate medical assistance and to confess. A forensic expert later concluded he had no injuries when examined on 31 January.

The prosecutor terminated proceedings on 25 February for lack of evidence, relying on officers’ denials and the forensic conclusion. On 26 March the town court quashed that decision because cellmates had not been questioned. On 24 April ambulance records reported blunt abdominal trauma and his beating complaint. Proceedings were terminated again on 25 April. A cellmate testified that the applicant was absent for 40–60 minutes and returned saying two policemen had forced him to refuse medical treatment and beaten him, leaving a red cheek/cheekbone and swollen liver; another cellmate said the applicant told him policemen beat him to force a confession. Officer So denied involvement and said he was at work; ITT surveillance had not been working from 26 January to 4 February.
