In **G.S.B. v. Switzerland** (ECtHR, Third Section, 22 December 2015, app. no. 28601/11), the applicant, a Saudi Arabian and American binational living in Miami, complained that Switzerland’s transmission of his banking data to US tax authorities under a Swiss–US mutual assistance arrangement violated Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. The Court communicated those complaints; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The case arose from the UBS tax affair. In 2008, the IRS discovered that thousands of US taxpayers held undeclared UBS accounts or economic rights in such accounts. UBS faced criminal prosecution. In February 2009, UBS entered a deferred prosecution agreement and paid USD 780 million. The IRS then issued a “John Doe summons” seeking identities and account data for some 52,000 US customers. To avoid a Swiss–US legal conflict, Switzerland and the United States concluded Agreement 09 on 19 August 2009. Under it, Switzerland agreed to process the IRS mutual assistance request concerning UBS’s American customers under the 1996 Swiss–US double taxation convention (CDI-US 96), covering approximately 4,450 open or closed accounts. The IRS requested data on US taxpayers who, between 2001 and 2008, had authority to sign or other access rights to UBS accounts in Switzerland. The Swiss Federal Tax Administration (AFC) ordered UBS to provide complete customer files.

UBS transmitted the applicant’s file to the AFC on 19 January 2010. On 7 June 2010, the AFC granted mutual assistance and ordered the documents to be sent to the IRS. The applicant appealed. On 21 September 2010, the Federal Administrative Court set aside the decision because his right to be heard had been breached, and remitted the case. After receiving the applicant’s observations, the AFC again granted mutual assistance on 4 November 2010. The applicant appealed, alleging that the decisions lacked a legal basis and violated the ECHR and other treaties, including the prohibition of retroactivity, respect for private life, the presumption of innocence, equality and non-discrimination, and the right to remain silent.

On 2 March 2011, the Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It held that Protocol 10, which amended Agreement 09 (“Convention 10”), was binding on Swiss authorities and, as later international law, took precedence over earlier treaties such as the ECHR, absent *jus cogens*. It found that even if Article 8 ECHR applied, the interference was justified under Article 8 § 2: Convention 10 provided a sufficient legal basis, and Switzerland’s interest in honouring its international commitments and avoiding serious diplomatic and financial consequences outweighed the applicant’s interest in keeping his financial affairs secret. It rejected the retroactivity complaint, finding that the parties intended retroactive application and that mutual assistance procedural rules could apply retroactively. As to Article 14, the applicant alleged that Convention 10 discriminated by singling out UBS customers rather than customers of other banks. The court said it could not review Convention 10’s conformity with the Constitution or earlier treaties and applied it despite the different treatment.

The Federal Court declared the applicant’s further appeal inadmissible on 11 April 2011. The applicant’s banking data were transmitted to the US tax authorities on 14 December 2012. As of 2014, he stated that the US tax inspection was ongoing and that he had not been criminally charged. The ECtHR’s examination therefore focused on whether the disclosure and transfer of his banking data, and the UBS-specific scheme, breached Articles 8 and 14.

In *Alves v. Portugal* (Application no. 79925/12), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, Committee) gave judgment on 30 April 2015. The applicant, Ms Cretka Ivanic Alves, a Slovenian national born in 1953 who lives in Braga, Portugal, lodged an application under Article 34 of the Convention on 4 December 2012. The application was communicated to the Portuguese Government on 4 March 2014. The Slovenian Government was informed of its right to intervene but did not do so. The applicant was represented by a Braga lawyer, and the Portuguese Government by the Deputy Attorney General.

The domestic case concerned a civil liability action for professional negligence. On 22 November 2006, the applicant sued F., a lawyer who had represented her in earlier proceedings, in the Braga Court, claiming damages. F. was notified on 12 December 2006. On 25 January 2007, F. filed his defence and requested that his professional liability insurer be joined to the proceedings. The applicant filed a reply on 8 March 2007. On 11 July 2007, the Braga Court accepted the insurer’s intervention. The insurer was summoned on an unknown date and filed submissions on 14 September 2007; the applicant replied on 11 October 2007.

Between January and April 2008, the parties disputed whether the applicant had legal capacity to be a party. On 28 April 2008, the judge issued a despacho saneador and absolved F. from the proceedings because the applicant allegedly lacked legal capacity. The applicant appealed to the Guimarães Court of Appeal. By decision of 4 December 2008, the Court of Appeal held that she did have legal capacity and ordered the first-instance court to re-examine the case. In February 2009, the proceedings were allocated to the Braga Court. On 29 April 2009, the judge issued directions identifying established and outstanding matters.

From 28 May to 6 November 2009, the parties made three requests, to which the judge responded within less than one month. The case was set for hearing on 10 March 2010, but it was adjourned to 15 June 2010. A second hearing took place on 7 October 2010. On 29 October 2010, the Braga Court partially found in favour of the applicant. Both parties appealed to the Guimarães Court of Appeal, which dismissed the appeals on 20 October 2011. The parties then challenged that decision before the Supreme Court, which dismissed the appeals on 29 May 2012.

Thus, the domestic civil proceedings lasted approximately five years and six months from filing to final decision: about three years and eleven months at first instance, one year on appeal, and seven months before the Supreme Court. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are the overall length of the proceedings and the procedural stages that may explain or contribute to delay, including the insurer’s intervention, the dispute over the applicant’s legal capacity and the ensuing appeal, the remittal of the case, and the adjournment of hearings. Although the excerpt does not set out the legal complaint, the chronology indicates that the case concerned the alleged excessive length of civil proceedings, primarily under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

In *Rozhnov and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 7501/22 and two others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of Carlo Ranzoni (President), Lado Chanturia, and María Elósegui, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, delivered a judgment on 20 July 2023. The judgment was adopted after private deliberations on 29 June 2023. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The case originated in three applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on the dates shown in the appended table. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants complained principally of the inadequate conditions of their detention and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. They also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The appended table sets out the key facts relevant to the alleged violations. The first applicant, Yaroslav Dmytrovych Rozhnov (born 1997), lodged application no. 7501/22 on 28 January 2022 through representative Andriy Vitaliyovych Pustyntsev, based in Dnipro. He was held in Chernigiv Detention Facility from 20 August 2019, with detention pending at the relevant time, for more than three years, nine months and nineteen days. The space per inmate was 2.5 m². He alleged overcrowding, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, lack of toiletries, poor quality of food, and no or restricted access to a shower.

The second applicant, Anatoliy Vasylyovych Lun (born 1983), lodged application no. 7513/22 on 28 January 2022, also represented by Pustyntsev. He was held in the same Chernigiv Detention Facility from 20 August 2019, also pending, for more than three years, nine months and nineteen days. The space per inmate was again 2.5 m². His specific grievances were overcrowding, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, lack of privacy for the toilet, poor quality of food, and no or restricted access to a shower.

The third applicant, Anatoliy Oleksandrovych Nikolayev (born 1985), lodged application no. 26434/22 on 20 May 2022 through representative Sergiy Oleksandrovych Kulbach, based in Limoges. He was detained in Dnipro Detention Facility no. 4 from 29 April 2020, with detention pending at the relevant time, for more than three years, one month and ten days. The space per inmate was 2.88 m². He complained of overcrowding, lack of fresh air, no or restricted access to potable water, lack of privacy for the toilet, passive smoking, and lack or insufficient physical exercise in fresh air.

These factual allegations underpin the applicants’ central complaints that their conditions of detention were inadequate and that they had no effective remedy in domestic law. The excerpt mainly records the procedure and the individual detention circumstances relevant to the alleged violations; it does not set out the Court’s full reasoning or final conclusions on the merits.

**Summary of *Metalla and Others v. Albania* (Applications nos. 30264/08, 42120/08, 54403/08, 54411/08)**

The case of *Metalla and Others v. Albania* concerns four applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by nine Albanian nationals between June and October 2008. The applicants alleged violations under the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, specifically regarding the Albanian authorities' failure to enforce final domestic administrative decisions that awarded them compensation for property that could not be physically restored. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, referencing *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The facts of each application centre on decisions by local commissions recognising the applicants' inherited property titles under Albania's post-communist restitution laws. In each instance, while part of the property was restored, the remaining portion was occupied and the applicants were to be compensated "in one of the ways provided for by law." Crucially, these commission decisions remained unenforced.

In Application no. 30264/08 (*Metalla*), a 1995 decision by the Shijak Commission recognised the applicants' title to 1,020 sq. m of land. Of this, 747 sq. m were restored, but the remaining 272 sq. m were occupied, entitling the applicants to compensation. This decision was never enforced.

In Application no. 42120/08 (*Bushati*), a 1995 decision by the Shkodër Commission recognised the applicant's and other heirs' title to a two-storey building and a surrounding 500 sq. m plot. The building was to be restored, but as the 500 sq. m plot was occupied, compensation was awarded. The applicant noted that a third party had built unauthorised constructions on the land. This decision also remained unenforced.

In Application no. 54403/08 (*Metalla and Others*), a 1994 decision by the Shijak Commission recognised the applicants' title to 5,527 sq. m of land. While 5,000 sq. m were restored, the remaining 527 sq. m were occupied, leading to a compensation award that was never enforced.

In Application no. 54411/08 (*Metalla and Others*), a 2007 decision by the Durrës Commission recognised the applicants' title to 65,000 sq. m of land. Of this, 60,000 sq. m were restored, but the remaining 5,000 sq. m—described as arable land, roads, and channels—were occupied. The applicants were to be compensated, but this decision likewise remained unenforced.

The core of the alleged violation is the Albanian state's systemic failure to execute these final administrative decisions. The judgment references the relevant domestic law and practice, as detailed in prior cases like *Manushaqe Puto* and *Ramadhi v. Albania*. It also draws on Council of Europe materials, including decisions from the Committee of Ministers between 2013 and 2015. These documents highlight the Albanian government's acknowledgement of the structural problem and its efforts to establish a compensation mechanism, including approving property valuation maps and drafting new legislation. However, the Committee of Ministers expressed regret that deadlines were not met and encouraged authorities to intensify their efforts. The applicants' central grievance is that despite recognising their rights, the state failed to provide the compensation awarded, leaving them in a state of legal limbo for years.

Yegorov v. Slovakia (Application no. 27112/11) is an ECtHR case brought by a Ukrainian national, Volodymyr Yegorov, alleging violations of Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 of the Convention. The complaints concerned his bringing before Bratislava I District Court on 16 June 2010, his arrest on 27 July 2011, remand orders of 16 July 2010 and 29 July 2011, and the proceedings on his interlocutory appeal against the 29 July 2011 remand.

The applicant was continuously deprived of liberty in Slovakia from 25 June 2002 to 19 September 2013. He was initially remanded on several charges, including what later became a charge of conceiving, setting up and supporting a criminal and terrorist group. That charge was separated in 2005. He was later convicted of attempting to legalise proceeds of crime and released on 13 July 2010. Immediately upon release, he was taken to the Border and Foreigners Police, ordered administratively expelled, banned from re-entry for five years, and detained at Medveďov pending expulsion.

While at Medveďov, on 16 July 2010 he was seized by police and brought to Bratislava I District Court for questioning in a murder case. After a private session, the District Court remanded him in pre-trial detention on the murder charge. He stated on record that he wished to appeal and would give reasons once he received the written decision. On 19 July he submitted written reasons in Russian (received 21 July); the written remand decision was served on 21 July, and the file was sent to the Regional Court the same day. He sent further reasons on 26 July (received 28 July). On 28 July the Regional Court dismissed his appeal as unfounded, stating he had submitted no reasons. The Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible on 7 December 2010. It found no arbitrariness: the submissions had not been available to the Regional Court, remand appeals must be decided swiftly (within five working days), the applicant had been heard at first instance, and his lawyer had taken no effective steps.

On 27 July 2011, after acquittal on the first murder charge, the applicant was released but immediately re-arrested and served with a 2003 charge concerning a criminal and terrorist group. On 28 July the prosecution sought detention on several charges. On 29 July the Specialised Criminal Court remanded him under Article 71(1)(a) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prevent flight and further offending. It cited his non-national status, unstable residence, foreign travel, other pending charges, and prior conviction. The applicant appealed, arguing that his arrest was unlawful because he was not informed of the reasons, contesting the detention grounds, complaining of over nine years’ deprivation of liberty, and alleging a pattern of arbitrary consecutive remands. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 8 August 2011.

On 19 September 2011 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, relying mainly on Article 5 §§ 1 and 3. He repeated that he had not been informed of the reasons for his arrest, that the courts ignored the unlawfulness argument, and that his detention was arbitrary, particularly because he had faced the charges for eight years and been continuously detained. On 18 October 2011 the Constitutional Court declared the complaint inadmissible. It found the arrest report sufficient, considered the Supreme Court to have dealt with the lawfulness argument implicitly, and held that, although total detention exceeded nine years, the contested decision concerned only detention from 27 July 2011 and had not yet become unconstitutional. The Supreme Court later released him on 22 February 2012, expressing doubts that ten years’ detention might be arbitrary and self-serving, that statutory maxima had been exceeded, and that his detention involved one criminal matter including offences for which he had already been detained from 2002 to 2005. Other Constitutional Court judgments found Article 5 violations concerning speediness and the repeated-remand pattern, but no just satisfaction was awarded.

text:
The European Court of Human Rights case *O.J. and J.O. v. Georgia and Russia* (Applications nos. 42126/15 and 42127/15) concerned two Georgian nationals arrested on 15 March 2012 in Tagiloni, Gali Region, Abkhazia, by a special-forces team of the de facto Abkhaz Security Services. A search of the second applicant’s house allegedly found two hand grenades and a hunting knife. The applicants complained that they were ill-treated during arrest and subsequent detention, held unlawfully, and denied a fair hearing before the de facto Supreme Court of Abkhazia, which convicted them of espionage and sentenced them to imprisonment for endangering the constitutional order of Abkhazia.

The prosecution alleged that in early 2011 the applicants, acting on instructions from Georgia’s Department of Military Intelligence, recruited D.K.—a soldier in the Russian border-guard unit at Tagiloni—as an informant and acted as intermediaries transmitting information to Georgian authorities. Both applicants were charged with espionage on 23 March 2012; the second applicant was also charged with unlawful possession of ammunition and a cold weapon.

The applicants alleged that they were beaten while handcuffed to chairs and subjected to waterboarding during questioning about their ties to Georgian intelligence and the Russian informant. The first applicant alleged that his teeth were loosened with extraction forceps and that he was threatened with rape and internet publication of footage. The second applicant alleged that a rope was tied around his neck to simulate strangulation. Lawyers assigned on 19 March 2012 allegedly advised them to confess to stop the beatings. Both then admitted ties to Georgian military intelligence, though they later claimed the confessions were extracted under torture. They said ill-treatment continued, though less frequently, during twice-weekly questioning by de facto security services and Russian Federal Security Service staff.

The applicants were held for six months at de facto security premises in Sukhumi, then three months at temporary detention facilities of the de facto Abkhaz Ministry of Interior, and later at Dranda Prison. On 16 April 2013, the de facto Supreme Court of Abkhazia convicted them and relied partly on their confessions, despite their claims that the statements were obtained through torture. The first applicant received eleven years and six months’ imprisonment; the second received thirteen years. Although an appeal was theoretically possible within ten days, the applicants considered it futile and did not appeal. They were released on 10 March 2016 after negotiations and interventions by Georgian authorities.

The case also raised issues of State responsibility. The applicants submitted that Russia had exercised effective control over Abkhazia through military forces since 1993. Georgia argued that the de facto Abkhaz authorities survived only through Russian military, economic, financial and political support, and that Abkhazia had been absorbed into Russian military, security and administrative structures. Russia denied involvement, stating that its peacekeepers had withdrawn by 2008, that the events occurred in 2012, and that the applicants were arrested and detained by Abkhaz security services not subordinate to Russia. Russia did not contest the applicants’ factual account but denied evidence of Russian agents’ involvement. Georgia stated it could not obtain information on the facts and did not challenge the applicants’ assertions. The applicants’ complaints thus concerned alleged ill-treatment, unlawful detention, unfair trial and lack of effective remedy, with key factual disputes centering on the circumstances of their arrest, interrogation, confession, trial and detention in Abkhazia.

**Case: Ivković and Others v. Serbia**  
*European Court of Human Rights, Second Section, Committee Judgment, 22 July 2021*  
*Application no. 62554/19 and four others*

The case originated in five applications against Serbia lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants complained of the excessive length of civil and administrative proceedings. The Serbian Government was given notice of the applications. The Court’s judgment was adopted by a Committee composed of Judges Koskelo, Lubarda, and Bošnjak.

The appended table sets out the key facts for each applicant. All applicants alleged that domestic proceedings had lasted unreasonably long. In each case, the table also records a prior domestic decision concerning the length complaint, and in each instance the domestic authority found no violation.

**Ranko Ivković**, born in 1979 and represented by Goran Stamenić of Čačak, lodged application no. 62554/19 on 21 November 2019. The domestic proceedings began on 31 December 2010 and ended on 15 May 2019. They lasted 8 years, 4 months, and 16 days across two levels of jurisdiction. The Smederevo Court of First Instance, in decision R4R.br.27/2017 of 22 September 2017, found no violation.

**Zoran Đorđević**, born in 1966 and represented by the same lawyer, lodged application no. 4559/20 on 10 January 2020. The proceedings began on 6 January 2011 and ended on 30 November 2018, lasting 7 years, 10 months, and 25 days across two levels. The Smederevo Court of First Instance, in decision R4R.br.25/2017 of 28 September 2017, found no violation.

**Jovica Marković**, born in 1966 and represented by the same lawyer, lodged application no. 22108/20 on 23 April 2020. The proceedings began on 14 July 2011 and ended on 20 September 2019, lasting 8 years, 2 months, and 7 days across two levels. The Smederevo Court of First Instance, in decision R4R.br.31/17 of 22 September 2017, found no violation.

**Dušan Janošević**, born in 1930 and without a listed representative, lodged application no. 32920/20 on 20 July 2020. The proceedings began on 19 January 2011 and ended on 8 March 2017, lasting 6 years, 1 month, and 18 days at one level of jurisdiction. The Constitutional Court, in decision Už-3645/2017 of 24 December 2019, found no violation.

**Slavoljub Aksić**, born in 1971 and represented by the same lawyer, lodged application no. 44445/20 on 11 September 2020. The proceedings began on 14 July 2011 and ended on 8 November 2018, lasting 7 years, 3 months, and 26 days across two levels. The Smederevo Court of First Instance, in decision R4R.br.7/2017 of 17 July 2017, found no violation.

The central alleged violation is therefore the excessive length of domestic civil or administrative proceedings, contrary to the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The durations at issue range from just over six years to more than eight years and four months. Most applicants pursued two levels of jurisdiction, while one pursued one level. Although each applicant had previously raised the length issue domestically, the domestic authorities concluded that no violation had occurred. The applicants then brought the matter to Strasbourg. The excerpt provided covers the procedure and facts; it does not include the Court’s subsequent reasoning or final conclusions on the merits or just satisfaction.

In *Milenković and Veljković v. Serbia* (Apps. nos. 7786/13 and 47972/13), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) examined complaints by two Serbian nationals, Ms Dobrica Milenković (born 1957) and Mr Miroslav Veljković (born 1966), both from Vladičin Han. They had been employed by DP “PK Delišes,” a socially-owned company based in Vladičin Han. The case concerned Serbia’s alleged failure to enforce final domestic judgments awarding them salary arrears and social insurance contributions.

The first applicant obtained a judgment from the Vladičin Han Municipal Court on 20 October 2003 ordering the debtor to pay specified salary arrears and social insurance contributions. It became final and enforceable by 31 October 2003. On 31 December 2003, at her request, the same court ordered enforcement and awarded her enforcement costs. The second applicant obtained a similar judgment on 18 February 2004, which became final and enforceable by 11 April 2004. On 4 May 2004, the court ordered enforcement and awarded him enforcement costs.

Despite these final and enforceable judgments, the debtor did not pay. The debtor’s status and subsequent proceedings were central to the non-enforcement. On 18 February 2004, the Privatisation Agency ordered the restructuring of the debtor. Later, on 30 January 2014, the Leskovac Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against it. The applicants duly reported their claims based on the judgments to the insolvency administration. At the time of the Strasbourg judgment, the insolvency proceedings were still ongoing, and the applicants had still not been paid.

The alleged violations therefore concerned the State’s failure to ensure enforcement of final domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour. The key facts were that the applicants held final, enforceable, and undisputed monetary claims against their employer; enforcement orders were issued; the debtor nevertheless failed to comply; and the debtor’s restructuring and insolvency prolonged the non-enforcement for many years. The applicants appeared to bear no fault for the delay. The ECtHR was called upon to assess whether this situation breached Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, guaranteeing access to court and fair trial, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, protecting property. Those provisions require the State to secure effective enforcement of final judgments and to respect possessions.

The domestic-law context involved the status of socially-owned companies and Serbian rules on enforcement and insolvency, as outlined in cases such as *R. Kačapor and Others v. Serbia*, *Jovičić and Others v. Serbia*, *Marinković v. Serbia*, and *Ferizović v. Serbia*. Procedurally, the first application was lodged on 18 December 2012 and the second on 5 July 2013. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The Court deliberated on 29 September 2015 and delivered judgment on 20 October 2015.

In essence, the case turned on whether Serbia could justify the prolonged non-enforcement of final judgments because the debtor was a socially-owned company subject to restructuring and later insolvency, and whether that situation violated the applicants’ rights under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Lambert and Others v. France* (Application no. 46043/14), the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights examined an application brought by the parents, half-brother and sister of Vincent Lambert. They alleged that permitting the withdrawal of Vincent’s artificial nutrition and hydration (“ANH”) would breach France’s obligations under Article 2 of the Convention, amount to ill-treatment contrary to Article 3, and infringe his physical integrity under Article 8.

Vincent Lambert sustained severe head injuries in a road-traffic accident on 29 September 2008. He became tetraplegic, completely dependent, and from June 2009 was cared for in Reims University Hospital, where he received enteral ANH via a gastric tube. In 2011 the Liège Coma Science Group described him as being in a chronic neuro-vegetative state characterised as “minimally conscious plus”. However, in 2014 a court-appointed expert panel found that he was in a vegetative state, that his condition had deteriorated since 2011, that brain damage was irreversible, that he could not communicate functionally, and that his reactions to care and painful stimuli were non-conscious.

Under the French “Leonetti Act” of 22 April 2005, treatment may be withdrawn where it is futile or disproportionate or has no other effect than to sustain life artificially. In 2013 Dr Kariger, Vincent’s doctor, began the statutory collective procedure. A first decision to withdraw nutrition and reduce hydration was implemented in April 2013 but was suspended by an urgent administrative court in May 2013 because the parents had not been properly informed and the procedure was defective.

A second collective procedure began in September 2013. Dr Kariger consulted six doctors and held family meetings. Vincent’s wife, Rachel Lambert, and six of his siblings supported withdrawing ANH; the applicants opposed it. On 11 January 2014 Dr Kariger concluded that continuing ANH amounted to unreasonable obstinacy, citing irreversible brain damage, poor prognosis, and Vincent’s previously expressed wishes not to be kept alive artificially in such a dependent state.

The applicants sought urgent court protection. On 16 January 2014 the Châlons-en-Champagne Administrative Court suspended Dr Kariger’s decision. It accepted that ANH was a form of treatment but found that Dr Kariger had incorrectly assessed Vincent’s wishes and that, given possible minimal consciousness, the treatment was not necessarily futile or disproportionate. On appeal, the Conseil d’État ordered an expert medical report and received general observations from medical and ethics bodies. On 24 June 2014 the Conseil d’État set aside the lower judgment and dismissed the applicants’ claims. It held that the statutory conditions had been met: the procedure was lawful, the family had been consulted despite disagreement, the expert findings confirmed an irreversible vegetative state and poor prognosis, and Vincent’s prior wishes had been sufficiently established. It therefore found the withdrawal decision lawful.

The applicants then brought the case to the European Court of Human Rights, which applied an interim measure under Rule 39 to prevent withdrawal pending the proceedings. They argued that withdrawal would violate Vincent’s right to life and physical integrity, particularly in the absence of advance directives, amid family division and because he was not terminally ill. The Grand Chamber examined whether the French legal framework and the decision-making process complied with positive obligations under Articles 2, 3 and 8. It ultimately held that there would be no violation of Article 2, no violation of Article 8, and that no separate issue arose under Article 3.

**Case: O’Keeffe v. Ireland (Application no. 35810/09), European Court of Human Rights, Grand Chamber, 28 January 2014**

The applicant, Louise O’Keeffe, an Irish national born in 1964, attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned by trustees of the Catholic Bishop of Cork and Ross, the recognised patron, and was managed locally by a parish priest acting for the bishop. The school had two teachers, one of whom, L.H., was principal.

In 1971, a parent complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. This complaint was not reported to the police, the Department of Education, or any other State authority, and the manager did not act on it. During the first six months of 1973, the applicant was subjected to approximately twenty sexual assaults by L.H. during music lessons in his classroom. She and her parents were unaware of the 1971 complaint at that time.

In September 1973, other parents brought similar allegations about L.H. to the attention of the applicant’s parents. After a parents’ meeting chaired by the manager, L.H. went on sick leave and resigned. Again, the allegations were not reported to the police or State authorities. The manager later notified the Department only that L.H. had resigned and named his replacement. L.H. subsequently taught at another national school until his retirement in 1995. Between 1969 and 1973, a State inspector visited Dunderrow National School six times—an above-average number—met L.H., and considered his teaching satisfactory. No complaint about L.H. was made to the inspector.

The applicant suppressed the abuse and suffered significant psychological difficulties without initially connecting them to the abuse. In 1996, police investigating a 1995 complaint by another former pupil contacted her. She made a statement in 1997. L.H. was charged with 386 sexual offences involving about twenty-one former pupils; in 1998 he pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was imprisoned. His teaching licence was later withdrawn.

The applicant received an ex gratia award from the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal. She also brought a civil action against L.H., the Minister for Education, Ireland, and the Attorney General. Against the State defendants, she claimed negligence in the recognition, examination and supervision of the school; failure to put in place measures to prevent and stop L.H.’s abuse; vicarious liability for L.H.; and breach of constitutional rights. The High Court non-suited the negligence claim and later found no vicarious liability, holding that national schools were privately and clerically managed. The Supreme Court, by majority, dismissed her appeal, finding that the State funded and inspected schools but did not directly control them; L.H. was employed by the manager, not the State, and the State was not liable for the manager’s failure to report the 1971 complaint. One judge dissented, viewing primary education as a joint Church-State enterprise creating sufficient connection for State liability.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant principally complained under Article 3 that Ireland’s primary education system failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973, and under Article 13 that she lacked an effective domestic remedy. She also relied on Article 8 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, alone and with Article 14. Complaints about the length of civil proceedings were settled. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the prior 1971 complaint, the failure to report abuse to State authorities, the State’s regulatory and inspection role, the managerial/denominational structure of national schools, and the unsuccessful domestic civil remedies.

In **Z v. Iceland** (Application no. 3538/21), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints that Icelandic authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into alleged sexual harassment and discriminated on gender grounds in handling such cases, contrary to Articles 2, 8 and 14 of the Convention. The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 2002, was 16 at the time.

On 14 June 2019 the applicant attended a festival. In the early hours of 15 June she went to a co-worker’s tent. At 6:20 a.m. she sent a friend a video showing she was unwell; the footage captured the back of O.’s head, a 23-year-old man. She alleged that O. was groping her without consent, though this was not visible in the video. She said she passed out from intoxication and woke around 8:00 a.m. with her underwear on but trousers pulled down and jumper lifted to her breasts. She heard a belt being loosened. O. was beside her with his jumper removed and belt undone. She alleged he touched her breasts and genitals over and under her clothing. She pushed him away about three times and told him to stop; he stopped only when she left the tent.

On 15 June she attended the Emergency Reception Unit for Victims of Sexual Abuse. She declined a gynaecological examination but requested STD testing. Child Protection Services were notified because she was a minor. On 19 June she gave a police statement with a child protection worker present and provided the video.

O. was interviewed on 15 July. He denied guilt but admitted acting “a little wrong” before asking. He claimed he found the applicant half-asleep, they cuddled for warmth, and he touched her breast under her jumper with her bra between them. He said he stopped immediately when she appeared uncomfortable and shook her head, lasting about five seconds. He denied touching her genitals or removing clothing, but acknowledged she was a minor. Shown the video, he recognised himself and said it looked “very wrong,” explaining he had been trying to squeeze her.

The case was investigated under Article 199 of the General Penal Code on sexual harassment. Police took ten witness statements; none were direct witnesses. Several witnesses confirmed the applicant described waking to a man groping her with her trousers down and jumper up, and saw her shortly afterwards in shock, traumatised and crying. One described a later panic attack upon seeing O., requiring an ambulance. Three witnesses said they received Snapchat messages from the applicant that night describing unwanted sexual advances and a man not letting her out of the tent, with photos of her crying and a man’s head on her chest. Because Snapchat messages delete automatically, they were not preserved. Police did obtain a screenshot of two witnesses expressing concern that she said she was held against her will.

On 30 March 2020 the District Prosecutor discontinued the case, finding conviction unlikely. It cited her limited recollection, the lack of preserved messages, unclear video evidence, and a medical report containing no information about the alleged violations. Although O. admitted touching her breast, the prosecutor gave him the benefit of the doubt because he said he stopped upon realising lack of consent, leaving uncertainty about intent under Article 199. The State Prosecutor upheld that decision on 7 August 2020, again noting insufficient evidence and uncertainty as to intent.

The applicant complained that the authorities failed to effectively investigate the alleged sexual violence and discriminated against her on gender grounds in handling such cases. The Court gave notice of those complaints under Articles 2, 8 and 14; the remainder was inadmissible. The AIRE Centre intervened.

The case of *Lambertné Bársony v. Hungary* (Application no. 48689/10) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning a Hungarian national’s complaint about domestic civil proceedings. The applicant, Ms Klára Lambertné Bársony, was born in 1955 and lives in Miskolc. She lodged her application against the Republic of Hungary on 18 August 2010 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Hungarian Government were represented by Mr Z. Tallódi, Agent at the Ministry of Public Administration and Justice. On 6 March 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. A Second Section Committee composed of Judges Helen Keller (President), András Sajó and Egidijus Kūris, with Stanley Naismith as Section Registrar, adopted the judgment on 25 March 2014.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation stem from a civil dispute initiated by the applicant on 20 April 1998. On that date, she brought an action seeking division of the property of her common-law partnership with a person identified as Mr F. The case was heard at first instance by the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Court. It then proceeded on appeal to the Debrecen Court of Appeal. The final judgment in the domestic proceedings was delivered by the Supreme Court on 2 March 2010.

The central fact for the alleged violation is the duration of those domestic proceedings. From 20 April 1998, when the applicant commenced her action, until 2 March 2010, when the Supreme Court gave final judgment, the civil case lasted approximately eleven years and ten months. This period included proceedings at three judicial levels: a county court, a court of appeal, and the Supreme Court. The applicant lodged her Convention application on 18 August 2010, about five and a half months after the final domestic decision. That timing is relevant because applications to the European Court generally must be submitted within six months of the final domestic decision, and her application therefore appears timely in that respect.

Although the provided excerpt does not expressly set out the applicant’s specific complaints in the Court’s own words, the factual chronology indicates that the principal alleged violation concerned the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The key facts relevant to that complaint are the total elapsed time, the successive stages of domestic review, and the subject matter of the dispute, namely division of property from a common-law partnership. The nature of the dispute could affect the assessment of complexity and what was at stake for the applicant. The provided materials do not describe the reasons for the delay, the conduct of the parties, or any periods of inactivity, which would ordinarily be relevant to the Court’s reasonableness assessment. They also do not indicate whether the applicant raised a separate complaint, such as an alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy for the length of proceedings under Article 13 of the Convention. The available text ends after recording the Supreme Court’s final judgment and does not include the Court’s legal reasoning or conclusion.

In *Martynovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 69358/13), the European Court of Human Rights examined the temporary suspension of the applicant’s licence to practise as an advocate. The applicant, Roman Yuryevich Martynovskiy, a Ukrainian national born in 1965, received his advocate’s licence in 1993 and worked in Sevastopol, Crimea. In October 2012, the Sevastopol Bar elected him to represent it in the Higher Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Bar (“HQDCB”), a governing body of the Ukrainian Bar.

On 7 December 2012, the HQDCB held its first meeting. The applicant did not attend, saying he had not been informed. Lawyer D. complained to the HQDCB that the applicant’s absence violated Article 62 of the Rules of Professional Conduct, adopted on 17 November 2012 and published on 18 January 2013, which required advocates elected to self-government bodies to refrain from actions that could block those bodies’ work. D. claimed that the HQDCB had posted notice of the meeting on its website and asked that the applicant’s licence be suspended.

On 24 January 2013, the head of the HQDCB transferred D.’s complaint to the Qualification and Disciplinary Commission of the Regional Bar of Zakarpattya (“QDC of Zakarpattya”), relying on Article 63 § 2 of the Rules, which required complaints against advocates elected to self-government bodies to be examined by a regional Bar outside the region where they were elected. The applicant learned of the complaint in February 2013. On 5 March 2013, he objected that the website notice did not mention him by name or address; that the HQDCB had adopted its Rules at the 7 December meeting, showing its work had not been blocked; that D. wrongly stated he had been elected by the Chernigiv Bar rather than Sevastopol; and that the transfer was unlawful under the Law on the Bar, which required complaints to be examined where the advocate practised. He also questioned how D.’s rights had been violated.

On 17 April 2013, in the applicant’s absence, the Disciplinary Chamber of the QDC of Zakarpattya suspended his licence for six months for failing to attend the meeting and violating Article 62. It asserted, without concrete evidence, that all HQDCB members had been informed via the website. The applicant was informed on 22 April 2013. The decision was upheld on 16 May 2013. His appeal to the HQDCB did not have suspensive effect. He complained that the QDC lacked competence, that the HQDCB head had no power to transfer the complaint, and that his right to equality of arms was violated because he was not informed before the hearing. His suspension also prevented him from attending an HQDCB meeting on 19 April 2013.

The HQDCB’s review stalled. It held hearings in 2013 but reached no decision, and held none in 2014. In July 2014, the Bar Council changed the HQDCB’s Rules so that a draft decision was rejected unless a majority of members voted in favour. In 2016, the rapporteur prepared a draft granting the applicant’s appeal and annulling the disciplinary decisions. On 22 July 2016, 19 of 30 members attended; 11 voted in favour, 6 against, and 2 abstained. Under the amended Rules, the draft was rejected, so the licence suspension remained.

The applicant sought judicial review in October 2016, arguing that the Rules had been applied retroactively, that he had not been informed of the December 2012 meeting, that the transfer was unlawful, and that he learned of the 17 April 2013 hearing only after it occurred. Related proceedings and delays followed. In April 2021, the Kyiv District Administrative Court found the Bar bodies’ decisions lawful; the Supreme Court gave a final decision on 9 December 2021. The applicant claimed he could only access that decision in November 2022.

The ECtHR application, lodged on 19 September 2013, concerned alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention arising from the suspension of the applicant’s advocate’s licence. The key facts relevant to those allegations include the in-absentia disciplinary sanction, allegedly inadequate notice and evidence, the contested transfer of the complaint, retroactive application of rules, lack of suspensive effect and effective judicial review, prolonged proceedings, and the resulting interference with the applicant’s professional and private life.
