In *Halet v. Luxembourg*, Raphaël Halet, a French national born in 1976, worked for PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) in Luxembourg. PwC provided auditing, tax advice, and consultancy services, including preparing tax returns and obtaining Advance Tax Agreements (ATAs), also called tax rulings, from Luxembourg tax authorities. Halet coordinated a five-person team, although the Government disputed this description and characterized his role as administrative.

Between 2012 and 2014, several hundred ATAs and tax returns prepared by PwC were published, revealing advantageous tax agreements between PwC, multinational clients, and Luxembourg tax authorities. An earlier leak came from auditor A.D., who copied 45,000 pages of documents in October 2010 and gave them to journalist E.P. in 2011. These documents were used in a May 2012 *Cash Investigation* programme.

After that first programme, Halet contacted E.P. in May 2012 and offered further documents. Between October and December 2012, he transferred sixteen documents: fourteen tax returns and two covering letters. Some were used in a second *Cash Investigation* programme in June 2013. In November 2014, the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists posted the sixteen documents online as part of “LuxLeaks.” PwC’s internal investigation identified Halet. PwC and Halet entered a settlement in December 2014, under which PwC limited its claim to one euro and registered a €10 million mortgage on his assets. Halet was dismissed.

Following PwC’s complaint, Halet, A.D., and E.P. were prosecuted. In June 2016, the Luxembourg District Court convicted Halet of theft from his employer, fraudulent access to a data-processing system, breach of commercial secrecy, breach of professional secrecy, and laundering/possession. He received a nine-month suspended prison sentence and a €1,000 fine. On appeal in March 2017, the Court of Appeal upheld convictions for theft, fraudulent access/retention, breach of professional secrecy, and laundering, but set aside commercial secrecy. It accepted that the LuxLeaks disclosures concerned a public-interest debate on multinational taxation, tax transparency, and ATAs, and that the documents were authentic.

However, the Court of Appeal refused Halet full whistle-blower protection under Article 10 of the Convention. It found his sixteen documents were of limited relevance: they did not provide essential new information, did not significantly contribute to the already ongoing public debate, and caused reputational and client-confidence damage to PwC. It also noted that the ATA practice had already been exposed through A.D.’s earlier disclosures. Nevertheless, it recognized mitigating circumstances—honourable motive, disinterested action, and no prior criminal record—and imposed only a fine, dispensing with prison.

In January 2018, the Court of Cassation dismissed Halet’s appeal, holding that the whistle-blower assessment fell to the lower courts and was sufficiently reasoned. Halet applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 7 May 2018. He alleged that his criminal conviction for disclosing sixteen documents covered by professional secrecy to a journalist amounted to a disproportionate interference with his right to freedom of expression under Article 10. The Grand Chamber granted referral and held a hearing in February 2022. The central issue was whether Luxembourg’s criminal conviction and refusal to grant whistle-blower protection struck a fair balance between professional secrecy and PwC’s interests, on one hand, and Halet’s right to impart information in the public interest, on the other.

In *Gavrysh and Kosynets v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 62835/19 and 10392/25), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 22 January 2026. The judgment was adopted after private deliberations on 18 December 2025. It is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The case originated in two applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The Ukrainian Government were given notice of the applications.

The applicants are two Ukrainian nationals: Andriy Yuriyovych Gavrysh, born in 1973, and Sergiy Vitaliyovych Kosynets, born in 1972. Kosynets is represented by Mykhaylo Vasylyovych Kozachuk, a lawyer based in Kyiv. The central complaints in both applications concern the excessive length of civil proceedings before the domestic courts and the lack of any effective remedy in Ukrainian law for that delay. Such complaints ordinarily engage the fair-trial guarantee under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and the right to an effective remedy under Article 13.

The appended table provides the key factual details relevant to the alleged violations. In application no. 62835/19, Gavrysh introduced his application on 25 November 2019. The underlying civil proceedings commenced on 30 March 2007 and ended on 30 November 2020. The proceedings therefore lasted 13 years, 8 months and 1 day and passed through three levels of jurisdiction. This exceptionally long duration forms the factual basis of his complaint that the domestic courts failed to determine his civil case within a reasonable time. Because the proceedings were still pending when he applied to the European Court, his complaint also raises the question whether he had an effective domestic remedy to challenge or obtain redress for the delay.

In application no. 10392/25, Kosynets introduced his application on 21 March 2025. His civil proceedings began on 21 September 2021 and were still pending at the time the case was before the Court. Their duration was therefore more than 4 years, 2 months and 13 days, and the case had already passed through two levels of jurisdiction. As with Gavrysh, Kosynets complained that the length of the civil proceedings was excessive and that no effective remedy existed in domestic law. Because his proceedings remained pending, the alleged violation is continuing.

The judgment records the procedural history and factual details relevant to those alleged violations, including the dates of introduction, the start and end dates of the domestic civil proceedings, the total duration of each case, and the number of jurisdictional levels involved. The applicants’ core allegation is that the civil proceedings to which they were parties exceeded a reasonable time and that Ukrainian law did not provide them with an effective remedy for that delay. No further substantive details of the underlying civil disputes are set out in the provided extract. The Court’s assessment would therefore turn on the length and complexity of the proceedings, the conduct of the parties and authorities, what was at stake for the applicants, and the availability and effectiveness of domestic remedies for delay.

The case of *Ljajić v. Serbia* (Application no. 58385/13) originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Serbia with the European Court of Human Rights on 8 July 2013. The applicants were four Serbian nationals: Mr. Fuad Ljajić, Ms. Alma Ljajić, Mr. Ertan Ljajić, and Ms. Samra Ljajić. They were represented by a lawyer, and the Serbian Government was represented by its Agent.

The central facts of the case concern the failure of the Serbian authorities to enforce a final domestic judgment. The applicants’ late wife and mother, Ms. Sadija Ljajić, was employed by “Raška” Holding kompanija AD Novi Pazar, a company that, at the relevant time, was predominantly comprised of socially-owned capital. On 14 December 2005, the Municipal Court in Novi Pazar issued a judgment ordering the debtor company to pay Ms. Ljajić a certain amount for salary arrears and social insurance contributions, plus the costs of the civil proceedings.

Subsequently, on 10 October 2006, upon Ms. Ljajić’s request, the same Municipal Court ordered the enforcement of the 2005 judgment by means of a bank transfer. The court also ordered the debtor to pay the costs of these enforcement proceedings. Despite these final and binding decisions, the judgment remained unenforced.

A significant development occurred on 24 April 2013, when Ms. Sadija Ljajić passed away. Following her death, on 9 September 2013, the Novi Pazar First Instance Court declared Mr. Fuad Ljajić as the sole inheritor of her estate. Consequently, the applicants’ representative informed the Court that Ms. Alma Ljajić, Mr. Ertan Ljajić, and Ms. Samra Ljajić no longer intended to pursue the application. This left Mr. Fuad Ljajić as the sole applicant, pursuing the claim as the inheritor of the original creditor.

The failure to enforce the judgment was further compounded by the debtor’s financial situation. On 25 October 2013, the Commercial Court in Kraljevo opened insolvency proceedings in respect of the debtor company. In response, on 5 January 2014, Mr. Fuad Ljajić submitted his claims for payment, based on the 2005 judgment, within these insolvency proceedings. As of the date of the Court’s judgment, these insolvency proceedings were still pending.

The applicants’ complaint before the European Court of Human Rights was therefore based on the prolonged non-enforcement of the final judgment of 14 December 2005 rendered in their late mother’s and wife’s favour. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are: the existence of a final domestic judgment ordering payment by a socially-owned company; the subsequent order for enforcement that proved ineffective; the significant delay of over seven years between the judgment and the initiation of the application, during which time no payment was made; and the eventual insolvency of the debtor company, which left the claim unresolved and subject to pending insolvency proceedings. The case thus concerned the respondent State’s failure to ensure the enforcement of a final judgment against a company under its control or influence, a matter falling under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Summary of M.A. v. Austria (Application no. 4097/13)**

The case of *M.A. v. Austria* concerns an Italian father's complaint that Austrian authorities failed to enforce court orders for his daughter's return to Italy, thereby violating his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, an Italian national, had a daughter in December 2006 with D.P., an Austrian national, while living together in Vittorio Veneto, Italy. Under Italian law, both parents held joint custody. In January 2008, the relationship deteriorated, and D.P. left the family home with the child. On 8 February 2008, the Venice Youth Court issued a travel ban preventing the child's removal from Italy. However, on the same day, the applicant discovered that D.P. had already taken the child to Austria.

The Venice Youth Court subsequently lifted the travel ban in May 2008, granting preliminary joint custody and authorizing the child to reside with her mother in Austria, considering the child's young age and close relationship with her mother. The court also granted the applicant access rights twice monthly and appointed an expert to gather information for a final custody decision. Visits between the applicant and his daughter took place in Austria between October 2008 and June 2009 but later ceased due to the mother's alleged obstruction.

The applicant pursued multiple legal avenues. Under the 1980 Hague Convention on Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, his initial return application was dismissed by the Leoben District Court in July 2008, a decision set aside on appeal due to procedural issues. On reconsideration in November 2008, the court again refused return, citing Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention—finding a grave risk of psychological harm if the child were separated from her mother. The Leoben Regional Court upheld this in January 2009.

Meanwhile, in March 2009, D.P. initiated custody proceedings in Austria, and the Judenburg District Court awarded her sole custody in March 2010. Concurrently, the Venice Youth Court ordered the child's return to Italy in July 2009 under Article 11(8) of the Brussels IIa Regulation, issuing a certificate of enforceability. The applicant sought enforcement in Austria, and after initial refusal, the Leoben Regional Court granted enforcement in January 2010. This decision was appealed to the Austrian Supreme Court, which requested a preliminary ruling from the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU).

In July 2010, the CJEU ruled that the Italian courts retained jurisdiction and that the Venice Youth Court's return order was enforceable, with any changed circumstances to be raised before Italian courts. The Austrian Supreme Court subsequently dismissed D.P.'s appeal and directed enforcement. However, the applicant failed to provide proof of adequate accommodation as required by the Venice Youth Court's original conditions, leading to further delays.

In November 2011, the Venice Youth Court awarded sole custody to the applicant and ordered the child's return to Italy to live with him. The Leoben Regional Court granted enforcement in June 2012, ordering D.P. to hand over the child. D.P. did not comply and lodged an extraordinary appeal, which the Supreme Court rejected in September 2012, confirming the return order's enforceability.

Enforcement proceedings continued in 2013. The Wiener Neustadt District Court ordered handover by July 2013, but an attempted enforcement on 24 July 2013 failed because D.P. and the child were absent. Meanwhile, D.P. applied to the Venice Youth Court to stay enforcement and sought sole custody, alleging changed circumstances. The Italian proceedings remained pending. The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights in January 2013, alleging Austria's failure to enforce the return orders violated his family rights. The Court granted interim measures in December 2012 but lifted them in February 2013.

**Summary of *Svystoruk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 50067/13)**

The case of *Svystoruk v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Viktor Petrovych Svystoruk, a Ukrainian national, on 26 July 2013. The application alleged that the Ukrainian authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation into the murder of his daughter, Inna Puzyr.

The underlying facts are as follows. On 11 August 2007, Inna Puzyr was found stabbed to death by the roadside. The Poltava Regional Police immediately instituted criminal proceedings for suspected murder. Initially, the applicant was summoned only as a witness, and his request to join the proceedings as an aggrieved party was refused. Subsequently, on 18 August 2007, his other daughter, V.K., was admitted as an aggrieved party.

The investigation was marked by a series of arrests and releases. On 25 August 2007, a local resident, O.T., was arrested. He initially confessed but later retracted his statement, alleging police ill-treatment. The proceedings against him were discontinued due to a lack of corroborating evidence. On 7 September 2007, V.K. formally complained to the police about the investigation's ineffectiveness and her inability to meaningfully participate, noting she was denied access to the case file and poorly informed of progress. The police denied any irregularities.

The investigation was suspended on 10 October 2007 due to a lack of leads, but this decision was quickly quashed by the prosecutor's office, which noted the investigation had been "perfunctory." In November 2007, V.K. again complained of ineffectiveness, suspecting her sister's husband, R.P., and pointing to investigative delays that had resulted in the loss of important evidence.

In January 2008, the police acknowledged significant inadequacies in the investigation, reprimanded supervisors, and replaced the lead investigator. A breakthrough appeared to occur on 5 March 2008, when R.P. was arrested and confessed to the murder. However, he later retracted his confession, claiming it was given under duress. Consequently, on 15 August 2008, the proceedings against him were also discontinued due to irreconcilable discrepancies between his retracted confession and other evidence. The case was suspended again.

Over the next several years, the investigation was repeatedly renewed and suspended. In May 2009, the Deputy Minister of Interior ordered a renewal after reviewing the file, noting that leads to at least two potential perpetrators had not been properly followed and that virtually no action had been taken in 2008. Despite this, the pattern of suspension and renewal continued into 2011 due to insufficient investigative measures.

A key development occurred on 15 April 2013, when, under a new Code of Criminal Procedure, the applicant was finally admitted as an aggrieved party and granted access to the case file. After reviewing the file, the applicant complained to the Minister of Interior on 19 August 2013. He argued that the entire investigation had been marred by prohibitive delays and inactivity, with authorities having focused excessively on a single theory (the husband's involvement) rather than conducting a prompt and comprehensive examination of objective evidence. He provided specific suggestions for further investigative steps, including potential witnesses and the type of weapon used.

The authorities responded by stating that while no new leads had been uncovered, his suggestions would be considered. This pattern of acknowledging suggestions but reporting no progress continued in response to further complaints. The applicant's core complaint to the Strasbourg Court was that the investigation into his daughter's murder was ineffective and protracted, violating Ukraine's obligation under Article 2 of the Convention to conduct a thorough and prompt investigation into a death caused by violence.

In *Temchenko v. Ukraine* (Application no. 30579/10), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Anatoliy Georgiyevich Temchenko, a Ukrainian national born in 1942 and formerly rector of a State-owned university. He was arrested on 29 September 2009 on suspicion of receiving bribes as rector and detained in Kryvyy Rig’s temporary detention facility and later the SIZO remand centre.

Before arrest, the applicant had type-2 diabetes, and an endocrinologist had advised that insulin treatment be commenced and adjusted in hospital. The domestic courts ordered and extended his detention, citing risks that he might abscond, hinder the investigation, or continue criminal activity, though often without concrete supporting facts. appellate courts upheld detention relying on unspecified evidence and medical documents indicating he was fit for detention.

While in detention, the applicant’s health deteriorated. He was diagnosed with ischemic heart disease, hypertension, chronic pancreatitis, kidney pathology, and diabetes. The SIZO medical unit lacked specialist staff and equipment. Medical staff and outside doctors repeatedly stated that he required in-patient treatment in a specialist endocrinology or cardiology institution; the head of the SIZO medical unit even asked the judge to change the preventive measure because adequate treatment was impossible in the SIZO. The judge did not respond. The applicant received insulin in the SIZO, partially bought by himself or supplied by relatives, and had intermittent hospital treatment. Forensic medical reports of 12 November 2010, 28 January 2011, and 8 June 2011 found his condition grave and unstable, worsened by inadequate treatment, and at risk of fatal complications such as cardiac arrest, brain haemorrhage, or aortic dissection unless he received comprehensive specialist in-patient care. They also considered transportation undesirable or potentially fatal.

The applicant repeatedly requested release in 2010 and 2011, arguing poor health and that he could no longer hinder the investigation because he was no longer rector. The District Court rejected those requests, saying he could influence witnesses and was receiving medical aid, without citing concrete facts or assessing the adequacy of treatment. On 16 March 2011, under Rule 39, the European Court indicated that the Government should ensure he received treatment in the specialised institutions identified in the January 2011 report. He was later hospitalised locally and, in July 2011, taken to Kyiv, where heart surgery was prescribed. In May 2011 he was convicted of bribery and sentenced; in October 2011 the sentence was changed to suspended imprisonment and he was released.

A separate alleged Article 5 issue concerned his detention from 29 January to 9 March 2010, which was not covered by any court decision. The District Court nevertheless found it justified because he had been awaiting committal for trial.

As to conditions, the applicant alleged dampness and poor food in the SIZO, and that the prescribed special diet was not provided there but brought by relatives. He complained of transportation in an ordinary van 26 times and a police car once, with inadequate ventilation and heating, sometimes lasting up to three hours; later he was transported by ambulance with a doctor 19 times. He also alleged that the train carriage to Kyiv was unsuitable and that he was handcuffed to hospital beds, though he did not raise the handcuffing complaint domestically. His complaints to prosecutors were rejected. The key alleged violations therefore concerned Article 3 (inadequate medical care, detention conditions, and transportation) and Article 5 (unlawful or unjustified detention).

CASE OF BOTEZATU v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA (Application no. 17899/08) concerned a Moldovan police officer, Radu Botezatu, who complained to the European Court of Human Rights about the failure of the Moldovan authorities to enforce a final domestic judgment ordering the Chișinău municipality to provide social housing for him and his family. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are as follows.

On 21 July 2004 the Centru District Court ordered the municipality to provide social housing. This judgment was upheld by the Chișinău Court of Appeal on 19 October 2004 and became final on 4 November 2004. Enforcement proceedings began on 11 May 2005, but the judgment remained unenforced for years. The applicant alleged that this non-enforcement breached his rights under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The applicant lodged his application with the ECtHR on 21 March 2008. On 10 November 2009 the application was communicated to the Government following the pilot judgment in Olaru and Others v. Moldova. Meanwhile, Moldova introduced Law no. 87, effective 1 July 2011, creating a domestic remedy for unreasonable length of proceedings and non-enforcement of final judgments, allowing acknowledgment and compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. On 2 August 2011 the applicant used this remedy, seeking enforcement plus compensation: EUR 10,000 non-pecuniary; MDL 129,700 pecuniary, including MDL 123,200 in rent paid from September 2004 to December 2011 for alternative accommodation; and costs. He submitted four lease contracts, each for less than three years.

The Ministry of Finance disputed the leases as fictitious: the landlady was a relative, had no commercial registration, the contracts were not tax-registered until 2011, and had never been registered in the land register. On 30 November 2011 the Rîșcani District Court found violations of Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 due to non-enforcement exceeding seven years. It rejected the Ministry’s arguments, noting that leases under three years did not require land-register registration and that the landlady’s tax and commercial failures were not imputable to the applicant. It awarded MDL 112,000 (about EUR 7,050) non-pecuniary and granted pecuniary damage and costs in full.

On appeal, on 29 February 2012, the Chișinău Court of Appeal quashed that judgment. It acknowledged only an Article 6 violation from non-enforcement for 78 months (11 May 2005 to 30 November 2011). It awarded MDL 36,000 (about EUR 2,270) non-pecuniary and MDL 8,965 (EUR 565) costs. It dismissed pecuniary damage as unsubstantiated, holding the lease contracts ineffective vis-à-vis the State under Article 876 of the Civil Code due to the Ministry’s objections. That judgment became final.

Finally, on 8 August 2012 the municipality issued the applicant an occupancy voucher for a new flat. The Government informed the ECtHR that the final judgment had been enforced on that date, which the applicant did not dispute. The facts thus centre on a lengthy failure to enforce a final housing judgment, the applicant’s attempt to obtain compensation through the new domestic remedy, and the domestic courts’ divergent assessments of the violation and of the lease-based pecuniary claim.

**Case Summary: Jovičić and Others v. Serbia (Applications nos. 37270/11 et al.)**

The case of *Jovičić and Others v. Serbia* originated from eight separate applications lodged against the Republic of Serbia with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were all Serbian nationals and former employees of Raketa-Putnički Saobraćaj AD, a company based in Užice (hereinafter "the debtor"). They were represented by a lawyer from Novi Pazar. The applications were declared admissible on 15 October 2013.

The key facts revolve around the applicants' inability to enforce final domestic court judgments due to the debtor company's insolvency proceedings.

**Background and Civil Claims:**
Since the debtor company failed to meet its obligations toward its employees, all the applicants initiated numerous separate civil claims seeking payment of salary arrears and various social security contributions. They were successful in these proceedings and obtained final court decisions ordering the debtor to pay them specified sums. The essential details of these domestic proceedings are outlined in an appended table to the judgment.

**Insolvency Proceedings and Impact on Enforcement:**
A pivotal event occurred on 12 July 2010, when the Užice Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings in respect of the debtor. This decision had an immediate and severe consequence: in accordance with domestic insolvency law, all ongoing enforcement proceedings against the debtor were automatically stayed. This legal measure prevented the applicants from enforcing their final court judgments.

The decision to open insolvency was posted on the Commercial Court's notice board on the same day, 12 July 2010, and was subsequently published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia on 4 August 2010. The applicants complied with the insolvency procedure by duly reporting their claims, based on their court decisions, to the insolvency administration.

**Insolvency Process and Debtor's Status:**
The court examined the reported claims over a series of hearings held between 30 September 2010 and 8 June 2011. On 8 June 2011, the court partially accepted the applicants' claims.

The liquidation of the debtor's assets was slow. On 17 April 2012, some of the debtor’s property was sold. The remaining assets were advertised for sale, and a public auction was scheduled for 29 June 2012. However, it was not known whether any assets were sold at that auction. Critically, at the time of the Court's judgment, the insolvency proceedings in respect of the debtor were still ongoing.

Separately, the debtor's status had been the subject of prior changes. It was privatised on 30 December 2002. This privatisation was annulled on 17 July 2007 because the buyer had failed to fulfil his contractual obligations. Following the annulment, the State owned 58.18% of the shares in the debtor. However, on 11 December 2008, the State sold its shares to a private company.

**The Alleged Violation:**
The core of the applicants' complaint before the European Court was that they had obtained final court decisions, which remained unenforced. The State's responsibility was engaged because the opening of insolvency proceedings, a legally mandated process initiated by a state court, automatically stayed the enforcement of their final judgments. This situation, where final and binding judicial decisions in their favour remained unexecuted for a prolonged period due to the ongoing, state-supervised insolvency process, formed the basis of their alleged violation of rights protected under the Convention, specifically the right to a fair trial and the right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The relevant domestic law, including the Insolvency Act, which governs these proceedings and their effect on enforcement, was also reviewed by the Court.

In *Sagvolden v. Norway*, the applicant, Torill Sagvolden, was a Norwegian national who acquired an apartment in Housing Cooperative X in March 2004. Before moving in, the cooperative discovered that her son, Mr A, had caused serious problems in Housing Cooperative Y, where the applicant had previously lived and where her son had cohabited with her. The Board therefore asked for a written undertaking that Mr A would not move into the new apartment. In May 2004, the applicant’s lawyer confirmed that she, not her son, would move in and that her household would consist of one person. The Board maintained its approval on that basis.

Mr A later moved into the applicant’s apartment. Between 2005 and 2008, he repeatedly engaged in violent assault, frightening behaviour, and harassment against neighbours in Housing Cooperative X. He was convicted by Oslo City Court on 10 March 2006 and 23 June 2008, receiving prison sentences. The courts described him as aggressive, intrusive, and prone to conspiracy perceptions, and found that his conduct seriously harmed neighbours’ sense of safety in their homes. He was also subjected to several restraining orders prohibiting contact with four neighbours between 2007 and 2009.

In April 2009, the cooperative issued an order requiring the applicant to sell her apartment under the Housing Cooperative Act 2003, relying on serious disturbance and nuisance. When she refused, the cooperative instituted proceedings for compulsory sale. The applicant objected, arguing that the Board’s decision did not validly authorise compulsory sale, that her son’s offences were dated and the situation had improved, that she was eighty years old and increasingly dependent on her son, that she had no realistic alternative housing, and that less intrusive measures should be considered. She also requested an oral hearing under the ordinary procedure, since domestic law required such examination if objections against compulsory sale were not “clearly groundless.”

On 26 April 2010, Oslo City Court rejected her objections as clearly groundless and ordered compulsory sale. It held that the part owner was responsible for household members’ conduct, that Mr A’s behaviour constituted substantial default, and that no prior warning was needed because the conditions for eviction under section 5-23 were met. It further found that the applicant’s age did not outweigh the neighbours’ interests. The High Court rejected her appeal on 5 August 2010, deciding on the written file without an oral hearing and agreeing that the objections were clearly groundless. The Supreme Court’s Appeals Leave Committee refused leave on 1 October 2010.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 about the absence of an oral hearing before the national courts in the compulsory-sale proceedings, despite the serious consequences for her home. She complained under Article 8 that the compulsory sale was not “necessary” in a democratic society. The key facts relevant to those complaints were the domestic-law requirement of an ordinary procedure with an oral hearing unless objections were clearly groundless; the national courts’ determination that her objections were clearly groundless and could be decided in writing; the long-running serious harassment by her son; the applicant’s confirmation that only she would occupy the flat; her age and dependence on her son; and her claims that the situation had improved and that less intrusive measures were available. Subsequent proceedings validated the sale and led to eviction steps. The applicant died in November 2015.

In *Qerimi and Canaj v. Albania* (Applications nos. 12878/10 and 74858/12), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 8 September 2016. The case originated in two applications lodged by two Albanian nationals under Article 34 of the Convention. The Albanian Government were represented by Agent A. Hicka of the State Advocate’s Office. The applications were communicated to the Government on 20 December 2013. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, citing *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*. The applicants failed to submit claims for just satisfaction within the time-limit allowed under Rule 60 of the Rules of Court.

The facts concerned the recognition of inherited property rights and the subsequent failure to provide restitution or compensation. In application no. 12878/10 (*Qerimi*), on 1 November 2002 the Durrës Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties recognised the applicant’s inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 8,000 sq. m. Because the plot was occupied, the applicant and other heirs were to be compensated in kind with an equivalent plot of land. In application no. 74858/12 (*Canaj*), on 23 November 2001 the Fier Commission recognised the applicant’s inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 1,121 sq. m. Of that, 598 sq. m were restored to the applicant. Since the remaining 523 sq. m was occupied, the applicant and other heirs were to be awarded compensation in the sum of 251,040 Albanian Lek (ALL).

The relevant domestic law and practice were described in prior judgments, including *Ramadhi v. Albania*, *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*, and *Sharra and Others v. Albania*. Relevant Council of Europe materials were also referred to in *Sharra and Others*, *Metalla and Others*, *Siliqi and Others*, and *Karagjozi and Others*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that final decisions of the domestic property commissions recognised the applicants’ property rights and either ordered compensation in kind (*Qerimi*) or monetary compensation (*Canaj*), but the authorities apparently failed to execute those decisions. The Court’s reliance on *Manushaqe Puto* indicates that the alleged violations concerned the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in the context of property restitution and compensation. Such failure engages Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial, including the right to execution of final judgments) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). The systemic nature of the problem had already been established in the Court’s case-law concerning Albania’s failure to enforce property compensation decisions.

Thus, the case is essentially one of delayed or non-executed property restitution/compensation decisions, where the applicants had final domestic decisions in their favour but did not receive the awarded compensation or equivalent land. The Court treated the matter as a repeat case under well-established case-law. Since the applicants did not submit just satisfaction claims, no separate award of just satisfaction was sought by them in the proceedings. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

The case *Kyryk and Gonchar v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 6200/25 and 7881/25) concerns two separate criminal proceedings in Ukraine, lodged with the European Court of Human Rights in February 2025. The Fifth Section Committee delivered judgment on 16 April 2026.

In the first application, Stefaniya Mykhaylivna Kyryk (born 1987) complained about the investigation into her husband’s death. On 12 August 2018, her husband was riding a motorcycle when he collided with a car driven by V. He sustained severe injuries, and a criminal case was opened. He died in hospital on 25 August 2018. Although the applicant repeatedly requested victim status, she was granted it only on 14 November 2018. Investigators questioned witnesses and took other steps. On 26 December 2018, the case was closed for lack of evidence of a criminal offence; expert conclusions stated that V. had no technical possibility to avoid the collision. On 21 January 2019, an investigative judge overturned that closure, doubting the thoroughness and completeness of the investigation. After reopening, a crime scene reconstruction was conducted with the applicant, and forensic metallurgical and engineering examinations of the motorcycle were carried out. On 31 March 2021, the case was closed again for absence of a criminal offence. On 11 May 2021, the investigative judge annulled that decision as premature, noting that investigators had failed to exhaust all means of verifying key circumstances and to address the applicant’s arguments. It is unclear whether further investigative actions occurred, apart from a road traffic technical examination appointed in 2022. On 24 June 2024, an expert report concluded that traffic organisation at the intersection did not comply with regulatory standards. Nevertheless, on 29 August 2024, the investigator closed the case, finding no traffic violations by V. directly linked to the accident. On 14 October 2024, the appellate court upheld the first-instance decision and dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the closure. These facts are relevant to alleged violations concerning the length and effectiveness of the investigation into the death.

In the second application, Mykhaylo Ivanovych Gonchar (born 1950) complained about criminal proceedings arising from a road accident. On 29 July 2019, while riding a scooter, he was cut off by a car driven by P. He fell and sustained injuries classified as moderate by a forensic medical expert. Criminal proceedings were initiated the next day. On 19 March 2020, P. was served with a notice of suspicion, and the two-month pre-trial investigation period began. An indictment was issued on 17 June 2020 and sent to the trial court on 22 June 2020. On 24 June 2020, the applicant lodged a civil claim within the criminal proceedings. On 15 September 2021, the local court convicted P. of traffic rules violations and sentenced him to two years of community service. However, on 20 October 2025, the Sumy Court of Appeal quashed the verdict and terminated the criminal proceedings. The appellate court held that, under mandatory legal provisions, the proceedings had to be terminated because the two-month pre-trial investigation time-limit had expired and had never been extended, while the bill of indictment was submitted to the trial court after that period. These facts are relevant to alleged violations regarding the length of proceedings and the eventual termination of the case on procedural grounds, which prevented a final determination of the criminal charge and the applicant’s civil claim.

**A.T. v. Luxembourg** (Application no. 30460/13) concerned a British national, A.T., who complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the European Convention on Human Rights that his criminal proceedings in Luxembourg were unfair because he lacked a lawyer during police questioning and did not receive effective legal assistance during questioning by the investigating judge.

The charges arose from an investigation ordered on 9 October 2009 into alleged rape and indecent assault of a girl under sixteen, aggravated by the perpetrator’s position of authority over her. On 4 December 2009 A.T. was arrested in the United Kingdom under a European Arrest Warrant. He was surrendered to Luxembourg on 17 December 2009. On arrival at Luxembourg airport at 2.45 p.m., he was served with the warrant. At 3.20 p.m., he was questioned at a police station in the presence of an interpreter. The police report stated that A.T. initially refused to make any statement and, referring repeatedly to British legislation, claimed his right to legal assistance. After receiving explanations about Luxembourg procedure, he agreed to take part in questioning. No lawyer was present. He was informed of the victim’s statements and the suspicions against him, denied all charges, and gave his version of events. At the end of the interrogation, he requested legal assistance for the next day’s interrogation before the investigating judge. He was then transferred to Luxembourg Prison.

On the morning of 18 December 2009, A.T. was questioned by the investigating judge with an interpreter. He was informed of his right to choose a defence lawyer or have one officially appointed. He availed himself of that right and was assigned Mr W. as officially appointed counsel. He was then questioned in the presence of his lawyer and interpreter, made statements on the facts, and confirmed his police statements. He was later released on 10 March 2010 subject to conditions.

At trial, the District Court on 31 March 2011 sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment with a three-year partial probation period. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 7 February 2012. A.T.’s lawyer complained that after extradition he had been heard by police without legal assistance, despite requesting it. The Court of Appeal relied on the police report and concluded that, although A.T. had initially requested a lawyer, after the applicable procedure was explained he agreed to give statements without counsel. On 22 November 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed his appeal, finding no violation of Article 6 § 3 because he had agreed to make statements absent counsel.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, A.T. alleged unfairness, specifically the lack of effective assistance before the police and the investigating judge. On 4 November 2013, the Court communicated the complaint concerning lack of effective assistance before the police and the investigating judge to the Luxembourg Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The British Government declined to intervene, while Fair Trials International was granted leave to intervene.

Later, in 2013, Luxembourg prosecutors corresponded with UK authorities regarding extradition to serve his sentence. They stated that the police report showed A.T. had neither been assisted by nor offered a lawyer during the 17 December 2009 police hearing. As to the 18 December 2009 interrogation, they said an officially appointed lawyer assisted him and that access to counsel before interrogation had not been restricted.

The key alleged violation therefore centred on the initial police interrogation after surrender, where A.T. had requested legal assistance but was questioned without counsel. The domestic courts treated his eventual agreement to speak as a waiver. The case engaged the Salduz line of authority and Luxembourg’s subsequent circulars and Police Memorandum No. 49/2011, which extended effective lawyer access to police interrogations in preparatory investigations.

In *El Ghatet v. Switzerland*, the applicants—Saleh El Ghatet, a Swiss and Egyptian national living in Switzerland, and his son Mohamed Saleh El Ghatet, an Egyptian national living in Egypt—complained that Switzerland’s refusal of family reunification breached their right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The father entered Switzerland in 1997 and applied for asylum, which was rejected. His son remained in Egypt with his mother. In 1999 the father married a Swiss national and obtained a residence permit; a daughter was born in 2000. The son visited Switzerland for three months in 2002 on a tourist visa and re-entered in July 2003 for family reunification. In 2004 the father obtained a permanent residence permit and then Swiss nationality. However, after difficulties at school and with his stepmother, the son returned to Egypt in January 2005, where he was cared for by his mother and paternal grandmother. The father separated from his wife in 2006.

On 1 March 2006, when the son was 15½, the father applied for family reunification, relying on his custody under Egyptian law. The Cantonal Migration Office refused the request in February 2007. On appeal, the Cantonal Court in September 2007 granted it. Although the statutory requirements under Article 17 § 2 of the Residence of Foreign Nationals Act were not met, the court held that the applicants’ Article 8 interests prevailed over public interests and ordered a residence permit. The Migration Office then sought the Federal Office of Migration’s consent. In March 2008 the Federal Office refused, finding the requirements unmet and the cantonal decision contrary to Federal Supreme Court case-law.

The applicants appealed to the Federal Administrative Court. In July 2009 they informed authorities that the son’s mother had moved to Kuwait with a new spouse, leaving the son in the exclusive care of his paternal grandmother. In February 2010 the Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. It found the statutory requirements unmet and held that Article 8 could not be relied on because the son had reached adulthood and was not dependent on his father.

A further appeal to the Federal Supreme Court was dismissed in July 2010. That court found the relationship between father and son was not “paramount,” despite the father’s custody under Egyptian law. It noted the father had not sought reunification immediately after arriving in Switzerland; the son had been cared for by his mother and grandmother in Egypt until he was 18; he had lived almost all his life in Egypt and had stronger social and personal ties there; and he had returned to Egypt after a prior 1½-year stay with his father. The court also observed that the father had then preferred the son to live with his mother, that integration in Switzerland would now be harder, and that the father had close ties to his daughter in Switzerland and could not be expected to relocate. It distinguished *Tuquabo-Tekle v. the Netherlands* because there the sole surviving parent had sought reunification promptly and the child faced forced marriage. The ECtHR later refused an interim measure under Rule 39.

The applicants alleged that this refusal violated Article 8. The key issues concerned the son’s minority at application but adulthood by decision, dependency, custody, the delay in applying, care arrangements in Egypt, and the strength of family ties versus integration prospects.

**Case: Bouyid v. Belgium (Application no. 23380/09, Grand Chamber, 28 September 2015)**

The case concerned two Belgian brothers, Saïd and Mohamed Bouyid, who alleged that they were slapped in the face by police officers while at the Saint-Josse-ten-Noode police station in Brussels. Their complaint was brought under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment.

The applicants lived with their family next to the local police station and described a long history of tense relations with the police. They alleged that problems began in 1999 after an officer suspected their brother of scratching his car, leading to what they described as police harassment and reprisals. They filed numerous complaints over the years, including an allegation that the first applicant, then aged 13, had been beaten by an officer in 1999 and suffered a perforated eardrum.

The first alleged incident occurred on 8 December 2003. The first applicant, Saïd, said that at around 4 p.m. he was outside his home with a friend, ringing the doorbell because he had forgotten his keys. A plain-clothes officer, A.Z., asked to see his identity card. Saïd refused and asked the officer to show his credentials. The officer then allegedly grabbed him by his jacket, tearing it, and took him to the police station. While alone with A.Z. in a room, Saïd claimed the officer slapped him in the face as he protested about his arrest. A medical certificate issued the same day at 7:20 p.m. recorded that he was in a state of shock and had erythema on his left cheek and left external auditory canal. The Government disputed the slap, saying Saïd had refused identification, caused a scene, insulted an officer, and was released after his identity was verified; A.Z. filed a criminal complaint against him.

The second incident occurred on 23 February 2004. Mohamed Bouyid was at the police station being interviewed by Officer P.P. about an altercation involving him and his mother. He alleged that P.P. slapped him after telling him not to lean on his desk, and then threatened to put him in a cell if he did not sign his statement. A same-day medical certificate noted bruising on his left cheek. The Government stated that Mohamed had been arrogant, slouching, leaning on the desk, laughing, changing his statement, and threatening officers. P.P. admitted grabbing Mohamed’s arm to make him leave but denied slapping him.

The applicants complained to the Standing Committee for oversight of police services and joined criminal proceedings as civil parties. Officers A.Z. and P.P. were charged with violence and arbitrary acts. However, the investigation found insufficient evidence. In 2005 the Crown Prosecutor sought discontinuance; in 2007 the Committals Division discontinued the case, a decision upheld by the Court of Appeal in 2008. The Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal later that year.

A Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights found no violation of Article 3 in 2013. The Grand Chamber, on referral, reversed that finding. It held that a slap inflicted by police on a person under their control can amount to degrading treatment, even without serious injury. The Government had failed to provide a plausible explanation for the applicants’ injuries, and the Grand Chamber found a violation of Article 3 in respect of each applicant.

Case Oliari and Others v Italy (Applications nos. 18766/11 and 36030/11) concerned six Italian nationals in three same-sex couples: Enrico Oliari and Mr A.; Gian Mario Felicetti and Riccardo Zappa; and Riccardo Perelli Cippo and Roberto Zaccheo. They lived in stable, committed relationships and complained that Italian law prevented them from marrying or entering any other type of civil union, leaving their relationships without legal recognition and discriminating against them because of their sexual orientation. They invoked Articles 8, 12 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court communicated the complaints under Article 8 alone and in conjunction with Article 14.

Oliari and Mr A. requested marriage banns in Trent in July 2008; the request was refused. They challenged the refusal before the Trent Tribunal, arguing that Italian law did not expressly prohibit same-sex marriage and that any exclusion was unconstitutional. The Tribunal rejected the claim, holding that the Civil Code required spouses to be of opposite sex, that there was no fundamental right to marry, and that there was no discrimination because the limitation applied generally. On appeal, the Trent Court of Appeal referred the constitutional issue to the Italian Constitutional Court. In judgment no. 138/2010, the Constitutional Court declared the challenge inadmissible. It accepted that homosexual unions, understood as stable cohabitation between two people of the same sex, fell within Article 2 of the Constitution and deserved legal recognition of relevant rights and duties. However, it held that Parliament had discretion to decide the form of recognition and that marriage under Article 29 and the Civil Code referred only to opposite-sex marriage. It found no unreasonable discrimination. The Court of Appeal then rejected the applicants’ claims in September 2010.

Felicetti and Zappa began their relationship in 2003, moved in together, registered their cohabitation, and designated each other as guardians in case of incapacity. In February 2011 they requested marriage banns; their request was refused in April 2011. They did not pursue the Civil Code remedy because, after the Constitutional Court judgment, it was considered ineffective.

Perelli Cippo and Zaccheo had cohabited since 2002, opened a joint bank account, and registered their cohabitation. In November 2009 they requested marriage banns; the request was refused. They challenged the refusal before the Milan Tribunal, which rejected their claim in June 2010, relying on Constitutional Court judgment no. 138/2010. They did not appeal further because the remedy was considered ineffective.

Under Italian law, same-sex couples could not marry, and no alternative civil union or registered partnership existed, either for same-sex or heterosexual couples. “Cohabitation agreements” were not specifically regulated, though later private contracts could govern some financial aspects of living together. Some municipalities established symbolic civil union registers, but these had no legal effect. Italian case law, including Court of Cassation judgments in 2012 and 2015, recognized that same-sex couples had a right to respect for private and family life and that the legislature should act, but held that there was no right to marry or to register a foreign same-sex marriage.

The applicants alleged that Italy’s failure to provide any legal framework allowing same-sex couples to marry or enter a civil union violated their right to respect for private and family life and discriminated against them. They stressed their stable relationships, mutual support, cohabitation, and repeated attempts to obtain official recognition, all of which were refused. The domestic authorities consistently left recognition to Parliament, which had not enacted legislation. Comparative European material showed that many Council of Europe states had introduced same-sex marriage or civil partnership. The case therefore concerned whether Italy’s lack of any legal recognition or alternative to marriage for same-sex couples breached Article 8 and Article 14 of the Convention.

In *Moog v. Germany* (Applications nos. 23280/08 and 2334/10), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Claus Moog, a German national, that German court decisions concerning contact with his son, D., violated his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant lodged the applications in 2008 and 2010, the second also on behalf of his son.

D. was born in July 1998. His parents separated in 1999, and D. lived with his mother, Ms K. From 1999 onward, the parents were in continuous dispute over contact and custody. Initially, the father was granted contact, later fixed at eight hours every Saturday. The mother was repeatedly accused of failing to cooperate, and the Family Court warned and eventually fined her. In 2002, an expert considered that D. enjoyed contact with his father but that the parents instrumentalised the child and could not communicate, so joint custody was impossible. The mother was granted custody, while the father received six hours of contact per week and a contact facilitator was appointed.

In 2003, the Cologne Court of Appeal found that the mother had “intentionally sabotaged” contact and warned that custody might have to be reconsidered. However, later that year the same court quashed a fine against her, relying on a paediatrician’s report that D. showed mental abnormalities after contact with the father, caused by parental conflict; enforcing contact would therefore harm the child. In 2005, the mother applied to suspend contact. D. told the court he no longer wished to see his father. In 2006, the child’s paediatrician stated in an affidavit that D. had been deeply traumatised by forced contact and parental hostility, had aggressive outbursts, and needed psychotherapy. Attempts at supervised contact failed after the mother and child were advised not to speak to the applicant on medical grounds.

In 2007, the kindergarten director recommended continuing contact, finding D. overly controlled by his mother and in need of a counterbalancing authority figure. The Family Court provisionally granted monthly contact, ordered the mother to prepare D. and not influence him against his father, and warned of fines. The first visit failed when D. refused to leave with the applicant. The Youth Office reported that D. wanted peace and did not want to see his father, while his teacher said the father lacked empathy. The Family Court fined the mother EUR 3,000.

In February 2008, the Court of Appeal quashed the fine. It cited a psychologist’s certificate that the mother suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder and doubted her ability to prepare D. for contact. It also noted D.’s stated unwillingness and preferred therapy to forced contact. In December 2008, the Family Court suspended the applicant’s contact until 31 December 2011. It found that the severe parental conflict would create a serious loyalty conflict for D., that the mother’s stress disorder prevented cooperation, that forced contact could retraumatise the child, and that D. needed trauma therapy.

The applicant appealed. In January 2009, a custody expert preliminarily opined that contact would not endanger D.’s welfare. In May 2009, custody remained with the mother, although the court noted her obstructive attitude. In June 2009, the Court of Appeal confirmed the contact suspension, acknowledging that the mother had effectively achieved her aim, but relying on D.’s repeated statements that he did not want to see his father and associated him with court proceedings. It considered a period of respite necessary and stated that the loyalty conflict was not solely the mother’s fault. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider the applicant’s complaint in August 2009. The applicant alleged that these decisions, especially the three-year suspension of contact, violated his Article 8 right to respect for family life.

CASE OF OTGON v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA (Application no. 22743/07) is a European Court of Human Rights case. The applicant, Ms Svetlana Otgon, a Moldovan national born in 1963 and living in Călărași, complained under Article 8 of the Convention that she had received insufficient compensation after domestic courts established a violation of her rights. The application was lodged on 20 April 2007 and communicated to the Moldovan Government, represented by Agent V. Grosu, on 30 November 2009.

The facts arose on 26 October 2005, when the applicant and her twelve-year-old daughter drank tap water in their apartment and soon felt unwell. On 29 October 2005 the daughter was admitted to hospital with a diagnosis of serious acute dysentery. The applicant was admitted with the same diagnosis on 31 October 2005 and discharged on 13 November 2005, one day after her daughter.

The applicant sued the local utilities provider, a State-owned company, seeking 100,000 Moldovan lei (MDL), approximately EUR 6,700 at the time, in compensation for harm to her health and related inconveniences, including subsequent investigations and disinfection.

On 1 March 2006 the Călărași District Court found in her favour. It relied on sanitary, medical and technical reports which showed that near the applicant’s apartment block the sewage pipe was situated above the drinking-water pipe and was leaking. The water pipe had cracked on 26 October 2005, allowing sewage water to infiltrate the drinking-water pipe. The court also found that the pipes had been in use since 1977, although their expected lifespan was fifteen years. Five people who had drunk water from the same pipe were admitted to hospital with the same diagnosis around the same time as the applicant. Taking into account the physical and mental suffering caused to the applicant and her daughter, the District Court awarded MDL 10,000, approximately EUR 648 at the time.

Both parties appealed. On 26 April 2006 the Chişinău Court of Appeal rejected the applicant’s appeal and partly accepted the provider’s appeal. It reduced the award to MDL 5,000, approximately EUR 310, on the basis that both the sum claimed by the applicant and the sum awarded to her were exaggerated. The parties appealed further. On 25 October 2006 the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the judgment of 26 April 2006. It found that the lower court had considered the nature and seriousness of the mental suffering caused to the applicant and the degree of guilt of the defendant. That judgment was final.

The applicant then applied to the European Court of Human Rights. Her central complaint was that, despite the domestic courts’ establishment of a violation of her rights, the compensation ultimately awarded was insufficient. The key facts relevant to that alleged violation were therefore the confirmed contamination of the drinking-water supply by sewage; the resulting serious illness of the applicant and her daughter; the finding that the State-owned utilities provider was responsible; and the domestic courts’ decisions on damages, which reduced the initial award from MDL 10,000 to MDL 5,000. The European Court was thus called upon to assess whether that compensation was adequate for the purposes of Article 8 of the Convention.
