text:
In *Geotech Kancev GmbH v. Germany* (Application no. 23646/09, judgment of 2 June 2016), the applicant was a German limited company specialising in soil sampling by drilling for geological examination, including assessing building-site suitability and constructing wells. It complained that its obligation to participate in and contribute to the Social Welfare Fund in the German building industry (“SOKA-BAU”) violated its right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention, particularly the negative aspect of that right, and its right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

The Fund was jointly set up by employers’ associations in the building industry and the trade union IG Bauen-Agrar-Umwelt through collective agreements, notably the Collective Agreement on Social Welfare Proceedings in the Building Trade (“VTV”). The VTV regulated contributions and entitlements relating to the Supplementary Pension Scheme for the Construction Industry (“ZVK”) and the Holiday and Wage Equalisation Fund (“ULAK”). The Federal Ministry for Labour and Social Affairs declared the VTV generally binding under the Law on Collective Agreements. As a result, all employers in the building industry, including those not belonging to an employers’ association, were obliged to contribute 19.8% of gross wages to the Fund.

The applicant was not a member of any employers’ association party to the collective agreements. However, the authorities considered its drilling activities to fall within the VTV’s scope; Article 1 § 2(v) no. 6 expressly listed drilling as a covered activity. In 2004 the Fund sent the applicant information about the welfare schemes and contributions. The applicant did not respond. In 2005, after enquiries, the Fund informed the applicant of its duty to contribute and opened an account. The applicant’s lawyer objected in April 2005.

In October 2007 the Wiesbaden Labour Court ordered the applicant to pay EUR 63,625.58 in welfare fund arrears to the ZVK for September 2002 to March 2004, and to submit wage slips for January 2006 to June 2007. The court found that the VTV bound all building employers and covered the applicant’s drilling activities. The applicant appealed, arguing that the generally binding effect violated the negative aspect of its freedom of association because it was forced to contribute to a fund jointly established by employers’ associations and a trade union, despite belonging to neither. It also claimed the obligation prevented it from founding its own association due to lack of funds.

In June 2008 the Hesse Labour Court of Appeal rejected the appeal. It held that the generally binding effect did not oblige the applicant to join either an employers’ association or the Fund. Although non-members could not control the Fund through the associations, that disadvantage and any pressure to join were insufficient to breach the negative aspect of freedom of association. The obligation also did not prevent the applicant from founding its own association, and most contributions would be reimbursed if properly declared. The court found the scheme served the public interest by addressing high employee fluctuation and preventing distortion of competition. The Federal Labour Court rejected a further complaint in December 2008, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the applicant’s constitutional complaint in February 2009.

Relevant facts also included that the Fund did not make individual employers or employees members; only the collective agreement parties were members. It administered supplementary welfare schemes financed on a solidarity basis, operated as a non-profit entity, was state-supervised, and published annual reports. Insolvency proceedings over the applicant were opened in March 2010, but the administrator authorised counsel to continue the European Court proceedings.

**Morari v. the Republic of Moldova (Application no. 65311/09, judgment of 8 March 2016)** concerned an allegation of police entrapment and the fairness of criminal proceedings.

In January 2008, the Balti police organised an undercover operation to identify a criminal group producing and circulating forged documents. They placed an advertisement in a local newspaper stating: “Need help with obtaining passport (Romanian-Bulgarian)” and provided a telephone number. The applicant, Oleg Morari, a Moldovan national interested in obtaining a Romanian passport to facilitate work in Romania or the European Union, called the number. He met a person identifying himself as E., who claimed also to be seeking a Romanian passport. They agreed to inform each other if either found an easy way to obtain one.

Later, the applicant’s friend D. recommended a person called Z., who could arrange a Romanian passport quickly. Both D. and Z. later confirmed that D. had made this recommendation in March 2008. Z. asked for EUR 1,500, which the applicant did not have.

About three weeks after first meeting E., E. called the applicant to ask whether he had found a way to obtain a passport. The applicant told him about Z. and proposed putting E. in contact with Z. E. refused direct contact, said he lacked money, but mentioned an acquaintance, T., also interested in a Romanian passport. E. proposed that the applicant act as intermediary between Z. and T., telling T. the price was EUR 2,300; the EUR 800 difference between Z.’s price and T.’s payment would be split between the applicant and E. The prosecution did not contest this account. The applicant agreed.

The applicant then discussed matters with Z., who gave him a list of documents needed for T.’s new Romanian identity card. The applicant claimed he believed the card would not be forged and that Z. would merely represent T. before the Romanian authorities. Z. disputed this, stating he had told the applicant from the outset that the identity card would be false and he should avoid travelling to Romania with it.

On 3 April 2008, the applicant met T., obtained documents and an advance of EUR 750, and gave T. a receipt. He passed the money and documents to Z. The identity card was produced in the United Kingdom and reached Z and then the applicant by mid-April 2008. On 16 April 2008, the applicant met T., gave him the identity card in exchange for the remaining money, and was arrested.

A criminal investigation began on 17 April 2008 for manufacturing and trading forged official documents. Z. concluded a plea agreement, admitted guilt, and received a suspended four-year sentence.

During proceedings, the applicant argued he had been entrapped by E. and T. and asked for them to be heard. The first-instance court refused, citing the law permitting undercover officers to testify only if they consented. On 17 December 2008, the Balti District Court convicted the applicant of participating in producing and selling a false Romanian identity card, fining him about EUR 200. The judgment did not address his entrapment claim.

His appeal complained that the offence resulted from police incitement and that E. and T. had not been heard. The Court of Appeal initially agreed to hear them but later reversed that decision. On 4 March 2009, it dismissed the appeal, rejecting entrapment solely because the applicant had first telephoned the newspaper number. It found no need to hear E. and T. since their statements were not used against him. The Supreme Court of Justice dismissed his appeal on 8 July 2009.

The applicant alleged before the European Court of Human Rights that he had been the victim of entrapment, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The key fair-trial issue was whether the domestic courts adequately examined his incitement claim and his inability to confront the undercover individuals allegedly involved.

In *Meier v. Switzerland* (Application no. 10109/14), Third Section, judgment of 9 February 2016, the applicant was Beat Meier, a Swiss national born in 1946, detained in Regensdorf. In 2003 the Zurich Court of Appeal sentenced him to four years and four months’ imprisonment for multiple sexual acts with minors and multiple acts of sexual coercion. In 2010 the execution of that sentence was suspended and replaced by preventive detention designed to prevent reoffending. Because he was subject to a custodial measure, Swiss law—Article 90(3) of the Criminal Code—applied the prison work rules by analogy.

The alleged violations arose from the requirement that Meier continue working after reaching retirement age. In December 2011 he requested exemption from the prison work requirement. On 19 March 2012 the Judicial Enforcements Office of the Canton of Zurich refused. After he refused to work, Pöschwies Prison on 29 May 2012 placed him under a stricter regime, confining him to his cell and confiscating his television and computer for fourteen days. That disciplinary decision was revoked on 31 July 2012, but the refusal of exemption was upheld by the Directorate of Justice and Internal Affairs on 20 June 2012, the Administrative Court of Zurich on 10 January 2013, and the Federal Court on 18 July 2013.

The Federal Court held that compulsory prison work was not in itself contrary to human rights or Article 4 of the Convention. It pursued aims such as developing or maintaining work capacity, structuring daily life, maintaining order, fostering social behaviour, and, for prisoners over 65, avoiding the harmful effects of isolation and mental or physical deterioration. Work had to be tailored to the prisoner’s abilities; lighter or therapeutic activity could be used. Pension rules under the Old-Age and Survivors’ Insurance Act did not apply because prison work was not comparable to competitive employment. Voluntary work was considered insufficient to achieve the aims of compulsory prison work.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, Meier complained that requiring him to work after retirement age breached Articles 4 and 14 of the Convention—prohibition of forced or compulsory labour and discrimination. Relevant domestic law included Articles 7 and 10 of the Federal Constitution (human dignity and personal freedom), Articles 74, 75, 81 and 90 of the Criminal Code (dignity, resocialisation, normal life, support, and compulsory work matched to ability), and Article 103 of the Zurich Justice Enforcement Order.

International materials included ILO Convention No. 29, Article 2(2)(c) of which excludes work exacted as a consequence of conviction under public supervision; European Prison Rules 2006 Rule 105.2, stating that sentenced prisoners who have not reached normal retirement age may be required to work subject to fitness; and CPT concerns about older prisoners required to work beyond retirement age. Switzerland replied that the work requirement applied to all inmates but was tailored, medically unfit prisoners were exempt, and special arrangements existed for retired prisoners. A comparative survey showed that 16 Council of Europe States did not require prisoners to work beyond retirement age, while 12 had no explicit rule but often granted practical exemptions. The central alleged violation was that Switzerland’s continued work requirement for a retired preventive-detention prisoner amounted to compulsory labour and age- or status-based discrimination.

**Wenner v. Germany** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, App. No. 62303/13, judgment 1 September 2016) concerned a German prisoner’s complaint that the refusal to provide him with drug substitution treatment during imprisonment—and the refusal to have the medical necessity of such treatment examined by an external addiction expert—violated Article 3 of the Convention.

The applicant, born in 1955, had been addicted to heroin since 1973. He also suffered from hepatitis C since 1975 and had been HIV-positive since 1988. He was considered 100% disabled and received a disability pension. Between 1991 and 2008, his heroin addiction was treated with medically prescribed substitution therapy, mainly Polamidon. From 2005, he reduced the dosage and additionally consumed heroin.

In 2008, he was arrested on drug-trafficking suspicion and detained on remand in Kaisheim Prison. His substitution treatment was interrupted against his will. In June 2009, he was convicted and sentenced to several years’ imprisonment. The court also ordered his placement in a drug detoxification facility. He was transferred to a rehabilitation centre in Günzburg in December 2009, where he received abstinence-based treatment without substitution. In April 2010, the detoxification order was terminated and he was returned to Kaisheim Prison.

While in prison, the applicant suffered chronic pain from polyneuropathy, often spending most of his time in bed. An external doctor, H., suggested that the prison medical service reconsider substitution treatment, and recommended examination by a drug-addiction specialist. The applicant also obtained an opinion from Dr B., an external addiction specialist, who concluded that substitution treatment was medically necessary. Dr B. stated that substitution was internationally recognised as the best therapy for long-standing opioid addicts, that forced abstinence caused serious physical and mental strain, and that substitution could prevent deterioration, reduce infection risks, and make hepatitis C treatment possible.

In June 2011, the applicant requested Diamorphin, Polamidon, or another heroin substitute, or alternatively that an external specialist examine whether substitution was necessary. He relied on the Federal Medical Association’s Guidelines for Substitution Treatment of Opiate Addicts, arguing that substitution was the standard treatment for his condition and should be continued in detention.

The prison authorities refused the request in January 2012. They argued that substitution was neither medically necessary nor suitable for rehabilitation. Relying on the prison doctor, they said the applicant no longer suffered physical withdrawal symptoms after three years in detention, his HIV and hepatitis C were stable, and no treatment requiring substitution was needed. They also claimed he could use prison to wean himself off opioids, that prior substitution had not prevented drug use or crime, and that he had consumed drugs in detention, so substitution could pose risks. The Augsburg Regional Court upheld the refusal and found no need for an external addiction expert. The Munich Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, and the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint.

Relevant domestic law under the Bavarian Execution of Sentences Act entitled prisoners to medical treatment if necessary to detect, cure, prevent aggravation of, or alleviate illness. Federal Medical Association Guidelines recognised substitution as a scientifically tested therapy for opiate addiction and required continuity of substitution during imprisonment. Council of Europe standards required equivalence of prison health care with community care. Statistical data showed that opioid substitution programmes were available in prisons in many Council of Europe states.

The applicant alleged that refusing him substitution treatment, and refusing an external expert review, amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 3, given his severe chronic pain, long-term addiction, and medical conditions.

Cunha Martins da Silva Couto v. Portugal (Applications nos. 69053/13, 69374/13, 69377/13, 71135/13 and 8088/14) is a case before the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, brought by Mr José Luís Cunha Martins da Silva Couto, a Portuguese national born in 1961 and residing in Porto. The case originated in five applications lodged against Portugal under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Portuguese Government was represented by Mrs M. F. da Graça Carvalho, Deputy Attorney General. On 21 November 2014, the applications were communicated to the Government.

The applicant complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of an effective remedy in that respect. These allegations engage Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and Article 13, which requires an effective remedy for arguable Convention violations.

The appended table provides the key factual details of each application. In Application no. 69053/13, introduced on 28 October 2013, the domestic proceedings began on 21 April 2009 and ended on 13 February 2014. Their total duration was approximately 4 years, 9 months and 25 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.

In Application no. 69374/13, introduced on 30 October 2013, the proceedings began on 20 February 2009 and, according to the last information received by the Court on 26 May 2015, were still pending. Their length at that point was approximately 6 years, 11 months and 13 days, again across two levels of jurisdiction.

Application no. 69377/13, also introduced on 30 October 2013, concerned proceedings that likewise began on 20 February 2009 and were still pending as of 26 May 2015. The total duration was also approximately 6 years, 11 months and 13 days, with two levels of jurisdiction.

In Application no. 71135/13, introduced on 1 November 2013, the civil proceedings started on 16 May 2009 and ended on 28 November 2014. They lasted approximately 5 years, 6 months and 14 days, across two levels of jurisdiction.

Finally, in Application no. 8088/14, introduced on 30 December 2013, the proceedings began on 13 October 2010 and ended on 27 June 2014. Their total length was approximately 3 years, 8 months and 14 days, also across two levels of jurisdiction.

The central facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the prolonged duration of several civil proceedings involving the same applicant, with some cases remaining unresolved for nearly seven years by the time the Court last received information. The applicant alleged not only that the proceedings were excessively long, but also that the Portuguese legal system failed to provide an effective domestic remedy to challenge that length. The Court would need to assess whether the duration of each set of proceedings exceeded the “reasonable time” requirement under Article 6 § 1, taking into account factors such as complexity, the conduct of the applicant and the authorities, and what was at stake. It would also need to determine whether an effective remedy existed under Article 13 for the length complaints.

The judgment is dated 26 April 2016 and is stated to be final, although it may be subject to editorial revision. The excerpt supplied focuses primarily on the procedural and factual background and the applicant’s complaints, rather than setting out the Court’s ultimate reasoning or disposition.

**Topallaj v. Albania** (Application no. 32913/03, judgment 21 April 2016) concerned Albanian civil and property proceedings. The applicant, Marketin Topallaj, later a U.S. citizen, became involved in 1996 with land near the Tirana–Durrës road on which fuel tanks and a petrol station stood. Albanian courts had recognised certain landowners’ inherited rights over 24 hectares. In April 1996 the Tirana District Court quashed a property commission’s refusal and allocated the landowners 56,500 sq. m, ordering that the fuel tanks and installations be restored at no cost because their value was less than 20% of the land’s value. That judgment became final in May 1996, and the landowners obtained a property certificate.

Acting on the landowners’ behalf, the applicant concluded agreements in January and February 1996 to finance privatisation of the fuel tanks and installations in exchange for future ownership. In May 1996 he concluded a notarised sales contract for almost all of the fuel tanks and installations for USD 100,000 and registered title in his name. He also concluded two loan agreements with one landowner. He thereafter represented the landowners in proceedings protecting their property rights.

Between 1996 and 2000, State bodies repeatedly challenged the landowners’ rights. After the Supreme Court dismissed one challenge in 1999, the Ministry of Economy and State-owned oil companies obtained supervisory review. In May 2000 the Supreme Court Joint Benches reopened the proceedings. The case was reheard through several remittals until 2009, ultimately in the landowners’ favour. In 2007 the property agency recognised inherited rights over 24 hectares and ordered compensation for 183,500 sq. m, a compensation issue later pursued in separate proceedings.

Separately, in 2002 and again in 2005, the landowners sued the applicant to annul the 1996 agreements and sales contract as absolutely null and void. The applicant alleged that the fresh claim was signed only by the landowners’ lawyer, without proper authority, and was time-barred. He also alleged forgery, sought a stay pending a criminal complaint, and repeatedly challenged the bench. The presiding judge withdrew, but the District Court President set aside that withdrawal. In April 2006 the District Court declared the agreements and contract absolutely null and fictitious. It found that the property was State-administered when concluded, no rights had been transferred to the landowners, no joint company or loans existed, and the sales price matched the alleged loans. It ordered erasure of the applicant’s May 1996 property registration.

The Court of Appeal upheld that decision in May 2007. A dissenting judge found no evidence that the transactions were fictitious, considered the claim time-barred and unauthorised, and stated that the applicant’s procedural requests had been ignored. The Supreme Court declared the applicant’s appeal inadmissible in January 2010, and the Constitutional Court rejected his appeal in November 2010, finding no impartiality breach and deferring to the lower courts’ factual assessment.

The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key facts relevant to those alleged violations were the annulment of his registered contracts and erasure of his property registration, allegedly depriving him of possessions; alleged unfairness, bias, and improper court composition, including military judges in the Court of Appeal; rejection of requests for withdrawal and evidence; lack of reasoned decisions; complaints that the claim was unauthorised and time-barred; the excessive length of proceedings; and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

In *B.A.C. v. Greece* (Application no. 11981/15), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section) examined an application by a Turkish national, born in 1977 and living in Athens, who complained about Greece’s prolonged failure to decide his asylum request. He alleged violations of Article 8 § 1 of the Convention, alone and in conjunction with Article 13, and of Articles 3 and 13 taken together, on account of the Ministry of Public Order’s failure for twelve years to take any decision on his asylum application.

The applicant had been a pro-communist and pro-Kurdish political activist while studying in Turkey between 1994 and 1999. In 1997 he opened a literary café frequented by people sympathetic to those political views. In 2000 the Turkish police arrested him, and he was prosecuted for infringing the State constitutional order under Article 146 of the Turkish Criminal Code. He was held in the “white (isolation) cells” at Kandra Prison. He went on hunger strike for 171 days, causing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, a condition capable of causing irreversible damage or death. Because his life was at risk, the Turkish authorities released him.

In 2002 the applicant fled to Greece and applied for asylum on 15 January 2002. On 18 February 2002, the General Secretary of the Ministry of Public Order rejected the application at first instance with summary reasons. On 21 March 2002, the applicant appealed. On 29 January 2003, having been summoned before the Advisory Board on Asylum, he submitted documents showing he had suffered torture in Turkey because of his political opinions, including a medical report from the Greek Medical Centre for the Rehabilitation of Torture Victims and an Amnesty International document. That same day, the Advisory Board issued a favourable opinion. Under Article 3 § 5 of Presidential Decree No. 61/1999, the Minister for Public Order should then have decided within twenty-four hours whether to grant international protection. However, by the time the application reached the Court, the Minister had taken no decision and had neither ratified nor rejected the Board’s opinion.

Between 2003 and 2015, the applicant lived in Athens and attended a police station every six months to renew his asylum-seeker’s card. Under domestic law, that card was not a residence permit. It only prevented expulsion and allowed him to remain in Greece with “tolerated status” while his application was pending. Asylum seekers in his position could not work, undertake vocational training, marry, obtain a driving licence, hold a bank account, or apply for family reunion.

In 2003 his wife joined him from Turkey, but her presence became lawful only in 2008 when she obtained a short-term work permit. In 2010 they had a son. In 2011 his wife returned to Istanbul with the child because of health problems, and the couple divorced in 2012.

Separately, on 5 August 2005, the Turkish Interpol Office issued an extradition request based on accusations similar to those already assessed during the asylum proceedings. On 12 March 2013 the applicant was arrested in Patras. On 26 March 2013, the indictment division of the Patras Court of Appeal unanimously rejected extradition, citing the risk of ill-treatment for his political opinions and the vague and abstract description of the alleged offences. The prosecutor appealed, but on 26 April 2013 the Court of Cassation upheld the rejection.

The applicant repeatedly sought a final decision. He wrote to the Ombudsman on 21 March and 25 June 2012, and to the Minister for Public Order on 19 November 2013, 16 June 2014, and 27 February 2015. Correspondence among authorities on 23 February 2007, 16 October 2012, 14 November 2012, and 28 January 2015 confirmed that his asylum application was still pending before the Minister. These facts formed the basis of his complaints about prolonged uncertainty, restrictions on his private and family life, and the absence of an effective remedy.

In *Armani Da Silva v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 5878/08, Grand Chamber, 30 March 2016), the applicant was Patricia Armani Da Silva, cousin of Jean Charles de Menezes. Her complaint concerned the fatal shooting of de Menezes by Metropolitan Police officers at Stockwell Underground Station on 22 July 2005 and the subsequent decision not to prosecute any individual officer. The alleged violation was of the procedural limb of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which requires an effective investigation capable of establishing the facts, determining whether lethal force was justified, and identifying and, if appropriate, punishing those responsible.

The shooting occurred in a counter-terrorism context. After the 7 July 2005 London suicide bombings and the failed 21 July attacks, police launched Operation THESEUS 2 to locate suspects, including Hussain Osman, thought to be at Scotia Road. The plan was to conduct covert surveillance, follow anyone leaving, and stop them safely with specialist firearms officers (SO19) in support. However, SO19 was deployed late.

On 22 July 2005 de Menezes left 17 Scotia Road. Surveillance officers followed him, regarding him as a possible but not confirmed match for Osman. Control room personnel apparently believed a positive identification had been made. He boarded a bus and later entered Stockwell station. The Designated Senior Officer ordered that he be stopped before getting on a train; the order was relayed to SO19. De Menezes entered a train and sat down. Firearms officers rushed in, he was pinned down, and two officers shot him multiple times. He was entirely unconnected to the bombings.

The IPCC Stockwell One Report identified serious failings: briefings that heightened fears of suicide bombers without adequate warnings; delayed deployment of SO19; command, communication and planning failures; delay in handing the scene to the IPCC; an altered surveillance log; and missing CCTV/hard-drive evidence. It found no evidence of a cover-up, however, and experts disagreed over the log alteration.

The CPS considered prosecutions for murder, gross negligence manslaughter, misconduct in public office, forgery and perverting the course of justice. It concluded that no individual officer should be prosecuted. The main reason was insufficient evidential prospect: the two shooters claimed genuine self-defence, and the evidence could not disprove their honest belief that de Menezes was a suicide bomber. Other accounts were conflicting, contemporaneous records were lacking, and the identified errors did not meet the criminal threshold. The CPS did prosecute the Office of the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis under health and safety legislation, but not individuals.

The applicant argued that the absence of individual prosecutions breached Article 2. The Grand Chamber held that there was no violation. While Article 2 required an effective investigation, it did not require criminal prosecution in every case. The investigation was independent, thorough and capable of leading to accountability, and the prosecutorial decision was not arbitrary. The authorities had thus complied with the procedural obligation.

**Bujković v. Montenegro (Application no. 40080/08)** concerns a Montenegrin national’s complaint about the length of civil proceedings relating to a plot of land. The applicant, Vladimir Bujković, born in 1972 and living in Sutomore, lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 31 July 2008. The application was communicated to the Montenegrin Government on 30 November 2009 and later assigned to the Second Section.

The underlying civil proceedings began on 24 April 2000, when the applicant sued the Municipality of Bar over a plot of land. After a remittal, the Court of First Instance in Bar ruled partly in his favour on 23 January 2003. On 27 April 2004, the High Court in Podgorica upheld part of that judgment but quashed the remainder. On 16 September 2004, the applicant simultaneously filed a request for reopening of the proceedings with the Court of First Instance and an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court, both concerning the upheld part.

The case file was sent to the Supreme Court on 2 February 2005 but returned to the Court of First Instance only on 20 December 2005. On 20 October 2006, the Court of First Instance dismissed the reopening request; the High Court upheld that decision on 9 May 2008. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on points of law on 13 June 2008.

Meanwhile, on 9 October 2008, the Court of First Instance joined the remaining part of the applicant’s claim with two earlier claims. The applicant filed further submissions in October 2008 and May 2009. On 18 June 2009, the hearing restarted because the case had been assigned to a new judge; the applicant withdrew one submission and specified his claim the following day. On 9 September 2009, the hearing again restarted after another change of judge. On 2 November 2009, the Court of First Instance declared that it lacked competence and rejected the claim. The High Court later quashed that decision, and by March 2010 the case was again pending before the Court of First Instance.

Between April and August 2010, the parties attempted a friendly settlement, without success. On 14 February 2011, the hearing started afresh after the case was assigned to yet another judge. On 17 February 2011, the Court of First Instance ruled against the applicant, but the High Court quashed that decision on 20 September 2011. On 10 May 2012, the Court of First Instance again ruled against him. The High Court upheld that judgment on 19 October 2012, and the Supreme Court upheld it on 7 February 2013.

Other relevant facts include that in 2003 and 2004 the applicant sought suspension of a separate set of civil proceedings until the 2000 proceedings concluded, and in November 2006 requested their continuation. In March 2013, he instituted another set of civil proceedings, then pending before the High Court.

The domestic legal framework includes the Right to a Trial within a Reasonable Time Act, in force from 21 December 2007. It allows a party to seek expedition through a request for review and, where certain conditions are met, to claim compensation through an action for fair redress. Section 33 requires prior use of a request for review and filing of the compensation action with the Supreme Court within six months of receipt of the final decision in the impugned proceedings.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the almost thirteen-year duration of the civil proceedings, repeated appellate remittals, changes of judges causing hearings to begin anew, the competence rejection, and the availability of a domestic length-of-proceedings remedy only from late 2007.

**Kleutin v. Ukraine (no. 5911/05)** concerned an application lodged on 7 January 2005 by Mr Denis Vasilyevich Kleutin, a Ukrainian national born in 1979, against Ukraine. He alleged that he had been beaten by police during apprehension on 22 January 2004 and that no effective investigation followed. He also complained that his arrest and pre-trial detention were unlawful, that he lacked effective judicial review of his detention, and that conditions in Odesa SIZO were inhuman and degrading.

On 22 January 2004, criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant and two others in connection with a robbery committed the previous night. The same day, an investigator arrested him at 1:40 p.m. on suspicion of robbery. The applicant alleged that police officers, including K.—the brother of an alleged accomplice—came to his apartment, threatened him with firearms, struck him on the head and body, and fractured two ribs while trying to force him to confess. He said he was then forced to go to the police station. His sister, who was in another room, testified that she heard raised voices but did not witness the alleged beating. The Government maintained that no force or pressure was used and that the applicant voluntarily agreed to go with officers. A police officer later stated that no physical force was needed because the applicant did not resist. On 4 June 2007, the prosecutor refused to institute criminal proceedings against the police officer, finding no force had been applied. The applicant’s complaints during the criminal trial led the District Court to order the prosecutor’s office to investigate the ill-treatment allegations in March 2005 and again in May 2007, but these orders were not complied with in time. The applicant also alleged that K. forced his sister to give false evidence. Medical records were disputed: authorities said he was healthy on admission to Odesa SIZO and had no complaints, while the applicant alleged an X-ray showed he lacked part of his third left rib.

As to detention, on 24 January 2004 the Prymorsky District Court of Odesa remanded the applicant in custody in the absence of the applicant and without setting a maximum duration, relying on the gravity of the charge, his previous convictions, and risks of absconding or obstructing justice. On 18 March 2004, again in his absence, detention was extended for one month. After the investigation was completed and the case sent to trial, committal hearings on 5 May 2004 made no ruling on further detention. The case was twice remitted for additional investigation, on 18 June 2004 and 18 April 2005, without addressing his continued detention. On 15 September 2005, the District Court maintained detention without reasons or time-limits. The applicant repeatedly requested a non-custodial preventive measure, but the court replied that such petitions had to be lodged and examined at a hearing. On 8 June 2007, he was convicted of group robbery and involving minors in a crime, sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, and released on 22 January 2009 after the Supreme Court rejected his appeal.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant was held in Odesa SIZO from 26 January 2004 to 23 November 2007. He alleged insufficient living space, poor sanitation, prolonged confinement indoors, and no outdoor activity. Government records listed cells mostly measuring about 6.7–7.9 square metres intended for four detainees, with some larger cells. The Government claimed conditions were adequate, with furnishings, partitioned toilets, ventilation, natural light, and running water. The CPT had recommended at least 4 square metres per prisoner. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s Convention complaints.

**Summary of A.K. v. Liechtenstein (Application no. 38191/12)**

The case originated in an application against Liechtenstein lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by A.K., a German national, on 14 May 2012. The applicant alleged in particular that the five judges of Liechtenstein’s Constitutional Court had been partial, notably because of the procedure they used to reject his motions for bias, in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. The Court communicated only that impartiality complaint to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying facts concerned a long-running dispute between the applicant and F.H. over property rights in 75% of the bearer shares in two Liechtenstein companies, EMK and EMK Engineering. In December 2009, the Regional Court granted an interim injunction preventing the Real Property and Commercial Registry from registering certain changes decided at an extraordinary shareholders’ meeting of 23 July 2004. Those changes included F.H.’s removal as a representative and supervisory board member and the applicant’s election as managing director. The injunction confirmed an earlier provisional order.

After the Court of Appeal quashed the first injunction in March 2010 and remitted the case, the Regional Court issued a fresh identical injunction on 30 July 2010. It found that the applicant had not acquired 75% of the bearer shares and had therefore not validly represented that shareholding at the shareholders’ meeting. It held that interim injunctions could secure declaration claims and preserve the status quo, and that such measures were necessary to prevent irreversible damage to F.H. The Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 23 September 2010.

On 22 October 2010 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against the Court of Appeal’s decision. On 7 November 2011 the Constitutional Court informed him that judges B., Bu., S., V. and W. would deliberate on his complaint in private on 28 November 2011. Shortly before that date, the applicant—then unrepresented—filed motions for bias against all five judges and against the secretary, V.

His bias allegations were extensive. He claimed the Constitutional Court had previously failed to quash decisions of lower courts in related proceedings, had taken over a year to assign judges, and discriminated against German nationals. More specifically, he alleged that judge B. had refused suspensory effect and interim measures in related proceedings and belonged to committees whose members included Supreme Court judges and judge H., F.H.’s brother. Judge Bu. allegedly worked for the Government by preparing expert reports and teaching government seminars and worked regularly with judge H. Judge S. was said to be a member of the supervisory board of a state-owned company. Judge V. had been a professor at Liechtenstein University, had worked for the Government, and was a close friend of judge H. Judge W. was allegedly a partner of a lawyer against whom the applicant had brought inheritance proceedings; another lawyer in his firm had represented EMK Engineering, and W. had previously worked in judge H.’s law firm.

On 28 November 2011 the Constitutional Court dismissed the bias motions. It stated that each challenged judge had not participated in the decision on his own motion, with the four remaining judges deciding. It reasoned that prior adverse decisions, five-year judicial terms, previous government work, and regular contact or friendship with F.H.’s brother did not objectively cast doubt on impartiality. It added that, in a small country such as Liechtenstein, excessively strict standards would disproportionately obstruct justice. The same day, the Constitutional Court allowed the applicant’s complaint only as regards the length of proceedings and dismissed the remainder.

The key alleged violation before the European Court was therefore that the Constitutional Court lacked impartiality under Article 6, especially because the challenged judges themselves effectively took part in the process by which the bias motions against them were rejected.

The case of *Halimi and Others v. Albania* (Application no. 33839/11) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (First Section, sitting as a Committee) on 7 April 2016; the judgment was rectified on 26 April 2016 under Rule 81 of the Rules of Court. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention by nine Albanian nationals against the Republic of Albania. The applicants were represented by Mr S. Puto, a lawyer practising in Tirana, and the Government were represented by Ms A. Hicka of the State Advocate’s Office. The application was communicated to the Government on 20 December 2013. In its judgment, the Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, referring in particular to *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are essentially undisputed. On 30 May 1995, the Vlora Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 10,000 square metres. Because that plot was occupied by others, the applicants could not obtain restitution of the land itself. Instead, Albanian law provided that they would be compensated in one of the ways established by law. Despite this formal recognition of their entitlement, no compensation had been paid by the time the case reached the Court. Thus, for more than two decades, the applicants held a recognised right to compensation that remained entirely unfulfilled.

These facts formed the basis of the alleged Convention violations. The applicants’ central complaint was that the Albanian authorities failed to enforce the compensation entitlement, thereby interfering with their right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The prolonged failure to pay compensation, combined with the absence of any meaningful domestic mechanism to secure payment, also raised issues under Article 13 concerning the right to an effective remedy. In related Albanian property-compensation cases, similar facts have also engaged Article 6 § 1, particularly where proceedings became excessively long or where access to a determination of compensation was effectively blocked.

The Court observed that the relevant domestic law and practice on property compensation had been described in earlier cases, including *Ramadhi v. Albania*, *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*, and *Sharra and Others v. Albania*. It also had regard to relevant Council of Europe materials, as set out in *Sharra*, *Metalla and Others*, *Siliqi and Others*, and *Karagjozi and Others*. The essential factual pattern was therefore not novel: a final domestic recognition of a right to compensation for property that could not be returned, followed by a prolonged failure by the State to provide that compensation. Because the issue was already covered by well-established case-law, the Court was able to adopt a committee judgment.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the 1995 recognition of the applicants’ inherited property rights, the occupied status of the land, the statutory promise of compensation, and the continuing failure to pay any compensation, leaving the applicants without redress for an extended period.

In *Colloredo Mannsfeld v. the Czech Republic* (Apps. nos. 15275/11 and 76058/12, ECtHR First Section, 15 December 2016), the applicant, Jerome Colloredo Mannsfeld, a Czech national, pursued restitution of movable property formerly kept at Opočno Castle. The property had been confiscated from his predecessor in 1942 by the German Secret State Police as an enemy of the Reich. After World War II, the Czechoslovak State confiscated it again in 1945 under the Beneš decrees because the predecessor was considered German. That expropriation was quashed in January 1947 after authorities found him to be of Czechoslovak nationality and loyal to the State. The property’s later fate was disputed.

In 1992 the applicant’s father and his cousin sought restitution. The applicant entered the proceedings as heir after his father died in 1998. One earlier set of proceedings returned 68 paintings and is not part of these applications. The two later sets form the basis of the case.

In the second proceedings (application no. 15275/11), the Pardubice District Court on 27 October 2006 ordered the National Heritage Institute to return certain movable property. It found that the applicant’s predecessor had owned the property on the critical restitution date, 25 February 1948, and that the statutory conditions were met. On 18 October 2007, however, the Hradec Králové Regional Court reversed and dismissed the action, finding that the property had been taken before 25 February 1948 and that restitution legislation therefore did not apply.

The key fair-trial complaint arose from how the Regional Court reached that conclusion. At the hearing on 8 October 2007, the court did not raise new evidence or questions with the parties; it merely heard their comments before adjourning for judgment. Its decision relied on two documents: a letter of 24 June 1947 from the national administrator of Opočno Castle and a decision of the Ministry of Agriculture of 30 April 1947 declaring the castle State cultural property (“the 1947 decision”). The 1947 decision had not been disclosed or raised with the parties, and they had no opportunity to comment on it. The Regional Court noted it was aware of the document through the exercise of its functions.

On 11 February 2009, the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law. It noted the appellate court’s reliance on the 1947 decision but did not address the applicant’s argument that he had not seen it and could not comment. On 11 August 2010, the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal as manifestly ill-founded, holding that the requirements of Article 121 of the Code of Civil Procedure were met and that facts generally known or known to the court through its functions need not be proved.

In the third proceedings (application no. 76058/12), the District Court dismissed the remainder of the restitution claim on 22 April 2009, referring to the earlier judgments. On 27 January 2011, the Regional Court upheld that decision, relying on a Ministry of Agriculture letter of 27 May 1957 referring to the 1947 decision. Despite repeated requests, the 1947 decision was not produced to the parties. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal on 28 November 2011, and the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal on 19 April 2012 as manifestly ill-founded.

The applicant alleged that he had not had a fair trial and that his property rights had been breached. The central facts relevant to those alleged violations were the domestic courts’ use of the 1947 decision without disclosing it to the parties or allowing them to comment, allegedly violating fair-hearing and equality-of-arms guarantees, and the resulting rejection of his restitution claim, which affected his asserted property rights.

**Summary of *Guk v. Ukraine* (Application no. 16995/05)**

The case of *Guk v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Viktor Guk, a Ukrainian national, on 21 April 2005. The applicant alleged multiple violations of the Convention, primarily under Articles 3, 8, 13, and 34.

In 2001, the applicant was convicted of murder, attempted murder, and illegal possession of firearms, receiving a life sentence. This was later reduced to fifteen years in 2009. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations pertain to his detention conditions and treatment in various penal institutions.

**Alleged Ill-Treatment (Article 3):** The applicant claimed that upon his arrival at Sokalska Prison on 15 October 2004, he was beaten by several guards, resulting in an eye injury (later diagnosed as traumatic mydriasis) and multiple bruises. He alleged that his complaints to prison officials went unheeded and that he received no medical assistance for these injuries. His attempts to send complaints to a prosecutor were allegedly obstructed by prison authorities. When his complaint was eventually addressed in 2006, the prosecutor refused to open a criminal investigation, citing a lack of evidence, a decision later upheld by domestic courts.

**Conditions of Detention (Article 3):** The applicant described severe conditions in Sokalska Prison from 2004 to 2007. He was held in a twelve-square-meter cell with three others, spending 23 hours a day inside without physical exercise. He alleged the cells were damp, unventilated, and inadequately heated, and that he was for a time detained with inmates suffering from open tuberculosis. He further complained of humiliating treatment when outside his cell, including being handcuffed, escorted by guards with a dog, and having a felt bag placed over his head. He also alleged inadequate food and water, and that his complaints about these conditions were not examined.

**Medical Assistance (Article 3):** The applicant, who suffered from hypertension, claimed he did not receive adequate medical treatment and was not allowed to keep necessary medication. A prosecutor's inquiry in 2005 found the medical assistance adequate, a finding the applicant unsuccessfully challenged in domestic courts.

**Restrictions on Family Life (Article 8):** During his detention, the applicant's contact with his family was severely restricted. He was entitled to visits only once every six months, for a maximum of four hours. These visits were often shorter due to high demand. He was separated from his family by a glass partition, placed in a cage, and conversations were monitored. He was denied any intimate contact with his wife. Furthermore, he was allegedly not allowed any telephone calls between October 2004 and November 2005, and subsequently only once every three months.

**Hindrance of the Right of Application (Article 34):** The applicant also complained that in 2012, while at Zamkova Prison, his correspondence with the Court was opened and read by the administration, and that he was persecuted for communicating with the Court, including being placed in solitary confinement for several months and having his documents and pen confiscated.

The applicant initially also complained of being obstructed in substantiating a previous application to the Court by being denied access to his criminal case file.

The case of *Bouyid v. Belgium* originated from an application lodged by two Belgian brothers, Saïd and Mohamed Bouyid, against the Kingdom of Belgium. They alleged that they were slapped in the face by police officers while at the Saint-Josse-ten-Noode police station, complaining of degrading treatment in violation of Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants claimed these incidents occurred against a background of tense and hostile relations between their family and the local police force.

The first incident occurred on 8 December 2003. The first applicant, Saïd Bouyid, was outside his home when a plain-clothes police officer, A.Z., asked to see his identity card. Bouyid refused, asking the officer to first show his credentials. The officer then grabbed him by his jacket and took him to the police station. While alone in a room with the officer, Bouyid alleged that A.Z. slapped him in the face. A medical certificate issued later that day confirmed he was in a state of shock and had erythema (redness) on his left cheek and ear canal. The police officer disputed this account, stating that Bouyid had been uncooperative and insulting.

The second incident took place on 23 February 2004. The second applicant, Mohamed Bouyid, was at the same police station being interviewed by Officer P.P. about a complaint filed against him by a third party. During the interview, Bouyid alleged that the officer slapped him in the face after he leaned on his desk and then forced him to sign his statement by threatening to put him in a cell. A medical certificate from that day documented bruising on his left cheek. The police officer admitted to grabbing Bouyid by the arm to escort him out but denied slapping him, describing Bouyid as arrogant and disrespectful during the interview.

Both applicants filed complaints with the Belgian authorities. An investigation was initiated by the Standing Committee for the oversight of police services (Committee P) and a judicial investigation was opened. The officers involved were charged with using violence in the course of their duties, but the case was ultimately discontinued. The Brussels Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal, finding no evidence to justify committing the officers for trial. The court noted the inconsistent statements of the parties and referenced a report describing the Bouyid family's generally problematic and confrontational conduct towards the police, which shed light on the context of the events. A subsequent appeal on points of law was dismissed by the Court of Cassation.

The applicants then brought their case to the European Court of Human Rights. A Chamber of the Court initially ruled that there had been no violation of Article 3, but the applicants successfully requested a referral to the Grand Chamber. The key factual dispute for the Grand Chamber was whether the slaps had occurred, as there was no conclusive evidence and the domestic proceedings had found the officers' consistent denials more credible than the applicants' accounts, given the overall context of family-police hostility.

**Paposhvili v. Belgium** (Application no. 41738/10, Grand Chamber, 13 December 2016) concerned a Georgian national, born in 1958, who arrived in Belgium in November 1998 with his wife and child and applied for asylum. His asylum application was ultimately rejected. He also had a significant criminal record, including convictions for theft, robbery with violence, and, in 2005, three years’ imprisonment for involvement in a criminal organisation. In 2007 the Belgian Minister of the Interior issued a ministerial deportation order and barred him from re-entering Belgium for ten years.

The case’s central facts concerned the applicant’s grave medical condition. In 2006 he was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL), which later progressed to stage C and then to lymphocytic lymphoma. He also suffered from tuberculosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hepatitis C, and the after-effects of a stroke. While in Belgium he received chemotherapy and later Ibrutinib, a targeted cancer therapy. His treating doctors stated that discontinuing Ibrutinib would likely lead to death within about three months, and that a donor stem-cell transplant offered the only prospect of a cure. They also indicated that he would not have access to Ibrutinib or such a transplant in Georgia. His wife and three children were granted indefinite leave to remain in Belgium in 2010, so his removal would separate him from his family.

The applicant made several requests for regularisation on exceptional grounds and on medical grounds under the Belgian Aliens Act. His medical regularisation requests under section 9ter were rejected because he was excluded from that provision on account of serious crimes he had allegedly committed. As a result, the Belgian authorities did not examine his medical evidence or assess whether appropriate treatment would be available and accessible in Georgia. In July 2010 the Aliens Office refused his exceptional regularisation request and issued an order for him to leave Belgium, together with a detention order. The European Court of Human Rights then indicated an interim measure under Rule 39, suspending removal pending domestic proceedings. Domestic courts later dismissed his appeals, often reasoning that no removal measure was then being enforced or that medical risk should be assessed at the time of actual removal. The applicant died in June 2016, and his family continued the proceedings.

Before the Court, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 2, 3, and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Under Articles 2 and 3, he argued that removal to Georgia would expose him to a life-threatening lack of appropriate medical treatment, causing premature death and inhuman or degrading treatment. He contended that Belgium had failed to assess the real risk he faced and the availability and accessibility of treatment in Georgia. Under Article 8, he argued that removal would permanently separate him from his wife and children, with whom he had established family life in Belgium. The Government maintained that his condition was controlled, that treatment might be available, and that his criminal record and public-order concerns justified removal.

The Grand Chamber found that, if the removal decision were enforced, there would be a violation of Article 3. It clarified that removing a seriously ill alien may breach Article 3 where substantial evidence shows a real risk of serious, rapid, and irreversible decline in health causing intense suffering or a significant reduction in life expectancy due to the absence of or lack of access to treatment. The Belgian authorities had failed to adequately assess that risk. The Court found no need to examine Article 2 separately and also considered Article 8.

**Ruban v. Ukraine** (Application no. 8927/11), a 2016 judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), concerned an alleged violation of Article 7 of the Convention—the prohibition of punishment without law and the requirement that the most lenient applicable criminal law be applied retroactively.

The applicant, Mr Vladimir Nikolayevich Ruban, a Ukrainian national born in 1972, was serving a life sentence. The case arose from criminal proceedings concerning serious crimes committed in 1996 and 1999. In August 1996, an investigation began into the murder of four persons in the Mykolayiv region. In October and November 1999, separate investigations began in the Donetsk region into the murder of A. and hooliganism concerning R. These investigations were joined on 22 November 1999. Several suspects, including the applicant, were suspected of acting as a group.

On 14 December 1999, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office charged the applicant in absentia with these crimes and placed him on the wanted list. The investigation against him was suspended until his apprehension. Other suspects were convicted in 2002. In 2004, a local court ordered the applicant’s detention. He was apprehended in Russia on 28 June 2007 and extradited to Ukraine. On 31 March 2008, the investigation resumed and he was formally charged with participation in an organised criminal group, strangling A., killing four persons with another suspect in 1996, and inflicting grievous bodily harm on R. in a murder attempt connected with extortion. The investigation was completed in May 2008.

The key legal issue concerned the sentencing law. Under the 1960 Criminal Code, Article 93 provided that aggravated murder was punishable by eight to fifteen years’ imprisonment or by the death penalty. On 29 December 1999, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine declared the death penalty unconstitutional and void with immediate effect. However, life imprisonment as a replacement was only introduced by Law no. 1483 of 22 February 2000, which entered into force on 29 March 2000. Therefore, between 29 December 1999 and 29 March 2000, there was an interval in which the death penalty was no longer available but life imprisonment had not yet been introduced. The applicant argued that this interim version of Article 93 was the most favourable law applicable to his case, meaning the maximum penalty should have been fifteen years’ imprisonment.

On 10 July 2009, the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, acting as a first-instance court, found the applicant guilty of aggravated murder and banditry and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 15 July 2010, the Supreme Court of Ukraine upheld that judgment. The applicant’s lawyer submitted an additional appeal arguing that the courts should have applied the most favourable wording of the Criminal Code in force between 29 December 1999 and 29 March 2000. The Supreme Court rejected this argument, stating that the sentence had been imposed correctly.

Later, on 26 January 2011, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine interpreted the relevant provisions and held that the interim period after the abolition of the death penalty did not create a new, more lenient law. It considered that only Law no. 1483, which replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment, was a new mitigating law with retroactive effect. However, this decision came after the applicant’s conviction had already become final.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that the domestic courts had failed to apply the most lenient criminal provisions, contrary to Article 7 of the Convention. The Court examined whether the life sentence was compatible with the requirement that no heavier penalty be imposed than the one applicable at the time of the offence, and that any subsequent law providing for a lighter penalty must be applied retroactively. The central factual dispute was thus whether the interval between the death penalty’s abolition and the introduction of life imprisonment constituted the most favourable applicable sentencing regime. The Court ultimately found a violation of Article 7, concluding that the domestic courts had failed to apply the most lenient version of the relevant criminal law to the applicant’s sentencing.

**Case summary: Lindstrand Partners Advokatbyrå AB v. Sweden (Application no. 18700/09)**

The applicant was a Swedish law firm, Lindstrand Partners Advokatbyrå AB (formerly Hagenfeldt Advokatbyrå AB). The case arose from tax audits and coercive measures carried out by the Swedish Tax Agency in 2006–2008 concerning three companies, including SNS-LAN Trading AB (“SNS”) and Draupner Universal AB (“Draupner”). The Tax Agency suspected tax evasion through irregular transactions with a Swiss company and considered that Mr Toivo Jurik, who was connected to the Swedish companies, had a decisive role.

In March 2008, the Tax Agency applied to the County Administrative Court for permission to use coercive measures against SNS, including search and seizure of documents. Since SNS had been liquidated and had no premises, the Agency sought to search two locations connected to Mr Jurik: a flat/registered address of Draupner and the offices of the applicant law firm, where Mr Jurik had an office. The Agency requested that SNS not be notified in advance because of the risk that documents might be destroyed. On 10 March 2008, the County Administrative Court granted the application and made it immediately enforceable.

The search took place on 14 March 2008. At the flat, 19 files, an external hard disk drive, and a torn document were seized; a computer hard disk and a USB memory stick were copied. The law firm’s premises were then searched, including the offices of Mr Jurik and Mr Möller, but no relevant material was found there. During the flat search, the Tax Agency decided on-site to audit Draupner and took an interim decision to use coercive measures against it, allowing searches at both the flat and the law firm. That decision was later confirmed by the County Administrative Court.

The applicant requested that the seized and copied material—especially the external hard disk and USB stick—be exempted from the audit, arguing that it was protected by attorney-client privilege because SNS and Draupner were clients and the devices had been used by Mr Jurik in his law practice. The courts dismissed the request, finding that the applicant lacked legal standing because the coercive measures had not been directed against the law firm and the material had been seized from Draupner. The Administrative Court of Appeal held that the applicant was not sufficiently affected to appeal; the Supreme Administrative Court refused leave to appeal.

Draupner also sought exemption of documents. The courts generally rejected those requests, holding that material found at Draupner’s premises was presumed to belong to its business and be eligible for audit. They found no attorney-client privilege because the Tax Agency had not ordered the law firm to provide information and the documents had not been seized at the law firm. Some private documents were later exempted.

The applicant also challenged the impartiality of a co-opted judge in the Administrative Court of Appeal who was a Tax Agency civil servant on leave. The objection was rejected by the domestic courts.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key complaints concerned the search and seizure at a law firm, the copying and potential examination of privileged material, the refusal to recognize the applicant’s standing to seek exemption, the alleged lack of effective judicial review, and the alleged lack of impartiality. The audits were eventually discontinued, no tax decisions were issued, and all documents were returned.

Korošec v. Slovenia (Application no. 77212/12; ECtHR Fifth Section, 8 October 2015) concerned an Article 6 § 1 complaint that judicial proceedings were unfair. The applicant, Tadej Korošec, a Slovenian national born in 1980, suffers from progressive spinal muscular atrophy and requires twenty-four-hour assistance with daily activities.

In 2006 the Pensions and Disability Insurance Institute of Slovenia awarded him an assistance and attendance allowance at 70% of the reference amount. On 28 May 2009 his general practitioner applied for an increase because his condition, especially respiratory function, had worsened. The GP stated that he needed twenty-four-hour assistance from a family member or lay care assistant, together with permanent professional assistance. At that time the applicant relied on hired students and family members for care.

The Institute’s first-instance disability commission, composed of an internal-medicine specialist and an occupational-medicine specialist, examined the medical documentation and the applicant. On 9 July 2009 it reported that he did not need permanent professional medical assistance. The Institute dismissed the request on 20 July 2009. On appeal, the second-instance disability commission, composed of an occupational-medicine specialist and a neuropsychiatrist, examined the file and concluded that he did not need permanent professional assistance; his care could be provided by assistants without specific medical knowledge and by family members. On 24 September 2009 the Institute dismissed the appeal, relying on the 1998 Decision on Assistance and Attendance Allowance, which allowed a higher allowance only where the beneficiary needed twenty-four-hour family assistance and further professional medical assistance.

On 22 October 2009 the applicant brought court proceedings against the Institute before the Ljubljana Labour and Social Court and requested an independent medical expert. On 30 September 2010 the court heard him, reviewed the file and dismissed the claim. It refused to appoint an independent expert, finding that the opinions of the Institute’s first- and second-instance disability commissions, together with other evidence, sufficiently showed that he did not need professional assistance. The applicant appealed, arguing that the court lacked medical expertise and should have appointed an independent expert. On 24 January 2011 the Higher Labour and Social Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the commissions were composed of experts and had considered his medical records.

The applicant then sought leave to appeal on points of law, relying on Supreme Court decision no. VIII Ips 3/2006. That decision held that opinions of the Institute’s disability commissions could not be treated as independent expert opinions in judicial proceedings against the Institute, because they were opinions of representatives of one of the parties. The Supreme Court nevertheless dismissed his application on 17 May 2011, finding no departure from established case-law. His constitutional complaint was dismissed on 11 June 2012 under section 55.b of the Constitutional Court Act.
