**Summary of Seton v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 55287/10)**

The case of *Seton v. the United Kingdom* concerns the applicant, Mr. John Edward Seton, who was convicted of murder in 2008 and alleged a violation of his right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The conviction stemmed from the shooting death of Mr. Jon Bartlett on March 31, 2006. The prosecution’s case was that Seton, a drug dealer who owed the victim £24,000, shot him and then fled to the Netherlands before being extradited to the UK.

The central issue arose from Seton’s defense. He claimed that the murder was committed by a third party, Mr. Pearman, a man with previous convictions for drug, firearm, and murder offenses who was serving a life sentence at the time. According to Seton, he had been involved in a drug deal with both Bartlett and Pearman, and it was Pearman who had driven off in the silver Vauxhall Vectra used in the shooting.

During the investigation, police interviewed Pearman, who answered "no comment." Subsequently, Pearman made two phone calls from prison—to his son and his wife—in which he denied any involvement in the murder and claimed he had never heard of Seton. As a category A prisoner, Pearman would have known these calls were being recorded. At Seton’s trial, the prosecution sought to admit these recordings as hearsay evidence under section 114(1)(d) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The defense objected, but the trial judge ruled the recordings admissible.

In his ruling, the judge considered the factors in section 114(2) of the Act. He found the evidence had "extremely strong probative value" as Pearman appeared to be expressing genuine outrage at being implicated. While Pearman refused to testify, the judge noted that police enquiries had found no connection between Pearman and either the victim or the applicant, and no evidence of his involvement. The judge acknowledged the defense’s argument that the statements were self-serving, as Pearman knew he was being recorded, but considered this a matter of weight for the jury, not a ground for exclusion. He also noted the evidence was reliable (taped) and that Pearman’s bad character had already been put before the jury. The recordings were played at trial, and the jury asked to hear them a second time during deliberations.

Seton was convicted by a majority verdict and sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 30 years. His appeal to the Court of Appeal was dismissed. The Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge's decision, finding that he had properly considered all relevant matters under section 114(2). It noted that compelling Pearman to attend court would have been a "fruitless exercise" as he would have refused to give evidence, and that the defense could still argue the statements were self-serving.

It was this admission of hearsay evidence—the recorded phone calls of an absent witness whom the defense could not cross-examine—that formed the basis of Seton’s application to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that it rendered his trial unfair.

In *Hakobyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 21350/19), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application lodged on 15 April 2019 by Hrayr Hakobyan, born in 1959, represented by Yerevan lawyer D. Shakhramanyan. The application was communicated to the Armenian Government. The applicant complained that his criminal trial was unfair because he had no opportunity to put questions in court to the witness whose testimony played a significant role in securing his conviction. The final domestic decision was a Court of Cassation judgment of 16 October 2018. The applicant had been convicted of misappropriation of State funds—swindling in particularly large amounts—and forgery of official documents.

The central facts concern the witness identified as H.Z. During the pre-trial investigation, H.Z. was interviewed twice. She made incriminating statements against the applicant only during the second interview. According to the appended information, H.Z.’s statement was the only direct evidence implicating the applicant in the act of swindling State funds and played the decisive role in his conviction on that count. There was no other direct evidence linking the applicant to the crimes with which he was charged. This made H.Z.’s evidence central to the prosecution case and, consequently, to the fairness of the trial.

In court, H.Z. retracted her incriminating statements. She claimed that the investigator had inaccurately recorded her words and had tried to confuse her. Because her earlier statement was decisive, the defence needed to question her about the contradictions between her accounts, including her statement that she had passed money to the applicant and the circumstances surrounding that alleged transfer. However, the presiding judge did not allow H.Z. to respond to the defence’s questions relating to the charges against the applicant or to her relevant incriminating statement. The judge relied on formalistic grounds: H.Z. had been summoned for an additional examination

**Gyuleva v. Bulgaria** (Application no. 38840/08) concerned a Bulgarian national, Ms Valentina Atanasova Gyuleva, born in 1947 and living in Plovdiv. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention because she was not notified of civil proceedings brought against her and could not defend herself.

The case arose from an earlier restitution dispute over a flat occupied by the applicant and her family. Between 1992 and 2000, proceedings ended with the pre-nationalisation owners being recognised as the true owners. That earlier matter led to a prior Strasbourg judgment finding violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1 due to the length of proceedings. In February 2002, those owners sold the flat to Mr and Mrs P. They then brought *rei vindicatio* proceedings against the applicant. The first-instance court allowed their claim in October 2002. Although appeals continued, the applicant vacated the flat on 10 January 2003 and moved to Hrabrino, registering her address there on 4 February 2003.

On 4 May 2005, Mr and Mrs P. brought a new action against the applicant for unjust enrichment, claiming compensation for her occupation of the flat between 1 February 2002 and 10 January 2003. On 16 May 2005, the Plovdiv District Court issued a summons, sent to the mayor of Hrabrino for service. On 16 June 2005, the mayor returned it, stating that “no such person has been registered” in the village. On 8 July 2005, at the claimants’ request, the Plovdiv Regional Directorate of the Interior issued a certificate confirming that the applicant’s last declared address was in Hrabrino. Despite this, the District Court made no further attempts to locate her. On 26 August 2005, it concluded that her address was unknown and published a notification in the State Gazette under Article 50 § 1 of the 1952 Code of Civil Procedure.

The court then appointed an ex officio lawyer to represent the applicant, and all subsequent documents were served on that lawyer. The applicant alleged that the lawyer failed to contact her, failed to appeal, made no evidentiary requests, and did not meaningfully contest the claimants’ arguments, including a possible partial time-bar objection.

On 6 April 2006, the Plovdiv District Court allowed the unjust enrichment claim, ordering the applicant to pay BGN 3,573 plus interest. On appeal by Mr and Mrs P., the Plovdiv Regional Court, in a final judgment of 10 July 2006, ordered her to pay an additional BGN 1,006.21. The applicant only learned of the proceedings and judgments on 22 February 2008, when a bailiff notified her to pay. She ultimately paid BGN 8,767.07, approximately EUR 4,473.

The applicant relied on additional facts suggesting the authorities could have found her. In 2004, she was appointed as a juror at the Plovdiv District Court for 2005–2009 and received hearing notices at her brother’s address in Plovdiv. At that same address, in 2007 and 2008, she received two summonses relating to other proceedings brought by Mr and Mrs P., as well as the February 2008 bailiff notice. She was also a well-known piano teacher at the Academy of Music, Dance and Fine Arts in Plovdiv, whose workplace could have been known to the authorities.

Domestic law required summonses normally to be served by court officials, municipality, village mayor, registered mail, or at the person’s workplace. Service by publication in the State Gazette was a last resort where the address was genuinely unknown, but the court had to satisfy itself through checks that this was so. Reopening civil cases was possible if a party had been deprived of participation or had an ex officio representative appointed despite a known address, subject to strict time limits.

The key alleged violation was therefore that the authorities treated the applicant as of unknown address and served her only by publication, despite available information, then appointed a lawyer who allegedly did not adequately defend her, leaving her unable to participate in the unjust enrichment proceedings until after final judgment and enforcement.

The applicant, Juozas Pugžlys, a Lithuanian national born in 1966, complained to the European Court of Human Rights about his treatment during criminal proceedings in Poland. He was arrested in the Netherlands in April 2003 on suspicion of leading an international organised criminal group and of six counts of kidnapping for ransom. He was detained on remand and transferred to Poland in October 2003. In a separate case, he was convicted of armed robbery in 2005 and served that sentence from January 2006 to July 2010. In the main case, he was indicted in April 2004; after jurisdictional issues, the trial proceeded before the Lublin Regional Court. In January 2010 he was convicted of six kidnappings and leading an organised criminal gang and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment. His appeal was dismissed in December 2010, and the Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal in April 2012.

The main alleged violations concerned the “dangerous detainee” regime, courtroom conditions, defence rights, and family contact. On 21 October 2003, the Lublin Remand Centre Penitentiary Commission classified him as a “dangerous detainee” under the Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences. The authorities relied on the suspicion that he had committed offences within an organised criminal group, the violent and ruthless nature of the alleged crimes, his personal situation, his knowledge of boxing and combat techniques, and an alleged “high degree of depravity.” The regime was reviewed and reaffirmed every three months until it was lifted on 25 July 2012—about nine years. The renewal decisions and requests used similar wording, referring to the charges or convictions, his personal circumstances, low moral character, and lack of participation in social rehabilitation. His appeals against these decisions were dismissed by domestic courts, which found the measures lawful and based on thorough assessments.

As to courtroom conditions, the Government acknowledged that during hearings before the Lublin Regional Court the applicant was held in a metal cage separating him from judges and the public, and that while in the cage his hands remained handcuffed. The applicant alleged he was placed in the cage, with hands and legs shackled, during all approximately 104 trial hearings. The Government claimed this occurred only at some hearings. The dimensions of the cage and the position of guards were unclear. This formed part of his Article 3 complaint.

Regarding fair trial and defence rights, the applicant was Lithuanian. Interpreters were generally provided—initially Lithuanian, occasionally Russian if he agreed, and Lithuanian from January 2007. His court-appointed lawyer spoke only Polish. The applicant asked for a different lawyer, saying he could not communicate with him, but the request was refused. He could meet the lawyer during trial recesses, but allegedly in the presence of an interpreter and police officers or court personnel; requests for unsupervised meetings were denied. He had access to the case file with an interpreter, and the trial court agreed to provide translations of documents, though he later argued translations were not actually supplied unless he paid. The appeal court found no breach of defence rights; the Supreme Court held that guards were necessary because he was detained on remand and that translations of essential documents sufficed.

Finally, he complained under Article 8 about restrictions on family contact. He was allowed two ten-minute phone calls per week, sometimes one fifteen-minute call, plus additional calls. Visits by his common-law wife and daughter occurred regularly, between two and four times yearly from 2004 to 2009 and eight times in 2010, lasting thirty minutes to two hours. Correspondence was not restricted. The Court communicated complaints under Articles 3, 6, 6 § 3(b), (c), (e), 8, and 13; other parts were declared inadmissible.

In *Menéndez García and Álvarez González v. Spain* (European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, Applications nos. 73818/11 and 19420/12, judgment of 15 March 2016), the applicants were two Spanish nationals: Gerardo Menéndez García, born in 1964 and living in Gargantada, and Sigifredo Álvarez González, born in 1956 and living in Sant Jordi de Cercs. The first applicant was represented by a lawyer; the second was self-represented.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation concern the excessive length of criminal proceedings. In 2000 the applicants acted as intermediaries or purchase agents in the sale of three cars to a company. On 20 November 2000, criminal investigations were opened by the Gijón investigating judge against the applicants and eight other suspects for fraud and forgery of documents. In April 2001 the applicants were detained, charged with document forgery, informed of their rights as detainees, and interrogated by the Guardia Civil in the presence of counsel.

A significant delay followed. On 8 November 2004, the investigating judge issued a decision ordering the opening of oral proceedings and sent the case file to the Asturias Audiencia Provincial. However, the hearings before the Audiencia Provincial did not take place until 6 May 2009—approximately four and a half years after committal and eight and a half years after the investigation began. On 5 June 2009, the Audiencia Provincial convicted the first applicant and sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment, and convicted the second applicant and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment, for fraud and document forgery.

The applicants requested a sentence reduction for undue delay under Article 21 of the Criminal Code. The Audiencia Provincial refused. It acknowledged that the proceedings had been “unusually” long but attributed the duration to the complexity of the case: difficulties gathering evidence in different jurisdictions, the large number of parties, problems notifying some defendants, and the applicants’ lawyers’ lack of celerity in presenting submissions.

The applicants appealed in cassation. On 27 May 2010, the Supreme Court partially ruled in their favour, sentencing both to three years and eight months’ imprisonment for fraud. It rejected their undue-delay claims, accepting that the proceedings might have appeared excessively long but finding that the Audiencia Provincial had provided a sound and detailed justification. Both applicants then filed amparo appeals with the Constitutional Court, complaining, among other things, about the excessive length of proceedings. By decisions of 20 May and 12 September 2011, served on 25 May and 23 September 2011, the Constitutional Court declared the appeals inadmissible for lack of constitutional relevance under Article 50 § 1(b) of the Organic Law on the Constitutional Court.

The applicants lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights on 18 November 2011 and 22 March 2012. On 12 September 2013, the complaints concerning the length of proceedings were communicated to the Spanish Government, while the remainder of the applications was declared inadmissible by the President of the Section under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The central alleged violation was therefore that the criminal proceedings lasted excessively long, contrary to the right to a hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The key timeline runs from the investigation in November 2000 to final domestic decisions in 2011, with notable delays between investigation and committal and between committal and hearing.

In *Krahulec v. Slovakia* (Application no. 19294/07), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 5 July 2016; it became final on 5 October 2016. The applicant, Mr Štefan Krahulec, a Slovak national born in 1945 and living in Zvolen, lodged his application on 30 April 2007. He alleged that Slovakia’s rent-control scheme imposed restrictions on his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The Court declared the application partly admissible on 7 June 2011.

The property at issue was a house in Piešťany built by the applicant’s grandfather in 1929. The family retained ownership under the communist regime, and ownership was transferred to the applicant from his mother on 21 December 1998. The house contained four flats: two measuring 108 sq. m and two measuring 123 sq. m.

At the time the application was lodged, the flats were occupied by tenants under regulated rents. The tenants or their predecessors had acquired the right to use the flats through municipal decisions taken between 1953 and 1986. After 1 January 1992, that right of use was transformed into tenancies with regulated rent for an indefinite period. Under the applicable legislation, the applicant had to accept that the flats were occupied by those tenants and could charge no more than the maximum rent fixed by the State. He had no possibility of unilaterally terminating the leases.

In 1999, the maximum monthly rent chargeable for the flats was the equivalent of approximately EUR 13 to EUR 33. Following several increases, by 2004 the applicant could charge EUR 115 per month for each smaller flat and EUR 124 per month for each larger flat. The applicant claimed that in practice he received less than the statutory maximum and pursued several property disputes with tenants and the local municipality.

The parties disputed the market rent. The applicant relied on data from the National Association of Real Estate Agencies, claiming that monthly market rent for similar flats reached EUR 600 to EUR 800 between 2004 and 2007. The Government submitted an expert valuation putting the monthly market rent in 2010 at EUR 265.50 and EUR 325 for the applicant’s flats. Rent control ended for the first flat in May 2007, for the second and third flats in August 2007, and for the fourth flat in April 2008.

The relevant domestic law and practice concerning Slovakia’s rent-control scheme were set out in *Bittó and Others v. Slovakia* (no. 30255/09, 28 January 2014). In *Bittó*, the Court found that the rent-control scheme violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Under Article 46, it held that the violation originated in a systemic legislative and practice problem affecting many flat owners, with 13 other applications pending concerning about 170 persons. The Court noted gradual measures, including Law no. 216/2011 allowing annual 20% rent increases from late 2011, and a possible right from 2017 for landlords to claim the difference between market and controlled rent if municipalities had not housed hardship tenants by the end of 2016. However, those measures did not address the prior situation. The Court stated that further measures were needed and that Slovakia should introduce a specific, clearly regulated compensatory remedy. Implementation of *Bittó* remained pending.

The key alleged violation was therefore that the rent-control scheme forced the applicant to keep tenants, capped his rent far below market levels, and prevented him from terminating leases, thereby interfering with his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In **Bimuradova v. Russia** (Application no. 3769/11), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 12 November 2015 (final 14 March 2016), the applicant was Toita Bimuradova, a Russian national born in 1966 and living in Bas-Gordali, Chechnya. She is the sister of Magomed Bimuradov, born in 1972. The application, lodged on 2 December 2010, alleged that in May 2002 her brother had been abducted by State servicemen in Chechnya and that no effective investigation into the disappearance had taken place. The Russian Government did not dispute the applicant’s account of the facts but denied any involvement by State servicemen.

According to the applicant, at about 3 p.m. on 27 May 2002 (some documents refer to 26 May 2002), Magomed Bimuradov was abducted from a street near his home in Bas-Gordali by a group of armed masked men in a white car. He was forced into the car, which drove away toward the village of Shuani in the Nozhay-Yurt district of Chechnya. The abductors allegedly belonged to the federal forces. He has been missing since. The applicant claimed that fellow villagers E.Ts. and Kh.Ts. witnessed the abduction, but she did not submit their statements to the Court, and they do not appear to have given statements to the official investigation. She did submit an undated joint statement by herself and two sisters, none of whom were present during the abduction.

The official investigation began after relatives complained on 5 June 2002 that Magomed had gone out and not returned. On 1 October 2002 the Nozhay-Yurt district prosecutor’s office opened criminal case no. 71056 under Article 105 of the Criminal Code (murder). On 14 October 2002 the applicant was granted victim status. In October and November 2002 investigators sent inquiries to various law enforcement agencies about the possibility that Magomed was being detained; all replies were negative. On 2 December 2002 the investigation was suspended for failure to identify suspects. In July 2003 investigators provided the applicant’s relatives with statements confirming that Magomed had gone missing and had not been involved in an illegal armed group. On 31 March 2004 the military prosecutor’s office of military unit no. 20116 replied to a request from the applicant’s sister that it was impossible to verify the theory that military servicemen were involved in the disappearance. On 19 April 2005 the investigation was resumed, but on 20 May 2005 it was again suspended for failure to identify suspects. Between June 2005 and November 2010 the applicant and her relatives made further requests to the authorities. On 8 November 2010 they complained to the North Caucasus Department of the Prosecutor General’s Office about abductions by federal servicemen and the lack of effective investigations; no reply was given. On 1 December 2011 the investigation was resumed following a complaint by the applicant’s relatives, and the criminal proceedings remain pending.

The main witness statements in the criminal file were limited. On 14 October 2002 the applicant told investigators that her brother had left home and not returned, and that earlier she had seen a suspicious white VAZ-2106 car without a registration number driving around the village. On 3 May 2005 investigators questioned her sisters Z.Kh. and Kh.B. and the head of the Bas-Gordali village administration, E.K. Their accounts were similar, but none had witnessed the abduction; they had only seen a white VAZ car without registration plates that day.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the alleged abduction of Magomed Bimuradov by State servicemen, the absence of direct witness statements in the official file, the repeated suspension and resumption of the investigation, the failure to identify suspects, and the authorities’ inability or unwillingness to verify military involvement. These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint that the State had failed to protect the right to life and to conduct an effective investigation into the disappearance.

In Kulyk v. Ukraine (Application no. 30760/06, judgment 23 June 2016), the applicant, Anatoliy Kulyk, alleged that police officers had ill-treated him, that the investigation into his complaints was ineffective, and that his right of individual application to the European Court of Human Rights had been interfered with.

The relevant events began on 30 December 2002. Kulyk saw three young men on the premises of the nearby Shargorodskiy Food Products Factory. Because of earlier thefts from the factory, he climbed over the fence, entered an abandoned building through an opening in the wall, heard adult voices, and quickly returned home. Five to ten minutes later, police officer L. arrived at his house. Kulyk alleged that L. had a gun, swore at him, grabbed him by the collar, struck him on the head with the gun handle, and kicked him after he fell. His mother-in-law intervened and asked L. to stop. L. then took Kulyk to the police station and accused him of stealing aluminium sheets.

At the police station, Kulyk alleged that L. kicked him in the kidneys in the presence of two officers. Later, L. and another officer, P., allegedly beat him about the head and body for 15–20 minutes, and officer G. joined them, seeking a confession to theft. Kulyk was then placed in a cell. That night he complained of headache and sickness. A man in a white coat gave him Analgin and Dimedrol, but later medical-unit information indicated he received no ambulance assistance. On the morning of 31 December 2002, he was taken to court, fined for disobeying police, returned to the station, and signed a statement that no physical force had been used and that he had no complaints. The same day, authorities decided not to prosecute him for theft, finding he had no intent and had entered the factory out of curiosity.

Kulyk later suffered headaches, nausea and fever. He was hospitalised from 3 January to 11 February 2003. Medical records noted bruises mostly on the left side, scratches, and a large left-thigh bruise. Diagnoses included closed brain injury, brain contusion of medium severity, two broken ribs, post-traumatic pneumonia, and kidney, face and body injuries. A May 2003 forensic report found medium-severity injuries caused by a blunt hard object, possibly on 30 December 2002.

The police version was that factory employees had asked L. to check noises. They saw Kulyk run, fall when climbing through a conveyor opening and over a fence, and later fall at his house. He hid in a coal bunker. Police denied beating him. Kulyk’s mother-in-law testified that she saw L. aim a blow or kick at Kulyk while he lay on the ground. Experts said the injuries could have resulted from falls or beatings.

After Kulyk complained in February 2003, prosecutors repeatedly refused or terminated proceedings for lack of evidence; those decisions were often quashed and reinvestigated. Proceedings for abuse of power began in October 2004, and officers P. and L. were charged in April 2005. However, the case was terminated in October 2008 for absence of evidence, with authorities concluding the injuries likely resulted from falls and no evidence could be found after six years. The investigation was criticised for delays and failures to question witnesses or doctors, obtain medical records, and conduct timely reconstructions.

Separately, in September–October 2010, premises connected to Kulyk’s representative were searched/inspected in unrelated criminal proceedings concerning online pornographic material. Police seized three computers from an office used by the representative/human rights organisation. One allegedly contained confidential correspondence with the Court in this case. Complaints about the seizure led to a refusal to institute criminal proceedings. The representative was reportedly acquitted in August 2013.

The applicant therefore alleged violations of Article 3 (ill-treatment and ineffective investigation) and Article 34 (interference with the right of individual petition).

In *Salikhova and Magomedova v. Russia* (Application no. 63689/13, judgment of 26 January 2016), the applicants were the mother and wife of Mr Sakhrab Abakargadzhiyev. They alleged that he had been abducted by State agents in Dagestan, Russia, had subsequently disappeared, and that the authorities had failed to investigate the matter effectively.

At the material time, Mr Abakargadzhiyev lived with the applicants and other relatives in Makhachkala. For about eighteen months before the incident, he had allegedly been suspected of illegal activities and followed by Dagestani law-enforcement agencies, particularly the Centre against Extremism (CPE). On 20 May 2013, at about 6 p.m., he drove his white GAZ Volga-3110 car to visit relatives. At about 6.45 p.m., on Engelsa Street, his car was stopped and he was abducted by eight armed, masked men dressed in civilian clothing. They drove two civilian vehicles: a silver VAZ-21014 with a registration number partly reading “A067” and a black VAZ-21099. A relative called Mr Abakargadzhiyev during the abduction and heard him screaming. Shortly afterwards, the first applicant and a relative went along his route and found his car with police officers from the Sovetskiy district police station. The police said he had been abducted minutes earlier and told them to wait at home; they took his car to the police station.

About twenty days later, CPE officers searched the applicants’ home. Around 20 June 2013, the applicants obtained video footage of the abduction from a local resident. They recognised one abductor’s voice as that of a CPE officer named “Shakir” and informed the authorities. On 1 July 2013, a burnt male corpse was found near Gurbuki village. On 23 December 2013, the authorities identified the body as Mr Abakargadzhiyev through DNA testing. The applicants disputed this, stating that the corpse had several gold teeth while their relative had none.

The applicants complained of the abduction to the Sovetskiy police immediately and again on 24 May 2013. A criminal case was opened on 14 June 2013. Investigators examined the crime scene on 3 June and the car on 6 June, but collected no useful evidence; fingerprints were unfit for identification. They questioned witnesses, including Mr Ma.Ma., who had recorded the abduction on his mobile telephone. The video was seized on 21 June. The first applicant provided DNA samples. In June and July 2013, she received anonymous text messages claiming her son had become a “shahid” and had been set up by a neighbour working for the police. On 5 September 2013, a caller claiming to be an FSB officer said he was holding the victim and demanded a ransom; RUB 50,000 was deposited, after which the number was disconnected. Call logs placed the caller in Volgograd.

The applicants requested voice analysis of the abduction video. It was ordered, but experts found the voice unfit for identification. CPE officer Shakir N. was questioned; he admitted participating in the June search of the applicants’ home but denied any involvement in the abduction. He claimed the victim supported Wahhabism and had aided terrorist groups. An internal inquiry could not verify the allegations due to conflicting statements. The investigation was suspended on 30 December 2013, resumed in January 2014, joined with the case concerning the burnt corpse, and remained pending.

The Government denied State involvement but did not dispute the applicants’ factual account. The applicants alleged that the abduction and disappearance were attributable to State agents and that the authorities failed to conduct an effective investigation.

This case concerns an application lodged on 19 September 2018 by A.L., a Slovak national; S.M., a Norwegian national; their child X; and J.L., the child’s grandmother, against Norway. The applicants complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights about Norwegian child welfare proceedings and measures concerning X. The Court gave notice of the Article 6 and Article 8 complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

X was born in mid-January 2015. On 26 March 2015, when she was about two months old, she was taken into emergency foster care. The emergency decision stated that the hospital had contacted child welfare services after the parents left with X even though the hospital had indicated that she needed treatment and was not ready to leave. Child welfare services had offered close follow-up because the family needed substantial practical guidance on feeding, nursing, sleep and routines. Concerns included that the parents left X alone on a nursing table or sofa, and that A.L. switched off an alarm that vibrated to alert S.M. that X was crying. A.L. had also “shooed” the child when she cried. X reportedly developed irregularly due to lack of interaction and social stimuli. The parents refused an offered stay at a family centre. The foster home’s address was not disclosed, and the parents initially received supervised contact for one hour every fourteen days.

The emergency placement was confirmed by the County Social Welfare Board on 31 March 2015, upheld by the District Court on 25 June 2015, and became final when the High Court refused leave to appeal on 30 October 2015. A care order application followed. In November 2015, contact was reduced to one hour every sixth week, upheld by the Board in February 2016. The Board rejected the care order in March 2016, after which contact was increased to one hour every third week. In September 2016, the District Court upheld the Board’s decision. In November 2016, the High Court quashed that judgment on procedural grounds because one judge had been biased. The Supreme Court dismissed a further appeal in January 2017.

The case was retried before a different District Court in October 2017. The first and second applicants were present with legal aid counsel, gave evidence, and twenty witnesses were heard. A court-appointed expert and a privately appointed expert provided reports. The Commission of Child Welfare Experts found no significant issues with the court-appointed expert’s report but identified major shortcomings in the private expert’s report.

In its judgment of 16 November 2017, the District Court noted that X had been in emergency foster care since March 2015. It considered evidence of early developmental concerns, delayed motor skills, elevated care needs, and limited interaction between parents and child. Expert evidence indicated both parents had reduced caring skills: the mother had difficulty understanding X’s needs, possibly linked to her own psychological and traumatic background, while the father was described as intense and invasive. The mother’s hearing disability was not considered decisive. Although contact sessions had improved, X showed adverse reactions, and the parents had not benefited sufficiently from guidance. The court found serious deficiencies in care if X were returned and set contact at three times a year for one hour, supervised. It also authorised non-disclosure of the foster home’s address due to pressure from the parents and X’s need for peace. Contact was to take effect immediately. The High Court refused leave to appeal in March 2018, and the Supreme Court’s Appeals Committee dismissed the appeal in June 2018.

Before the ECtHR, the Article 8 complaints concerned interference with family life through emergency placement, the care order, restricted contact, and non-disclosure of the foster home. The Article 6 complaints concerned the fairness of the proceedings, including the retrial, expert evidence, appeal restrictions, and procedural safeguards. The Slovak and Czech Governments and the Ordo Iuris Institute intervened.

In *Simoncini v. San Marino*, the applicant, Massimiliano Simoncini, a San Marinese national, complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention about domestic proceedings no. 37/2020, which concerned the annulment of his appointment as *Commissario della Legge* (CoL), a first-instance judicial office. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of those complaints to the San Marinese Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The case arose from a dispute over the lawful composition of the Judicial Council in plenary session (*Consiglio Giudiziario Plenario*, “CGP”), the body responsible for judicial appointments. The applicant had served as an *Uditore Commissariale* since 2009 and was confirmed in that office in 2012. Having more than four years’ experience, he was eligible for appointment as CoL. In 2018 the CGP began a recruitment procedure for a CoL post. On 12 February 2019, by eleven votes in favour, the CGP decided to proceed by internal recruitment and appointed the applicant as CoL. Parliament acknowledged the appointment on 15 March 2019, and the applicant took up service on 22 March 2019.

However, two other *Uditori Commissariali*, X and Y, who had also been potential candidates, challenged the appointment in administrative proceedings no. 13/2019. They alleged, among other things, that the CGP had not been lawfully composed because judge C, a Judge of Appeal still serving a probationary period and not yet confirmed on a permanent basis, had participated in the CGP. They also complained of missing reports, lack of criteria, absence of reasons, and failure to notify interested candidates. The applicant did not initially participate in those proceedings and later failed to intervene because his request was out of time.

The legal background involved conflicting interpretations of the rules governing the CGP’s composition. In 2018 the CGP had taken the view that supplementation could include judges in the same category/functions even if not permanently confirmed. Later, Qualified Law no. 1/2020 introduced an authentic interpretation, with retroactive effect, providing that the CGP should be composed primarily of magistrates confirmed on permanent basis. On 28 September 2020, relying on that interpretation and on a *pro veritate* opinion, the CGP of its own motion (*autotutela decisoria spontanea*) annulled both the recruitment decision and the applicant’s appointment, on the ground that the CGP had been defectively composed when it appointed him. The applicant then brought proceedings no. 37/2020 challenging that annulment.

The domestic courts rejected the applicant’s claims. The first-instance judge found that the retroactive legislative interpretation pursued a compelling public interest and was not arbitrary; that the CGP could annul its own administrative act ex officio under domestic law; and that the presence of C had vitiated the appointment. On appeal, the Judge of Appeal for Civil Liability Actions of Magistrates upheld that reasoning on 9 January 2024. It held that the annulment was justified by the defective composition of the CGP, that the legislative intervention was necessary, reasonable, and proportionate, and that the applicant had no subjective right to retain an unlawful appointment. It found no violation of Articles 6, 8, 13, or 14, and considered parts of the appeal abusive or delaying. The applicant was ordered to pay costs.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court on 9 May 2024. The key alleged violations under Articles 6 and 8 concern whether the annulment of his judicial appointment, following a retroactive legislative change and an ex officio decision by the CGP, breached his right to a fair trial and his private life.

**Case: Fürst-Pfeifer v. Austria (Applications nos. 33677/10 and 52340/10)**

The case originated in two applications lodged against Austria with the European Court of Human Rights by Ms Gabriele Fürst-Pfeifer, an Austrian psychiatrist born in 1964. Since 2000, she had been registered as a psychological expert for court proceedings, particularly in custody and contact-rights disputes, public-care decisions and child-abuse cases. Her work focused mainly on psychological examinations of children and adolescents in custody and contact disputes.

On 23 December 2008, an article was published online on “meinbezirk.at” and in the free regional weekly print publication *Bezirksblatt*. The article was headlined “Disclosed: Court Expert for custody proceedings a case for therapy” and alleged that the applicant suffered from mood swings, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, hallucinations and paranoid ideas, yet continued to work as a court-appointed expert. It stated that she had examined over 3,000 married couples in custody disputes over the previous 12 years. The article relied on a 1993 psychological expert report by Dr. M., commissioned in civil proceedings concerning an alleged breach of promise of marriage, which reportedly found those impairments and suggested they were hereditary. It added that the applicant had later been introduced to the expert community at the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court and that her integrity had been beyond reproach for a decade. The article also included comments from a Green Party member who had filed a criminal complaint against her, the Youth Advocate at the Lower Austria Regional Government, and the Vice-President of the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court. It noted that she had stopped answering her phone and withdrawn from her cases.

Following publication, the applicant faced questions from colleagues and patients, and proceedings were initiated at the Wiener Neustadt Regional Court to determine whether she remained fit to serve as a court-appointed expert. Her mental status was also to be examined.

The applicant brought separate actions against the online and print publishers under section 8a of the Austrian Media Act, seeking damages and publication of the judgment. She claimed that the article, especially the passages about the 1993 psychological report, violated her intimate personal sphere and compromised her publicly. She did not argue that the expert report itself had been obtained unlawfully.

The St. Pölten Regional Court and the Innsbruck Regional Court initially allowed her actions, awarding €5,000 in damages each and ordering publication. They found that an average reader would link the 1993 opinion to her current work and question her professional quality. The article touched her intimate sphere, was incomplete, exaggerated and manipulative, and was not directly linked to her public life because custody proceedings were not public. They also considered that she appeared able to manage her illness and work without impairment.

However, the Vienna Court of Appeal (30 November 2009) and the Innsbruck Court of Appeal (11 February 2010) set aside those judgments and dismissed her actions. They agreed that the article affected her intimate personal sphere and was capable of compromising her, but found the published information true and sufficiently balanced. They held that her work as a registered court expert belonged to the public sphere, was closely linked to the administration of justice and had considerable influence on judges’ decisions. Given the sensitivity of custody proceedings and the dominant role of experts, any well-founded doubt about an expert’s psychological integrity warranted investigation in the public interest. The courts therefore treated the article as justified reporting on a matter of public concern.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that the Austrian courts had failed to protect her reputation and private life against the defamatory allegations. The key issue was whether the publication of intimate psychiatric details was justified as true information directly related to public life and the public interest in the fitness of court experts.

**Case: Jurišić v. Croatia (No. 2), app. no. 8000/21, Judgment 7 July 2022**

In this case, Mr Stjepan Jurišić alleged a fresh violation of Article 8 of the Convention because of his prolonged inability to have contact with his son, I.R. (born 2006). A prior judgment, *Jurišić v. Croatia* (no. 29419/17, 16 January 2020), had already found a violation of Article 8 due to non-enforcement of contact decisions; its execution remained pending before the Committee of Ministers. The new application concerned the subsequent period.

A final 2010 contact order granted the applicant contact every other weekend and part of school holidays. In enforcement proceedings, the child’s treating psychiatrist, J.G., warned that further expert evaluation or court questioning would harm the child; he proposed gradual meetings in his office. The applicant refused, claiming bias and manipulation. On 29 January 2020 the Slavonski Brod Municipal Court again terminated enforcement of the 2010 order. Relying on expert reports recommending gradual contact and finding coercive enforcement of the outdated order counterproductive and traumatising, the court held the order impossible to enforce. The Zagreb County Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal on 17 June 2020, and the Constitutional Court declared his complaint inadmissible on 21 October 2020.

In parallel, the mother initiated fresh contact proceedings in 2019. A guardian ad litem reported that I.R. was willing to give his father “one final chance” at Dr J.G.’s office; the applicant refused. The Social Welfare Centre proposed weekly Friday meetings in a neutral place without the mother. On 2 November 2020 the court issued a fresh contact order for supervised weekly contact, later progressing to every other weekend and holidays once contact was continuous and trust established. The court strongly criticised both parents: the mother had obstructed contact, ignored professional help, and delayed proceedings; the applicant denied the child’s medical issues, questioned experts’ competence, insisted on contact on his own terms, involved police during disputes, and refused to cooperate with the treating doctor. The court stressed that contact is the child’s right, not the parent’s, and that both parents’ conduct harmed I.R. The Zagreb County Court upheld this decision on 10 May 2021.

Attempts to enforce the new order also failed. On 2 and 9 January 2021, visits to the child’s home resulted in no contact. On 25 June 2021, the mother brought the child to a meeting, but the parents argued and the child left, saying he was fourteen and did not wish to be there. On 2 July 2021, the parents argued again; the applicant told the child his mother could go to prison, and the child left. On 7 July 2021, the child immediately refused contact, alleging past abuse. On 20 and 27 August 2021, he refused to speak, and on 8 September 2021 the applicant did not attend.

The mother was convicted twice of obstructing contact: for December 2015–August 2016 and April–June 2015, receiving suspended sentences. Three further criminal complaints for later periods remained pending. The key alleged violation was whether Croatia failed, under Article 8, to enforce contact rights and protect the applicant’s family life despite the prior judgment and fresh contact order.

In *Armani Da Silva v. the United Kingdom* (2016), the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights considered whether the United Kingdom breached the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights by failing to prosecute any individual police officers after the fatal shooting of Jean Charles de Menezes. The applicant, Ms Patricia Armani Da Silva, was Mr de Menezes’s cousin. She complained that the decision not to prosecute anyone meant the investigation was not effective, as Article 2 requires an official investigation capable of establishing the facts, determining whether the force used was justified, and identifying and, if appropriate, punishing those responsible.

The shooting occurred on 22 July 2005, two weeks after the London suicide bombings of 7 July and one day after failed bomb attacks on 21 July. The Metropolitan Police launched Operation THESEUS 2 to locate suspects. Intelligence suggested Hussain Osman might be at 21 Scotia Road, London. Mr de Menezes lived at 17 Scotia Road. On the morning of 22 July, surveillance officers followed him after he left the building. There were serious doubts about whether he was the suspect: he was initially described as a “possible likeness,” later as “not identical,” yet the control room apparently believed a positive identification had been made.

The police plan was to deploy specialist firearms officers from SO19 to Scotia Road to stop and arrest suspects safely. However, because SO19 was not in place in time, Mr de Menezes was simply followed. Briefings given to firearms officers were later criticised for heightening their belief that they might confront suicide bombers and for failing to warn them that persons leaving Scotia Road could be innocent. When Mr de Menezes entered Stockwell Underground Station, Commander Cressida Dick ordered that he be stopped. The order was interpreted by firearms officers as an armed interception. On a train, officers confronted Mr de Menezes, pinned him down, and two officers shot him multiple times. He was unarmed and had no connection to the bombings.

After the shooting, the Independent Police Complaints Commission conducted an independent investigation. Its Stockwell One Report identified numerous failings: inadequate briefings, delayed deployment of firearms officers, command and control problems, uncertain identification, an altered surveillance log, and missing CCTV footage. It found no evidence of a cover-up, but referred possible criminal offences to the Crown Prosecution Service. These included murder or self-defence issues for the shooters, gross negligence manslaughter for senior commanders, and misconduct or perverting the course of justice for others.

The CPS decided there was no realistic prospect of convicting any individual officer. It concluded that the shooters genuinely believed they faced a lethal threat, and that the mistakes of commanders and others did not meet the criminal threshold for gross negligence manslaughter or other offences. The CPS did prosecute the Office of the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis under health and safety law; it was convicted and fined. An inquest later returned an open verdict. No disciplinary charges were ultimately upheld against the frontline officers.

The Grand Chamber held that there had been no violation of Article 2. It accepted that the procedural obligation required an effective, independent investigation capable of leading to accountability, but it did not guarantee that every case would end in prosecution or conviction. Prosecutorial decisions had to be reasonably and impartially reached, not arbitrary. Given the complex operational context, conflicting evidence, self-defence issues, the detailed CPS review, the independent IPCC investigation, the inquest, and the health and safety prosecution, the authorities had not failed in their Article 2 obligations. The decision not to prosecute individuals did not make the investigation ineffective.

In *Ruban v. Ukraine*, the applicant, Vladimir Ruban, a Ukrainian national born in 1972 and serving life imprisonment, complained under Article 7 of the Convention that the domestic courts had failed to apply the most lenient criminal provisions when sentencing him.

The case arose from investigations in 1996–1999 into the murder of four persons, the murder of A., and hooliganism/grievous bodily harm concerning R. The investigations were joined, and several suspects, including Ruban, were suspected of acting as an organised group. On 14 December 1999 Ruban was charged in absentia and placed on a wanted list; proceedings against him were suspended. Co-accused G., P., and F. were convicted in 2002. Ruban was arrested in Russia in June 2007, extradited, and in March 2008 formally charged with participation in an organised criminal group, strangling A., killing four persons with G. in 1996, and grievous bodily harm in an attempted murder linked to extortion.

In July 2009 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal, acting as a first-instance court, convicted Ruban of aggravated murder and banditry and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The Supreme Court upheld that judgment in July 2010. Ruban’s lawyer submitted an additional appeal arguing that the courts should have applied the most favourable version of the Criminal Code—the law in force between 29 December 1999 and 29 March 2000, when the death penalty had already been abolished but life imprisonment had not yet been introduced. The Supreme Court rejected that argument.

The Article 7 issue concerned the applicable punishment. Under the 1960 Criminal Code, before 29 December 1999, aggravated murder was punishable by 8–15 years’ imprisonment or the death penalty. On 29 December 1999 the Constitutional Court declared the death penalty unconstitutional and null and void from that date, ordering Parliament to align the Code. However, Law no. 1483, which replaced the death penalty with life imprisonment, was adopted on 22 February 2000 and entered into force only on 29 March 2000. Thus, for an interim period, the death penalty had been abolished but life imprisonment had not yet been introduced. Ruban argued that this interim

Paposhvili v. Belgium (Application no. 41738/10, Grand Chamber, 13 December 2016) concerned a Georgian national, Mr Georgie Paposhvili, who arrived in Belgium in 1998 with his wife and child. His asylum request was refused, and he later received several criminal convictions, including for theft, robbery and involvement in a criminal organisation. In 2007 the Minister of the Interior issued a deportation order barring him from re-entering Belgium for ten years on public-order grounds.

The applicant suffered from severe health problems. In 2006 he was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, which later progressed to Binet stage C and to lymphocytic lymphoma. He also had tuberculosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hepatitis C and, after a stroke, permanent paralysis of one arm. He received multiple courses of chemotherapy and later Ibrutinib, a targeted therapy available in Belgium. Medical reports stated that discontinuing Ibrutinib would likely result in death within about three months, that he needed specialised haematological supervision, and that a donor stem cell transplant—identified as his only prospect of cure—would not be available in Georgia. Belgian medical advisers, however, considered that his condition was serious but currently controlled and did not amount to a “critical” or terminal state under N. v. the United Kingdom.

The applicant made several requests for regularisation, both on exceptional grounds and on medical grounds under section 9ter of the Aliens Act. The medical requests were rejected after the Aliens Office excluded him from the scope of section 9ter because of his serious criminal offences, without first examining his medical evidence. The Aliens Appeals Board upheld that approach, holding that medical risk would be assessed, if necessary, at the time of removal. A request for regularisation on exceptional grounds was also refused in July 2010, accompanied by an order to leave Belgium. His wife and children were granted indefinite leave to remain in 2010, but he was not.

On 23 July 2010 the applicant applied to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that removal to Georgia would expose him to risks to his life and physical well-being and would breach his right to family life, relying on Articles 2, 3 and 8 of the Convention. On 28 July 2010 the Court indicated an interim measure under Rule 39, requesting Belgium not to remove him pending the domestic proceedings. A Chamber judgment in 2014 found no violation of Articles 2 and 3 and no violation of Article 8. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber. The applicant died in June 2016, and his family continued the proceedings.

Before the Grand Chamber, the central issue was whether the Belgian authorities had adequately assessed the risk that removal would entail for the applicant’s health and whether he would have access to appropriate treatment in Georgia. The Grand Chamber clarified that Article 3 may be engaged where removal would lead to a real risk of serious, rapid and irreversible decline in health causing intense suffering, or a significant reduction in life expectancy due to the absence or lack of access to appropriate treatment. It found that Belgium had failed to carry out an adequate assessment of those risks, and held that there had been a violation of Article 3. The facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore centred on the applicant’s life-threatening illness, his dependence on specialised treatment unavailable in Georgia, the exclusion of his medical regularisation request without substantive examination, and the outstanding removal order that triggered his complaint under Articles 2, 3 and 8.

In *Prilutskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 40429/08), a Fifth Section judgment of 26 February 2015, final on 26 May 2015, the applicant, Mr Igor Prylutskyy, a Ukrainian national born in 1960 and living in Donetsk, alleged that the State had failed to take appropriate preventive measures to protect his son in a life-threatening situation and that the criminal proceedings concerning his son’s death had been ineffective. The application was lodged on 31 July 2008 and communicated to the Government on 3 September 2012.

The events arose on the night of 30 September 2006 during “AutoQuest”, a location-based driving game in Donetsk. Teams moved by car between locations, solved riddles to find the next destination, and competed to reach the final point first. The applicant’s son was a passenger in P.’s car. P. lost control and collided with a pillar. P. was injured, while his three passengers, including the applicant’s son, died.

On 1 October 2006 the Donetsk Region police opened an investigation under Article 286 § 3 of the Criminal Code concerning the fatal accident. The applicant was admitted as a victim on 3 October 2006. On 19 February 2007 the prosecutor’s office told him the case was complicated, required expert examinations, and that the activities of the game’s organisers were being examined. On 23 February 2007, however, the police refused to institute criminal proceedings against the organisers.

Psychiatric examinations became central. On 10 July 2007 experts found that P. had been aware of and able to control his actions at the time of the accident, but had later developed a chronic mental disability, including organic brain impairment and amnesic syndrome, and required mandatory psychiatric treatment. On 24 October 2008 the regional prosecutor’s office rejected the applicant’s complaint about investigative ineffectiveness and found no grounds to replace the investigator. The case was referred to the Kuybashevskyy District Court on 5 February 2009 to decide on compulsory medical measures. On 15 March 2010 the chairman of the Donetsk Region Council of Judges requested prompt consideration, noting repeated adjournments and unreasonable length. A repeat psychiatric report on 28 February 2011 confirmed the earlier conclusions.

On 8 June 2011 the first-instance court found that P. had committed a crime by violating traffic safety rules, exceeding the speed limit and losing control, causing the deaths. Nevertheless, relying on the psychiatric reports, it ordered compulsory outpatient psychiatric assistance because P. had later become unable to control his actions. The applicant appealed, arguing that the medical findings were wrong and that P. should have been brought to the hearings. On 24 January 2012 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal quashed the decision and remitted the case for additional pre-trial investigation, noting witness statements suggesting P. might have made a sharp turn to avoid a pedestrian; it found the facts had not been properly established. After further investigation, the case was again referred to the first-instance court on 31 October 2012. The authorities maintained that P. had exceeded the speed limit, lost control and caused the deaths, but proposed compulsory medical measures because of his post-accident mental disability. As of 26 March 2013 the proceedings remained pending.

Relevant domestic law included Article 286 of the Criminal Code and section 36 of the Automobile Roads Act 2005, which required local authorities, with approval of road-management and traffic-safety bodies, to regulate use of public roads for mass events and required permission for motor sports competitions on public roads. These provisions were relevant to the alleged failure to prevent the dangerous driving game.

In *Gherardi Martiri v. San Marino* (Application no. 35511/20, judgment of 15 December 2022), the applicant, an Italian national, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1 about San Marino’s alleged failure to protect her property from an organised fraud and about delays in related civil proceedings. The central facts concerned her dealings with Banca Commerciale San Marinese S.p.A. (“the bank”), its employees and third persons.

In 2005 the applicant sold property in Rimini. The buyer required an account at the bank, and €200,000 as an advance, later followed by €1,300,000 sale proceeds, were paid into a current account there. In 2009 she learned that the account balance was zero and that €80,000 of a credit had been used. Bank documents showed that from 2005 M.R., a person she had only recently met, had made investments and transfers using a power of attorney which she denied having knowingly given. She claimed the mandate was undated, unregistered in the bank’s system, bore no bank employee signature or stamp, and contained a contested scribbled signature. On a day in 2005 when she was at the bank, M.R. and bank management allegedly made three high-risk investments totalling €1,100,000. Funds were also transferred to persons she did not know. Criminal investigators later found that the transactions caused her a loss of about €700,000 and that M.R. had acted without a regular mandate; the bank’s information system recorded no such mandate, and bank officials were aware of the irregular operations. Some repayments were made, but the fraud charge was time-barred and neither M.R.’s profit nor wilful intent was fully proven.

In 2011 the applicant reported the matter to San Marino’s banking supervisory authority (“BA”). The BA said it would gather information but lacked power to settle disputes between banks and customers, which fell to the judiciary. In late 2011 the bank was placed under extraordinary administration, and in 2012 it ceded its branch and legal relations to Asset Banca S.p.a. Criminal proceedings began in 2012 on the applicant’s fraud complaint. In 2014 the investigating judge discontinued them as time-barred. The appeals judge reopened the investigation, finding it incomplete, but in 2017 the investigating judge again discontinued the case as time-barred, while confirming that M.R. had acted without a regular mandate, that the bank had not objected to the high-risk transactions, and that serious irregularities had occurred.

In 2015 the applicant brought a civil action against M.R., bank officials, the bank and Asset Banca, seeking compensation. In 2017 Asset Banca was placed in administrative compulsory winding-up. In 2018 the civil judge declared the action inadmissible against Asset Banca and impossible to continue against the other defendants because the applicant had pleaded joint and several liability. She then sought inclusion as a creditor in the winding-up liabilities, but the liquidators refused. Her objection was initially assigned to the wrong judge; in 2019 the judge found a lack of competence and ordered reopening before the competent judge. Those proceedings remained pending. In 2021 the Magistrate confirmed inadmissibility while the winding-up remained registered; although the winding-up was later declared illegal in 2022, the company remained inoperative and reimbursement impossible.

The applicant therefore alleged that San Marino breached its positive obligations under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 by failing to protect her property from organised fraud by the bank and third persons, and that the civil proceedings were excessively delayed under Article 6 § 1. The Court gave notice of these complaints and declared the remainder inadmissible.

Chakvetadze v. Georgia (Application no. 55949/10) concerned a Georgian national, Zurab Chakvetadze. On 25 December 2008 police stopped him in Tbilisi and searched him, allegedly seizing a Subutex tablet and a bullet. A search of his apartment that same day found heroin, another bullet, and USD 230,050 in cash. The cash was seized as evidence and deposited with the National Bank of Georgia. The applicant was charged with unlawful acquisition and possession of narcotic substances and ammunition.

On 23 September 2009 the Tbilisi City Court acquitted him of the heroin charge but convicted him in respect of the Subutex tablet and bullet. He received one year’s imprisonment and a fine of GEL 352,000. Crucially, the trial court found that the seized cash was not linked to the criminal proceedings and ordered its return to the applicant, unless he chose to use it to pay the fine. On 4 December 2009 the Tbilisi Court of Appeal maintained only the criminal fine and ordered his immediate release. The Supreme Court rejected his appeal on points of law on 12 March 2010.

On 14 April 2010 the Court of Appeal issued two writs of enforcement: one for the criminal fine and one requiring the police to return the seized cash. The applicant was informed that the police had been instructed to enforce the return order. On 25 April 2010 the National Bureau of Enforcement invited him to pay the fine voluntarily, together with a 7% enforcement fee of GEL 24,640. The applicant gave a power of attorney to another person to receive the cash, transfer USD 220,000 to individuals he claimed were co-owners, and use USD 10,050 to partly pay the fine. However, the police did not return the money. In May 2010 the applicant repeatedly asked the police to comply with the return order and complained to the prosecutor about the delay, but apparently received no response.

The return order remained unenforced for almost two years. On 30 November 2011 the police retrieved the cash from the National Bank and called the applicant to the police station. After he signed a report confirming return of the cash, a bailiff appeared and seized the entire amount to enforce the criminal fine and the related enforcement fee—before the applicant had physically taken possession of the money. The remaining excess of GEL 4,714 was returned to him on 4 February 2012.

The applicant alleged that the prolonged failure to enforce the final judgment ordering return of his cash violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. He also argued that the formal return on 30 November 2011 was a sham because the money was seized immediately, and that the authorities’ delay had prevented him from paying the fine voluntarily, making the 7% enforcement fee unlawful and unfair. Domestic courts rejected his challenge, holding that the enforcement fee became due in April 2010. The European Court of Human Rights gave notice of the complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The key alleged violations therefore concern the delayed enforcement of a final judgment in the applicant’s favour and the resulting interference with his possessions.

In the ECtHR case of *Strøbye and Rosenlind v. Denmark* (Apps. 25802/18 and 27338/18, 2 February 2021), two Danish nationals complained that they had been wrongly denied the right to vote in the 18 June 2015 parliamentary election because they had been deprived of their legal capacity. They alleged a breach of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, alone and read with Article 14, arguing that their disenfranchisement violated their right to free elections and discriminated against them as persons with disabilities.

The first applicant, born in 1966, was declared legally incompetent by Copenhagen City Court in 1984 to manage his financial and personal affairs. The second applicant, born in 1987, was placed under financial guardianship and deprived of legal capacity by Roskilde District Court in 2009. The 2009 order found that mental disability made him unable to manage his finances and that deprivation was necessary to prevent further debt. Under Article 29 of the Danish Constitution and section 1 of the Parliamentary Elections Act, persons who were “legally incompetent” did not have the right to vote in general elections. Consequently, both applicants were excluded from the 2015 parliamentary election. A 2016 statutory amendment granted persons deprived of legal capacity the right to vote in European Parliament and local/regional elections, but not in national parliamentary elections.
