**P.H. v. Slovakia** (Application no. 37574/19) concerned a 16-year-old Roma girl who was arrested on 17 January 2017 after being caught committing petty theft at a shopping mall. She was transported by Officers A and B to a county police station. According to the applicant, during the car journey the officers threatened to put her in a cage, insulted her because of her Romani origin, and each slapped her once. The Government denied any physical or verbal abuse, relying on police records stating that no coercive measures were used because she was a minor, cooperative, and not expected to abscond.

At the police station, the applicant admitted further thefts. A prosecutor instructed that she should not be detained and should be released after paperwork. A female officer searched her. Officer A then completed records alone with her. When she asked to use the toilet, he accompanied her. The bathroom area was on the second floor at the end of a corridor with a window measuring 116 by 140 cm, with a sill 90 cm high, opening by tilting. Officer A stated that he showed her the toilet, stood less than a metre away, and turned his back to wait. He then saw her falling out of the open window. She fell 770 cm to the ground, suffering severe injuries, including an endocranial injury, four rib fractures, four other skeletal fractures, a pneumothorax, and lung contusions. She was initially unconscious and reportedly in a coma for over a month. She later said she had no recollection of the fall but believed the mistreatment from the car likely continued at the station. Her brother submitted a statement saying he heard her shouting to be released and heard threats, insults, and racial slurs, before officers ran downstairs saying she had jumped.

The investigation was fragmented. Criminal proceedings were opened, quashed, and reopened against unknown officers for failing to guard the applicant under an internal police decree. The prosecution service found no grounds for criminal prosecution but considered it a disciplinary matter. Officer A was disciplined with a one-off 5% salary reduction for turning his back and failing to ensure proper guarding; mitigating factors included that the applicant was not dangerous and was expected to be released. A separate investigation into the alleged abuse in the police car was terminated in July 2017, finding no suspicion of wrongdoing. It reasoned that coercion was unnecessary, that slapping from the front seats was implausible, and that the applicant’s retrograde amnesia made her selective memory of abuse doubtful.

The applicant’s requests for review were dismissed. The prosecution service stated that the investigation was limited to the police-car ill-treatment, while the circumstances of her fall were outside its scope. The Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, noting no standalone right to criminal prosecution of third parties. The Ombudsperson found no violation.

The applicant alleged that Slovakia failed its positive obligations to protect her life and well-being while in police custody and to conduct an effective, prompt, independent, and adequate investigation into her fall, the alleged ill-treatment, and possible racial motives.

Fischer v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 24314/13, judgment of 24 February 2022) concerned a German national, Václav Fischer, and his minority shareholding in the Czech joint-stock company Cestovní kancelář FISCHER, a.s. Fischer originally owned 100% of the company. In November 2003 he entered into a consortium agreement with K & K Capital Group a.s., controlled by K.K. The agreement provided that if the company’s share capital were increased, both parties would have the right to participate proportionally. Fischer then transferred 75% of the shares to K & K Capital Group, retaining 25%.

On 3 March 2004, the company’s general meeting, using K & K Capital Group’s votes, adopted a resolution to increase the company’s share capital from CZK 1,000,000 to CZK 11,000,000. The shareholders’ pre-emptive subscription rights were excluded so that the newly issued shares could be offered to Kapitálová společnost K & K a.s., another company controlled by K.K. The stated aim was to reinforce the company’s internal financial resources because of negative equity and insufficient capital. Fischer objected and voted against the resolution. As a result, his shareholding fell from 25% to 2.3%.

Fischer applied to the Prague Municipal Court to have the capital-increase resolution set aside. He argued that the resolution breached Article 204a § 5 of the Commercial Code and the consortium agreement. In his view, pre-emptive rights could be excluded only for a serious reason, and no such reason existed: the new shareholder brought nothing valuable that existing shareholders could not have provided. He alleged the real purpose was for K.K. to seize control of the company.

Before that application was decided, the company’s general meeting on 17 December 2004 approved a merger with three other companies. The merger was recorded in the Commercial Register on 18 March 2005. It substantially increased the merged company’s share capital and diluted Fischer’s holding further, from 2.3% to 0.07%. Fischer also challenged the merger resolution, arguing that he still held 25% and that the merger had not been approved by the required 90% majority.

In the capital-increase proceedings, the Prague Municipal Court dismissed Fischer’s application on 13 April 2005. It found the resolution lawful and noted that, even if unlawful, it could not be set aside under Article 131 § 3(c) of the Commercial Code because the later merger had already been recorded in the Commercial Register. The High Court upheld that decision. The Supreme Court later quashed it, holding that Article 204a § 5 had not been complied with. On remittal, however, the High Court again upheld the dismissal. It accepted that the resolution breached the consortium agreement, was contrary to good morals, and circumvented the law, but held that it could not be set aside under Article 131 § 3(b) because third parties had acquired bona fide rights through the merger. The Supreme Court endorsed that reasoning, observing that Fischer could seek damages and just satisfaction under Article 131 § 4. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint, finding that his access to court was secured by the Supreme Court’s review and that share ownership did not guarantee unchanged influence over the company.

In the merger challenge, the Prague Municipal Court dismissed Fischer’s application on 17 January 2012. It reasoned that, because the capital-increase challenge had failed, he no longer held 25% at the relevant time; the merger had been approved by the required majority; and, in any event, Article 131 § 3(c), and possibly (b), barred setting the resolution aside because the merger was already registered. The High Court upheld that judgment on 17 May 2013.

Fischer complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 of the Convention that the domestic courts refused him access to a court to protect rights breached by the general meeting resolution. He also complained that, as a consequence, his property rights had been violated.

In *Fu Quan, s.r.o. v. the Czech Republic* (Application no. 24827/14), the applicant was a Czech limited liability company whose two associates, one also its managing director, were prosecuted for tax evasion in 2005. On 27 April 2005 the Prague Municipal Prosecutor’s Office ordered the seizure of the company’s property under Article 347 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, including clothing merchandise and a leased vehicle, on suspicion that the accused might transfer assets to China. The merchandise, valued at CZK 62,424,027 (about EUR 2.4 million), was seized between May and June 2005 and entrusted to the Office for Government Representation in Property Matters. Complaints against the seizure were dismissed. The associates were eventually acquitted on 27 February 2009; the court found it unproved that the alleged tax evasion had occurred. The seized funds were returned in 2010, and on 22 July 2010 the Municipal Court ordered the merchandise returned to the company. The goods were handed back in September 2010 after roughly five years’ storage.

In January 2011 the company sought compensation from the Ministry of Justice under the State Liability Act, claiming CZK 63,294,609. It primarily alleged that the stored clothing had deteriorated, become unsaleable, and sold for only CZK 536,663. It also claimed for stolen office equipment, enforcement due to unpaid telephone bills, and a leasing penalty. The Ministry dismissed the claims, stating it was not liable for the passage of time and that the alleged depreciation was unsubstantiated. The company then brought court proceedings.

The domestic courts dismissed the action. The District Court found the company lacked locus standi because it had not been a party to the criminal proceedings against its managing director and associate; it could not therefore claim damage arising from those proceedings. The Municipal Court upheld that reasoning, holding that claims under sections 8 and 9 of the State Liability Act for unlawful prosecution or custody belonged to the prosecuted individuals, not the company. It also found no causal link between the custody/indictment and the alleged damage from five-year storage, and noted that the company had not argued irregular official conduct. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on points of law in November 2012, reiterating that only a party to proceedings in which an unlawful decision was issued could claim compensation for that decision. The Constitutional Court dismissed the constitutional complaint in September 2013 as manifestly ill-founded, finding no arbitrariness.

Before the ECtHR, the company alleged violations of Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key facts relevant to those allegations are that the company owned the seized merchandise but was not a party to the criminal proceedings; the goods were stored for five years and allegedly deteriorated; the prosecution ended in acquittal; and the domestic courts refused compensation mainly because the company was not a party to the criminal case and had not framed its claim as one for irregular official conduct. The applicant complained that this formalistic and restrictive interpretation of national law deprived it of access to a court and an effective remedy, and that the seizure, storage, return of its property, and refusal of compensation violated its property rights. The ECtHR First Section judgment was delivered on 17 March 2022; the case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 1 June 2023.

The case concerns an application by Mr Isteyfo Özçelik, a Netherlands national born in 1959, against the Netherlands. He complained under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention that the lawfulness of his continued detention had not been decided “speedily”. The detention arose from a measure of placement in a Persistent Offenders Institution (ISD).

On 21 May 2010 the Almelo Regional Court convicted the applicant of shoplifting and imposed an ISD measure for two years. The measure aims to protect society and prevent reoffending, and may last a maximum of two years from the date the judgment becomes final. The Regional Court ordered a review six months after the judgment became final on 5 June 2010. On 1 December 2010 the Regional Court declined to terminate the measure because there was still a high risk of reoffending. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed by the Arnhem Court of Appeal on 19 April 2011.

On 19 May 2011 the applicant’s personal case officer reported that his placement at FPA De Cederborg was progressing reasonably, but that if the measure were terminated he would immediately have no income, housing or daily activities, making the risk of reoffending high. Continuation was recommended. On 9 June 2011 the Regional Court prolonged the measure, finding a considerable likelihood of reoffending after release.

The applicant appealed against that prolongation on 15 June 2011. This appeal is central to the alleged violation. On 8 November 2011 his counsel inquired about the progress of the appeal and requested priority. On 18 November 2011 counsel requested an interpreter speaking Aramaic or Assyrian and named a suitable interpreter.

On 12 December 2011 a hearing took place before the Court of Appeal. The applicant could not understand the Assyrian interpreter. With his agreement, the case was adjourned for up to three months to allow written questions to be put to his counsellors and for the case officer to be heard as an expert witness, with an Aramaic interpreter required at the next hearing. After three months, counsel again inquired about progress on 13 March and 2 April 2012. The hearing resumed on 10 May 2012. The case officer testified that the applicant was no longer addicted, that the risk of reoffending was maximally reduced, that treatment possibilities had been exhausted, and that the applicant was in a halfway house awaiting sheltered accommodation. Accommodation became available on 11 May 2012.

On 16 May 2012 the Court of Appeal delivered its decision. It held that the appeal had not been dealt with speedily within the meaning of Article 6 ECHR, as more than ten months had passed since the appeal was lodged, and considered that finding sufficient satisfaction. It nevertheless terminated the measure because execution had not been sufficiently expeditious at all stages, the difficult progress could not be attributed solely to the applicant, the institution could have signalled earlier that no further treatment was possible, and accommodation and reduced risk made continuation unnecessary.

Under domestic law, the ISD measure is governed by Article 38m of the Criminal Code and has a maximum duration of two years. Interim reviews are possible, and if continuation is no longer required the measure must be terminated. Article 509gg of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires the Court of Appeal to decide as speedily as possible on appeals involving the ISD measure. The key facts relevant to the Article 5 § 4 complaint are therefore the continued detention measure, the 15 June 2011 appeal against its prolongation, repeated requests for progress, the interpreter-related adjournment, the resumed hearing on 10 May 2012, and the decision of 16 May 2012—approximately eleven months after the appeal was lodged.

Balajevs v. Latvia (Application no. 8347/07) concerned a Latvian national, Mr Murads Balajevs, who alleged under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights that he had been ill-treated by three detainee escort officers at Riga Regional Court on 8 May 2006 and that Latvia had failed to conduct an effective investigation.

On 8 May 2006 the applicant was transferred from Central Prison to Riga Regional Court and placed in a holding cell. At 11:25 a.m. he asked escort officers to call an ambulance because he had waist pain and nausea. The ambulance arrived at 11:35 a.m.; he was found to have kidney stones and renal colic and was given painkillers. Later, when the pain returned, he again asked for an ambulance, shouting and cursing. The Government claimed that officer M.P. entered the cell to calm him, the applicant tried to hit M.P., and M.P. used physical force and a restraint technique under the Law on Police to prevent the attack. The applicant alleged that around 1:30 p.m. the officers refused to call an ambulance; when he continued asking for medical help, an officer entered the cell and kicked him in the chest, causing him to fall. While he tried to stand, he was kicked several more times. Other officers allegedly came, one forced him to the floor and kicked him in the back. At 1:48 p.m. the officers called an ambulance, which arrived at 2:04 p.m. The applicant told staff he had been hit on his left side and had previously suffered a right kidney rupture. The ambulance log noted no visible injuries. He was taken to Olaine prison hospital, where he was diagnosed with a fracture of the third lumbar vertebra and contusion of the left kidney. He was discharged on 19 May 2006.

Medical evidence was disputed. The Government relied on an extract stating that an X-ray on 6 May 2006, two days before the incident, had already revealed a lumbar vertebra fracture, and that his condition appeared “similar” after an X-ray on 9 May 2006. The prison hospital recorded a transverse process fracture and left kidney contusion but no bruises or scratches. It could not provide information about his care before 8 May 2006.

The applicant’s complaint was received by the Internal Security Office of the State Police on 17 May 2006, and criminal proceedings for exceeding official authority began on 2 June 2006. A forensic expert concluded on 19 September 2006 that the lumbar fracture was moderately severe and could have been caused by a blunt object on 8 May 2006, but a fall against a solid object could not be excluded. The applicant could not identify the officers from photographs; the officers denied excessive force. A witness, S.Š., said he saw two or three officers enter the applicant’s cell and kick “something,” and heard groaning. The first investigation closed in October 2006, accepting the officers’ account. The deputy chief prosecutor quashed that decision in January 2007, finding the investigation superficial and requiring scene inspection, verification of statements, and expert clarification on whether the injury pre-dated 8 May 2006.

A second expert report in March 2007 stated that the applicant could have remained mobile after the fracture and that the injury might have pre-dated 8 May 2006. The investigation closed again, but the chief prosecutor quashed it in June 2007, citing failure to properly verify the officers’ evidence at the scene, failure to consider S.Š.’s evidence, and failure to question other detainees. In the third round, the scene was visited, S.Š. was questioned again, and fourteen detainees were questioned; some had heard noise and shouts. The investigation closed on 24 April 2009, finding discrepancies in the applicant’s accounts, no corroboration of chest or head injuries, and the possibility that the fracture resulted from a fall against a hard object, matching the officers’ version. The prosecutor upheld that decision in May 2009, finding no offence and that force had complied with the Law on Police. The applicant did not appeal further, and the prosecution later said the time-limit had expired.

**Summary of *A and B v. Georgia* (Application no. 73975/16)**

The case of *A and B v. Georgia* concerns a complaint lodged by two Georgian nationals, A (the mother) and B (the son), regarding the state's failure to protect their daughter and mother, C, from domestic violence, resulting in her death, and the subsequent lack of an effective investigation. The application, submitted to the European Court of Human Rights on 16 September 2016, alleges violations of Articles 2 (right to life) and 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention.

The facts center on C, who was born in 1994. In 2011, at age seventeen, she was kidnapped for marriage by D, a twenty-two-year-old police officer. Though the marriage was never registered, C cohabited with D until June 2012, enduring regular physical and psychological abuse fueled by his jealousy. Even after leaving while pregnant, C and her family remained targets of D's threats and violence. He repeatedly invoked his status as a police officer and his connections within law enforcement to intimidate them. The family reported some of the most violent incidents but feared broader reporting.

A critical incident occurred on 31 August 2013, when D assaulted C at her parents' home over child support. Police officers, who were D's acquaintances, responded. They interviewed C in D's presence, allowed him to mock and threaten her, and coerced her into signing a report that minimized the attack as a "minor family altercation." One officer told her that wife-beating was commonplace and warned her not to waste police time. C subsequently filed a criminal complaint with the public prosecutor's office, detailing the abuse and D's threats to kill. The prosecutor interviewed C, D, and one officer, but accepted D's written undertaking to cease abuse and decided not to launch a criminal investigation.

Between 2011 and 2014, numerous witnesses confirmed D's pattern of using his official position to abuse C, including flaunting his service pistol and making threats. On 5 July 2014, C complained to the General Inspectorate of the Ministry of the Interior about further assaults. During an interview on 25 July 2014 regarding these complaints, she reiterated the systematic abuse. Shortly after leaving, D stalked and fatally shot her five times with his service pistol in a public park.

Following C's murder, D was convicted of premeditated murder and sentenced to eleven years. Separately, the first applicant filed complaints against the law enforcement authorities for failing to protect C. A criminal case was opened into the police officers' negligence, but it stalled. A civil action against the Ministry of the Interior and the Chief Public Prosecutor's Office resulted in a judgment on 24 July 2015, finding a causal link between the authorities' inactivity and C's death. The court awarded damages, citing a breach of the obligation to respond effectively to discrimination and failure to take measures to protect C's life.

The case before the European Court of Human Rights focuses on whether the respondent State failed to fulfill its positive obligations to protect C from lethal domestic violence and to conduct an effective investigation, potentially influenced by gender-based discrimination.

The case concerns Vegotex International S.A., a Belgian company based in Antwerp, and complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention arising from tax-recovery proceedings. In 1995 the tax authorities rectified Vegotex’s 1993 tax return, disallowing deductions linked to a stock-exchange transaction and investment costs, and imposed a 50% penalty. After its administrative objection was rejected in 2000, Vegotex brought court proceedings in December 2000 seeking to set aside the penalty. Meanwhile, on 24 October 2000, the tax authorities served a “demand for payment interrupting the limitation period,” expressly stating that it was not aimed at enforcing the disputed tax debt but only at interrupting the limitation period.

In 2004 the Court of First Instance largely upheld the assessment and penalty, reducing the penalty to 10% only as regards investment costs. Vegotex appealed, arguing that the State’s right to recover the 1993 tax was time-barred. It relied on Court of Cassation case-law from 2002 holding that a demand for payment in respect of a disputed tax debt did not validly interrupt the limitation period. While the appeal was pending, the Belgian legislature enacted the Miscellaneous Provisions Act of 9 July 2004. Section 49 provided that a demand for payment must be interpreted as interrupting the limitation period under Article 2244 of the Civil Code even where the disputed tax debt was not certain and of a fixed amount. The provision was intended to apply retrospectively to pending proceedings.

In 2007 the Antwerp Court of Appeal found that the 2000 demand did not interrupt the limitation period under Article 2244, and that section 49 was not applicable. However, it held that the limitation period had been suspended under Article 2251 of the Civil Code while the tax debt was contested, so recovery was not time-barred.

Vegotex appealed on points of law. The advocate-general at the Court of Cassation proposed substituting new grounds for those of the Court of Appeal: the limitation period had been interrupted by the demand under section 49, so Vegotex’s ground of appeal was inadmissible for lack of interest. Vegotex received the submissions on 5 March 2009 and filed a memorandum on 9 March 2009. It argued that if the Court of Cassation substituted its own grounds, it would breach Article 6 by depriving Vegotex of any opportunity to challenge the new grounds. It also said that objections remained, including that retroactive application of section 49 violated Article 6, and that these should be debated before lower courts.

On 13 March 2009 the Court of Cassation followed the advocate-general’s approach. It held that section 49 was not interpretative but had to be applied retrospectively in accordance with the legislature’s intention. The demand of 24 October 2000 therefore interrupted the limitation period, and recovery was not time-barred. The contested decision had a proper legal basis in the new ground, so Vegotex’s appeal was inadmissible for lack of interest.

The alleged Article 6 § 1 violations were therefore: (1) legislative intervention during pending judicial proceedings, through retrospective application of section 49, affecting the outcome; (2) breach of the right of access to a court and the adversarial principle because the Court of Cassation substituted its own grounds for those of the Court of Appeal, allegedly preventing Vegotex from effectively challenging the new basis for the decision; and (3) failure to comply with the reasonable-time requirement, given proceedings from the mid-1990s until 2009.

In *Kiril Zlatkov Nikolov v. France*, the applicant was a Bulgarian national convicted in France in connection with an international prostitution ring. He lodged two applications with the European Court of Human Rights in 2011 and 2012. The Court gave notice of the case to the French Government in respect of complaints under Article 5 § 3 (prompt judicial review of detention), Article 14 read in conjunction with Article 6 § 1 (discrimination in fair-trial rights), and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy). Other complaints were declared inadmissible.

The investigation began in 2009 into an international prostitution ring. Telephone interceptions authorised by the Chambéry liberties and detention judge captured two conversations on 4 September 2009 that appeared to incriminate the applicant. A judicial investigation was opened on 2 October 2009 for living on the earnings of prostitution as part of an organised gang, human trafficking as part of an organised gang, and criminal conspiracy. An arrest warrant was issued on 28 July 2010 and later converted into a European arrest warrant. The applicant was arrested in Germany and handed over to the French authorities at 11:45 a.m. on 16 December 2010. He was brought before the Strasbourg public prosecutor and immediately placed in administrative detention. He first appeared before the investigating judge at 10:56 a.m. on 20 December 2010, when he was placed under formal investigation. At about 5 p.m. that same day, the Lyons liberties and detention judge interviewed him and remanded him in custody. The nearly four-day period between his transfer to France and his first appearance before a judge was central to the Article 5 § 3 complaint.

Although the alleged offences were classified as serious crimes, the interviews and confrontations during the investigation were not video-recorded, relying on an exception in the seventh paragraph of Article 116-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for organised crime. On 17 June 2011 the applicant applied to the Investigation Division of the Lyons Court of Appeal to have various procedural steps declared void, including the detention order, interviews and confrontations, and telephone interceptions. He also submitted preliminary rulings on constitutionality concerning Articles 64-1 and 116-1. On 6 September 2011 the Investigation Division dismissed most of his application and referred the constitutional questions to the Court of Cassation. On 14 September 2011 he appealed on points of law, relying on Articles 5 § 3, 6 § 1 and 14 of the Convention and the constitutional principle of equality.

On 18 January 2012 the Court of Cassation referred the constitutional questions to the Constitutional Council. On 6 April 2012 the Constitutional Council declared the seventh paragraphs of Articles 64-1 and 116-1 unconstitutional because they infringed equality, but the abrogation was prospective only, applying to persons questioned or interviewed after publication of the decision. On 10 May 2012 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It held that the constitutional ruling did not benefit him retroactively; that he had not been questioned in police custody; and that the absence of video recording of his interviews by the investigating judge did not violate his Convention rights because he had legal assistance, could review the transcripts, request corrections, and challenge his statements. It also held that only the person concerned could complain about the lack of video recording of others’ questioning. The Article 13 complaint concerned the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy for these matters. The applicant was convicted and ultimately released in June 2015 after serving his sentence.

**Case: Ferhatović v. Slovenia (Application no. 64725/19), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, Judgment of 7 July 2022 (final 14 November 2022).**

The case concerned the seizure of copper wire from the applicant, Mr Sebastjan Ferhatović, and the police’s decision to hand part of it to Company E, the alleged victim of theft. The applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention that this amounted to an unlawful interference with his property.

In February 2009, police investigating burglaries at Tobačna Street in Ljubljana, in which copper cable was stolen from Company E, noticed the applicant and others unloading what appeared to be copper wire into the applicant’s garage. On 8 February 2009, following a search order, police seized eight large canvas bags containing mostly copper wire from the applicant’s address. A seizure certificate was issued to the applicant. Police later concluded that the wire in three of the bags matched the dimensions of cables stolen from Company E.

On 24 April 2009, without a court order, police handed those three bags over to Company E under section 110(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, which permits items to be delivered to an injured party before the end of criminal proceedings only if they “without doubt” belong to that party and are not needed as evidence. The remaining five bags were returned to the applicant in May 2009.

In April 2010, police filed a criminal complaint against the applicant for concealment, alleging he accepted and hid copper wire knowing it came from a crime. Charges were lodged in December 2011, but the prosecution withdrew them in November 2012, and the criminal proceedings were discontinued in December 2012.

In January 2013, the applicant asked the District Court for the return of the three bags. He was informed that they had already been given to Company E. He then brought a civil claim against the State for EUR 13,750, the alleged value of the wire. He claimed he collected waste metals and had stored the wire for over two years to sell in larger quantities. He relied on section 224 of the Criminal Procedure Act, under which seized items should be returned to the owner or holder if criminal proceedings are discontinued and no confiscation order is made.

The domestic civil courts dismissed his claim. Although the Local Court noted that the conditions for returning the wire to Company E under section 110(1) may not have been met, it found that the police had acted with reasonable care and diligence, so their conduct was not unlawful. The Higher Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the applicant had failed to prove ownership of the wire and therefore could not have suffered compensable damage, even if the police conduct had been unlawful. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court later refused further review.

Before the European Court, the applicant argued that the police had unlawfully deprived him of the three bags by handing them to Company E without a court order or proof of ownership, and that the domestic courts’ refusal of compensation left him without redress. The Court examined the case under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It found that the handover had interfered with the applicant’s possession of the wire and that the domestic authorities had failed to comply with the strict statutory condition that the items “without doubt” belong to the injured party. The Court concluded that there had been a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and awarded the applicant compensation.

In the European Court of Human Rights case *Gerasyutin and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 23698/20 and 3 others), the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 29 September 2022. The case concerned four applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates in 2020 and 2021. The Ukrainian Government was given notice of the applications. The applicants’ common complaint was that criminal proceedings against them had been excessively long and that Ukrainian law provided no effective domestic remedy for that delay. The relevant facts were set out in an appended table.

The first applicant, Oleg Vladyslavovych Gerasyutin (born 1969), represented by Maksym Igorovych Bezukh, lodged application no. 23698/20 on 25 May 2020. His criminal proceedings began on 25 September 2012 and ended on 26 November 2019. They therefore lasted 7 years, 2 months and 2 days and passed through three levels of jurisdiction.

The second applicant, Sergiy Oleksiyovych Butenko (born 1983), represented by Sergiy Oleksandrovych Kulbach, lodged application no. 53149/20 on 25 November 2020. His proceedings started on 22 November 2016 and ended on 24 May 2021. Their total duration was 4 years, 6 months and 3 days across two levels of jurisdiction.

The third applicant, Igor Mykolayovych Bidun (born 1968), lodged application no. 27783/21 on 21 May 2021. His criminal proceedings began on 21 February 2009 and ended on 18 November 2020. The total length was 11 years, 8 months and 29 days across three levels of jurisdiction. The judgment was rendered in his absence and served on him at a later date, a fact relevant to the procedural history and the overall duration of the case.

The fourth applicant, Viktor Ivanovych Chernyak (born 1947), represented by Andriy Bogdanovych Romanyuk, lodged application no. 30696/21 on 4 June 2021. His criminal proceedings began on 10 February 2009 and were still pending at the time of the application. They had therefore lasted more than 13 years, 6 months and 9 days and had involved three levels of jurisdiction.

These facts are central to the alleged violations. The applicants did not complain about the substantive outcome of the criminal proceedings as such; rather, they alleged that the duration of those proceedings was unreasonable and that no effective remedy existed in domestic law to address the delay. In Convention terms, these complaints engage Article 6 § 1, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and Article 13, which guarantees an effective remedy for arguable Convention violations. The durations range from approximately four and a half years to more than thirteen and a half years, with most cases passing through multiple levels of jurisdiction. One case was still pending, and one involved a judgment rendered in absentia. These features form the factual basis for the applicants’ claims of excessive length and lack of effective redress. The provided excerpt records the procedural background and the applicants’ complaints, but it does not include the Court’s full legal reasoning or final disposition. It states that the Court deliberated on 8 September 2022 and delivered the judgment on 29 September 2022, which is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

**Mickovski v. North Macedonia** (ECtHR, Fifth Section, judgment 24 March 2022; final 5 September 2022; applications nos. 39107/18 and 39726/18) concerned the alleged violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The applicant, Vlado Mickovski, a Macedonian citizen born in 1964, lived in Vraneshtica and had operated a registered bailiff practice in Kichevo since registering with the Chamber of Bailiffs in 2006. He applied both as a natural person and on behalf of his bailiff practice as a legal person.

The key facts began on 3 February 2011, when the Gostivar Court of First Instance opened a criminal investigation against the applicant for negligence in the performance of his duties as a bailiff. The allegation concerned the alleged double enforcement of a pecuniary claim. On 11 April 2011, the Chamber of Bailiffs ordered the suspension of his bailiff practice as a compulsory measure under section 60(2) of the Enforcement Act. The Minister of Justice appointed a deputy bailiff, M.D. from Struga, to carry out necessary activities during the suspension. Income from services provided by the deputy bailiff on behalf of the applicant was credited to the applicant’s practice, except for certain fees charged by the deputy.

On 22 June 2011, the Constitutional Court rejected as res judicata the applicant’s request for an abstract constitutionality review of section 60(2). On 21 November 2011, after the criminal investigation was terminated for lack of evidence, the Chamber lifted the suspension. The relevant suspension period was therefore from 11 April to 21 November 2011.

The applicant subsequently sued the State and the Chamber under the Obligations Act, seeking compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage caused by the suspension. He claimed approximately EUR 10,418 for actual damage, including employee salaries and office maintenance costs; approximately EUR 23,845 for loss of income; and approximately EUR 15,450 for harm to reputation.

On 2 March 2016, the Kichevo Court of First Instance granted the claim against the State for EUR 10,418 in actual loss, relying on an expert report, employment-suspension decisions, bank statements, utility bills and a services agreement. It dismissed the non-pecuniary claim, finding that the applicant had neither been convicted nor fined, and found no need to examine the claim against the Chamber. On 10 November 2016, the Gostivar Court of Appeal accepted the established facts but overturned the judgment and dismissed all claims. It held that the State could not be liable in the absence of wrongful conviction or imprisonment under sections 549 and 553 of the Criminal Proceedings Act. On 17 May 2018, the Supreme Court upheld that judgment. The applicant also made several requests between April and December 2011 and on 17 January 2018 to initiate disciplinary proceedings against the public prosecutor and judge involved in the criminal investigation; no such proceedings were initiated.

The relevant legal framework included the Obligations Act’s general compensation provisions, the Criminal Proceedings Act’s compensation rules limited to unjustified deprivation of liberty or conviction, and the Enforcement Act. At the time, section 60(2) allowed suspension of a bailiff’s practice after a criminal investigation was opened relating to official duty. A later 2016 amendment provided that suspension could occur only if an indictment had been confirmed.

The alleged violation was that the temporary suspension of the applicant’s bailiff practice, following a criminal investigation that was eventually terminated for lack of evidence, together with the domestic courts’ refusal to award compensation, interfered with his rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The ECtHR gave notice to the Government only of that complaint and declared the remainder of the applications inadmissible.

The case of *Šilović v. Serbia* (Application no. 32883/08) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 8 November 2016 by a Committee of the Third Section. The applicant, Goran Šilović, was a Serbian national born in 1952 who lived in Belgrade. He lodged his application against Serbia on 19 March 2008. The case primarily concerned the length of civil proceedings and the availability of an effective domestic remedy for that delay.

The key domestic facts relevant to the alleged violation are as follows. On 10 June 2002, the applicant filed a claim with the former Supreme Military Court in Belgrade seeking payment of certain benefits. At some point thereafter, the Supreme Military Court ceased to function and its jurisdiction was taken over by the Supreme Court of Serbia. On 10 August 2007, the Supreme Court rejected the applicant’s claim. The applicant received that judgment on 2 October 2007. The proceedings therefore lasted approximately five years and four months from the initial filing to the applicant’s receipt of the final decision. The case was decided at one final-instance level after the transfer of jurisdiction from the military court to the Supreme Court.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that these proceedings had been excessively long, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time. The central facts for that complaint are the date the claim was filed, the date of the final rejection, and the period of delay attributable to the domestic authorities. The transfer of jurisdiction from the former Supreme Military Court to the Supreme Court appears to have contributed to the duration of the proceedings. There is no indication in the provided excerpt that the applicant was responsible for significant delay. The applicant also complained, under Article 13 of the Convention, that he lacked an effective domestic remedy in respect of the excessive length of the proceedings. The relevant fact supporting that complaint is that the Supreme Court’s decision of 10 August 2007 was final, leaving no further ordinary domestic avenue through which he could seek relief for the delay.

Procedurally, the application was communicated to the Serbian Government on 18 December 2014. The Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee of the Court. After considering that objection, the Court rejected it. The Committee was composed of Judges Pere Pastor Vilanova, Branko Lubarda, and Georgios A. Serghides, with Fatoş Aracı as Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 11 October 2016 and adopted the judgment on 8 November 2016.

Case: **Lings v. Denmark** (Application no. 15136/20) concerns a Danish retired physician, Mr Svend Lings, convicted under Article 240 of the Danish Penal Code for assisted suicide and attempted assisted suicide. He complained that his conviction violated Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, arguing he had merely provided general information about suicide.

Lings, born in 1941, practised as a physician until 2010. Around 2015, he founded “Physicians in Favour of Euthanasia” and prepared an online guide, “Medicines suited for suicide.” It contained a detailed suicide procedure, a list of about 300 common pharmaceuticals, doses, combinations, caveats, and advice on ensuring death, including combining medication with a plastic bag over the head and a rubber band around the neck. Publishing the guide was lawful in Denmark.

In February 2017, in a radio interview, Lings said he had assisted a patient with a terminal pulmonary condition to die by administering Fenemal. The Patient Safety Authority reported him to police for violating section 240 and withdrew his medical licence, meaning he could no longer prescribe medication. He was charged with two counts of assisted suicide and one count of attempted assisted suicide.

Count 1 concerned an attempted assisted suicide on 23 March 2017. A, who had neurological diseases, wanted to commit suicide. Lings spoke and emailed with A and asked a co-defendant to prescribe Fenemal for A, knowing A would use it for suicide; Lings could not prescribe it himself after losing his licence. The attempt failed.

Count 2 concerned B, who was paralysed after a stroke, no longer found life worth living, and wanted to die. Lings visited B and advised him how to commit suicide according to his guide. He also discussed procuring pills with another person. B’s former wife later contacted Lings; a supply was obtained, and B died in May 2017. The Supreme Court found Lings had procured medications for B knowing they were intended for suicide, although Lings denied personally providing them.

Count 3 concerned C, an 85-year-old woman with many infirmities but not seriously ill. She wished to die and had already procured pills herself. Between 17 July and 6 August 2018, she exchanged at least nine emails with Lings. He asked what medication she had, confirmed it was “excellent,” recommended the general guide, helped her find it, and advised combining the medication with a plastic bag over her head, stating: “If you are able to go through with it, you will be 100% certain. Remember in that case that it is necessary to put a rubber band around the neck.” C was found dead on 10 August 2018 with a plastic bag over her head.

The Supreme Court upheld convictions on all three counts and imposed 60 days’ suspended imprisonment. The majority held that Lings’ advice to C was specific and significant assistance, not exempt because it was based on a lawful general guide, and found no Article 10 breach. A minority would have acquitted on count 3, finding that he merely passed on information already publicly available, did not encourage suicide, and that Article 10 protected giving and receiving information. Lings maintained that his conviction violated Article 10.

**Case of Gloveli v. Georgia (Application no. 18952/18)**

The case concerns an unsuccessful judicial candidate’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that she had no effective access to a court to challenge the refusal to appoint her to a judicial post. The applicant, Marina Gloveli, a Georgian national, was a practising lawyer with over twenty years’ experience and had previously served as a judge in the Tbilisi Court of Appeal from 1999 to 2005. She had applied unsuccessfully for judicial positions six times.

The relevant events arose from a judicial competition announced by the High Council of Justice (HCJ) on 18 October 2017. Gloveli applied for a vacant appellate court judgeship. The HCJ admitted her to the competition, interviewed her, and assessed her using score sheets. On 20 January 2018, she was notified that her application had been rejected because she did not meet the minimum competency score. She later obtained the individual score sheets of the HCJ members.

On 2 February 2018, Gloveli appealed to the Supreme Court’s Qualifications Chamber, a body created by 2017 amendments to the Courts Act to review HCJ decisions refusing judicial appointments. She alleged that the decision was arbitrary and discriminatory. In support, she submitted a recording of a televised statement by N.J., a non-judicial member of the HCJ, who claimed that several HCJ members had favoured “protégé” candidates and arbitrarily lowered the scores of other candidates. She argued that the very low scores she received indicated such bias.

On 6 February 2018, the Qualifications Chamber declared her appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that because Gloveli had failed to achieve the minimum competency score, her candidacy had never been put to a vote before the HCJ. Therefore, the precondition under section 35(12) of the Courts Act was not met, and the HCJ had not issued a formal “decision refusing appointment” capable of being challenged under section 354. The Chamber further stated that it did not have “full jurisdiction” to review the facts of the case, and its decision was final and not appealable.

The background included a prior constitutional complaint brought by Gloveli and others. They alleged that the Courts Act provided no court jurisdiction over judicial appointment disputes. After amendments effective 10 March 2017 allowed HCJ appointment refusals to be appealed to the Qualifications Chamber, the Constitutional Court on 7 April 2017 rejected the complaint, finding that the new remedy resolved the access-to-court issue. The Constitutional Court also held that judicial appointments fell within the right of access to public service under Article 29 of the Georgian Constitution and required fair procedure and judicial protection under Article 42. It emphasised that HCJ decisions must be subject to judicial control to prevent arbitrary, unsubstantiated, or biased refusals.

The alleged violation was therefore that, despite the new statutory appeal mechanism, the Supreme Court’s restrictive interpretation denied Gloveli any judicial review of the HCJ’s scoring and refusal. The key issue was whether excluding candidates who fail the minimum competency threshold from appealing to the Qualifications Chamber breached the right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1. The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that the applicant had been denied access to a court to challenge the allegedly arbitrary and discriminatory refusal of her judicial appointment.

In *P.C. v. Ireland* (Application no. 26922/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 1 September 2022, final on 1 December 2022. The applicant, P.C., an Irish national born in 1940, had made Pay Related Social Insurance contributions and qualified for the State Pension (Contributory) (“SPC”) at age 66 in February 2006. He received approximately €230 per week.

In March 2011, the applicant was convicted of sixty counts of sexual assault and fourteen counts of rape. He was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment, with the final three years suspended, and expected release in March 2020. Under section 249(1)(b) of the Social Welfare Consolidation Act 2005, persons undergoing imprisonment or detention in legal custody were disqualified from receiving benefits under Part 2 of the Act, including the SPC. As a result, his pension payments ceased when he was imprisoned.

The applicant alleged that this disqualification left him practically destitute. His only income was a prison gratuity, initially €18.90 per week and later reduced to €11.90 because age-related ailments and a wrist injury prevented him from doing prison work. He claimed he had no money for extra food, personal clothing or small electronic appliances, and that the stoppage would cost him over €100,000. He further noted that prisoners with private pensions or other income could receive funds lodged into their prison accounts, whereas his contributory State pension was stopped.

In 2013, the applicant issued proceedings against the State. He sought a declaration that the impugned provision was unconstitutional and incompatible with the Convention, damages, and an injunction requiring payment of his pension. He invoked Articles 3, 5, 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and sought a declaration under section 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003 together with compensation.

Evidence before the High Court showed that the SPC is non-means-tested; about 30–40 prisoners had their SPC payments stopped each year; the average annual cost of maintaining a prisoner was approximately €65,000; and some prisoners in the applicant’s age group worked in prison for €4.50 per week.

The High Court dismissed the case in April 2016. It held that the contributory SPC was not a property right for constitutional or Convention purposes, emphasising the partly tax-funded nature of social welfare and the State’s need for flexibility, with a wide margin of appreciation in economic and social matters. It rejected the discrimination claim, finding the comparison with private pensions not like-for-like and noting that the rule applied to all social welfare benefits. Withholding the SPC was considered objectively rational and proportionate because the benefit was intended for basic living costs, while imprisonment met essential needs. The High Court also rejected the Convention claims under Articles 3, 5, 6 and 8, and found no breach of Article 14.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained that the statutory disqualification interfered with his rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, discriminated against him contrary to Article 14 read with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and denied him an effective remedy under Article 13 because the Supreme Court allegedly did not determine his Convention complaints or award adequate redress. The Court gave notice of those complaints and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible.

In *Razgon and Others v. Russia*, the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered a judgment on 10 November 2022 concerning six applications (nos. 5386/20 and 5 others) lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention. The applications were introduced between 10 January and 2 March 2020. The applicants were ten individuals: Leonid Razgon, Danil Levenstam, Pavel Merkulov, Kirill Chirkin, Renaldo Dzhindzholiya, Maksim Balabin, Dmitriy Znamenskiy, Mariya Isayeva, Mikhail Rives-Korobkov, and Polina Anisimova. In *Vool and Toomik v. Estonia* (ECtHR, 2022), two Estonian nationals complained under Article 14 read with Article 8 about Estonia’s statutory rule that remand prisoners may not receive unsupervised long-term family visits, while convicted prisoners generally may. Both applicants were held on remand and denied long-term visits by prisons relying on section 94(5) of the Imprisonment Act, despite prosecutorial restrictions on contacts later being lifted or relaxed.

The first applicant, Mr Vool, was suspected of extortion and membership in a criminal organisation and was remanded in April 2014. Initially, the Prosecutor General imposed complete isolation and restricted visits, correspondence and telephone use. In September 2014, these restrictions were partly lifted to allow short-term visits, letters and calls with his cohabiting partner, mother and brother; in November 2014, all additional restrictions were lifted. However, Tallinn Prison refused his repeated applications from February 2015 for long-term visits with his partner, citing section 94(5). Between September 2014 and November 2016, he had 51 short visits—32 with his partner—along with 351 telephone calls, correspondence and parcels. He was convicted in September 2016 and became eligible for long-term visits after the judgment took effect in November 2016. Domestic administrative courts dismissed his challenge. In 2016, the Supreme Court refused to declare section 94(5) unconstitutional, finding the ban proportionate. It emphasised the risk that unsupervised visits could facilitate witness manipulation or evidence destruction, referring to the criminal organisation’s support networks and use of threats and violence. It also found different treatment of remand and convicted prisoners justified because convicted prisoners could no longer obstruct ongoing proceedings. In 2017, it upheld the refusal.

The second applicant, Mr Toomik, was suspected of handling large quantities of narcotics and was remanded in December 2011. The prosecutor initially prohibited short and long visits, correspondence and telephone use with next of kin. In August 2012, the Court of Appeal allowed correspondence, telephone use and short-term visits; in December 2013, it lifted all restrictions. From September 2012 to June 2014, he had 46 short visits—35 with his partner and 8 with his daughter—plus letters, calls and parcels. He was convicted in May 2013; the conviction became final in June 2014, after which he could seek long-term visits. In April 2014, Tartu Prison refused his request for a long-term visit with his partner under section 94(5). The administrative court awarded €500 compensation, but the appellate court reversed. In October 2017, the Supreme Court upheld the refusal as proportionate, citing the charges, repeated convictions and risk of influencing proceedings; it noted his remand status ended less than a month after the refusal. A dissenting judge argued the ban was disproportionate because all additional restrictions had already been lifted in December 2013.

In 2019, in an unrelated case, the Supreme Court en banc declared section 94(5) unconstitutional *ex nunc*, holding that it did not allow separate proportionality assessment of long-term visit bans from detention justification and disproportionately interfered with family life in practice. It gave limited retroactive effect. Both applicants sought reopening; the Supreme Court refused in 2020. The alleged violations concerned discriminatory and unjustified interference with family life: although the applicants had short visits, calls and letters, they were categorically denied unsupervised long-term family visits solely because they were remand prisoners. Domestic courts initially justified this by risks to criminal proceedings, but the later constitutional decision criticised the absence of individualised balancing.

**CASE OF D.S. AND OTHERS v. HUNGARY**  
(Applications nos. 41602/17 and 9 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, First Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 31 March 2022. The applications were lodged against Hungary under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on various dates shown in the appended table. The Hungarian Government were given notice of the applications. The central complaint was the excessive length of the applicants’ pre-trial detention. Some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The appended table lists ten applicants and the relevant detention facts. **D.S.** (born 1992), represented by Karsai Dániel András, Budapest, was detained in three periods: 12 June 2014 to 12 December 2014 (6 months 1 day); 22 December 2014 to 11 August 2015 (7 months 21 days); and 19 August 2015 to 15 October 2015 (1 month 27 days). He was also under house arrest from 12 to 22 December 2014 and from 15 October 2015 to 26 May 2017. His application was introduced on 31 May 2017.

**Zsanett Horváth** (born 1989), represented by Karsai Dániel András, was detained from 6 September 2017 to 9 April 2021, a total of 3 years 7 months 4 days. Her application was introduced on 2 February 2021. **Viola Mező** (born 1990), same representative, was detained from 5 April 2019 and remained in detention at the time of application, exceeding 2 years 10 months 4 days; the application was introduced on 29 January 2021. **János Norbert Bodnár** (born 1991), represented by Kiss Dominika Szilvia, was detained from 31 January 2019 and remained in detention, exceeding 2 years 11 months 25 days; application introduced 11 February 2021. **Máté Mihály Gémes** (born 1988), represented by Karsai Dániel András, was detained from 2 June 2019 and remained in detention, exceeding 2 years 8 months 7 days; application introduced 11 February 2021.

**Anita Király** (born 1978) and **Csaba Király** (born 1970), represented by Kiss Dániel Bálint, were each detained from 25 January 2018 to 5 October 2021, a total of 3 years 8 months 11 days. Their applications were introduced on 26 March 2021. **László Szilárd Bedő** (born 1978), represented by Kiss Dominika Szilvia, was detained from 25 April 2019 to 21 May 2021, a total of 2 years 27 days; application introduced 25 March 2021. **József Horváth** (born 1975), same representative, was detained from 21 June 2019 to 17 June 2021, a total of 1 year 11 months 28 days; application introduced 12 April 2021. **Melinda Kolompár** (born 1988), represented by Karsai Dániel András, was detained from 18 July 2018 and remained in detention, exceeding 3 years 6 months 22 days; application introduced 16 April 2021.

These facts were relevant to the alleged violation of the right to liberty and security, in particular the requirement under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that detained persons be entitled to trial within a reasonable time or to release pending trial. The applicants complained that their pre-trial detention was excessively long. The case therefore concerned lengthy, and in several instances ongoing, pre-trial detention, multiple separate detention periods, and one instance of house arrest. The Court’s judgment addressed those complaints, while some applicants also raised additional Convention issues.

The case *Tetik and Others v. Turkey* (Application no. 25885/19 and 37 others) is a 2022 European Court of Human Rights judgment concerning 38 Turkish applicants. The central complaint was the non-enforcement of final domestic court decisions awarding them compensation against Yüksekova Municipality, despite earlier findings by Turkey’s Compensation Commission that the non-enforcement breached their right to a fair trial.

Between 2008 and 2010, the Yüksekova Civil Court of First Instance ruled in three sets of civil proceedings that the applicants were owed compensation for receivables arising from labour agreements with the Municipality. The judgments became binding. However, the Municipality did not pay the awarded sums, except for the compensation in the first set of proceedings brought by the applicants in application no. 26026/19. This persistent failure to execute the judgments formed the core of the applicants’ complaints.

In 2011, 2012 and 2013, the applicants applied to the ECtHR, alleging non-enforcement of domestic judicial decisions in their favour. In 2013, the Court declared those applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies. It held that the applicants should first use the Compensation Commission established under Law no. 6384, which provided a domestic remedy for complaints including non-enforcement of domestic decisions.

In 2014, the Compensation Commission awarded the applicants non-pecuniary damage for the excessive length of the proceedings. It also transmitted its decision to the Municipality and requested that the judicial decisions be executed. Despite this, the underlying compensation awards remained unpaid. The Commission’s decision thus acknowledged a fair-trial breach but did not secure actual enforcement of the judgments. In the same year, the applicants applied to the Constitutional Court, complaining that the Municipality had still failed to enforce the relevant judicial decisions despite the Compensation Commission’s decision.

While those Constitutional Court applications were pending, in July 2018 a provision was added to Law no. 6384. It empowered the Compensation Commission to deal with applications pending before the Constitutional Court concerning, among other things, non-enforcement complaints. Later in 2018, the Constitutional Court found the applicants’ applications inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, namely the Compensation Commission. This left the applicants in a procedural cycle: the ECtHR had sent them to the Compensation Commission; the Commission found a breach but did not enforce payment; the Constitutional Court then sent them back to the same Commission. On unspecified dates, some minor parts of the receivables were paid to some applicants, but the essential awards remained unexecuted.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore: final and binding domestic judgments in the applicants’ favour; prolonged non-payment by a public municipality; a domestic compensation remedy that only awarded non-pecuniary damages and requested execution without success; and subsequent inadmissibility decisions that failed to provide effective redress. The alleged violations concern the continuing non-enforcement of judicial decisions, implicating the right to a fair trial in its execution-of-judgments aspect and, in substance, the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions, because the applicants were deprived of the compensation they had been awarded. The Government’s objection to examination by a Committee was rejected. The Court deliberated on 22 February 2022 and delivered judgment on 15 March 2022.
