text:
**Metalla and Others v. Albania** (Applications nos. 30264/08, 42120/08, 54403/08 and 54411/08) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided on 16 July 2015. Four applications were lodged against Albania by nine Albanian nationals between 13 June and 8 October 2008. The central complaint was that final domestic administrative decisions recognizing their inherited property rights and awarding compensation for occupied land had not been enforced.

The applicants’ claims arose from decisions of local property restitution commissions. In each case, the commission recognized the applicants’ inherited title to property, restored part of it physically, but found that the remaining portion was occupied. For that occupied portion, the applicants were to receive compensation “in one of the ways provided for by law.” The key facts were as follows:

- **Application no. 30264/08 (Metalla):** On 9 August 1995, the Shijak Commission recognized title to 1,020 sq. m of land. Of this, 747 sq. m were restored; the remaining 272 sq. m were occupied and subject to compensation. The decision remained unenforced.
- **Application no. 42120/08 (Bushati):** On 8 February 1995, the Shkodër Commission recognized title to a two-storey building and 500 sq. m of surrounding land. The building was to be restored, while the occupied 500 sq. m plot was to be compensated. The applicant had previously brought actions against a third party but discontinued them. A third party apparently built unauthorized constructions on the land. The decision remained unenforced.
- **Application no. 54403/08 (Metalla and Others):** On 12 May 1994, the Shijak Commission recognized title to 5,527 sq. m. Of this, 5,000 sq. m were restored; the remaining 527 sq. m were occupied and subject to compensation. The decision remained unenforced.
- **Application no. 54411/08 (Metalla and Others):** On 13 August 2007, the Durrës Commission recognized title to 65,000 sq. m. Of this, 60,000 sq. m were restored; the remaining 5,000 sq. m, consisting of arable land, roads and channels, were occupied and subject to compensation. The decision remained unenforced.

The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already covered by well-established case-law, particularly **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania** (2012). Relevant domestic law and practice had also been described in **Ramadhi v. Albania** (2007). Albania later approved property valuation maps in 2013 and 2014, but the compensation mechanism remained incomplete.

Council of Europe material showed that the Committee of Ministers had repeatedly examined Albania’s failure to enforce final judicial and administrative decisions awarding compensation in lieu of physical restitution. In 2014 and 2015, the Committee welcomed Albania’s action plan and draft law but noted that deadlines under the pilot judgment had not been met and that a functioning compensation mechanism was still needed.

The alleged violations concerned the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions. The applicants could neither obtain possession of the occupied portions of their property nor receive the compensation to which those decisions entitled them. This raised complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the execution of final decisions and access to a fair hearing, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The case formed part of a structural problem in Albania involving the failure to compensate owners for occupied property.

**Case: Goulandris and Vardinogianni v. Greece (Application no. 1735/13)**

The applicants, Georgios Goulandris and Christianna Vardinogianni, are Greek nationals and a married couple living in London. On 17 September 2003 they purchased a coastal plot in Korakia near Kranidi, Argolida. On 5 October 2004, an urban-planning inspection found that two stone walls had been built on the property without the required building permit: one wall was 119.5 metres long and 1.9 metres high, and the other was 99.4 metres long and 1.8 metres high. The inspection report named the first applicant as owner, declared the constructions unlawful, and imposed an administrative construction fine of EUR 18,102 plus an annual preservation fine of EUR 1,802 for each year the walls remained.

The report was received by an employee of the applicants on 4 November 2004. No complaint was filed against the fines. In March 2005, after a reduction, the first applicant paid EUR 7,414.78, covering the construction fine and stamp duties. In November 2011, the municipality issued notices to recover preservation fines of EUR 5,379.80 from each applicant as co-owners. On 29 November 2011, the first applicant paid the total amount of EUR 10,759.60.

Separately, the inspection report was sent to the public prosecutor in January 2005. In July 2006 a bill of indictment was issued against both applicants. On 17 September 2008, the one-member Nafplio Criminal Court of First Instance convicted them of jointly and intentionally constructing the walls without a permit. The building permit relied on authorised only a 0.6-metre-high fence. The court sentenced them to seven months’ imprisonment, taking into account the offence’s severity and their personal circumstances, and converted the sentence into a fine of EUR 10 per day.

The applicants appealed, arguing that the administrative fines were criminal in nature and had become final when paid, so the later criminal prosecution and conviction breached the ne bis in idem principle under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the Convention, as well as domestic res judicata rules. On 16 December 2011, the Nafplio Court of Appeal dismissed that plea. It held that administrative acts do not have res judicata effect for criminal courts; that the construction and preservation fines were not criminal sanctions but administrative measures aimed at ensuring compliance with urban-planning law; and that the fines did not amount to a final criminal conviction. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction and sentence, suspending the sentence for three years.

On 4 June 2012, the applicants appealed on points of law, again complaining of a breach of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. On 11 September 2012, the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It reasoned that res judicata under Article 57 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies only to final criminal judgments; that criminal sanctions are imposed by criminal courts for criminal justice purposes, while administrative sanctions exercise an administrative function; and that administrative sanctions cannot be considered criminal punishment under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. Therefore, the cumulative imposition of administrative fines and criminal sanctions for the same unlawful constructions did not violate ne bis in idem.

The applicants later submitted the walls for regularisation under Law no. 4178/2013, completed in October 2017. Before the European Court of Human Rights, they alleged that Greece had violated their right not to be tried and punished twice for the same offence under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, focusing on whether the administrative fines constituted criminal penalties and whether the later criminal conviction duplicated punishment for the same conduct.

**Case: Ferhatović v. Slovenia (Application no. 64725/19)**

The case concerns the seizure of three large bags of copper wire from the applicant, Mr Sebastjan Ferhatović, a defendant in criminal proceedings, and the police’s decision to hand the wire over to Company E., from which the wire had allegedly been stolen. The applicant complained that this handover breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention (protection of property).

In February 2009, police noticed three men pushing an unlicensed white Mazda van while the applicant drove behind in a car. They later learned that an identical Mazda had been seen near two burglaries at Tobačna Street in Ljubljana on 5 and 6 February 2009, where a large quantity of copper cable was stolen from Company E. Police then saw several people unloading copper products and wire from a Mazda van into the applicant’s garage; the van resembled one captured on surveillance footage from the burglary scene.

On 8 February 2009, acting under an investigating judge’s search order, police searched the applicant’s address and seized eight large canvas bags containing mostly copper wire. A seizure certificate indicated the wire had been seized from the applicant. Police later concluded that the dimensions of wire in three of the bags corresponded to cables stolen from Company E. On 24 April 2009, without a court order, police gave those three bags to Company E. The remaining five bags were returned to the applicant on 11 May 2009.

In April 2010, police filed a criminal complaint accusing the applicant of concealment under Section 217(1) of the Criminal Code—accepting peeled copper cables knowing they came from a crime. Damage to Company E was estimated at about EUR 23,000. Charges were lodged in December 2011, but in November 2012 the prosecutor withdrew them, and the criminal proceedings were discontinued in December 2012.

In January 2013, the applicant asked the Ljubljana District Court to return the three bags, each allegedly weighing around 800 kg. The court replied that they had been handed to Company E in April 2009.

The applicant then sued the State for EUR 13,750, the alleged value of the unreturned wire. He claimed he collected and sold waste metals and had stored the wire for over two years to sell in larger quantities at a higher price. He relied on Section 224 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which requires seized items to be returned to their owner or holder if criminal proceedings are discontinued and no confiscation occurs.

In the civil proceedings, Company E’s representative said the wire had later been sold and the money given to the company director. He could not confirm the wire came from the stolen cables because it had been cleaned and cut and was not examined when collected. A police officer testified that the seized wire certainly originated from the kind of cables stolen from Company E, but such cables were available everywhere. He said police considered the wire belonged to Company E due to the chain of events, but the bags were not weighed and no court order authorized the handover.

Domestic courts ultimately dismissed the applicant’s compensation claim. A local court found he had not proved ownership of the wire with certainty and that, although the wire likely came from the stolen cables, it could not reliably be established that it belonged to Company E. It suggested the conditions for return to Company E under Section 110(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act had therefore not been met. However, it held that the police had acted with due care and reasonable grounds, so their conduct was not unlawful. The Higher Court dismissed the appeal, finding no compensable damage because the applicant had not proved ownership. The Supreme Court dismissed his further appeal, and the Constitutional Court declined to consider his constitutional complaint.

The key legal issue was whether the police’s handover of the copper wire to Company E without a court order and without conclusive proof of ownership violated the applicant’s property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Alleleh and Others v. Norway** (App. no. 569/20, ECtHR, 23 June 2022) concerned an Article 8 complaint about Norway’s expulsion of the first applicant, Ms Neima Aden Alleleh, and the alleged effects on her family life with her Norwegian husband and their four Norwegian children.

The first applicant arrived in Norway in September 2001 and applied for asylum, falsely claiming to be Somali and giving a detailed but untrue personal history. Her asylum application was rejected in 2002 and her appeal dismissed in 2003. She remained in Norway and later sought revision of the refusal, again giving false information and presenting false identity papers. In 2002 she met the second applicant, a Norwegian citizen. They married in April 2004 while she had no lawful residence. She then applied for residence based on the marriage, repeating the same false Somali identity and history. She was granted temporary residence in September 2005, renewed in 2006. In 2007 she was granted Norwegian citizenship based on her false Somali identity.

The couple had four children: born in 2005, twins in 2009, and another child in 2013. In 2014, during a police inquiry into persons claiming to be Somali, the first applicant was questioned and maintained her false identity. Later that year she was warned about possible withdrawal of citizenship and expulsion. In December 2014 she finally disclosed her correct Djiboutian identity and origin. In June 2015 her Norwegian citizenship was withdrawn. In November 2015 she was expelled with a two-year re-entry ban. Her administrative appeal was dismissed in March 2016.

The Immigration Appeals Board considered the children’s best interests but found expulsion proportionate. It noted that the second applicant could adequately care for the children in Norway, or the family could move to Djibouti, where the first applicant had family and cultural ties. It treated her repeated unlawful conduct, general deterrence, and respect for immigration law as decisive.

The applicants challenged the expulsion in court. In 2017 the Oslo City Court ruled for the Government. It found the first applicant’s violations gross, repeated, and intentional over about 13 years. It accepted that separation from their mother would sadden the children but held this was not disproportionate or exceptional. The Borgarting High Court reversed in 2019, finding the expulsion invalid as disproportionate for the children. It emphasized that the mother was the primary caregiver, the children were more attached to her than to the father, the father worked long hours, two twins were somewhat vulnerable, and the youngest was closely attached to the mother. It found a risk that separation would impose an unusually heavy burden and that the father might not manage sufficiently.

The Supreme Court reversed in December 2019 and upheld the expulsion. It held that because the first applicant’s residence had been precarious and obtained through false information, expulsion would generally breach Article 8 only in “exceptional circumstances” or where it imposed an “unusually great burden.” It stressed the seriousness of her long-running fraud, that family life was established while her status was precarious, that there was no insurmountable obstacle to family life in Djibouti, that the children were generally well-functioning, and that the two-year ban was limited. It found no extraordinary circumstances and declared the expulsion valid.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged that the expulsion violated Article 8 by disrupting their family life. The Court ultimately found no violation of Article 8.

In *Anatoliy Yeremenko v. Ukraine*, the applicant was a Ukrainian journalist working for the weekly newspaper *Dzerkalo Tyzhnya*. On 12 March 2005 it published his article “Black triad: nothing else matters in the case,” later posted on the newspaper’s website. The article alleged systemic corruption in the Donetsk commercial courts. It described case no. 27/37, in which a judgment had allegedly been based on a forged copy of a guarantee letter even though the original was in a criminal case file, and said the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal had relied on that copy. It also described an alleged scheme under which clients paid a law firm, cases were assigned to the “right judge,” and a “black triad” ensured the desired outcome. The article quoted Ch., a company director, who claimed an organised group operated in the Donetsk Regional Commercial Court and the Donetsk Commercial Court of Appeal, citing case no. 8/55 and a letter to a parliamentary sub-committee. No judge was named in the article.

On 7 April 2005 six judges from those courts applied for “preventive measures and securing of evidence.” They claimed the article contained false, negative statements damaging their honour, dignity and professional reputation, including references to an “organised group,” the “pressure of the system,” cases being distributed to the right judge, and the “black triad.” They asked for the article’s removal from the website. On 8 April 2005 the Voroshylovsky District Court ordered the editorial board to remove the article from the newspaper’s website pending defamation proceedings. The decision merely restated the claimants’ request and cited Article 152 § 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, without real reasoning. On 26 August 2005 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the removal, reasoning that internet information was publicly accessible and difficult to control, so removal was the only protective measure. It acknowledged that the legal basis cited was erroneous because no defamation claim had yet been lodged, but refused to quash the ruling. The Kyiv Court of Appeal later rejected the applicant’s cassation appeal on 15 January 2008. The article was removed by 18 August 2005.

Defamation claims were filed in April and August 2005. The judges sought retraction and damages, arguing that the article undermined judicial authority. On 20 October 2005 the Petrovskyy Local Court partly allowed the claim. It found paragraphs 8 and 9 defamatory and untrue. It held that statements about an “organised group” and a corrupt scheme amounted to accusations of criminal offences, which under the presumption of innocence required proof by a court verdict; no such proof existed, and the security service had found no evidence of an organised group. The court rejected the applicant’s reliance on the Press Act because Ch. was not a State official and his letter was not an official document. It treated the applicant and Ch. as co-authors, but considered the applicant less culpable, though he had failed to verify the information. The court ordered the newspaper to publish a retraction and the applicant to pay UAH 333 in non-pecuniary damages per claimant plus legal and court fees, amounting to about EUR 331 and EUR 430.51; Ch. was ordered to pay UAH 1,000 per claimant. The Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the merits on 27 January 2006, reducing fees, and the Kyiv Court of Appeal rejected the final cassation appeal on 5 November 2007 without detailed reasoning. The applicant complained under Article 10 that the interim removal order and the defamation judgments violated his freedom of expression, particularly in relation to public-interest allegations of judicial corruption.

In *Armani Da Silva v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 5878/08), the applicant, Patricia Armani Da Silva, is the cousin of Jean Charles de Menezes, a Brazilian national shot dead by Metropolitan Police officers at Stockwell Underground Station on 22 July 2005. She complained under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the decision not to prosecute any individual officer after his death breached the procedural obligation to conduct an effective investigation capable of establishing the facts, determining whether lethal force was justified, and identifying and, if appropriate, punishing those responsible.

The shooting occurred during Operation THESEUS 2, launched after the failed London bombings of 21 July 2005. Intelligence indicated that suspect Hussain Osman was linked to an address at Scotia Road. Commander McDowall’s plan was to place surveillance at Scotia Road, follow anyone leaving, and arrest them safely once firearms officers from SO19 were in place. Commander Cressida Dick was the Designated Senior Officer; DCI C was Silver/ground commander; Trojan 80 and 84 advised. However, the SO19 unit was not deployed at Scotia Road in time. Briefings portrayed suspects as deadly suicide bombers and omitted warnings that not everyone leaving was a bomber or that the KRATOS lethal-force policy applied only as a last resort with positive identification.

On 22 July, Menezes left 17 Scotia Road and was followed by surveillance officers. Because SO19 were not in position, he was not stopped. He took a bus; surveillance officers described him variously as a possible likeness and later not identical, but the control room apparently believed he was Osman. He entered Stockwell station. Dick ordered a stop, then directed SFOs to prevent him boarding a train; Code Red was declared. On the train, Menezes was restrained and pinned down by officers; two SFOs, Charlie 2 and Charlie 12, shot him multiple times. He was entirely unconnected to the bombings.

After the shooting, the IPCC referral was delayed and the Anti-Terrorist Branch initially controlled the scene. The two SFOs made statements about 36 hours later, after learning Menezes was innocent; some details proved false or doubtful. The surveillance log was allegedly altered, and CCTV recordings had gaps. The IPCC Stockwell One Report identified serious failings: inadequate briefings, failure to implement McDowall’s strategy and deploy SO19, command and communication problems, delayed IPCC access, and concerns about the log. It referred possible criminal liability of the SFOs, Dick, Trojan 84, and others. The IPCC later decided no disciplinary action had a realistic prospect. The CPS decided not to prosecute any individual: it found insufficient evidence to disprove the SFOs’ genuine belief in self-defence, and other errors did not meet criminal thresholds. It prosecuted the Office of the Commissioner as employer under health and safety law.

The applicant’s Article 2 complaint therefore concerned whether this lack of individual prosecution meant the investigative and prosecutorial response was not effective. The Grand Chamber ultimately held that there had been no violation of the procedural aspect of Article 2.

In *Vékony v. Hungary*, the applicant, László Vékony, a Hungarian national born in 1950, ran a family grocery in Sopron. From 1994 the family sold excise goods, including alcohol and tobacco, initially under his mother’s excise licence. Tobacco retail represented about one-third of the family business. Vékony obtained a shop-keeping licence in 1999, qualified as a trader and shop manager in 2001, and registered as an excise-goods trader in 2005.

In September 2012 Parliament enacted Act no. CXXXIV of 2012 on the Repression of Smoking of the Youth and on Tobacco Retail. The final version entered into force on 1 July 2013. It converted tobacco retail—previously carried on at around 42,000 retail points—into a State monopoly exercised through ND Zrt. Retailers were to be licensed through a concession tender advertised on 15 December 2012. Applicants had to submit business plans reflecting public-health policy, especially limiting minors’ access to tobacco. New tobacco shops required separate entrances, dark windows, and a limited range of other goods. The application deadline was 22 February 2013. Existing tobacco retailers had no privilege in the tender, which was decided by ND Zrt; about 6,800 licences were granted nationwide.

Vékony applied on 4 February 2013 for a concession for the family enterprise and amended his application on 20 February 2013. The Government later said his application was very brief and lacked an adequate business plan. Vékony claimed he was never given information about how the tender was assessed. On 23 April 2013 he was informed that he had not obtained a concession. The decision contained no reasons, no score on the 120-point assessment sheet, and was not subject to legal remedy. His family had to stop selling tobacco by 14 July 2013. Wholesalers were obliged to buy back outstanding stock. The remaining business became unprofitable and was wound up. No compensation was available for former tobacco retailers who lost part of their livelihood after failing to obtain a concession. Vékony said he had considerable difficulty supporting his family, including a minor son.

He alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 alone and read together with Article 14 of the Convention. He argued that the loss of his tobacco retail licence amounted to an unjustified deprivation of possessions in discriminatory circumstances. He claimed that others in comparable situations—and even some who had never previously sold tobacco—received concessions, and that this difference could only be explained by political adherence. He also noted that some successful tenderers obtained multiple concessions for several selling points.

The Constitutional Court admitted related complaints on 14 January 2014 but dismissed them on the merits in decision no. 3194/2014 (VII.14.). It held that long-standing tobacco retail activity did not create acquired possessions or constitutionally protected legitimate expectations. Before 1 July 2013, the applicants had no specific tobacco retail licence; the excise licences were non-transferable, revocable permits and not possessions. The legislation did not prevent them from applying for concessions. Although the right to pursue an entrepreneurial activity was protected, it was not absolute. The restriction pursued public health aims, was proportionate, and fell within the State’s wide margin of appreciation.

The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 October 2013 and communicated to the Government on 15 November 2013. The case was decided by the Second Section on 13 January 2015 and became final on 1 June 2015.

text:
The case *Jovanović v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 21497/13 and 21907/13) originated in two applications lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 March 2013 by Mr Radoslav Jovanović, a Serbian national born in 1943 and living in Niš. He complained about the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in his favour against socially/State-owned companies, because enforcement proceedings were stayed while the debtors underwent privatisation-related restructuring. The applications were communicated to the Serbian Government on 16 September 2014. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The first set of enforcement proceedings concerned the company “FŽV Želvoz a.d. Smederevo.” On 28 April 2010 the applicant brought an enforcement action before the Smederevo Court of First Instance. On 15 December 2010 that court ordered direct enforcement of an outstanding invoice based on a credible document. On 15 June 2011, however, the Privatisation Agency ordered the debtor’s restructuring as part of the privatisation process. Consequently, on 25 October 2011 the enforcement proceedings were stayed. The applicant appealed on 3 November 2011, but his appeal was rejected on 10 February 2012. On 21 March 2013 he urged the court to continue enforcement. On 7 June 2013 the court informed him that the debtor was still undergoing restructuring and that enforcement could not continue. It appears the applicant did not appeal against that decision.

The second set concerned “Vagonka a.d. Niš.” On 11 January 2010 the applicant brought an enforcement action before the Niš Commercial Court. On 29 January 2010 that court ordered direct enforcement of an outstanding invoice. However, on 4 November 2009 the Privatisation Agency had already ordered the debtor’s restructuring. On 4 February 2010 the enforcement proceedings were stayed because the debtor was undergoing restructuring. The applicant did not appeal, and that decision became final on 17 February 2010. On 20 March 2013 he urged the court to continue enforcement. On 22 March 2013 the court informed him that the debtor was still undergoing restructuring and that enforcement could not continue.

The relevant domestic law referred to cases such as *R. Kačapor and Others v. Serbia*, *Vlahović v. Serbia*, *Crnišanin and Others v. Serbia*, *Adamović v. Serbia*, and *Marinković v. Serbia*, which set out the Serbian framework on enforcement and the restructuring of socially/State-owned companies.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are that the applicant held final enforcement orders in his favour, but those orders remained unexecuted for years. In both cases, the debtors were socially/State-owned companies undergoing restructuring ordered by the Privatisation Agency. The domestic enforcement courts stayed the proceedings and later refused to continue them solely because restructuring was ongoing. In the first case, the applicant appealed the stay but was unsuccessful; in the second, he did not appeal the stay. The applicant’s repeated requests in 2013 to continue enforcement were also unsuccessful. The case therefore concerns complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, concerning the right of access to court and execution of final judgments, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, concerning protection of property, arising from the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions against State/socially-owned debtors in restructuring.

**Case: Nadtochiy v. Ukraine (Application no. 32899/13)**  
The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) examined a Ukrainian applicant’s complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, alleging unlawful and disproportionate deprivation of her property.

The applicant, Ms Zinayida Sergiyivna Nadtochiy, was granted a plot of land by the Sumy Town Council on 4 June 2008, free of charge, for the construction of a house as part of the privatisation process. She planned to begin construction within two years but did not do so, instead using the land primarily for gardening.

In August 2011, the Deputy Prosecutor of the Sumy Region brought civil proceedings against the applicant, seeking to have her title to the land declared void. This became the first set of proceedings. The prosecutor argued that the designated use of the land contradicted the town’s general zoning plan and violated the town’s right to construct apartment buildings on the land. On 9 February 2012, the Sumy Regional Court of Appeal gave a final decision rejecting the prosecutor’s action. The court found that the prosecutor had not challenged the Council’s decision of 4 June 2008 and that the applicant’s use of the land for gardening was not a reason to deprive her of it.

In February 2012, the prosecutor brought a second action, this time against both the Council and the applicant. The second action relied on similar grounds but additionally argued that the Council’s decision of 4 June 2008 had not been based on a detailed zoning plan or specific construction limits. On 25 July 2012, the Kovpakivskyy District Court of Sumy allowed the prosecutor’s second action. That judgment was ultimately upheld by the Higher Specialised Court of Civil and Criminal Matters on 18 January 2013. The courts declared the Council’s decision of 4 June 2008 and the applicant’s title to the land void, and the land was returned to the municipality. The courts held that, when transferring the land to the applicant, the Council had failed to develop a detailed zoning plan and specific construction limits, thereby failing to serve the interests of the community.

Before the European Court, the applicant complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that she had been deprived of her land for no legitimate purpose, since no apartment building had been erected on it. She also alleged a violation of the principle of legal certainty, arguing that the second set of proceedings—which led to her deprivation—had re-examined matters already determined with final effect in the first set of proceedings. Finally, she complained that no compensation had been paid to her, even though it had been the fault of the authorities that she was deprived of the land.

The key alleged violation therefore concerned the annulment of her land title and the return of the plot to the municipality. The central factual issues were the original free transfer of land for housing construction, the applicant’s failure to build and use of the land for gardening, the prosecutor’s two successive challenges, the final rejection of the first claim, the later success of the second claim based on deficient zoning and construction planning, and the absence of any compensation. The Court was thus called upon to assess whether the interference with the applicant’s property was lawful, pursued a legitimate aim, was proportionate, and struck a fair balance, including with respect to procedural certainty and compensation.

In *Qerimi and Canaj v. Albania* (Applications nos. 12878/10 and 74858/12), the European Court of Human Rights, First Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 8 September 2016. The case concerned two Albanian nationals who complained that the Albanian authorities failed to enforce final decisions of property restitution and compensation commissions, thereby depriving them of the effective benefit of their inherited property rights. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already covered by well-established case-law, particularly *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The first applicant, Qerimi, relied on a decision of the Durrës Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties dated 1 November 2002. That decision recognised, among others, the applicant’s inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 8,000 square metres. Because the plot was occupied, the Commission decided that the applicant and other heirs would be compensated in kind with an equivalent plot of land. The key fact for the alleged violation was that this final decision was not enforced: the applicant did not receive the equivalent land, and the compensation award remained unrealised.

The second applicant, Canaj, relied on a decision of the Fier Commission dated 23 November 2001. That decision recognised, among others, the applicant’s inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 1,121 square metres. Of that area, 598 square metres were restored to the applicant. However, the remaining 523 square metres were occupied, so the Commission ordered that the applicant and other heirs be awarded compensation in the amount of 251,040 Albanian Lek. As with Qerimi, the central factual complaint was that this final compensation decision was not enforced, leaving the applicant without the compensation due.

Procedurally, the applications were lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention. On 20 December 2013, they were communicated to the Albanian Government, which was represented by the State Advocate’s Office. The applicants failed to submit claims for just satisfaction within the time-limit set by Rule 60 of the Rules of Court, meaning the Court did not make any award under Article 41.

The legal context was well known to the Court. Relevant domestic law and practice had been described in cases such as *Ramadhi v. Albania*, *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*, and *Sharra and Others v. Albania*. Council of Europe materials had also been referred to in *Sharra and Others*, *Metalla and Others*, *Siliqi and Others*, and *Karagjozi and Others*. These cases concerned Albania’s systemic difficulties in enforcing final property restitution and compensation decisions.

The applicants’ alleged violations arose primarily under Article 6 §1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair trial and includes the right to execution of final binding decisions, and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects property. They argued that the State’s failure to enforce the commissions’ final decisions rendered their property rights illusory and deprived them of compensation. Applying its well-established case-law, the Court found violations of Article 6 §1 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Because no just satisfaction claims were submitted in time, no separate compensation was awarded by the Court.

In *A and Others v. Iceland*, four Icelandic nationals—parents A and B and their children X (born 2008) and Y (born 2011)—complained about child-protection proceedings that culminated in the parents’ loss of custody. The case concerned alleged violations of the right to respect for private and family life, particularly the authorities’ handling of sexual-abuse allegations after the father was acquitted in criminal proceedings.

In October 2015, X’s school notified the municipal child protection committee that X had described domestic violence and drawn a picture suggesting her father had touched her and her brother on their “private parts.” X reportedly said the drawing showed “the penis which entered my vagina.” The father was arrested, questioned, and held in pre-trial detention for four days. At Children’s House interviews, X initially did not disclose abuse, but later described her father touching her private parts with his penis and finger and applying cream. Y initially denied any touching, but after being placed in foster care in September 2016, his foster mother reported urinary and bowel problems and said Y had disclosed that his father applied cream to his genitals and told him not to tell his mother. In a later interview, Y said his father rubbed his penis, applied cream, and inserted a finger into his rectum.

Child-protection authorities found the family home disordered and the children badly cared for. The mother was receiving treatment for depression and anxiety. The children were temporarily placed outside the home, then returned to their mother after the father moved out. In February 2016, X was placed in temporary foster care. In September 2016, Y was also removed and placed in the same foster home after concerns that he was having extensive contact with the father. A psychologist later concluded that the mother lacked sufficient capacity to have custody, citing neglect, possible violence, emotional problems, and her failure to protect the children, including by allowing contact with the father and pressuring X to change her statement. Reports in 2017 found neither parent fit to care for the children, and the committee sought custody deprivation.

In March 2017, the father was indicted for sexual offences against X and Y. On 22 November 2017, the Reykjanes District Court acquitted him of all charges, finding guilt not established beyond reasonable doubt. The prosecution did not appeal.

In the separate custody proceedings, a court-appointed psychologist in May 2018 found the children’s accounts consistent and credible, the parents’ custody capacity lacking, and both children genuinely afraid of their father. The children had bonded with their foster parents and wished to remain there. The Reykjavik District Court granted custody deprivation in June 2019. The Court of Appeal overturned that decision in November 2019, finding the committee had failed to reconsider the case after the acquittal and that less intrusive measures had not been properly explored. On 10 March 2020, the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeal and deprived both parents of custody. It held that the criminal acquittal was not determinative in child-protection proceedings, which must be assessed under the children’s best interests. It found the children had severe fear of the father and that the mother, despite efforts, could not provide adequate protection, partly because she intended to remain married to the father and the children mistrusted her.

The children remained in permanent foster care, with limited contact for the mother and no contact for the father. The applicants’ surviving complaints concerned Article 8, especially whether the custody deprivation and contact restrictions were justified and whether the authorities improperly relied on abuse allegations after the father’s acquittal.

**Case Summary: Bahtić v. Bosnia and Herzegovina**  
*(Application no. 4034/22, European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, judgment of 27 October 2022)*

The case originated in an application lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Anfisa Bahtić, born in 1973, was represented by Kenan Buljubašić, a lawyer practising in Zenica. The respondent Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were given notice of the application. The application was introduced on 11 January 2022 and was decided by a Committee of the Fourth Section composed of Judges Armen Harutyunyan, Jolien Schukking, and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar.

The central factual basis of the applicant’s complaint was the non-enforcement of a domestic decision issued in her favour. Specifically, on 9 October 2020, the Zenica Municipality Court issued a decision in the applicant’s favour against the City of Zenica. Despite that domestic court decision, the authorities did not enforce it. The relevant period of non-enforcement began on 23 November 2020. By the time the case was examined by the European Court of Human Rights, the enforcement proceedings remained pending. The appended table records the length of the enforcement proceedings as “more than 1 year(s) and 9 month(s) and 23 day(s),” with no end date because enforcement had not been completed.

The applicant therefore complained to the European Court that the domestic decision issued in her favour had not been enforced. This failure to enforce a final or enforceable domestic decision formed the core of her alleged violation. In the Convention context, such a complaint ordinarily concerns the obligation of the State to ensure that judicial decisions are executed and to protect the applicant’s rights under the fair-trial guarantees and the right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions. However, the factual summary provided focuses primarily on the prolonged non-enforcement itself: a domestic court decision in the applicant’s favour against a public authority, the City of Zenica, remained unsatisfied for an extended period, and enforcement proceedings were still pending.

Procedurally, the Court, sitting as a Committee, deliberated in private on 6 October 2022 and adopted the judgment on 27 October 2022. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore limited but significant: (1) the applicant obtained a domestic decision in her favour on 9 October 2020; (2) the decision was against the City of Zenica, a public authority; (3) enforcement did not begin effectively or was not completed, with the non-enforcement period starting on 23 November 2020; (4) the enforcement proceedings were still pending at the relevant time; and (5) the applicant turned to the European Court on 11 January 2022, complaining that the domestic decision remained unenforced. The essence of the case is the State’s alleged failure to secure timely enforcement of a domestic court decision in the applicant’s favour.

In *Marina Aucanada Group S.L. v. Spain* (App. no. 7567/19, Third Section, judgment 8 November 2022), the applicant is a Spanish limited liability company. It complained under Article 6 § 1 ECHR that it had not been directly served with a summons in judicial administrative proceedings concerning annulment of a public call for tenders, despite being an identifiable interested party.

On 4 February 2015, the Port Authority of the Balearic Islands published a call for tenders for management of moorings at the old Port of Alcúdia. On 7 April 2015, the Alcúdia City Council brought judicial administrative proceedings before the High Court of the Balearic Islands, seeking annulment of the call because it allegedly infringed a 2004 agreement between the City Council and the Port Authority. The proceedings were admitted on 20 April 2015. The High Court requested the administrative file and ordered that it be provided to “any interested party” within five days, with nine days to appear as interested parties.

Meanwhile, on 5 May 2015, the applicant company submitted a tender. On 18 May 2015, its tender and three others were accepted for consideration. On 7 May 2015, following the High Court’s instructions and relying on section 49 of the Administrative Jurisdiction Law and section 59 of Law 30/1992, the Port Authority published a public notice (*edicto*) in the Official Gazette of the Balearic Islands, dated 27 April 2015, informing interested parties of the proceedings and inviting them to participate. None of the tenderers was directly served with a summons, either then or later. Press articles in 2015 and 2016 reported the proceedings and identified the applicant company as a tenderer; one article dated 8 June 2015 expressly linked the tender procedure to the City Council’s appeal.

The City Council later sought suspension of the tender as a precautionary measure. The Port Authority objected, noting that tenders had been opened and were under consideration, and added the relevant minutes to the file. On 18 May 2016, while proceedings no. 113/2015 remained pending, the Port Authority selected the applicant company’s tender as the most advantageous. On 31 March 2017, the High Court upheld the City Council’s claim and annulled the call for tenders and secondary acts because it violated prior undertakings. The applicant said it learned of the proceedings through the press and applied on 20 April 2017 to intervene and appeal.

The applicant appealed in cassation to the Supreme Court, arguing that identifiable interested parties had to be directly summoned. On 17 April 2018, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that publication of the *edicto* complied with section 49 and that a party acquiring a legitimate interest *ex post facto* could still appear; it did not examine the merits. A plea of nullity was rejected by the High Court on 14 June 2018 on the same basis. The applicant then lodged an *amparo* appeal, complaining that its right to be directly summoned and to a fair hearing had been breached because the authorities and courts knew its identity but failed to inform it of the pending proceedings, even though it had won the tender before judgment. On 18 December 2018, the Constitutional Court declared the *amparo* inadmissible for lack of constitutional relevance.

The alleged violation therefore concerns Article 6 § 1: whether Spain failed to ensure that the applicant company, as a known and identifiable interested party whose successful tender was later annulled, was directly summoned and given a real opportunity to participate in the administrative judicial proceedings. The domestic courts considered the published *edicto* sufficient; the ECtHR gave notice of the Article 6 § 1 complaints.

Case of Razgon and Others v. Russia is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, delivered on 10 November 2022. The case originated in six applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention: nos. 5386/20, 6001/20, 6789/20, 8737/20, 11553/20, and 12772/20. They were introduced between 10 January 2020 and 2 March 2020. The applicants are ten individuals: Leonid Abramovich Razgon, Danil Alekseyevich Levenstam, Pavel Andreyevich Merkulov, Kirill Vadimovich Chirkin, Renaldo Zaurovich Dzhindzholiya, Maksim Nikolayevich Balabin, Dmitriy Dmitriyevich Znamenskiy, Mariya Dmitriyevna Isayeva, Mikhail Yuryevich Rives-Korobkov, and Polina Vadimovna Anisimova. They were represented by Ernest Aleksandrovich Mezak, the Memorial Human Rights Centre, and Aleksey Nikolayevich Laptev.

All applicants were subjected to Russian administrative-offence proceedings. Each received a fine of RUB 10,000. Their final domestic decisions were rendered by the Moscow City Court on various dates in 2019. Specifically, the final decisions were: 12 November 2019 for Razgon and Levenstam; 30 July 2019 for Merkulov; 26 August 2019 for Chirkin and Dzhindzholiya; 24 October 2019 and 26 August 2019 for Balabin and Znamenskiy respectively; 8 November 2019 and 24 September 2019 for Isayeva and Rives-Korobkov respectively; and 30 August 2019 for Anisimova. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications.

The key alleged violation concerned the lack of impartiality of the tribunal. The applicants complained that in their administrative-offence proceedings the prosecuting party was absent. Because no representative of the prosecution participated in the hearings, the court was left to examine the case without an adversarial prosecuting presence. The applicants argued that this absence undermined the impartiality of the tribunal, contrary to the fair-trial guarantees of the Convention. They also raised other complaints under the Convention, but the central complaint was the tribunal’s alleged lack of impartiality due to the absence of the prosecuting party.

Procedurally, the Court’s Third Section, sitting as a Committee composed of Darian Pavli (President), Andreas Zünd, and Frédéric Krenc, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar, deliberated in private on 20 October 2022 and adopted the judgment on 10 November 2022. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The appended table provides the specific details of each application, including the applicants’ names, years of birth, representatives

**Halimi and Others v. Albania (Application no. 33839/11)**

**Judgment: 7 April 2016**

The case of *Halimi and Others v. Albania* concerns the failure of the Albanian authorities to provide compensation for property that was recognized as belonging to the applicants but which they could not physically recover.

**Key Facts:**

The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by nine Albanian nationals against the Republic of Albania. The central event occurred on 30 May 1995, when the Vlora Commission officially recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 10,000 square meters. This decision affirmed their legal ownership.

However, the recognition of their rights came with a critical caveat: the plot of land was already occupied by third parties. In accordance with Albanian law at the time, when property could not be returned in kind because it was occupied, the original owners were entitled to compensation. The law provided for specific methods by which this compensation should be determined and paid.

Despite the 1995 decision in their favour, the applicants never received any form of compensation for the land. The judgment notes succinctly that "to date, no compensation has been paid," a period spanning over two decades. This failure to provide compensation, despite a formal and binding administrative decision recognizing their entitlement, formed the basis of their complaint to the European Court.

**Legal Context and Proceedings:**

The applicants were represented by Mr S. Puto, a lawyer practising in Tirana. The Albanian Government was represented by its Agent, Ms A. Hicka. The application was communicated to the Government on 20 December 2013.

The Court noted that the underlying legal issue—the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions regarding property compensation—was already the subject of well-established case-law. It specifically referenced the leading case of *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania* (2012), among others like *Ramadhi v. Albania* and *Sharra and Others v. Albania*. These cases had extensively documented the systemic problem in Albania where individuals who had their property rights recognized were left in a legal limbo, unable to either recover their property or receive the compensation guaranteed by law.

The applicants in this case, like many others, had a final and enforceable decision from a domestic body confirming their right to compensation. The Government's prolonged failure to act upon this decision meant the applicants were deprived of their possessions without adequate redress. This situation constituted a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to the peaceful enjoyment of one's possessions. The Court’s judgment in this case was therefore a direct application of its prior findings, holding Albania responsible for failing to ensure the effective implementation of property compensation decisions and to provide a remedy for the affected individuals.

In **Tolmachev v. Estonia** (Application no. 73748/13), the applicant was an Estonian national, Kirill Tolmachev. On 17 September 2012, a police officer fined him EUR 80 in misdemeanour proceedings for breach of public order, namely breaking a glass panel of a bus shelter. The applicant contested the decision before the Viru County Court. He denied the act, challenged the assessment of witness statements, complained that the police had failed to present him to a witness for identification, and alleged that the police decision did not specify the local public-order provisions he had allegedly breached.

The County Court summoned the applicant to a hearing on 21 March 2013 at 12:30 p.m., stating that his participation was mandatory. The summons warned that under Article 126 § 2 of the Code of Misdemeanour Procedure, if a complainant failed to appear despite being notified of the obligation to participate, and the hearing was not adjourned, the court would refuse to examine the complaint. The applicant’s counsel, a police representative and witnesses were also summoned. The summons sent to the applicant’s known address could not be served personally on 4 February 2013 because he was absent; his mother refused to accept it and said he was living abroad. Counsel received the summons on 8 February 2013. On 20 March 2013, the County Court admitted the complaint and scheduled the hearing.

On 21 March 2013, the applicant did not appear. His counsel asked the court to examine the matter without him because he was abroad and his return date was unknown. The applicant’s father, present as a spectator, said the applicant would not return to Estonia within five years. The County Court refused to examine the complaint, issuing reasons on 2 April 2013. It found that the applicant had failed to inform the authorities of his new address, but concluded that because his father knew the hearing time and the applicant’s intention not to return, the applicant must have been aware of the hearing through his parents and counsel.

The court held that the case could not be examined without the applicant. A misdemeanour court had to hear the matter in full and verify the factual and legal basis of the police decision. The applicant had specifically complained that the police failed to present him for identification; interviewing him and presenting him to the witness were therefore important steps impossible in his absence. Adjournment would serve no purpose because he would not return within the one-month maximum adjournment period, and counsel had not requested an adjournment but examination without the applicant. The court relied on Article 126 § 2.

Counsel appealed, relying, inter alia, on Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention—the right to defend oneself through legal assistance of one’s own choosing. The receipt of the summons was not disputed. On 23 May 2013, the Tartu Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and upheld the first-instance ruling. It noted that under Article 126 § 1 the court could decide whether the complainant’s participation was necessary and that the County Court had given reasons why it was. It was unclear how the County Court could have remedied the alleged failure to present the applicant for identification without him. No further appeal lay against that ruling.

The applicant alleged that the refusal to examine his complaint because he was absent, even though his counsel was present, violated his right to a fair trial and his right to defend himself through legal assistance of his own choosing.

text:
M.T. and Others v. Sweden (ECtHR, First Section, App. No. 22105/18, 20 October 2022) concerned Sweden’s refusal to grant residence permits to a Syrian mother and her minor son in Syria based on family reunification with another son/brother who had subsidiary protection in Sweden. The applicants alleged that the refusal breached Article 8 (family life) and Article 14 read with Article 8 (discrimination), because the Temporary Act suspended family reunification for subsidiary-protection beneficiaries while refugees retained a more favourable regime.

The first applicant (M.T.) is the mother of the second (A.A.K.) and third (M.A.K.) applicants. The second applicant arrived in Sweden in March 2016 at age 15 and applied for asylum. In November 2016, the Migration Agency granted him a 13-month temporary residence permit as a person eligible for subsidiary protection under the Aliens Act and the Temporary Act, based on the security situation in Syria. It found no individual reasons for refugee status. His permit was extended in October 2017 for two years.

In February 2017, while the second applicant was still a minor, the first and third applicants applied at Sweden’s embassy in Khartoum for residence permits citing family ties to him. The third applicant, also a minor, additionally cited an eye injury requiring medical care, study plans, and reunion with brothers in Sweden. The first applicant’s husband/father lived in Saudi Arabia; several siblings were in Sweden, Germany, or Turkey.

In August 2017, the Migration Agency rejected the applications. It noted that under Chapter 5, section 3(4) of the Aliens Act, a parent of an unmarried child who is a refugee or otherwise in need of protection could normally receive a permit if the child had arrived in Sweden separately from both parents. However, under section 7 of the Temporary Act, that rule did not apply if the person in Sweden had a temporary residence permit as a subsidiary-protection beneficiary and had applied after 24 November 2015. Because the second applicant applied after that date and held subsidiary-protection status, the mother could not receive a permit. The third applicant’s application was rejected on the same basis and because no other grounds existed. The Agency found no breach of Sweden’s international commitments.

The Migration Court upheld the refusal in October 2017, and the Migration Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal in November 2017. The applicants relied on Article 8 alone and with Article 14. They argued that the Temporary Act had suspended their right to family reunification and that treating subsidiary-protection beneficiaries differently from refugees was discriminatory. The second applicant turned 18 in August 2018, after which he would generally no longer be eligible for reunification with parents or siblings.

The Temporary Act, in force from July 2016 to July 2019, was introduced after Sweden received about 163,000 asylum seekers in 2015. It reduced family reunification to EU minimum standards: refugees were limited essentially to the nuclear family, while reunification for subsidiary-protection beneficiaries was suspended. It contained a safety provision allowing a permit if refusal would breach an international convention. The preparatory works considered the restrictions compatible with Articles 8 and 14, reasoning that refugees generally have longer-lasting protection needs. UNHCR and the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights criticised the distinction and its impact on Syrians, most of whom received subsidiary protection. The case thus concerned whether this blanket temporary suspension and the differential treatment of subsidiary-protection beneficiaries breached the applicants’ family-life and non-discrimination rights.

text:
In *Atristain Gorosabel v. Spain* (Application no. 15508/15), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention. The applicant, Javier Atristain Gorosabel, a Spanish national, alleged that while held incommunicado he was denied a lawyer of his own choosing and was unable to communicate with his lawyer before and during police questioning, leading him to make self-incriminating statements that supplied evidence used for his conviction.

The case arose from an anti-terrorist investigation by the Audiencia Nacional concerning the Basque terrorist group ETA. On 29 September 2010, the Guardia Civil arrested the applicant. On 30 September 2010, investigating judge no. 2 of the Audiencia Nacional authorised his detention incommunicado to prevent frustration of the ongoing investigation, which primarily sought to locate explosives. The detention was ordered and supervised by a judge. Once authorised, the applicant was assigned State-funded legal aid. He was informed of his rights, including the right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself. However, because of the incommunicado regime, he could neither choose his own lawyer nor meet privately with the assigned legal-aid representative before being interviewed by police.

During the incommunicado detention, the applicant gave two statements to the Guardia Civil, both in the presence of the legal-aid representative. On 1 October 2010, he stated that he had “cooperated” with ETA, describing attempted kidnapping, verifying a businessman for possible assassination, and providing information about police officers so an attack could be planned. He also indicated a storage room where explosives were kept. A subsequent search there revealed explosives, detonators, USB keys, terrorist manuals, ammunition, and other material. On 3 October 2010, after again being informed of his rights, and despite his legal-aid representative’s opposition, he gave a second statement revealing a hidden firearm, cartridges, USB keys, and false licence plates. Those items were later found at his home. His legal-aid representative repeatedly tried to contact him but was told that communication was restricted because of the incommunicado detention.

The applicant was examined daily by a forensic doctor. He reported no mistreatment but claimed that the Guardia Civil had threatened to arrest his girlfriend if he did not cooperate. On 4 October 2010, he was brought before the investigating judge. He stated that his police statements had been obtained during five days of incommunicado detention and were therefore self-incriminatory. His incommunicado detention was then lifted, and he was able to appoint a lawyer of his own choosing.

On 16 April 2013, the Audiencia Nacional convicted him of membership of a terrorist group and possession of explosives, sentencing him to seventeen years’ imprisonment. The conviction was based essentially on seized computer material, explosives found at his home and at locations he had indicated, statements by co-defendants, witness evidence, and his silence at trial. The courts ruled out mistreatment and found that his statements had been given freely and voluntarily. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction on 18 March 2014. The Constitutional Court declared his *amparo* appeal inadmissible on 7 November 2014 for failure to justify its constitutional relevance.

The ECtHR complaint therefore focused on the impossibility of being represented by a lawyer of his own choosing and communicating with that lawyer before and during incommunicado detention. The applicant argued that this breached his fair-trial rights and tainted the self-incriminatory statements and derivative evidence used against him.

text:
**Case: Arnar Helgi Lárusson v. Iceland**  
**ECtHR, Third Section, Application no. 23077/19, judgment 31 May 2022 (final 10 October 2022).**

The applicant, Arnar Helgi Lárusson, is an Icelandic national born in 1976 who lives in Reykjanesbær. After an accident in 2002, he was left permanently paralysed from the chest down and uses a wheelchair for mobility.

In 2015, the applicant and an association of people with spinal injuries brought civil proceedings against the municipality of Reykjanesbær and its holding company, F., which owned one of the buildings. They challenged the lack of wheelchair access in two buildings housing municipal arts and cultural centres. They sought a declaratory judgment requiring accessibility improvements.

The first building, Duushús, was a three-storey arts and cultural centre made up of two adjoining houses built in 1877 and 1954–70, extensively renovated between 2006 and 2014. The applicant requested a wheelchair lift between floors, ramps between ground-floor galleries no steeper than 1:20 as required by building regulations, and changes to the main entrance threshold. The second building, 88 Húsið, was a two-storey former engine house built in 1963 and used as a municipal youth centre since 2004. The applicant requested a wheelchair lift between floors, ramps no steeper than 1:20 from the car park to the building and between rooms, and a designated disabled parking space within 25 metres of the entrance. He also sought ISK 1,000,000 (about EUR 7,300) in non-pecuniary damages.

The plaintiffs argued that the buildings did not comply with applicable building regulations and that the lack of access prevented the applicant and other wheelchair users from enjoying their private life on an equal basis with others, contrary to the Icelandic Constitution, the European Convention on Human Rights, and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD).

A court-appointed assessor found that Duushús had no lift between floors, a ramp between ground-floor halls with an incline of approximately 1:7 and a width of 96–161 cm, and a 51 mm threshold at the main entrance. At 88 Húsið, there was no lift between floors, no lift or ramp between the different halls, a ramp from the car park to the entrance with an incline of approximately 1:9, and no designated disabled parking space by the entrance.

On 24 November 2016, the Reykjanes District Court ruled in favour of the defendants. It found that access needed improvement but that the buildings did not violate the applicable building regulations because they had been built before those regulations took effect. The municipality was nevertheless under a legal obligation to work towards improving wheelchair access to public buildings and public service institutions. The court noted that the municipality had begun an accessibility initiative and held that municipalities had a margin of appreciation in prioritising such projects; separation of powers prevented courts from ordering specific action where authorities had discretion.

The plaintiffs appealed. Before the Supreme Court, they did not expressly rely on the Convention but referred to their earlier submissions and invoked equality and non-discrimination. On 25 October 2018, the Supreme Court upheld the lower judgment. It noted that the CRPD had been ratified but not incorporated into domestic law, so it could not be directly relied on, although domestic law should be interpreted harmoniously with international obligations where possible. It held that the municipality had complied with its legal duty to devise an accessibility strategy under legislation enacted with regard to international human rights obligations, including the CRPD, and had acted on that strategy. Disability matters had been transferred from the State to municipalities in 2010; municipalities were autonomous in matters entrusted to them by law and in the use of their funds, and had a wide margin of appreciation in prioritising improvements. The Supreme Court did not address the Convention or the equality and non-discrimination arguments.

The ECtHR gave notice to the Government only of the complaints under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention; the remainder of the application was inadmissible. The core alleged violations concerned the lack of wheelchair access to public cultural and social buildings and alleged discrimination in the enjoyment of private life and social participation.

In *Centroprom Holding AD Beograd v. Montenegro* (Application no. 30796/10), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 10 February 2022. The case originated in an application lodged under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by Centroprom Holding AD Beograd, a company, against Montenegro. The application was introduced on 10 May 2010. The applicant company was represented by Ms V. Čejović, a lawyer practising in Bar. The Montenegrin Government were given notice of the application.

The Court sat as a Committee composed of Lətif Hüseynov (President), Lado Chanturia and Arnfinn Bårdsen, judges, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. It deliberated in private on 20 January 2022 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment was final but remained subject to possible editorial revision.

The applicant company’s principal complaint was the excessive length of civil proceedings. It also raised other complaints under the Convention, although the provided extract does not identify those additional complaints or describe them in detail. The key facts relevant to the length complaint are set out in the appended table.

According to that table, the relevant starting point for the length of proceedings, or the date of entry into force of the Convention in respect of Montenegro, was 3 March 2004. The domestic civil proceedings ended on 2 April 2015. The total length of the proceedings was therefore 11 years and 1 month. The proceedings involved three levels of jurisdiction.

The fact that the Convention entered into force in respect of Montenegro on 3 March 2004 is significant for the Court’s temporal jurisdiction. In principle, the Court could examine the length of the civil proceedings only from that date onward, unless earlier periods were relevant as background. The table indicates that the relevant period for the excessive-length complaint was calculated from 3 March 2004 until the final termination of the proceedings on 2 April 2015. This produced a total duration of over eleven years across three judicial levels.

The application was lodged on 10 May 2010, while the domestic civil proceedings were still pending. The domestic proceedings continued for approximately another five years after the application was introduced, ending on 2 April 2015. Thus, the applicant company complained that the domestic courts had failed to decide the civil case within a reasonable time, as required by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. That provision guarantees, among other things, a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.

The provided judgment extract does not set out the underlying subject matter of the civil dispute, the specific procedural steps taken by the domestic courts, or the Court’s ultimate conclusions on the merits and just satisfaction. Rather, it focuses on the procedural history and the duration of the proceedings. The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the application was lodged on 10 May 2010; the relevant Convention period began on 3 March 2004; the civil proceedings ended on 2 April 2015; they lasted 11 years and 1 month; and they passed through three levels of jurisdiction. Those facts formed the basis of the applicant company’s complaint that the length of the civil proceedings was excessive and incompatible with the reasonable-time requirement under the Convention.

Armani Da Silva v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 5878/08) concerned the fatal shooting of Jean Charles de Menezes, the applicant’s cousin, by Metropolitan Police officers at Stockwell Underground Station on 22 July 2005. The applicant complained that the United Kingdom breached the procedural aspect of Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights because no individual police officer was prosecuted for the killing.

The shooting occurred amid heightened terrorism fears. After the 7 July 2005 London bombings and the failed 21 July attacks, police launched Operation THESEUS 2. Intelligence suggested a suspect, Hussain Osman, was staying at 21 Scotia Road. Menezes lived at 17 Scotia Road and left the same building on 22 July. Surveillance officers followed him because he resembled a suspect. Commander Cressida Dick, the Designated Senior Officer, intended that he be stopped and arrested. However, specialist firearms officers from SO19 were not deployed to Scotia Road in time. Menezes boarded a bus and then entered Stockwell station. Firearms officers, briefed that they might confront a suicide bomber, were ordered to stop him. On a train, they tackled and shot him multiple times; he was later found to be entirely innocent.

The IPCC conducted a major investigation, Stockwell One. It identified serious operational failings: late deployment of firearms officers, inadequate briefings that failed to caution officers about the KRATOS suicide-bomber policy, communication failures, and mistaken identification. It also noted post-incident problems, including delayed IPCC involvement, inconsistent police accounts, an altered surveillance log, and missing CCTV recordings, though it found no evidence of a cover-up. The investigation was extensive, taking nearly 890 witness statements and over 800 exhibits, and the family received regular briefings. The IPCC referred potential offences to the CPS, including murder, gross negligence manslaughter, misconduct in public office, and perverting the course of justice.

The CPS decided not to prosecute any individual officer. It concluded there was insufficient evidence to prove that the two shooting officers did not genuinely believe they were acting in self-defence against a suspected suicide bomber. Although some accounts were questionable, that did not provide a realistic prospect of a murder conviction. The CPS also found insufficient evidence to prosecute commanders or other officers for gross negligence manslaughter or other offences. Detailed Review Notes explained evidential difficulties, including the absence of contemporaneous records and inconsistent accounts. It instead prosecuted the Office of the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis under health and safety law.

The applicant argued that this decision not to prosecute breached the Article 2 procedural duty to conduct an effective investigation capable of identifying and punishing those responsible. The Grand Chamber examined whether the investigation and prosecutorial decision were independent, thorough, and reasonably reasoned. It emphasised that Article 2 does not guarantee a prosecution in every case; what matters is whether the investigation was capable of leading to accountability and whether the decision was based on adequate reasons.
