The case **Halimi and Others v. Albania** (Application no. 33839/11) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, First Section, sitting as a Committee. The judgment was delivered on 7 April 2016 and rectified on 26 April 2016. It originated in an application lodged under Article 34 of the Convention by nine Albanian nationals against Albania. The applicants were represented by Mr S. Puto, a lawyer practising in Tirana. The Albanian Government were represented by Ms A. Hicka of the State Advocate’s Office. The application was communicated to the Government on 20 December 2013.

The key facts concerned inherited property and the failure to pay compensation. On 30 May 1995, the Vlora Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 10,000 square metres. However, the plot was occupied. Because the land was occupied, the applicants were not to be given restitution of the actual property but were instead entitled to compensation in one of the ways provided by law. Despite this official recognition of their entitlement, no compensation had been paid to the applicants by the time the case was examined by the Court.

The applicants therefore complained about the Albanian authorities’ prolonged failure to provide the compensation owed to them. The essential factual basis for the alleged violation was that the applicants held a recognised legal entitlement to compensation for inherited property that was occupied, yet the State had failed for many years to honour that entitlement. This raised issues under the Convention, principally concerning the protection of property under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The case formed part of a broader line of Albanian cases involving the non-execution of final decisions or administrative acts granting property compensation.

The Court noted that the relevant domestic law and practice had already been described in earlier judgments, including **Ramadhi v. Albania**, **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania**, and **Sharra and Others v. Albania**. Relevant Council of Europe materials were also referred to in **Sharra and Others**, **Metalla and Others**, **Siliqi and Others**, and **Karagjozi and Others**. Importantly, the Court observed that the underlying legal issue in the application was already the subject of well-established case-law, specifically **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania** (nos. 604/07, 43628/07, 46684/07 and 34770/09, 31 July 2012).

The facts relevant to the alleged violation were therefore focused on: the existence of a valid, final recognition of the applicants’ inherited property rights; the occupied status of the land; the statutory substitution of compensation for restitution; and the continuing failure of the Albanian authorities to pay any compensation. In substance, the case concerned the State’s failure to implement a property-compensation entitlement, a factual pattern already found problematic in the Court’s earlier Albanian property cases. The reference to well-established case-law indicates that the legal issue was repetitive rather than novel, and that the Court would assess the applicants’ complaints against its prior findings concerning similar failures to compensate persons whose property rights had been recognised but not satisfied. Thus, the central facts relevant to the alleged violation were the 1995 Vlora Commission decision, the occupied nature of the 10,000-square-metre plot, the legal entitlement to compensation, and the long-standing non-payment by the Albanian authorities.

**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Vasilevska and Bartoševič v. Lithuania* (Applications nos. 38206/11 and 18054/12) concerns the annulment of inherited property rights and the subsequent, protracted restitution process, raising issues under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicants, Lithuanian nationals, are the heirs of their grandfather, P.S. In 1991, P.S. applied for the restoration of his property rights to land nationalized by the Soviet regime. In 1994, authorities acknowledged his right to restitution. Consequently, on 28 September 2004, the Vilnius County Administration (VCA) restored his rights by granting him 8.17 hectares of land near Vilnius.

In 2005, P.S. sold two portions of this land: 0.50 hectares to S.M. and 1.27 hectares to Ž.J. The sales were notarized. P.S. passed away in July 2005, and the applicants received their inheritance certificate in December of that year.

Subsequently, the prosecutor of the Vilnius Region initiated three separate legal actions to annul parts of the original restitution. The prosecutor argued that certain plots, totaling 3.52 hectares, were covered by forest of "national importance." Under domestic law, such forests within city limits could only be owned by the State.

The domestic courts ruled in favor of the prosecutor in all three cases. They annulled P.S.'s property rights to 2.50 hectares, 0.15 hectares, and 0.87 hectares. As the applicants were P.S.'s heirs, the courts also annulled the sale agreements for the land sold to S.M. and Ž.J. and ordered the applicants to reimburse the buyers. The applicants were ordered to pay S.M. approximately EUR 14,340 and Ž.J. approximately EUR 54,660 (which they paid in 2013, along with bailiff’s expenses).

Regarding the annulled 2.50 hectares that had not been sold, the applicants were simply deprived of this land. In total, they lost rights to 3.52 hectares of land and incurred significant financial liabilities.

Following these annulments, a subsequent restitution process was initiated by the National Land Service (NLS) to compensate the applicants for the 3.52 hectares. This process proved to be lengthy and complex. The applicants expressed a preference for a residential plot in Vilnius or the return of land in Kryžiokai. They were informed of long waiting lists (over 4,800 candidates) and were offered various alternatives, including land in rural areas or monetary compensation, which they declined.

Over the years, the applicants participated in meetings to select substitute plots. They chose several plots in 2012 and 2016, but the process was fraught with delays. In 2012, chosen plots were not allocated. In 2018, they refused a plot offered in joint ownership. By October 2018, over a decade after the annulment process began, the NLS had only restored their rights to a fraction of the land—0.23 hectares—leaving 3.29 hectares still unresolved.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights. The core of their case is that the annulment of their property rights effectively imposed an excessive and disproportionate individual burden on them. They lost land they had inherited and were forced to pay substantial sums to third parties, while the state's subsequent attempts to provide restitution were plagued by excessive delays and failed to adequately remedy their losses. The key factual issue is whether the Lithuanian authorities, through their actions, struck a fair balance between the public interest (protecting state-owned forests) and the applicants' fundamental right to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions.

Pukhyr and Others v. Ukraine (Applications nos. 10791/20 and six others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, delivered on 24 February 2022. The case concerned seven Ukrainian nationals who applied to the Court between 2020 and 2021. The Government was given notice. The applicants complained principally of inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. They also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The first applicant, Yuriy Pukhyr (b. 1990), was held in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 28 May 2012 to 14 August 2019—7 years, 2 months, and 18 days. He allegedly had only 1.5–2 m² of personal space and suffered overcrowding, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of fresh air, insufficient natural light, restricted access to potable and warm water, poor water quality, restricted showers, inadequate hygiene facilities, no toiletries, poor bedding and bed linen, inadequate temperature, poor and insufficient food, insufficient outdoor exercise, and no privacy for the toilet.

Valentyn Tunitovskyy (b. 1986) was held in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 31 March 2015 to 22 February 2021—5 years, 10 months, and 23 days—with 2.5–2.7 m². His complaints included lack of fresh air, inadequate hygiene, a mouldy or dirty cell, poor bedding, and insufficient outdoor exercise.

Andriy Zakharchenko (b. 1981) was detained in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 14 April 2017 to 11 March 2021—3 years, 10 months, and 26 days—with 2.04–2.98 m². He alleged overcrowding, insects/rodents, mould or dirt, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, no toilet privacy, restricted warm water, no toiletries, poor bedding, poor and insufficient food, restricted showers, inadequate hygiene, and insufficient electric light.

Yevgeniy Nemchenko (b. 1962) had been held in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility since 2 September 2019—more than 2 years, 4 months, and 13 days at introduction—with 2.5–6.1 m². He complained of lack of fresh air, insufficient electric light, poor bedding, insufficient food, restricted showers, poor food, no toiletries, and overcrowding.

Igor Podushkin (b. 1978) was detained in Cherkasy Pre-Trial Detention Facility from 3 December 2018—more than 3 years, 1 month, and 12 days—with 2.27–4.26 m². His grievances included insects/rodents, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygiene, insufficient outdoor exercise, no toiletries, insufficient food, mould or dirt, restricted showers, overcrowding, passive smoking, and no toilet privacy.

Yanush Kondrashov (b. 1990) was held in Dnipro Penitentiary Facility no. 4 since 2 April 2018—more than 3 years, 9 months, and 13 days—with 3.6–3.65 m². He alleged overcrowding, insects/rodents, lack of fresh air, inadequate hygiene, restricted showers, poor potable water, mould or dirt, no toiletries, poor food, insufficient outdoor exercise, and poor bedding.

Sergiy Raulets (b. 1996) had been held in Kyiv Pre-Trial Detention Facility since 23 February 2018—more than 3 years, 10 months, and 23 days—with 2.4–2.9 m². He complained of restricted showers, overcrowding, mould or dirt, lack of fresh air, poor potable water, poor bedding, no toiletries, passive smoking, and insufficient outdoor exercise.

The core alleged violations thus concern prolonged detention in overcrowded, unsanitary, poorly ventilated and lit conditions, with inadequate access to water, showers, hygiene, food, bedding, and outdoor exercise, and the absence of effective domestic remedies.

In *Dolenc v. Slovenia* (Application no. 20256/20, judgment of 20 October 2022), the applicant was a Slovenian neurosurgeon who in 1992 performed surgery in Ljubljana on Israeli citizen E.M. E.M. later suffered severe disability. In 1995 E.M. sued the applicant for medical negligence in Israel, serving the claim during the applicant’s visit there. The proceedings continued before the Tel Aviv District Court. The applicant, represented by an Israeli lawyer, submitted a defence, medical expert opinions, his own written statement, and statements from eleven witnesses—mostly doctors and nurses at Ljubljana University Hospital—as well as an expert opinion on Slovenian law.

The key procedural dispute concerned the examination of the applicant and his witnesses. In 1999 the Israeli district court decided they would be examined by video link. The Slovenian Ministry of Justice stated that no bilateral civil legal assistance treaty existed with Israel, but the Hague Evidence Convention applied; however, neither the Convention nor Slovenian law allowed direct video-link examination. The applicant refused video-link examination and repeatedly requested that he and his witnesses be examined before a Slovenian court under the Hague Evidence Convention. Israeli courts rejected those requests, finding video-link examination balanced the parties’ interests and was technically possible. In June 2003, after the applicant maintained his refusal, the Israeli district court excluded his main written statement and ordered that his witnesses be examined in Slovenia under the Hague Evidence Convention.

The Hague request was sent in September 2003. In January 2004 the Ljubljana District Court raised issues concerning translation, interpretation, costs, cross-examination under Slovenian law, and participation of foreign lawyers. The Slovenian Ministry forwarded these concerns to Israel, but delays and unanswered queries followed. E.M. allegedly later sought to discontinue the Hague procedure due to difficulties. In April 2004 the applicant cancelled his Israeli lawyer’s power of attorney. The Israeli court ordered that documents be served at the former representative’s office; the applicant disputed being informed of this and later decisions. After no progress for fifteen months, in September 2004 the Israeli district court cancelled the Slovenian examination and decided to take evidence in Israel. Hearings in late 2004 proceeded without the applicant appearing; additional deadlines for a concluding statement were allegedly not communicated to him.

In June 2005 the Israeli district court excluded the applicant’s witness statements and Slovenian-law expert opinion because the witnesses had not been directly examined, attributing this to the applicant’s conduct. Since foreign law was not proven, the court applied Israeli law and found the applicant fully liable for E.M.’s damage, relying on evidence including alleged failure to perform a CT scan and inadequate postoperative care.

The applicant’s admitted complaint under Article 6 § 1 concerned the Slovenian courts’ recognition of those Israeli judgments. He alleged that recognition violated his fair-trial rights because the Israeli proceedings had not examined his witnesses, had excluded his evidence and submissions, and had served court documents on his former representative rather than on him. The central facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the video-link/Hague Convention dispute, the exclusion of his evidence, the service on former counsel, and Slovenia’s subsequent recognition of the resulting Israeli judgment.

text:
**Case: Bjarki H. Diego v. Iceland (Application no. 30965/17), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 15 March 2022.**

The applicant, Bjarki H. Diego, an Icelandic lawyer and former director of the loan division and member of the group credit committee of Kaupþing Bank hf., complained that his indictment and conviction for financial offences after Iceland’s 2008 financial crisis violated his right to a fair trial. The ECtHR communicated two main alleged violations: the lack of an independent and impartial tribunal, and the manner in which he was interviewed during the investigation. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

Kaupþing collapsed on 9 October 2008. A Special Prosecutor was later established. Following a Financial Supervisory Authority complaint of 1 October 2009 concerning alleged market manipulation, several investigations were opened into Kaupþing’s pre-collapse trading. The applicant was among twelve former employees investigated. From 9 March to May 2010, the Vesturland District Court authorised telephone tapping of the applicant’s numbers. The Special Prosecutor’s initial request cited four investigations—Al Thani, Holt, CLN and Desulo—and suspected that the applicant had taken part in decisions concerning allegedly criminal conduct. Later reports referred to him as a “suspect.”

On 19 April 2010, the applicant was questioned in the Al Thani investigation but was not prosecuted in that case. On 14 May 2010, he was questioned in the Holt investigation as a witness, not as a suspect. He was not accompanied by a legal representative and does not appear to have been notified of any right to have one. He was informed of his obligation to testify truthfully and of his right not to incriminate himself. On 12 November 2011, he was questioned again in the Holt investigation, this time as a suspect, with defence counsel present.

On 15 March 2013, the applicant was indicted on seven counts of fraud through abuse of position. Three counts concerned allegedly improper loans to Holt Investment Group Ltd.; four concerned allegedly improper loans to Desulo Trading Ltd. He was accused of participating in decisions to grant loans in disregard of the bank’s rules and without properly protecting its interests. On 26 June 2015, the Reykjavik District Court convicted him on six counts and acquitted him on one Holt count, sentencing him to two and a half years’ imprisonment. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Iceland, by judgment of 6 October 2016, partly overturned the lower judgment, convicted him on all seven counts, and upheld the sentence.

Before the Supreme Court, the applicant argued that the case should be dismissed because he had been questioned as a witness on 14 May 2010 while actually being treated as a suspect. He also sought dismissal based on the telephone tapping and the use of transcripts of calls between him and two lawyers; those requests were rejected because the lawyers were not his defence counsel.

A further impartiality issue arose on 5 December 2016, when media disclosed Supreme Court judges’ financial interests. The applicant learned that Justice V.M.M., who had adjudicated his case, had owned shares in Kaupþing and Landsbanki before their collapse. Justice V.M.M. had owned 36 Kaupþing shares, with a nominal value of ISK 360 but a real value of about EUR 140 in October 2008, and Landsbanki shares acquired for ISK 14,753,256, valued at ISK 8,518,692 (about EUR 62,860) on 3 October 2008, before being lost in the collapse. Justice V.M.M. was appointed to the Supreme Court in September 2010.

Relevant domestic law included Article 70 of the Icelandic Constitution, guaranteeing a fair trial before an independent and impartial court, and section 6 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which disqualifies judges where circumstances may justifiably raise questions about impartiality.

text:
The case *Metalla and Others v. Albania* (Applications nos. 30264/08, 42120/08, 54403/08 and 54411/08) is a 2015 judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section). It concerned four applications lodged in 2008 by nine Albanian nationals. The applicants complained that the Albanian authorities failed to enforce final administrative decisions recognising their inherited property rights and awarding compensation for portions of land that could not be physically restored because they were occupied. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, in particular *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

In Application no. 30264/08 (*Metalla*), the Shijak Commission on 9 August 1995 recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 1,020 sq. m of land. Of this, 747 sq. m were restored, but the remaining 272 sq. m were occupied, so the applicants were to receive compensation in one of the forms provided by law. The decision remained unenforced.

In Application no. 42120/08 (*Bushati*), the Shkodër Commission on 8 February 1995 recognised the applicant’s and other heirs’ inherited title to a two-storey building and 500 sq. m of surrounding land. The building was to be restored to them, but the 500 sq. m plot was occupied, so compensation was due. The applicant claimed that a third party had built unauthorised constructions on the plot. He had instituted two legal actions in 1995 and 1997 but discontinued them because of pending proceedings in other cities. This commission decision also remained unenforced.

In Application no. 54403/08 (*Metalla and Others*), the Shijak Commission on 12 May 1994 recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 5,527 sq. m of land. Of this, 5,000 sq. m were restored, while the remaining 527 sq. m were occupied and subject to compensation. The decision remained unenforced.

In Application no. 54411/08 (*Metalla and Others*), the Durrës Commission on 13 August 2007 recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 65,000 sq. m of land. Of this, 60,000 sq. m were restored, but the remaining 5,000 sq. m, consisting of arable land, roads and channels, were occupied and subject to compensation. That decision also remained unenforced.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore that, in each case, a final domestic administrative decision had recognised the applicants’ property rights and either restored part of the property or required compensation for the occupied portion. Under Albanian law, when physical restoration was impossible, compensation had to be provided in one of the ways prescribed by law. Nevertheless, the authorities failed to enforce the decisions for many years, leaving the applicants without either full restoration or the compensation to which they were entitled.

The applicants alleged violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the Convention. The Court referred to domestic law and practice described in *Manushaqe Puto* and *Ramadhi v. Albania*. It also noted Council of Europe Committee of Ministers decisions from 2014 and 2015 criticising Albania’s failure to enforce final decisions awarding compensation in lieu of restitution. Those decisions recorded that Albania had adopted an action plan and was preparing draft legislation to create a compensation mechanism, but the pilot judgment deadline had not been met. The case thus concerned a structural problem: the prolonged non-enforcement of final property compensation decisions. Following its established case-law, the Court found violations of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 13.

Mortier v. Belgium (Application no. 78017/17) concerned the euthanasia of the applicant Tom Mortier’s mother, G.T., without the applicant or his sister being informed beforehand. The applicant complained under Articles 2, 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

G.T. had suffered from chronic depression and a personality/mood disorder for around forty years and had been treated by a psychiatrist, Dr B., for several years. In 2011 she sought euthanasia. Her general practitioner declined to act as main doctor, so she was referred to Professor D., who became her main doctor under Belgium’s 2002 Euthanasia Act. She consulted several psychiatrists. Dr V. initially considered her request premature and suggested further treatment. Later, Dr T. and Dr V.D. concluded that G.T. was clear-sighted, suffered intolerable and incurable mental suffering, and could be assisted to die. On 14 February 2012, G.T. lodged a formal handwritten euthanasia request. Because her death was not imminent, Belgian law required a second psychiatric consultation and a waiting period of at least one month. Euthanasia was performed by Professor D. on 19 April 2012 in a public hospital.

A central issue was the lack of contact with the applicant. G.T. had been estranged from her son and grandchildren for about two years. On 31 January 2012, she emailed both children informing them of her euthanasia request. The applicant did not reply; her daughter replied that she respected her mother’s wishes. Doctors repeatedly encouraged G.T. to contact her children by phone and to write a goodbye letter

The case of *Hakobyan v. Armenia* (Application no. 21350/19) concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention on 15 April 2019. The applicant, Hrayr Hakobyan, born in 1959, was represented by Diana Shakhramanyan, a lawyer practising in Yerevan. The Armenian Government were notified of the application. The applicant complained of an unfair criminal trial, specifically that he had not been given an opportunity to put questions in court to the witness whose testimony played a significant role in securing his conviction. The final domestic decision was a Court of Cassation judgment of 16 October 2018.

The applicant had been convicted of misappropriation of State funds—described as swindling in particularly large amounts—and forgery of official documents. The central issue in the application concerns the evidence of a witness identified only as H.Z. According to the appended factual details, H.Z.’s statement was the only direct evidence directly implicating the applicant in the alleged swindling of State funds and played the decisive role in his conviction on that count. There was no other direct evidence linking the applicant to the crimes with which he had been charged.

The circumstances of H.Z.’s evidence were disputed. H.Z. was interviewed twice during the pre-trial investigation. Only during the second interview did she make incriminating statements against the applicant. Later, in court, she retracted those statements. She claimed that the investigator had inaccurately recorded them and had tried to confuse her. This retraction made the defence’s ability to question her about the reliability and consistency of her evidence particularly important.

At trial, however, the presiding judge did not allow H.Z. to respond to defence questions related to the charges against the applicant and to her relevant incriminating statement. The judge’s reasons were described as formalistic. In particular, the judge refused to allow the applicant’s representative to question H.Z. about discrepancies between her statements, including about having passed money to the applicant and the circumstances surrounding it. The judge justified this restriction on the ground that H.Z. had been summoned for an additional examination only with regard to the criminal case against herself, and she could not therefore be questioned about other matters.

In substance, the applicant’s complaint was that the domestic courts deprived him of an opportunity to challenge the decisive witness evidence against him. Because H.Z.’s testimony was the sole direct evidence on the swindling count, and because she had changed her account and later retracted it, the refusal to permit defence questioning about the inconsistencies and circumstances of her statements allegedly undermined the fairness of the proceedings. The application therefore raised issues under Article 6 of the Convention, particularly the right to a fair trial and the right to examine witnesses against the accused. The Court, sitting as a Committee of the Fifth Section, communicated the case to the Government and delivered judgment on 2 April 2026.

In *Kin v. Ukraine* (Application no. 46990/07), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints brought by Vira Maksymivna Kin, a Ukrainian national born in 1956 and principal of a private school in Dubno, Rivne Region. The case concerned criminal proceedings against her and events of 29 May 2000, raising issues under Article 3, Article 5 § 1, and Article 8 of the Convention, as well as the length of criminal proceedings under Article 6 § 1.

On 30 March 2000 criminal proceedings were initiated against the applicant for failure to comply with a court decision ordering the reinstatement of a teacher at the private school. According to the applicant, at about 9:00 a.m. on 29 May 2000, Dubno police officers broke down the front door of her house. Inside, an investigator from the Dubno inter-district prosecutor’s office ordered her to go to his office for questioning. When she refused, the investigator asked police officers to ensure her compulsory appearance. The police allegedly beat her, twisted her arms behind her back, and forced her out of the house barefoot. She was placed in a police car and taken to the investigator’s office. She was released at about 1:00 p.m. The next day, a doctor noted injuries to her shoulders.

On 2 June 2000 the applicant complained to the Rivne regional prosecutor’s office. A medical expert found five bruises to her shoulders and injured left shoulder ligaments, caused by blunt solid objects; the expert stated the injuries could have been sustained in the circumstances she described. On 30 June 2000, after a pre-investigation inquiry, the prosecutor’s office refused to initiate criminal proceedings against the police officers for lack of constituent elements of a criminal offence. On 20 March 2001, following her complaint, the Prosecutor General’s Office reversed that decision as unsubstantiated and ordered an additional inquiry. The applicant was not informed of the decision taken within that inquiry. In 2016 the Office of the Government Agent learned that the file on those inquiries had been destroyed after expiry of the statutory retention period.

Separately, the criminal case against the applicant proceeded slowly. On 9 April 2001 the investigation was discontinued because of the insignificance of the offence. On 2 August 2001 the Dubno Town Court quashed that decision as unfounded and ordered further investigation. On 14 August 2001 the investigation was completed and the case was referred to the Dubno Town Court. On 30 January 2004 and 13 March 2006 the Dubno Town Court issued judgments, which were quashed by the Rivne Regional Court of Appeal. On 30 January 2007 the Dubno Town Court convicted the applicant of failure to comply with a court decision and fined her, but released her from punishment because the statute of limitation had expired. On 17 April 2007 the Rivne Regional Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and upheld the judgment. On 13 November 2007 the Supreme Court refused to examine her cassation appeal because she had not complied with procedural rules.

On 29 May 2003 the applicant lodged a civil claim seeking damages for violation of the inviolability of her home and her unlawful arrest and ill-treatment on 29 May 2000. On 9 July 2007 the Dubno Town Court found that she had been ill-treated and unlawfully taken from her home to the investigator’s office. It found that the authorities had acted unlawfully and violated her rights to inviolability of home, liberty, and respect for human dignity. It awarded her UAH 500 (approximately EUR 73) in non-pecuniary damage. On 26 May 2008 the Lviv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that judgment. The applicant appealed on points of law, contesting the amount. On 8 May 2009 the Higher Administrative Court found the appeal improperly prepared and set a time-limit to rectify shortcomings. On 13 July 2009 it returned the appeal without examining the merits because she had failed to comply with procedural requirements.

The Court gave notice of the complaints under Article 3, Article 5 § 1, and Article 8 concerning the events of 29 May 2000, and under Article 6 § 1 concerning the length of the criminal proceedings. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

This case concerns Mr Zouhair Dahman Bendhiman, a Spanish national born in 1975, married with two children. He and his wife were long-term unemployed; the family lived on social welfare benefits of €662.89 per month until May 2020, when this increased to €876.85. In March 2011 the Madrid Housing Authority (IVIMA) allocated him public housing in Navalcarnero and signed a seven-year subsidised tenancy agreement. Rent was €393.21 per month, plus communal expenses and property tax; non-payment allowed termination. IVIMA later granted rent reductions of 75%, then 90%, reducing his monthly rent to €49.10.

In October 2013 IVIMA sold 32 public-housing blocks, including the applicant’s, to a private company, A.G., later transferred to E.C. E.C. became the applicant’s landlord. It stated that the tenancy terms were maintained, but refused to recognise the 90% reduction, demanded the full rent plus communal expenses, property tax and CPI adjustments. From November 2013 to October 2017, the applicant paid the reduced €49.10 for only eleven months.

In November 2017 E.C. brought summary civil verbal proceedings seeking €14,420.72 in arrears and the applicant’s eviction. The applicant opposed the claim, arguing that E.C. lacked standing because an administrative court had declared the sale of the housing blocks null and void; that the amount claimed was wrong; that summary eviction proceedings were inadequate to address complex ownership and validity issues; and that, if the 90% reduction remained valid, he owed the legitimate owner €8,637.72. The first-instance civil court initially stayed the proceedings pending the administrative decision, but the Madrid Audiencia Provincial overruled the stay in May 2019 and resumed the case.

On 10 July 2019 the first-instance court ordered the applicant to vacate the dwelling and pay €14,420.72, finding that he had not proven payment of the rents due. The applicant appealed. On 7 October 2019 his appeal was declared inadmissible because he had not paid or secured the debt as required by section 449 of the Civil Procedure Act. His further appeal (recurso de queja) was dismissed on 9 January 2020, without examination of the merits. Although the applicant had been granted legal aid, Spanish law and case-law treated the section 449 payment/security requirement as essential and not exempted by legal aid, which covered court fees and appeal deposits but not the overdue rent debt.

In parallel administrative proceedings, the sale by IVIMA was declared null and void on 21 May 2018, upheld on 14 May 2019 and final in 2020, because tenants had not been heard and public-interest and approval requirements were not met. The applicant was not a party. Enforcement remained pending, and the effects of the nullity on individual tenants were left to the civil courts. His eviction was repeatedly postponed and adjourned sine die in July 2021.

The applicant’s amparo appeal to the Constitutional Court alleged breach of access to a court and discrimination based on lack of economic means and social origin. It was declared inadmissible on 8 July 2020 for failure to show special constitutional importance. Before the European Court of Human Rights, he complained under Article 6 § 1 that the summary first-instance proceedings had not duly answered his submissions and that the appeal bar denied him access to a court, and under Article 14 that this was discriminatory because his inability to pay or secure the debt stemmed from his indigence and social origin. The central issue was whether requiring an indigent tenant, despite legal aid, to pay or secure overdue rent before appealing unjustifiably restricted access to court and discriminated against him.

The case of **Qerimi and Canaj v. Albania** (Applications nos. 12878/10 and 74858/12) is a European Court of Human Rights First Section Committee judgment delivered on 8 September 2016. It originated in two applications lodged by Albanian nationals under Article 34 of the Convention. The Albanian Government was represented by Ms A. Hicka of the State Advocate’s Office. The applications were communicated to the Government on 20 December 2013. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue—non-enforcement of property restitution and compensation decisions—was already the subject of well-established case-law, particularly **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania**.

The facts concern Albania’s post-communist property restitution and compensation scheme. In both applications, the applicants’ inherited property rights were recognised by local commissions, but because parts of the properties were occupied, the applicants were entitled to compensation rather than full restitution. The alleged violations arose from the authorities’ failure to enforce those final decisions, meaning the applicants did not receive the substitute land or monetary compensation awarded to them.

In **Application no. 12878/10 (Qerimi)**, on 1 November 2002 the Durrës Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties recognised, among others, the applicant’s inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 8,000 sq. m. Since the plot was occupied, the applicant and other heirs were to be compensated in kind with an equivalent plot of land. The key issue was that this decision was not effectively executed, leaving the applicant without the compensation in kind that had been determined.

In **Application no. 74858/12 (Canaj)**, on 23 November 2001 the Fier Commission recognised, among others, the applicant’s inherited property rights over a plot measuring 1,121 sq. m. Of that, 598 sq. m were restored. The remaining 523 sq. m were occupied, so the applicant and other heirs were to receive compensation in the amount of 251,040 Albanian Lek (ALL). Again, the relevant complaint concerned the failure to enforce that compensation award.

The legal context is important. The relevant domestic law and practice had been described in earlier cases such as **Ramadhi v. Albania**, **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania**, and **Sharra and Others v. Albania**. Those cases established that the prolonged failure of Albanian authorities to enforce final decisions of restitution and compensation commissions raised Convention issues, principally under Article 6 § 1 (right to a fair hearing, including execution of final decisions) and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property). In **Qerimi and Canaj**, the Court therefore treated the applicants’ complaints as falling within that established line of case-law.

The applicants did not submit claims for just satisfaction within the time-limit allowed under Rule 60 of the Rules of Court. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. In substance, the case is a property non-enforcement case: two applicants had final administrative decisions recognising inherited property rights and awarding compensation, but the decisions were not implemented, leading to alleged violations of their right to effective execution of final decisions and their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions.

Case No. 41749/12, *Martinović v. Bosnia and Herzegovina*, concerned an application lodged on 12 June 2012 by Božana Martinović, a Bosnian national born in 1955 and living in Assemini, Italy. She complained about the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions in her favour, raising issues under the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time and the protection of property. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The first set of proceedings began with a decision of 4 December 2006 by the Cantonal Prosecutor of the Hercegovina-Neretva Canton granting the applicant reimbursement of witness costs of BAM 519. Enforcement then stalled. On 29 February 2008 the Mostar Municipal Court rejected enforcement as unenforceable; the Cantonal Court quashed that decision on 18 September 2008. A writ of execution followed on 19 November 2008, but an objection was upheld on 19 June 2009. On 1 April 2010 the Cantonal Court again quashed and remitted the case. On 18 February 2011 the Municipal Court partly accepted the objection, especially concerning interest from 4 January 2007 and interest on enforcement costs; the Cantonal Court upheld this on 2 December 2011. The Supreme Court dismissed revision on 19 September 2013. On 23 December 2013 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina found a violation of the applicant’s right to trial within a reasonable time because the 18 February 2011 decision had not been enforced. It ordered the Canton to take enforcement measures but awarded no non-pecuniary damages. On 21 October 2014 the Constitutional Court confirmed that the decision remained unenforced. It was finally enforced on 18 December 2014, when the applicant was paid in cash.

The second set concerned a Municipal Court judgment of 3 April 2009, final on 16 December 2009, ordering a certain P.M. to pay the applicant BAM 1,959 in civil proceedings costs. The applicant requested enforcement on 31 October 2010. She sought acceleration on 14 September 2011, 4 November 2011 and 5 October 2012. Only on 5 December 2012 did the Municipal Court issue a writ of execution. After an objection was dismissed on 13 June 2013, P.M. appealed. On 17 September 2013 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the reasonable-time right due to the duration of the enforcement proceedings before the Municipal Court. It ordered the Cantonal Court to rule urgently on P.M.’s appeal but again awarded no non-pecuniary damages. The Cantonal Court dismissed the appeal on 16 October 2013. On 11 June 2015 the Municipal Court issued another writ of execution, and on 4 August 2016 the judgment was enforced by payment into the applicant’s bank account in Bosnia and Herzegovina; she apparently still lived in Italy.

These facts were relevant to the alleged violations because both final decisions in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced for years. Domestic courts repeatedly delayed or remitted enforcement, and although the Constitutional Court recognised unreasonable delay, it did not compensate the applicant. The case therefore focused on the length and effectiveness of enforcement proceedings and the lack of adequate redress.

**Summary of Aganikyan v. Armenia (Application no. 21791/12)**

The case of *Aganikyan v. Armenia* originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Armenia with the European Court of Human Rights on 2 April 2012 by Mr. Hrayr Aganikyan, an American national residing in Yerevan. The applicant’s sole complaint, which was communicated to the Armenian Government, concerned the excessive length of criminal proceedings brought against him. All other aspects of the application were declared inadmissible. The central facts of the case relate to the protracted nature of these proceedings, which spanned nearly seven years from the initial investigation to the final appeal.

The proceedings began on 30 December 2004, when an investigator instituted a criminal case against the applicant for alleged usury. Over the next year and a half, the investigation expanded to include additional charges. On 20 June 2005, the applicant was formally charged with professional usury. Subsequently, on 15 October 2005, a separate case concerning fraud was initiated and merged with the usury case. By 7 March 2006, the charges against the applicant were significantly amended to include fraud in large amounts, extortion, usury, and forgery of evidence. During this pre-trial phase, the authorities ordered a search of his apartment, confiscated his property, and imposed a written undertaking not to leave his residence. He was later detained for two months following a successful prosecutor's appeal against an initial refusal of detention.

On 14 July 2006, the bill of indictment was approved and the case was sent to the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court. The trial phase, which commenced on 18 August 2006, was characterized by numerous adjournments. Between August 2006 and October 2007, the court held twelve hearings that were postponed, primarily due to the absence of victims and witnesses. The proceedings were further delayed when the presiding judge's powers were suspended in October 2007, leading to a new judge taking over and ordering the examination of the case to start anew in November 2007.

From November 2007 to December 2010, the trial continued with an additional forty hearings. These were adjourned for various reasons, including the absence of the applicant or his lawyer (and applications lodged by them), the absence of victims or witnesses, and applications by the prosecutor or the court’s own motion. Throughout the proceedings, the court heard from forty-seven witnesses and examined extensive documentary and expert evidence. On 31 January 2011, the District Court delivered its judgment, finding the applicant guilty on five counts, including fraud, extortion, and usury, and sentencing him to nine years' imprisonment, property confiscation, and a fine.

The applicant and the prosecutor both appealed. On 3 October 2011, the Criminal Court of Appeal rejected the appeals and upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law. On 21 November 2011, the Court of Cassation declared the appeal inadmissible for lack of merit, thus finalizing the domestic proceedings. The applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights focused on the length of this entire process.

Case De Legé v. the Netherlands (Application no. 58342/15) concerns an alleged breach of the privilege against self-incrimination under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, Mr Levinus Adrianus de Legé, is a Dutch national born in 1934, resident in Spain since 2000. In 2005, Dutch tax authorities obtained from Belgian counterparts information about Luxembourg X Bank accounts, including balances from 1994 and 1996. The information had been stolen from the bank and discovered in a Belgian criminal investigation. Luxembourg banking secrecy prevented lawful transmission of such data to foreign tax authorities without the account holder’s cooperation. The applicant was identified as an account holder.

On 7 March 2007, the tax inspector wrote to the applicant, stating that he appeared to hold foreign bank accounts not declared in his income or capital tax returns. He was asked to complete forms declaring past or present foreign bank accounts after 31 December 1994 and to provide copies of all bank statements for 1 January 1995 to 31 December 2000. The inspector relied on section 47(1) of the General State Taxes Act, which obliged taxpayers to provide relevant information and documents. The applicant, through counsel, refused, invoking the privilege against self-incrimination. He argued that such requests were followed by additional tax assessments and fines, making Article 6 applicable under its criminal head, and that the authorities could not obtain the information without his cooperation. His spouse similarly refused.

On 25 July 2007, the inspector warned that estimated additional assessments would be issued. On 22 November 2007, he informed the applicant that he intended to increase taxable income for 1995 and taxable capital for 1996 based on estimates and to impose statutory fines of 100% of the additional assessments without remission. The fines could be reduced to 50% if he complied before assessments, or 75% if he cooperated during objection. The applicant did not respond. On 28 December 2007, additional income and capital tax assessments were issued with 100% fines.

The applicant objected in January and March 2008. While those proceedings were pending, the State brought civil interim proceedings to compel disclosure of foreign accounts and documents. On 27 November 2008, the provisional-measures judge ordered the applicant to declare whether he held foreign bank accounts after 31 December 1995 and to provide information and documents, including bank statements for 1996–2000. Compliance was required within fourteen days on pain of penalty payments of EUR 5,000 per day, up to EUR 50,000. The applicant did not appeal. On 9 December 2008, he submitted forms declaring a joint X Bank Luxembourg account and provided bank statements and portfolio summaries.

In the resumed tax proceedings, the inspector used the actual figures from these documents to recalculate the assessments downward. The fines were reduced to approximately EUR 1,400 and EUR 825, and later further reduced by the courts for length of proceedings, but the fines remained. The applicant challenged the use of the compelled documents to recalculate the tax fines, arguing that this breached his privilege against self-incrimination. Domestic courts rejected the complaint. They classified bank statements and portfolio summaries as “will-independent” material under Saunders v. the United Kingdom, holding that Article 6 did not preclude their use for tax fines. The Supreme Court affirmed, reasoning that forced surrender of existing bank documents does not make them will-dependent and that the inspector could assume their existence after identifying the account holder.

The applicant lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 19 November 2015, relying on Article 6 § 1. The central alleged violation is that documents obtained under threat of substantial penalty payments were used to recalculate punitive tax fines, thereby compelling him to provide evidence against himself in proceedings amounting to a criminal charge for Convention purposes.

In A.M. v. Norway (Application no. 30254/18, ECtHR 24 March 2022), the applicant, a Norwegian national, complained under Articles 8 and 14 about Norway’s refusal to recognize her as the legal mother of a child, X, born through gestational surrogacy in the United States, and about the denial of contact rights.

The applicant and her former partner, E.B., began a relationship in 2002. After unsuccessful natural conception, IVF and egg donation, they pursued surrogacy in the United States. Their relationship deteriorated and ended definitively by early 2013, but they continued the surrogacy process. In 2013, an embryo created with E.B.’s sperm and a donated egg was implanted in a US surrogate. X was born on 19 March 2014. A Texas court recognized the surrogacy agreement and declared A.M. the legal mother; her name appeared on the US birth certificate.

In Norway, E.B. acknowledged paternity in May 2014. The authorities registered him as X’s father with sole parental responsibility. They refused to register A.M. as mother. Under section 2 of the Children Act, the woman who gives birth is the legal mother. A.M. had no genetic or biological link to X, and the surrogate remained the legal mother under Norwegian law absent adoption. The Tax Directorate stated A.M. could not be registered as mother without a valid adoption.

A.M. and E.B. initially shared care on an equal, daily basis, but their conflict increased. Child welfare services expressed concern about the arrangement’s impact on X. In August 2015, E.B. cut off contact, and X lived with him thereafter.

A.M. applied to Norwegian authorities for recognition of maternity or, alternatively, adoption. The application was rejected in 2015. The temporary Surrogacy Act did not apply because the filing deadline had passed and because A.M. and E.B. had not had a shared wish to raise the child together. Ordinary or stepparent adoption required the consent of the person with parental responsibility; E.B. did not consent. Stepparent adoption was also unavailable because X already had two legal parents—the surrogate mother and the biological father.

The Oslo City Court (2016) and Borgarting High Court (2017) dismissed A.M.’s claims. They held that Norwegian law allowed maternity only through birth or adoption, that the Texas judgment was not enforceable in Norway, and that the refusal did not breach X’s best interests, the Constitution, the UNCRC or the ECHR. The courts also refused contact rights, finding no legal basis and no indication that contact served X’s best interests given the conflict and his stable life with E.B.

Before the ECtHR, A.M. alleged that the refusals violated her right to respect for private and family life under Article 8. She argued that Norway failed to recognize her de facto family life with X, ignored X’s best interests, and left her without legal status despite the US judgment. She also alleged discrimination under Article 14, claiming she was treated differently as an intended/social mother in a surrogacy case, especially because E.B.’s refusal of consent blocked adoption. Key facts for those complaints were that A.M. lacked a genetic link, was not the surrogate, the couple separated before conception, E.B. had legal parenthood and parental responsibility, and X had lived with E.B. since 2015. The Court found no violation of Article 8 and no violation of Article 14.

**Bradshaw and Others v. Malta** (Application no. 37121/15) concerns twenty-four Maltese nationals and a Maltese company who jointly owned 274 Republic Street, Valletta—a four-storey, 864-square-metre property known as the King’s Own Band Club (“KOBC”). In 1946, the applicants’ ancestors voluntarily leased the property to KOBC for GBP 500 annually (approximately EUR 1,164.69). In 1955, Maltese law introduced specific rules for leases to band clubs. Under the Civil Code and the Re-letting of Urban Property (Regulation) Ordinance, the applicants were obliged to renew the lease annually and could not demand an increase in rent. The applicants claimed that by 2014 the property’s market rental value was EUR 269,100 per year. Part of the property was used as a band club, while part operated as a restaurant and bar, which the applicants said generated around EUR 150,000 or more annually for the caterer.

The applicants alleged an ongoing violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, arguing that they were denied peaceful enjoyment of their property without adequate compensation. They also alleged discrimination under Article 14, taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. They pointed out that 2009 amendments to the Civil Code allowed increases in certain commercial rents and established a cut-off date of 2028 for existing protected commercial leases, but those amendments did not cover properties leased to clubs. As a result, club leases remained subject to annual renewal and frozen rent, unlike commercial leases.

In 2011, the applicants brought constitutional redress proceedings against the Attorney General, the Prime Minister, and KOBC. In 2013, the Civil Court (First Hall), in its constitutional jurisdiction, found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. It held that the interference was disproportionate, noting the disparity between the rent received and the property’s estimated rental value or the income generated from the bar/restaurant. It awarded EUR 300,000 in damages, payable half by the Attorney General and Prime Minister jointly and half by KOBC. The court found no discrimination.

On appeal, the Constitutional Court reversed in 2015. It accepted that the applicants owned the property but held that, because the 1946 lease had been entered into voluntarily with knowledge of its consequences, the applicants could not complain of a violation. Even if inflation had made the rent low, the principle of *pacta sunt servanda* applied. It also found that the 2009 amendments did not affect the applicants’ position. A request for retrial was rejected in 2016.

Meanwhile, in 2014, new regulations increased club rents by 10% annually until 2016, then by 5% until 2023, and thereafter by inflation. From 2015, tenants also had to pay an additional 5% of annual income from economic activity. As a result, the applicants received only EUR 2,876.26 in 2015 and EUR 3,017.20 in 2016.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the long-standing statutory rent control, the applicants’ inability to terminate the lease or increase rent, the voluntary origin of the 1946 lease, the dramatic gap between actual rent and market value, the profitable commercial use of part of the premises, and the differential treatment of club leases compared with commercial leases after the 2009 reforms. These facts formed the basis of the complaints of disproportionate interference with property rights and discriminatory treatment.
