The case *Alleleh and Others v. Norway* concerns an Article 8 complaint about Norway’s expulsion of the first applicant, Ms Neima Aden Alleleh, and its effects on her family life with her Norwegian husband and four Norwegian citizen children.

The first applicant arrived in Norway in September 2001 and applied for asylum, falsely claiming to be Somali and giving a detailed but untrue personal history. Her asylum application was rejected in 2002, and her appeal dismissed in January 2003. She remained in Norway unlawfully. In May 2003 she sought revision of the refusal, admitted giving false information before, but then gave a new false story and false identity papers—still claiming Somali origin. The Immigration Appeals Board refused revision in November 2005.

Meanwhile, in 2002 she met the second applicant, a Norwegian citizen. They married in April 2004, while she had no lawful residence in Norway. Less than two weeks later, she applied for residence based on the marriage, repeating the same false information. She was granted temporary residence in September 2005, renewed in November 2006. In 2007 she applied for and was granted Norwegian citizenship by claiming Somali citizenship, signing a declaration that the information was correct and that citizenship could be revoked if she had given false information or concealed relevant facts. The couple’s children were born in 2005, 2009 (twins), and 2013.

In 2014, police suspected she was actually Djiboutian. When questioned in June 2014, she maintained her false account. In November 2014 she was warned of possible citizenship withdrawal and expulsion; in December 2014 she finally gave her correct identity and country of origin. In June 2015 her Norwegian citizenship was withdrawn, and in November 2015 she was expelled with a two-year re-entry ban. The Immigration Appeals Board dismissed her appeal in March 2016. It accepted that expulsion would negatively affect the children but found that the father could adequately care for them in Norway, that the family could move to Djibouti, and that the seriousness of her repeated immigration violations and general deterrence outweighed the children’s best interests.

Before the domestic courts, the Oslo City Court upheld the expulsion in 2017, finding her false information gross, repeated, and intentional over roughly 13 years. The children were denied standing and acted only as interveners. The Borgarting High Court reversed in April 2019, finding the expulsion disproportionate vis-à-vis the children: the mother was the primary caregiver, the children were strongly attached to her, two twins were somewhat vulnerable, the youngest was closely attached, and the father worked long hours, creating a risk of unusually heavy burden. The Supreme Court reversed in December 2019 and upheld the expulsion. It stressed that her residence and citizenship were based on false identity and information, making family life precarious from the outset. It found no exceptional circumstances or unusually great burden on the children: they were generally well-functioning, had not suffered prior separations, would remain with their father and siblings in a familiar environment, the two-year ban was limited and could be lifted, contact was possible, and there was no insurmountable obstacle to family life in Djibouti.

The alleged violation was therefore Article 8 ECHR, requiring a fair balance between immigration control, the seriousness of the first applicant’s prolonged falsehoods, and the children’s best interests and family life.

In *Bondarenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 27052/09 and 11 others), the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered judgment on 28 June 2018. The case originated in twelve applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government. The central alleged violation was that the applicants’ pre-trial detention had been excessively long. Some applicants also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The applicants were held in pre-trial detention in Ukraine during criminal proceedings. According to the appended table, Borys Bondarenko was detained from 23 October 2006 to 20 August 2010, a period of 3 years, 9 months and 29 days. Oleg Galimon was detained twice: from 14 February to 2 November 2007 (8 months and 20 days) and from 4 August 2009 to 25 October 2010 (1 year, 2 months and 22 days). Sergey Kukhtin was detained from 7 November 2010 to 6 December 2011 (1 year and 1 month). Gleb Zelenov was detained from 8 February 2008 to 9 August 2010 (2 years, 6 months and 2 days) and again from 15 February 2011 to 5 June 2012 (1 year, 3 months and 22 days).

Vadim Tokunov was detained from 22 September 2009 to 22 July 2014 (4 years, 10 months and 1 day). Oleg Volokin had three separate periods: 3 July 2008 to 27 July 2009 (1 year and 25 days), 4 November 2009 to 28 March 2012 (2 years, 4 months and 25 days), and 17 September 2012 to 15 November 2013 (1 year, 1 month and 30 days). Tamara Nekrasova was detained from 2 March 2012 to 23 September 2015 (3 years, 6 months and 22 days). Aleksandr Grebeshkov had four periods: 21 September 2009 to 16 December 2010 (1 year, 2 months and 26 days), 26 April 2011 to 13 March 2012 (10 months and 17 days), 10 July to 21 December 2012 (5 months and 12 days), and 11 March to 19 June 2014 (3 months and 9 days).

Gennadiy Chernov was detained from 26 August 2005 to 15 December 2008 (3 years, 3 months and 20 days) and again from 20 May 2010 to 10 June 2014 (4 years and 22 days). Oleksandr Kharkiv was detained from 9 August 2010 to 27 September 2012 (2 years, 1 month and 19 days) and again from 1 March 2013 to 26 June 2015 (2 years, 3 months and 26 days). Aleksandr Tverdokhleb was detained from 1 March 2011 to 25 June 2013 (2 years, 3 months and 25 days). Andriy Yolkin was detained from 24 July 2012 and remained in detention at the time of the application, a period exceeding 5 years and 9 months.

These facts underpinned the applicants’ complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial. The applicants alleged that the Ukrainian authorities had kept them in pre-trial detention for unjustifiably long periods without adequate justification. The case therefore required the Court to assess whether the length of the detention, whether continuous or cumulative across separate periods, exceeded the reasonable-time requirement and whether the domestic authorities had provided sufficient reasons for prolonging detention.

In *Annen v. Germany (No. 2)*, the applicant, Klaus Günter Annen, a German national born in 1951 and living in Weinheim, was an anti-abortion campaigner who operated the website *babycaust.de*. The site compared abortion with the Holocaust. Its starting page showed graves and the text “then: Holocaust”; clicking led to “Abortion – the new Holocaust?” A link titled “Life or death?” led to “Prayer requests for Germany,” from which users could reach a location-based alphabetical list of doctors who performed abortions, including their names and practice addresses, and requests to pray for them. The site stated: “Perverted doctors murder unborn children at the request of the mothers.” It also urged prayers for doctors “who personally undertake the AGGRAVATED MURDER of abortion killing,” and said counselling centres were enabling “the unpunished aggravated murder of children in their mother’s womb.” These statements formed the basis of the later injunction.

Dr Q., one of the listed doctors, first sought a civil injunction to remove his name and address. On 23 May 2006, the Mannheim Regional Court refused, holding that it was a fact Dr Q. performed abortions and that the rest was covered by freedom of expression; it found no comparable “pillory effect.” Dr Q. appealed and modified his request, seeking an order that Annen desist from labelling abortions, such as those performed by Dr Q., “aggravated murder.” On 28 February 2007, the Karlsruhe Court of Appeal granted the injunction. It found the website could be understood as a personalised accusation that Dr Q. had committed the criminal offence of aggravated murder. Although “aggravated murder” could be a moral judgment, the overall presentation did not exclude a criminal-law reading. The applicant had emphasised the term, compared abortion to the Holocaust, and had not mentioned section 218a of the Criminal Code, which exempted abortions such as Dr Q.’s from criminal liability. The Federal Court of Justice refused legal aid for an appeal, and on 2 July 2009 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to admit Annen’s constitutional complaint without reasons.

On 15 January 2010, Annen applied to the European Court of Human Rights. He alleged that the domestic order to desist from labelling abortions “aggravated murder” on his webpage violated his freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. On 3 January 2017, the Court communicated the Article 10 complaint to the Government and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3.

The relevant German law included Article 5 of the Basic Law, which protects expression but limits it by general laws and personal honour; Criminal Code provisions on aggravated murder (Art. 211), abortion (Art. 218), and the exception to liability (Art. 218a); and Civil Code provisions (Arts. 823 and 1004) allowing injunctions to prevent violations of personality rights. The Federal Constitutional Court’s 1993 judgment regarded abortions performed within twelve weeks after counselling as unlawful but not punishable. The domestic courts therefore treated the applicant’s statements as potentially actionable accusations of criminal conduct against a named doctor, rather than merely abstract moral criticism. The key alleged violation was that the civil injunction disproportionately restricted Annen’s Article 10 right to express his anti-abortion views.

**Metalla and Others v. Albania** (Applications nos. 30264/08, 42120/08, 54403/08 and 54411/08) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section, Committee) delivered on 16 July 2015. Four applications were lodged by nine Albanian nationals between 13 June and 8 October 2008. The applications were communicated to the Albanian Government on 21 January 2010. The core complaint was the Albanian authorities’ failure to enforce final decisions of local property restitution commissions. Those decisions recognised the applicants’ inherited title to property and, where portions of land or buildings were occupied and could not be physically restored, ordered that the applicants receive compensation in one of the ways provided for by law. The Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already covered by well-established case-law, particularly **Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania**.

The relevant facts in each application were similar. In application no. 30264/08 (**Metalla**), on 9 August 1995 the Shijak Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 1,020 sq. m of land. Of that, 747 sq. m were restored, while the remaining 272 sq. m were occupied; the applicants were therefore to be compensated under law. The decision remained unenforced.

In application no. 42120/08 (**Bushati**), on 8 February 1995 the Shkodër Commission recognised the applicant’s and other heirs’ inherited title to a two-storey building and a surrounding plot of 500 sq. m. Because the 500 sq. m plot was occupied, compensation was to be provided, and the building was to be restored to them. The applicant claimed he brought legal actions in 1995 and 1997 against a third party for vacation and restoration of the property, but discontinued them because of pending judicial proceedings in other cities. The third party apparently built unauthorised constructions on the plot. The Commission decision remained unenforced.

In application no. 54403/08 (**Metalla and Others**), on 12 May 1994 the Shijak Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 5,527 sq. m. Of that, 5,000 sq. m were restored, while 527 sq. m were occupied; compensation was to be provided. The decision remained unenforced.

In application no. 54411/08 (**Metalla and Others**), on 13 August 2007 the Durrës Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited title to 65,000 sq. m. Of that, 60,000 sq. m were restored, while the remaining 5,000 sq. m—described as arable land, roads and channels—were occupied; compensation was again ordered. The decision remained unenforced.

The domestic law and practice concerning such restitution and compensation claims had been set out in earlier cases such as **Manushaqe Puto** and **Ramadhi v. Albania**. In 2013 and 2014, Albania approved new property valuation maps containing reference prices per square metre. At the Council of Europe level, Committee of Ministers decisions in 2014 and 2015 addressed the execution of judgments concerning Albania’s failure to enforce final domestic judicial and administrative decisions awarding compensation in lieu of physical restoration. The Committee welcomed an action plan and draft law but noted delays and the need for an effective compensation mechanism.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore that final domestic decisions granting restoration or compensation remained unexecuted for years, that occupied portions of property were not compensated, and that no effective redress was provided. The applicants alleged violations arising from this continuing non-enforcement, principally under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Sandu and Others v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (ECtHR, Second Section, 17 July 2018, final 3 December 2018), eight applications were lodged by 1,646 Moldovan natural persons and three companies. The applicants lived in the villages of Doroțcaia, Pîrîta, Molovata Nouă, Pohrebea and Cocieri, on the left bank of the Dniester in the Dubăsari region, an area under Moldovan control. Their farmland was located near these villages, but across a road linking the northern and southern parts of the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Transdniestrian Republic” (“MRT”). That road, cutting through Moldovan-controlled zones, was controlled by the “MRT” authorities. The applicants alleged that they were denied access to their land, in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, and that they had no effective remedies.

The applicants had obtained title to their plots from Moldova through the “Pamântul” land privatisation programme. Some land was later transferred by gift or inheritance. The three applicant companies rented land from owners during the relevant period. Farming was the applicants’ main source of income. To reach their land, they had to cross the “MRT”-controlled road.

Between 1992 and 1998, the applicants used or rented the land without interference. In 1998, the “MRT” authorities set up checkpoints to monitor agricultural products crossing the road, and the applicants had to pay various taxes and fees to the “MRT”. In August 2004, the “MRT” authorities declared that the land owned or rented by the applicants belonged to the “MRT”. The applicants were told they could continue working it only if they paid rent to the local “MRT” authorities. They refused, because they were already lawful owners or renters under Moldovan law. As a result, all access to the land was blocked, the harvest was lost, and some agricultural machines were seized. No work was done for the following two years, making it difficult to restore the land’s productivity.

The applicants complained repeatedly to the “MRT” authorities, requesting a right of passage, but were refused on the basis that the land was “MRT” property. They also complained to the Moldovan authorities, who replied that they had no means to compel the “MRT” to allow free passage. The applicants asked the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office to open a criminal investigation. Complaints to the Russian embassy and the OSCE were unsuccessful, and protests took place in 2005 asking Russia to intervene.

Specific company applicants documented losses. Agro-Tiras S.R.L. rented 450 hectares across the road; “MRT” customs seized a tractor and wheat for alleged failure to declare importation. Posedo-Agro S.R.L. rented land in Cocieri; “MRT” customs seized barley and apples, imposed fines and temporarily seized trucks and tractors. It complained to the Moldovan Government, OSCE and Dubăsari prosecutor. Agro-S.A.V.V.A. S.R.L. also showed it rented land and could not cultivate it.

The Moldovan Government cited laws compensating villagers for losses, including price differences, pensions, tax breaks, credits, diesel fuel, and direct compensation of almost 39 million Moldovan lei (about EUR 2.3 million) in 2004–2007. In 2006, Moldova negotiated a temporary “MRT” registration mechanism allowing landowners to cultivate the land and be exempt from “MRT” payments; it was renewed annually.

The applications were lodged in 2004–2006 and communicated to the Governments in 2013. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were the “MRT” control over access, the 2004 property declaration and rent demand, the resulting blocked access, lost harvests and seizures, and the alleged absence of effective remedies.

Boldijar and Others v. Romania (Application no. 46831/14 and 15 others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 29 March 2018. It originated in 16 applications lodged against Romania under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates between 2014 and 2016. The applications were communicated to the Romanian Government. The applicants complained of inadequate conditions of their detention.

The applicants were detained in a range of Romanian police arrest facilities, prisons and a prison hospital. Their detention periods varied from several weeks to several years; some were still pending when the applications were lodged. Facilities included Miercurea-Ciuc, Codlea, Bistrița, Ialomița County Police Arrest, Poarta Albă Prison Hospital, Slobozia, Rahova, Cluj County Police Arrest, Gherla, Colibași, Bucharest General Police Arrest, Craiova, Drobeta Turnu Severin, Târgu-Jiu, Gorj County Police Arrest, Teleorman County Police Arrest, Giurgiu, Jilava, Ploiești and Arad prisons.

The core alleged violation concerned Article 3 ECHR, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The applicants alleged that the material conditions of detention were so poor that they reached the threshold of severity. The appended table shows that overcrowding was a central issue. Many applicants had extremely limited personal space, often ranging from 0.87 to 2.14 sq m, 1.08 to 1.48 sq m, 1.13 to 1.98 sq m, 1.21 to 1.7 sq m, 1.44 to 1.72 sq m, 1.47 to 2.7 sq m, 1.57 to 2.52 sq m, or around 1.88–1.97 sq m. In some facilities the space was greater, for example 3.39–9.2 sq m, but applicants still alleged other serious deficiencies.

The recurring grievances included overcrowding; insufficient sleeping places; lack or inadequacy of hygienic facilities; no or restricted access to showers or warm water; lack of privacy for toilets; poor-quality bedding and bed linen; lack or inadequate furniture; mouldy or dirty cells; infestation with insects or rodents; lack of fresh air; insufficient natural or electric light; inadequate temperature; passive smoking; poor-quality food and potable water; lack or insufficiency of outdoor physical exercise; and lack or restricted access to leisure or educational activities. Some complained of cells being constantly lit or lacking toilets.

Specific examples illustrate the allegations: Remus Boldijar complained of 0.87–2.04 sq m and overcrowding at Miercurea-Ciuc and Codlea; Romeo Gabriel Ardelean and Robert Andreas Bedners alleged similar overcrowding at Miercurea-Ciuc; Vasile Meterez alleged multiple facilities with spaces as low as 1.97–2.2 sq m; Grigore-Alin Gornoavă alleged 1.08–1.48 sq m at Craiova; Costel Păun alleged 1.44–1.72 sq m at Jilava for nearly three years; Claudiu-Florian Isac alleged overcrowding and rodent infestation at Jilava and Ploiești; Florin Șumăndan alleged poor food and infestation at Arad.

The case therefore concerns whether the cumulative effect of overcrowding and poor material conditions amounted to degrading treatment contrary to Article 3. Severity would be assessed by duration, space, sanitation, ventilation, food, exercise and cumulative conditions.

In *A.M. v. Norway*, the applicant, a Norwegian woman, complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights about Norway’s refusal to recognise her as the legal mother of X, a child born through gestational surrogacy in the United States, and about the denial of contact rights. The key facts concern her role as intended/social mother, the breakdown of her relationship with the biological father, and the resulting conflict under Norwegian parentage law.

A.M. and her former partner, E.B., tried for years to have a child. After unsuccessful natural conception, IVF and egg donation, they pursued surrogacy in the United States. Their relationship deteriorated and E.B. moved out in September 2012, but they continued cooperating in the surrogacy process. In 2013, an embryo created using E.B.’s sperm and an anonymous donor egg was implanted in a US surrogate. X was born in March 2014. A Texas court declared A.M. the legal mother under Texas law, and she was named as mother on the US birth certificate. E.B.

**Case Summary: Bosyy v. Ukraine (Application no. 13124/08)**

The case of *Bosyy v. Ukraine* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Vasyl Ivanovych Bosyy, a Ukrainian national, on 8 February 2008. The applicant was convicted of aggravated robbery in 2006 and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. The Court declared the complaints regarding the fairness of the criminal proceedings inadmissible, focusing instead on the conditions of the applicant's detention, alleged ill-treatment, monitoring of correspondence, and hindrance of his right to individual application.

The facts concern the applicant’s detention in various facilities from 2005 to 2012. He was held in a pre-trial detention centre (SIZO) in Kropyvnytskyi, followed by correctional colonies no. 6 and no. 78. The applicant alleged that the conditions in the correctional colonies were inadequate. Specifically, he claimed severe overcrowding, stating he was held in a dormitory measuring 6 by 8 square meters with twelve double bunk beds. He also complained of regular electricity cuts, inadequate lighting, poor quality food, and unsanitary conditions involving pests such as cockroaches, mice, and rats. The Government disputed these claims, submitting that the dormitory measured over 41 square meters with ten beds and that food and sanitation were compliant with regulations, though they admitted to reducing voltage for energy-saving purposes.

Regarding ill-treatment, the applicant alleged he was beaten by guards upon arrival at the first colony in October 2006, tortured, humiliated, and placed in a disciplinary cell. He further claimed that in March 2007, guards attempted to place him in a psychiatric clinic. The Government denied all allegations of ill-treatment. The applicant lodged numerous complaints with domestic authorities regarding this alleged persecution, though he later withdrew two complaints in 2010, citing heightened emotions.

A significant portion of the case concerned the monitoring of the applicant’s correspondence and his right to communicate with the Court. Under domestic law at the time (Article 113 of the Code on the Enforcement of Sentences), prison authorities automatically monitored prisoner correspondence, except for specific exemptions. While correspondence with the Court and the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights was exempt from monitoring by law, the applicant alleged that prison authorities intercepted, reviewed, blocked, and delayed his mail, including letters to the Court, and intimidated him for applying to the Court. The Government denied these allegations. Records indicated that despite monitoring domestic mail, the applicant corresponded extensively with international and domestic entities.

Finally, the applicant complained of hindrances to his right of individual application. He alleged that authorities denied him access to his criminal case file, preventing him from obtaining necessary documents. The Government countered with evidence showing the applicant had examined his file in late 2011 and early 2012. Additionally, there were procedural issues regarding the applicant's legal representation where he twice revoked and then reinstated the authority of his lawyer, Mr. E. Markov, leading to administrative complications with the Registry.

The Court delivered its judgment on 22 November 2018, assessing these facts against the Convention articles concerning the prohibition of torture and inhuman treatment, the right to respect for correspondence, and the right to individual application.

**Summary of *Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria* (Application no. 5734/14)**

The case of *Aviso Zeta AG v. Austria* originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Austria with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 January 2014. The applicant, Aviso Zeta AG, was a bank based in Vienna that purchased and held shares, predominantly in the "IF" company, for third parties. The applicant company and IF were closely related, sharing management personnel and staff. A separate investment advisory firm, the "A. company," acted as a key distribution partner for the applicant.

Following a significant decline in the value of the IF shares beginning in the second half of 2007, numerous legal proceedings were initiated against Aviso Zeta AG. The case at issue concerned a civil action brought in 2009 by two clients, F.M. and H.H., who sought to annul their purchase of IF shares. The Vienna Commercial Court ruled in favour of the clients in April 2012, holding the applicant company liable for inadequate advice provided by the A. company, citing the close professional ties between the two entities.

While the Vienna Court of Appeal overturned this decision in September 2012, the Supreme Court, in a judgment delivered on 17 June 2013 by a five-judge panel, restored the Commercial Court's ruling. The Supreme Court found the applicant company liable, reasoning that its significant interest in selling IF shares meant it was responsible for the inadequate information provided to the clients by the A. company.

The central violation alleged in this case stems from the involvement of Judge N. on the Supreme Court panel that delivered the 17 June 2013 judgment. The applicant company later discovered that Judge N. had a personal conflict of interest. Specifically, Judge N. had personally purchased IF shares whose value had subsequently dropped.

Crucially, Judge N. had previously declared himself biased in other comparable cases involving IF shares and had been permitted by the Supreme Court to withdraw from them. In those prior cases, Judge N. had even considered filing a personal lawsuit for his own financial losses, with the applicant company being a potential defendant. The applicant only learned of Judge N.'s participation in its case upon receiving the Supreme Court's judgment, making a prior challenge impossible.

The applicant company subsequently filed an action for nullity, which was heard by a different section of the Supreme Court. The Court acknowledged Judge N.'s history but rejected the action. It ruled that under Austrian law, judicial bias was not a ground for nullifying a final decision, unlike the legal exclusion of a judge. The Supreme Court found that Judge N.'s situation was not “particularly grave” enough to warrant an exception.

The applicant company alleged that this situation constituted a breach of the principle of impartiality under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. It argued that the participation of a judge with a known personal financial interest in the case, who had previously withdrawn from similar matters, objectively compromised the impartiality of the proceedings before the Supreme Court. The domestic courts, by refusing to nullify the judgment, failed to remedy this fundamental procedural defect.

**Case: Halimi and Others v. Albania**  
**Application no. 33839/11 — European Court of Human Rights, First Section Committee**  
**Judgment: 7 April 2016 (rectified 26 April 2016)**

The case originated in an application lodged under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights by nine Albanian nationals against Albania. The applicants were represented by Mr S. Puto, while the Albanian Government were represented by Ms A. Hicka. The application was communicated to the Government on 20 December 2013. In its judgment, the Court noted that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, particularly *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation concern the applicants’ property rights and the failure to pay compensation. On 30 May 1995, the Vlora Commission recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights over a plot of land measuring 10,000 sq. m. However, the plot was occupied by others. Because the property could not be returned in kind, Albanian law provided that the applicants were to be compensated in one of the ways prescribed by law. Despite this official recognition of their entitlement, no compensation had been paid to date. Thus, more than two decades after the domestic recognition, the applicants remained without the compensation they were legally entitled to receive.

The relevant domestic law and practice had been described in earlier cases, including *Ramadhi v. Albania*, *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania*, and *Sharra and Others v. Albania*. Council of Europe materials were also referenced in *Sharra*, *Metalla and Others v. Albania*, *Siliqi and Others v. Albania*, and *Karagjozi and Others v. Albania*. These sources provided the background against which the Court assessed Albania’s compliance with its Convention obligations.

The alleged violation arose from the prolonged non-payment of compensation after the applicants’ inherited property rights had been formally recognised. In substance, the applicants complained that the failure to provide compensation violated their right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. They had a recognised property interest—or at least a legitimate expectation—in receiving compensation for the occupied land. The State’s indefinite delay and complete failure to compensate them imposed a disproportionate burden. Depending on the application, there may also have been an associated complaint under Article 13 concerning the lack of an effective domestic remedy to enforce the compensation entitlement or to obtain redress for the delay.

The Court’s reference to well-established case-law indicates that this case formed part of the wider, systemic problem of Albania’s failure to execute property compensation decisions or to pay compensation for recognised but occupied property. The essential facts for the alleged violation are therefore: (1) the Vlora Commission’s 1995 recognition of the applicants’ inherited rights over 10,000 sq. m. of land; (2) the fact that the land was occupied, which triggered a compensation entitlement rather than restitution; (3) the statutory promise of compensation under Albanian law; and (4) the continued failure, up to the date of the application and judgment, to pay any compensation. These facts made the application suitable for determination under the Court’s established case-law on Albanian property compensation.

**Summary of Jishkariani v. Georgia**

The case of *Jishkariani v. Georgia* (Application no. 18925/09) concerns a complaint lodged by Ms. Mariam Jishkariani, a Georgian psychiatrist and director of the NGO "Empathy," which provided rehabilitation services to torture victims. The applicant alleged that the domestic courts failed to protect her right to reputation under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights against defamatory statements made by the then Minister of Justice.

The events stem from a professional agreement between the applicant's NGO and the Ministry of Justice in October 2003 to create a psychosocial rehabilitation office in Tbilisi Prison No. 1. The applicant was also a member of the Public Monitoring Commission and the Inmates' Mental Health Research and Monitoring Commission. In September 2005, an inmate with mental health issues, transferred to the prison hospital based on the applicant's medical opinion, physically assaulted hospital staff. This incident, alongside a separate inmate death, fueled media allegations of corruption and mismanagement in the penal system's medical department.

On 16 September 2005, the Minister of Justice, Mr. K.K., spoke live on Rustavi 2 television, explicitly naming the applicant. He accused her of "grossly exceeding her powers," writing illegal medical conclusions, and being involved in corrupt "business" dealings. He claimed her "scribbles" led to the unjustified transfer of inmates and that she would be investigated alongside the Medical Department director. On 20 September 2005, the newspaper *Rezonansi* published an interview where the Minister further alleged the applicant was the "most important figure" in corruption, had "made a nest" in the monitoring council for personal gain, and was an "accomplice" in taking money from inmates.

The applicant filed a civil defamation suit against the Minister. She argued her conclusions were based on verifiable medical documents and that the corruption allegations were false, noting she was never formally accused. However, the domestic courts ruled against her. The Tbilisi City Court applied the Freedom of Expression and Speech Act, classifying the applicant as a "public figure," which required her to prove three cumulative conditions for defamation: the statement's falsity, resulting damage, and the speaker's knowledge of falsity or gross negligence.

While the court found the Minister's accusations "may have contained erroneous facts," it held the applicant failed to prove the other two conditions. It reasoned she did not demonstrate specific harm and that the Minister had taken "measures to verify" information by ordering an internal investigation three days prior to his televised statement, thus negating a finding of gross negligence. The court deemed his statements part of an important public discussion and acceptable criticism. The Court of Appeal upheld this judgment, emphasizing the applicant's obligation as a public figure to tolerate such criticism. The Supreme Court declared her appeal inadmissible in May 2008.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the domestic courts' failure to grant her any redress for the Minister's defamatory statements violated her right to respect for private life, specifically her professional reputation, under Article 8 of the Convention. The core of her alleged violation is that the national legal framework and its application failed to provide adequate protection for her reputation against false, public accusations of criminal and unethical conduct made by a senior government official.

In *Boguta and Tereshchenko v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, Committee) examined two Ukrainian applications alleging that domestic authorities failed to conduct effective investigations into the deaths of the applicants’ relatives. Application no. 13094/19 was lodged by Volodymyr Boguta on 28 February 2019; application no. 37726/19 was lodged by Yuliya Tereshchenko on 7 July 2019. The Ukrainian Government was given notice, and the Court adopted its judgment on 13 January 2022.

Boguta’s son, B., was found dead on 13 January 2007 on the ground floor of an unfinished 18-storey building in Truskavets, where he had been on vacation with his wife and friends. A same-day inspection and medical examination concluded that he died from multiple injuries caused by a fall from height, with no signs of violent death. Between January and May 2007, the Truskavets Town Prosecutor’s Office issued three decisions refusing to institute criminal proceedings; these were set aside as premature. A June 2007 medical examination found injuries atypical for a fall from height, repeatedly confirmed in 2009 and 2012. In January 2008, a criminal investigation into possible intentional murder was opened and transferred to Truskavets police. In March 2008, an investigator closed it for lack of evidence, accepting accident; that decision was quashed in April 2008. In October 2009, the case was transferred to Lviv Region police. Between October 2011 and October 2013, the investigator terminated proceedings four times; each decision was set aside by prosecutors and the Galytskyy District Court of Lviv. Those rulings noted failures to resolve discrepancies between witness statements and medical expert conclusions and to perform investigative steps ordered by prosecutors and courts. In March 2015, the case was transferred to Ternopil Region police. In March 2020, the investigator again closed it for lack of evidence; the Ternopil City Court quashed that decision in August 2020 as ill-reasoned. The investigation remained ongoing.

Tereshchenko’s daughter, U., was found dead on 25 June 2016 near a multi-apartment building in Kharkiv where her acquaintance Ye. lived. A criminal investigation for possible intentional murder began the same day. The applicant alleged that Ye., who had several convictions, was involved. A 27 June 2016 medical examination found minor head injuries, bruises and cuts on the left forearm, and an injection mark on the right arm. The expert concluded that death was caused by cardiomyopathy and blood circulation disorder against a background of medium alcohol intoxication. Between June 2016 and March 2017, the investigator issued three decisions closing the investigation for lack of crime, treating the death as natural. These were set aside by the Kominternivskyy District Prosecutor’s Office and District Court, which noted failures to question persons who had seen U. before her death (including Ye), to assess the evidence properly, especially the origin of the injuries, and to follow instructions on investigative steps. In March 2017 and October 2018, the Kominternivskyy District Court ordered police investigators to step out because of unjustified protraction. The investigation was still pending.

In both applications, the applicants complained of ineffective investigation into the death of their relatives, raising the procedural aspect of the right to life under Article 2 of the Convention.

In *Prokhorenko and Others v. Russia* (Application no. 12204/15 and 2 others), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) delivered judgment on 29 March 2018. The applications were lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants’ principal complaint was the inadequate conditions of their detention. In application no. 12204/15, the applicant also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The facts are set out in the appended table. The first applicant, Artem Aleksandrovich Prokhorenko, born 1 July 1985, introduced application no. 12204/15 on 15 February 2015. He was detained at IZ-47/1 St Petersburg from 21 November 2008 to 26 April 2015, a total of 6 years, 5 months and 6 days. He was held with 4 inmates and had approximately 2 m² of personal space. His specific grievances included overcrowding, lack of privacy for the toilet, lack of fresh air, passive smoking, insufficient natural light, insufficient electric light, no or restricted access to a shower, insufficient physical exercise in fresh air, inadequate temperature, and constant electric light. These conditions formed the factual basis for his alleged violation concerning detention conditions.

The second applicant, Yevgeniy Valeryevich Petrov, born 12 January 1975, introduced application no. 63371/16 on 20 October 2016. He was detained at IZ-1 Nizhniy Novgorod from 5 September 2016 to 3 October 2016, a period of 29 days. The cell held 11 inmates, with approximately 2.6 m² per inmate. His grievances included lack of fresh air, poor quality food, infestation of the cell with insects or rodents, a mouldy or dirty cell, lack of privacy for the toilet, lack or poor quality of bedding and bed linen, and lack of requisite medical assistance. These conditions were central to his complaint of inadequate detention.

The third applicant, Denis Sergeyevich Bankin, born 12 April 1977, introduced application no. 77886/16 on 12 December 2016. He was detained at IZ-6 Moscow from 15 August 2015 to 22 July 2016, lasting 11 months and 8 days. The table records 1.2 m² per inmate. His specific grievances were overcrowding, no or restricted access to running water, and no or restricted access to a toilet. These facts pointed to particularly severe overcrowding and lack of basic sanitation.

Overall, the case concerns three applicants held in different Russian pre-trial detention facilities over different periods. Their complaints focus on allegedly inhuman and degrading conditions of detention, including overcrowding, poor sanitation, lack of privacy, insufficient ventilation, light, exercise, shower access, and, in one case, inadequate medical assistance. The Court deliberated in private on 8 March 2018 and adopted the judgment on 29 March 2018. The judgment is final but subject to editorial revision. The appended list provides the detailed factual matrix relevant to the alleged violations.

In *Muhammad v. Spain*, the applicant, Mr Zeshan Muhammad, a Pakistani national who had lived in Spain since 2005 and held a long-term residence permit, alleged that a police identity check was carried out because of his dark skin colour. On 29 May 2013, while walking in a Barcelona street known for pickpocketing, he and his friend K.A. were stopped by two National Police officers. According to the applicant, when he asked whether he was being stopped because of his skin colour, an officer replied: “Yes, because you are black, and that’s all. I am not going to stop a German citizen.” He protested, and the officer allegedly slapped him, arrested him, called him “monkey”, and threatened negative consequences for his residence permit. His friend K.A. was also reportedly asked to show identification and complied. The police disputed this account. They claimed they approached the applicant only after he laughed at them and used disrespectful slang; he then refused to identify himself. He was taken to a police station, where he showed his NIE, was released, and received an administrative notice for refusing to identify himself and showing an insolent attitude. The police report did not mention K.A.

The applicant attempted to file a criminal complaint the same day but claimed two police stations refused to accept complaints against officers. The next day he lodged a handwritten criminal complaint. Criminal proceedings were opened and then discontinued, later briefly revived on appeal, but ultimately dismissed. Those proceedings concerned alleged defamation, bodily harm, unlawful detention, humiliation, intimidation, and forgery—not the allegedly discriminatory identity check. The police maintained that the applicant had refused to show his documents. K.A. could not be summoned, though the applicant submitted his notarised witness statement. No relevant video footage was found. The criminal proceedings were discontinued in 2015 and that decision became final in 2016.

In parallel, on 7 April 2014, the applicant brought an administrative State liability claim, alleging that the identity check was discriminatory and caused humiliation, exclusion, and marginalisation. He sought acknowledgment of unlawfulness, a public apology, EUR 3,000 in non-pecuniary damages, and publication of the judgment. He submitted statistical expert reports, reports from the Spanish Ombudsperson, ECRI, CERD, and NGOs documenting widespread racial profiling by Spanish police. He requested that the officers be heard and that video footage be obtained. The police submitted a report denying racial motive and citing his defiant attitude. The administrative authorities discontinued the claim on 6 November 2014 for lack of evidence and no causal link. Judicial review rejected his proposed evidence—including the friend, officers, and expert—and dismissed the appeal in September 2015, finding contradictory evidence and no causal link. A voidness application and an *amparo* appeal were unsuccessful.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, relying on Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12, the applicant complained that he had been required to identify himself solely because of his race, amounting to racial discrimination and a violation of his private life, and that the domestic authorities had failed to effectively investigate his allegations of racial profiling. The key alleged violation was therefore discriminatory identity checking and the State’s alleged failure to investigate and remedy racial discrimination.

In *Theo National Construct S.R.L. v. the Republic of Moldova* (Application no. 72783/11, ECtHR, judgment of 11 October 2022), the applicant, a Romanian road-construction company, alleged a “raider attack”: the illegal seizure of its goods with the assistance of allegedly corrupt courts and law-enforcement agencies. The complaint was examined under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

In 2007 the applicant agreed with a Moldovan businessman and political party leader, Mr Ș., to enter Moldova’s road-construction market. Under an agreement of 4 April 2007, the applicant was to acquire a 50% stake in company Q., contributing twenty-three pieces of road-construction equipment. The Moldovan Chamber of Commerce (MCC) valued the equipment at EUR 1,031,965. Elmazova and Others v. North Macedonia (Apps. 11811/20 and 13550/20) concerns alleged segregation of Roma primary-school pupils in two state-run schools in Bitola and Shtip. Eighty-seven Roma applicants—children and parents—complained under Article 14 ECHR and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12 that they suffered discriminatory treatment in education. They were represented by the European Roma Rights Centre and a Skopje lawyer. The ECtHR gave notice only of the Article 14 and Protocol No. 12 complaints.

In Application no. 11811/20, applicants lived in Bair, Bitola. G.S. and T.A. were state primary schools in the same catchment area, with G.S. designated as the compulsory-admission school. Parents could request transfer to another school with the admitting school’s consent. The applicants alleged that Roma children from Bair were enrolled at G.S., while ethnic Macedonian children from the same or neighbouring catchment attended T.A. T.A. allegedly allowed transfers of Macedonian pupils from G.S. but refused Roma pupils. In 2018/19, T.A. had seven Roma pupils and G.S. had five ethnic Macedonian pupils. Over 80% of G.S. pupils were Roma, and it was known as the “Romani or Gypsy school.” The applicants alleged inferior education at G.S.—fewer courses, less-skilled teachers, inadequate resources—and that segregation prevented interethnic contact and Roma integration. The Constitutional Court found 83.5% Roma at G.S. and 95.1% Macedonian at T.A., and stated that Bair children attended two ethnically divided schools. It nevertheless rejected the complaint, finding statistics insufficient; the applicants had not shown concrete transfer requests or refusals, and parents had voluntarily enrolled them at G.S. Three judges dissented, finding sufficient evidence of different treatment. By 2021/22, all 77 first-grade pupils at G.S. were Roma. In 2022, the domestic Commission found indirect discrimination/systemic segregation and recommended stricter catchment enforcement.

In Application no. 13550/20, the child applicants attended G.D. in Shtip. They alleged that in 2017/18 and 2018/19 first grade had three classes—two mixed and one Roma-only, each with 18 pupils—excluding Roma pupils from regular education and equal opportunities. The Constitutional Court found fewer ethnic Macedonian pupils enrolled because many transferred to out-of-catchment schools; Roma made up 64% of first-grade pupils in 2017/18 and 67% in 2018/19. It confirmed a Roma-only class but found no evidence Roma pupils received inferior education or different treatment. It held that ethnic composition alone did not automatically prove discrimination and that the complaint was premature because ordinary civil remedies under the Discrimination Act should be exhausted. In 2021/22, of 78 first-grade pupils, 63 were Roma, 14 Macedonian, and one Turkish; they were divided into four classes, two Roma-only. The Commission again found indirect discrimination and systemic segregation.

Domestic law required schools to admit catchment-area children, while transfers required consent. The Discrimination Act allowed civil discrimination claims, and Ombudsman reports since 2011 had documented Roma segregation and non-compliance with catchment rules in Bitola and Shtip.

In *Sinkova v. Ukraine* (no. 39496/11), the applicant, a Ukrainian national and member of the St Luke Brotherhood artistic group, complained under Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 5 and Article 10 of the Convention. The case arose from a December 2010 performance at Kyiv’s Eternal Glory Memorial and Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. On 16 December 2010, Sinkova and three others fried eggs in a frying pan over the Eternal Flame; two companions grilled sausages on skewers; another filmed. The participants made no speeches and displayed no posters. To reach the flame, Sinkova stepped over a wreath sculpture and on the inscription “Glory to the Unknown Soldier.” Police approached, said the behaviour was inappropriate, but did not interfere. Sinkova posted the video online with a statement protesting the pointless burning of natural gas at the memorial, estimating monthly taxpayer costs and suggesting Communist Party members keep eternal flames lit manually. The video used a Soviet song and titles such as “Recipe of the day” and “Eternal fried eggs on the eternal flame.”

After public complaints, criminal proceedings were opened. One participant, D., was questioned, admitted participating in a protest against gas waste, expressed regret, and identified Sinkova from passport-office photographs. Investigators questioned Sinkova’s grandmother and mother, who said she did not live at her registered address, was away in western Ukraine, and gave no contact details. On 18 February 2011, the case against Sinkova and two unidentified persons was severed, and she was declared wanted the same day. Her lawyer later claimed no summons had been sent before her arrest and that she learned of the charge only when arrested.

On 17 March 2011, the investigator sought her detention pending trial, citing the serious charge (three to five years’ imprisonment), her having absconded/wanted status, and risks of reoffending or obstructing truth. On 25 March, a court ordered her arrest to bring her before court. She was arrested on 29 March at another person’s flat. On 31 March, with counsel, she confessed and expressed remorse. On 1 April, the Pecherskyy District Court remanded her in custody, relying again on the serious charge, her wanted status, and risk of obstruction; it rejected character evidence and did not discuss personal guarantees from deputies. The Kyiv City Court of Appeal upheld this on 11 April. She was indicted on 25 May. On 17 June, her release application was refused based on the charge’s seriousness, nature/circumstances, and wanted status; she was released on 30 June under an undertaking not to leave town.

On 4 October 2012, she was convicted of desecrating the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier by a group following prior conspiracy and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment, suspended for two years. The court rejected her claim that the act was only a protest and noted she showed no remorse. On 18 December 2012, the appellate court upheld the conviction, saying desecration could be insulting or disrespectful regardless of motive, and that any Article 10 restriction was lawful and pursued a legitimate aim. Her cassation appeal was rejected on 11 April 2013. The key allegations were thus that her pre-trial detention violated Article 5 and that her prosecution and conviction for the performance violated her Article 10 freedom of expression.

Case Abdilla v. Malta (Application no. 36199/15) concerned an application against Malta by Jean Pierre Abdilla, a Maltese national born in 1975 and detained at the Corradino Correctional Facility, Paola. He was serving a sixteen-year prison sentence and a EUR 40,000 fine for drug-related offences, imposed on 3 December 2009 and confirmed on appeal on 19 September 2013. He lodged his application on 25 September 2015, alleging a violation of Article 3 of the Convention because of the conditions of his detention and a lack of an effective remedy under Article 13 read together with Article 3. The application was communicated to the Government on 8 February 2017.

The applicant was placed in Division 2, cell no. 88, on 10 December 2009. He remained in various Division 2 cells, except for two brief periods in 2011 in Division 6, a high-security unit, lasting nine and eleven days, the latter ending on 4 December 2011. From 4 December 2011 until 26 December 2014 he was held in cell no. 45, and thereafter in cell no. 70. He alleged that Division 2 was around 200 years old, required extensive maintenance, and lacked light and air. The windows were triple-barred, and three skylights were kept closed even during summer, causing excessive heat. He described the environment as squalid and foul-smelling.

As to cell no. 45, the applicant claimed it was nearly underground, structurally condemned, poorly ventilated, and affected by fumes and excessive heat from a nearby bakery. It was humid and cold in winter, and the triple bars meant he could barely see outside. Cell no. 70 was very small, had little ventilation, and made him feel claustrophobic. He also claimed he hardly ever had access to running water.

The applicant complained that food in Division 2 was poor quality, non-nutritious, and served in too-small portions. Between 1 and 4 September 2015, prisoners allegedly had to be taken to hospital because of food poisoning, and mice were found dead in a dirty kitchen. Toilets had no automated flushing system; inmates had to flush using a bucket. Running water in cells was intermittent, and available water was not potable. Inmates could buy bottled water, but their ability to do so was limited by lack of money. Showers often lacked hot water, were dirty, and were insufficient: mostly only one shower was available for all Division 2 inmates, with two in summer. One shower tray was broken and cracked, creating a risk of injury.

Telephone calls were very expensive and became more costly on 3 December 2014. Complaints to the prison authorities were unsuccessful. The prison allowance was too low, making tuck-shop goods expensive and affecting inmates’ ability to buy water and make calls. The applicant also alleged health issues and being confined to bed; the emergency buzzer in his cell never worked. When he tried to use it, no one came for thirty minutes, and staff then reprimanded him. Petitions and other inmates’ constitutional cases about the conditions produced no change.

The relevant domestic law was set out in Story and Others v. Malta, and relevant material in Yanez Pinon and Others v. Malta. CPT standards cited in the case state that a single-occupancy cell should measure 6m² plus space for a sanitary annexe, usually 1m² to 2m². The case therefore focused on whether the cumulative detention conditions amounted to inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3 and whether Malta provided an effective domestic remedy under Article 13.

In *Ruiz Pena and Perez Oberght v. Malta* (Applications nos. 25218/15 and 25251/15), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section) delivered judgment on 17 July 2018, final on 17 October 2018. Both applicants were detained at Corradino Correctional Facility in Paola, Malta, and alleged that their conditions of detention violated Article 3 of the Convention.

The first applicant, Mr Ruiz Pena, a Venezuelan national, had been detained since September 2009 and was serving a ten-year sentence imposed on 21 March 2012. Since 10 January 2013 he had been held in Division 3, cell no. 148. He never requested a transfer because this would have meant losing his individual cell and being placed in a dormitory, harming his privacy. He alleged that his cell had one window and one air vent, but the vent was clogged and the window was too high, requiring him to climb onto the sink to open or close it. Ventilation was inadequate, and the cell was extremely hot in summer and cold in winter. He claimed he was not given a heater despite requests and had only one blanket, with additional blankets and clothes coming from NGOs. In summer temperatures reached 35–40°C, and two fans he purchased merely circulated hot air. He had to flush the toilet with a bucket because of low water pressure, sometimes using more than one bucket, which was especially deplorable in summer. The old building’s ceiling released dust allegedly harmful to his lungs. Tap water was rusty and filthy, so he purchased drinking water. His prison job paid only €0.60 per day. The Government stated he received €34.77 every four weeks under “gratuity” and “Work and Pay” schemes since 2015, and that a six-pack of water cost €2.24.

The second applicant, Mr Perez Oberght, a Dominican national, had been detained since 24 November 2009 and was serving a nine-year sentence imposed on 15 October 2012. Since 27 January 2012 he had been in Division 3, cell no. 155, except one day in Division 6 on 3 October 2015. The Government said that after the complaint was communicated, he was asked whether he wanted a transfer and refused. He alleged that his cell window was over two metres high and difficult and dangerous to open; metal bars limited natural light; and although there were two ventilation openings, one was blocked, so ventilation was insufficient. The water was not drinkable, so he bought water. The Government stated he received €41.58 every four weeks from gratuity and Work and Pay schemes. He claimed ceiling dust affected his asthma; the Government said the dust was normal for Maltese stone and that he never requested paint. He also alleged humidity and lack of a heater caused frequent flu; the Government attributed humidity to his blocking the vent with a towel and failing to maintain the cell. He complained of poor light, making reading difficult; the Government cited ceiling and wall lights, a portable lamp, three skylights, and 400W bell lamps. Finally, he alleged the spiral staircase was unsafe for emergencies, as a stretcher could not be carried down and evacuation two at a time was impossible; the Government pointed to a walkway between divisions.

The applications were lodged on 1 July 2015. The complaint was communicated to the Government on 25 February 2016, and the remainder of application no. 25218/15 was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. Relevant domestic law appeared in *Story and Others v. Malta*, and relevant material in *Yanez Pinon and Others v. Malta*.

**Ciocodeică v. Romania** (Application no. 27413/09) concerned a Romanian national, Maria Ciocodeică, who alleged under Article 6 § 1, Article 13, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the State failed to effectively assist her in enforcing a final judgment awarding salary entitlements and that she had no effective remedy for the non-enforcement.

In 2004 the applicant sued her employer, private company C.G.H.T., seeking annulment of her dismissal and salary entitlements. On 29 September 2004 the Timișoara Court of Appeal gave a final judgment in her favour, ordering the company to revoke its dismissal decision and pay all salary entitlements from 17 October 2003 until the judgment, updated and index-linked, plus costs. The judgment was validated by the Timiș County Court on 15 November 2004.

On 21 January 2005 the applicant began enforcement through bailiff office M.S.R. & S.A.I. The bailiff served a payment notice on the company in January 2005, but the company refused to comply and challenged the enforcement. In February 2005, at the company’s request, the Timișoara District Court suspended enforcement, subject to a deposit of ROL 4,000,000, about EUR 90. The applicant sought urgent lifting of the suspension in May 2005, arguing she needed the salary payments for herself and her infant, but the court dismissed the request for lack of imminent damage.

In June 2005 the District Court allowed the company’s objection and annulled the enforcement because the bailiff had failed to serve the company with a copy of the enforceable judgment. The applicant’s appeal on points of law was dismissed in October 2005, making that annulment final. The company also obtained annulment of a bank-account restriction because it had been issued after the suspension. The bailiff later issued another payment notice in June 2005, posted with the enforceable judgment at the company’s entrance in July 2005. In November 2005 the applicant asked whether the company had complied; the bailiff replied that it had not. After that, no further exchange occurred. In May 2007 the bailiff issued a report declaring the enforcement time-barred under Article 389 of the old Code of Civil Procedure, because six months had passed since the last enforcement act and the creditor had remained passive. It was unclear whether the applicant received that report.

The applicant pursued other remedies. In May 2005 she sought immediate enforcement under Article 5803 of the old Code. In August 2005 the District Court ordered a coercive fine of ROL 500,000 per day, but in December 2005 the County Court allowed the company’s appeal, holding that the fine was not appropriate because the debt could be enforced by a bailiff. She also complained to the Ministry of Justice in July 2005; the complaint was rejected because the underlying judgment was final. In 2005 she filed criminal complaints alleging refusal to execute the judgment. An investigation began in December 2006 against the company administrator, M.D., but in February 2008 the prosecutor discontinued proceedings, finding no offence, and imposed an administrative fine of RON 1,000, about EUR 250. Her challenges were dismissed through January 2009. The company was later liquidated and struck off the register in 2014.

The applicant therefore alleged that the Romanian authorities failed to assist her in enforcing a final judgment against a private debtor and that available remedies—complaints against the bailiff, disciplinary or civil liability, and criminal proceedings—were ineffective.

**CASE OF VUJOVIĆ v. MONTENEGRO** (Application no. 75139/10) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section, Committee), delivered on 15 May 2018. The applicant, Mr Igor Vujović, was a Montenegrin and Norwegian national born in 1973, living in Oslo, Norway. He was represented by Mr Đ. Čepić, a lawyer practising in Belgrade. The Montenegrin Government was represented by its Agent, Ms V. Pavličić.

The case arose from criminal proceedings connected with a traffic accident in which a child died. On 26 April 2000 criminal proceedings were brought against the applicant and one other person. On 25 February 2003 the Court of First Instance in Podgorica convicted the applicant of endangering public traffic and sentenced him and his co-accused to one year and six months’ imprisonment. In 2006 the High Court in Podgorica quashed that judgment and remitted the case back to the Court of First Instance.

On 18 April 2007 the Court of First Instance again convicted the applicant and his co-accused, but reduced the sentence to one year and four months’ imprisonment. On 13 November 2009 the High Court reduced the sentence of the applicant’s co-accused, but upheld the first-instance judgment in respect of the applicant. The applicant’s appeal against that judgment was rejected on 14 June 2010.

The applicant then lodged a further appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 26 October 2010 the Supreme Court rejected it. On 11 December 2010, complaining about the overall length of the criminal proceedings, the applicant lodged an action for fair redress with the Supreme Court. That action was rejected on 31 December 2010. On 19 April 2013 the Constitutional Court rejected his ultimate appeal.

The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 13 December 2010 under Article 34 of the Convention. On 3 December 2014 the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings was communicated to the Government. Pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court, the complaint concerning the outcome of the criminal proceedings was declared inadmissible. Therefore, the only alleged violation examined by the Court concerned the excessive length of the criminal proceedings, an issue falling under the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The key facts for the length complaint are the chronology and duration of the proceedings. The criminal case began on 26 April 2000. A first-instance conviction was reached on 25 February 2003. It was quashed in 2006 and remitted. A second conviction followed on 18 April 2007. Appellate proceedings continued until the High Court decision of 13 November 2009 and the rejection of the applicant’s appeal on 14 June 2010. The Supreme Court rejected his further appeal on 26 October 2010. Thus, from the institution of proceedings to the final criminal-law decision, the case lasted approximately ten and a half years. The applicant also pursued domestic remedies specifically directed at the length complaint, but the Supreme Court rejected his fair-redress action on 31 December 2010 and the Constitutional Court rejected his appeal on 19 April 2013.

This procedural history, particularly the repeated remittal and successive appeals, formed the factual basis for the alleged violation of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The Court adopted its judgment on 15 May 2018.

In *Patalakh v. Germany* (Application no. 22692/15), the applicant, Ivan Patalakh, a Russian national, complained under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention that the German courts failed, or significantly delayed, reviewing the lawfulness of his remand detention. He alleged this caused the automatic and arbitrary continuation of his detention, violating his right to liberty and security.

On 30 October 2013, the Frankfurt am Main District Court issued an arrest warrant against the applicant on strong suspicion that he had aided aggravated fraudulent conversion, corruption, corruption in commercial practice and aggravated tax evasion involving several million euros. The warrant was based on a risk of absconding, given the possible heavy sentence, his lack of legal residence or significant ties to Germany, and the fact that his wife was a co-accused. There was also a risk of collusion. He was arrested the same day and placed in remand detention. The warrant was later expanded, and in December 2014 the prosecution charged him with multiple counts of aiding aggravated fraudulent conversion, corruption and tax evasion. The main proceedings opened in May 2015, trial began in June 2015, and in July 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment. The conviction was not final at the time of the Strasbourg proceedings. The arrest warrant was set aside in October 2016.

The detention-review history was central. From January 2014, the applicant unsuccessfully challenged his remand detention. On 28 July 2014, the Frankfurt am Main Court of Appeal ordered the prolongation of detention and directed that the file be resubmitted by 28 October 2014 for the next periodic review. It transferred competence for further reviews to the court with general jurisdiction until then. On 24 October 2014, the prosecution submitted the file to the Court of Appeal and requested an extension under Articles 121 et seq. of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant requested release on 7 November 2014 and later lodged complaints of bias against judges and complained about delay. The Court of Appeal encountered difficulties in obtaining the file, making enquiries of the Frankfurt Regional Court and later the Darmstadt Regional Court. The applicant’s lawyer submitted material in March 2015, and the applicant twice asked for a prompt decision. On 21 April 2015, he lodged a constitutional complaint alleging that the absence of a decision violated his right to liberty. The Federal Constitutional Court refused to accept it on 27 April 2015 without reasons. On 15 May 2015, the applicant was served with the Court of Appeal’s decision, taken on 15 April 2015 and issued on 13 May 2015, ordering continued remand detention. The Court of Appeal found a continuing risk of absconding and no undue delay in the criminal proceedings, considering detention proportionate. It did not address the duration of the review proceedings or give reasons for the delay.

Under German law, remand detention may exceed six months only where particular difficulty, unusual extent of investigation or another important reason justifies it. The Court of Appeal reviews such extensions and further reviews at least every three months. There is no fixed time-limit for the Court of Appeal’s decision, and time is suspended if the file is submitted before the deadline. The applicant’s complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 were communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

Delecolle v. France (Application no. 37646/13), ECtHR Fifth Section, judgment of 25 October 2018. The applicant, Roger Delecolle, a French national born in 1937, lived in Paris. In June 2009, aged 72, the guardianship judge placed him under enhanced protective supervision (curatelle renforcée) for five years at his adoptive daughter’s request. Medical reports excluded dementia but found slight cognitive impairment, psychological fragility and vulnerability, and a need to protect his assets. The Paris Regional Court upheld the measure in December 2009, finding he could no longer manage his real property, business interests or tax returns or dispose of property, though he could retain a bank account and cash card.

The alleged violation concerned Article 12 ECHR, the right to marry. In 2009 Delecolle asked his supervisor to authorise his marriage to M.S., a friend since 1996 and partner since 2008. They stressed the religious importance of marriage. On 17 December 2009 the supervisor refused, saying she had known him only a few months and lacked background to authorise a wedding. Under French Civil Code Article 460(1), a person under curatelle may marry only with the supervisor’s authorisation or, failing that, the guardianship judge’s authorisation.

The guardianship judge ordered a social inquiry by the UDAF and a medical opinion. On 18 January 2010 a psychiatrist found intellectual disorders; while Delecolle could consent to marriage, he was incapable of dealing with its property and financial consequences. **Salakhbekov and Abukayev v. Russia** (Applications Nos. 28368/09 and 28636/09) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by two Russian nationals against the Russian Federation under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants had taken part in the clean-up operation at the Chernobyl nuclear disaster site and were entitled to certain social benefits. In 2008 they applied for a recalculation of those benefits. Their claims were granted by domestic courts, which issued judgments in their favour. These judgments therefore became final domestic decisions recognizing the applicants’ entitlement to recalculated social benefits.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Convention violations arose after those favourable final judgments. The applicants complained that the time limits for lodging appeals against the final judgments were extended and that the final judgments in their favour were subsequently quashed. In other words, although domestic courts had already resolved the benefit recalculation claims in the applicants’ favour, the appellate process was later reopened through an extension of appeal time limits, and the final judgments were set aside. The Court communicated to the Government the complaints concerning the extension of the time limits for lodging appeals and the subsequent quashing of the final judgments. The remainder of application no. 28368/09 was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

Procedurally, the applications were lodged with the European Court of Human Rights. The applicant in application no. 28636/09 was represented by Mr Z.S. Salimov, a lawyer practising in Makhachkala. The Russian Government were represented initially by Mr G. Matyushkin, Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights, and later by his successor, Mr M. Galperin. On 24 April 2017, the complaints concerning the extension of appeal time limits and the quashing of the final judgments were communicated to the Government. The Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee, but after considering that objection, the Court rejected it.

The Court also noted that the relevant domestic law and practice governing the restoration of time limits for appeal were summarized in **Magomedov and Others v. Russia** (nos. 33636/09 and 9 others, §§ 35–43, 28 March 2017). That reference frames the central legal issue: the domestic practice permitting appeal time limits to be restored or extended, thereby allowing final judgments to be challenged and quashed. For the applicants, this practice was directly linked to the loss of their final judgments granting recalculation of Chernobyl-related social benefits.

The alleged violations therefore focused not on the initial benefit eligibility dispute, but on the fairness and legal certainty of the domestic proceedings after the applicants had already obtained final judgments in their favour. The case concerned whether the retrospective reopening and quashing of those final judgments, through extended appeal deadlines, infringed the applicants’ Convention rights. The Third Section Committee comprised Branko Lubarda (President), Pere Pastor Vilanova and Georgios A. Serghides, with Stephen Phillips as Section Registrar. The judgment was delivered on 29 May 2018, following private deliberations on 7 May 2018.
