text:
In *Lysak v. Ukraine* (Application no. 52299/14), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint by Ms Svitlana Vasylivna Lysak, a Ukrainian national born in 1949 and living in Cherkasy. The applicant was a private entrepreneur. The Court gave notice only of her complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. Her essential allegation was that equipment belonging to her and located on municipal land had been unlawfully dismantled, and that she had been unable to obtain compensation for that interference.

The facts concerned three kiosks—temporary structures for selling goods—that the applicant owned and operated on municipal land in three locations in Cherkasy. The municipal authorities considered that her rights to use the land had expired. The applicant challenged that assessment before the Cherkasy Regional Commercial Court. That court issued preliminary injunctions on 14 August 2008 and 19 May 2009 prohibiting the municipal authorities from dismantling her equipment. In a final decision of 31 March 2010, the commercial court declared the authorities’ assessment unlawful and ruled that the applicant continued to have the right to rent the land in question.

Separately, on 28 April 2009, the city executive committee ordered the municipal working group dealing with unlawful structures to proceed with the removal of the applicant’s equipment. Mr K., a member of that group and director of a municipal company, was directed to provide equipment for the dismantling operation and to arrange storage of the dismantled equipment. On 28 May 2009, despite the commercial court’s interim injunction, the municipal working group dismantled the applicant’s equipment and its contents—kiosks, cash registers and a stock of goods for sale—and placed them in storage. The applicant alleged that the equipment had been damaged during dismantling and had become unusable, and that the stock of goods had been lost.

Subsequent domestic proceedings confirmed elements of unlawfulness. On 21 September 2010, the Cherkasy Sosnivsky District Court, in a final decision, declared the executive committee’s decision of 28 April 2009 unlawful. It specifically noted that the decision had been taken in disregard of the commercial court’s injunctions. The applicant also lodged a criminal complaint accusing city officials of abuse of public office and other crimes. Mr K. was eventually charged with criminal dereliction of duty. Within those criminal proceedings, the applicant brought a civil claim for damages against Mr K. and the State Treasury. On 4 October 2013, Mr K. was found guilty but released from serving his sentence. The civil claim was dismissed, with the court stating that it could be resubmitted in separate civil proceedings. The conviction was later quashed and the case remitted for further investigation, most recently on 16 February 2016; no further developments were reported.

The applicant also sued the city council and the city executive committee in the administrative courts, seeking a declaration that their actions in removing her equipment had been unlawful, as well as damages. On 22 January 2014, the High Administrative Court upheld the lower courts’ decisions rejecting the claim. Those courts reasoned, in particular, that it would be appropriate for the applicant to seek compensation within the framework of the criminal proceedings against Mr K.

Thus, the key facts relevant to the alleged violation under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 are that the applicant’s possessions were dismantled despite court injunctions; a final domestic decision later declared the underlying removal decision unlawful; and the applicant was nevertheless unable to obtain compensation through criminal or administrative proceedings. The ECtHR’s review focused on whether this amounted to an unlawful interference with her property rights and a failure to provide compensation.

The case of **Çeki v. Turkey** (Application no. 50070/10) was a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Second Section) delivered on 10 July 2018. The applicant, Mesut Çeki, a Turkish national born in 1977, was detained at Kırıkkale F-type prison when he lodged the application on 25 June 2010. He was represented by lawyer C. Tombul, and the application was communicated to the Turkish Government on 4 September 2012.

The facts concerned the applicant’s arrest and prolonged detention in criminal proceedings for membership of a terrorist organisation. On 1 October 2004, he was taken into police custody on suspicion of being a member of a terrorist organisation. On 5 October 2004, he was brought before a judge at the Ankara Assize Court, who ordered his detention on remand. The judge relied on the nature of the offence, the state of the evidence, and the severity of the potential penalty. On 15 March 2005, the Ankara public prosecutor indicted him before the Ankara Assize Court for membership of a terrorist organisation.

On 31 January 2008, the Ankara Assize Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment. It also ordered that his detention continue. On 6 May 2009, the Court of Cassation quashed that judgment and remitted the case to the Ankara Assize Court for further examination. On 10 November 2009, the 11th Chamber of the Ankara Assize Court held a further hearing; both the applicant and his lawyer were present. At the end of that hearing, the court again ordered the continuation of the applicant’s detention.

On 10 December 2009, the applicant’s lawyer filed an objection against the 10 November 2009 detention decision. On 21 December 2009, the 12th Chamber of the Ankara Assize Court dismissed the objection without holding a hearing. In doing so, it relied on the written opinion of the public prosecutor, which had not been communicated to the applicant or his representative. This non-communication and absence of a hearing formed a central element of the alleged Convention violations, particularly regarding the judicial review of detention under Article 5 §4. The applicant complained that the procedure for challenging his continued remand was not adversarial and did not allow him or his lawyer to respond to the prosecutor’s submissions.

Subsequently, on 28 August 2012, the Ankara Assize Court once more convicted the applicant and sentenced him to 15 years’ imprisonment. On 8 July 2013, the Court of Cassation upheld that judgment. The relevant domestic law was described by reference to *Altınok v. Turkey*, *Demir v. Turkey* (dec.), and *A.Ş. v. Turkey*.

In essence, the case concerned the lawfulness and procedural fairness of the applicant’s detention on remand, especially the refusal of his objection to continued detention without a hearing and without disclosure of the public prosecutor’s written opinion. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore: the initial remand in 2004; the lengthy criminal proceedings and continued detention; the 2009 quashing of the first conviction; the 10 November 2009 continuation order; and the 21 December 2009 dismissal of the applicant’s objection on the basis of an uncommunicated prosecutor’s opinion. These facts raised issues under the Convention, principally the right to have the lawfulness of detention reviewed by a court in an adversarial procedure.

**Ashayev and Others v. Ukraine** (Applications nos. 24329/08 and six others) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 14 June 2018, adopted after private deliberations on 24 May 2018, and is final subject to editorial revision. The applicants lodged their applications against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates, and the applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

The common complaints were that civil proceedings in Ukrainian courts had been excessively long and that there was no effective remedy in domestic law for that length. These allegations correspond to complaints commonly examined under the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time and the right to an effective remedy (typically Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention). The appended table sets out the key factual details for each applicant.

**Application no. 24329/08**, introduced on 14 May 2008, was brought by Aleksey Dmitriyevich Ashayev (born 17 December 1948). His civil proceedings ran from 5 November 1997 to 6 July 1999 (1 year, 8 months and 2 days) and from 27 August 2000 to 15 November 2007 (7 years, 2 months and 20 days). Both sets of proceedings went through three levels of jurisdiction.

**Application no. 32126/11**, introduced on 17 May 2011, was brought by Lyudmila Grigoryevna Denisenko (born 10 May 1942).

In *Nicholas v. Cyprus* (Application no. 63246/10), the European Court of Human Rights examined a complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that a Cypriot Supreme Court judge was not objectively impartial because of a family and professional connection to the lawyer representing the opposing party. The applicant, Charalambos Nicholas, a Cypriot and British national born in 1951, lived in Larnaca. He had been dismissed from Cyprus Airways Ltd as a trainee pilot. On 26 June 1998 he brought a civil action in the Nicosia District Court against the company for wrongful dismissal and defamation (civil action no. 7562/98). The defendant company was represented by a law firm. On 29 December 2006 the District Court dismissed his action. On 9 February 2007 he appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 43/07). A three-judge bench heard the appeal. At the hearing on 11 March 2007, Mr P.G.P., the managing partner of the defendant’s law firm, appeared for the defendant and addressed the Supreme Court. Until then, other lawyers from the same firm had appeared before the appeal bench on behalf of the defendant. On 21 April 2010 the Supreme Court unanimously dismissed the appeal.

The alleged impartiality problem emerged after the appeal judgment. The applicant discovered that the son of one of the judges on the bench, Judge A.K., and the daughter of Mr P.G.P. were married, and that both worked at Mr P.G.P.’s law firm. This meant that the judge and the opposing lawyer were connected through their children’s marriage, and the judge’s son was employed by the opposing lawyer’s firm. The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee, delivered a judgment on 13 October 2022 in the case of *Khuren-Ool and Others v. Russia*. The case originated in applications lodged against Russia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Russian Government were given notice of the applications. The applicants complained principally of permanent video surveillance of detainees in pre-trial or post-conviction detention facilities. They also raised other complaints under the Convention. The Court deliberated in private on 15 September 2022 and adopted the judgment on that date. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

The key facts are set out in the appended table. The case involved six applications. The first applicant, Ivan Alimovich Khuren-Ool, born in 1973, lodged applications nos. 77300/17, introduced on 20 October 2017, and 29430/18, introduced on 5 May 2018. He was detained in IK-23 in the Krasnoyarsk Region from 23 January 2018 to 14 November 2018. The specific circumstance relevant to the surveillance complaint was that the video surveillance was conducted by opposite-sex operators.

The second applicant, Artem Mikhaylovich Lazarev, born in 1986, lodged application no. 33010/18, introduced on 16 August 2017. He was detained in IK-34 in the Krasnoyarsk Region from 13 July 2015 to 11 August 2017. The relevant specific circumstance was again the use of opposite-sex operators for video surveillance.

The third applicant, Roman Vladimirovich Chernoknizhnyy, born in 1979, represented by Nataliya Yevgenyevna Reyzer of Syktyvkar, lodged application no. 41663/18, introduced on 22 July 2018. He was detained in SIZO-1 in the Komi Republic from 17 April 2021, and remained detained at the time of the application. The alleged violation involved opposite-sex operators and detention in different cells with video surveillance.

The fourth applicant, Vladimir Fedorovich Ivanyutenko, born in 1972, represented by Leonid Leonidovich Krikun of St Petersburg, lodged application no. 58934/19, introduced on 12 November 2019. He was detained in SIZO-6 in St Petersburg from 22 February 2019 to 15 February 2020. The specific circumstance was video surveillance by opposite-sex operators.

The fifth applicant, Gulruz Nurilloyevich Azizulloyev, born in 1983, lodged application no. 23017/21, introduced on 13 April 2021. He was detained in IK-25 and IK-31 in the Komi Republic from 9 June 2019 to 21 November 2021. The alleged violation again involved opposite-sex operators and detention in different cells with video surveillance.

Overall, the case concerns allegations that permanent video surveillance of detainees, particularly where monitored by opposite-sex operators and across different cells, violated the applicants’ rights under the Convention. The applicants also raised other complaints, but the principal facts relevant to the alleged violation are the continuous surveillance in the listed detention facilities during the stated periods.

In *Kartvelishvili v. Georgia*, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints under Article 3 and Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) of the Convention. The applicant, Giorgi Kartvelishvili, a Georgian national, was serving sentences for murder and for refusing to obey a prison officer. On 6 January 2006 he was placed in Tbilisi Prison No. 7.

On 8 August 2006 prison officers conducted a surprise search of his cell. The inmates, including the applicant, were ordered into the corridor while the search was filmed. A written report stated that a penknife had been found under the mattress on a bed later identified as the applicant’s. The applicant was never shown or asked to sign that record. On 11 August 2006 he was charged with possessing a prohibited item under Article 378 § 2 of the Criminal Code.

At trial, which began on 12 February 2007, the prosecution relied mainly on the prison officers who had conducted the search. The applicant asked the court to examine the seven inmates who had shared his cell, arguing that they could describe the exact circumstances of the search, including whether the officers abused their powers or whether the knife could have been planted in his bed. He stressed that the charge rested solely on the officers’ statements and that the cellmates had never been interviewed during the pre-trial stage. The prosecutor opposed the request, noting that the cellmates were convicted prisoners. The Tbilisi City Court refused the application as unsubstantiated, finding that the applicant had not sufficiently demonstrated the need for those witnesses and that they were not trustworthy because of their criminal convictions.

The officers later gave inconsistent accounts of where the knife was found: between the mattress and blanket near the footboard; between the mattress and sheet near the headboard or pillow; or falling to the floor when the mattress was lifted. They also said the cell door had been open, so the cellmates could have observed from the corridor. The video recording showed officers examining the mattress about one metre above the floor; a metal object fell and was picked up, but it was unclear whether it had fallen from the mattress. The prosecutor conceded that the video did not establish with certainty where the knife was found. The applicant argued that a cellmate could have planted the knife and repeatedly sought the cellmates’ examination before the trial court, the appellate court, and the Supreme Court. On 1 March 2007 the Tbilisi City Court convicted him and sentenced him to three years. The Tbilisi Court of Appeal rejected his request to examine the cellmates, upheld the conviction, and increased the sentence to four years. On 11 February 2008 the Supreme Court rejected his cassation appeal without an oral hearing. These facts formed the basis of his Article 6 complaint that he could not obtain the attendance and examination of defence witnesses under the same conditions as prosecution witnesses.

As to Article 3, the applicant complained about detention conditions and inadequate medical treatment. On 7 November 2007 he reported fever and a cough and was transferred to the prison hospital. He was diagnosed with advanced pulmonary tuberculosis and early-stage hepatitis C. Doctors planned anti-TB DOTS treatment first, followed later by anti-HCV drugs. He began DOTS on 13 November 2007, received intensive hospital treatment, and continued antibiotics in prison. Tests later showed negative sputum cultures and no recurrence of TB. In 2010 blood tests showed low HCV activity; doctors prescribed anti-HCV drugs, warned of side effects, and the applicant postponed treatment in a written note dated 2 June 2010. The case file contained no further health information.

**TB Inžinjering d.o.o. v. Bosnia and Herzegovina** (Application no. 8181/21) is a European Court of Human Rights case concerning the prolonged non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment obtained by a private company against a public authority. The applicant company, TB Inžinjering d.o.o., was represented by Mustafa Alić, a lawyer practising in Tešanj. The application was lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms on 10 December 2020. The respondent Government were given notice of the application.

The central factual basis of the alleged violation was that the applicant company had obtained a domestic decision in its favour, but that decision was not enforced. The relevant domestic decision was issued by the Zenica Municipal Court on 4 October 2017. It was issued against the municipality of Maglaj, meaning that the debtor was a local public authority. The applicant therefore held a final and enforceable domestic judgment, but the authorities failed to secure its execution.

According to the appended table, the non-enforcement period began on 2 July 2018. At the time of the proceedings before the European Court, enforcement remained pending. The length of the enforcement proceedings was recorded as more than three years, eight months, and twenty-seven days. This prolonged failure to enforce the domestic decision formed the core of the applicant’s complaint.

The applicant complained specifically of the non-enforcement of the domestic decision issued in its favour against the municipality of Maglaj. In Convention terms, such a complaint typically raises issues under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, which guarantees the right to a fair hearing, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which protects the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The essential allegation was not that the domestic court had decided the underlying dispute incorrectly, but that the State had failed to ensure that a final judicial decision in the applicant’s favour was actually executed. Because the debtor was a municipality, the failure to enforce the judgment engaged the responsibility of the respondent State, which is required to organise its legal and administrative systems so that final judgments are executed within a reasonable time.

The case was heard by the Fourth Section of the Court, sitting as a Committee composed of Armen Harutyunyan, President, Jolien Schukking, and Ana Maria Guerra Martins, judges, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Court deliberated in private on 5 May 2022 and delivered its judgment on 25 May 2022. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: the applicant company obtained a favourable domestic decision from the Zenica Municipal Court on 4 October 2017; the debtor was the municipality of Maglaj; enforcement did not occur; the non-enforcement period started on 2 July 2018; and enforcement remained pending for over three years and eight months. These facts indicate that the applicant was unable to realise the benefit of a final judgment for a substantial period. The case thus concerns the State’s obligation to enforce final domestic decisions, especially where the debtor is a public body, and the alleged breach arising from the prolonged failure to do so. The excerpt provided does not include the Court’s full legal reasoning or final disposition, but it clearly identifies the non-enforcement of a final domestic judgment as the factual foundation of the applicant’s complaint.

The case *Marcinkevičius v. Lithuania* (application no. 24919/20) concerns an alleged violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, freedom of expression. The applicant, Mindaugas Marcinkevičius, a Lithuanian businessman and founder/shareholder of Vilniaus Prekyba, one of the largest retail groups in the Baltic region, was involved in a public and hostile conflict with N.N., another founder and major shareholder. In 2015 the applicant complained to law-enforcement authorities that Vilniaus Prekyba had used financial deals to avoid taxes, damage the State, and unjustly enrich N.N. A pre-trial investigation began in August 2015 but was discontinued in August 2016; that decision was upheld in November 2016. The applicant asked for reopening, submitting new material, but in December 2016 the prosecutor refused. The tax authorities later opened an inquiry into N.N.’s tax compliance, which remained pending.

On 1 December 2016 the applicant answered questions from a Delfi journalist; the article appeared on 2 January 2017. It quoted him alleging that companies belonging to Vilniaus Prekyba were used to transfer shareholders’ money to N.N.’s personal accounts, avoid Lithuanian

In *Vaščenkovs v. Latvia* (Application no. 30795/12, ECtHR, 15 December 2016), the applicant, Maksims Vaščenkovs, a Latvian national born in 1986, complained under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that the Latvian courts had failed to provide sufficient reasons for the suspicion that he had committed robbery when extending his pre-trial detention. He died on 3 November 2015, and his grandmother informed the Court that she wished to pursue the proceedings on his behalf. The application was lodged on 16 May 2012. On 10 July 2014, the complaint was communicated to the Government under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4, while the remainder was declared inadmissible.

The relevant facts began in July and August 2011, when the police opened four criminal investigations into three thefts and one robbery; these were joined on 29 August 2011. On 12 August 2011, the police arrested the applicant on suspicion of robbery. He was held on that basis until 14 August 2011, when he was placed under arrest on suspicion of theft. On 15 August 2011, the police applied to the Ludza District Court for his pre-trial detention in relation to the theft investigation.

On 16 August 2011, an investigating judge granted that application. The judge’s reasoning referred only to a suspicion of theft under section 175(3) of the Criminal Law, said to be confirmed by evidence gathered in the criminal case. The applicant appealed, but on 2 September 2011 the Latgale Regional Court dismissed the appeal, stating that the suspicion of theft was confirmed by information in the file. No further appeal lay against that decision.

On 19 September 2011, the public prosecutor charged the applicant with robbery, theft, involving a minor in theft, and petty theft. On 28 September 2011, the case was transferred to the Ludza District Court for adjudication, with the prosecution setting out its case and evidence. On 17 October 2011, the investigating judge decided to keep the applicant in detention, reasoning that the accusations of theft, robbery, petty theft, and involving a minor in theft were confirmed by evidence. No appeal lay against this decision.

On 28 December 2011 and 23 April 2012, the applicant’s detention was extended. The judge stated that detention was based on suspicion of theft, noted that in other criminal proceedings the applicant had been declared a suspect for petty theft and robbery, and said there had been no change in the reasons given in the 16 August 2011 detention order, which had been re-examined in subsequent decisions. In February, June, and August 2012, the applicant complained to the Ludza District Court that it had failed to assess his detention in relation to the alleged robbery.

On 6 August and 2 November 2012, and on 25 January 2013, the judge continued the detention using largely the same wording. She additionally noted that the twenty-four-month maximum period under section 277(7) of the Criminal Procedure Law had been observed because the applicant was also accused of an especially serious offence—robbery—under section 176(2). Those decisions were not subject to appeal.

Under domestic law, section 277(6) allowed a maximum of twelve months’ detention for a serious offence, while section 277(7) allowed up to twenty-four months for an especially serious offence. The alleged violation therefore concerned whether the domestic courts gave sufficient, specific reasons for the suspicion that the applicant had committed robbery, particularly when later extensions and the longer statutory maximum relied on that robbery charge, while the courts’ reasoning largely repeated earlier theft-based justifications and generic references to evidence.

Ciobotaru and Others v. Romania (Application no. 23572/14 and 3 others) is a case before the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), judgment delivered on 14 June 2018 by a Committee. The applicants—Vasilică Ciobotaru, Marius Galan, Marian Dragotă and Vasile-Adrian Panaite—lodged applications against Romania under Article 34 of the Convention on the dates shown in the appended table. The applications were communicated to the Romanian Government. The common complaint was that the applicants’ conditions of detention were inadequate, raising issues under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment. The key facts are set out in the appended table.

Ciobotaru (application 23572/14, introduced 28 April 2014; born 4 June 1980) was detained in Focșani Penitentiary from 15 February 2013 to 5 September 2014, a period of 1 year, 6 months and 22 days. He allegedly had only 1.43 m² of personal space. His specific grievances were overcrowding, lack of toiletries and infestation of the cell with insects or rodents.

Galan (application 73773/14, introduced 13 November 2014; born 18 September 1972; represented by Alina Gherman, Iași) was held in Iași Penitentiary and Botoșani Penitentiary from 28 October 2011 onward. The duration was described as more than 6 years, 5 months and 17 days and was still pending at the relevant time. His space per inmate ranged from 1.26 to 2.2 m². He complained of overcrowding, lack or inadequate hygienic facilities, insect or rodent infestation, no or restricted access to showers, poor quality food, lack of toiletries, lack or poor quality bedding and bed linen, lack or insufficient outdoor physical exercise, and inadequate temperature.

Dragotă (application 22053/15, introduced 25 May 2015; born 18 November 1958) was detained in Rahova Penitentiary from 10 September 2014 to 21 January 2016, i.e. 1 year, 4 months and 12 days. His space was 1.93–2.4 m² per inmate. He alleged overcrowding, lack or inadequate hygienic facilities, no or restricted access to warm water, lack of fresh air, inadequate temperature, lack or inadequate furniture, lack or poor quality bedding and bed linen, and infestation with insects or rodents.

Panaite (application 41700/15, introduced 16 October 2015; born 14 June 1974) was first held in Timișoara Arrest Centre from 17 January 2009 to 15 March 2009, a period of 1 month and 27 days. He was then held in Timișoara, Rahova and Arad Penitentiaries from 15 March 2009 to 14 October 2015, a period of 6 years and 7 months. His space was 2–2.7 m² per inmate. He complained of inadequate sanitary facilities, lack of fresh air, lack or insufficient electric light, lack or poor quality bedding and bed linen, lack or inadequate furniture, lack of toiletries, lack or insufficient outdoor physical exercise, insect or rodent infestation, bunk beds, no or restricted showers and poor food. He also alleged overcrowding, except during two periods in Arad Penitentiary: 5 November 2010–14 May 2012 and 25 May 2012–9 August 2012.

Overall, the case centres on allegations that detention in Romanian facilities, with very small living space and poor material conditions, amounted to inadequate conditions of detention under the Convention.

**CASE OF OTEGI MONDRAGON AND OTHERS v. SPAIN** concerned five Spanish nationals—Mr Arnaldo Otegi Mondragón, Mrs Jacinto García, Mr Díez Usabiaga, Mrs Zabaleta Tellería and Mr Rodríguez Torres—who lodged applications with the European Court of Human Rights in January 2015. The only complaint communicated to the Spanish Government was an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, namely the right to a fair hearing before an impartial tribunal. The applicants alleged that the panel of the Audiencia Nacional’s Fourth Section that tried them in the so-called “Bateragune” case lacked impartiality because it included a presiding judge who had previously shown bias against the first applicant.

The factual background involved two sets of criminal proceedings. In the first, on 2 March 2010, the first applicant was convicted by the Fourth Section of the Audiencia Nacional of encouragement of terrorism and acquitted of unlawful assembly and association. During the oral hearing, after the applicant had given evidence, the presiding judge asked him whether he condemned ETA’s violence. He refused to answer, and the judge replied that she “already knew that he was not going to give an answer to that question.” On appeal, the Supreme Court ruled on 2 February 2011 that this question and the judge’s reaction objectively revealed a preconceived opinion about the applicant’s guilt. It declared the judgment void and ordered a retrial before a different panel. On 22 July 2011, a new panel acquitted the first applicant.

Meanwhile, in 2009, criminal proceedings were brought against all five applicants in the Bateragune case. They were accused of belonging to, and being linked with, the terrorist organisation ETA, specifically through an alleged attempt to create a political party under ETA’s control. These proceedings were allocated to the same Fourth Section of the Audiencia Nacional, composed of the same judges who had sat in the earlier case against the first applicant, including the same presiding judge, though she was not the judge rapporteur. The first applicant challenged the entire panel, arguing that the presiding judge’s previously established bias created an objectively justified doubt about the impartiality of the whole section. On 26 April 2011, a special chamber of the Audiencia Nacional rejected the challenge, finding that the new proceedings concerned different charges and that no bias was shown.

On 16 September 2011, the Audiencia Nacional convicted the first and third applicants of membership and leadership of a terrorist organisation, sentencing them to ten years’ imprisonment. The second, fourth and fifth applicants were sentenced to eight years for belonging to a terrorist organisation. All were also disqualified from standing in elections for the same periods. On appeal, the Supreme Court, by a 3-to-2 majority on 7 May 2012, reduced the sentences to six years and six months for the first and third applicants and six years for the others, but rejected the impartiality complaint. It held that bias shown in previous, different proceedings did not automatically contaminate the judges in later proceedings. Two dissenting judges disagreed; one found a violation of impartiality, while the other considered the evidence insufficient for conviction.

The applicants then lodged amparo appeals. On 22 July 2014, the Constitutional Court, by 7 votes to 5, rejected the main appeals, finding that the doubts about the presiding judge’s impartiality were not objectively justified because the earlier and later proceedings concerned different offences. Five dissenting judges considered that the applicants’ right to an impartial tribunal had been violated. A separate amparo by the third applicant was also rejected on 22 September 2014. The key issue before the ECtHR was therefore whether the prior finding of bias against the presiding judge, combined with her participation in the later Bateragune trial, created objectively justified doubts about the impartiality of the tribunal for all applicants.

**Case:** *Qerimi and Canaj v. Albania* (ECtHR, First Section, 8 September 2016; Applications nos. 12878/10 and 74858/12)

The case originated in two applications lodged by two Albanian nationals under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants complained, in substance, about the Albanian authorities’ failure to enforce final decisions of local property restitution and compensation commissions. The Court noted at the outset that the underlying legal issue was already the subject of well-established case-law, referring in particular to *Manushaqe Puto and Others v. Albania* (2012).

**Key facts – Application no. 12878/10 (Qerimi):**  
On 1 November 2002, the Durrës Commission on Restitution and Compensation of Properties recognised the applicant’s inherited property rights, together with other heirs, over a plot of land measuring 8,000 sq. m. Because the plot was occupied, the Commission decided that the applicant and the other heirs would be compensated in kind with an equivalent plot of land. The decision therefore acknowledged a property entitlement and provided for substitute land, but the compensation was apparently not delivered. This failure formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint.

**Key facts – Application no. 74858/12 (Canaj):**  
On 23 November 2001, the Fier Commission recognised the applicant’s inherited property rights, together with other heirs, over a plot of land measuring 1,121 sq. m. Of that area, 598 sq. m were restored to the heirs. The remaining 523 sq. m were occupied, so the Commission awarded financial compensation in the amount of 251,040 Albanian Lek (ALL). As with Qerimi, the decision was not effectively enforced or the compensation was not paid, which prompted the applicant to apply to the European Court.

**Procedure:**  
The applications were communicated to the Albanian Government on 20 December 2013. The Government were represented by the State Advocate’s Office. The applicants failed to submit claims for just satisfaction within the time-limit set by Rule 60 of the Rules of Court. The Court referred extensively to the relevant domestic law and practice described in earlier cases such as *Ramadhi*, *Manushaqe Puto*, *Sharra and Others*, *Metalla and Others*, *Siliqi and Others*, and *Karagjozi and Others*. It also referred to relevant Council of Europe materials.

**Relevance to alleged violations:**  
The essential alleged violation was the non-enforcement of final domestic decisions recognising property rights and awarding restitution or compensation. The facts indicate that the applicants had obtained favourable decisions from the competent restitution commissions, but those decisions remained ineffective: Qerimi did not receive the equivalent plot, and Canaj did not receive the monetary compensation for the occupied portion. Such prolonged non-enforcement engages Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (protection of property) because it interferes with the applicants’ peaceful enjoyment of their possessions and with the compensation owed to them. It also engages Article 6 § 1 of the Convention (right to a fair trial/access to court), since the final decisions were not executed and the applicants lacked an effective means of obtaining enforcement.

Because the Court considered the issue already settled by its case-law, the case did not require new factual or legal development. The central facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the two commission decisions, the property areas involved, the compensation awarded—in kind for Qerimi and partly monetary for Canaj—and the authorities’ failure to enforce those awards.

In *Yalanskyy and Galunka v. Ukraine*, the European Court of Human Rights examined two applications lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention. The Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, was composed of André Potocki (President), Síofra O’Leary and Mārtiņš Mits, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 3 May 2018, adopted after private deliberations on 12 April 2018, and is final but subject to editorial revision. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

Application no. 15131/17 was introduced on 8 February 2017 by Yaroslav Igorovych Yalanskyy, born 17 January 1975, represented by Olena Viktorivna Shapoval in Kyiv. The key fact for his complaint is that criminal proceedings involving him began on 22 September 2008 and were still pending at the time the application was lodged. By then, the proceedings had lasted more than nine years and five months and had passed through three levels of jurisdiction. The alleged excessive length was therefore continuing, rather than a completed delay.

Application no. 36543/17 was introduced on 12 May 2017 by Nadiya Mykhaylivna Galunka, born 27 October 1959, represented by Mykhaylo Yosypovych Bordyuk in Chervonograd. Her criminal proceedings began on 15 February 2010 and were also still pending. They had lasted more than eight years and one month and had involved one level of jurisdiction. As with Yalanskyy, the central factual basis for her complaint was the prolonged duration of the criminal case against her.

Both applicants complained of the excessive length of criminal proceedings and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. In Convention terms, such complaints normally concern the right to a hearing within a reasonable time and the right to an effective remedy for that delay. The applicants alleged that the Ukrainian authorities had failed to determine their criminal cases within a reasonable period and that no effective domestic mechanism existed to provide redress for the delay. These complaints were the principal matters communicated to the Government.

In addition, in application no. 36543/17, Galunka raised another complaint under Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention. The provided text does not set out the factual background of that additional complaint or the Court’s assessment of it. It is therefore not possible to summarize its specific factual basis from the excerpt. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are thus the dates and duration of each applicant’s criminal proceedings, their pending status at the time of application, the number of jurisdictional levels involved, and the alleged absence of an effective domestic remedy. The applicants were not, in this excerpt, challenging the merits of the criminal charges as such; their complaints focused on delay and the lack of remedy. The portion of the judgment supplied does not include the Court’s final legal findings or conclusions on the merits.

In *Sergey Smirnov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 36853/09), the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Mr Sergey Aleksandrovich Smirnov, a Ukrainian national born in 1965. On 3 April 2008 the applicant shot and seriously injured a person and was arrested at the scene. He remained in detention during criminal proceedings, mainly at the Kharkiv pre-trial detention centre. On 14 April 2009 the Kharkiv Court of Appeal sentenced him to ten years and six months’ imprisonment with confiscation of property; the Supreme Court upheld that judgment on 29 December 2009. He served his sentence in several correctional colonies, including the Slovyanoserbsk Correctional Colony in the Luhansk Region from 11 May 2010 to 7 April 2011. He was transferred to a semi-open institution in May 2015 and released in December 2015.

The Court communicated four main sets of complaints to the Ukrainian Government: conditions of detention at the Slovyanoserbsk Colony, allegedly inadequate medical assistance in detention, alleged interception and monitoring of his correspondence, and the alleged lack of an effective domestic remedy. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection without reasons.

As to conditions of detention, the applicant was placed in a single-occupancy cell on 13 May 2010 at his own request because he feared attacks by other inmates. Later prison reports stated that he refused to move to a dormitory, citing fear of violence. He claimed that the isolation cell measured 4.5 sq. m in total, including toilet and washbasin, with only about 1 sq. m of living space. After the case was communicated, he further alleged that average living space in the colony’s dormitories was 2.8 sq. m per inmate, relying on a CPT report of 23 November 2011 which noted overcrowding in most dormitories.

Regarding correspondence, the applicant alleged systematic monitoring of all his mail. He stated that on 22 July and 9 September 2009 the prison administration handed him two letters from the Court, and on 18 December 2010 a letter from the parliamentary secretariat, all of which had been opened. Prison registers showed that between July 2009 and December 2010 he sent at least forty-seven letters to public entities covered by monitoring, including courts, the High Council of Justice, the prison department and Parliament. These entries often contained brief summaries or were marked as applications, petitions or complaints. By contrast, letters to the Court and his lawyer were marked as “sealed letter.” Under domestic law, correspondence with the Court, international institutions and prosecutors was exempt from monitoring; from February 2010, correspondence with lawyers was also exempt.

On medical care, the applicant alleged inadequate treatment for digestive, back and other conditions. He was diagnosed with chronic gastroduodentitis in January 2010 and treated in the Kharkiv SIZO medical unit in April 2010. In February 2011 a colony doctor recommended transfer to Luhansk SIZO hospital for examination and treatment, but no transfer followed. In October 2011 a civilian hospital diagnosed acute pancreatitis, duodenopathy, gastric stasis, oesophagitis and chronic hepatitis and prescribed medication and a diet. The next day a colony doctor recommended hospitalisation at Temnivka prison hospital; the applicant refused, saying he mistrusted prison doctors. He later alleged that medication and dietary recommendations were not provided. He had osteochondrosis since 1998; in 2012 an MRI was performed and a surgeon recommended specialist neurological examination and treatment, which he alleged was not implemented. In 2013 a traumatologist prescribed painkillers, anti-inflammatory medication and a back-support device, also allegedly not implemented. In 2015 he underwent spinal surgery in a civilian institution and was later recognised as a Category 2 disabled person. He also suffered bronchitis, fungal nail infection and heart-related conditions.

The case therefore centred on the applicant’s allegations that his detention conditions, medical care and correspondence while imprisoned violated the Convention, and that no effective domestic remedy existed for those complaints.

In *Grytsenko and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 56576/08 and three others), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee) considered applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The Committee comprised André Potocki (President), Síofra O’Leary and Mārtiņš Mits, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was adopted on 1 February 2018 and delivered in Strasbourg on 22 February 2018. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government.

The applicants complained primarily of the excessive length of civil proceedings and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. In application no. 56576/08, the applicant also raised other complaints under the Convention, but the appended table does not set out their details.

The key facts concern four applicants and the duration of their civil proceedings:

**Application no. 56576/08** was introduced on 10 November 2008 by Leonid Ivanovych Grytsenko (born 1956). His civil proceedings began on 30 June 1997 and ended on 6 June 2006, lasting 8 years, 11 months and 8 days across three levels of jurisdiction.

**Application no. 21916/09** was introduced on 31 March 2009 by Sergey Gennadiyevich Nefedov (born 1959). It concerned four separate sets of proceedings: 11 May 2005 to 16 November 2006 (1 year, 6 months and 6 days, two levels); 29 March to 23 April 2007 (26 days, two levels); 6 August 2007 to 3 December 2008 (1 year, 3 months and 28 days, two levels); and 5 May 2010 to 7 February 2012 (1 year, 9 months and 3 days, two levels). These formed the basis of his length complaint.

**Application no. 54466/09** was introduced on 1 October 2009 by Georgiy Volodymyrovych Khrykin (born 1945). It involved two civil cases: 24 November 2003 to 20 October 2006 (2 years, 10 months and 27 days, three levels); and 22 February 2007 to 11 June 2010 (3 years, 3 months and 21 days, three levels).

**Application no. 26724/17** was introduced on 31 March 2017 by Volodymyr Fedorovych Kunayev (born 1960). It concerned two sets of proceedings: 25 June 2007 to 8 February 2008 (7 months and 15 days, one level); and 13 May 2011 to 23 November 2016 (5 years, 6 months and 11 days, three levels).

The alleged violations therefore arise from the length of civil proceedings in each applicant’s domestic cases. Under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, civil disputes must be determined within a reasonable time. The applicants argued that delays ranging from several months to almost nine years, and in some cases spanning multiple proceedings and appeal levels, were excessive. They further complained under Article 13 that Ukrainian law did not provide an effective remedy to challenge or obtain redress for those delays. The Grytsenko application additionally raised other Convention complaints, but only the length-and-remedy allegations are detailed in the provided factual table. The Court’s factual focus was thus the duration of each proceeding, the number of jurisdictional levels involved, and the absence of an effective domestic remedy.

In *Voykin and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 47889/08), four Ukrainian applicants—Mr Voykin, his wife, his mother-in-law, and his mother—complained under Articles 3, 5, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The case arose from an alleged assault by a police officer, subsequent criminal proceedings against the first applicant, and police searches of family homes.

The central Article 3 complaint concerned the second applicant. On the night of 18–19 June 2008, she alleged that M., a police officer and colleague of her husband, approached her in the street while heavily drunk and in plain clothes. She claimed he searched her bag, grabbed her by the neck, strangled her, and hit her head with a heavy object. She sought medical help and was diagnosed with neck bruises, concussion, and situational neurosis. She immediately called the police and later complained to the prosecutor’s office.

The investigation was protracted and repeatedly restarted. On 28 June 2008 the Kalyninskyy police refused to open a criminal case. After the second applicant complained, the Kalyninskyy prosecutor’s office quashed that refusal on 25 July 2008, noting that the investigation had wrongly been handled by the police force to which M. belonged. Further refusals followed on 1 and 14 August 2008; each was annulled as premature or incomplete. Forensic examinations in August and October 2008 found a neck bruise and concussion caused by blunt objects, consistent with her account, though no visible head injuries were documented. M. and his witnesses denied ill-treatment, claiming the second applicant was drunk and aggressive and that he had not touched her. Prosecutors repeatedly refused to charge M., relying on conflicting witness statements, the insignificance of injuries, and the fact that M. had not acted in an official capacity. Higher prosecutor complaints were dismissed or forwarded, leaving her without a criminal investigation.

The first applicant, a district police officer, alleged that after his wife’s complaint, the Kalyninskyy police threatened him and his family with dismissal, prosecution, or worse. In September 2008, criminal proceedings were opened against him for abuse of power and forgery relating to a 2008 administrative offence report. He was summoned, but stayed away, citing fear and knee surgery. On 13 September 2008 a court authorised his arrest, and on 19 September he was declared wanted. He was arrested on 29 June 2009 at the home he shared with his wife. On 3 July 2009 the court ordered his pre-trial detention without detailed reasoning. On 21 July 2009 the Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal quashed that ruling and released him, finding the first-instance court had failed to justify the strictest preventive measure. He was later convicted of abuse of office, forgery, and bribe-taking, with various appeals and reclassifications.

The Article 8 complaints concerned searches of the flats of the third and fourth applicants. In September 2008, police searched the third applicant’s flat, allegedly breaking the door, threatening the occupants, failing to show a warrant, and planting cannabis. The fourth applicant’s flat was searched on 16 September 2008, and again in February 2009, with documents allegedly planted or irrelevant items seized. The third and fourth applicants complained repeatedly, but prosecutors refused to investigate the police actions, and the courts did not provide copies of the search authorisations.

Overall, the facts alleged ill-treatment by police and a failure to investigate it, retaliatory criminal proceedings and unjustified detention, and unlawful home searches without effective remedies.

Pázsi and Others v. Hungary (Application no. 72595/13 and eight others) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fourth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 15 November 2018 and adopted after private deliberations on 25 October 2018. The case arose from nine applications lodged against Hungary under Article 34 of the Convention between 2013 and 2015. The applicants were János Pázsi, Ferenc Sánta, Beshir Ademi, György Hunvald, Ali Zaki Toohaw, Bertalan Kovács, Mihályné Zsíros, Bettina Zsíros-Vagyóczki, and Leonárd Weinek. Notice of the applications was given to the Hungarian Government.

The applicants’ principal complaint was that the criminal proceedings against them were excessively long, contrary to the right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 §1 of the Convention. In application no. 39649/15, brought by Leonárd Weinek, the applicant also complained under Article 13 that he had no effective domestic remedy for the excessive length of the proceedings.

The appended table set out the key facts. Pázsi’s proceedings ran from 8 August 2008 to 3 July 2013, a total of 4 years, 10 months and 26 days at one level of jurisdiction. Sánta’s ran from 10 May 2009 to 17 April 2014, 4 years, 11 months and 8 days at two levels. Ademi’s ran from 27 August 2009 to 2 September 2014, 5 years and 7 days at two levels. Hunvald’s ran from 1 October 2010 to 12 February 2015, 4 years, 4 months and 12 days at two levels. Toohaw’s ran from 31 December 2008 to 27 November 2014, 5 years, 10 months and 28 days at three levels. Kovács’s ran from 22 March 2010 to 1 May 2015, 5 years, 1 month and 10 days at two levels. Mihályné Zsíros’s ran from 15 February 2010 to 6 May 2015, 5 years, 2 months and 22 days at two levels. Zsíros-Vagyóczki’s ran from 16 April 2010 to 6 May 2015, 5 years and 21 days at two levels. Weinek’s ran from 30 November 2010 to 12 February 2015, 4 years, 2 months and 14 days at two levels.

Thus, the alleged delays ranged from about four years and two months to nearly five years and eleven months. Most proceedings involved two levels of jurisdiction, one involved one level, and one involved three. The applications were introduced on various dates between 13 November 2013 and 6 August 2015. The underlying criminal charges are not described in the provided extract; the case focuses on the duration of the proceedings and, for Weinek, the availability of an effective remedy. These facts formed the basis for the complaints that the domestic criminal proceedings failed to satisfy the reasonable-time requirement under Article 6 §1 and, in one application, that Hungarian law lacked an effective remedy under Article 13 for that delay.

text:
The case of *Starenkiy and Rudoy v. Ukraine* (Applications nos. 44807/10 and 15752/14) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee composed of Judges André Potocki (President), Síofra O’Leary, and Mārtiņš Mits, with Liv Tigerstedt as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was delivered in Strasbourg on 11 January 2018 and adopted after private deliberations on 7 December 2017. Both applications were lodged against Ukraine under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Ukrainian Government was notified of the applications. The applicants principally complained of inadequate conditions of detention and the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. They also raised other complaints under Convention provisions.

The first applicant, Demyan Ivanovych Starenkyy, born 23 November 1968, introduced application no. 44807/10 on 20 May 2008. He was detained in Sokalska correctional colony no. 47 from 21 June 2006 to 27 March 2012, a total of 5 years, 9 months, and 7 days. During this period, he had approximately 3 square metres of personal space per inmate. His specific grievances were that the shower was available only once a week; there was no isolated toilet; nutrition was bad; the cell lacked ventilation; and in summer the cell became very hot and lacked fresh air. These conditions formed the factual basis for his complaint that detention conditions were inadequate and that no effective domestic remedy existed to address them.

The second applicant, Igor Vasilyevich Rudoy, born 26 May 1969, was represented by Vyacheslav Yuryevich Malyar of Odessa. He introduced application no. 15752/14 on 27 January 2014. He was held in Kyiv SIZO no. 13 from 10 November 2010 to 25 January 2014, a total of 3 years, 2 months, and 16 days. He had approximately 2 square metres per inmate. His specific grievances were severe overcrowding—20 inmates in a cell measuring 30.2 square metres; lack of heating in the cell; lack of hot water; lack of ventilation; other inmates smoking in the cell; lack of drinking water; lack of daylight; high humidity and mould on the cell walls; lights kept on for 24 hours; shower available only once a week; and bad nutrition. These facts underpinned his Convention complaint about inadequate conditions of detention and the absence of an effective remedy.

The Court’s judgment concerned the alleged violations arising from these conditions and the alleged lack of domestic redress. The available text does not set out the Court’s full reasoning or final conclusions on each complaint, but it records that the applications were communicated to the Government and that the Court deliberated and adopted its judgment. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the duration of detention, the amount of space per inmate, and the specific material conditions—especially overcrowding, sanitation, ventilation, heating, humidity, lighting, and nutrition—experienced by each applicant.

**Summary of *Cabral v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 37617/10)**

The case of *Cabral v. the Netherlands* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Euclides Cabral, a Netherlands national, on 25 June 2010. The applicant alleged that his criminal conviction for a street mugging was based solely or to a decisive extent on the statements of a witness, identified as V., whom he had not been able to effectively examine, in violation of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention, which guarantees the right to examine witnesses against the accused.

The factual background involves four charges against the applicant: three supermarket robberies and one street mugging outside a discotheque. The prosecution's case heavily relied on statements made to the police by V., an accomplice in the supermarket robberies who also implicated the applicant in all four crimes. V. initially confessed to police and named the applicant as a co-perpetrator.

The domestic proceedings unfolded across three levels. Before the Regional Court, V. was summoned as a defence witness. Regarding the street mugging, V. was not a suspect, so he was compelled to testify. He provided a statement disculpating the applicant, claiming he had not witnessed the robbery and had only heard from bystanders that the perpetrators did not include the applicant. This exculpatory statement was disbelieved by both the prosecutor and the court, leading to V. being charged with perjury. The Regional Court convicted the applicant on all four counts.

On appeal, V. was again summoned but this time remained silent on all charges, including the street mugging for which he was facing a perjury prosecution. Despite his refusal to be cross-examined, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on all charges. For the fourth charge (the street mugging), the evidence cited in the judgment consisted of the supermarket manager's report, a cashier's statement, and V.'s confession to the police naming the applicant.

The applicant then appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that using V.'s police statements without allowing for cross-examination violated his defence rights. The Advocate General advised that V.'s evidence was "sole and decisive" for the fourth charge. However, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, relying on its existing case-law. It held that the applicant had been given a sufficient opportunity to cross-examine V. The fact that V. refused to answer questions did not, in itself, render his prior police statement inadmissible under Article 6 § 3 (d).

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore: (1) The applicant's conviction on at least one charge was based decisively on statements made by V. to the police. (2) V. was summoned by the defence at both the trial and appellate stages. (3) During the appeal, where the conviction was finalised, V. refused to answer any questions, thereby denying the applicant any opportunity for effective cross-examination on his police statements. (4) Despite this refusal, the domestic courts used V.'s untested police statements to ground the conviction, finding that the opportunity to summon him was sufficient. This situation formed the basis of the applicant's complaint to the European Court that his right to examine a decisive witness against him had been violated. The case also notes a subsequent shift in Dutch Supreme Court case-law in 2013, which reversed the position held at the time of the applicant's conviction.

The case *Kešelj and Others v. Montenegro* (Application no. 33264/11) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 May 2011 by ten nationals of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The applicants complained about the continued non-enforcement of a final court settlement concluded in their favour. On 12 January 2017, the Court communicated to the Montenegrin Government the complaints concerning non-enforcement of that settlement, while declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

The central facts concern a court-approved settlement reached on 28 February 1996 before the Cetinje Municipal Court between the applicants and the debtor, JSP “Tara” Cetinje. Under that settlement, the debtor undertook to pay the applicants specified amounts in respect of both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. The settlement became final on the same date, meaning it was binding and enforceable. The debtor eventually paid only part of the amounts due under the settlement.

On 26 May 1997, the Podgorica Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against the debtor. On 19 August 1997, the applicants submitted their respective claims based on the settlement. During the insolvency proceedings, the Podgorica Commercial Court acknowledged the applicants’ claims. On 23 December 2009, the Podgorica Commercial Court formally terminated the insolvency proceedings against the debtor but continued the proceedings against the debtor’s estate.
