*N.V. and C.C. v. Malta* (Application no. 4952/21) concerned a Maltese mother, N.V., and her British partner, C.C., who complained under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights about a Family Court order that severely restricted their family life.

N.V. had a son, E., from a prior marriage to J. After separating, N.V. obtained custody of E., while J. had access rights. In 2009 N.V. moved to Malta with E. and began living with C.C.; they later had a child together in 2016.

In 2012 J. brought Family Court proceedings concerning access. Tensions included C.C.’s presence during visits. In July 2015, after an incident, J. alleged that C.C. had come to his house, threatened to kill E., and had psychological problems. N.V. claimed instead that C.C. had been the victim of violence. J. sought custody and the forced removal of E.

On 1 October 2015, relying in part on a sealed Children’s Advocate report that was not disclosed to the parties, the Family Court ordered N.V. not to expose E. to C.C., with immediate effect. It also warned N.V. about hindering J.’s access and ordered monitoring. N.V. asked for variation and for C.C. to be heard and evaluated. On 28 October 2015, without a hearing, the court dismissed her requests, citing only “some of the reasons” in the objection and giving no specific reasoning.

A psychologist’s report of 25 November 2015 later found that E. was fond of C.C., missed him, and that there was nothing dangerous or untoward in their relationship; it recommended continued contact. Despite this, the October decree remained in force. As a result, N.V. and C.C., while expecting their child, could not live together or be together when E. was present; C.C. could not assist N.V. in everyday needs.

In constitutional redress proceedings in 2016, the applicants alleged breaches of Article 8 and Article 6. Under Article 8, they argued that the decree unjustifiably interfered with their de facto family life. Under Article 6, C.C. complained that an order affecting him was made although he was never a party to the Family Court proceedings, never heard, and despite requesting to be heard. Both applicants complained that the Children’s Advocate report was sealed and inaccessible. N.V. complained that decisions affecting her were made without oral hearings and without reasoning, and that she had no effective remedy because challenges had to be brought before the same judge who had issued the decrees. They sought annulment and damages.

In September 2016, as their child’s birth approached, the applicants sought an interim measure allowing them to be together when E. was present. The constitutional court declined but invited a cautious arrangement in the child’s best interests; after the birth, they resumed living as a family.

The First Hall, Civil Court, in 2019 found breaches of Articles 8 and 6 and annulled the 1 October 2015 decree. On appeal, the Constitutional Court in 2020 set aside the Article 8 finding as unnecessary because the decree had been annulled, and dismissed C.C.’s Article 6 claim because he was not a party to the original proceedings. It confirmed Article 6 violations regarding N.V., particularly the lack of oral hearings and unreasoned decisions. The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 January 2021.

**Summary of *Bakchizhov v. Ukraine* (Application no. 24874/08)**

The case of *Bakchizhov v. Ukraine* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 May 2008 by Mr Aleksandr Viktorovich Bakchizhov, a Ukrainian national born in 1969. The applicant was convicted of inflicting bodily injuries and sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, a conviction upheld on appeal. He served his sentence in Boryspil Correctional Colony from 13 April 2007 until his release on probation on 17 June 2011.

The core of the applicant’s complaints concerned the conditions and treatment during his detention. He alleged that he was held in overcrowded, dirty cells with poor ventilation and insufficient winter heating. He claimed that healthy prisoners were housed with inmates suffering from HIV and tuberculosis and that food and water were unsatisfactory. He provided details of four cells where he was held, citing severe overcrowding, such as a 70-square-metre cell accommodating 50 prisoners and a 45-square-metre cell holding 35.

The applicant further alleged ill-treatment by guards, including physical and verbal abuse, threats, and arbitrary solitary confinement. He complained of frequent cell searches during his absence, which left his belongings in disarray, and of nighttime searches, which caused him stress. He also stated that personal documents from his case file went missing.

Regarding medical care, the applicant contended that he received inadequate assistance. He claimed he did not undergo a thorough examination or receive a long-term treatment strategy, only occasional symptomatic care.

Additionally, the applicant alleged that under threat of disciplinary punishment, he was forced to perform overtime labour, often twelve to fourteen hours a day, seven days a week, without adequate remuneration.

He also complained that prison authorities monitored all his correspondence, including letters to and from the Court, selectively failing to send or delaying them. He cited an instance where a letter to the Court was not sent and claimed a letter from the Court was received a month late. Consequently, he resorted to sending some letters via friends.

The Government contested the applicant’s account. They submitted that inmates with tuberculosis were detained separately, food and water were of adequate quality, and heating maintained temperatures between 18°C and 20°C. They provided medical records showing the applicant received treatment for various conditions, including bronchitis, radiculoneuritis, and dermatitis, and claimed his health was generally stable. The Government could not provide information on alleged ill-treatment or searches, as records had been destroyed. They denied forced labour, stating he performed standard prison work with remuneration or unpaid maintenance work for no more than two hours daily. They also denied monitoring all correspondence.

Separately, the applicant complained about hindrance in accessing his criminal case file. While he was provided with some documents upon request, the Brovary Town Court informed him in 2008 that the file did not contain certain cassation appeals or Supreme Court judgments. He was only provided with a copy of the Supreme Court’s judgment in April 2009, after the Court requested it. Full access to his case file was granted only after his release in 2011.

In *Kalda v. Estonia*, the applicant, Romeo Kalda, an Estonian national born in 1974 who was serving a life sentence, alleged that his right under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights to receive information through the Internet without interference by public authorities had been violated. The case concerned prison refusals to allow him access to certain Internet resources.

At Pärnu Prison, on 21 July 2005, Kalda asked the prison governor for access to the online version of *Riigi Teataja* (the State Gazette), the online decisions of the Supreme Court and administrative courts, and the HUDOC database of European Court of Human Rights judgments. The governor refused. After domestic court proceedings, the Supreme Court of Estonia, on 31 May 2007, held that refusing access to the online *Riigi Teataja* was lawful because a paper version was available. However, it found that refusing access to the administrative court rulings and HUDOC was unlawful. It noted that from 1 January 2007 the primary official version of *Riigi Teataja* was online and only five printed control copies existed. Prisons therefore had to ensure detainees could reasonably search and familiarize themselves with legal acts. The Supreme Court also held that prisoners’ constitutional right to obtain information disseminated for public use under Article 44 § 1 of the Estonian Constitution had to be protected equally, absent statutory restrictions.

Kalda was later transferred to Tartu Prison. On 18 October 2007, he requested access to three websites: www.coe.ee (Council of Europe Information Office in Tallinn), www.oiguskantsler.ee (Chancellor of Justice), and www.riigikogu.ee (Estonian Parliament). He claimed he was involved in legal disputes with prison authorities and needed the sites to defend his rights in court. The Ministry of Justice dismissed his complaint on 23 November 2007. On 17 July 2008, Tartu Administrative Court granted access only to www.coe.ee, ordering supervised access via a specially adapted computer. It reasoned that HUDOC contained ECtHR rulings only in English and French, while Estonian translations were available on www.coe.ee; the burden of translation should not fall on Kalda. It found www.coe.ee similar to the judicial decisions database permitted under section 31-1 of the Imprisonment Act. Access to the other two sites was not foreseen by that provision, and Kalda could request information directly. The Tartu Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 31 October 2008.

On further appeal, the Supreme Court’s plenary session, on 7 December 2009, dismissed Kalda’s appeal and upheld Tartu Prison’s appeal, quashing access to www.coe.ee. The Supreme Court examined section 31-1 of the Imprisonment Act, in force from 1 June 2008, which prohibited prisoners from using the Internet except on specially adapted, supervised prison computers allowing access only to official legislation databases and the judicial decisions database. The three requested sites did not fall within those exceptions. The Supreme Court accepted that the restriction interfered with the right to obtain information under Article 44 § 1 of the Constitution but found it constitutional and justified by the aims of imprisonment: protecting public safety, maintaining legal order, and steering detainees toward law-abiding behaviour. It cited risks of misuse, prohibited communication, security threats, and increased control costs. It noted that detainees could access the ECtHR website, ratified Council of Europe treaties via *riigiteataja.ee*, printed works in prison libraries, and could contact the Parliament and Chancellor of Justice by post or information request. The restriction was considered “low intensity.” Four judges dissented, finding access to all three sites should be allowed because the sites did not generally threaten safety, supervised computers existed, and the information aided court access. Kalda lodged his application on 16 March 2010.

**Summary of *Smirnov and Others v. Russia* (Applications nos. 74889/16 and 7 others)**

The case of *Smirnov and Others v. Russia* was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) by eight Russian nationals. The applications, lodged between November 2016 and October 2017, concerned the inadequate conditions of their detention in various Russian penal colonies (IK). The applicants primarily complained under Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment, and some also raised complaints under Article 13 regarding the lack of an effective domestic remedy for their grievances.

The core facts of each application revolve around the specific, severe deficiencies in the detention facilities where the applicants were held. A central and recurring issue was severe overcrowding. In several facilities, the personal space allotted to each inmate was drastically below acceptable standards. For instance, in IK-6 in the Republic of Chuvashiya (applicant Troitskiy), 50 inmates shared a space providing only 1.5 square meters per person. Similarly, in IK-8 in the Bashkortostan Republic (applicant Shiyanov), the space was 1.4 square meters per inmate among 180 prisoners. In IK-11 in the Nizhniy Novgorod Region (applicants Klokov and Tolstykh), the space per inmate was 1.6 and 1.4 square meters, respectively. This lack of space was frequently coupled with an insufficient number of sleeping places, forcing inmates to share beds or sleep in shifts.

Beyond overcrowding, the applicants detailed a range of other degrading conditions. Sanitary and hygiene facilities were widely reported as inadequate or severely restricted. Many applicants complained of a lack of privacy for using the toilet, restricted access to toilets, and insufficient access to showers and warm water. For example, in IK-6, 50 inmates had to share a single toilet. The quality and quantity of food were also a common grievance, described as poor, with some applicants noting a lack of access to potable water.

Environmental factors contributing to the poor conditions included a lack of fresh air and insufficient natural and electric light. Several applicants reported infestations of their cells with insects or rodents and the presence of mould. A significant health concern raised was the practice of sharing cells with inmates infected with contagious diseases, a complaint lodged by applicants Smirnov, Troitskiy, and Klokov.

Furthermore, the applicants faced material deprivations. These included a lack of or inadequate furniture, poor or non-existent hygienic facilities, and a lack of basic toiletries. Access to activities was also limited, with one applicant (Shiyanov) noting a lack of or restricted access to leisure or educational activities. In one case (Troitskiy), the applicant also alleged a lack of requisite medical assistance.

The durations of detention under these conditions varied significantly. Applicant Klokov endured the longest period, over five years in IK-11, from June 2012 to August 2017. Other applicants faced periods ranging from just over one year (Smirnov and Shalyakin) to more than two and a half years (Tolstykh and Poskrebyshev). For some, like Tolstykh, Poskrebyshev, Shalyakin, and Artemenkov, their detention was ongoing at the time of application.

In summary, the applications detailed a systemic failure to provide humane detention conditions, characterized by extreme overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, poor nutrition, and environmental health hazards. These factors collectively formed the basis of the applicants' claims that their treatment violated Article 3 of the Convention, and that they lacked an effective remedy at the national level to address these violations, contrary to Article 13.

**Gloveli v. Georgia** (Application no. 18952/18), judgment of 7 April 2022, concerned an alleged violation of Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights—the right of access to a court.

The applicant, Marina Gloveli, was a Georgian lawyer and former judge of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal. She had unsuccessfully applied for judicial positions six times. The case arose from her October 2017 application for an appellate court vacancy announced by the High Council of Justice (“HCJ”). She was admitted to the competition, interviewed, and assessed by HCJ members using competency and integrity score sheets. On 20 January 2018, she was notified that her application had been rejected because she did not meet the minimum competency score. She later obtained copies of the individual score sheets.

The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court’s Qualifications Chamber, a remedy introduced by amendments to the Courts Act that entered into force in March 2017. Under the amended law, unsuccessful judicial candidates could challenge HCJ decisions refusing appointment where they alleged bias, discrimination, or abuse of power by HCJ members. The applicant alleged that the refusal was arbitrary and discriminatory. In support, she relied on a televised statement by N.J., a non-judicial HCJ member, who claimed that some HCJ members had “protégé” candidates and arbitrarily lowered the scores of other candidates. She argued that the very low scores she received indicated such bias.

On 6 February 2018, however, the Qualifications Chamber declared her appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that because she had failed the minimum competency score, her candidacy was never put to a vote before the HCJ. Therefore, the HCJ had not issued a decision “refusing appointment” within the meaning of the relevant provisions, and no appealable decision existed. The Chamber stated that its decision was final and not subject to appeal.

The domestic background was significant. Following an earlier constitutional complaint by Gloveli and others, the Constitutional Court of Georgia had held on 7 April 2017 that judicial office is a form of public service under Article 29 of the Georgian Constitution, and that candidates must have access to a court under Article 42 to challenge arbitrary refusals. The Constitutional Court considered that the newly created Qualifications Chamber remedy resolved the previous lack of judicial review. The European Court of Human Rights therefore examined why that remedy did not operate in the applicant’s case.

The central alleged violation was that the applicant could not obtain any judicial review of the refusal to appoint her, contrary to Article 6 § 1. The key facts were that the only available judicial remedy was interpreted by the Supreme Court as excluding candidates rejected at the competency-scoring stage, even though such rejection effectively ended their candidacy and despite serious allegations of bias and discrimination. The ECtHR found that this interpretation deprived the applicant of access to a court. It also referred to international standards—including the UN Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary, Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)12, Venice Commission opinions, GRECO, and the Dublin Declaration—which require that unsuccessful judicial candidates receive reasons and have an opportunity to challenge appointment decisions or procedures. The Court accordingly found a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

**Summary of *Grabovskiy v. Ukraine* (Application no. 4442/07)**

The case of *Grabovskiy v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr. Nikolay Aleksandrovich Grabovskiy, a Ukrainian national born in 1969, regarding criminal proceedings against him and the conditions of his detention.

The events stem from an incident on 22 July 2005, when a sales clerk, G., was attacked in a Kharkiv shop, suffering multiple cuts including a penetrating chest wound. She identified the applicant, whom she knew, as her attacker. The domestic courts found that the applicant attacked G. and seized cash belonging to her employer. The applicant, however, maintained throughout proceedings that G. owed him money. He claimed he went to the shop to collect the debt, but G. attacked him with scissors. He stated that while defending himself, he hit her, seized the scissors, and stabbed her. When an alarm sounded, he took the money and fled.

The applicant was arrested late on 22 July 2005. He alleged that his request for a lawyer during police questioning was ignored. However, police records dated 23 July 2005 indicated that his procedural rights, including the right to legal aid, were explained to him, and that he chose to waive his right to legal assistance. On 25 July 2005, a forensic medical examination noted injuries to the applicant's jaw and hand, consistent with his account of a fight.

The applicant was charged with aggravated robbery. During his trial before the Kharkiv Kyivsky District Court, which began on 17 October 2005, the applicant stated he wished to defend himself and waived his right to legal assistance. He later alleged he was forced to do so by police guards in the courtroom. He repeated his version of events and requested certain witnesses be called, but the trial court refused, stating he failed to identify them and deemed his allegations an obfuscation tactic. On 18 October 2005, the applicant was convicted and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment. The court relied on, among other things, the applicant's trial admissions, the victim's testimony denying any debt, and testimony from the applicant's girlfriend and the victim's relatives who also denied knowledge of any debt.

The applicant appealed on 14 November 2005, raising evidentiary matters and requesting a lawyer. He reiterated this request on 6 January 2006. On 2 February 2006, the Court of Appeal's Vice-President asked the regional Bar association to assign a lawyer, but there was no follow-up. The Court of Appeal upheld the conviction on 20 July 2006, with the applicant present but unrepresented. His subsequent request to the trial court for a lawyer to prepare a cassation appeal was denied on 28 August 2006. The Supreme Court rejected his appeal on points of law on 28 February 2007.

Regarding detention conditions, the applicant was held in various facilities, including the Kharkiv pre-trial detention centre (SIZO) from 17 August 2005. He complained of overcrowding, specifically a cell with 24 sleeping places holding over 50 inmates. The Government provided cell occupancy data showing varying square metres per sleeping place, ranging from 1.34 to 2.09. The applicant was also treated for various medical issues during detention.

Finally, the applicant complained that domestic authorities failed to provide him with copies of certain documents needed for his application to the Court, including witness statements and records, despite having copies that were of poor quality.

**Case Name:** *R.I. and Others v. Romania* (Application no. 57077/16)

The case concerned a Romanian mother, R.I., and her two children, M.I. and I.I. The mother had been in a stable relationship with R., but after the relationship ended in 2010, the children initially remained with her, while R. was to have unrestricted access and participate in their upbringing. In November 2013, however, R. took the children from the mother’s home without her consent. From then until May 2014, the mother saw them only occasionally and always in the father’s presence; after 6 June 2014, all contact stopped.

The mother began custody proceedings on 25 November 2013 and sought an interim injunction. On 5 May 2014, the Bucharest County Court issued a final interim decision ordering that the children reside with their mother and that the father pay monthly child support. The mother immediately sought enforcement. On 6 June 2014, she went to the children’s school to collect them, but the father appeared, became abusive, and the police had to intervene; she could not take the children home. Subsequent bailiff meetings failed: on 17 July 2014 the father and children did not attend, and on 14 August 2014 the children attended but refused absolutely to return to their mother, alleging that she had shouted at and occasionally beaten them. Enforcement therefore could not proceed.

The child protection authority became involved. Reports in early 2014 found the children well cared for at the father’s home and no signs of abuse, but noted anxiety and distress caused by parental conflict. A psychologist later recommended counselling. A social assistant in February 2015 reported that the children refused to see their mother because of alleged beatings and meanness. A more detailed expert psychological report of 17 November 2015 found no indication of physical abuse by the mother, but found indicators of psychological abuse in the form of parental alienation exercised by the father. It described the father as corresponding to the profile of an “alienator parent” and recommended counselling and ending the children’s involvement in the parental conflict.

Meanwhile, on 24 September 2014, the Bucharest District Court granted the mother physical custody and ordered child support. The father initially appealed but later withdrew. Enforcement was extended to the return of the children. The father moved with the children to Năvodari, contested enforcement, and in September 2017 obtained a stay pending appeal. His appeal was dismissed in May 2018. On 16 July 2018, at a bailiff meeting, the children again refused absolutely to move in with their mother.

In separate custody proceedings, on 20 March 2017 the Bucharest District Court awarded physical custody to the father, relying on the children’s long stay with him, their refusal to move, and their attachment to him. On 24 April 2018, the Bucharest County Court reversed that decision. It found that the mother was not at fault for the non-enforcement of the 5 May 2014 decision, that the Romanian State had a positive obligation to take urgent measures to return the children to her, and that the father’s alienation of the children had been allowed to continue. It warned that family ties risked becoming permanent broken and that future visiting arrangements would be illusory.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations therefore centre on the Romanian authorities’ prolonged failure to enforce final court decisions granting the mother custody or residence and to prevent the father’s alleged parental alienation. Despite repeated requests to bailiffs, police, and child protection authorities, and despite expert findings of alienation, the children remained with the father for years. The application alleged that this failure breached the applicants’ right to respect for family life, and possibly their right of access to court, under the Convention.

**Gloveli v. Georgia** (Application no. 18952/18, judgment of 7 April 2022) concerned a Georgian lawyer, Marina Gloveli, who complained under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that she had been denied access to a court to challenge the refusal to appoint her to a judicial post.

The applicant had more than twenty years’ legal experience and had previously served as a judge in the Tbilisi Court of Appeal between 1999 and 2005. She applied unsuccessfully for judicial vacancies six times. The present case arose from her latest application in October 2017, when the High Council of Justice (“HCJ”) announced a competition for a vacant appellate court position. Gloveli applied, was admitted to the competition, underwent a background check, and was interviewed and individually scored by HCJ members on 29 December 2017.

On 20 January 2018, she was notified that her application had been rejected because she did not meet the minimum competency score. She later obtained copies of the score sheets. On 2 February 2018, she appealed to the Supreme Court’s Qualifications Chamber under section 354(3)(b) of the Courts Act, alleging that the decision was arbitrary and discriminatory. In support, she relied on a televised statement by N.J., a non-judicial member of the HCJ, who claimed that several HCJ members had “protégé” candidates and had arbitrarily lowered the assessment scores of other candidates. Gloveli argued that the very low scores she received from certain HCJ members indicated bias.

On 6 February 2018, the Qualifications Chamber declared her appeal inadmissible for lack of jurisdiction. It reasoned that because she had failed to achieve the minimum pass score in the competency component, her candidacy had never been put to a vote before the HCJ. As a result, the precondition in section 35(12) of the Courts Act was not met. The HCJ had therefore not examined her application for appointment and had not issued a “decision refusing appointment” capable of being challenged before the Qualifications Chamber. The Chamber also stated that it did not have “full jurisdiction” to review the facts of the case, and its decision was final and not subject to appeal.

The case had an important background. In 2016, Gloveli and two other unsuccessful candidates had lodged a constitutional complaint arguing that no court had jurisdiction to review disputes over judicial appointments. In March 2017, amendments to the Courts Act created the Qualifications Chamber to hear appeals against HCJ decisions refusing judicial appointments. In April 2017, the Constitutional Court rejected the earlier complaint, holding that the new legislative amendments had essentially resolved the access-to-court issue. However, the Qualifications Chamber’s subsequent practice limited its jurisdiction to formal refusals issued after a vote, thereby excluding candidates rejected at the preliminary scoring stage.

The Constitutional Court had held that judicial appointment is a form of public service, that procedural fairness is required at every stage of recruitment, and that candidates should have access to a court to challenge arbitrary refusals. Council of Europe and other international materials similarly provide that unsuccessful judicial candidates should be able to challenge selection decisions or at least the procedure followed.

The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 § 1. Although States may impose conditions on access to court, the Qualifications Chamber’s restrictive interpretation deprived the applicant of any judicial review of an allegedly arbitrary and discriminatory refusal. The domestic remedy created after the 2017 reform was thus ineffective in her situation, impairing the very essence of her right of access to a court.

The applicant, Edvin Starkevič, was a Lithuanian police officer. In October 2015, police arrested V.M. on suspicion of burglary. V.M. later told the police internal affairs division that, during his detention, the applicant had asked him to steal goods. V.M. said he subsequently met the applicant and persons linked to him in public places on 25 October and 11 November 2015.

On 12 November 2015, internal affairs opened a pre-trial investigation into suspected abuse of office. Based on V.M.’s statements and security-camera footage, a prosecutor sought court authorisation to intercept the applicant’s electronic communications, conduct secret surveillance, and use a criminal conduct simulation model. The court authorised these measures on 16 November 2015. V.M. was allowed, no more than twice, to agree to the applicant’s demands to obtain stolen goods in exchange for payment, with the actions recorded.

On 8 January 2016, V.M. met the applicant in a public place and gave him a bottle of whiskey. The applicant was arrested in flagrante delicto. A notice of suspicion alleged that, between 25 October 2015 and 8 January 2016, the applicant—acting with his wife, I.S., and another person, J.R.—had asked V.M., a suspect in another case, to illegally obtain handbags, sports shoes, and whiskey. The applicant denied the accusations but refused to testify.

On 29 January 2016, the applicant was notified of a disciplinary investigation based on information that he had possibly committed abuse of office, thereby damaging the police’s prestige and possibly discrediting an officer’s name. He was invited to provide an explanation by 5 February 2016. He instead asked the police to rely on his statements from the pre-trial investigation, where he had refused to testify. The disciplinary proceedings were suspended pending the criminal investigation.

On 9 September 2016, the prosecutor discontinued the pre-trial investigation. He found no corpus delicti because there was no significant pecuniary or non-pecuniary damage to the State or police, no major public reaction, and no disruption of police work. However, he considered that the applicant’s conduct contained elements of a disciplinary violation and forwarded the file to the police for disciplinary assessment. The prosecutor’s decision relied on evidence from the criminal conduct simulation model, V.M.’s testimony, other witnesses, CCTV footage, telephone data, and the whiskey bottle. The applicant did not appeal that decision.

On 26 October 2016, a disciplinary investigation report found that the applicant’s actions were contrary to law and had features of a crime. It stated that he had used his police position for personal gain, encouraged another person to break the law, and breached police ethics and service rules. It concluded that he had discredited an officer’s name. On 27 October 2016, the police dismissed him under the Statute of Internal Service.

The applicant challenged his dismissal in administrative proceedings, arguing that disciplinary and criminal proceedings had different grounds, that he should have had a proper opportunity to explain and submit evidence, that the disciplinary findings lacked concrete evidence, and that evidence obtained through the criminal conduct simulation model should not have been used in disciplinary proceedings. He did not expressly raise the presumption of innocence. The administrative courts dismissed his claims, finding that the misconduct notice was sufficiently clear, that his refusal to explain was his own defence tactic, and that the prosecutor’s decision was admissible proof. They also held that, even excluding the simulation-model evidence, other evidence sufficiently supported the dismissal.

The case before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the applicant’s complaints about the right to a fair hearing, the presumption of innocence, and respect for private life, mainly because information obtained during the criminal investigation—including secret surveillance and simulated criminal conduct—was used in the subsequent disciplinary proceedings that led to his dismissal.

**Summary of *Yakushev v. Ukraine* (Application no. 15978/09)**

The case of *Yakushev v. Ukraine* concerns an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by Mr Igor Viktorovych Yakushev, a Ukrainian national born in 1971, on 7 March 2009. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, concerning his right to respect for private and family life. The core of the complaint related to the domestic courts' refusal to allow him to challenge his legal paternity of a child, K., despite conclusive genetic evidence that he was not the biological father.

The key facts are as follows: On 17 November 1993, a woman identified as M. gave birth to a daughter, K. At the time, the applicant had been having relations with M., although he was married to another woman and did not cohabit with M. On 2 December 1993, based on his belief that he was the father, the applicant submitted a formal declaration accepting paternity of K., thereby becoming her legal father.

Several years later, in 2005, the applicant began to have doubts about his paternity. In July 2006, shortly after his marriage to M. ended in divorce, he initiated proceedings in the Malyn District Court to challenge his paternity of K. The central issue in the domestic proceedings was the interpretation of Article 56 § 2 of the Ukrainian Marriage and Family Code. This provision stated that a person who had registered as a child's father based on his own declaration did not have the right to challenge that paternity if, at the time of the declaration, he had been aware that he was not the child's father.

On 24 March 2008, the District Court ruled in favour of the applicant. The court's decision was based on a genetic expert's opinion which excluded him as K.'s biological father. Crucially, the court found that the applicant had the right to challenge his paternity because there was no evidence in the case file to suggest he knew he was not the father when he accepted paternity in 1993.

This decision was overturned on appeal. On 29 May 2008, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal quashed the ruling and dismissed the applicant’s claim. The appellate court held that under Article 56 § 2, the applicant did not have the right to challenge his paternity. It reasoned that at the time he accepted paternity, he was aware he was not the biological father. To support this conclusion, the Court of Appeal pointed to circumstantial evidence: the applicant and M. had not been married before K.'s birth, they had not been living together (noting in particular that the applicant lived in another town between February and April 1993), and the applicant had been married to another woman at the time.

The applicant then appealed on a point of law to the Supreme Court of Ukraine, arguing that the Court of Appeal had no evidentiary basis to conclude he had known he was not the father in 1993. He contended that the appellate court had overstepped its authority in drawing such a conclusion. On 9 September 2008, the Supreme Court of Ukraine rejected his appeal as unfounded, effectively finalising the domestic decisions against him.

Consequently, the applicant brought the case to the European Court of Human Rights. He had exhausted all domestic remedies and complained that the dismissal of his claim, which prevented him from legally severing his paternal link to a child who was proven not to be his, constituted a violation of his right to respect for his private life under Article 8 of the Convention. The Court gave notice of this specific complaint to the Ukrainian Government.

The case *Hovhannisyan and Nazaryan v. Armenia* (Applications nos. 2169/12 and 29887/14) concerned the death of A. Nazaryan, a 31-year-old Armenian army officer, on 27 July 2010 at military base no. 12. The first applicant was his mother and the second applicant his sister. They complained under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the State had failed to protect his life and had not conducted an effective investigation into his death.

The official initial report stated that A. Nazaryan had fatally shot himself in the trench with his assigned assault rifle. Criminal proceedings were opened for incitement to suicide. However, the scene examination described his body seated next to a rock, with the rifle barrel in his mouth and the stock between his legs. A fired cartridge, blood-like traces, and a magazine containing twenty-nine bullets were seized. Captain H.M., present at the base, removed A. Nazaryan’s notebook from his pocket and gave it to Major M.N., asking him to keep it secret because he feared his fingerprints might be on it. The notebook contained a note stating that A. Nazaryan was “tired of everything” and that it was no one’s fault but his and his parents’. Forensic document examination attributed the note to A. Nazaryan, but the applicants disputed this.

Evidence gathered during the investigation indicated that A. Nazaryan had been subjected to humiliation, physical violence, and systematic ill-treatment by superiors and conscripts. Captain H.M. admitted hitting him on 19 July 2010 during an argument; Lieutenant V.H. also allegedly beat him. Several conscripts—A.H., M.M., and H.K.—reportedly mocked and abused him. A Minister of Defence order later found that Captain H.M. had abused his position, assaulted A. Nazaryan in front of staff, created an unhealthy moral environment, and that this led to ill-treatment by conscripts and ultimately to A. Nazaryan’s suicide. The order also found that the situation had been concealed from command.

The autopsy concluded that death resulted from a gunshot wound to the mouth. It also found other bruises and abrasions on A. Nazaryan’s body, some inflicted shortly before death, and alcohol intoxication. A later forensic commission concluded that self-infliction was possible, but did not rule out that another person could have inflicted the injury; it found no traces of the body being moved. A posthumous psychological examination linked the suicide to humiliation, debasement, and ill-treatment by officers and conscripts.

Captain H.M., Lieutenant V.H., A.H., M.M., and H.K. were charged and convicted in 2013, receiving prison sentences. Nevertheless, the applicants alleged that the investigation was ineffective. Key procedural concerns included that numerous servicemen were placed in disciplinary isolation after the death and questioned while confined; several later retracted pre-trial statements, alleging duress, beatings, and prolonged interrogation. The trial court refused to exclude those pre-trial statements. The applicants also complained that requests for further forensic examination—including handwriting analysis abroad and testing of blood traces and other injuries—were refused, and that discrepancies existed regarding the scene examination date, cartridge serial numbers, initial reports of death in a trench versus beside a rock, and missing photographs. The Court of Appeal reviewed the case in a cassation-style manner without a full evidentiary hearing, and the Court of Cassation declared the appeals inadmissible. The applicants therefore alleged that Armenia violated its substantive and procedural obligations under Article 2.

The case *Hülya Ebru Demirel v. Turkey* (Application no. 30733/08, judgment of 19 June 2018) concerned alleged sex discrimination in access to public employment and unfairness in administrative court proceedings. The applicant, a Turkish woman born in 1976, passed a civil-service examination on 17 October 1999. She was informed by the State Personnel Department that she had been appointed as a security officer at the Kilis branch of TEDAŞ, the State-run Turkish Electricity Distribution S.A. TEDAŞ later refused to appoint her because she did not meet the requirements of “being a man” and “having completed military service.”

On 4 September 2000 the applicant challenged that refusal before the Gaziantep Administrative Court. On 9 May 2001 the court stayed execution of the refusal, finding that being male was not a requirement for the post. On 23 July 2001 TEDAŞ offered her a six-month probationary contract, and she began working. On 4 October 2001 the Gaziantep Administrative Court annulled the refusal. It held that the military-service requirement applied only to male candidates and that no rule prevented women from serving as security officers at TEDAŞ; rejecting her solely because of her sex was unlawful.

TEDAŞ appealed. On 12 April 2002 the Twelfth Division of the Supreme Administrative Court stayed execution of the lower judgment. On 11 June 2002 TEDAŞ informed the applicant that her contract had been terminated on 27 May 2002 as a result. On 26 December 2002 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the 4 October 2001 judgment. It reasoned that because the post required completion of military service, it had been reserved for male candidates, so the refusal had been lawful. On 23 October 2003 the Gaziantep Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s case following that reasoning.

The applicant appealed, arguing that this interpretation breached equality and Turkey’s positive obligation of non-discrimination. She relied on the Constitution, CEDAW Article 2(d), ICESCR Article 3, and EU rules prohibiting sex discrimination in access to employment. On 16 November 2007 the Twelfth Division upheld the dismissal without addressing those arguments.

A related development occurred on 6 December 2007. The Supreme Administrative Court’s General Assembly of Administrative Proceedings Divisions decided the case of R.B., another female TEDAŞ candidate rejected for the same reasons. The General Assembly held that the military-service requirement applied only to men and that refusing to appoint R.B. on that ground was unlawful.

The applicant then sought rectification of the 16 November 2007 decision, relying on R.B. and her right to a fair hearing. The judge rapporteur opined that the decision should be rectified in light of R.B. and Turkey’s CEDAW Article 11 obligations regarding equal employment opportunities. On 24 June 2009, however, the Twelfth Division dismissed the rectification request, finding that none of the applicant’s grounds fell within the exhaustive list in section 54(1) of the Administrative Procedure Act.

The applicant alleged violations under Article 14 in conjunction with Article 8 of the Convention, complaining that the refusal to appoint her and her subsequent dismissal were discriminatory on grounds of sex. She also complained under Article 6 that the administrative proceedings were unfair, particularly because the courts failed to address her discrimination arguments and refused rectification despite the inconsistent General Assembly ruling in R.B.’s case. The Court communicated the Article 14/Article 8 and Article 6 complaints; the remainder of the application was inadmissible.

The case originated in an application lodged against Bosnia and Herzegovina with the European Court of Human Rights by the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Vrhbosna, a Roman Catholic community based in Sarajevo, on 16 May 2013. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1; those complaints were communicated to the Government on 28 March 2017, while the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The central factual background concerns the authorities’ prolonged failure to enforce a final domestic decision ordering the relocation of public schools from property belonging to the applicant in Travnik.

By a decision of 9 May 2003, which became final on 4 September 2003, the Human Rights Chamber for Bosnia and Herzegovina found that the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina had discriminated against the applicant in its enjoyment of the right to freedom of religion under Article 9 of the Convention. It ordered the Federation to ensure that public schools housed in the Archdiocese High School building in Travnik were relocated and to reinstate the applicant in the premises within one year. The Chamber rejected the applicant’s request for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

Implementation was not completed within the ordered period. By an agreement of 21 May 2004, the Federation undertook to reinstate the applicant by 1 July 2006. The Travnik Municipal Council subsequently adopted implementing decisions, and one public school was moved from the premises. However, full compliance remained outstanding.

Enforcement proceedings then became protracted. On 23 June 2010 the Travnik Municipal Council issued a writ of execution. On 5 October 2011 the Travnik Cantonal Court quashed that decision and remitted the case. On 17 October 2011 the Travnik Municipal Court held that it lacked jurisdiction. On 16 May 2012 the Cantonal Court quashed that decision and remitted the case again. On 3 July 2012 the Municipal Court held that decisions of the Human Rights Chamber were not subject to enforcement proceedings. The applicant appealed on 12 July 2012, but as of 28 August 2017 the Cantonal Court had still not ruled on that appeal.

On 30 October 2012 the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina determined that the Federation had not yet fully enforced the 9 May 2003 decision. In February 2017 the applicant initiated civil proceedings against the public school still occupying its premises, seeking relocation and damages for use of the premises between 1 February 2014 and 1 June 2017. On 14 July 2017 the Municipal Court in Travnik ruled in the applicant’s favour, awarding 270,360 convertible marks in pecuniary damages and 6,713 marks for costs and expenses, and ordering the respondent to vacate the premises within 30 days. On 20 December 2017 the Cantonal Court in Novi Travnik upheld that judgment. By 20 February 2018, however, the Central Bosnia Canton had submitted a revision petition to the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the public school had still not been relocated.

These facts were relevant to the alleged violations under Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In substance, the applicant complained that the final decision in its favour remained unenforced for years, that enforcement proceedings were repeatedly frustrated by jurisdictional and procedural obstacles, and that it continued to be deprived of the use of its property despite the final ruling. The case therefore concerned whether the domestic authorities’ failure to secure timely compliance with a binding decision violated the applicant’s right of access to a court and its right to the peaceful enjoyment of its possessions.

In *Goryayeva v. Ukraine* (Application no. 58656/10, judgment of 6 October 2016), the applicant, Ms Zoya Georgiyivna Goryayeva, complained about the death of her son, A.G., while in police detention and the subsequent domestic investigation. A.G., born in 1966, suffered from tuberculosis, AIDS, drug addiction, and an infected phlegmon on his right shin. On 4 May 2007 he was arrested on suspicion of drug-related crimes and placed in a temporary detention centre (“ITT”) belonging to the Mykolayiv police. On 7 May 2007 the Tsentralnyy District Court of Mykolayiv ordered his pre-trial detention. While in the ITT he was attended by ambulance doctors; on 19 May 2007 he was transferred to a local hospital’s surgical ward for treatment of his phlegmon. After treatment, doctors considered that he could remain in detention, and he was returned to the ITT.

On 23 May 2007, at about 9:30 p.m., an ITT officer heard moaning from A.G.’s cell. A.G. was alone, with his mouth open, breathing heavily, and saying he felt bad and needed air. Officers removed him to the entrance area for fresh air and gave first aid. An ambulance arrived at 9:43 p.m. and confirmed that A.G. was dead. The post-mortem report found that he died from ischaemic heart disease aggravated by acute heart failure. Linear strangulation bruises on his neck indicated interrupted asphyxiation; asphyxiation had been attempted about ten minutes before death and could have aggravated his chronic illnesses.

Domestic authorities conducted repeated inquiries. Between 2007 and 2012, investigators at the local prosecutor’s office refused more than fifteen times to initiate criminal proceedings. Supervising prosecutors and courts quashed those refusals as unsubstantiated and ordered further pre-investigation inquiries. On 14 December 2012 criminal proceedings were initiated under the 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure. On 27 March 2013 an investigator terminated the proceedings, finding no elements of a crime by the ITT officers. On 24 July 2013 the Zavodskyy District Court of Mykolayiv quashed that decision as unfounded, noting that the investigator had failed to take necessary measures. On 3 October 2013 the investigator again terminated the proceedings, concluding that there was no evidence that ITT staff had caused the death.

The investigator admitted that certain evidence could not be obtained. Bed linen and a rope fashioned from bed linen found in the cell had been destroyed after the post-mortem examination, preventing further examination or reconstruction. Although a site inspection occurred on 24 May 2007, no video-recordings, sketches, or photographs were made.

The investigator concluded that shortly before death A.G. had unsuccessfully attempted suicide by asphyxiating himself with a bed-linen rope. Latest medical findings stated that death resulted from interrupted mechanical asphyxiation, and neck injuries suggested heart failure from attempted strangulation. As to detention conditions, medical evidence suggested no acute condition requiring hospital admission during ITT detention; he had been medically supervised. His TB and HIV meant his physical condition would gradually deteriorate in any event. The investigator found that ITT officers could not have envisaged the fatal outcome and that A.G. had received appropriate nutrition and had not refused food.

These facts are relevant to alleged violations concerning the right to life and the State’s positive and procedural obligations. Key issues include whether authorities adequately protected A.G. given his serious medical conditions, whether returning him to the ITT after hospital treatment was proper, and whether the investigation was effective. The repeated refusals, destruction of crucial evidence, failure to preserve the scene, delayed criminal proceedings, and inability to reconstruct events raise concerns about compliance with the obligation to conduct an adequate and prompt investigation into a death in custody.
