text:
In *Goryayeva v. Ukraine* (Application no. 58656/10), the European Court of Human Rights considered the death of the applicant’s son, A.G., while in police detention and the subsequent domestic investigation.

The applicant, Ms Zoya Georgiyivna Goryayeva, is a Ukrainian national born in 1938. Her son, A.G., was born in 1966 and suffered from tuberculosis, AIDS, drug addiction, and an infected phlegmon on his right shin. On 4 May 2007, A.G. was arrested on suspicion of drug-related crimes and placed in a temporary detention centre (“ITT”) belonging to the Mykolayiv police. On 7 May 2007, the Tsentralnyy District Court of Mykolayiv ordered his pre-trial detention.

While in the ITT, A.G. was attended by ambulance doctors and received medical treatment. On 19 May 2007, he was transferred to the surgical ward of a local hospital for treatment of his phlegmon. After treatment, doctors considered that he could be held in detention facilities, and he was returned to the ITT.

According to domestic investigations, at about 9:30 p.m. on 23 May 2007, an ITT officer heard moaning from A.G.’s cell. A.G. was alone. The officer checked the cell and saw him with his mouth open, breathing heavily, and saying that he felt bad and needed air. ITT officers removed him from the cell, took him to the entrance area for fresh air, and administered first aid. An ambulance arrived at 9:43 p.m. and confirmed that A.G. was dead.

A post-mortem examination concluded that A.G. died from ischaemic heart disease aggravated by acute heart failure. Linear strangulation bruises were found on his neck, indicating interrupted asphyxiation. The report stated that asphyxiation had been attempted about ten minutes before death and could have aggravated his chronic illnesses.

The domestic investigation was protracted and repeatedly restarted. Between 2007 and 2012, investigators at the local prosecutor’s office refused more than fifteen times to initiate criminal proceedings. Those decisions were quashed as unsubstantiated by supervising prosecutors and courts, and further pre-investigation inquiries were ordered. On 14 December 2012, criminal proceedings were initiated under the 2012 Code of Criminal Procedure. On 27 March 2013, an investigator terminated the proceedings, finding no elements of a crime on the part of the ITT officers. On 24 July 2013, the Zavodskyy District Court of Mykolayiv quashed that decision as unfounded, noting that the investigator had failed to take necessary measures.

On 3 October 2013, the investigator again terminated the proceedings, concluding that there was no evidence that ITT staff had caused A.G.’s death. He admitted that certain evidence could not be obtained: bed linen and a rope fashioned from bed linen found in the cell had been destroyed after the post-mortem examination, so they could not be further examined; reconstruction of events was therefore impossible. A site inspection had been carried out on 24 May 2007, but no video-recordings, sketches, or photographs were made.

Based on the available evidence, the investigator found that A.G. had unsuccessfully attempted suicide shortly before his death by asphyxiating himself with a rope made from bed linen. Medical findings indicated death by interrupted mechanical asphyxiation, with neck injuries suggesting heart failure resulting from the attempted strangulation. As to his detention conditions, medical evidence suggested no acute condition requiring hospital admission during his stay in the ITT; he had been medically supervised. His serious illnesses, including tuberculosis and HIV, meant his physical condition would gradually deteriorate in any event. The investigator concluded that ITT officers could not have envisaged the fatal outcome, and that A.G. had received appropriate nutrition and had not refused food.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the death of a detainee with known serious health conditions and drug addiction, possible self-harm or suicide in custody, the adequacy of medical supervision and emergency response, and the repeated failures, delays, and evidential deficiencies in the domestic investigation. These matters implicate Ukraine’s positive obligations under Article 2 of the Convention to protect the life of a person in detention and to conduct an effective investigation into a death in custody.

In *R.Š. v. Latvia*, the applicant, a Latvian national and licensed pilot undergoing aviation training, was a passenger on a private flight on 16 August 2008 from Riga to Tukums. The flight was organised by KD.C., a company providing private flights and pilot training. D.K. was its sole shareholder and board member. KD.C. did not operate commercial flights and had not been certified as an air operator. The aircraft, a Piper PA-31, was owned by KD.C. It was piloted by G.V., who had begun but not completed differences training for that aircraft type and lacked authorisation from the Civil Aviation Agency to fly it. Shortly after take-off, G.V. lost control in cloudy weather; the aircraft crashed and caught fire. The pilot died. The applicant and other passengers suffered serious injuries. The applicant sustained life-threatening injuries, permanently lost vision in his right eye, and suffered lasting health damage. He could later work only with limitations and could not operate aircraft independently.

The Transport Accident and Incident Investigation Bureau found that the primary cause was human error: G.V.’s insufficient skills and experience to operate a multi-engine Piper PA-31 under instrument flight rules. Contributing factors included poor weather and “unsafe supervision” by the Civil Aviation Agency in ensuring compliance with aviation legislation and visual flight rules. The report also found that KD.C. had failed to follow up on G.V.’s training, check his documents, or properly verify his qualifications before handing him the aircraft. It recommended a mandatory handover procedure to prevent unqualified pilots from flying. Yet the investigation and later testimony indicated that, at the material time, Latvian law did not regulate how general-aviation aircraft should be handed over or who must verify a pilot’s qualifications. Commercial aviation was regulated; general/private aviation was not.

Criminal proceedings were brought against D.K. for negligence and air-traffic safety violations. He was convicted at first instance but acquitted on appeal, and the Supreme Court upheld the acquittal. The courts found that D.K. had not been shown to have committed the required offence, that he was not a transport employee or aviation specialist, and that the duty not to fly without qualifications rested on the pilot. The Senate also noted that no domestic rule at the time required an aircraft owner to verify pilot qualifications; owner liability under the Chicago Convention arose only from 18 November 2010, and a domestic prohibition on handing over aircraft to unqualified pilots was added to the Law on Aviation only in 2013.

The applicant also sued KD.C., D.K., and the insurer for damages. KD.C. was declared bankrupt and later dissolved with no successor. The civil courts dismissed the claims: D.K. was not the aircraft owner; the pilot was not his employee; no unlawful act or causal link was established; and the pilot had acted arbitrarily contrary to the plan to fly with an instructor. The insurer refused coverage because the pilot lacked the right to operate the aircraft. The applicant therefore received no compensation. Before the European Court of Human Rights, he alleged under Articles 2 and 8 that he could not obtain compensation for harm from the accident and that the State should be responsible for shortcomings in the legal regulation of private-flight safety. Those complaints were communicated to the Latvian Government.

Big Brother Watch and Others v. the United Kingdom concerned three joined applications brought against the UK by companies, charities, organisations and individuals. The applicants alleged that UK electronic surveillance programmes, disclosed after Edward Snowden’s revelations, violated their rights under Articles 8, 10 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed their electronic communications were likely to have been intercepted by UK intelligence services, obtained from foreign governments, or acquired from communications service providers.

The case focused on two principal surveillance routes. First, GCHQ allegedly operated a bulk interception programme, referred to as TEMPORA, tapping fibre-optic cables and storing large volumes of data. Under section 8(4) of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000, the Secretary of State could authorise warrants for “external communications”. Two processing systems were described: one using simple selectors such as email addresses, and another using processing rules and complex queries to identify material of intelligence value. Section 16 of RIPA prohibited selecting intercepted material for examination by reference to an individual known to be in the British Islands, but this protection did not apply equally to related communications data.

Second, the applicants complained about UK access to material obtained by the US National Security Agency through PRISM and Upstream. PRISM involved targeted requests to internet service providers under US Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act approval. Upstream involved collecting content and communications data from fibre-optic cables and infrastructure. Leaked documents suggested GCHQ had access to PRISM from July 2010 and had acquired information obtained through it.

Domestically, the first applicants sought declarations that relevant legislation was incompatible with the Convention, but were told the Investigatory Powers Tribunal had exclusive jurisdiction over human rights complaints against intelligence services. The second applicants brought no domestic proceedings, believing no effective remedy existed. The third applicants—ten human rights organisations—complained to the IPT that the intelligence services and the Home and Foreign Secretaries had violated Articles 8, 10 and 14 by accessing or receiving intercepted communications and data from the US under PRISM and Upstream, and by intercepting, inspecting and retaining their communications under TEMPORA and section 8(4). They sought disclosure of relevant policies and guidance.

The Government adopted a “neither confirm nor deny” approach. The IPT therefore proceeded on assumed facts: that the NSA had obtained the applicants’ communications and data via PRISM or Upstream and passed them to GCHQ, where they were retained, stored, analysed and shared; and that GCHQ had intercepted their communications under TEMPORA and similarly retained, stored, analysed and shared them. The IPT held public hearings and a closed hearing, assisted by Counsel to the Tribunal, to examine secret internal arrangements.

In its December 2014 judgment, the IPT found that PRISM/Upstream engaged Article 8 but that adequate safeguards, signposting and oversight existed; it also found the section 8(4) bulk interception regime Convention-compliant and rejected discrimination and separate Article 10 claims. In February 2015, however, it declared that, before certain disclosures were made, the PRISM/Upstream regime had contravened Articles 8 and 10, though it now complied. In June 2015, it found that Amnesty International’s emails had been lawfully intercepted under section 8(4) but retained too long, and that Legal Resources Centre communications were lawfully intercepted but an internal selection procedure was not followed. Both amounted to Article 8 breaches, but no compensation was awarded.

The Strasbourg applicants maintained that the scope and magnitude of these surveillance programmes violated the Convention, particularly through bulk interception, foreign intelligence sharing, insufficient legal safeguards and discriminatory distinctions affecting non-UK persons. The case was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 25 May 2021.

**CASE OF ILIĆ v. SERBIA** (Application no. 26739/16), a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 23 October 2018, concerned a Serbian national, Mr Njegoš Ilić, born in 1960 and living in Kragujevac. The only complaint communicated to the Serbian Government on 5 October 2017 was the length of civil proceedings; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The key facts concern civil proceedings instituted by the applicant on 14 December 2006 against the Kragujevac Clinical Centre, seeking damages. During the first-instance proceedings, eleven hearings were held, while five scheduled hearings were not held. On 20 May 2011, the Kragujevac Court of First Instance rejected the applicant’s claim as unfounded. On 26 December 2011, the Kragujevac Appellate Court quashed that decision and remitted the case for reconsideration.

In the resumed proceedings, the applicant twice sought recusal of the acting judge, but both motions were rejected. On 4 October 2012, after three held hearings, two hearings that were not held, expert examination, and an increase in the applicant’s claim, the case was transferred to the Kragujevac High Court. On 20 March 2013, following two further recusal requests—one of which was granted—the High Court rejected the damages claim as unfounded. The applicant appealed. On 21 August 2014, the Appellate Court rejected his appeal and upheld the High Court’s decision. The applicant then filed an appeal on points of law, which the Supreme Court of Cassation rejected only on 21 December 2016.

In parallel, on 7 February 2013, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court complaining about the length of the still-pending civil proceedings. He sought €3,000 in non-pecuniary damages and publication of the Constitutional Court’s decision. The Constitutional Court transferred the case file to the Appellate Court, which was competent under Article 8a of the Law on the Organization of the Courts to deal with length complaints in pending cases. However, on 23 September 2014, the Appellate Court held that it no longer had jurisdiction because the civil proceedings had ended. The file was returned to the Constitutional Court. On 6 November 2014, the Constitutional Court sent it back to the Appellate Court, which on 28 November 2014 again found it lacked jurisdiction and forwarded the file to the Supreme Court of Cassation. The applicant appealed.

On 22 January 2015, the Supreme Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s appeal and upheld the 28 November 2014 decision. It also partially accepted his complaint concerning the length of proceedings and awarded him €200 for non-pecuniary damage, rejecting the remainder of his claim. On 21 October 2015, the Constitutional Court rejected the applicant’s appeal regarding the length of proceedings. It found that although the impugned proceedings had lasted seven years and eight months, they were very complex, the applicant had largely contributed to their length, and the competent courts had acted efficiently.

The alleged violation therefore concerned the length of civil proceedings under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The central facts are the approximately decade-long civil litigation, repeated remittals, recusal motions, transfers, delayed appellate/final review, and the applicant’s domestic length complaint, which resulted only in a €200 award. The ECtHR’s examination was limited to whether that duration and the domestic response complied with the reasonable-time requirement.

In *Leonov v. Russia*, the applicant, Sergey Aleksandrovich Leonov, a Russian national living in Moscow, complained about domestic court decisions concerning his son, A., born in August 2007. The child initially lived with both parents at Leonov’s flat, where he was registered, received paediatric care, and attended nursery school. In November 2009, the mother, Ch., left Leonov, moved to her parents’ home, and took A. with her. A. remained with his mother thereafter.

In March 2010, Leonov applied for a residence order so that A. would live with him. Ch. counterclaimed for residence with her and requested an interim measure pending the proceedings. She alleged that Leonov might abduct A. to Belarus and had already tried to take him from nursery school. On 26 April 2010, the Timiryazevskiy District Court granted the interim measure, forbidding Leonov from contacting A. or collecting him from nursery without Ch.’s prior permission. The court reasoned that the child was then living with his mother and that the measure was proportionate to ensure execution of the future judgment. Leonov learned of the order on 30 April 2010, when nursery staff refused to let him see his son.

Childcare authorities inspected both parents’ flats and found both suitable. In June 2010, one childcare authority said that, because of his young age, A. should live with his mother until five or six. The court ordered a psychological expert examination. In November 2010, the experts found that A. was equally attached to both parents, that both were equally capable of raising him, that contact with both was beneficial, and that the serious parental conflict could harm the child psychologically. In December 2010, another childcare authority nonetheless recommended that A. live with his mother, citing his age, established routine, and nursery attendance.

The proceedings were also affected by conflict between the parents. In June 2010, Ch. physically attacked Leonov when he hugged A. at a public beach. She was later convicted of assault and battery. Leonov also objected to the trial judge, alleging she had said that the Timiryazevskiy District Court always made residence orders in favour of mothers. In February 2011, the Moscow City Court quashed the interim measure as unconnected to the subject matter, disproportionate, and prejudicial; a fresh request was rejected in April 2011.

On 12 April 2011, the District Court granted residence to Ch. and dismissed Leonov’s claim. It found a serious parental conflict, but accepted that both parents were capable and that the child was equally attached to each. It noted Ch.’s criminal conviction was not yet final and held the charges were not decisive. It emphasised that A. was under four, had an established life with his mother and attended nursery there, and that changing residence would harm him. Leonov’s better housing and finances were not decisive, and the childcare authorities favoured the mother. The court called Leonov’s request “premature,” suggesting he could reapply when A. was older. The Moscow City Court upheld that judgment in June 2011. Later, in December 2011, a court set a contact schedule for Leonov and the paternal family after Ch. prevented contact.

Leonov complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the refusal to make a residence order in his favour and the interim measure restricting contact during the proceedings violated his right to respect for family life, the principle of equality of spouses, and amounted to sex discrimination. The key facts concern the alleged reliance on a maternal presumption, the interim contact ban, the expert finding of equal parental attachment and capacity, and the domestic courts’ preference for the mother based on the child’s young age and established residence.

The case of **Fabbri and Others v. San Marino** (Applications nos. 345/21, 6319/21, 6321/21 and 9227/21) concerned four applications brought by Mario Foschi, Stellino Fabbri, Andrea Forcellini—all San Marinese nationals—and Angelina Marro, an Italian national. The applicants were injured parties or complainants in separate criminal investigations in San Marino. Their common complaint was under **Article 6** of the Convention: because criminal proceedings against the alleged offenders were discontinued after the charges became time-barred due to the authorities’ inactivity, the applicants could not have their civil claims determined within the criminal proceedings, as San Marino law permitted.

In **Mr Foschi’s case**, in August 2014 he lodged a complaint with the Italian police against MKT, a Bulgarian national, for fraud and misappropriation of EUR 354,370. The Italian investigation found insufficient evidence, considered the matter essentially civil, and concluded that most transfers occurred outside Italian jurisdiction. The file was transferred to San Marino in July 2015, and a criminal investigation was opened. However, the assigned investigating judge took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice invited submissions on the non-observance of investigation time-limits. A new investigating judge was assigned in February 2020. In March 2020, that judge found the offence time-barred because no investigative act had occurred after the file was opened. The Prosecutor agreed to discontinuation without prejudice to any future civil claims. The discontinuation decree was issued in March 2020.

In **Fabbri and Marro’s case**, in April 2016 they complained against N., a national of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for personal injury. They stated their intention to join the eventual proceedings as civil parties, asked to be informed if proceedings were discontinued, and appointed lawyers. A criminal investigation was opened, but the investigating judge again took no steps. In May 2019 the Acting Chief Justice invited submissions concerning the investigation time-limits. In November 2020 a newly assigned investigating judge declared the charge discontinued because it had become time-barred. He noted that no investigative measures had been undertaken and that N. had not even been notified of the investigation. In any event, absent evidence, no criminal proceedings could ensue. The Prosecutor agreed later that month.

In **Mr Forcellini’s case**, defamation proceedings had been initiated in 2015 by a teacher against his parents. In March 2018 the trial judge found the parents guilty and sent the file to the investigating judge to consider investigating third persons. A criminal file was opened against V. and D. for private violence and persecution against the fourth applicant, then a minor. A request to join the proceedings as a civil party was submitted. The assigned investigating judge took no steps. In November 2020 a newly assigned judge archived the case, finding it time-barred and noting that no investigative acts had been undertaken and no evidence collected. The Prosecutor agreed.

The legal framework, notably Law no. 93/2008, required the investigating judge to complete investigations within peremptory time-limits. Once those limits expired, proceedings were considered published and the case could be discontinued. Criminal Code Article 54 imposed a three-year limitation for relevant offences. The Code of Criminal Procedure allowed injured parties to pursue civil actions separately or within criminal proceedings, and time-bar did not bar civil action unless the civil action was also time-barred. Victims could join as civil parties, but had no right to know investigative acts before publication.

The alleged violation arose from the authorities’ failure to conduct timely investigations, causing charges to become time-barred and proceedings to be discontinued. As a result, the applicants allegedly lost the opportunity to have their civil claims determined by the criminal court, contrary to Article 6. The Chamber judgment was later referred to the Grand Chamber, which delivered judgment on 24 September 2024.

**Maslák and Others v. Slovakia** (Application no. 11037/12) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by three Slovak nationals, Miroslav Maslák, Tomáš Ďuriš and Vladimír Haviar. Relying on Article 5 §§ 4 and 5 of the Convention, they alleged that they had been denied (i) a speedy procedure for judicial review of the lawfulness of their pre-trial detention and (ii) an enforceable right to compensation for the alleged breach of the “speediness” requirement. Their complaints concerned several unsuccessful requests for release—dated 2 May 2010, 10 May 2010 and December 2010 (amended in January 2011)—and an interlocutory appeal against a detention order of 4 April 2011. On 25 June 2014, those complaints were communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

Since 2007, the applicants had faced multiple charges, mainly concerning alleged violent offences linked to organised crime. They were repeatedly arrested, remanded, released, re-arrested and re-remanded. The application directly related to three release requests following their arrest on 1 April 2010 on a perjury charge, and later to their remand on an extortion charge after arrest on 1 April 2011.

As to the first applicant’s request of 2 May 2010, it was received by the Považská Bystrica District Court on 11 May and amended on 19 May. At a hearing on 21 May, he challenged the judge for bias; that challenge was dismissed the same day, and his appeal against that decision was dismissed by the Trenčín Regional Court on 10 June, served on 21 June. His release request was then dismissed by the District Court on 25 June 2010 and, on appeal, by the Regional Court on 20 July 2010, served on 26 July. He filed a constitutional complaint on 27 September 2010. On 4 October 2011, the Constitutional Court declared it inadmissible, finding the length complaints manifestly ill-founded and the remaining complaints partly out of time and partly manifestly ill-founded. It was served on 23 November 2011.

The second and third applicants requested release on 10 May 2010, offering a pledge. The request was filed with the prosecution service, which transmitted it to the District Court on 17 May; the court received it on 21 May. The file was incomplete and was completed only on 2 June. The applicants waived an oral hearing on 27 May. The District Court dismissed the request on 3 June 2010; the Regional Court dismissed their appeal on 15 July 2010. Service was delayed because one of their lawyers had stopped representing them without informing the court. Their constitutional complaint of 30 September 2010 was declared inadmissible on 9 November 2011. The Constitutional Court acknowledged delays caused by the incomplete file and by the lawyer’s failure, but found the length compatible with Article 5 § 4. It was served on 19 December 2011.

On 22 December 2010, the applicants lodged a fresh release request. On 3 January 2011, the District Court replied that, absent new relevant information, a new request could not be lodged until thirty days

**Case: Sharxhi and Others v. Albania (Application no. 10613/16), judgment of 11 January 2018.**

The applicants were eighteen Albanian nationals and one Italian national. In 2009 the first two applicants purchased a plot of land in Vlora, in the Uji i Ftohtë–Tuneli coastal area. In 2010 the Vlora Municipal Council for Territorial Planning issued a building permit for a five-storey residential and commercial building, the “Jon Residence.” The remaining applicants bought flats in the planned building. Construction was completed in 2012, the building was registered with the Immovable Property Registration Office, most flats were occupied, and a pool bar/pizzeria opened.

On 3 November 2013, without prior notice, officials of the National and Vlora Construction and Urban Planning Inspectorates (NUCI and MUCI), supported by State Police, surrounded and cordoned off the Jon Residence with yellow police tape marked “Crime scene – no entry.” Residents were prevented from entering their flats or retrieving valuables. The authorities said they were inspecting the legality of the building permit. No formal administrative act was presented. The applicants learned of the situation through the media or security guards. The Ombudsman later wrote that the building had been seized without a formal act and that the cordoning off was unlawful.

The applicants sought urgent judicial protection. On 7 November 2013 the Vlora Administrative District Court issued an interim order under the Code of Civil Procedure and the Administrative Disputes Act. It stayed administrative actions by any public authority that could interfere with the applicants’ peaceful enjoyment of their properties, pending a decision on the merits, provided the applicants brought a merits claim within ten days. The court found that the applicants had legally acquired their flats, were being prevented from accessing them, and faced irreparable harm. It also noted that the authorities had not documented their administrative action. The interim order was executable despite appeal. The applicants’ lawyer informed the NUCI and urged enforcement, but received no reply. The NUCI appealed.

Despite the interim order, the authorities continued. On 27 November 2013 the Council of Ministers ordered the expropriation in the public interest of properties affected by environmental rehabilitation of the Uji i Ftohtë–Tuneli coastline. It awarded compensation of approximately ALL 462,919,230 for the building, with a deadline of 28 December 2013. The decision was published on 3 December; the applicants learned of it through the media. On 2 December the mayor of Vlora requested NUCI assistance with demolition. The Jon Residence was demolished with explosives between 4 and 8 December 2013. On 20 January 2014 the Administrative Court of Appeal terminated the interim-order proceedings because the building had already been demolished and the subject matter had ceased to exist.

On the merits, the District Court on 28 January 2014 declared the authorities’ actions of 3 November 2013 arbitrary and in flagrant breach of Albanian law. The Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 6 May 2016. In separate expropriation proceedings, the District Court on 6 March 2014 found the expropriation unlawful and a “de facto expropriation,” increased compensation, and found serious procedural violations. The Court of Appeal largely upheld this in September 2014, but in January 2015 the Supreme Court stayed execution of the decision, and the case remained pending. No compensation was paid to the applicants. The Immovable Property Registration Office refused to issue ownership certificates because the building no longer existed. Criminal complaints against officials were rejected.

The applicants alleged that the authorities’ disregard of the administrative court injunction violated Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. They also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that the cordoning off, expropriation and demolition interfered with their peaceful enjoyment of possessions; under Article 8 that preventing access to their homes interfered with respect for their homes; and under Article 13 that no effective domestic remedy existed for these violations. The core facts are that, despite a binding interim order prohibiting interference pending the merits, the authorities sealed, expropriated and demolished the applicants’ lawfully built and acquired homes and shops, rendering the injunction moot and leaving the applicants without compensation or effective redress.

Case Dainelienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 23532/14) is a European Court of Human Rights case against Lithuania lodged on 18 March 2014 by Ms Dalia Regina Dainelienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1944. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the independence and impartiality of the Supreme Court. On 13 September 2017 that complaint was communicated to the Government; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying criminal case began in April 2009, when the applicant was notified that she was suspected of organising the embezzlement of high-value property. She was charged in May 2009 and denied guilt. In July 2011 the Vilnius Regional Court found the charges incorrectly classified because the total value of the allegedly embezzled property was not high. It reclassified the charges as a less serious offence, held that prosecution had become time-barred, and discontinued the proceedings. The prosecutor appealed. In October 2011 the Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case.

On re-examination, in June 2013 the Vilnius Regional Court convicted the applicant, imposed a fine of LTL 12,000 (about EUR 3,475), and ordered her to pay part of the damages claimed by a company, amounting to LTL 2,800 (about EUR 810). In October 2013 the Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and upheld the conviction in full.

In January 2014 the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law with the Supreme Court. On 17 February 2014, a three-judge selection panel refused to examine the appeal, finding that it did not comply with Article 368 § 2 and Article 369 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (“CCP”), which set formal and legal requirements for cassation appeals. The chair of that selection panel, Judge V.G., was the father of M.G., the prosecutor who had acted in the applicant’s case before both the first-instance and appellate courts. This relationship is central to the alleged violation.

Domestic law provided that parties could seek removal of judges. Under Article 58 § 1(1) of the CCP, a judge could not participate in proceedings if he or she was a close family member or relative of a prosecutor in those proceedings, and Article 59 required a judge to withdraw on that basis. However, the cassation admissibility procedure was different. Under Article 372 § 2, the President of the Supreme Court or the Chair of the Criminal Division composed a panel of three judges to decide whether to accept an appeal. The appeal was admitted if at least one judge voted in favour, and a judge on that panel was not precluded from later deciding the merits. The decision was final and not appealable, though reasons had to be given.

Crucially, the CCP contained no provisions allowing parties to be informed of the composition of the initial three-judge selection panel or to request removal of those judges. Only after an appeal had been accepted and set for written examination did Article 3741 § 1 require that parties be informed of the chamber’s composition and of their right to request removal of judges.

The alleged Article 6 § 1 violation was therefore that the Supreme Court’s refusal to admit the applicant’s cassation appeal was decided by a panel chaired by the father of the prosecutor who had prosecuted her, creating an appearance of bias or lack of impartiality. The key facts are the close familial relationship between the selection-panel judge and the prosecutor in the same case; the judge’s participation in a final, unreviewable admissibility decision; the general domestic prohibition on judges related to prosecutors participating; and the absence of any procedure allowing the applicant to learn the panel’s composition or seek recusal at that preliminary stage.

**Abdi Mahamud v. Malta** (Application no. 56796/13) concerned a Somali national, Ms Sagal Abdi Mahamud, born in 1992, who entered Malta irregularly by boat on 6 May 2012. On arrival she was registered by immigration police, given an identification number, and served with a Return Decision and a Removal Order under Article 14(2) of the Immigration Act. The Return Decision stated she was a prohibited immigrant because she had no means of subsistence and was liable to become a charge on public funds. The Removal Order, issued after her request for voluntary departure was rejected, provided that she would remain in custody until removal and that an entry ban would be issued. Both documents advised her of a right to appeal to the Immigration Appeals Board within three working days.

On 9 May 2012 the applicant submitted a preliminary questionnaire indicating her wish to apply for asylum. She was interviewed by the Office of the Refugee Commissioner on 21 May 2012. Her asylum application was rejected on 30 June 2012, partly because she allegedly gave insufficient convincing evidence that she came from central or southern Somalia. The Refugee Appeals Board dismissed her appeal on 18 December 2012. By the date she lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights, 19 August 2013, no steps had been taken regarding her removal. In practice, Malta did not effect removals to Somalia or Somaliland.

The applicant’s detention was central to her complaints. She was held at Lyster Barracks Detention Centre in Ħal Far. She alleged that her continued detention was arbitrary and unlawful and that she had no effective remedy to challenge its lawfulness, relying on Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention. She also complained about detention conditions under Article 3.

A significant factual issue concerned her vulnerability. From arrival she suffered from headaches, earaches, fainting, and other medical problems, and was frequently hospitalised. She showed severe anxiety and depression, which worsened after her asylum rejection. In October 2012 the Jesuit Refugee Service referred her to the Agency for the Welfare of Asylum Seekers (AWAS) for release from detention on vulnerability grounds. In December 2012 she was interviewed briefly by AWAS, in English, assisted by another detainee who was not fluent in the language. On 10 August 2013 she was verbally informed she would be released, but she remained detained when she applied to the Court on 19 August 2013. She was eventually released on 12 September 2013. The applicant argued that the AWAS vulnerability assessment procedure had a determining impact on continued detention yet was not adequately regulated by law, gave no written reasons, and offered no appeal.

As to conditions, the applicant described Lyster Barracks as prison-like and basic. Zone C held over eighty women and was so crowded that some slept on metal tables. Zone D was less crowded but lacked privacy and sanitation. She complained of a lack of constructive activities, overcrowding, limited open-air access, communication difficulties, lack of information, and extreme temperatures. She also highlighted the lack of female staff: male soldiers allegedly entered the women’s dormitory each morning while they slept and removed sheets during head counts, forcing her to sleep fully dressed, including her headscarf. She further complained of limited access to medical care and a lack of interpreters for medical communication.

The case therefore focused on whether her prolonged immigration detention, the absence of judicial review, and the conditions at Lyster Barracks violated Articles 3 and 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention.

In *Novotný v. the Czech Republic* (ECtHR, App. no. 16314/13, judgment of 7 June 2018), the applicant, František Novotný, alleged violations of Articles 6, 8 and 14 of the Convention. The case concerned his inability to challenge a final judicial declaration of paternity after DNA evidence proved he was not the biological father.

The applicant was born in 1942. In 1965 he had a sexual relationship with a woman who gave birth to a daughter, Z., on 2 March 1966. The applicant denied paternity. Z.’s legal guardian brought proceedings on her behalf in the Jihlava District Court. After Z.’s birth, but before those proceedings, the mother married another man.

On 23 April 1970 the District Court declared the applicant to be Z.’s father and ordered him to pay maintenance. The court relied on witness evidence, documentary evidence, a “bio-hereditary” blood test, and a finding that the applicant had had intercourse with the mother between 300 and 180 days before Z.’s birth. Under Article 54 of the Family Code, a man who had intercourse with the mother in that period was presumed to be the father unless there were serious grounds to exclude paternity. Another man had also had intercourse with the mother at the relevant time, but the blood test excluded him. The applicant appealed and requested another expert opinion. The Brno Regional Court refused, finding the facts sufficiently proved, and upheld the judgment on 2 June 1970. It became final on 10 June 1970.

In 2011 the applicant asked the Prosecutor General to challenge his paternity in court. By letter of 21 June 2011, he was told that the requirements of Article 62 of the Family Code were not met: Z., by then an adult, did not want to challenge paternity, it was not in her interests, and the applicant had not produced expert evidence credibly disproving paternity.

On 29 February 2012 the applicant and Z. underwent a DNA examination. The report of 19 April 2012 unequivocally confirmed that the applicant was not Z.’s father. On 9 May 2012 the applicant made a new request to the Prosecutor General. On 12 September 2012 the Prosecutor General refused, explaining that paternity had been determined by a judicial declaration under Article 54 of the Family Code, not by a statutory presumption under Articles 51 and 52. Once such a judgment became final, Czech law provided no possibility to challenge it. The Prosecutor General’s competence under Articles 62 and 62a applied only to statutory presumptions of paternity.

Relying on Article 6 § 1, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor General’s decision. He argued that he had proved he was not Z.’s biological father, requested that the Prosecutor General be ordered to initiate proceedings, and claimed that Articles 61 § 1 and 62 § 1 of the Family Code were unconstitutional. On 13 December 2012 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint. It noted that his paternity had been established by a final judicial decision and that the Prosecutor General’s competence could apply only if all legal requirements were fulfilled, which was not the case.

The relevant domestic law allowed a court to declare paternity under Article 54 and allowed the Prosecutor General to challenge paternity under Article 62 where the child’s interests required it and parental time-limits had expired. However, the Prosecutor General treated that power as unavailable where paternity had already been established by a final judgment. Constitutional case-law, including references to *Paulík v. Slovakia*, recognised Article 8 and Article 6 concerns where alleged fathers lacked any procedure to deny paternity, but the Constitutional Court found no such avenue available to the applicant because his paternity had been judicially determined and had become final. The ECtHR application was lodged on 19 February 2013 and communicated to the Government on 19 February 2015.
